questions.title: Bucket Allocation II
questions.problem: You and $100$ other players are each given $3$ tickets to distribute into three buckets with prizes $\$20, \$80,$ and $\$200$. One winning ticket is drawn from each bucket, and the winner gets the associated prize. A single person can win multiple buckets. You are the last person to put in your tickets and are told that the number of tickets in each bucket are currently allocated proportionally to the size of the prize of the bucket. Assuming your utility is binary past $\$10$ (i.e. you get $1$ utility from $\$11$ and $\$100$, but $0$ utility from $\$9$), how should you arrange your tickets to maximize expected utility? Report the expected utility under this strategy.
questions.solution: Since the $\$20, \$80,$ and $\$200$ buckets all yield $1$ utility, you want to maximize your probability of winning. The bucket with $\$20$ in it has, by far, the least tickets inside, so the optimal strategy is to put all three of your tickets in there. $3$ is small compared to the bucket sizes, so the incremental probability increase for each ticket in the $\$20$ bucket is larger than the other buckets. This yields an expected utility of $3/23$, as $3$ of the $23$ tickets in the bucket are yours.

questions.title: Product Rolls II
questions.problem: Suppose you roll two standard fair $4-$sided dice. You can pay $\$c$ to reroll either the dice, and this decision can be made as many times as you'd like. Your payout is the product of the upfaces of your final roll. Assuming optimal play, what is the smallest value of $c$ such that taking the first roll is the best strategy?
questions.solution: If the penalty is large enough, the optimal strategy will be to always take the first outcome no matter what. Therefore, we will want to roll as few times as possible, so we only need to find the value of $c$ such that taking a threshold of $t = 1$ yields a higher expected value than $t = 2$ only (using the notation of the previous part). This is because the expected payout would be decreasing in the number of times that rerolls must occur, so $t = 3$ and $t = 4$ would have even lower expected values than $t = 2$ for sufficiently large $c$. Using the work of the previous problem, the expected profit with $t = 1$ is $25/4$, while substituting in $2$ as $c$ for the cost yields an expected profit with $t = 2$ as $9 - 2c/3$. Setting these equal yields 25 4 = 9 − 2 3 ⟺ = 33 8 4 25 =9− 3 2 c⟺c= 8 33 Therefore, if $c \geq 33/8$, the strategy with $t = 1$ is optimal.

questions.title: Tourney Ending II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play in a tennis tournament such that the winner of each round receives $1$ point, while the loser loses $1$ point. The tournament ends as soon as one of the players reaches $2$ points or $2n$ games have been played, whichever comes first. Alice has probability $0 < p < 1$ of winning each round. Let $E(n,p)$ be the expected number of games played in the tournament. If it exists, compute lim → ∞ (, ) n→∞ lim E(n,p) when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: From the first part of the question, we know that (, ) = 2 ⋅ 1 − ( 1 − ) E(n,p W )=2⋅ p W 1−(1−p W ) n As = 2 + ( 1 − ) 2 p W =p 2 +(1−p) 2, it's easy to substitute in and take the limit directly. Namely, (, ) = 2 ⋅ 1 − ( 1 − 2 − ( 1 − ) 2 ) 2 + ( 1 − ) 2 E(n,p)=2⋅ p 2 +(1−p) 2 1−(1−p 2 −(1−p) 2 ) n The entire parenthesized term is at most $1$ in magntiude, so it tends to $0$ in limit, meaning that lim → ∞ (, ) = 2 2 + ( 1 − ) 2 n→∞ lim E(n,p)= p 2 +(1−p) 2 2 This intuitively makes sense: As $n \rightarrow \infty$, the threshold of playing "at most $n$ rounds" becomes less and less important, as it becomes less likely that there is nobody that has won two consecutive games within $n$ rounds as $n$ increases. Thus, in limit, the tournament is really unrestricted, and the expected number of rounds would be $1/p_W$, so the expected number of games is $2/p_W$, which is the answer above. With the specified values, the answer is $3.6$.

questions.title: Partial Placement
questions.problem: $n$ balls labelled $1-n$ are placed into $n$ urns labelled $1-n$ such that ball $i$ is equally likely to be placed in any of urns $1-i$. Find the expected number of empty urns when $n = 25$.
questions.solution: As we are looking to compute the expected count of dependent events, linearity of expectation is a good approach. We're looking to compute the expected number of empty bins, so let $I_i$ be the indicator that bin $i$ is empty. = 1 + ⋯ + T=I 1 +⋯+I n yields the total number of empty bins. By linearity of expectation, [ ] = ∑ = 1 [ ] E[T]= i=1 ∑ n E[I i ] [ ] E[I i ] is the probability that bin $i$ is empty. The only possible ball numbers that can go in bin $i$ are balls $i,i+1,\dots, n$. For any ball $j > i$, the probability that ball $j$ goes in bin $i$ is $1/j$, as the selection is uniform, so the probability ball $j$ doesn't go in bin $i$ is $\frac{j-1}{j}$. As the ball placements are independent, the probability that none of the balls $i,i+1,\dots,n$ go in urn $i$ is [ ] = ∏ = − 1 = − 1 ⋅ + 1 ⋅ ⋯ ⋅ − 1 = − 1 E[I i ]= j=i ∏ n j j−1 = i i−1 ⋅ i+1 i ⋅⋯⋅ n n−1 = n i−1 As a sanity check, when $i = 1$, the answer is $0$, as ball $1$ always goes in urn $1$. Plugging this in, [ ] = ∑ = 1 − 1 = 1 ∑ = 0 − 1 = − 1 2 E[T]= i=1 ∑ n n i−1 = n 1 i=0 ∑ n−1 i= 2 n−1 With $n = 25$, the answer is $12$.

questions.title: Beer Pong Betting
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play beer pong, but also want to spice it up by betting on the outcome. Per game, each of them bet $\$1$. Bob won $m$ games, but lost $n$ dollars. How many games did Alice and Bob play? Provide your answer when $m=3$ and $n=2$.
questions.solution: For Bob to win $m$ games, but lose $n$ dollars, he must have $n$ more losses than wins to account for his net loss. Therefore, he must have $m+n$ total losses. The first $m$ losses take him to neutral profit, and the next $n$ losses account for his loss in dollars. Thus, the total number of games played must be $m+(m+n)$ or $2m+n$. The result is $8$ when solved for $m=3$ and $n=2$.

questions.title: Star System Alignment
questions.problem: There is a star with three planets orbiting it. The planets have orbital periods of $60, 84,$ and $140$ years, respectively. If the planets are currently aligned with the sun, when is the next time they will be aligned again? By aligned, we mean the planets all lie on a diameter passing through the sun.
questions.solution: When considering problems involving a period, it's best to first reduce the periods to be relatively prime, and then find their least common multiple. This allows us to account for the condition that the planets can be aligned on any diameter through the sun. The largest number that all three orbital periods are divisible by is $4$. This gives us $15, 21, 35$ as the "reduced" periods. We cannot further reduce these numbers, so now we can find the lowest common multiple of all three. We can see fairly easily see that $105$ is the LCM: $105 = 15 \cdot 7 = 21 \cdot 5 = 35 \cdot 3$. As the planets can lie on a diameter, they can be off-cycle by a half-revolution with one another and still be aligned. This holds here: After $105$ years, the planets with periods $60$ and $140$ is $3/4$ done with a revolution, while the planet with period $84$ years is $1/4$ done with a revolution.

questions.title: Lots of Change II
questions.problem: A person asks you to break their dollar for change. You are unable to do so because you don't have change for a dollar. What is the maximum value of currency that you can have satisfying this condition? Use denominations of U.S. Currency.
questions.solution: Using the highest denomination of U.S. Currency, we can start with $1$ quarters ( $\$0.25$). Next up, we can include $9$ dimes ( $\$0.90$), as we cannot mix the dimes and quarters to get exact change for a dollar. We can't include another quarter because $2$ quarters and $5$ dimes could make a dollar. We choose $9$ dimes because it's the maximum amount that can be included without making a dollar just from dimes. No nickels can be included, as a quarter, a nickel, and $7$ dimes can make a dollar. However, the maximum amount that can be added in pennies is $4$ cents, so that amounts ending in $9$ are possible, but having the next tens place is not possible. Thus, the combination is $1$ quarter, $9$ dimes, and $4$ pennies, which sums to $\$1.19$. This can alternatively be achieved with $3$ quarters, $4$ dimes, and $4$ pennies, which intuitively makes sense, as we substitute $5$ dimes for $2$ quarters.

questions.title: Sine Summation II
questions.problem: Let $1 \leq r \leq 90$ be an even integer. Evaluate $\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^r \sin^2\left(\dfrac{k\pi}{2r}\right)$. Report the answer when $r = 30$.
questions.solution: As we see a $\sin^2(x)$ term here, we should immediately think to use the identity $\sin^2(x) + \cos^2(x) = 1$ in some way. Testing the first and last terms, we get $\sin^2(0) = 0$ and $\sin^2(\pi/2) = 1$. These two terms sum to $1$, while the interior radian measures add to $\pi/2$. Using the identity $\cos(x) = \sin(\pi/2 - x)$ for all real $x$, we see that $\sin^2(x) + \sin^2(\pi/2 - x) = 1$ for all real $x$. This duality between the first and last term suggests that we may want to pair up certain terms that sum to $\pi/2$. In particular, the ith and $(r-i)$ th terms satisfy this condition, as $\frac{\pi i}{2r} + \frac{\pi (r-i)}{2r} = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Using this, we conclude that the ith and $(r-i)$ th terms of the sum add to $1$. Since $r$ is even, there are an odd number of terms in the sum, as $k = 0$ is included. As there are an odd number of terms $k = r/2$ will be a standalone element of the sum. This is because $r/2 = r - r/2$, so it's paired with itself. This implies there are $r/2$ pairs that sum to $1$, and then the $r/2$ term. Therefore, ∑ = 0 sin 2 ( 2 ) = [ sin 2 ( 0 2 ) + sin 2 ( 2 ) ] + ⋯ + [ sin 2 ( ( / 2 − 1 ) ⋅ 2 ) + sin 2 ( ( ( / 2 + 1 ) ⋅ 2 ) ] + sin 2 ( ( / 2 ) 2 ) = + 1 2 k=0 ∑ r sin 2 ( 2r kπ )=[sin 2 ( 2r 0π )+sin 2 ( 2r rπ )]+⋯+[sin 2 ( 2r (r/2−1)⋅π )+sin 2 ( 2r ((r/2+1)⋅π )]+sin 2 ( 2r (r/2)π )= 2 r+1 With the specified value, the answer is $15.5$ 15.5.

questions.title: Average Speed III
questions.problem: John and Charlie are competing in a dirtbike race. If John does a lap in three minutes, and Charlie does a lap in four, how many minutes until John laps Charlie?
questions.solution: The two people will intersect each other at the LCM of their lap times, since that is when they will have completed an integer number of laps at the same time. The LCM of $3$ and $4$ is $12$, so after $12$ minutes, they will intersect.

questions.title: Fetty Wap's Equation
questions.problem: Fetty Wap asks you to solve the following equation for $x$: $(x-1000)^3 = 369^3 + 492^3 + 615^3$
questions.solution: The key is to notice a common factor of all terms on the RHS. Namely, we can see $(x-1000)^3 = (3\cdot123)^3+(4\cdot123)^3 + (5\cdot123)^3 \iff \left(\dfrac{x-1000}{123}\right)^3 = 3^3 + 4^3 + 5^3 = 216 = 6^3 \iff \dfrac{x-1000}{123} = 6 \iff x = 1738$

questions.title: COVID Spread
questions.problem: There are $4000$ people at a convention. One of these individuals has COVID, while the rest of them do not. Every $5$ minutes, each individual talks to another at random with no restrictions. If an individual talks to someone with COVID, they will immediately get COVID and have the ability to get others sick. What is the minimum amount of time until everyone gets COVID? Provide your answer in hours.
questions.solution: We want to solve for the lowest value of $n$ interactions that satisfies $2^n > 3999$, as the number of people with COVID can at most double per interaction: Every healthy person talks to a sick person. From this, we see that $2^{12}=4096$ will be the minimum integer satisfying our condition. Therefore, we have $12$ interactions, and if each interaction takes $5$ minutes, the minimum time for everyone to get COVID is $1$ hour.

questions.title: Minimum Unlocks
questions.problem: You have $n$ locks and $n$ keys. Each key unlocks only one lock. What is the maximum number of attempts needed to figure out all of the key-lock pairs using an optimal strategy? Report the answer when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: The naive strategy is indeed optimal here, as we don't have any additional information on which key unlocks each lock. Thus, we will have to test the first key on $n-1$ locks (if it doesn't unlock the first $n-1$ locks, it must unlock the last), the second on $n-2$, and so on, so that the number of total attempts is given by $(n-1) + (n-2) + \dots + 1 = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $45$.

questions.title: Diluted Juice I
questions.problem: You begin with two glasses: One is half full of juice, and the other has $1/3$ of its capacity filled with juice. However, the second glass has twice the capacity of the first glass. Then, you fill both cups to the brim with water and put them both in the same bowl. What proportion of the bowl is juice?
questions.solution: With these combining problems, it's best to break them up into the individual components, and then recombine. Let the capacity of the two cups be $1$ and $2$, respectively. In each cup, the amount of juice is given by $1/2 \cdot 1 = 1/2$ and $2 \cdot 1/3 = 2/3$. Once combined, the total amount of juice in the bowl is $1/2 + 2/3 = 7/6$, and the total volume in the bowl is $3$, so the proportion of the bowl that's juice is $(7/6)/3 = 7/18$.

questions.title: Head Game
questions.problem: You play a game where you keep flipping a fair coin with your goal being to maximize the ratio between the number of heads you get and the total flips. What is your expected ratio of heads to flips, assuming you will not stop until you get a ratio greater than or equal to $1/2$?
questions.solution: The maximum possible ratio occurs if you get a heads on your first flip, which yields a ratio of $1$. Otherwise, the number of heads and tails will equalize at some point with probability $1$ by the Law of Large Numbers (heads and tails are equally likely on a fair coin), and at this point, under the given strategy, you would stop flipping, meaning the ratio is $1/2$. Thus, the expected ratio is $1 \cdot 1/2 + 1/2 \cdot 1/2 = 3/4$.

questions.title: Fibonacci Property
questions.problem: Let $F_n$ be the sequence of Fibonacci numbers. Define the sequence $R_n = \dfrac{F_1 + \dots + F_{3n}}{F_3 + F_6 + \dots + F_{3n}}$. Find $R_{100}$.
questions.solution: Whenever you see Fibonacci numbers, you should think of the recurrence $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$. The common terms between the numerator and denominator are multiplies of $3$, so we should use this recurrence on all multiplies of $3$. This yields $\dfrac{F_1 + F_2 + F_3 + \dots + F_{3n-2} + F_{3n-1} + F_{3n}}{F_3 + F_6 + \dots + F_{3n}} = \dfrac{F_1 + F_2 + (F_1 + F_2) + \dots + F_{3n-2} + F_{3n-1} + (F_{3n-2} + F_{3n-1})}{(F_1 + F_2) + \dots + (F_{3n-2} + F_{3n-1})}$ The numerator is really just twice the denominator, as $F_{3k-2}$ and $F_{3k-1}$ appear twice in the numerator, while they only appear once in the denominator, so the answer is $R_n = 2$ for all $n$.

questions.title: Event Generation
questions.problem: Let $E$ be any event of positive probability in some sample space. What is the smallest value of [ ] P[E] such that $E$ can be simulated by rolling a $6-$ sided die $3$ times and flipping a fair coin twice?
questions.solution: Since the dice and coins are fair, finding probabilities involving them boils down to counting outcomes. For $E$ to be represented via simulation on the dice and coins, it must correspond to some subset of outcomes. As all outcomes are equally likely, the smallest such subset is $1$ event, so the minimum probability of $E$ is $\Omega$∣ P[E]=1/∣Ω∣, where Ω Ω is our sample space of all outcomes. There are $6^3 \cdot 2^2 = 864$ outcomes from the three dice ( $6$ outcomes per die) and $2$ coins ( $2$ outcomes per coin), so the answer is $1/864$.

questions.title: Boat Crossing
questions.problem: There are $n$ people $n-2$ of which are adults, and $2$ of which are children. There is a boat on a river which will carry two children, or one adult. The boat needs at least 1 person in it in order to function. How many trips will it take to transport all of the people across the river using the boat? Report the answer when $n = 100$.
questions.solution: The key here is to recognize that you need to move the children back and forth, as they will control the boat movement. They control the movement because there always needs to be one child to send the boat back once an adult crosses. If there isn't, the adult would just have to return to where they were. Thus, a natural first step is to send both children across. Now, you iterate the following process: Send one child back with the boat. Send an adult across. Send the child that already crossed the river back with the boat. Pick up the other child, and both children cross back over. The children can repeat this process until every adult is across. This process can't be made any quicker due to the fact that the boat can't hold both a child and an adult. After one cycle of the process above, both children are back across the river with $1$ additional adult crossed. Therefore, the total number of trips is equal to the number of trips to set up the process $(1)$ and the number of trips to get everyone across, which is $4(n-2)$. In total, this takes $1+4(n-2)=4n-7$ trips. With $n = 100$, the answer is $393$.

questions.title: Octopus Truth
questions.problem: There is a colony of octopuses where $6-$ legged and $8-$ legged octopuses tell the truth, while $7-$ legged octopuses lie. In a group of $4$ octopuses, each one claims there are a different amount of legs between them: The $4$ octopuses claim there are $28,27,26,$ and $25$ legs between them, respectively. How many legs are there between them?
questions.solution: There can only be one correct leg count, so there must be $3$ octopuses that are lying. Since they are lying, they each must have $7$ legs, yielding $21$ legs to start. Now, one of them must be telling the truth, so that octopus must have either $6$ legs or $8$ legs. Since $21 + 8 = 29$ is not an option (all $4$ would be lying in this case), the total number of legs must be $27$, as the last octopus would have $6$ legs.

questions.title: Binomial Swap II
questions.problem: Does there exist a non-negative integer ≠ 0, 1 k ≠ =0,1 such that ( 2070 ) = ( 2070 2 ) ( k 2070 )=( k 2 2070 )? If so, report the value of $k$. Otherwise, report $-1$.
questions.solution: Since ≠ 0, 1 k ≠ =0,1, it must be the case that ≠ 2 k ≠ =k 2. Thus, the only equality identity we have is ( ) = ( − ) ( k n )=( n−k n ). For the two coefficients to be equal, we must have $k = n-k^2 \iff n = k(k+1)$ for some positive integer $k$. Since $45^2 = 2025$ and we note $45^2 + 45 = 2070,$ we can conclude $k = 45$ satisifes our condition, meaning $45$ is the answer.

questions.title: Uniform Equilibria II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play the following game: Both of them pick any real number in $[0,1]$. Bob pays Alice the absolute value of the difference between the selected numbers. Under rational play from both players, what is Alice's expected payout?
questions.solution: In such game questions, it's best to first consider if there is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. If not, what would a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium look like? As for a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, we showed in "Uniform Equilibria I" that there is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. The key idea is that Bob should first try to limit the maximum amount he can lose first. To do this, he should select the central value $1/2$, since the maximum he can lose is $1/2$ at $0$ and $1$. If he selects a value not equal to $1/2$, one of $0$ or $1$ would be further than $1/2$ away in distance, so the maximum loss would be larger. From there, what should Alice do? Naturally, Alice should only select the values as far away as possible from $1/2$, which are $0$ and $1$. If Alice were to always select $0$, Bob could change his value to be closer to $0$, resulting in a small loss, and similar to $1$. Thus, Alice should have a mixed strategy of selecting $0$ and $1$ with some probabilities $1-p$ and $p$, respectively. To make Bob indifferent to moving in one direction or another $p = 1/2$. If ≠ 1 / 2 p ≠ =$1/2$, Alice would be more biased to one side, so Bob could reduce his expected loss by moving his value closer to the more likely value. In other words, if Bob always selects 1 / 2 1/2 and Alice selects $0$ or $1$ with equal probabilities, neither player can unilaterally improve their expected payout. Thus, this is a Nash equilibrium. Alice receives a payout of $1/2$ from both $0$ and $1$, so her expected payout is $1/2$.

questions.title: Even Stopped
questions.problem: A standard fair $(2n)-$ sided die is repeatedly rolled until the value $2n$ appears for the first time. Find the probability that the sum of all upfaces viewed is even when $n=10$.
questions.solution: The probability that the sum of all upfaces is even depends on the value observed at the first roll: The first value being even or odd changes the required parity of the sum of remaining rolls. Additionally, we could even stop rolling after the first turn. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on the first roll. Let $p$ be the probability of our event of interest. If the first roll is $2n$(occurs with probability $1/(2n)$), the cumulative sum is $2n$, meaning it's even. If the first roll is even, but not the value $2n$, (occurs with probability $\frac{n-1}{2n}$, as there are $n-1$ other even values on the die that aren't $2n$), we're essentially in the same position as before: The sum of the remaining rolls must be even, which is what we started with. Thus, there is probability $p$ of the event occurring in this case. Lastly, if the first value rolled is odd, (occurs with probability $1/2$, as $n$ of the $2n$ values are odd), the remaining rolls must sum to an odd value. This is the complementary situation of the case above, since we required the remaining sum to be odd in the above. Therefore, the probability of obtaining an even final sum (i.e. odd sum after the first roll) in this case is $1-p$. By the Law of Total Probability $p = \dfrac{1}{2n} \cdot 1 + \dfrac{n-1}{2n} \cdot p + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1-p) \iff p = \dfrac{n+1}{2n+1}$ As a sanity check, when → ∞ n→∞, the answer tends to $1/2$, which makes sense: The probability of rolling $2n$ on the first roll tends to $0$, so that small edge to the even cumulative sum vanishes, rendering it close to equally likely that the sum is even or odd. With $n = 10$, the answer is $11/21$.

questions.title: Rabbit Population
questions.problem: A rabbit population that initially consists of one male and one female rabbit reproduces as follows: Any given rabbit takes $4$ months to reach maturity. Once a female rabbit reaches maturity, there is a pregnancy period of $1$ month, after which $2$ male and $2$ female rabbits are born. All female rabbits give birth every month after reaching maturity. No rabbits die in the process. How many rabbits are in the population after $1$ year?
questions.solution: The number of rabbits in the population is twice the number of pairs. Only female rabbits are pregnant, so it's best to make a recurrence on the number of pairs of rabbits in the population. We can multiply by $2$ to get the number of total rabbits. Let $P_n$ be the number of rabbits in the population at the end of $n$ months. We are given that $P_0 = 1$. Now, let's think about how the rabbits reproduce (no, not in that way). At time $n$, all of the rabbits from time $n-1$ are still alive, as no rabbits die. Which group of rabbits give birth at time $n$? It takes a total of $5$ months to go from newborn to birthing rabbits ( $4$ months to reach maturity and $1$ month of pregnancy). Therefore, all of the rabbits alive at time $n-5$ are giving at time $n$. There are $P_{n-5}$ pairs of rabbits at time $n-5$, and each yield $2$ pairs of rabbits. Thus $2P_{n-5}$ pairs of rabbits are born at time $n$. We obtain the recurrence $P_n = P_{n-1} + 2P_{n-5}$ As for initial conditions, we know that $P_0 = P_1 = P_2 = P_3 = P_4 = 1$, as no rabbits are born during the first $4$ months. Using our recurrence, we want to find $P_{12}$. Doing so $P_5 = P_4 + 2P_0 = 3$$P_6 = P_5 + 2P_1 = 5$$P_7 = P_6 + 2P_2 = 7$$P_8 = P_7 + 2P_3 = 9$$P_9 = P_8 + 2P_4 = 11$$P_{10} = P_9 + 2P_5 = 17$$P_{11} = P_{10} + 2P_6 = 27$$P_{12} = P_{11} + 2P_7 = 41 $Since there are $ 41 $pairs of rabbits after $ 12 $months, there are $ 2 \cdot 41 = 82$total rabbits.

questions.title: Kevin's Kids II
questions.problem: Kevin has $2$ children. You're visiting Kevin at his house and knock on his door. One of the two children uniformly at random comes to open the door for you. You see that a boy opens the door. Find the probability that the other child is a boy. You may assume that both genders are equally likely at birth, and genders are independent between child.
questions.solution: In this question, you are given information about Kevin's children, so conditional probability is the way to go. This situation isn't exactly the same as the first part, as the boy is chosen by chance, rather than being told directly. To set this up, let $D$ be the event that a boy opens the door for you, and $BB$ be the event that Kevin has two boys. We are looking to compute [ ∣ ] P[$BB$∣D]. By the definition of conditional probability, [ ∣ ] = [ ∩ ] [ ] P[BB∣D]= P[D] P[BB∩D] For the numerator, if we know the counts of each gender of child, we can easily compute the probability that a boy opened the door. Therefore, we reverse the direction of the conditional probability to be given the information BB. Doing this, [ ∩ ] = [ ∣ ] [ ] = 1 ⋅ 1 / 2 2 = 1 / 4 P[BB∩D]=P[D∣BB]P[BB]=1⋅$1$/2 2 =1/4 The conditional probability is 1 1 because both children are boys, so a boy is guaranteed to open the door. For the denominator, we do the same process of conditioning on the children's genders. This yields [ ] = [ ∣ ] [ ] + [ ∣ ] [ ] + [ ∣ ] [ ] + [ ∣ ] [ ] P[D]=P[D∣BB]P[BB]+P[D∣BG]P[BG]+P[D∣GB]P[GB]+P[D∣GG]P[GG] Since all $4$ combinations are equally likely without additional information, [ ] = [ ] = [ ] = [ ] = 1 / 4 P[GB]=P[GG]=P[GB]=P[BB]=1/4. Given the genders, it's easy to compute the probability that a randomly selected child is a boy: Just take the number of boys, and divide by $2$. Doing this, we get [ ] = 1 ⋅ 1 / 4 + 1 / 2 ⋅ 1 / 4 + 1 / 2 ⋅ 1 / 4 + 0 ⋅ 1 / 4 = 1 / 2 P[D]=1⋅1/4+$1/2$⋅1/4+1/2⋅1/4+0⋅1/4=1/2 Plugging in, our answer is [ ∣ ] = 1 / 4 1 / 2 = 1 / 2 P[BB∣D]= 1/2 1/4 =1/2 We did not do anything incorrectly, so what happened? In this scenario, the child approaching the door was selected by chance to be a boy. Therefore, if there were to be a girl in the house, it would be less likely (probability 1 / 2 1/2) that the child going to the door was actually a boy, whereas if there are two boys, it's guaranteed the child going to the door is a boy.

questions.title: WLS Contains OLS?
questions.problem: For what choice of weight matrix $W$ is running WLS equivalent to running OLS under the standard assumptions? Suppose that $\sigma^{2}$ is some positive constant $W = I_n$ $W = I_{p+1}$ $W = \sigma^2 I_n$ $W = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}I_n$ $W = 1_n$, where $1_n$ is the $n \times n$ matrix of all ones. = 2 1 W=σ 2 1 n $W = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}1_n$ There is no general choice of $W$ that makes the two regressions equivalent. SUBMIT
questions.solution: The fitted coefficient for WLS is given by, ^ = ( ) − 1 β ^ WLS =(X T WX) −1 X T WY and the fitted coefficient for OLS is given by, ^ = ( ) − 1 β ^ OLS =(X T X) −1 X T Y Inspecting the fitted coefficients, it is clear that by setting $W = I_{n}$, the identity matrix, that we will then have, ^ = ^ β ^ WLS = β ^ OLS. Thus the correct answer is Option (1).

questions.title: Decreased Variance
questions.problem: Which of the following are most likely to decrease the variance of our estimates for the regression coefficients, ^ $\hat{\beta}$^ i, in ordinary least squares? Sampling more data. Removing predictors that are not explanatory. Removing any predictors. Adding in more predictors. None of the above are likely to reduce the variance of ^ β ^. SUBMIT
questions.solution: The variance of the OLS estimator is Var ( ^ ) = 2 ( ) − 1 Var( β ^ )=σ 2 (X T X) −1. We can't change $\sigma^2$, but we can edit the X T X term by increasing the amount of data points. The variance is inversely proportional to X T X, and more data allows us to gain more information on the true value of ^ $\hat{\beta}$^, so our estimates have less variance. Thus, the first answer is correct. Reducing the number of predictors can decrease the variance of ^ $\hat{\beta}$^ if the removed predictors were contributing little to the explanation of the dependent variable or were highly correlated with other predictors (multicollinearity). Removing such predictors simplifies the model and can lead to more stable estimates of the remaining coefficients. Thus, the second choice is correct. However, removing informative predictors is detrimental to the model and may add variance to estimates, so the third choice is incorrect. The fourth choice is incorrect because it can create multicollinearity, which would increase variance.

questions.title: Why Multicollinearity? I
questions.problem: When performing OLS, why is perfect multicollinearity an issue mathematically? The matrix X T X will not be invertible. The $R^2$ will be $0$. The adjusted $R^2$ will be $0$. The matrix $X$ T X will be positive definite. SUBMIT
questions.solution: Mathematically, if one column is a linear combination of other columns, the matrix will not be of full rank. It turns out that $X$ T X is invertible exactly when $X$ is full rank, so $X$ must be full rank for ( ) − 1 (X T X) −1 to exist. Therefore, we can't have any columns in X be linearly dependent. Option (1) is correct by the above discussion. Option (2) and Option (3) are incorrect, as $R^{2}$ has nothing to do with multicollinearity. Option (4) is incorrect by the above discussion. If X T X were positive definite then it would be invertible.

questions.title: Missing Predictor

Which of the following residual plots is most likely to indicate that the there is a missing predictor? The residuals show non-constant variance with no particular pattern. The residuals appear to have a large constant variance. The residuals appear to have a non-constant variance that exponentially increases with the predictor. None of the above. SUBMIT
questions.solution: Option (1) is incorrect because the plot with a missing predictor would have a trend that is dependent on the predictor. Option (2) is incorrect because constant variance of residuals is acceptable! Constant variance is an assumption of OLS. Option (3) is correct, as one sees an exponential trend that varies with the predictor, so one should add a predictor in the form $e^{x_i}$, or something similar.

questions.title: Fair Die?
questions.problem: A quality control engineer at a dice company rolls a new die $600$ times to test for fairness. He observes the values $1-6$ from the die, $95,105,100,90,110,$ and $100$ times, respectively. Conduct a hypothesis test at significance $\alpha = 0.05$ and interpret the results. If the relevant critical value is 11.07, what should the conclusion of the test be? The calculated test statistic is less than the critical value, so we reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is less than the critical value, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is greater than the critical value, so we reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is greater than the critical value, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: Since we are looking to see if a given distribution (in this case, discrete uniform over $1-6$) is a good fit for our data, the $\chi^2$ GOF test is most appropriate. Letting $p_i$ being the probability of side $i$ appearing in a given roll, our null and alternative hypotheses are $H_0:$ $p_i = 1/6$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 6$ against $H_1:$ $p_i \neq 1/6$ for at least one $1 \leq i \leq 6$. The two hypotheses respectively encapsulate the die being fair/not fair. The test statistic for the $\chi^2$ GOF test is $\chi^2_{GOF} = \sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}$ In the above formula, $n$ is the number of groups (in this case, $n = 6$) $E_i$ is the expected number of occurrences of group $i$ (in this case, $100$ per group, as the die is theoretically fair) $O_i$ is the observed number of occurrences of group $i$ (these are the values in the question) To compute the test statistic, it's easiest to make a table as follows: | $i$ | $O_i$ | $E_i$ | $\frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}$ | |---|---|---|---| | $1$ | $95$ | $100$ | $0.25$ | | $2$ | $105$ | $100$ | $0.25$ | | $3$ | $100$ | $100$ | $0$ | | $4$ | $90$ | $100$ | $1$ | | $5$ | $110$ | $100$ | $1$ | | $6$ | $100$ | $100$ | $0$ | | Sum | $600$ | $600$ | $2.5$ | The right-most column contains the value of our test statistic: 2.5. The $\chi^{2}$ test for independence is a right-sided test. This means that we will reject the null hypothesis if our test statistic is larger than the relevant critical value. Since $2.5 < 11.07$, we will fail to reject the null hypothesis. Thus, there isn't statistically significant evidence to support $H_1$, so the engineer can conclude that the data supports the die being fair. Thus, Option (2) is the correct answer.

questions.title: McDonald's Weight V
questions.problem: McDonald's wants to test if their Quarter Pounder has a standard deviation of $0.1$ ounces. To test their hypothesis, they weigh a sample of $400$ Quarter Pounders and find that the sample variance of the Quarter Pound weights is $s^2 = 0.012$. Assuming that the Quarter Pounder weights are Normally distributed, test their hypothesis at significance $\alpha = 0.05$. If the relevant left critical value is 345.55 and the relevant right critical value is 456.24, what should the conclusion of the test be? The calculated test statistic is less than the left critical value, so we reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is less than the right critical value, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is greater than the right critical value, so we reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is greater than the left critical value, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: As we are testing the variance of a population, a $\chi^2$ variance test is appropriate. Since the test is non-directional, our hypotheses are $H_0: \sigma^2 = 0.01$ against $H_1: \sigma^2 \neq 0.01$. We had to square the theoretical standard deviation $\sigma_0 = 0.1$. Our test statistic is provided by $X = 399 \cdot \dfrac{0.012}{0.01} = 478.8$ As stated in the problem, the relevant critical value is 456.24. Since our alternative hypothesis is that $H_1: \sigma^2 \neq 0.01$, we will only reject the null hypothesis if the value of our test statistic is less than the left critical value or greater than the right critical value. Since our test statistic, $X$, is equal to 478.8, and $456.24 < 478.8$, we will reject the null hypothesis. Thus, Option (3) is the correct answer.

questions.title: USA Heights Hypothesis Test
questions.problem: A researcher reads that the standard deviation of heights is $3$ inches, but they disagree: They think it's more than $3$ inches. To test this, they randomly and independently sample $100$ people and measure their heights. The researcher finds that the sample variance of the collected heights is $s^2 = 10$ inches. Assuming that heights are Normally distributed, test their hypothesis at significance $\alpha = 0.05$. If the relevant critical value is 123.22, what should the conclusion of the test be? The calculated test statistic is less than the critical value, so we reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is less than the critical value, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is greater than the critical value, so we reject the null hypothesis. The calculated test statistic is greater than the critical value, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: As we are testing the variance of a Normal population, a $\chi^2$ variance test is appropriate. The test is directional to the right tail, so our hypotheses are $H_0: \sigma^2 = 9$ against $H_1: \sigma^2 > 9$. The value for $\sigma^{2}$ is 9 since we had to square the theoretical standard deviation $\sigma_0 = 3$ to get a variance. Our test statistic is provided by $X = 99 \cdot \dfrac{10}{9} = 110$. As stated in the problem, the relevant critical value is 123.22. Since our alternative hypothesis is that $H_1: \sigma^2 > 9$, we will only reject the null hypothesis if the value of our test statistic is greater than the critical value. Since our test statistic, $X$, is equal to 110, and $100 < 123.22$, we will fail to reject the null hypothesis. Thus, Option (2) is the correct answer.

questions.title: Interaction Interest
questions.problem: Consider a multiple regression model where you suspect an interaction effect between two predictors might be statistically significant. What is the most appropriate method to test for the significance of this interaction? Include an interaction term in the model and use a $t-$test to assess the significance of it's coefficient. Perform a separate regression analysis excluding one predictor each time. Use an F-test to compare the fit of models with and without the interaction term. Test the hypothesis $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2$, where $\beta_{1}$ is the coefficient for the first predictor and $\beta_{2}$ is the coefficient for the second predictor. None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (1) is correct. The $t-$statistic is used to test whether or not a coefficient is statistically different from a particular value or not. In this case, we would include the interaction term in our regression model, and then use a $t$-test to test whether or not the coefficient for the interaction term is statistically significantly different from 0 or not. Option (2) is incorrect. It's not clear what this method really means and how it would be used to determine if the interaction is statistically significantly different from 0. Option (3) is incorrect. For example, if the two predictors were the exact same, the interaction term wouldn't tell us anything new that the individual predictors don't already say, so the fit wouldn't be better, even though there is an interaction. Option (4) is incorrect. This test simply checks if the coefficient for the two different predictors are equal. It is possible that their individual coefficients are equal and there is no interaction effect, but it is also possible that their individual coefficients are not equal and there is an interaction effect. Thus, this test tells us nothing about whether or not the interaction term is needed.

questions.title: Typical Kolmogorov Null
questions.problem: Which of the following would be a typical null hypothesis for the one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test? The data are uniformly distributed. The data do not follow a specified theoretical distribution. The data does follow a specified theoretical distribution. The data set is independent of another data set. None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (3) is correct. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test determines if data follows a prescribed distribution, so the null hypothesis would be the third option.

questions.title: Alternate Sample Variance III
questions.problem: Let $X_1,\dots, X_n \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ IID. Define $V = \dfrac{1}{2(n-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} (X_{i+1} - X_i)^2$ Find the efficiency of $V$ relative to $s^2$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$, where $s^{2}$ is the typical expression for sample variance. NOTE: It is highly recommended to complete Alternate Sample Variance I, Alternate Sample Variance II, and Sample Variance Variance before attempting this question.
questions.solution: The variance of $s^2$ is given by $\var{s^2} = \frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}$, while $\var{V} = \frac{(3n-4)\sigma^4}{(n-1)^2}$. To find the efficiency of $V$ relative to $s^2$, we must take the limit of the ratio $\frac{\var{s^2}}{\var{V}}$, as this represents the asymptotic variances of the estimators. This yields $E_V = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{\frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}}{\frac{(3n-4)\sigma^4}{(n-1)^2}} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{2n-2}{3n-4} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ One can intuitively interpret this as: For a given large sample size $n$, the estimator $s^2$ of $\sigma^2$ has a variance approximately $2/3$ as large as $V$.

questions.title: Uniform MLE I
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1\mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim \text{Unif}[0,\theta]$ IID. If it exists, find the MLE of $\theta$ with the dataset $\{1,2,3,4,0.5\}$. If it doesn't, report $-1$.

questions.title: Geometric MLE
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \theta,\dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim \geom{\theta}$ IID. If it exists, find the MLE of $\theta$ with the data $\{2,5,3,4\}$. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$.
questions.solution: The PMF of each $X_1 \mid \theta, \dots , X_n \mid \theta$ is $p(k \mid \theta) = \theta(1-\theta)^{k-1}$ for all integer $k \geq 1$. Taking the product, the joint likelihood is $L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \theta (1-\theta)^{x_i - 1} = \theta^n(1-\theta)^{\sum x_i - n}$ We leave off the joint support for simplicity. It's easier to consider the log-likelihood most of the time when taking derivatives, so we get $l(\theta) = \ln(L(\theta)) = \ln\left(\theta^n(1-\theta)^{\sum x_i - n}\right) = n\ln(\theta) + \left(\sum x_i - n\right)\ln(1-\theta)$ Taking the partial derivative, we get $\partial l/\partial \theta = \dfrac{n}{\theta} - \dfrac{\sum x_i - n}{1-\theta} = 0 \iff \theta = \dfrac{n}{\sum x_i}$ Therefore, $\hat{\theta}_{MLE} = \dfrac{n}{\sum X_i}$. This intuitively makes sense: The mean of the Geometric distribution is $1/p$, so to get the estimator of $p$, we take the reciprocal of our standard estimator for the mean. With the specified values, the answer is $2/7$.

questions.solution: The Fisher Information of $\theta$ does not exist because the $\text{Unif}[0,\theta]$ distribution has a support dependent on the parameter $\theta$, meaning it's not well-defined. The answer is $-1$.

questions.title: Remaining Heart
questions.problem: Awooga shuffles a deck and then draws cards one-at-a-time without replacement until it only consists of Jacks, Queens, Kings, and Aces. What is the probability that the Ace of hearts is still in the deck?
questions.solution: Let's first think of the proper approach. Since we are drawing until there are no more non-Ace and non-face cards, we only care about the position of the Ace of hearts relative to the non-Ace and non-face cards. This is because it only matters that the Ace is in the deck after all of the other non-face or non-Ace cards have been drawn. If it's not the last one relative to these other $36$ cards, there would exist another non-face/Ace afterwards, and we'd keep drawing. The probability that the Ace of hearts is in this last position among the $37$ cards is $1/37$, since all orderings of the cards are equally likely.

questions.title: Ultra Reroll III
questions.problem: Albert has a fair $n-$sided die with the values $1$ to $n$. He rolls the die and observes the value. Afterwards, he has the choice to roll again or receive a payout equal to the value he rolled (in dollars). If he rolls again, there is a cost of $\$r$. He is allowed to exercise this reroll option as many times as he would like. Let $t^*(n,r)$ be the optimal threshold for the game described above, and define $v = r/n$. If it exists, along the path where $v$ is fixed, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{r,n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{t^*(n,r)}{n}$ Report the answer when $v = 1/50$.
questions.solution: From the second part of the problem, we found that $\dfrac{t^*(n,r)}{n} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{n} - \sqrt{\dfrac{2r}{n}}$ Since we are taking the limit along the path where $v = r/n$ is fixed, we can conclude that $\displaystyle \lim_{r,n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{t^*(n,r)}{n} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{n} -\sqrt{2v} = 1 - \sqrt{2v}$ With $v = 1/50$, the answer is $4/5$. This aligns closely with what was received in Ultra Reroll I, as the ratio would be $201/250 pprox 0.8$.

questions.title: Sharp Shooter
questions.problem: Abd and Belle Delphine both shoot at a target simultaneously. Abd and Belle Delphine each hit the target with respective probabilities $0 < p_A, p_B < 1$. Given that only one of the two people hits the target, find the probability it was Abd. You may assume that each person's shot lands independently of one another. Report the answer when $p_A = 4/5$ and $p_B = 3/5$.
questions.solution: Let's state the question in probabilistic language. Let $A$ be the event that Abd hits the target and $O$ be the event that only one person hits the target. We are looking to compute $\prob{A \mid O}$. By the definition of conditional probability, $\prob{A \mid O} = \dfrac{\prob{A \cap O}}{\prob{O}}$ For the numerator, $A \cap O$ is the event that Abd hits and Belle Delphine misses, as only one person can hit the target. The probability of this is $p_A(1-p_B)$ by independence and complementation. As for the denominator, there are two possible ways that one person can hit the target: Either Abd or Belle Delphine does it. These cases are disjoint, so we can add their probabilities together. By independence and casework, $\prob{O} = \prob{O \cap A} + \prob{O \cap A^c} = p_A(1-p_B) + p_B(1-p_A)$ Plugging these in, $\prob{A \mid O} = \dfrac{p_A(1-p_B)}{p_A(1-p_B) + p_B(1-p_A)}$ This result intuitively makes sense: If $p_A << p_B$, the answer is close to $0$, while if $p_A >> p_B$, the answer is close to $1$. With the specified values, the answer is $8/11$.

questions.title: Mean Pick
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n \geq 2$. Three integers are selected uniformly at random without replacement from the set $[2n] = \{1,2,\dots, 2n\}$. Find the probability that one of the integers is the average of the two other when $n = 11$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we are selecting $3$ integers uniformly at random from the set $[2n]$. As the integers are selected uniformly at random, we can compute the probability by converting it into a counting problem: Count the number of selections of $3$ integers satisfying the condition, and the divide by the total number of ways to select $3$ integers. As we are selecting $3$ integers without respect to the order of which is the one that is the mean of the other two, there are $\binom{2n}{3}$ ways to pick $3$ integers without replacement and order irrelevant. As for the numerator, for one to be the mean of the other two, the mean must be an integer. For the mean of two integers, say $x$ and $y$, to be an integer, $x+y$ must be even, so $x$ and $y$ must have the same parity. Given $x$ and $y$ of the same parity, there is exactly one selection of the third integer (namely, $\frac{x+y}{2}$) that satisfies the condition. From the above, we need to count the number of pairs of integers $(x,y)$ of the same parity, as then the third integer in the set has only $1$ option. There are $2$ ways to pick which parity the integers are (even or odd), and then $\binom{n}{2}$ ways to pick the two integers, as the order of selection is irrelevant. Thus, there are $2\binom{n}{2}$ selections that satisfy the condition. Dividing and simplifying, the final answer is $\dfrac{2\binom{n}{2}}{\binom{2n}{3}} = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{\frac{2n(2n-1)(2n-2)}{3!}} = \dfrac{3}{2(2n-1)}$ With $n = 11$, the answer is $1/14$.

questions.title: Money Box II
questions.problem: A box contains $\$100$ of cash inside. You and your friend, who is a rational player looking to maximize their payout, each write down a non-negative integer of a slip of paper privately. Afterwards, you reveal your slips of paper to one another. If the sum of the two numbers written is at most $100$, each person receives the amount (in dollars) equal to the number they wrote; otherwise, neither player receives any payout. Your friend says he is going to write down the number $83$. He may or may not change his mind later. Assuming you are also rational, what number should you write down?
questions.solution: As per the previous part of the question, all pairs of the form $(x,100-x)$ are Nash equilbria. Your friend saying that he is going to write down $83$ means that he wants to go into the Nash equilibrium $(17,83)$. Since he is rational and knows that he gave this information, he will not choose a number larger than $83$, as he'd know you are entering the Nash equilibrium $(17,83)$. Thus, you should choose the number $17$.

questions.title: Negative Poisson
questions.problem: Suppose that $X \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ for some $\lambda  > 0$. If possible, compute $\ev{X(-1)^X}$ to the nearest thousandth when $\lambda = 2$. If it's not possible, report $-1$.
questions.solution: As the interior of this expectation is in the form of $Xc^X$, one might think to use the MGF, as $Xc^X = Xe^{\ln(c)X} = M_X(\ln(c))$. However, the issue here is that $c = -1$, and $\ln(-1)$ is not defined. Therefore, to compute this, we should LOTUS to compute this (somewhat complicated) expected value expression. The PMF of $X \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ is given by $\prob{X = k} = \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda}, k = 0,1,2,\dots$ Using this, we can write the LOTUS expression as $\ev{\textcolor{red}{X(-1)^X}} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \textcolor{red}{k(-1)^k} \cdot \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda} = e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k \cdot \dfrac{(-\lambda)^k}{k!}$ Since we have a $k$ and $k!$, we can write $k! = k \cdot (k-1)!$ and cancel out $k$. As we'll have a $(k-1)!$ in the denominator, we should start the sum at $k = 1$ instead of $k = 0$. Note that when $k = 0$, the expression is $0$, so we can change the lower index to $k = 1$ without any harm. Making these manipulations, we find $\ev{X(-1)^X} = e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k \cdot \dfrac{(-\lambda)^k}{k \cdot (k-1)!} = e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-\lambda)^k}{(k-1)!} = -\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-\lambda)^k}{(k-1)!}$ We take out one term of $-\lambda$ from $(-\lambda)^k$ because we want to have a consistent $k-1$ between the numerator and denominator, as the sum starts at $k = 1$. To compute the value of the sum, we can perform an index shift of $u = k-1$ to make the sum start at $u = 0$. Lastly, each instance of $k-1$ can be replaced with $u$, yielding the final summation $\ev{X(-1)^X} = -\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{u = 0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-\lambda)^u}{u!} = -\lambda e^{-\lambda} \cdot e^{-\lambda} = -\lambda e^{-2\lambda}$ We reduce the sum using the Taylor series for $e^x$ evaluated at $x = -\lambda$. In actuality, if we had a real-valued expression for $\ln(-1)$, our answer does turn out to be $M_X(\ln(-1))$ for $X \sim \poisson{\lambda}$, as the convergence of the Taylor series occurs for all real values. With $\lambda = 2$, the answer is $-0.037$.

questions.title: Equal Zetas
questions.problem: Suppose that $X, Y \sim \text{Zeta}(2)$ IID i.e. they have PMF $p(k) = \frac{6}{\pi^2k^2}$ for positive integers $k$. Compute $\prob{X > Y}$. You may find the following fact helpful: The PMF of a $\text{Zeta}(4)$ random variable is given by $m(k) = \frac{90}{\pi^4k^4}$ for positive integers $k$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we're looking for $\prob{X > Y}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, we can claim that $\prob{X > Y} = \prob{Y > X}$. In addition, the only possible case besides the two above is that $X = Y$. As these three events are disjoint (impossible for more than one to be true at once) and exhaustive (at least one is always true), we can conclude that $\prob{X > Y} + \prob{Y > X} + \prob{X = Y} = 1 \iff \prob{X > Y} = \dfrac{1 - \prob{X = Y}}{2}$ This fact can be used for any IID discrete random variables. We've obtained it from substitution of $\prob{Y > X} = \prob{X > Y}$. Therefore, we only need to compute $\prob{X = Y}$, and the rest falls into place. To compute $\prob{X = Y}$, we can just disjointify over all possible values of $k$ that $X$ and $Y$ can equal. This is because $X$ and $Y$ must both be equal to some positive integer, so we break the expresssion down and sum over all possible values of $k$. Doing this, we get $\prob{X = Y} = \sum_{k = 1}^{\infty} \prob{X = Y = k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{X = k}\prob{Y = k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{6}{\pi^2 k^2} \cdot \dfrac{6}{\pi^2 k^2} = \dfrac{36}{\pi^4}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{k^4}$ All of the above was from using the basic properties of PMFs and the fact that $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The hint comes in handy for computing the final sum. Since we're given that $m(k) = \frac{90}{\pi^4 k^4}$ is a PMF over the positive integers, we can conclude that $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{90}{\pi^4k^4} = 1 \iff \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{k^4} = \dfrac{\pi^4}{90}$ Substituting this in, we find $\prob{X = Y} = \dfrac{36}{\pi^4} \cdot \dfrac{\pi^4}{90} = 2/5$ With this fact, we conclude that $\prob{X > Y} = \dfrac{1 - 2/5}{2} = 3/10$

questions.title: Money Box IV
questions.problem: A box contains $\$100$ of cash inside. You and your friend, who is a rational player looking to maximize their payout, each write down a non-negative integer of a slip of paper privately. Afterwards, you reveal your slips of paper to one another. If the sum of the two numbers written is at most $100$, each person receives the amount (in dollars) equal to the number they wrote; otherwise, neither player receives any payout. You get to tell your friend that you're selecting any number of your choice, and they will believe you. What number do you tell your friend?
questions.solution: Since your friend is rational, they are looking to maximize the expected value for themselves. A natural thought is that you should say $100$ because that is the highest possible valid value. However, your friend receives no money in this scenario, so there's no incentive for them to pick $0$ instead of any positive value. Thus, you should pick $99$ so that your friend receives $\$1$ per turn and doesn't have incentive to go any higher, as $(99,1)$ is a Nash equilibrium.

questions.title: Unseated Table
questions.problem: Fix integers $1 \leq r \leq n$. There is a circular table with $n$ seats. $r$ people want to sit at the table for dinner. In how many distinct ways can this be done? Two arrangements are considered distinct if they are not rotations of one another. Report the answer when $n = 7$ and $r = 5$.
questions.solution: This seems like a standard circular table problem, except now all seats are being used. The first step to approaching such problems is to drop the constraint of the circle, and then add it back in later. On a standard table, to seat $r$ people in $n$ seats, we must perform two steps: Determine which $r$ seats of the $n$ will be occupied. Arrange the $r$ people among the $r$ seats. As for the first step, since the order of selection of seats is irrelevant, there are $\binom{n}{r}$ ways to pick the $r$ seats to be occupied. Once they are selected, there are $r!$ ways to arrange the $r$ people among the $r$ seats, as this is just creating a permutation between them. With no restrictions, the number of arrangements is given by $\binom{n}{r}r!$ However, we have the restriction of having a circular table. Thus, for each arrangement of the $r$ people, we need to count out the repeated arrangements that can be obtained by rotating the table. Given any fixed arrangement, the table has $n$ rotations that can be performed, so the previous quantity overcounts by a factor of $n$. Dividing this through, we get the final answer: $\dfrac{ inom{n}{r} r!}{n} = \dfrac{ rac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} \cdot r!}{n} = \dfrac{(n-1)!}{(n-r)!}$ As a sanity check, when $r = n$, the answer is $(n-1)!$, which is the solution to the (more common) question where it's $n$ seats and $n$ people. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{6!}{2!} = 360$

questions.title: Sharpe Ratio Sum II
questions.problem: Let $X$ be any non-constant random variable with finite mean and variance. We define the $\textit{sharpe ratio}$ of $X$ to be $SR(X) = \dfrac{\ev{X}}{\sqrt{\var{X}}}$ Suppose $X_1$ and $X_2$ are random variables with sharpe ratios $SR(X_1)$ and $SR(X_2)$, respectively, and correlation $\rho$. Assume that $\var{X_1} = \var{X_2} < \infty$. It turns out that $SR(X_1+X_2) > SR(X_1)$ if and only if $SR(X_2) > c(\rho) \cdot SR(X_1)$ for some constant $c$ dependent on $\rho$. Find $c$ when $\rho = 0.28$.
questions.solution: In this question, we assume the same conditions as the first part, but we now want to find a condition on $SR(X_1)$ and $SR(X_2)$ that ensures $SR(X_1 + X_2) > SR(X_1)$. We have the expression from the first part of the question that $SR(X_1 + X_2) = \dfrac{SR(X_1) + SR(X_2)}{\sqrt{2(1+\rho)}}$ Thus, to solve $SR(X_1 + X_2) > SR(X_1)$, we just plug in the prior expression to the inequality to obtain $\dfrac{SR(X_1) + SR(X_2)}{\sqrt{2(1+\rho)}} > SR(X_1) \iff \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2(1+\rho)}}\right) \cdot SR(X_1) > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2(1+\rho)}} \cdot SR(X_2) \iff SR(X_2) > \left(\sqrt{2(1+\rho)} - 1\right)\cdot SR(X_1)$ With $\rho = 0.28$, we find that $c = \sqrt{2.56} - 1 = 3/5$.

questions.title: Triangular Partition I
questions.problem: Each of the vertices of the base of a triangle is connected by straight lines to $n$ distinct points on the side opposite it. Into how many parts do these $2n$ lines divide the interior of the triangle? Report the answer when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: WLOG, suppose that triangle $ABC$ is our triangle, with $B$ and $C$ being our base vertices. Suppose we draw all $n$ lines from vertex $B$ to side $AC$ first. These $n$ lines divide up the area of the triangle into $n+1$ distinct regions. Now, when drawing the lines from vertex $C$ to side $AB$, each of these $n+1$ regions is going to be split via $n$ lines, making $n+1$ regions inside each region. Thus, the resulting triangle has $(n+1)^2$ distinct parts. With $n = 10$, the answer is $121$.

questions.title: Binomial Counter I
questions.problem: For any positive integer $n$, find a closed-form for $\binom{n}{0} + \frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{1} + \frac{1}{3}\binom{n}{2} + \dots + \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{n}{n}.$ Report the answer when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: We can write the expression in summation form as $\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^n \dfrac{1}{k+1}\binom{n}{k}$. We can try to simplify the summand by expanding out the definition of the binomial coefficient. Doing so, we get $\dfrac{1}{k+1} \binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{1}{k+1} \cdot \dfrac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} = \dfrac{n!}{(k+1)!(n-k)!} = \dfrac{1}{n+1} \cdot \dfrac{(n+1)!}{(k+1)!(n-k)!} = \dfrac{1}{n+1} \binom{n+1}{k+1}$ Plugging this in and reindexing the sum yields $\sum_{k=0}^n \dfrac{1}{k+1}\binom{n}{k} = \sum_{k=0}^n\dfrac{1}{n+1} \binom{n+1}{k+1} = \dfrac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}{k} = \dfrac{1}{n+1} \left[\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}{k} - 1\right] =\dfrac{2^{n+1} - 1}{n+1}$ In the above, used the fact that the sum before the final equality counts the number of subsets of a set of size $n+1$, which is just $2^{n+1}$.

questions.title: Binomial Counter II
questions.problem: For any positive integer $n$, find a closed-form for $\binom{n}{1} + 2\binom{n}{2} + 3\binom{n}{3} + \dots + n\binom{n}{n}.$ Report the answer when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: We can write the expression in summation form as $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^n k\binom{n}{k}$. The form of the summation gives a hint as to the problem for this sum counts: $\binom{n}{k}$ picks a subset of size $k$ from a set of size $n$. $k$ picks out one element from the set of size $k$. In the order above, we first pick the subset of size $k$, and then pick the element from it. Instead, since we aggregate over all set sizes, we could reverse the order of operations: Pick the special element first, and then determine if every other element is in the subset. There are $n$ ways to pick the special element. For the other $n-1$ elements, each can be included or not in the subset, so there are $2^{n-1}$ possible subsets of the other $n-1$ elements that can be included with the special element. In the above, we can choose a subset of any size to include with the special element because we sum over all set sizes. Therefore, the solution to the above counting problem, and hence the sum, is $n \cdot 2^{n-1}$. With $n = 10$, the answer is $10 \cdot 2^9 = 5120$.

questions.title: Correl Check I
questions.problem: Determine if the following statement is True or False: There exists random variables $X$ and $Y$ such that $X \geq 0$ always, $Y \leq 0$ always, and $\corr{X}{Y} = 1$.
questions.solution: The definition of $\corr{X}{Y} = 1$ implies that $Y = aX + b$ for some constants $a > 0$ and $b$. Hence, we could imagine that if the $b$ relating $X$ and $Y$ is negative enough, $Y \leq 0$ always. For example, suppose $X \sim \unif{0}{1}$ and $Y = X - 1$. As $0 \leq X \leq 1$ always, $-1 \leq Y \leq 0$, so $Y \leq 0$ always, but $\corr{X}{Y} = \corr{X}{X-1} = \corr{X}{X} = 1$. Hence, the statement is true.

questions.title: 4Head I
questions.problem: Varun has $4$ fair coins. He flips all $4$ at once and notes the parity of each. After seeing the outcomes, he may $\textbf{turn over}$ any pair of coins. Note that this means a heads becomes a tails and vice versa. Varun may not turn over a single coin without turning over another. He can iterate this process as many times as he would like. If Varun plays to maximize his expected number of heads, find the expected number of heads he will have.
questions.solution: The key item to note here is that Varun will always end up with either $3$ or $4$ heads. The final amount that he can obtain is going to depend on how many heads he obtains initially. If Varun obtains an even number of heads, he can select a pair of tails and turn both of them over. He can do this with any amount of tail pairs, so Varun will eventually end up with all heads. However, if Varun obtains either $1$ or $3$ heads on the first turn, he can't do any better than $3$ heads, as any pair of coins that he would select to attempt to do better would consist of one head and one tail. This implies that Varun will obtain $4$ heads precisely when his initial flipping yields an even number of heads, while he obtains $3$ heads precisely when his initial flipping yields an odd number of heads. The probability that Varun obtains an even number of heads from the $4$ flips is $\dfrac{1 + 6 + 1}{16} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ The above was obtained via the Binomial distribution. Therefore, the probability Varun obtains an odd number of heads from the $4$ flips is $1/2$. The expected number of heads Varun obtains is $\dfrac{4+3}{2} = \dfrac{7}{2}$

questions.title: 4Head II
questions.problem: Varun has $4$ fair coins. He flips all $4$ at once and notes the parity of each. After seeing the outcomes, he may flip any pair of coins again. Varun may not flip a single coin without flipping another. He can iterate this process as many times as he would like. If Varun plays to maximize his expected number of heads, find the expected number of heads he will have.
questions.solution: For each pair we flip again, we always have a positive probability ($1/4$ on each flip) of obtaining $2$ heads. Since there is a positive probability per trial of obtaining two heads, regardless of the initial outcome, if the pair is flipped enough times, Varun will end with a pair heads. This can be rigorously proven by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. If he repeats this for the two pairs, he will eventually have $4$ heads. Therefore, the answer is just $4$, as with probability $1$, Varun will obtain $HHHH$ at some point.

questions.title: Roll Again I
questions.problem: Kelly rolls a fair standard $6-$sided die. She observes the value on the face. Afterwards, she is given the option to either receive the upface (in dollars) as a payout or to roll again. If she rolls again, she receives the upface of the second roll (in dollars) as payout, regardless of what she rolled on the first turn. If Kelly plays optimally, what is her expected payout?
questions.solution: The idea here is that Kelly wants to maximize her expected value at each step. Therefore, Kelly should only roll again when she receives a value on the first roll than is smaller than the expected value rolling again. The expected value of a standard die is $3.5$, so if Kelly receives any value less than $3.5$, which would be $1,2,$ or $3$, she should roll again. This is because she would have another roll, which has expected value $3.5$, which is larger than the value currently showing on her die. Otherwise, if Kelly rolls a $4,5,$ or $6$, she should keep her value and cash out. We now need to compute a conditional expectation, conditioning on the value that Kelly observes on her first roll. Let $P$ be her payout and $X_1$ be the value on the first roll. By Law of Total Expectation, we have that $\mathbb{E}[P] = \mathbb{E}[P \mid X_1 \leq 3]\mathbb{P}[X_1 \leq 3] + \mathbb{E}[P \mid X_1 > 3]\mathbb{P}[X_1 > 3]$ The two probabilities are each $1/2$, as they cover $3$ of the $6$ possible values of the die. If $X_1 \leq 3$, Kelly rolls her die again, so her expected payout in this scenario is $3.5$, as it is the expected value of the second die roll. If Kelly receives larger than $3$ on the first roll, she stays with her current value, so the value she rolled is uniformly random among $\{4,5,6\}$, which has mean $5$. Her expected payout in this case would be $5$. Therefore, putting it all together, $\mathbb{E}[P] = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 3.5 + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 5 = \dfrac{17}{4} = 4.25$ Note that this is an improvement by $0.75$ over just a standard die roll.

questions.title: Coinsecutive I
questions.problem: Daniel flips a fair coin until he obtains $2$ consecutive heads. Find the expected number of flips that Daniel performs.
questions.solution: The idea here is to condition on what happens at the first flip and set up a Markov Chain. We need to think about our intermediate states that can occur before hitting $HH$. We could have no part of the sequence or one $H$ before hitting the sequence $HH$. Therefore, let $e_0$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe two consecutive heads given that no heads have been observed in our sequence yet. Similarly, let $e_H$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe two consecutive heads given that the previous flip was $H$. By conditioning on the first flip, we have that $e_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_0 + 1) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_H + 1)$ This is because if we obtain a tails (which occurs with probability $1/2$), it is as if we are still in a nothing state, but the number of flips we have performed now is $1$ instead of $0$. Therefore, our process is in the same state, but now we add $1$ to the counter. If we flip a heads on the first flip (also occurring with probability $1/2$), then we are in the state where our previous flip was $H$. We have to add $1$ for the same fact that we have now flipped and it must be added to our running total. We now need to compute $e_H$ in terms of $e_0$. Conditioning on the next flip, we have that $e_H = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1 + e_0) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1)$ If we obtain a tails on the next flip, then we go back to a nothing state, as we don't have any part of the sequence $HH$ presently. Therefore, we add $1$ to our counter and have expected time $e_0$ to obtain $HH$. If we obtain a heads on the next flip, then we now have the sequence $HH$, which means it took $1$ flip from our current state to obtain $HH$. We now have a system of two equations with two unknowns. By substituting in $e_H = \dfrac{1}{2}e_0 + 1$ into the first equation, we can solve for $e_0 = 6$. On an intuitive level, it should make sense that the sequences $HH$ (and also $TT$, assuming a fair coin) is the most difficult $2$ flip sequence to obtain consecutively. This is because of the fact that even if you have flipped a heads, flipping a tails restarts your sequence, whereas if your sequence is $HT$, if you flip a heads and then flip another heads, you don't have to restart your sequence. Therefore, it should take longer (on average) to see the sequence $HH$ than $HT$.

questions.title: Coinsecutive II
questions.problem: Daniel flips a fair coin until he obtains a heads immediately followed by a tails. Find the expected number of flips that Daniel performs. For example, if the sequence Daniel flips is $THHT$, then it took him $4$ flips total.
questions.solution: The idea here is to condition on what happens at the first flip and set up a Markov Chain. We need to think about our intermediate states that can occur before hitting $HT$. We could have no part of the sequence or one $H$ before hitting the sequence $HT$. Therefore, let $e_0$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe $HT$ given that no part of our sequence has been observed yet. Similarly, let $e_H$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe $HT$ given that the previous flip was $H$. By conditioning on the first flip, we have that $e_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_0 + 1) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_H + 1)$ This is because if we obtain a tails (which occurs with probability $1/2$), it is as if we are still in a nothing state, but the number of flips we have performed now is $1$ instead of $0$. Therefore, our process is in the same state, but now we add $1$ to the counter. If we flip a heads on the first flip (also occurring with probability $1/2$), then we are in the state where our previous flip was $H$. We have to add $1$ for the same fact that we have now flipped and it must be added to our running total. We now need to compute $e_H$ in terms of $e_0$. Conditioning on the next flip, we have that $e_H = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1 + e_H)$ If we obtain a tails on the next flip, then we have obtained the sequence $HT$. Therefore, it would have only taken one flip from $H$ to obtain our sequence of interest. If we obtain a heads on the next flip, then we remain in the state where the previous flip was a heads, but must add $1$ to our counter to account for the fact that we performed an additional flip. The above provides two equations with two unknowns, which we can solve for $e_0$. Solving for $e_H = 2$ in the second equation, we can solve for $e_0 = 4$ by substituting in $2$ for $e_H$ in the first equation. On an intuitive level, it should make sense that the sequences $HH$ (and also $TT$, assuming a fair coin) is the most difficult $2$ flip sequence to obtain consecutively. This is because of the fact that even if you have flipped a heads, flipping a tails restarts your sequence, whereas if your sequence is $HT$, if you flip a heads and then flip another heads, you don't have to restart your sequence. Therefore, it should take longer (on average) to see the sequence $HH$ than $HT$.

questions.title: Groggy Froggy
questions.problem: A frog starts at the center of a circular lily pad of radius 1 meter. The frog hops to a uniformly random point on the lily pad. Find the expected radial distance of the frog from the center of the lily pad.
questions.solution: Let $R$ be the radial distance. We use the complementary tail sum formula: $\ev{R} = \ctailsum{R}$. The event $\{R \geq x\}$ means the frog lands at distance at least $x$ from the center. We need $\prob{R \geq x}$. The area at distance at most $x$ from the center is a circle of radius $x$, which has area $\pi x^2$. The remaining area (at distance at least $x$) is $\pi(1-x^2)$. Since the frog lands uniformly on the lily pad of area $\pi$, $\prob{R \geq x} = \dfrac{\pi(1-x^2)}{\pi} = 1-x^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$. The lily pad has radius $1$, so $R$ is supported on $0 \leq x \leq 1$. Therefore, $\ev{R} = \intab{0}{1} \prob{R \geq x} dx = \intab{0}{1} 1-x^2~dx = \dfrac{2}{3}$

questions.problem: Find the number of anagrams of $$$$B$$$$$$O$$$OLAHUBBOO$ that have all of the B's before the first O.

questions.title: True Equation
questions.problem: Dan has a fair $6$ 6-sided die with faces labeled 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , + , $1,2,3,4,+,$ and − . −. In order to complete the equation ‾ ‾ ‾ = ‾ , = , Dan repeatedly rolls his die and fills in a blank with the character he obtained, starting with the leftmost blank and progressing rightward. Find the probability that, when all blanks are filled, Dan forms a true equation.
questions.solution: We know that the first, third, and last digits must be numerical values, as the expression would not make sense otherwise. If the second digit is also numerical, then the statement can't be true, as Dan would have a $3$ − 3−digit integer equal to a $1$ − 1−digit integer, which is not valid. Therefore, the second roll must be either a $$$$+$$$$ + or − −. This gives us two cases to consider. If the second roll is a + +, then by fixing the first roll as a 1 1, we can see the triples ( 1 , 1 , $2$ ) , ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) , $(1,1,2), (1,2,3),$ and ( 1 , 3 , 4 ) $(1,3,4)$ are the only valid roll combinations. Similarly, if 2 2 is the first roll, then ( 2 , 1 , 3 ) $(2,1,3)$ and ( 2 , 2 , 4 ) $(2,2,4)$ are the only valid roll combinations. Lastly, if 3 3 is the first roll, then ( 3 , 1 , 4 ) $(3,1,4)$ is the only valid combination. This implies that there are $$$6$$$ 6 combinations that are valid with a + +. However, if the second roll is a − −, we can see symmetry in this problem. If + = $a+b = c$ if valid, then − = c−b=a is also a valid combination with a − −. Therefore, we can match up the valid triples ( , , ) $(a,b,c)$ for + + with the triple ( , , ) $(c,b,a)$ for − − to get all of the valid combinations for − −. This implies there are also 6 6 triples with a − − in the middle that make a valid equation. Therefore, there are 6 + 6 = 12 $6 + 6 = 12$ total roll combinations that are valid. Since there are a total of 6 4 = 1296 6 4 =1296 total rolls that can be obtained, as there are 6 6 outcomes per roll, so the probability of a valid equation is 12 1296 = 1 108 1296 12 = 108 1

questions.title: Slow Ferry I
questions.problem: You are waiting for a ferry to go to the Statue of Liberty! The ferry runs on a fixed schedule of appearing every $10$ 10 minutes. If you arrive at a uniformly random time throughout the day, what is the expected time until the next ferry arrives (in minutes)?
questions.solution: The key observation here is that since the ferry runs on a fixed schedule of appearing every $$10$$ 10 minutes, the only quantity that matters is how many minutes before the next multiple of 10 10 minutes did you appear. Since you arrive at the ferry stop at a uniformly random time throughout the day, the time until the next ferry (and also the time since the last ferry) is Unif ( 0 , 10 ) Unif(0,10) distributed. Therefore, this distribution has mean $$5$$ 5, which means that you will have to wait 5 5 minutes for the next ferry on average.

questions.title: Disco Squares I
questions.problem: $$n$$ adjacent colorless squares are linear arranged. Each individual square is colored black or white with equal probability, independent of all other squares. A connected component is a maximal sequence of adjacent squares all with the same color. For example, BBWWBBBWBWWW has $6$ 6 connected components. Find the expected number of connected components in the line after coloring the squares when = 100 $n = 100$.
questions.solution: It is best to derive a recurre$$$$n$$$$ce relation for the quantity of interest. This approach makes sense, as when we add on another square to the line, we get another line of squares that is directly related to what already was there. In particular, suppose C n is the expected number of connected components in a line of n squares. We can find the expected number of connected components that the nth square brings in addition to the first − $$1$$ n−1. Since we have an equal probability of black or white at each step, the symmetry here makes this work nicely. The color of the ( − 1 ) (n−1)st square here is irrelevant, as each is equally likely. Therefore, we can fix the color of it arbitrarily. There is probability 1 / 2 $$$$1/2$$$$ that the nth square will match in color with the ( − 1 ) (n−1)st square. In this case, the expected number of connected component we would have in our line is − 1 C n−1 , as having another square of the same color does not add a new connected component. With probability 1 / 2 1/2 as well, the color of the nth square differs from the previous one, which means that we obtain − 1 + 1 C n−1 +1 connected components on average, as we have − 1 C n−1 on average from the first − 1 n−1 squares and an additional 1 1 component from the change in color. Putting this together, we obtain the recurrence = 1 2 ⋅ − 1 + 1 2 ⋅ ( − 1 + 1 ) = − 1 + 1 2 C n = 2 1 ⋅C n−1 + 2 1 ⋅(C n−1 +1)=C n−1 + 2 1 We have a boundary condition that 1 = 1 C 1 =1, as there will always be exactly one connected component in one square. questions.title: Blind Die
questions.problem: Alan has two 6 − 6−sided dice. One of the dice is a standard fair 6 − 6−sided die with the values 1 − 6 1−6 on the sides. Alan does not know the values on the other die. Note that the values on this other die do not necessarily need to be 1 − 6 1−6 and can also potentially be repeated. Whenever Alan tosses both dice, each of the integer sums 1 − 12 1−12, inclusive of both, are equally likely. What is the sum of the values on the sides of the die Alan doesn't know?
questions.solution: We know that the distribution of the sum of the two dice is uniformly distribute on the first $12$ 12 positive integers. The key here is to consider the expected value of the sum, as we can use this to find the expected value of the second die. Afterwards, since the die has $$6$$ 6 times, we can take the expected value of the second die and multiply it by the number of times to get the sum of all of the sides. We know that the expected value of the sum of the two dice is 12 + 1 2 = 1$3$ 2 2 12+1 = 2 13 , as the sum is uniform on { 1 , 2 , … , 12 } {1,2,…,12}. We also know that the expected value of a fair die is 7 2 2 7 , so by linearity of expectation, if $V$ is the expected value of the second die, then 7 2 + = 13 2 ⟺ = 3 2 7 +V= 2 13 ⟺V=3 This implies that the average value of the sides on the second die is 3 3. Since there are 6 6 sides on the second die, it must be the case that the sum of those sides is 3 ⋅ 6 = 18 $3 \cdot 6 = 18$.

questions.title: Jenga Stack
questions.problem: Jenga blocks are either $$1$$ 1 unit or $$2$$ 2 units tall. Assuming you have at least $$10$$ 10 of each type of block, how many distinct ways can a 10 10 unit tall tower be built?
questions.solution: This has a recursive flavor to it, as the $n$umber of ways that the tower can be built depends on the last block in the tower. Therefore, it is appropriate to break this up into two cases: the last block is $$$$$$2$$$$$$ 2 tall vs. $$$$$$$$1$$$$$$$$ 1 tall. Let T n be the number of ways to build a tower of height n.
