If the last block in the tower is 2 2 units tall, there are − 2 T n−2 ways to build the tower that is − 2 n−2 units tall and add a 2 2 unit tall block on top of it. These two cases are disjoint, as the last block in the tower can't be both 1 1 unit and 2 2 units tall. With this, we obtain a recurrence relation for T n given by = − 1 + − 2 T n =T n−1 +T n−2 The initial conditions on this are 1 = 1 T 1 =1 (only the 1 1 tall block works here) and 2 = 2 T 2 =2 (either 2 2 1 1 unit blocks or 1 1 2 2 unit block). We can see that this looks very similar to the Fibonacci numbers. questions.problem: How many subsets of { 1 , $$2$$ , … , 12 } {1,2,…,12} contain exactly 2 2 elements from { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } {$\{$\{1,2,3,4\}$\}$}?

questions.title: Pair of Cards
questions.problem: A standard deck of cards is shuffled uniformly at random and the top $2$ 2 cards are dealt from the deck. Find the probability that the cards have the same rank.
questions.solution: The key here is to note that each rank is equally likely on the first card dealt, so we can fix the rank of this card arbitrarily. This is because the calculation will be exactly the same for each of the $1$3$$ 13 ranks, so we can just fix one of them and work with that for the calculation. Once we have fixed this rank, we need to find the probability that we obtain a pair, which means that the second card dealt needs to match in rank to the first card. Once we have dealt out the first card, there will be 3 3 more cards of that same rank left in the deck, as there were originally $4$ 4 cards of each rank and we removed one card without replacement. There will be $51$ 51 cards left in the deck, so the probability that the second card matches in rank to the first is 3 51 = 1 17 51 3 = 17 1

questions.title: Cordial Handshake I
questions.problem: A business meeting begins with $2$ 2 representatives from $5$ 5 different companies. If every person at the meeting shakes hands with every other person at the meeting, how many handshakes occur total?
questions.solution: The key to this question is to think about what constitutes a handshake. A handshake is exactly a pair of people coming together, so counting the number of pairs of people that can be formed at the meeting is exactly the same as counting the number of handshakes that occur. This question now becomes how many pairs of people can be formed? Since there are 5 ⋅ 2 = $10$ $5 \cdot 2 = 10$ people at the meeting and we want to form pairs of people, the answer is just ( 10 2 ) = 45 ( 2 10 )=45, as each handshake consists of people two people from 10 10 to shake hands.

For this to happen, it must be the case that one of the two random variables takes a negative value, while the other takes a positive value. If this isn't the case, the region between the two will either be strictly positive or strictly negative in value, meaning $0$ 0 would not be contained inside. Since $$$$$$X$$$$$$ and $$$$$$Y$$$$$$ are IID, we can just consider one arrangement of X and Y being positive/negative and multiply this probability by the number of permutations of X and Y that there are. Since X and Y are independent random variables, we can say [ > 0 , < 0 ] = [ > 0 ] [ < 0 ] P[X>0,Y<0]=P[X>0]P[Y<0]. The event { > 0 } {X>0} is of length $4$ 4 inside the support, as it is the interval ( 0 , 4 ) $(0,4)$, while our total interval is of length $6$ 6, so [ > 0 ] = 4 / 6 = 2 / 3 P[X>0]=4/6=2/3. questions.title: Jar Match
questions.problem: Bob has $2$ 2 jars in front of him, say A and B. Jar A has $4$ 4 blue and $6$ 6 red marbles. Jar B has $5$ 5 blue and $3$ 3 red marbles. If Bob selects a uniformly random marble from each jar, find the probability that they match in color.
questions.solution: We want to compute the probability that Bob selects matching color marbles from each jar. Bob can obtain matching color marbles by either selecting a red marble or a blue marble from both jars. Since there are not identical amounts of blue and red marbles per jar, we should break this up into computing each case separately. The probability that Bob selects a red marble from Jar A is 6 / 10 = 3 / 5 $6/10 = 3/5$, meaning that he selects a blue marble from Jar A with probability 1 − 3 / 5 = 2 / 5 1−3/5=2/5. This is because he selects uniformly at random from the jar. Similarly, from Jar B, the probability a red marble is selected is 3 / 8 $3/8$, meaning the probability a blue marble is selected is 1 − 3 / 8 = 5 / 8 1−3/8=5/8. By the independence of the two draws, the probability that Bob draws a red marble from both is the product of the individual probabilities that he draws a red marble from each jar, which is 3 / 5 ⋅ 3 / 8 = 9 / 40 $3/5 \cdot 3/8 = 9/40$. The probability that Bob draws a blue marble from both is the product of the individual probabilities that he draws a blue marble from each jar, which is 2 / 5 ⋅ 5 / 8 = 10 / 40 $2/5 \cdot 5/8 = 10/40$. Adding these two together, we get a total probability of drawing the same color from both jars as 19 / 40 $19/40$.

questions.title: Group Project I
questions.problem: A class of $12$ 12 students must divide up into $4$ 4 groups of size $3$ 3 with group numbers 1 − 4 1−4 for a class project. How many distinct ways can the class perform this task?
questions.solution: This is a classic problem of dividing distinct objects (in this case, people), into groups. In this case, the groups are distinct, which makes this problem easier. Since all the groups are distinct, all that matters is the group label for a given person. Each assignment of the $$$1$$2$$$ 12 people to the groups corresponds to an anagram of the 12 12 character string consisting of $3$ 3 of each integer 1 − 4 1−4. For example, the anagram $123412341234$ 123412341234 corresponds to people 1 , 5 , $1,5,$ and $9$ 9 going to group 1 1, 2 , 6 , $2,6,$ and $10$ 10 going to group 2 2, and so on. This implies that counting the number of group arrangements is equal to counting the number of anagrams of the string above. The number of such anagrams is ( 12 3 , 3 , 3 , 3 ) = 369600 ( 3,3,3,3 12 )=369600.

questions.title: Almost Squares
questions.problem: We say a non-negative integer is "almost square" if it is not a perfect square, but all of its digits are perfect squares. For example, both $149$ 149 and $904$ 904 are almost square, but $144$ 144 and $936$ 936 are not. Find the number of positive integers less than $1000$ 1000 that are almost square.
questions.solution: Let's first break down the definition of an "almost square" integer. We know that all of the digits of the integer must be perfect squares, so all of the digits must be $0$ , 1 , $4$ , $$0,1,4,$$ or $$$9$$$ 9. We also know that the integer must not be a perfect square itself. Therefore, the idea here is that there are probably many more integers in the form above that are not perfect squares than are perfect squares, so we should count all of the integers that satisfy the form, and then subtract out those that are perfect squares. To count the number of integers less than $$10$00$ 1000 that are not perfect squares, we can account for integers with less than three digits by appending 0 0s out front to make the number $3$ 3 digits. For example, the integer $44$ 44 would become $044$ 044 and 9 9 becomes $009$ 009. With this, we can now count the number of integers satisfying this quite easily. There are 4 4 options for each of the three digits ( 0 , 1 , 4 , 9 ) $(0,1,4,9)$, so there are 4 3 = 64 4 3 =64 total integers that consist of only 0 , 1 , 4 , 0,1,4, and 9 9. We now need to see which of these integers are perfect squares and exclude them. A quick exhaustive check reveals that 0 , 1 , 4 , 9 , 49 , 100 , 144 , 400 , 441 , $0,1,4,9,49,100,144,400,441,$ and $900$ 900 are all perfect squares, so we must remove these 10 10 from our total, yielding 64 − 10 = 54 64−10=54 almost squares.

questions.title: Four of a Kind
questions.problem: A standard deck of cards is shuffled. You are dealt out $5$ 5 cards from the deck uniformly at random. Find the probability that you have $$4$$ 4 cards of the same rank in your hand.
questions.solution: We want to find the probability that there are $$$$$4$$$$$ 4 cards of the rank within a $$5$$ 5 card hand. First, we should count the number of ways a hand can be dealt. A hand consists of selecting 5 5 cards from $52$ 52, so the number of hands is just ( 52 5 ) ( 5 52 ). Then, to have 4 4 cards of a rank, we must choose the rank of the card that we want all 4 4 suits of first. Afterwards, we must select an additional card for the hand. There are $13$ 13 different ranks to select from for the rank to have all 4 4 suits of. Once the 4 4 cards of the suit have been selected, there are 52 − 4 = 48 52−4=48 cards left in the deck for us to select from for the last card. Therefore, the number of four of a kind hands is 13 ⋅ 48 $13 \cdot 48$. Combining the above, the probability of a four of a kind is 13 ⋅ 48 ( 52 5 ) = 1 4165 ( 5 52 ) 13⋅48 = 4165 1

questions.title: Soccer Shooter II
questions.problem: Cristiano Ronaldo is practicing his free kicks. He decides to perform $100$ free kicks to practice He scores his first free kick and misses his second free kick. For $n \geq 3$, the probability that Ronaldo scores the $n$th free kick is equal to the proportion of the first $n-1$ free kicks that he has scores. For example, if Ronaldo has scored $17$ of his first $30$ free kicks, the probability he scores the $31$st free kick is $17/30$. Find the expected number of shots that Ronaldo scores among the $100$ shots.
questions.solution: From Soccer Shooter I, we know that the probability that Ronaldo scores exactly $k$ among the first $n$ shots is $p(k,n) = \frac{1}{n-1}$ for each $1 \leq k \leq n-1$. In other words, the distribution of the number of shots that Ronaldo scores among the first $n$ is discrete uniform over the set $\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}$. This implies that the expected number of shots that Ronaldo scores among his first $n$ is $\frac{(n-1) + 1}{2} = \frac{n}{2}$. In particular, since $n = 100$ here, the expected number is $50$.

questions.title: Royal Firsts I
questions.problem: A deck of cards is well shuffled. Cards are dealt from this deck one-by-one until the first ace appears. Find the probability that no kings, queens or jacks appear before the first ace.
questions.solution: In this problem, we only care about the ordering of the first jack, queen, king, and ace. Therefore, we can ignore every other card in the deck and consider just the $4$ letters JQKA. We want to find the probability that in a random permutation of these $4$ letters, the letter A comes first. Since the permutation is random, each of the $4$ are equally likely to be first in this permutation, so the probability A is first is $1/4$.

questions.title: Royal Firsts II
questions.problem: A deck of cards is well shuffled. Cards are dealt from this deck one-by-one until the first ace appears. Find the probability that exactly one king, queen, and jack appears before the first ace. Note that other cards that aren't these $4$ ranks can appear before the first ace. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: In this question, we only care about the ordering of the $4$ suits of each of the four ranks jack, queen, king, and ace. Therefore, we can restrict our problem to the $16$ cards that are of these $4$ ranks. There are $16!$ orderings of the $16$ cards total. The first $3$ spots must be jack, queen, and king in any order. There are $3!$ ways to order these ranks around in the first $3$ spots. There are $4$ choices of suit for each of the ranks in the first $3$ spots, so we must also multiply by $4^3$. After these, the $4$th spot must be an ace. There are $4$ options for the ace in terms of suit. After this, the other $12$ cards can be permuted around in any order desired, as we have now satisfied our condition, so there are $12!$ permutations of the remaining $12$ cards after this. This means that there are $3! \cdot 4^3 \cdot 4 \cdot 12! = 3! \cdot 4^4 \cdot 12!$ total arrangements that satisfy our condition. This implies that the probability of the event is $\dfrac{3! \cdot 4^4 \cdot 12!}{16!} \approx 0.035$

questions.title: Royal Firsts III
questions.problem: A deck of cards is well shuffled. Cards are dealt from this deck one-by-one until the first ace appears. Find the probability that exactly one king, queen, and jack are the only cards to appear before the first ace. Round to the nearest millionth.
questions.solution: In this question, we care about the ordering of entire deck, so we can't do any restriction to some subset of the cards. However, we can use a similar combinatorial approach to Royal Firsts II. There are $52!$ total orderings of the entire deck. The first $3$ spots must be jack, queen, and king in any order. There are $3!$ ways to order these ranks around in the first $3$ spots. There are $4$ choices of suit for each of the ranks in the first $3$ spots, so we must also multiply by $4^3$. After these, the $4$th spot must be an ace. There are $4$ options for the ace in terms of suit. After this, the other $48$ in the deck cards can be permuted around in any order desired, as we have now satisfied our condition, so there are $48!$ permutations of the remaining $48$ cards after this. This means that there are $3! \cdot 4^3 \cdot 4 \cdot 48! = 3! \cdot 4^4 \cdot 48!$ total arrangements that satisfy our condition. This implies that the probability of the event is $\dfrac{3! \cdot 4^4 \cdot 48!}{52!} \approx 0.000236$

questions.title: Cheesy Guy I
questions.problem: Jon loves cheese. He decides to make $100$ blocks of cheese. The distribution of the weight (in grams) of each block he makes follows IID $\exponential{1/250}$ distribution. For consistency, let $W_i$ denote the weight of the $i$th block of cheese, and $T_{100}$ represent the total weight of the $100$ blocks of cheese. Using Markov's Inequality, find an upper bound for $\mathbb{P}[T_{100} > 26000]$.
questions.solution: The weight of the cheese is clearly non-negative, so Markov's Inequality applies here. Even better, we see that our statement is already in the form to apply Markov's Inequality. In particular, we have that $\prob{T_{100} > 26000} \leq \dfrac{\ev{T_{100}}}{26000}$. All that remains is computing $\ev{T_{100}}$. Since $T_{100}$ is the sum of $100$ IID random variables with mean $250$, by linearity of expectation, $\ev{T_{100}} = 100 \cdot 250 = 25000$. This implies that $\prob{T_{100} > 26000} \leq \dfrac{25}{26}$.

questions.title: St. Petersburg I
questions.problem: You are offered to play the following game: You flip a fair coin repeatedly until the first heads appears. If the first heads appears on the $n$th flip, you receive a payout of $\$2^n$. What is the fair value of this game? If the answer is infinite, report $-1$.
questions.solution: Let $N$ be the number of flips that are performed until you obtain your first heads. The payout of this game is $2^N$. We are looking to compute $\ev{2^N}$ here. We first need the distribution of $N$. Since $N$ is a waiting time until the first heads and flips are discrete, we know that $N$ follows a geometric distribution. Since the coin is fair, we can conclude $N \sim \geom{1/2}$. To compute the expectation at hand, we use Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS) to see $\ev{2^N} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^n \prob{N = n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^n \cdot \dfrac{1}{2^n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 1 = \infty$

questions.title: Rainbow Socks
questions.problem: There are $n \geq 2$ pairs of socks in a drawer, where each pair has a distinct color. You draw out $2$ socks at random without replacement. Find the probability that you obtain a matching pair when $n = 12$.
questions.solution: Since there are the same number of socks per color and the drawing is completely at random, fix the color of the first sock drawn arbitrarily. Now, there are $2n-1$ socks left in the drawer, of which $1$ is the same color as the first sock drawn, so the probability that you draw a matching pair of socks is $\dfrac{1}{2n-1}$. With $n = 12$, the answer is $1/23$.

questions.title: Excluded Number I
questions.problem: Eric rolls a fair standard die until he obtains a value other than $6$. He is then paid out the upface of the die in dollars. What is Eric's expected payout?
questions.solution: Since Eric can't obtain a $6$ as a payout, we can really exclude this from the sample space of values that Eric can obtain. Therefore, we want to find the conditional expectation of the die given that the die is not the value $6$. Given that Eric does not obtain a $6$, the other $5$ faces on the die are equally likely to appear. Therefore, the amount Eric is paid out is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. This means his expected payout is $\dfrac{1+2+3+4+5}{5} = 3$.

questions.title: Unchanged Die Pair
questions.problem: A pair of standard fair $6-$sided dice are rolled and the upfaces are observed. If the two dice are rolled again, find the probability that the values appearing on the dice will match those of the first roll. Note that these values can occur in any order.

questions.title: Unchanged Die Trio
questions.problem: Three standard fair $6-$sided dice are rolled and the upfaces are observed. If the three dice are rolled again, find the probability that the values appearing on the dice will match those of the first roll. Note that these values can occur in any order. Note: It may be helpful to solve Unchanged Die Pair before attempting this question.
questions.solution:
The key idea of "Unchanged Die Pair" was to condition on whether or not the values that appeared were the same. A similar idea applies here: Condition on the number of distinct values that appear on the dice, as this is what impacts how many permutations there are for the values onto the dice for the second roll. Let $V_i$ be the event that there are $i$ distinct values on the first roll for $i = 1,2,3,$, and let $M$ be the event that the set of values appearing on the second roll matches that of the first roll. By law of total probability with conditioning on the $V_i$ events, $ egin{align*}
\prob{M} = \prob{M \mid V_1}\prob{V_1} + \prob{M \mid V_2}\prob{V_2} + \prob{M \mid V_3}\prob{V_3} \
\end{align*}$ Let's first determine $\prob{V_i}$ for each $i$. The easiest ones to compute are for $V_1$ and $V_3$. The event $V_1$ is just the there is one distinct value appearing on the dice, which means that all $3$ dice show the same value. We know that there are $6^3 = 216$ total outcomes for the three dice by multiplication principle, and there are exactly $6$ outcomes with all the same value, as we only have $6$ options to pick what value is shown on all three dice. Thus, $\prob{V_1} = \dfrac{6}{216} = \dfrac{1}{36}$. Secondly, we have that $V_3$ is the event that three distinct values are shown among the dice. This means that the first die rolled has $6$ options of value, the second die roll has $5$ options (can't be the same as the first die), and the last die has $4$ options (can't be the same as either of the previous two), so there are $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 = 120$ total outcomes where the three dice all show distinct values. Therefore, $\prob{V_3} = \dfrac{120}{216} = \dfrac{5}{9}$. Lastly, we know that $\prob{V_1} + \prob{V_2} + \prob{V_3} = 1$, as there must always be either $1,2,$ or $3$ distinct values that show up between the three dice, so $\prob{V_2} = 1 - \prob{V_1} - \prob{V_2} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{36} - \dfrac{5}{9} = \dfrac{5}{12}$. Now, we need to compute all of the conditional probabilities. Suppose that all the dice share the same value. In other words, the outcome of the first roll is $(a,a,a)$ for some $a$. This means that there is only $1$ permutation of the values onto the dice for the second roll, so the second roll must exactly be the values $(a,a,a)$, which occurs with probability $\prob{M \mid V_1} = \dfrac{1}{216}$. Now, suppose that there are two distinct values between the dice, say $(a,a,b)$ for $a 
eq b$. There are now $3$ distinct permutations of these values onto the dice for the second roll, as there are $3$ options for which die shows $b$, so this means $\prob{M \mid V_2} = \dfrac{3}{216} = \dfrac{1}{72}$. Lastly, if all three values are distinct, say $(a,b,c)$ for $a
eq b
eq c$, there are $3! = 6$ permutations of the values onto the dice, as the three values can appear in any order, meaning $\prob{M \mid V_3} = \dfrac{6}{216} = \dfrac{1}{36}$. By plugging all of these values into the law of total probability above, we obtain the answer $\dfrac{1}{36} \cdot \dfrac{1}{216} + \dfrac{5}{12} \cdot \dfrac{1}{72} + \dfrac{5}{9} \cdot \dfrac{1}{36} = \dfrac{83}{3888}$

questions.title: Bivariate Correlation
questions.problem: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are jointly bivariate normal and marginally standard normal with $\corr{X}{Y} = \rho$. Compute $\cov{X}{Y^2}$ when $\rho = 1/4$.
questions.solution: Whenever you see a bivariate normal question where the normal distributions inside are not necessarily independent, it is best to work with the joint transformation that transforms $Z_1,Z_2 \sim \norm{0}{1}$ IID into the desired joint distribution $(X,Y)$. The transformation here is $X = Z_1$ and $Y = \rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2$. We can use this to compute $\cov{X}{Y^2}$, as working with independent random variables typically makes things cancel nicer. In particular, we have that $\cov{X}{Y^2} = \cov{Z_1}{(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2)^2} = \cov{Z_1}{\rho^2 Z_1^2 + (1-\rho^2)Z_2^2 + 2\rho\sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_1Z_2}$ We now use bilinearity of covariance to expand out this quantity to be $\rho^2\cov{Z_1}{Z_1^2} + (1-\rho^2)\cov{Z_1}{Z_2^2} + 2\rho\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\cov{Z_1}{Z_1Z_2}$ It now remains to compute the three covariance terms. We will use the fact that all odd moments of the standard normal are $0$, which can quickly be seen by the symmetry of the PDF about $0$. The easiest covariance to compute is the second. Note that $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are independent in this paradigm, so $\cov{Z_1}{Z_2^2} = 0$. To compute the first covariance, we use the fact above to obtain $\cov{Z_1}{Z_1^2} = \ev{Z_1^3} - \ev{Z_1}\ev{Z_1^2} = 0$ Lastly, to the compute the final covariance term, we use the independence of $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ to obtain $\cov{Z_1}{Z_1Z_2} = \ev{Z_1^2Z_2} - \ev{Z_1}\ev{Z_1Z_2} = \ev{Z_1^2}\ev{Z_2} - 0  = 0$ Therefore, $\cov{X}{Y^2} = 0$, regardless of what $\rho$ is!

questions.title: Car Wash I
questions.problem: The arrival of cars at a car wash is modelled well by a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$ per hour. Suppose that it takes $m$ minutes to serve each customer. Find the mean of the total service time (in minutes) for customers arriving in a one hour period when $\lambda = 8$ and $m = 10$.
questions.solution: We first need a random variable that counts the number of people arriving in a one hour period. Let $N$ be the number of people that arrive in a one hour period. Then $N \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ by the question itself. If $N$ cars arrive at the car wash, the total service time of all of the cars is $mN$, so we want $\ev{mN}$. By linearity, we have that $\ev{mN} = m\ev{N} = m\lambda$. With $\lambda = 8$ and $m = 10$, the answer is $80$.

questions.title: Car Wash II
questions.problem: The arrival of cars at a car wash is modelled well by a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$ per hour. Suppose that it takes $m$ minutes to serve each customer. Find the variance of the total service time (in minutes) for customers arriving in a one hour period when $\lambda = 8$ and $m = 10$.
questions.solution: We first need a random variable that counts the number of people arriving in a one hour period. Let $N$ be the number of people that arrive in a one hour period. Then $N \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ by the question itself. If $N$ cars arrive at the car wash, the total service time of all of the cars is $mN$, so we want $\var{mN}$. By linearity, we have that $\var{mN} = m^2\var{N} = m^2\lambda$. With $\lambda = 8$ and $m = 10$, the answer is $800$.

questions.title: Triangular Angle I
questions.problem: A right triangle is being formed with leg lengths $X$ and $Y$, where $X,Y \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Let $\theta$ be the measure of the (random) angle that is opposite of side $Y$. Find $\prob{\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{4}}$.
questions.solution: The key here is to keep in mind that we know the distributions of $X$ and $Y$, so we would want to relate $\theta$ to $X$ and $Y$. The way to do this is via trigonometric functions. In particular, we know that $\theta$ is opposite of $Y$ and adjacent to $X$, so $\tan(\theta) = \dfrac{Y}{X}$. We now need to get $\tan(\theta)$ inside our probability statement. Since $\tan(\theta)$ is strictly increasing in $\theta$ on $(0,\pi/2)$, we can apply the tangent function to both sides of the interior to obtain $\prob{\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{4}} = \prob{\tan(\theta) > \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} = \prob{\dfrac{Y}{X} > 1} = \prob{Y > X}$ Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, we have that they are exchangeable, so $\prob{Y > X} = \prob{X > Y}$ and the sum of the two terms is $1$, as $\prob{Y = X} = 0$ given that $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables. Therefore, $\prob{\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{4}} = \prob{Y > X} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.title: Triangular Angle II
questions.problem: A right triangle is being formed with leg lengths $X$ and $Y$, where $X,Y \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Let $\theta$ be the measure of the (random) angle that is opposite of side $Y$. Find $\prob{\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{3}}$. If necessary, round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: The key here is to keep in mind that we know the distributions of $X$ and $Y$, so we would want to relate $\theta$ to $X$ and $Y$. The way to do this is via trigonometric functions. In particular, we know that $\theta$ is opposite of $Y$ and adjacent to $X$, so $\tan(\theta)= \dfrac{Y}{X}$. We now need to get $\tan(\theta)$ inside our probability statement. Since $\tan(\theta)$ is strictly increasing in $\theta$ on $(0,\pi/2)$, we can apply the tangent function to both sides of the interior to obtain $\prob{\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{3}} = \prob{\tan(\theta) > \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)} = \prob{\dfrac{Y}{X} > \sqrt{3}} = \prob{Y > \sqrt{3}X}$ Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID $\unif{0}{1}$ random variables, we can just take the ratio of the area of the region of interest that is inside the joint support of $X$ and $Y$ and divide by the total area of the support. This is because of the uniformity. The total area of the square $[0,1] \times [0,1]$ in the plane is $1$. The region of interest that is inside our support is a triangle whose height is $1$ and base length is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so the area of this triangle is $\dfrac{1}{2}(1)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.289$, which is the probability we're after.

questions.title: Standard Deviation Sum
questions.problem: Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are two random variables with respective standard deviations $3$ and $4$. Find the standard deviation of $X+Y$ if $\corr{X}{Y} = -3/8$.
questions.solution: We know the variance of a sum formula $\var{X+Y} = \var{X} + \var{Y} + 2\cov{X}{Y}$. We can find $\var{X+Y}$ and then take the square root to get the standard deviation. We have that $\var{X} = 3^2 = 9$ and $\var{Y} = 4^2 = 16$, while $\cov{X}{Y} = \rho \sigma_X\sigma_Y = -\dfrac{3}{8} \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = -\dfrac{9}{2}$. Plugging these in, $\var{X+Y} = 9 + 16 - 9 = 16$ This means $\sigma_{X+Y} = \sqrt{\var{X+Y}} = 4$.

questions.title: Stoplight Switch I
questions.problem: A stoplight shows the colors red (stop!), yellow (slow down), and green (go). The colors occur in the sequence green $\rightarrow$ yellow $\rightarrow$ red and cycle back around. Green lights show for $60$ seconds before turning yellow for $10$ seconds. Afterwards, the light turns red for $30$ seconds, and the cycle repeats. If you observe the stoplight for a random $5$ second interval, find the probability that the stoplight changes colors.
questions.solution: Since the colors of the light cycle through the colors repeatedly, it is better to think about this problem in $100$ second cycles. In these cycles, $60$ are green, $10$ are yellow, and $30$ are red. Since we show up for a uniformly random $5$ second time interval, we need to find the proportion of time within the $100$ second cycle at which we can show up and observe a light change. We can show up within the last $5$ seconds of any color, as when we stay for $5$ seconds, we will observe a light change. This gives us $15$ seconds we can show up in, as there are $5$ seconds per light at which we can appear, and these appearance regions are completely disjoint. The regions are disjoint because all of the lights last more than $5$ seconds in duration. Therefore, the probability is just $\frac{15}{100} = \frac{3}{20}$.

questions.title: Greater Dice
questions.problem: You have two fair dice. One of them is $m-$sided, while the other is $n-$sided. The dice have respective values $1$ to $m$ and $1$ to $n$ on the sides. Suppose that $n > m$. Find the probability that the $n-$sided die shows a strictly larger value than the $m-$sided die. Solve this with $m = 20$ and $n = 30$.

questions.title: Sum of Primes I
questions.problem: Two distinct prime integers at most $20$ are uniformly at random selected. Find the probability that their sum is odd.
questions.solution: The primes at most $20$ are $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,$ and $19$. For the sum of two integers to be odd, it must be the case that one is odd and one is even. As the only even prime is $2$, this means that $2$ must be included in our selection of $2$ integers. As there are $8$ total prime integers that are at most $20$ and we are selecting $2$ of them, the probability that $2$ is one of the integers selected is $\frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$, as each would be equally likely to be selected and we select a subset of size $2$ from a set of size $8$.

questions.title: Sum of Primes II
questions.problem: Three distinct prime integers at most $20$ are uniformly at random selected. Find the probability that their sum is odd.
questions.solution: The primes at most $20$ are $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,$ and $19$. For the sum of three integers to be odd, it must be the case that either all three are odd or one is odd and two to be even. As the only even prime is $2$, the case of having $2$ evens is not possible. Therefore, we must select three odd integers. In other words, we just need to find the probability that $2$ is not selected. As there are $8$ total prime integers that are at most $20$ and we are selecting $3$ of them, the probability that $2$ is not selected is $\frac{5}{8}$, as each would be equally likely to be selected and we select a subset of size $3$ from a set of size $8$.

questions.title: Wild Card Room
questions.problem: Lewis is trapped in a room with $4$ doors. He selects a door uniformly at random. Two of the doors have paths of lengths $5$ and $7$ miles that lead to freedom. The other two doors have paths of lengths $2$ and $4$ miles that lead back to the room Lewis is currently in. If Lewis selects a door uniformly at random in each step, find the expected amount of miles that he travels before reaching freedom?
questions.solution: This is a classic Law of Total Expectation problem, as Lewis's expected value is very dependent on the path he selects. In particular, let $D$ be the distance he travels before reaching freedom. To compute $\ev{D}$, we should condition on what path he selects on the first trial. Let $P_i$ be the event that Lewis selects the path of length $i$ miles on the first trial. By Law of Total Expectation, $\ev{D} = \ev{D \mid P_2}\prob{P_2} + \ev{D \mid P_4}\prob{P_4} + \ev{D \mid P_5}\prob{P_5} + \ev{D \mid P_7}\prob{P_7}$. The paths of length $5$ and $7$ lead to freedom immediately, so $\ev{D \mid P_5} = 5$ and $\ev{D \mid P_7} = 7$. The paths of length $2$ and $4$ lead back to where he was before. Therefore, we can say that $\ev{D \mid P_2} = 2 + \ev{D}$ and $\ev{D \mid P_4} = 4 + \ev{D}$. This is because of the fact that Lewis is in the exact same spot as he was before, but now he has traveled $2$ (or $4$) miles already and faces the exact same scenario as when he started. Plugging these in with all of the probabilities equal to $1/4$ (each path is equally likely) $\ev{D} = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (2 + \ev{D}) + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (4 + \ev{D}) + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 5 + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 7 \implies \ev{D} = 9$.

questions.title: Carpenter Errors I
questions.problem: Nick makes rugs. The number of errors in rugs that Nick creates follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$ per square yard. Find the probability that a $n-$square yard rug that Nick makes has no errors when $n = 2$ and $\lambda = 3$. The answer is in the form $e^{-a}$ for some $a$. Find $a$.
questions.solution: The key property to use here is the scaling of Poissons. In particular, each of the $n$ square yards in the rug has a number of errors that is distributed as $\poisson{\lambda}$ IID. If $X_i$ is the number of errors in yard $i$, $1 \leq i \leq n$, then $T = X_1 + \dots + X_n$ gives the total number of errors in the rug. Since each of the $X_i \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ IID, $T \sim \poisson{n\lambda}$. Therefore, the probability there are no errors in the rug is just saying $\prob{T = 0} = \dfrac{(\lambda n)^0}{0!}e^{-\lambda n} = e^{-\lambda n}$. With our specified values here $\prob{T = 0} = e^{-6}$, so $a = 6$.

questions.title: Three Die Sum
questions.problem: Find the probability that sum of the upfaces is $10$ when three standard fair $6-$sided dice are rolled.
questions.solution: The easiest way is to count the combinations that sum to $10$ and count the number of distinct permutations that correspond to each. We have to consider each separately because not all of the combinations that yield a sum of $10$ have the same number of permutations onto the dice. These combinations are: $(6,2,2), (6,1,3), (5,1,4), (5,2,3), (4,4,2), (4,3,3)$. Note that there are $6^3 = 216$ total outcomes of three distinct dice because each individual die has $6$ outcomes. We now need to count the number permutations that correspond to each of these arrangements. The number of permutations that correspond to each combination above is, respectively, $3,6,6,6,3,3$. In the case that all the values are distinct, there are $3! = 6$ ways to arrange them distinctly onto the dice. If there is a repeated value, then we can choose the die that has the one distinct value in $3$ ways, and then the other two dice will have the repeated value. Adding all of these up, we get a sum of $27$ total outcomes that yield a sum of $10$, so the probability of a sum of $10$ is $\frac{27}{216} = \frac{1}{8}$.

questions.title: 60 Heads I
questions.problem: A fair coin is flipped $100$ times. Using the Central Limit Theorem without continuity correction, estimate the probability that at least $60$ heads are obtained. The answer is in the form $\Phi(a)$ for some $a$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution CDF. Find $a$.
questions.solution: We know that the number of heads that appear in $100$ trials is $N \sim \binomial{100}{1/2}$. Computing $\prob{N \geq 60}$ explicitly is quite difficult, as there is no exact way to evaluate the sum nicely. Therefore, it is advantageous to use the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to approximate this. The question then becomes why can we use CLT? Note that if $X \sim \binomial{n}{p}$, then $X = I_1 + \dots + I_n$, where $I_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$ IID. Since we can view $N$ as a sum of $100$ IID random variables, CLT applies here. By the properties of the Binomial distribution, $\ev{N} = 50$ and $\var{N} = 25$. Therefore, $\prob{N \geq 60} = \prob{\dfrac{N-50}{5} \geq \dfrac{60-50}{2}} \approx \prob{Z \geq 2} = 1 - \Phi(2) = \Phi(-2)$. CLT comes in the step where we do the approximation of the probability by $Z \sim N(0,1)$. This means $a = -2$ is the answer.

questions.title: Conic Cylinder
questions.problem: A uniformly random point $(X,Y,Z)$ is selected from the interior of a cylinder whose base has radius $r$ and has height $h$. Assume the the base of the cylinder is centered at $(0,0,0)$. Find the probability that the point also lies within the cone whose base and height is the same as the cylinder.
questions.solution: The volume of a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$ is $\pi r^2 h$. The volume of a cone with radius $r$ and height $h$ is $\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$. Since the point $(X,Y,Z)$ is selected uniformly at random from the cylinder, the probability that it lies in some sub-region inside the cylinder is just the ratio of the volume of that sub-region to the volume of the total region. In this case, since we know the volumes of the sub-region (the cone) and the full region (the cylinder), the probability the point lies inside the cone is $\dfrac{\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h}{\pi r^2 h} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.title: Introductory Gamma
questions.problem: Suppose that $X \sim \gam{3}{3}$ under the shape-scale parameterization. Compute $\ev{X^5}$.
questions.solution: To compute this, we can write out the LOTUS integral as a standard first step. This gives us $\ev{X^5} = \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} x^5 \cdot \dfrac{x^{3-1}e^{-x/3}}{3^3\Gamma(3)}dx = \dfrac{1}{3^3\Gamma(3)} \int_0^{\infty} x^{8-1}e^{-x/3}dx$. This remaining integral is in the form of a Gamma distribution as well, as it has $x$ to some point and an exponential term. In particular, by looking at the parameters, we can see this is a $\gam{8}{3}$ distribution without the normalization constant $8^3 \Gamma(3)$. Multiplying and dividing by this, we get $\dfrac{3^8\Gamma(8)}{3^3 \Gamma(3)}\int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{x^{8-1}e^{-x/3}}{3^8\Gamma(8)}dx = 3^5 \cdot \dfrac{\Gamma(8)}{\Gamma(3)} = 3^5 \cdot 2520 = 612360$. The integral evaluates to $1$ because it is the integral of a $\gam{8}{3}$ PDF over it's entire support. A similar argument can be used to more generally find $\ev{X^k}$ for $X \sim \gam{a}{b}$ as $\dfrac{b^{a+k} \Gamma(a+k)}{b^a \Gamma(a)} = b^k \cdot \dfrac{\Gamma(a+k)}{\Gamma(a)}$.

questions.title: Red Cube I
questions.problem: A $n \times n \times n$ cube is initially white in color. The faces of the cube are painted red and the cube is then cut into $n^3$ $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cubes. One cube is selected uniformly at random. Find the expected number of red faces of this cube when $n = 12$.
questions.solution: When the faces of the large cube are painted red, $6n^2$ faces of the tiny cubes are painted red, as there are $n^2$ faces on each side of the tiny cubes that would be painted red. Since the tiny cube is selected uniformly at random, we can just divide the number of red faces by number of cubes to find the expected number of red faces of the cube we select. In particular, this ratio is $\frac{6n^2}{n^3} = \frac{6}{n}$. With $n = 12$, the answer is $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.title: Red Cube II
questions.problem: A $n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3$ rectangular prism is initially white in color. The faces of the rectangular prism are painted red and is then cut into $n_1n_2n_3$ $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cubes. One cube is selected uniformly at random. Find the expected number of red faces of this cube when $n_1 = 8, n_2 = 10, n_3 = 12$.
questions.solution: When the faces of the rectangular prism are painted red, $2(n_1n_2 + n_2n_3 + n_1n_3)$ faces of the tiny cubes are painted red. This is because there are two faces of area $n_1n_2,$ two faces of area $n_2n_3$, and two faces of area $n_1n_3$. Since the tiny cube is selected uniformly at random, we can just divide the number of red faces by number of cubes to find the expected number of red faces of the cube we select. In particular, this ratio is $\dfrac{2(n_1n_3 + n_2n_3 + n_1n_2)}{n_1n_2n_3} = \dfrac{2}{n_1} + \dfrac{2}{n_2} + \dfrac{2}{n_3}$. With the values at hand, the answer is $\dfrac{2}{8} + \dfrac{2}{10} + \dfrac{2}{12} = \dfrac{37}{60}$.

questions.title: Minimizing Variance
questions.problem: Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be independent random variables with respective variances $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$. Find the value of $0 \leq c \leq 1$ that minimizes $\var{cX_1 + (1-c)X_2}$ when $\sigma_1^2 = 16$ and $\sigma_2^2 = 9$.
questions.solution: To minimize $\var{cX_1 + (1-c)X_2}$, we need to be able to treat this as a function in $c$. To attempt to make this a function in $c$, we can use the linearity of variance on independent random variables and note that we can pull out constants in front of variances with a square. Therefore, we want to minimize $f(c) = \var{cX_1  + (1-c)X_2} = \var{cX_1} + \var{(1-c)X_2} = c^2 \sigma_1^2 + (1-c)^2\sigma_2^2$. We can take the derivative in $c$ and set it equal to $0$ to maximize. By the chain rule, $f'(c) = 2c\sigma_1^2 - 2(1-c)\sigma_2^2 = 2c(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2) - 2\sigma_2^2 = 0$. To solve for $c$, divide by $2$ and isolate to get $c^* = \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}$. With the particular values here, $c^* = \dfrac{9}{25}$.

questions.title: Friendly Beef
questions.problem: Ian has $n \geq 2$ friends, of which he will invite $2 \leq k \leq n$ of them to a party. However, two of the friends have beef and refuse to attend together. How many ways can Ian choose a guest lists given this constraint with $n = 10$ and $k = 6$?
questions.solution: The easiest way to approach this would be to count the total number of ways Ian can invite $k$ friends and remove those that have both attending. This is complementary counting. Ian can select $k$ guests to invite in $\binom{n}{k}$ ways, as he picks $k$ from $n$ and order is irrelevant. Now, we must remove those guest lists that have both of the two people that dislike each other in the list. Fix both of those two people in the invite list. Ian now must select $k-2$ more people to invite from the remaining $n-2$ people. This can be done in $\binom{n-2}{k-2}$ ways. Therefore, subtracting these out, we have $\binom{n}{k} - \binom{n-2}{k-2}$ as the answer. With $n = 10$ and $k = 6$, the answer is $140$.

questions.title: Color Mix
questions.problem: How many distinct ways are there to arrange $n_1$ red balls, $n_2$ green balls, and $n_3$ yellow balls in a line? Assume $n_1 = 6, n_2 = 5,$ and $n_3 = 4$.
questions.solution: This is a classic anagrams problem, as you are assigning a label to the $n_1 + n_2 + n_3$ spaces in the line. In particular, if we view the $i$th letter in a string of length $n_1 + n_2 + n_3$ as the color of the ball in the $i$th position, then each arrangement of the balls in a line is exactly some distinct anagram of $R\dots RG\dots GY\dots Y$, where there are $n_1$ $R$s, $n_2$ $G$s, and $n_3$ $Y$s. By the anagrams paradigm, there are $\binom{n_1 + n_2 + n_3}{n_1, n_2, n_3} = \dfrac{(n_1 + n_2 + n_3)!}{n_1!n_2!n_3!}$ distinct ways to create an anagram of that string, and hence the number of distinct arrangements of the balls in the lines. With our specified values, the answer is $630630$.

questions.title: Prior Event I
questions.problem: Suppose you simulate some experiment repeatedly. Let $A$ and $B$ be disjoint events that can occur on each trial of the experiment such that $\prob{A} = p_1$, $\prob{B} = p_2$, and $0 < p_1 + p_2 \leq 1$. The simulation ends when either $A$ or $B$ occurs on some trial. Find the probability that $A$ occurred when $p_1 = 1/3$ and $p_2 = 1/6$.
questions.solution: The probability we are looking to compute here is $\prob{A \mid A \cup B}$, as we know either $A$ or $B$ occurred to end the experiment, so we want to find the probability that $A$ was the one that occurred and ended the experiment. Given this is a conditional probability statement, it would be best to use the definition of conditional probability here. Doing this, $\prob{A \mid A \cup B} = \dfrac{\prob{A \cap (A \cup B)}}{\prob{A \cup B}}$. As $A \subseteq A \cup B$, we can say $\prob{A \cap (A \cup B)} = \prob{A} = p_1$. For the denominator, since $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, we have that $\prob{A \cup B} = \prob{A} + \prob{B} = p_1 + p_2$. Therefore, the answer is $\dfrac{p_1}{p_1 + p_2}$. With our specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.title: Prior Die Sum I
questions.problem: Jeffrey is rolling a pair of standard fair $6-$sided dice until he obtains a sum of either $3$ or $5$ on the upfaces. Find the probability Jeffrey rolls a sum of $5$.
questions.solution: Since we are looking at the probability that an event occurs before some other event disjoint to it, the paradigm of "Prior Event I" is particularly appealing to solve this problem. Clearly, the events of rolling a sum of $3$ and a sum of $5$ are disjoint on a given trial. By writing out the PMF table of the sum of two dice, sums of $3$ and $5$ occur with respective probabilities $\dfrac{2}{36} = \dfrac{1}{18}$ and $\dfrac{4}{36} = \dfrac{1}{9}$. These sum to at most $1$, so the result of "Prior Event I" yields that the probability of obtaining a sum of $5$ before a sum of $3$ is $\dfrac{1/9}{1/9 + 1/18} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.title: Collector's Sculpture
questions.problem: You are an art collector bidding for a rare sculpture. You know that the value of the sculpture is uniformly at random somewhere between $\$0$ and $\$N$. If your bid is greater than the value of the sculpture, you win and sell it to an art museum at a price of $1.5$ times the true value. What is the optimal price to bid when $N = 1000$?
questions.solution: If you lose the auction, nothing happens, so we disregard this case. Suppose you win the auction and pay $x$ for the sculpture. We know that the distribution of the true price of the sculpture is $\unif{0}{N}$, so given that the sculpture is worth at most $x$, the true price is now $\unif{0}{x}$. The mean price of the sculpture given you purchased it for price $x$ is $x/2$. Therefore, the mean price you would sell it to the museum for would be $1.5 \cdot x/2 = 0.75x < x$. This means that, on average, you are losing money when you buy this sculpture! Therefore, you should not buy it and bet $\$0$, regardless of what the value of $N$ is.

questions.title: Parity Difference
questions.problem: You have a fair standard $6-$sided die and play the following game: You are paid the upface of every roll. If you roll an even value, the game is over. If you roll an odd value, you flip a fair coin. If it lands on tails, the game is over. If it lands on heads, you roll again and repeat the same coin flip process after your roll. Note that you do receive a payout that includes the roll the game ends. Find the expected payout from this game.
questions.solution: Let $T$ be the total payout. Let $E$ be the event that the first roll is even. By the Law of Total Expectation, $\ev{T} = \ev{\ev{T \mid E}} = \ev{T \mid E}\prob{E} + \ev{T \mid E^c}\prob{E^c}$. There are $3$ even values and $3$ odd values on the die, so $\prob{E} = \prob{E^c} = 1/2$. If the first roll is even, the game ends immediately with expected payout $\dfrac{2+4+6}{3} = 4$, so there are $3$ equally likely even outcomes and $\ev{T \mid E} = 4$. If the first roll is odd, the expected value of that roll is $\frac{1+3+5}{3} = 3$. Then we flip a coin: with probability $1/2$ the game ends, and with probability $1/2$ we continue with the same expected future payout $T$. So $\ev{T \mid E^c} = 3 + \frac{1}{2}T$. Putting it together: $\ev{T} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \ev{3 + \frac{T}{2}}$. Solving, $\ev{T} = 14/3$.

questions.title: Cubic Packing
questions.problem: Let $1 \leq k \leq n$ be integers. In how many ways can a $k \times k \times k$ cube be placed inside a $n \times n \times n$ cube? Assume that cubes can only be aligned at integer positions. Report the answer when $k = 4$ and $n = 12$.
questions.solution: Since the smaller cubes can only be aligned at integer positions, the key is that each $k \times k \times k$ cube that can fit inside the larger $n \times n \times n$ cube is uniquely determined by its starting point on each axis. Therefore, we need to find the number of ways that the smaller cubes can be aligned per axis. Since the cube is symmetric in all dimensions (all sides have the same length), all that needs to be computed is the number of starting positions on one side. We can observe the pattern quickly with some small numbers. If $k = 1$, there are $n$ possible starting positions. If $k = 2$, there are $n-1$ possible positions (any but the bottom possible position will be contained in the cube). More generally, we can see that it will be $n-k+1$ possible positions per side, as each dimension reduces the number of possible positions by $1$. Therefore, the total number of cubes that can be fit is $(n-k+1)^3$. With the numbers in the question, the answer is $9^3 = 729$.

questions.title: Scheduling Appointments
questions.problem: You have $n \geq 2$ students that you need to see $k$ times each over the next month. You have $nk$ total appointment spots available for students to select from. However, one of the students can't attend in the first time slot. How many different ways can these students be scheduled when $n = 4$ and $k = 3$.
questions.solution: The easiest way to compute this is to count the total number of ways that the students can be scheduled and multiply by the probability that the student in question does not get scheduled in the first time slot. This is because each arrangement is equally likely, so we can count the total number of arrangements and multiply by the proportion of those arrangements that satisfy our condition. Label the students $1-n$. Each arrangement of the students in the appointment slots corresponds to an anagram of the string $1\dots 1 \dots n \dots n$, where there are $k$ repetitions of each number to correspond to the $k$ times each student must schedule appointments. Therefore, there are $\binom{nk}{k,k,\dots,k} = \dfrac{(nk)!}{(k!)^n}$ total ways to arrange the numbers on the $nk$ blanks in distinct ways by a simple anagrams argument. Now, we need to compute the probability that the student in question (for simplicity, say student $1$) is not scheduled in the first time slot. As all $n$ students are equally likely to be scheduled in the first time slot, there is a probability $\frac{n-1}{n}$ that student $1$ is not scheduled in the first time slot, as there are $n-1$ other students that are not student $1$. Therefore, the total number arrangements that can be formed is $\dfrac{n-1}{n} \cdot \dfrac{(nk)!}{(k!)^n}$. With the specific values in the question, the answer is $277200$.

questions.title: Sublime Snowman
questions.problem: A snowman is formed by placing three spherical snowballs of radii $r_1 > r_2 > r_3$ inches on top of one another largest to smallest. Assume that every point on the surface of each snowball is visible. A uniformly random point is selected on the surface of the snowman. Find the probability that this point is at most $2r_1 + r_2$ inches off the ground when $r_1 = 10, r_2 = 8,$ and $r_3 = 6$.
questions.solution: Since the point is uniformly at random on the surface of the snowman, we can take ratios of surfaces areas to compute the probability. The total surface area of all three snowballs is $4\pi (r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2)$. Now, we need to find the surface area of the region at most a height $2r_1 + r_2$ above the ground. Since the radius of the largest snowball is $r_1$, the height of it is $2r_1$. The center of the second snowball would a radius $r_2$ above the top of the first snowball, so the points that are at most $2r_1 + r_2$ inches off the ground are those that are on the surface of the bottom snowball and on the bottom half of the middle snowball. This corresponds to a surface area of $4\pi r_1^2 + 2\pi r_2^2$. The coefficient of $2\pi$ for the middle comes from the fact that we consider only half of the total surface area of the second snowball. Therefore, the probability of our event is just the ratio of these surface areas, which is $\dfrac{2r_1^2 + r_2^2}{2(r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_3^2)}$. With our specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{33}{50}$.

questions.title: Weight Arrangement
questions.problem: There are $6$ weights of masses $1,2,3,4,5,$ and $6$ grams. $3$ weights are randomly put on each side of a scale. Find the probability that the side with the $6$ gram weight is heavier.
questions.solution: To compute this, we can fix the side the $6$ gram weight lies on arbitrarily, as it is equally likely to be on either side. Once we do this, we need to pick $2$ more weights to go on the same side as the $6$ gram weight. Once the weights on the same side are confirmed, there are exactly $3$ weights to go on the opposing side. There are $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ ways to pick the two other weights to be on the same side as the $6$ gram weight, so there are $10$ total distinct arrangements. The sum of all the weights is $21$ grams, so the side with the $6$ gram weight on it must be at least $11$ grams to be heavier. For this to be true, the sum of the other two weights must be at least $5$ grams. The only time this doesn't happen is if the two weights are $1$ and $2$ grams or $1$ and $3$ grams. Therefore, the probability the side with the $6$ gram weight is lighter is $\dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{1}{5}$, meaning it is heavier with probability $\dfrac{4}{5}$.

questions.title: Prime Dice
questions.problem: You have two fair $6-$sided dice before you. The sides of the dice have the integers $2,3,5,7,11,$ and $13$ on their sides. Find the probability that the sum of these two dice is a prime integer.
questions.solution: Prime integers are odd, so to get a prime integer as the sum, you must have the value $2$ appear to make the sum odd. If not, the remaining numbers are all odd, so the sum of two odds would be even and hence not prime. The pairs of values that can be obtained to get a sum that is prime are $(2,3), (2,5),$ and $(2,11)$. There are $2$ permutations of these values to the dice per outcome, as the values are distinct, so this yields $6$ total outcomes that result in a prime sum out of $6^2 = 36$ total outcomes of the dice, so the answer is $\dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.

questions.title: Reflip
questions.problem: $4$ fair coins are flipped. You receive a payout (in dollars) equal to the number of heads that appear. However, you also have the option to re-flip all $4$ coins at once one time for $\$1$. Assuming optimal gameplay, find your expected payout on this game.
questions.solution: The optimal strategy is to flip again precisely when the expected number heads that will appear by flipping again is larger than the number of heads that appear on the first trial. Since there are $4$ coins that are fair, the number of coins that appear among the $4$ coins is $X \sim \binomial{4}{1/2}$. This has mean $\ev{X} = 4 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 2$. This yields an expected payout of $\$2$. If you flip again, you must pay $\$1$ and you receive an average payout of $\$2$, so this means that the expected payout by flipping again is $\$1$. Thus, the optimal strategy is to flip again only when there are no heads that appear. The payout is dependent upon the number of heads that appear on the first trial. Therefore, we should condition on $X$ as defined above. If $P$ is the payout of this strategy, we have $\ev{P} = \ev{\ev{P \mid X}} = \sum_{k=0}^{4} \ev{P \mid X = k}\prob{X = k}$ If $X = 0$, $\ev{P \mid X = 0} = 1$, as you flip again. Otherwise, you keep the heads appearing on the first trial, so $\ev{P \mid X = k} = k$. Plugging these in, $\ev{P} = 1 \cdot \prob{X = 0} + \sum_{k=1}^4 k\prob{X = k} = 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{16} + 1 \cdot \dfrac{4}{16} + 2 \cdot \dfrac{6}{16} + 3 \cdot \dfrac{4}{16} + 4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{33}{16}$

questions.title: Absolute Uniform Difference
questions.problem: Suppose $X,Y \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Compute $\prob{X+Y \geq 3|X-Y|}$.
questions.solution: Sketching this region out in the plane is helpful. To do so, we can split the absolute value up into two expressions. The event $\{3|X-Y| \leq X+Y\} = \{3(X-Y) \leq X+Y\}\cap\{3(X-Y) \leq -(X+Y)\}$. Rearranging the expressions for an event in terms of $Y$ yields $\{Y \geq X/2\}\cap \{Y \leq 2X\}$. Sketching the lines $y = 2x$ and $y = x/2$ on the plane and the support, we see that the region is diamond-shaped and difficult to compute the exact area of. However, the complement of this region consists of two identical triangles. Therefore, the complement of this probability is easier to compute. The area of each triangle is $1/4$, as the two sides are of lengths $1$ and $1/2$. As there are two triangles in the complement, the total area of the complement is $1/2$. Since the total area of the support is $1$, the probability of the complement of our event of interest is $1/2$, so the probability of our event is $1/2$ as well.

questions.title: Maximin
questions.problem: Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete uniform IID over the set $S_n = \{-n,-n+1,\dots, n-1,n\} = [-n,n] \cap \mathbb{Z}$. Find $\prob{\max(0,X) = \min(0,Y)}$ when $n = 15$.
questions.solution: For the max to be equal to the min, it must be the case that $Y$ is non-negative and $X$ is non-positive. If both are positive, then the minimum term will be $0$, while the maximum is positive, and likewise with both being negative. We can't have $Y$ non-positive, as $\max(0,X) \geq 0$ always. There are $n+1$ integers that are non-positive $(-n,\dots, 0)$ and $n+1$ that are non-negative $(0,\dots, n)$ in the set. There are $2n+1$ total integers in the set. Therefore, the probability of having one non-positive and one non-negative is $2 \cdot \dfrac{n+1}{2n+1} \cdot \dfrac{n+1}{2n+1} = \dfrac{2(n+1)^2}{(2n+1)^2}$ With $n = 15$, the answer is $\dfrac{256}{961}$.

questions.title: Fresh Bagel
questions.problem: You have a devious older brother that wants to antagonize you. You are trying to make breakfast, and there are $N \geq 1$ fresh bagels and $N$ expired bagels. You can arrange them into two boxes however you would like. Afterwards, your brother selects a box at random and a bagel uniformly at random from the selected box. Afterwards, he takes the rest away. Suppose you are hungry and really like fresh bagels, so you want to maximize the probability of your brother drawing out a fresh bagel. Under an optimal strategy, what is the probability of your brother drawing a fresh bagel when $N = 100$?
questions.solution: A baseline strategy would be placing all $N$ fresh bagels in one boxes and all $N$ expired bagels in the other. This yields a $50\%$ chance of receiving a fresh bagel. However, note that you only really need one bagel in the box of fresh bagels to guarantee you receiving a fresh bagel when that box is selected. No matter if there are $N$ fresh bagels or $1$ fresh bagel in that box, you will always receive a fresh bagel from it when that box is selected. Therefore, you should instead put $1$ fresh bagel in one of the boxes and the remaining $2N-1$ bagels ($N$ expired and $N-1$ fresh) in the other box. Let $B_1$ be the event of selecting the box with the $1$ fresh bagel and $B_2$ be the event of selecting the box with the other $2N-1$ bagels. Lastly, let $F$ be the event that the bagel drawn is fresh. We have that $\prob{F} = \prob{F \mid B_1}\prob{B_1} + \prob{F \mid B_2}\prob{B_2}$ Since your brother selects uniformly at random, $\prob{B_1} = \prob{B_2} =1/2$. Given that your brother selects the box with $1$ fresh bagel, he will always draw the fresh bagel, so $\prob{F \mid B_1} = 1$. If your brother selects the box with the other $2N-1$ bagels, exactly $N-1$ of those are fresh, so $\prob{F \mid B_2} = \frac{N-1}{2N-1}$. This yields $\prob{F} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{N-1}{2N-1} = \dfrac{3N-2}{4N-2}$ With $N = 100$, the answer is $\dfrac{149}{199}$.

questions.title: Even Permutations
questions.problem: Define $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$. Find the number of permutations of $[10]$ that alternate between even and odd values.
questions.solution: If $n$ is even, then $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$. The integers $1,3,\dots, 2k-1$ are all odd, which is $k$ odd integers in the set, meaning the other $k$ integers in the set are even. A permutation of $[n]$ can be imagined as $n$ blanks, where we must arrange the integers $1-n$ on the blanks. To have no two odd integers adjacent, it must be the case that the integers are arranged in the following forms: $OEOE\dots OEOE$ or $EOEO\dots EOEO$, where $E$ is an even integer and $O$ is an odd integer. If we move one of the even integers ($E$) somewhere else, there will be two consecutive odds. The odd integers can be placed in the spots labelled $O$ in $k!$ ways, as there are $k$ total spots and $k$ odd integers. Similarly, the $k$ even integers can be permuted into the $k$ spots labelled $E$ in $k!$ ways. As there are $2$ arrangements, we multiply by $2$. By the multiplication principle, the answer is $2 \cdot k! \cdot k! = 2(k!)^2$, where $n = 2k$. In the case of $n = 10 = 2 \cdot 5$, the answer is $2(5!)^2 = 28800$.

questions.title: Longer Piece I
questions.problem: Suppose that you have a loaf of bread that is $1$ meter in length. You slice the piece of bread at a uniformly random point along it's length, creating $2$ slices. Find the expected length (in meters) of the longer piece of bread.
questions.solution: To solve this, we need to set up a random variable that represents the length of the longer piece. To do this, we need to model the point at which the loaf is cut. This can be done in many different ways, but the simplest is to just measure distance from an endpoint of the loaf. Let $X$ be the distance from the left endpoint of the loaf that it's cut at. We know that $X \sim \unif{0}{1}$ by the description in the question. The longer piece is of length $Y = \max(X,1-X)$. In other words, $Y = 1-X$ for $X \geq 1/2$ and $Y = 1-X$ for $X < 1/2$. The easiest thing to do would be to compute $\prob{Y \leq y}$, as we are taking the maximum of two random variables. We know that $Y \geq1/2$, as for the sum of the two lengths of the slices to be $1$, one of the two pieces must be of length $1/2$ or more. For $y \geq 1/2$, $\prob{Y \leq y} = \prob{\max(X,1-X) \leq y} = \prob{X \leq y, 1-X \leq y} = \prob{X \leq y, X \geq 1-y} = \prob{1-y \leq X \leq y}$ The second equality comes from saying that if $\max(x,y) \leq z$, then it must be true that $x \leq z$ and $y \leq z$. This last probability is easy to compute, as we know the distribution of $X$. The event $\{1-y \leq X \leq y\}$ is an interval of length $2y-1$ in a total interval of length $1$, so since $X$ is uniform, $\prob{Y \leq y} = 2y-1$ for $1/2 \leq y \leq 1$. By taking a derivative, the PDF of $Y$ is $f_y(y) = 2$ for $1/2 \leq y \leq 1$, meaning that $Y \sim \unif{1/2}{1}$, as it has a constant PDF on this interval. This means that $\ev{Y} = \dfrac{1+1/2}{2} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

questions.title: Longer Piece II
questions.problem: Suppose that you have a loaf of bread that is $1$ meter in length. You slice the piece of bread at a uniformly random point along it's length, creating $2$ slices. Find the variance of the length (in meters) of the longer piece of bread.
questions.solution: The distribution of $Y$, the length of the larger piece of bread, was found in the first part to be $\unif{1/2}{1}$. This means we can use the known formulas for variance to compute this. Namely, $\var{Y} = \dfrac{(1 - 1/2)^2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{48}$.

questions.title: Carpenter Errors II
questions.problem: Nick makes rugs. The number of errors in rugs that Nick creates follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$ per square yard. Find the expected number of errors in a $n-$square yard rug that Nick makes when $n = 2$ and $\lambda = 3$.
questions.solution: The key property to use here is the scaling of Poissons. In particular, each of the $n$ square yards in the rug has a number of errors that is distributed as $\poisson{\lambda}$ IID. If $X_i$ is the number of errors in yard $i$, $1 \leq i \leq n$, then $T = X_1 + \dots + X_n$ gives the total number of errors in the rug. Since each of the $X_i \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ IID, $T \sim \poisson{n\lambda}$. Therefore, $\ev{T} = n\lambda$. In this case, the answer would be $6$.

questions.title: Carpenter Errors III
questions.problem: Nick makes rugs. The number of errors in rugs that Nick creates follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$ per square yard. Find the variance in number of errors in a $n-$square yard rug that Nick makes when $n = 2$ and $\lambda = 3$.
questions.solution: The key property to use here is the scaling of Poissons. In particular, each of the $n$ square yards in the rug has a number of errors that is distributed as $\poisson{\lambda}$ IID. If $X_i$ is the number of errors in yard $i$, $1 \leq i \leq n$, then $T = X_1 + \dots + X_n$ gives the total number of errors in the rug. Since each of the $X_i \sim \poisson{\lambda}$ IID, $T \sim \poisson{n\lambda}$. Therefore, $\var{T} = n\lambda$. In this case, the answer would be $6$.

questions.title: Random Fixed Point
questions.problem: Let $f_n: [n] \rightarrow [n]$ be a uniformly random function selected from the set of all functions from $[n]$ to $[n]$, where $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Let $F_n$ be the number of fixed points the random $f_n$ selected. What is the limiting distribution of $F_n$? In other words, for any non-negative integer $k$, what does $\prob{F_n = k}$ converge to? Report $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \prob{F_n = 3}$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: To find the limiting distribution of $F_n$, it would be good to find the distribution of $F_n$ for a fixed $n$. $F_n$ counts the number of fixed points of the function. Each $1 \leq i \leq n$ maps to itself with probability $\dfrac{1}{n}$, as each value $i$ can map to any value $1-n$ uniformly at random, as we are considering all functions $[n] \rightarrow [n]$. Furthermore, the events of $i$ being a fixed point, $1 \leq i \leq n$, are independent, as there are no restrictions on how many times a value can be mapped to. For example, in a permutation, those events wouldn't be independent, as every value is mapped to exactly once. However, as we have $n$ independent events that each have probability $1/n$ of occurring and we are looking for the count of how many of those events occur (since $F_n$ counts number of fixed points), we can conclude that $F_n \sim \binomial{n}{1/n}$. By the Poisson Limit Theorem, we can conclude that $F_n$ converges to a Poisson distribution with parameter $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} n \cdot \dfrac{1}{n} = 1$. In other words, $F_n \implies F$, where $F \sim \poisson{1}$. With the specified values, the answer is $0.061$.

questions.title: Normal Practice
questions.problem: Suppose that $X \sim N(60,9)$. Find $\prob{X > 63}$. The answer is in the form $\Phi(a)$ for some real $a$.
questions.solution: To compute this probability, we need to standardize $X$. This allows us to use the standard normal CDF. Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, we get $\prob{X > 63} = \prob{\dfrac{X-60}{3} > \dfrac{63-60}{3}} = \prob{\dfrac{X-60}{3} > 1} = 1 - \prob{\dfrac{X-60}{3} \leq 1} = 1 - \Phi(1) = \Phi(-1)$ We know that $\dfrac{X-60}{3} \sim N(0,1)$ by standardization, so we then complement and use the definition of the CDF.

questions.title: Exponential Maxima
questions.problem: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots \sim \exponential{\lambda}$ IID. Let $p_n = \prob{M_n \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}}$, where $M_n = \max(X_1,\dots,X_n)$. Compute $\displaystyle \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} p_n$ when $\lambda  = 4$. The answer is in the form $e^{-a}$ for some $a$. Find $a$.
questions.solution: For a fixed $n$, computing $p_n$ would give the function we actually need to take a limit of, so it's best to start there. We have that $p_n = \prob{M_n \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}}$. Recall that $\prob{\max(X_1,\dots,X_n) \leq x} = \prob{X_1 \leq x,\dots, X_n \leq x}$, as the maximum of $n$ values being at most $x$ implies all of the $n$ values are at most $x$. We use this to say $\prob{M_n \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}} = \prob{X_1 \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda},\dots, X_n \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}} = \prob{X_1 \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}} \dots \prob{X_n \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}} = \left(\prob{X_1 \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}}\right)^n$ The first equality is by the fact above. The second equality comes from the independence of $X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n$. The last equality comes from the fact that the random variables are all identically distributed. Since $X_1 \sim \exponential{\lambda}$, the CDF of $X_1$ is $\prob{X_1 \leq x} = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x > 0$. Plugging in $x = \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}$ into it yields $\prob{M_n \leq \dfrac{\ln(n)}{\lambda}} = \left(1 - e^{-\ln(n)}\right)^n = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n$. This above function looks familiar, as the limit definition of $e^x$ is $e^x = \displaystyle \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \left(1 + \dfrac{x}{n}\right)^n$, so with $x=-1$, we get that $p_n$ converges to $e^{-1}$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$.

questions.title: Coin Swap I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play a game with a coin with probability $0 < p \leq 1$ of heads per flip. Alice starts with the coin and flips it. The game stops when someone flips a heads. If either player flip a tails, they pass the coin to the other player for them to flip. Find the probability that Alice is the winner when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: Alice's probability of winning is dependent on what happens in the first turn. Therefore, we should use the Law of Total Probability to condition on what happens on the first flip of each player. Let $a$ be the probability that Alice wins the game. With probability $p$, she flips a head on her first turn and immediately wins. Otherwise, she flips a tails with probability $1-p$. In this case, for Alice to have another shot at winning, Bob must also flip a tails, which occurs with probability $1-p$ as well. Afterwards, the coin would go back to Alice, and the probability of her winning would still be $a$, as the coin just performed one cycle and past outcomes don't influence future outcomes of the coin. Thus, we have the equation $a = p + (1-p)^2a \iff a = \dfrac{p}{1-(1-p)^2} = \dfrac{1}{2-p}$ With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $\dfrac{3}{5}$.

questions.title: Coin Swap II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play a game with a coin with probability $0 < p \leq 1$ of heads per flip. Alice starts with the coin and flips it. The game stops when someone flips a heads. If either player flip a tails, they pass the coin to the other player for their turn. However, Bob receives two flips on his turns, while Alice only receives one. Find the value of $p$ such that Alice and Bob are equally likely to win. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Alice's probability of winning is dependent on what happens in the first turn. Therefore, we should use the Law of Total Probability to condition on what happens on the first turn of each player. Let $a$ be the probability that Alice wins the game. With probability $p$, she flips a head on her first turn and immediately wins. Otherwise, she flips a tails with probability $1-p$. In this case, for Alice to have another shot at winning, Bob must also flip a tails on both of his flips, which occurs with probability $(1-p)^2$ by independence. Afterwards, the coin would go back to Alice, and the probability of her winning would still be $a$, as the coin just performed one cycle and past outcomes don't influence future outcomes of the coin. Thus, we have the equation $a = p + (1-p)^3a \iff a = \dfrac{p}{1-(1-p)^3} = \dfrac{1}{p^2 - 3p+3}$ To find the $p$ that makes Alice and Bob equally likely to win, we must set the above equation (as a function of $p$) equal to $1/2$. In other words, we must solve $\dfrac{1}{p^2 - 3p + 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. By inverting both sides and subtracting $2$, we get $p^2 - 3p + 1 = 0$ is the equation that must be solved. This has solutions $p = \dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}$. However, $\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2} > 1$, which means that $p = \dfrac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 0.382$ is the valid solution.

questions.title: Coin Swap III
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play a game with a fair coin. Alice starts with the coin and flips it. The game stops when someone flips both a heads and a tails (not necessarily in this order). The players repeatedly pass the coin to each other to alternate the flips until someone wins. Find the probability that Alice is the winner.
questions.solution: The key observation here is that this is a fair coin. This means that heads and tails are equally likely to occur. Regardless of what Alice and Bob get on their respective first turns, they will both need one side remaining. The sides that remain both have probability $1/2$ per trial of appearing. Thus, after the first turn for each player, it is as if they are playing the game from "Coin Swap I" with $p = 1/2$. To illuminate this, let's suppose that Alice and Bob land $H$ and $T$, respectively, on their first flips. This means that they respectively need $T$ and $H$ to win. Since those sides will appear with probability $1/2$ each, it is as if they are playing the game from the first part of this question, as there is the same probability per player (in this case, $1/2$) of winning per trial. Therefore, the answer is just the same as "Coin Swap I" with $p = 1/2$, which is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.title: Coin Swap IV
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play a game with coins. Alice has a coin that has probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads on each flip, while Bob has a coin that has probability $0 < q < 1$ of heads on each flip. Alice starts and flips her coin. The game stops when someone flips a heads. If either player flip a tails, the other player gets a turn to flip their coin. Find the probability that Alice is the winner when $p = 1/3$ and $q = 2/3$.
questions.solution: Alice's probability of winning is dependent on what happens in the first turn. Therefore, we should use the Law of Total Probability to condition on what happens on the first flip of each player. Let $a$ be the probability that Alice wins the game. With probability $p$, she flips a head on her first turn and immediately wins. Otherwise, she flips a tails with probability $1-p$. In this case, for Alice to have another shot at winning, Bob must also flip a tails, which occurs with probability $1-q$. Afterwards, the coin would go back to Alice, and the probability of her winning would still be $a$, as the coin just performed one cycle and past outcomes don't influence future outcomes of the coin. Thus, we have the equation $a = p + (1-p)(1-q)a \iff a = \dfrac{p}{1-(1-p)(1-q)}$ A good sanity check is to note that when $p = q$, the answer aligns with "Coin Swap I" (with some reduction). With our specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{3}{7}$.

questions.title: LinkedIn Networking I
questions.problem: You message $N$ quant researchers on LinkedIn in an attempt to get a referral. You created a personalized message for each, but forgot which one corresponds to each person. Therefore, you send each of them a random message, with each message being used exactly once. Find the expected number of quant researchers that receive the message you intended for them when $N = 20$.
questions.solution: Since you are looking to compute the expected number of some events that are not independent, linearity of expectation with indicators is the best tool to use here. Note that these events are not independent because you are permuting the messages to the people, so the knowledge that a person gets the correct or incorrect message influences the probability that the other people receive their correct message. We want to count the number of people that get the correct message, so let $M_i$ be the indicator of the event that the $i$th quant researcher, $1 \leq i \leq N$, receives the correct message. Then $T = M_1 + \dots + M_N$ gives the total number of quant researchers that receive the correct message, as it adds $1$ or $0$ per person that receives the correct or incorrect message, respectively. By linearity of expectation, $\ev{T} = \ev{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^N M_i} = \sum_{i=1}^N \ev{M_i}$ Since all of the labels on the quant researchers are arbitrary, as they all have the same probability of receiving their intended message, the random variables $M_1,\dots, M_N$ are exchangeable. This means they have the same distribution and same mean. Thus, $\ev{T} = N \ev{M_1}$. $\ev{M_1}$ is the probability that quant researcher $1$ receives their intended message. There are $N$ possible messages, of which $1$ is intended for quant researcher $1$, so $\ev{M_1} = 1/N$. This means that $\ev{T} = N \cdot 1/N = 1$, which is independent of the number of people $N$.

questions.title: Fruit Picker
questions.problem: James has a bowl with $s \geq 1$ strawberries and $o \geq 1$ oranges. He draws fruits one at a time without replacement until there are no oranges left. Find the probability that the bowl is empty when $s = 10$ and $o = 20$.
questions.solution: The key observation here is that for the bowl to be completely empty, it must be the case that the last fruit drawn out is an orange. If it's not, then it means that the last orange was drawn before the last strawberry, which would imply that there is still at least one strawberry left in the bowl when James is done drawing out fruits. Therefore, this question is really asking the probability that the last fruit drawn is an orange. Since drawing without replacement is an exchangeable process, the probability that the last fruit drawn is an orange is the same as the probability that the first fruit drawn is an orange, which is $\dfrac{o}{o+s}$. With our specific values, the answer is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.title: The Biggest Loser
questions.problem: Fred is playing a game that costs $\$1$ to play per round. He has a probability $0 < p < 1$ of winning each round. If Fred wins a given round, he receives an integer amount $\$k > 1$ (note that he does not receive the $\$1$ initially paid back). If Fred initially starts with an integer amount $\$s \geq 1$ in his bank, find the probability that Fred wins exactly once before going bankrupt when $s = 3, k = 4,$ and $p = 1/3$. Round to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution: The most crucial thing to note is that Fred must win within the first $s$ rounds of the game so that he doesn't go bankrupt without winning. If he wins exactly once, he will play a total of $s + k$ rounds of the game, as his original bankroll affords him to play $s$ rounds, while his remaining bankroll allows him to play $k$ additional rounds. We now need to find the probability that there is exactly one win the first $s$ rounds of the game and no wins in the last $k$ rounds of the game. The probability of winning each round is $p$, which means the probability of a loss in each round is $1-p$. Therefore, the probability that all of the last $k$ rounds of the game are losses is $(1-p)^k$ by independence. To compute the probability of $1$ win in the first $s$ rounds, we must consider both the location of the win and the probability of winning in each round. There are $s$ ways to pick the round in which Fred wins. He wins that round with probability $p$. Afterwards, the other $s-1$ rounds must be losses so that he has exactly $1$ win, which occurs with probability $(1-p)^{s-1}$ by independence. Multiplying all of these together, we have that the final probability of this event occurring is $sp(1-p)^{k+s-1}$ With our specified values, the answer is $0.0878$.

questions.title: Consecutive 1
questions.problem: On average, how many times must a fair standard die be rolled to obtain two consecutive $1$s?
questions.solution: The expected value here is very dependent on the outcome of the first roll. Therefore, use the Law of Total Expectation to condition on the first roll.
