Therefore, we want to compute $\ev{D_n} = R^2\ev{\displaystyle \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \cos	heta_iight)^2 + \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \sin	heta_iight)^2}$. The key here to compute this is to expand out each of the sums. In particular, each term in the expansion of $\displaystyle \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \cos	heta_iight)^2$ will either be in the form $\cos^2	heta_i$ or in the form $\cos	heta_i\cos	heta_j$ for $i 
eq j$. The same idea holds for the other sum. Therefore, we can break up each squared sum into the "$i = j$ terms" and "$i 
eq j$ terms", which is a similar idea of what you do when you compute variance of a sum. This yields $\ev{\displaystyle \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \cos	heta_iight)^2 + \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \sin	heta_iight)^2} = \ev{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n (\cos^2	heta_i + \sin^2	heta_i) + \sum_{1 \leq i 
eq j \leq n} (\cos	heta_i\cos	heta_j + \sin	heta_i\sin	heta_j)}$. Note that $\cos^2	heta_i + \sin^2	heta_i = 1$ for any $	heta_i$, as this is the Pythagorean identity. This implies the first sum inside the above expectation is just $n$, as each of the summands is $1$. To compute $\ev{\cos	heta_i\cos	heta_j + \sin	heta_i\sin	heta_j}$, one can directly use LOTUS to get a standard method. However, this is quite messy. Reaching back to pre-calculus, one can show that $\cos	heta_i\cos	heta_j + \sin	heta_i\sin	heta_j = \cos(	heta_i-	heta_j)$ via the sum and difference formulas. Therefore, we really need to compute $\ev{\cos(	heta_i - 	heta_j)}$ for $i 
eq j$. The computation goes as follows: The joint PDF of $	heta_i$ and $	heta_j$ is given by $f(	heta_i,	heta_j) = \dfrac{1}{4\pi^2}I_{(0,2\pi)}(	heta_i)I_{(0,2\pi)}(	heta_j)$ by independence. Using LOTUS, this expectation is given by $\displaystyle \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \dfrac{\cos(	heta_i - 	heta_j)}{4\pi^2}d	heta_id	heta_j$. The inner integral evaluates to $\displaystyle \int_0^{2\pi} -\dfrac{1}{4\pi^2}\left(\sin(2\pi-	heta_j) - \sin(-	heta_j)ight)d	heta_j = 0$, as $\sin(-	heta_j) = \sin(2\pi - 	heta_j)$ by periodicity. However, one could reason this result intuitively, as cosine is an even function and the region of integration is symmetric about the origin $(0,0)$. Regardless, this means that the entire second sum vanishes, as the summands are all $0$. This implies that $\ev{D_n} = nR^2$. With the specified values, the answer is $100$.

questions.title: Random Index
questions.problem: Let $S$ be a set of $n \geq 2$ distinct real numbers with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Two distinct values are selected from this set and form a random pair $(X_1,X_2)$. Compute $\corr{X_1}{X_2}$ when $n = 16, \mu = 10, \sigma^2 = 225$.
questions.solution: To compute the correlation, we must first compute the covariance. Since drawing without replacement is an exchangeable process, we know that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are identically distributed. This means that they both have variance $\sigma^2$. Using the definition of covariance, $\cov{X_1}{X_2} = \ev{X_1X_2} - \ev{X_1}\ev{X_2}$. We know $\ev{X_1} = \ev{X_2} = \mu$ by exchangeability. To compute $\ev{X_1X_2}$, we have to be a little creative. Since the mean of $S$ is $\mu$ and there are $n$ real numbers in $S$, the sum of all of them is $n\mu$. If we know $X_1$, the sum of the remaining elements is $n\mu - X_1$, and there are $n-1$ remaining elements in the set. Therefore, the mean of the remaining elements in the set is $\frac{n\mu - X_1}{n-1}$. Therefore, we should condition on the value of $X_1$. Namely, $\ev{X_1X_2} = \ev{\ev{X_1X_2 \mid X_1}} = \ev{X_1\ev{X_2 \mid X_1}} = \ev{X_1 \cdot \dfrac{n\mu - X_1}{n-1}} = \dfrac{n\mu}{n-1} \ev{X_1} - \dfrac{1}{n-1}\ev{X_1^2}$. We know that $\ev{X_1} = \mu$ and $\ev{X_1^2} = \var{X_1} + (\ev{X_1})^2 = \sigma^2 + \mu^2$. Plugging these in, we have $\cov{X_1}{X_2} = \dfrac{n\mu^2}{n-1} - \dfrac{\sigma^2 + \mu^2}{n-1} - \mu^2 = -\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n-1}$. Plugging into the correlation, we have $\corr{X_1}{X_2} = \dfrac{\cov{X_1}{X_2}}{\sqrt{\var{X_1}\var{X_2}}} = -\dfrac{1}{n-1}$. With our specified values, the answer is $-\dfrac{1}{15}$.

questions.title: Stick Split
questions.problem: A stick of length $1$ meter is broken at $2$ uniformly random spots along its length. Find the probability that the smallest piece is at least $s$ meters long, $0 \leq s \leq 1/3$. Compute this when $s = 1/10$.
questions.solution: Call $X$ and $Y$ be the distance of the two cutting points from the LHS. There are two cases: $X < Y$ and $X > Y$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, both of the cases will result in the same probability of our event, so we can arbitrarily assume $X < Y$ at the beginning and multiply the probability obtained by $2$ at the end to account for both cases. Assuming $X < Y$, the lengths of the resulting pieces will be $X, Y-X,$ and $1-Y$. We know that $X, Y\sim \unif{0}{1}$ by the fact that the cutting points are uniformly at random along the length of the stick and the stick is of total length $1$. We want to compute $\prob{\min(X,Y-X,1-y) \geq s}$. If the minimum of the lengths is at least $s$, this implies the lengths of all three pieces are at least $s$. Therefore, this is equivalent to $\prob{X \geq s, Y-X \geq s, 1-Y \geq s}$. Rearranging this, we obtain $\prob{X \geq s, Y \leq 1-s, Y \geq X+s}$. Plotting the region out in the plane, we obtain a right triangle whose sides are of both of length $1-3s$. The area of this triangle would be $\frac{(1-3s)^2}{2}$, while the total area of the support of $(X,Y)$ is $1$. Since we are dealing with uniforms, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities, so the probability that we have computed for this case is $\frac{(1-3s)^2}{2}$. By the statement from the beginning of this question, we must double this probability to account for the other case, so the final probability of the stick being at least $s$ meters long is $(1-3s)^2$. With the specified value, the probability is $\frac{49}{100}$.

questions.title: Brown Conditions II
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion and $0 < s < t$. Compute $\ev{W_s \mid W_t = M}$ when $s = 1, t = 2, M = 4$.
questions.solution: We want to be able to apply the result of "Brown Conditions I" to this problem. In particular, we need a way to reverse the order of $s$ and $t$. Since $s < t$, we know that $1/s > 1/t$, and we know by time-inversion that if $W_t$ is a Brownian Motion, $B_t = tW_{1/t}$ is also a Brownian Motion. In particular, this means $W_t = tB_{1/t}$ by rearranging the above and inverting in $t$. Using this, we have that $\ev{W_s \mid W_t} = \ev{sB_{1/s} \mid tB_{1/t}} = s\ev{B_{1/s} \mid B_{1/t}} = sB_{1/t} = \dfrac{s}{t}W_t$. The second equality comes from the fact that the $t$ in the information does not give us any new information, as we already know what $t$ is from the Brownian Motion. The third equality comes from the fact that $1/t < 1/s$, so we can apply the previous question to this, as $B_t$ is a Brownian Motion. The last equality comes from the equality $W_t = tB_{1/t}$. This result intuitively makes sense, as if we know the Brownian motion satisfies $W_0 = 0$ and $W_t = M$, the values should linearly increase over time from $0$ to $B$. Therefore, this result says that after $s$ units of time, the Brownian Motion is, on average, $s/t$ of the value at time $t$. With the specified values, the answer is $2$.

questions.title: Gamma Differential
questions.problem: Let $X_1,X_2 \sim \Gamma(50,2)$ (shape-scale parameterization) IID. Approximate $\prob{|X_1 - X_2| \leq 20}$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: We are looking for an approximation here, so we will want to find a reasonable way to not explicitly compute this probability. Recall that under the shape-scale parameterization, if $E_1,\dots,E_n \sim \exponential{\lambda}$ IID, then $E_1 + \dots + E_n \sim \gam{n}{\dfrac{1}{\lambda}}$. With $n = 50$ and $\lambda = 1/2$, we can say that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are each sums of a large number of IID random variables. This implies that we can use the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) here. Since $X_1, X_2 \sim \gam{50}{2}$ IID, $\ev{X_1 - X_2} = \ev{X_1} - \ev{X_2} = 0$ and $\var{X_1 - X_2} = \var{X_1} + \var{X_2} = 200 + 200 = 400$. Therefore, $\sigma_{X_1 - X_2} = \sqrt{400} = 20$. Standardizing to apply CLT, we have $\prob{|X_1 - X_2| \leq 20} = \prob{-20 \leq X_1 - X_2 \leq 20} = \prob{\dfrac{-20 - 0}{20} \leq \dfrac{(X_1 - X_2) - 0}{20} \leq \dfrac{20 - 0}{20}} \approx \prob{-1 \leq Z \leq 1} = \Phi(1) - \Phi(-1)$. The second equality is just by subtracting the mean and dividing by standard deviation (standardizing). The $\approx$ is by CLT.

questions.title: Dogecoin Diggers
questions.problem: Ben YOLO'd his money in Dogecoin. It turns out that he has $\$D$ of Dogecoin, but his computer died. Luckily, he has a local Geek Squad that he takes his computer to. Ben can have his choice on how many technicians to hire. Each technician has a probability $0 < p < 1$ of fixing his computer, independent between technicians. However, Ben must have $\$nk$ to Geek Squad if he chooses to hire $n$ technicians. If Ben doesn't get someone to fix his computer, the money is lost. How many technicians should Ben hire in order to maximize his expected profit? Find this when $D = 1000000, k = 3000,$ and $p = 0.3$. You may want to use a calculator.
questions.solution: To maximize his expected profit, we should compute his expected profit as a function of $k$ and then try to maximize in $k$. If Ben hires $n$ technicians, then he must pay $nk$ for them to search. The probability that at least one of the $n$ technicians fixes the computer is $1 - (1-p)^n$, as $(1-p)^n$ is the probability that none of the technicians are able to fix his computer. If they do fix his computer, his profit is $D - nk$, as he obtains $D$ and must pay out $nk$. If they don't fix his computer, his profit is $-nk$, as he has no payout. Using Law of Total Expectation, Ben's expected payout with $n$ technicians is $f(n) = (D - nk)(1 - (1-p)^n) - nk(1-p)^n$. Our goal now is to maximize this in $n$. This is a very complicated function, so it's best to use a calculator to plot this out with the specified values. Plotting this as a continuous function of $n$, we see that $f'(n) = 0$ when $n \approx 13.4$. This means that the optimal $n$ is either $13$ or $14$. Plugging in both, we see that $13$ is very slightly higher, so Ben should hire $13$ technicians.

questions.title: Paired Cards
questions.problem: A deck consists of $2n$ cards of values $1-n$ that each appear twice in the deck. You draw $2$ cards at a time uniformly at random from the deck. If they match in value, you remove them from the deck. Otherwise, they are put back into the deck. The game finishes once there are no more cards to draw. Each drawing of two cards is a turn. Find the expected number of turns until the deck is empty when $n = 30$.
questions.solution: We see that the expected number of draws needed to make the deck go empty is dependent on the outcome of the first draw, as we either end up in the state that we are currently in or we move to a state that have $n-1$ distinct values instead of $n$. Therefore, a recurrence relation is appropriate here. Let $E(k)$ be the expected number of draws that need to be performed to make the deck go empty. Let's condition on what happens at the first draw. If the two cards drawn match in rank, then we remove those two (which performs $1$ turn), and then we move to a state that has $k-1$ cards left. Thus, in this case, it takes an average of $1 + E(k-1)$ draws to finish the game. The probability of drawing two cards that match in rank is not difficult to compute. Since the cards are drawn uniformly at random and each of them appear twice, fix the first card drawn arbitrarily. Of the remaining $2k-1$ cards in the deck, exactly $1$ of them will match in rank to the first card, so the probability of drawing a matching pair is $\frac{1}{2k-1}$. Otherwise, with probability $1 - \frac{1}{2k-1} = \frac{2k-2}{2k-1}$, we remain in the same state we started in, so we perform one draw and stay in the same state. Thus, the expected number of draws to complete the game in this case is $1 + E(k)$. Using Law of Total Expectation, we get $E(k) = \dfrac{1}{2k-1} \cdot (1 + E(k-1)) + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2k-1}\right)(1 + E(k)) \iff E(k) = E(k-1) + (2k-1)$. We now have a simple recurrence relation. We recurse backwards starting from $n$. This yields $E(n) = E(n-1) + (2n-1) = E(n-2) + (2n-1) + (2(n-1) - 1) = \dots = E(1) + \displaystyle \sum_{k=2}^n (2k-1)$. Our base case is that $E(1) = 1$, as there is only one pair, so they will always be drawn matching on the first turn. Therefore, we have $E(n) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^n (2k-1) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} - n = n^2$. With $n = 30$, the answer is $900$.

questions.title: Linear Intersection I
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4 \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Draw a line segment between $X_{2i-1}$ and $X_{2i}$ for $i = 1,2, \dots, n$. Find the probability that the two line segments overlap.
questions.solution: One of the four points must be the left-most point. Since all of the random variables are IID, fix $X_1$ arbitrarily as the smallest/left-most point. We can now just consider the orderings of $X_2,X_3,$ and $X_4$ to compute this probability, as all of their respective orderings are equally likely. If $X_2$ is the minimum among the remaining three random variables, there is no intersection between the line segments, as the endpoint of the first line segment is before the start of the segment line segment. If $X_2$ lies between $X_3$ and $X_4$, there is an intersection. Similarly, if $X_2$ is the maximum, the segment between $X_1$ and $X_2$ contains the segment between $X_3$ and $X_4$, so there is an intersection. Therefore, as each of the three possibilities above are equally likely and $2$ of them result in an intersection, the probability of an intersection is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.title: Linear Intersection II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4 \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Draw a line segment between $X_{2i-1}$ and $X_{2i}$ for $i = 1,2, \dots, n$. Find the expected number of pairs of line segments that overlap when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: We are looking to count the expected number of events that are not independent, so counting with indicators is best here. Since there are $n$ line segments formed from the $2n$ points, there are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs of line segments. Label these pairs $1$ to $\binom{n}{2}$, and let $I_i$ be the indicator random variable of whether or not the line segments in pair $i$ intersect. We have that $T = I_1 + \dots + I_{\binom{n}{2}}$ is the total number of pairs of line segments that intersect. Since the labels of the line segments are arbitrarily, they are exchangeable, so each of the $I_i$ random variables have the same distribution, and hence same mean. By linearity of expectation, we have that $\ev{T} = \binom{n}{2}\ev{I_1}$. $\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that the line segments in pair $1$ intersect with each other. However, from "Linear Intersection I", we know this probability is just $\dfrac{2}{3}$, so $\ev{I_1} = \dfrac{2}{3}$. Plugging this in, $\ev{T} = \dfrac{2}{3}\displaystyle \binom{n}{2}$. With $n = 10$, the answer is $30$.

questions.title: Multiplicative Coin Flip
questions.problem: Alice and Bob respectively have coins with probability $0 < p < 1$ and $0 < q < 1$ of heads. They both flip until they obtain their first heads. Find the probability that it takes Bob strictly more than $k \geq 1$ times as many flips to obtain his first heads as Alice when $p = 1/3, q = 1/2,$ and $k = 3$.
questions.solution: We first need to frame this problem probabilistically. Let $A$ and $B$ be the number of flips needed for Alice and Bob to respectively obtain their first heads. Then $A \sim \geom{p}$ and $B \sim \geom{q}$ and you are looking to compute $\prob{B > kA}$. We get the distributions for $A$ and $B$ since they are waiting times for the first occurrence of some event. It is good to condition on the value of $A$ to remove a source of randomness. Namely, $\prob{B > kA} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \prob{B > kA \mid A = n}\prob{A = n} = \prob{B > kn}\prob{A = n}$. We know that $\prob{A = n} = p(1-p)^{n-1}$ by the PMF of a geometric random variable. To compute $\prob{B > kn}$, we note that this event exactly occurs when the first $kn$ flips are all tails. This occurs with probability $(1-q)^{kn}$, as each flip is independently tails with probability $1-q$. Therefore, we obtain $\prob{B > kA} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p(1-p)^{n-1} \cdot (1-q)^{kn} = p\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (1-p)^n[(1-q)^k]^n = p(1-q)^k \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[(1-p)(1-q)^k\right]^{n-1}$. The geometric series formula applies to the remaining sum with common ratio $r = (1-p)(1-q)^k$. This yields $\prob{B > kA} = \dfrac{p(1-q)^k}{1 - (1-p)(1-q)^k}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{22}$.

questions.title: Random Chord II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are two uniformly random points selected from the circumference of the unit circle. Let $L$ be the length of the chord (line segment) that connects $X_1$ and $X_2$. Find $\var{L}$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: We know that $\var{L} = \ev{L^2} - (\ev{L})^2$. The latter term was calculated in "Random Chord I", so all that's left is to compute $\ev{L^2}$. From the previous part, we found that $L = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{1-\cos\theta}$, where $\theta \sim \unif{0}{\pi}$. Thus, we have that $L^2 = 2(1-\cos\theta)$. To compute $\ev{L^2}$, we now just plug in and use linearity of expectation. Namely, we have $\ev{L^2} = 2\ev{1 - \cos\theta} = 2(1 - \ev{\cos\theta})$. All that remains is to compute $\ev{\cos\theta} = \displaystyle \int_0^{\pi} \cos\theta \cdot \dfrac{1}{\pi}d\theta = 0$. Therefore, $\ev{L^2} = 2$. Plugging this into the variance formula, $\var{L} = \ev{L^2} - (\ev{L})^2 = 2 - \dfrac{16}{\pi^2}$.

questions.title: Missing Values II
questions.problem: $n$ integers are going to be selected from the set $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$ with repetition allowed. Find the probability that exactly one integer is not selected when $n = 5$.
questions.solution: To compute this probability, we need to find the total number of ways in which we exclude one of the integers and divide that by the total number ways to select the $n$ values. If there are no restrictions, since we select with replacement, there would be $n$ options from $[n]$ that we can select at trial, so there would be a total of $n^n$ ways to select $n$ values by the multiplication principle. For there to be a missing value, we must select one of the integers twice and exclude one other. There are $n$ ways to pick the integer that is selected twice and $n-1$ ways to pick the integer that is excluded from the selection. Afterwards, there are $\binom{n}{2}$ ways to pick the locations of the draws in which the twice represented value is actually selected. This is because we are picking a subset of $2$ indices from $n$ total locations. Afterwards, there are $n-2$ values left that can be permuted to the remaining $n-2$ spots in any order, so there are $(n-2)!$ ways to do that. By the multiplication principle, this yields $\binom{n}{2} \cdot n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2)! = \binom{n}{2} \cdot n!$ ways in which exactly one integer is missing. Therefore, the probability is $\dfrac{\binom{n}{2} \cdot n!}{n^n}$. With $n = 5$, the answer is $\dfrac{240}{625} = \dfrac{48}{125}$.

questions.title: Circular Visitor
questions.problem: There are $2n$ positions in a circle labelled $0$ to $2n-1$ arranged increasing in CCW order starting from $0$. A particle starts at position $0$ and moves to position $i+1$ or $i-1$ with equal probability at each step (for position $0$, either $1$ or $2n-1$, and similar with $2n-1$). Find the probability that the particle has visited every other position at least once by the time it reaches position $n$ for the first time when $n = 100$.
questions.solution: The particle starts at position $0$ and position $n$ is diametrically opposed to position $0$. Before reaching position $n$, the particle must reach either $n-1$ or $n+1$, as it can only move one step at a time. Given that the particle reaches position $n-1$ or $n+1$, both of them are equally likely, as each of those two positions are equidistant from position $1$. One of them must occur first, so say it is $n+1$ arbitrarily, as each one is equally likely. If the particle hits position $n+1$ first, the particle must circle back all the way around to position $n-1$ before reaching position $n$. Imagine unraveling the circle, where position $n+1$ is the starting point and there is $1$ spot below (position $n$) and $2n-1$ spots above (all of the remaining spots, ending with position $n-1$). Therefore, we want to find the probability we hit the end of the upper tail (position $n-1$, which is $2n-2$ spots away) before hitting the end of the lower tail (position $n$). This is a standard gambler's ruin problem, where the answer is $\frac{1}{(2n-2) + 1} = \frac{1}{2n-1}$. With $n = 100$, the answer is $1/199$.

questions.title: Container Arc I
questions.problem: $n \geq 2$ points are uniformly at random selected from the circumference of the unit circle. These $n$ points divide the circle into $n$ arcs. Find the expected length of the arc that contains the point $(1,0)$ when $n = 5$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: An incorrect solution goes as follows: Since the $n$ arcs divide up the circle into $n$ pieces that should have exchangeable lengths, the answer is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}$, as the point $(1,0)$ will belong to one of them. The reason this is incorrect is because of the fact that the point $(1,0)$ really acts as another divider in this scenario, since we are measuring arc length inclusive of $(1,0)$. Therefore, there are really $n+1$ dividers here, and the arc that contains $(1,0)$ stretches from the point nearest to $(1,0)$ from both above and below. The arc containing $(1,0)$ is essentially contains two arcs: one above $(1,0)$ to the nearest point above and one below to the nearest point below $(1,0)$. As there are really $n+1$ dividers now, the average length of each arc is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n+1}$. Since the arc containing $(1,0)$ contains $2$ of these smaller arcs, the answer is $\dfrac{4\pi}{n+1}$. With $n = 5$, the answer is $\dfrac{2}{3}\pi$. One can prove the above rigorously by computing $\ev{L} = \ctailsum{L}$ for an appropriate choice of $L$. In this case, since we know that the arc containing $(1,0)$ really splits into two components, we can look at the expected length of one of those components. As all of these component arcs are the same length in expectation, we can look at the distance from $(1,0)$ to the nearest point above it. We can simulate a random point being selected by having $X_1,\dots,X_n \sim \unif{0}{2\pi}$ as a random angle, and minimum value of these is the one that is closest to $(1,0)$ from above it. Therefore, the event $\{L \geq x\} = \{\min(X_1,\dots,X_n) \geq x\} = \{X_1 \geq x,\dots,X_n \geq x\}$. This means $\ev{L} = \ctailsum{L} = \int_0^{\infty} \prob{X_1 \geq x,\dots, X_n \geq x}dx = \int_0^{2\pi} (\prob{X_1 \geq x})^n dx$. $\prob{X_1 \geq x} = 1 - \dfrac{x}{2\pi}$, as $X_1$ is uniform on $(0,2\pi)$ and $(x,2\pi)$ is of length $2\pi - x$. The upper bound of the integral is $2\pi$ because the minimum distance from $0$ and can anywhere in $(0,2\pi)$. Therefore, $\ev{L} = \int_0^{2\pi} \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{2\pi}\right)^n dx = \dfrac{2\pi}{n+1}$. This aligns with the intuition above.

questions.title: Container Arc II
questions.problem: $n \geq 2$ points are uniformly at random selected from the circumference of the unit circle. These $n$ points divide the circle into $n$ arcs. Given that $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ lie in the same arc, find the expected length of that arc when $n = 5$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Using the same intuition as the previous example, the arc consisting of $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ has a piece to the left of $(0,1)$ and below $(1,0)$. The arc containing $(1,0)$ is essentially contains two arcs: one above $(1,0)$ to the nearest point above and one below to the nearest point below $(1,0)$. The $n$ selected points split up the remaining $3\pi/2$ radians into $n+1$ pieces, as we can view the remaining part of the circle as a line segment of length $3\pi/2$. Since each of pieces has the same expected length by the uniformity of the selected points, each of the pieces dividing up the remaining arc has expected length $\frac{3\pi}{2(n+1)}$. The arc containing $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ consists of the arc of length $\pi/2$ between the two points, as well as $2$ of the remaining $n+1$ pieces: The one directly to the left of $(0,1)$ and below $(1,0)$. Therefore, the expected length of this arc is $\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2 \cdot \dfrac{3\pi}{2(n+1)} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{3\pi}{n+1}$. With $n = 5$, the answer is $\pi \approx 3.142$.

questions.title: Maximal Variant
questions.problem: Let $X$ be a random variable with support $S \subseteq [a,b]$ for $a < b$. Find the maximum possible variance of $X$ when $a = 3$ and $b = 5$.
questions.solution: Note that variance is independent of location, so we can shift the random variable $X$ to $X-a$ such that the support is $[0,b-a]$. Since $\var{X} = \var{X-a}$, this shift doesn't change the maximum. To maximize the variance, we want to maximize the spread and randomness of the random variable $X$. To maximize the amount of spread about the mean, we will want the random variable to take as few values as possible. To spread it out, we could pick $0$ and $b-a$, the endpoints of the interval. Now, we need to find $\prob{X = 0}$ such that it maximizes the variance. Intuitively, there is the most variance when there is the most randomness, which occurs when $\prob{X = 0} = \prob{X = b-a} = 1/2$, as it's the "most random" in terms of outcome (it is not biased either way). We can verify this with calculus. Let $\prob{X = 0} = p$, which means $\prob{X = b-a} = 1-p$. Then $\ev{X} = 0 \cdot p + (b-a) \cdot (1-p) = (b-a)(1-p)$. Similarly, $\ev{X^2} = 0^2 \cdot p + (b-a)^2 \cdot (1-p)$. Therefore, $\var{X} = \ev{X^2} - (\ev{X})^2 = (b-a)^2 \cdot p(1-p)$. We therefore need to maximize $f(p) = p - p^2$. We have that $f'(p) = 1-2p$, which is $0$ exactly when $p = 1/2$. Therefore, $p = 1/2$ maximizes the variance, as desired. The maximum variance here is $\var{X} = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{4}$ when plugging in $p = 1/2$ for the variance formula above. Therefore, shifting back by $a$, the random variable $X$ that has maximal variance is the one such that $\prob{X = a} = \prob{X = b} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, which has variance $\dfrac{(b-a)^2}{4}$. Therefore, with our specific values, the answer is $1$.

questions.title: Head Equalizer
questions.problem: Alice and Bob each flip a fair coin $n$ times. Find the probability that they obtain the same number of heads when $n = 6$.
questions.solution: It is easiest to disjointify this event based on how many times each of Alice and Bob obtain heads. Namely, let $A$ and $B$ represent the number of times that Alice and Bob each obtain heads in the $n$ flips. Then $A, B \sim \binomial{n}{1/2}$ IID. To compute $\prob{A = B}$, we can break this up based on Alice and Bob each obtaining $0$ heads, $1$ head, and so on. Namely, this is $\prob{A = B} = \sum_{k=0}^n \prob{A = B = k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \prob{A = k}^2$. The second equality is by the fact that $A$ and $B$ are IID. Since $A \sim \binomial{n}{1/2}$, $\prob{A = k} = \binom{n}{k}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$. In the following, we make use of the identity $\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}^2 = \binom{2n}{n}$, which can be proved via a combinatorial proof. $\sum_{k=0}^n \left(\binom{n}{k}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2^n}\right)^n = \dfrac{1}{4^n}\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}^2 = \dfrac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}$. With $n = 6$, the answer is $\dfrac{924}{4096} = \dfrac{231}{1024}$.

questions.title: Top Shagger
questions.problem: There are $n$ people in a line whose heights follows some continuous distribution. You then stand at the front of the line. You can see someone's head if they are taller than everyone that comes before them in the line. Let $N$ be the number of heads that you see. Find $\ev{N}$ when $n = 100$. Round your answer to the nearest thousandth.

questions.title: Odd Solutions
questions.problem: Find the number of non-negative odd integer solutions to $x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_{2r} = 2k$ where $1 \leq r \leq k$. Solve this when $r = 4$ and $k = 10$.
questions.solution: An odd integer $n$ is in the form $n = 2k+1$ for integer $k$. Therefore, we should try to write $x_i = 2y_i + 1$ for $y_i \geq 0$, as $x_i$ must be a non-negative odd integer. Doing so yields $(2y_1 + 1) + \dots + (2y_{2r} + 1) = 2k \iff y_1 + \dots + y_{2r} = k-r$. The above is by rearrangement. Note that this new equation only has the restriction that $y_1,\dots,y_{2r} \geq 0$ by the previous statement. The number of solutions to this equation is easily given by stars and bars to be $\binom{(k-r) + (2r) - 1}{2r-1} = \binom{k+r-1}{2r-1}$. With our specific values, the answer is $\binom{13}{7} = 1716$.

questions.title: Even Solutions
questions.problem: Find the number of non-negative even integer solutions to $x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_{r} = 2k$ with $r,k \geq 1$. Solve this when $r = 5$ and $k = 10$.
questions.solution: An even integer $n$ is in the form $n = 2k$ for integer $k$. Therefore, we should try to write $x_i = 2y_i$ for $y_i \geq 0$, as $x_i$ must be a non-negative even integer. Doing so yields $(2y_1) + \dots + (2y_{r}) = 2k \iff y_1 + \dots + y_{r} = k$. The above is by rearrangement. Note that this new equation only has the restriction that $y_1,\dots,y_{r} \geq 0$ by the previous statement. The number of solutions to this equation is easily given by stars and bars to be $\binom{k+r-1}{r-1}$. With our specific values, the answer is $\binom{14}{4} = 1001$.

questions.title: Random Equation
questions.problem: Suppose that $N$ is a random variable whose PMF is $\prob{X=k} = c_{\lambda} \cdot \dfrac{\lambda^k(k-1)!}{(2k-1)!}$ for integers $k \geq 1$. $c_{\lambda}$ is a normalizing constant on this. Find the expected number of non-negative integer solutions to the equation $x_1 + \dots + x_N = N$. The answer is in the form $K(\lambda)c_{\lambda}$ for some $K(\lambda)$. Find $K(2)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: The first thing to do is to find the number of solutions to the equation with $N$ known. If $N$ is known, by stars and bars, there are $\binom{2N-1}{N-1}$ solutions. Thus, we want to compute $\ev{\binom{2N-1}{N-1}}$, where $N$ has the prescribed distribution in the question. To compute this quantity, the best choice is LOTUS, as we only know the PMF of the random variable $X$. Namely, $\ev{\binom{2N-1}{N-1}} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\binom{2k-1}{k-1}\prob{X = k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(2k-1)!}{(k-1)!k!} \cdot c_{\lambda} \cdot \dfrac{\lambda^k \cdot (k-1)!}{(2k-1)!} = c_{\lambda} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!} = (e^{\lambda} - 1)c_{\lambda}$. The second equality is by the expansion of the binomial coefficient and plugging in the PMF. The third equality is by cancellation, while the last equality is by the Taylor Series of $e^x$ with $x = \lambda$. Note that the Taylor Series of $e^x$ starts at $k = 0$, so we have to subtract out the $k = 0$ term.

questions.title: Multidimensional Tic Tac Toe
questions.problem: In Tic Tac Toe, a player wins when their symbol (either $X$ or $O$) are all in a row, column, or diagonal of the grid. For example, one can check that there are $8$ winning paths in standard $3 \times 3$ Tic Tac Toe. How many winning paths are there in $3$D Tic Tac Toe in an $n \times n \times n$ grid when $n = 5$?
questions.solution: Let's start with the standard case to get some intuition. Imagine embedding the standard $3 \times 3$ Tic Tac Toe square in a $5 \times 5$ square i.e. add one more dimension in each direction of the standard square. Each winning path in the $3 \times 3$ grid corresponds to two distinct squares on the surface of the larger $5 \times 5$ grid if the path is extended outwards. Therefore, as each path corresponds to $2$ squares on the surface of the $5 \times 5$ squares, the number of squares on the outer surface of the $5 \times 5$ square is $2$ times as many as the number of winning paths. This is because we established a relationship that maps each path to $2$ squares on the outer surface. The number of squares on the outer surface of the $5 \times 5$ square is $5^2 - 3^2 = 16$, as that is the difference in area of the interior from the total region. Therefore, there must be $8$ winning paths, which is what's stated in the question. Now, we use this idea in $3$D. Imagine embedding the $n \times n \times n$ cube inside a $(n+2) \times (n+2) \times (n+2)$ cube. Each winning path in the $n \times n \times n$ cube corresponds to two unique squares on the surface of the $(n+2) \times (n+2) \times (n+2)$ cube. Therefore, the number of squares on the surface of the larger cube is $2$ times as large as the number of winning paths inside the $n \times n \times n$ grid. There are $(n+2)^3 - n^3$ total squares on the surface of the larger cube, as that is the difference of volumes. This means that there are $\dfrac{(n+2)^3 -n^3}{2}$ winning paths by the statement above. With $n = 5$, the answer is $109$.

questions.title: Complete Sub-Graphs
questions.problem: There are $n \geq 2$ points on a circle labelled $1-n$. For each pair of points, a line segment is drawn between them with probability $0 < p < 1$. A complete $k-$sub-graph, where $2 \leq k \leq n$, is a subset of $k$ points such that each pair of points in the subset has a line segment connecting them. Find the expected number of complete $k-$sub-graphs with $p = 1/4, n = 10,$ and $k = 4$.
questions.solution: We are looking to count the expected number of some events that are not independent, so linearity of expectation is best here. These are not independent because the existence of one complete $k-$sub-graph raises the probability of another one significantly. For example, if you were to replace one of the points in the sub-graph by another one, all that needs to occur is that the other $k-1$ points in the original $k-$sub-graph need to be linked to the new point, which is only $k-1$ connections that have to occur. There is a potential for a complete $k-$sub-graph in every subset of $k$ points from the $n$ points. In other words, the maximum number of complete $k-$sub-graphs is equal to the number of subsets of $k$ points from the $n$ points, which is $\binom{n}{k}$. Label the potential complete $k-$sub-graphs $1$ to $\binom{n}{k}$, and let $I_i$ be the indicator of the $i$th $k-$sub-graph being complete. Then $T = I_1 + \dots + I_{\binom{n}{k}}$ gives the total number of complete $k-$sub-graphs. Since the labels are arbitrary, the $I_i$ random variables are all exchangeable, which means they are identically distributed. In particular, they have the same mean. Thus, by linearity of expectation, $\ev{T} = \binom{n}{k}\ev{I_1}$. $\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that the first $k-$sub-graph is complete. The sub-graph is complete exactly when there is a line segment between each of pair of points among the $k$. There are $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs of points in the subset of $k$ points, and each one independently has a line segment between them with probability $p$. Therefore, the probability that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs of points have a line segment between them is $\ev{I_1} = p^{\binom{k}{2}}$. Substituting back in, $\ev{T} = \binom{n}{k}p^{\binom{k}{2}}$. With the values in the question, the answer is $\dfrac{105}{2048}$.

questions.title: Tricky House II
questions.problem: A very tricky house has $m+1$ doors labelled $1$ to $m+1$, where $m \geq 1$. Door $m+1$ leads to freedom immediately. Otherwise, behind door $1 \leq i \leq m$, there is a path that takes $i$ minutes to traverse and leads you back to the original room you were standing in. You select uniformly at random from the doors at each turn. Let $T$ be the total time it takes for you to reach freedom and $N$ be the number of turns needed. Find $\ev{T \mid N = n}$ when $n = 8$ and $m = 9$.

questions.title: Multichord I
questions.problem: $6$ points are selected uniformly at random from the circumference of a circle. These points are then split into $3$ pairs. A chord is drawn between each of the three formed pairs of points. Find the probability that none of these chords intersect.
questions.solution: The $6$ points are split into three pairs, so we need to first find the total number of pairs that can be formed. We are splitting the $6$ points into $3$ indistinguishable pairs, so we can first find the number of ways to do this if the pairs were distinguishable, and then remove the distinction of the pairs. If the pairs were distinguishable, there would be $\binom{6}{2,2,2}$ ways to do this, as we are forming groups $3$ groups of size $2$, and the other of the points in the pairs is irrelevant. The above treats the groups as distinct, so to remove the distinction between the groups, we have to divide by the number of ways to arrange "group labels" between them. There are $3$ groups, so there would be $3!$ ways to arrange the labels in indistinct ways, so the answer is $\dfrac{6!}{(2!)^3 \cdot 3!} = 15$. Now, we need to determine the number of these pairings of points that don't have the chords intersect. Arbitrarily pick one point on the circle as your "start". This start can be arbitrary since the circle can just be rotated around such that any point is your "start". For none of the chords to intersect, your starting point either has to connect to the point directly next to it on the left/right, or it has to connect to the middle point of the other $5$ points on the circle. If it connects to something that is $2$ away on the left or right (i.e. not the middle but not directly adjacent), there is a trapped point under the chord, which will have an intersection with the drawn chord, as it connects to something outside of the region pinned by the chord. We now analyze the two cases separately. In the first case, there are $2$ possible points you can connect to (point on left or right). Once this is done, there are $2$ ways that the remaining $4$ points can connect such that there is no intersection among them. This yields $4$ such arrangements of chords. In the second case, there is only one possible arrangement, as the chord splits the points "down the middle" and restricts the other points to stay on the same side of the circle. Adding up the two cases, there are $5$ total arrangements of chords that yield no intersection, so the probability is $5/15 = 1/3$.

questions.title: Frequent Upface
questions.problem: Fix $n > 1$. Abdul rolls a standard $n-$sided die with the values $1-n$ on the sides until he obtains the value $n$. The probability of side $i$ appearing $1 \leq i \leq n$ is $p_i > 0$. Find the probability that side $1$ appears exactly $k$ times. Solve this when $n = 10$, $p_i = 3/20$ if $i$ is odd and $1/20$ else, and $k = 5$.
questions.solution: The key insight to note here is that all rolls that aren't $1$ or $n$ are irrelevant. This is because of the fact that we only care about the number of $1$s that appear before the first $n$, which is not influenced by any other values not $1$ nor $n$. Therefore, we can just focus in on $1$ and $n$. Given that the roll is either $1$ or $n$, the probability it is $1$ is $\frac{p_1}{p_1 + p_n}$. One can show this using the definition of conditional probability. This means that the probability the value is $n$ is $\frac{p_n}{p_1 + p_n}$. We are looking at the distribution of the number of $1$s that appear before the first $n$. Since we only care about each value that is $1$ or $n$, we can use these rescaled probabilities in a geometric random variable to count the number of $1$s that appear before the first $n$. Namely, this distribution is $\geom{\frac{p_n}{p_1 + p_n}} - 1$, as there is a probability $\frac{p_n}{p_1 + p_n}$ per trial that, given the roll is either $1$ or $n$, that it is $n$. Since we are looking at the number of $1$s that come strictly before the first occurrence of $n$ (as opposed to the number of total times $1$ or $n$ occur), we need to subtract $1$ to account for the fact that there could be $0$ occurrences of $1$ before $n$. Thus, using the PMF of a geometric, the probability of exactly $k$ ones before the first $n$ is $\left(\dfrac{p_n}{p_1 + p_n}\right)\left(\dfrac{p_1}{p_1 + p_n}\right)^{k}$. This PMF is obtained via the Geometric PMF, with $k$ in place of $k-1$, as we start from $0$. With the specific values, the answer is $\dfrac{243}{4096}$.

questions.title: Infinite Origin Component
questions.problem: On the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$, you place an edge between each pair of vertices of distance $1$ with probability $0 < p < 1$. Using the bound provided by sub-additivity, the interval of values of $p$ such that the probability the origin is in an infinite connected component is in the form $(0,a)$ for some real value $a$. Find $a$.
questions.solution: Let $A_{\infty}$ be the event that the origin is in an infinite connected component. We can bound $\prob{A_{\infty}} \leq \prob{A_r}$ for every $r$, where $A_r$ is the event is that the origin is in a connected component of length $r$, as an infinite connected component will contain finite connected components of any length. The probability that a component of length $r$ occurs is $p^r$, as each of the line segments occurs with probability $p$ independently, and it must be of length $r$. The real question is that we need to bound how many such sequences there are passing through the origin of length $r$. The initial direction has $4$ options. Afterwards, for each of the other $r$ steps, there are at most $3$ directions the path can move in. This is because it can move in any direction that isn't the one it just came from. The reason it is at most $3$ is because, at some point, if the path is long enough, the path may not be able to move in other directions as well for it to not move on an edge it already moved on. Since the path is of length $r$, we have the initial movement ($4$ options) and the additional movements ($\leq 3$ options) $r-1$ times. Thus, a bound on the number of paths is $4 \cdot 3^{r-1}$. Therefore, $\prob{A_r} = \prob{\bigcup_{\gamma} A_{\gamma}} \leq 4 \cdot 3^{r-1} \cdot p^r$. The second expression is just expressing the event $A_r$ as the event that at least one path $\gamma$ of length $r$ passing through the origin exists, where the union is over all $\gamma$ satisfying the event. The final bound is by sub-additivity, as each such path has probability $p^r$ and there are most $4 \cdot 3^{r-1}$ of them. Thus, $\prob{A_{\infty}} \leq 4p(3p)^{r-1}$ for every $r$. For $\prob{A_{\infty}} = 0$, it must be the case that the bound on the RHS tends to 0. This is since the bound holds for all $r$. For this to happen, we need $3p < 1$, as if the ratio on the RHS is $< 1$, the limit is $0$ as $r \rightarrow \infty$. This occurs exactly when $p < 1/3$, which means $a = 1/3$.

questions.title: Identically Distributed Sum
questions.problem: A $6-$sided die with the values $1-6$ on the sides is weighted such that the probabilities of rolling a $2,3,4,5,$ and $6$ is the same if you roll once versus if you roll the dice twice and sum the upfaces. Find $p_1$, the probability of rolling a $1$ on this die. You may want to use a calculator in this question at some point. Round this answer to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: The question claims that this die is weighted such that the values $2-6$ appear with the same probability in $1$ roll as they do in $2$ rolls by summing the upfaces. Let $p_i$ be the probability of the face $i$ showing up on this die. We should relate the $p_i$ to each other by using the condition in the question. For $p_2$, the only way to get a sum of $2$ is to obtain two $1$s on the dice. This occurs with probability $p_1^2$, so $p_2 = p_1^2$. For $p_3$, the only way to get a sum of $3$ is to obtain a $1$ and a $2$ on the dice (in some order). There are $2$ permutations of these values on the dice, so by independence, the probability of rolling a $1$ and a $2$ is $p_3 = 2p_1p_2$. A sum of $4$ is where it starts to get more tricky, as there are multiple permutations now leading to this sum. A sum of $4$ can be obtained by a $1$ and $3$ (in some order) or two $2$s. There are $2$ permutations of the first case, so the probability of the first case is $2p_1p_3$. The probability of the second case is $p_2^2$, as there is only one arrangement. Therefore, we have $p_4 = p_2^2 + 2p_1p_3$. The details to compute $p_5$ and $p_6$ are quite similar. Using the above methodology, you can check that $p_5 = 2p_1p_4 + 2p_2p_3$ and $p_6 = 2p_1p_5 + 2p_2p_4 + p_3^3$. To solve for $p_1$, we want to get all the $p_i$ in terms of $p_1$. We want to do this because we know that $p_1 + p_2 + \dots + p_6 = 1$, as they represent the sum of probabilities of all outcomes of the die. Thus, if we can get each of the $p_i$ in terms of $p_1$, this allows us to have an equation for $p_1$. We already have $p_2 = p_1^2$, which is sorted. Since $p_3 = 2p_1p_2,$ $p_3 = 2p_1^3$ by the previous relation of $p_2 = p_1^2$. Next, $p_4 = p_2^2 + 2p_1p_3$, so using the previous relations, $p_4 = 5p_1^4$. By plugging in the other relations in a similar fashion, one can see that $p_5 = 14p_1^5$ and $p_6 = 42p_1^6$. Plugging all of these into $p_1 + \dots + p_6 = 1$, $42p_1^6 + 14p_1^5 + 5p_1^4 + 2p_1^3 + p_1^2 + p_1 = 1$. Plugging into a calculator, the solution only has one positive real root of $\approx 0.383$, so this must be the answer.

questions.title: Divided Plane I
questions.problem: Find the maximum number of disjoint regions the plane can be divided into by $n$ non-parallel lines. For example, one line splits the plane into two regions. Report the answer when $n = 20$.
questions.solution: The idea here is to derive a recurrence relation for $r(n)$, the number of regions that the plane can be split into with $n$ non-parallel lines. This is because the plane with $n+1$ lines inside of it is just adding in one more line to the plane that has $n$ lines in it, so the number of regions that are formed should be related to each other. Suppose that the max number of regions with $n$ lines is $r(n)$. Let's now add in the $(n+1)$st line. Given that this new line isn't parallel to any existing line and no three lines intersect at a single point (this reduces the number of regions, as there would be no "middle"), the new line must intersect every single one of the existing lines at some point. Therefore, the new line passes through $n+1$ regions and divides each of them into two new regions. This adds $n+1$ regions to our total when we input this new line, so we have derived $r(n+1) = r(n) + (n+1)$. By recursing backwards, we have that $r(n) = r(n-1) + n = r(n-2) + n + (n-1) = \dots = r(1) +  (n + (n-1) + \dots + 2) = (1 + 2 + \dots + n) + 1$. This can be reduced to $r(n) = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} + 1$ by the common formula $1+2+ \dots + k = \dfrac{k(k+1)}{2}$. This can also be written as $r(n) = \binom{n}{2} + \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{0}$. With $n = 20$, the answer is $211$.

questions.title: Tiny Target I
questions.problem: You are shooting two targets on the real line, say $T_1$ and $T_2$. The two targets are of radius $\varepsilon <<< 1$ and are centered at $x_1 \neq x_2$, respectively. This means $T_1$ covers $[x_1 - \varepsilon, x_1 + \varepsilon]$, and likewise for $T_2$. Assume that $|x_1 - x_2| > 2\varepsilon$ so that the two targets are disjoint. You have one dart to shoot at the line. Your goal is to maximize your probability of hitting one of the targets. You can choose where to center your throw on the line. If you choose to center your dart at $\mu$, the actual position that the dart lands on the real line is $X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $\sigma^2$ is fixed. Find the value of $\mu$ that maximizes the probability of hitting a target when $x_1 = -2, x_2 = 0,$ and $\sigma^2 = 9$. If necessary, round your answer to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Since the targets are extremely small, you can essentially treat them like individual points. Let $\phi(x; \mu,\sigma^2) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}$ be the PDF of a $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ random variable. We can say that the probability of landing in region $T_1$ is approximately $\phi(x_1; \mu,\sigma^2)2\varepsilon$ by the definition of a PDF. You can intuitively see this, as the probability of landing in some region is just the integral of the PDF under the region. However, since $\varepsilon$ is extremely small, the PDF is essentially constant on the interval $[x_1-\varepsilon,x_1 + \varepsilon]$. Thus, the region is essentially rectangular with base $2\varepsilon$ and height $\phi(x_1;\mu,\sigma^2)$. Similarly, the probability of landing in region $T_2$ is $2\varepsilon\phi(x_2;\mu,\sigma^2)$. As the two regions are disjoint, given $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$, the probability of landing in one of those regions is $p(\mu) = 2\varepsilon\phi(x_1;\mu,\sigma^2) + 2\varepsilon\phi(x_2;\mu,\sigma^2) = 2\varepsilon(\phi(x_1;\mu,\sigma^2) + \phi(x_2;\mu,\sigma^2))$. Our goal is to maximize $p(\mu)$ in $\mu$. To do this, we should take the derivative of $p(\mu)$ in $\mu$. Using the chain rule and power rules, we obtain $p'(\mu) = 2\varepsilon\left[\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x_1-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} \cdot \left(\dfrac{x_1 - \mu}{\sigma^2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x_2-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} \left(\dfrac{x_2 - \mu}{\sigma^2}\right)\right]$. Note that we can remove a lot of the constants out front, as they don't affect our optimization problem. Namely, we want to solve $(x_1 - \mu)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x_1-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} + (x_2 - \mu)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x_2-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2} = 0$. The trick here is to note that $x_1 - \mu$ and $x_2 - \mu$ appear in both terms, so we should try to make one the negative of the other so that, when added to each other, they cancel out. Namely, we need to solve $x_1 - \mu = -(x_2 - \mu) = \mu - x_2$. These are equal exactly when $\mu = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$. Intuitively, this makes a lot of sense, as the standard normal PDF is symmetric, so if we can center the normal distribution between them, the densities at those points will be equal. With the specified values, the answer is $-1$.

questions.title: Marble Transfer II
questions.problem: You have two bins in front of you, say $1$ and $2$. Bin $i$ has $r_i$ red and $b_i$ blue marbles inside. $1$ marble uniformly at random is selected from bin $1$ and is transferred to bin $2$. Afterwards, one bin is selected uniformly at random, and a marble from that bin is also uniformly at random selected. Find the probability that the marble drawn is blue when $r_1 = 4, b_1 = 3, r_2 = 5,$ and $b_2 = 3$.
questions.solution: The probability of drawing a blue marble is dependent on the color of the marble that is transferred from bin $1$. Therefore, the key idea is to condition on the color of the marble that is drawn from urn $1$. Let $B_1$ and $R_1$ be the events that a blue and red marble, respectively, are drawn from urn $1$. Similarly, let $B_2$ be the event that a blue marble is drawn on the second trial. Then $\prob{B_2} = \prob{B_2 \mid B_1}\prob{B_1} + \prob{B_2 \mid R_1}\prob{R_1}$. Since the marbles are drawn uniformly at random from bin $1$, $\prob{B_1} = \dfrac{b_1}{r_1 + b_1}$ and $\prob{R_1} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_1 + b_1}$. Now, we compute the conditionals. If a blue marble is transferred to bin $2$, there are $b_2 + 1$ blue and $r_2$ red marbles in bin $2$, while there are $b_1 - 1$ blue and $r_1$ red marbles in bin $1$. We now have to condition a second time on which bin you end up randomly selecting from. Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be the events that you select from bins $1$ and $2$, respectively. We have that $\prob{B_2 \mid B_1} = \prob{B_2 \mid B_1 \cap S_1}\prob{S_1} + \prob{B_2 \mid B_1 \cap S_2}\prob{S_2}$. We know that $\prob{S_1} = \prob{S_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ by the fact that the bin is selected uniformly at random. Then, given you select bin $1$, the probability of a blue is $\prob{B_2 \mid B_1 \cap S_1} = \dfrac{b_1 - 1}{b_1 + r_1 - 1}$ by the above values. Similarly, if you select from bin $2$, $\prob{B_2 \mid B_1 \cap S_2} = \dfrac{b_2 + 1}{b_2 + r_2 + 1}$. Therefore, $\prob{B_2 \mid B_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{b_1 - 1}{b_1 + r_1 -1} + \dfrac{b_2+1}{b_2 + r_2 + 1}\right]$. We now repeat the same paradigm to compute $\prob{B_2 \mid R_1}$. In particular, we must condition on whether we draw from bin $1$ or $2$ after the transfer. If we transfer a red, there are $b_1$ blue and $r_1 - 1$ red marbles in bin $1$, while there are $b_2$ blue and $r_2 + 1$ red marbles in bin $2$. Using the same notation, $\prob{B_2 \mid R_1} = \prob{B_2 \mid R_1 \cap S_1}\prob{S_1} + \prob{B_2 \mid R_1 \cap S_2}\prob{S_2}$. If a red marble is transferred and we select from bin $1$, the probability of a blue marble is $\prob{B_2 \mid R_1 \cap S_1} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_1 + r_1 - 1}$ by utilizing the counts above. Similarly, if we select from bin $2$, the probability is $\prob{B_2 \mid R_1 \cap S_2} = \dfrac{b_2}{b_2 + r_2 + 1}$. Plugging these values in, $\prob{B_2 \mid R_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{b_1}{b_1 + r_1 - 1} +\dfrac{b_2}{b_2 + r_2 + 1}\right]$. Plugging all of these values into the original Law of Total Probability expression, $\prob{B_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{2(b_1 + r_1)}\left[\dfrac{b_1 - 1}{b_1 + r_1 -1} + \dfrac{b_2+1}{b_2 + r_2 + 1}\right] + \dfrac{r_1}{2(b_1 + r_1)}\left[\dfrac{b_1}{b_1 + r_1 - 1} +\dfrac{b_2}{b_2 + r_2 + 1}\right]$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{17}{42}$.

questions.title: Unfair Coin?
questions.problem: There are $n+1$ coins in a box. $n \geq 1$ of these are fair, while one is double-headed. A coin is uniformly at random taken out and flipped $k \geq 1$ times. All of these flips appear heads. Find the probability that the double-headed coin was taken from the box when $n = 96$ and $k = 6$.
questions.solution: You are given information here about the flips, so use Bayes' rule to update your prior probability. Let $D$ be the event that the double-headed coin was selected. Similarly, let $H_k$ be the event that all $k$ flips of the selected coin were heads. These represent the events that we are given information about and the event that we want to compute the probability of. The statement we want to compute is $\prob{D \mid H_k} = \dfrac{\prob{D \cap H_k}}{\prob{H_k}}$. On the numerator, we know how to compute this probability if we are given that the double-headed coin is selected, so we should write $\prob{D \mid H_k} = \prob{H_k \mid D}\prob{D}$. Since the coin is selected uniformly at random, $\prob{D} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$. Similarly, given we selected the double-headed coin, the coin always landed heads, so $\prob{H_k \mid D} = 1$. For the denominator, we use the Law of Total Probability to condition on what coin was selected, as we know how to compute these probabilities once the coin is fixed. Namely, $\prob{H_k} = \prob{H_k \mid D}\prob{D} + \prob{H_k \mid D^c}\prob{D^c}$. We already computed $\prob{D} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$, meaning $\prob{D^c} = \dfrac{n}{n+1}$. $\prob{H_k \mid  D} = 1$ is inherited from the numerator. Given we select a fair coin, there is a probability $1/2$ per flip of obtaining a heads, so the probability of obtaining $k$ consecutive heads on a fair coin is $\prob{H_k \mid D^c} = \dfrac{1}{2^k}$. Plugging these values into the conditional probability formula, we have $\prob{D \mid H_k} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{n+1} \cdot 1}{\frac{1}{n+1} \cdot 1 + \frac{n}{n+1} \cdot \frac{1}{2^k}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \frac{n}{2^k}} = \dfrac{2^k}{2^k + n}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{2}{5}$.

questions.title: Distinct Wins
questions.problem: $n \geq 2$ teams play in a round-robin style tournament. This means that every team plays every other team exactly once. Suppose that every team is equally likely to beat any other team in a given match. Each team keeps track of how many wins they have. Find the probability that every team has won a distinct number of games at the end of the tournament when $n = 6$. Round to the nearest hundred-thousandth.
questions.solution: We must compute the total number of outcomes where the teams win a distinct number of games, and divide it by the total number of outcomes of the tournament. This can be done since each outcome is equally likely, as the question presumes that every team is equally skilled. We start with the latter, as it is easier to compute. The number of matches in the tournament is $\binom{n}{2}$, as every single pair of teams plays against each other once, and $\binom{n}{2}$ is the number of pairs that can be formed. In each game, there are $2$ outcomes: win or loss, so there are $2^{\binom{n}{2}}$ total outcomes of the tournament that are equally likely. To compute the total number of ways in which the teams win a distinct number of games, we must observe what this statement actually means. Each team plays $n-1$ games, so for each team to have won a distinct number of games, there must be a team that won $0,1,\dots, n-1$ games. Assigning the labels of how many games each team won fixes the outcome of the tournament, as there must be a unique configuration of wins/losses for each team that results in these counts of wins/losses. Furthermore, note that $0 + 1 + \dots + n-1 = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \binom{n}{2}$, so these labels being assigned to each team truly do fix the outcome of the tournament. As there are $n$ teams and $n$ labels, there are $n!$ ways to permute the labels to the teams, as each team must receive exactly $1$ label. Thus, the probability of this event is $\dfrac{n!}{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}$. With $n = 6$, the approximate probability is $0.02197$.

questions.title: Derivative Counter
questions.problem: Let $f: \mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where $f = f(x_1,\dots, x_N)$ is a smooth function (i.e. partial derivatives exist of all orders). How many $k$th order partial derivatives does $f$ have when $N = 8$ and $k = 6$? Some examples are $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1^6}$ and $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1^2\partial x_2^3\partial x_3}$.
questions.solution: The order of the partial derivative is $k$, which means that the sum of the orders of the partials with respect to each component is $k$. In other words, we can write a partial derivative of order $k$ in the form $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1^{n_1}\dots \partial x_N^{n_N}}$, where $n_1 + \dots + n_N = k$. Namely, we must also have that the $n_i$ are non-negative integers. Thus, the number of order $k$ partial derivatives of $f$ is just the number of non-negative integer solutions to the above equation, as we clearly see that if $(n_1,\dots, n_N)$ is a solution, then $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1^{n_1}\dots \partial x_N^{n_N}}$ is an order $k$ partial derivative, and vice versa. By stars and bars, the number of solutions is $\binom{N+k-1}{N-1}$. With the specific values, the solution is $\binom{13}{7} = 1716$.

questions.title: Greater Roll
questions.problem: Marcus rolls a fair standard $n-$sided die with the values $1-n$ on the sides. He records the value he rolled. Afterwards, he continues rolling the die until he obtains a value at least as large as the first roll. Let $N$ be the number of rolls after the first that he performs. Find $\ev{N}$ when $n = 6$.
questions.solution: The number of times that Marcus will need to roll the die is highly dependent on the value he rolls on the first turn. Therefore, computing the conditional expectation given the roll of the first term would remove a source of randomness and make computing this quantity easier. Let $X_1$ be the value of the first roll. By Law of Total Expectation, $\ev{N} = \ev{\ev{N \mid X_1}}$. Given $X_1$, Marcus must roll a value at least $X_1$ on another roll. There are $n+1 - X_1$ integers in the interval $X_1,X_1+1,\dots,N$ by direct counting, so the probability per turn that Marcus rolls a value at least $X_1$ is $1 - \frac{X_1 - 1}{n}$, as the die is fair. As $N$ counts the number of rolls needed to observe the first value at least $X_1$, $N \mid X_1$ must be Geometric with the above parameter. In other words, $N \mid X_1 \sim \geom{1 - \frac{X_1-1}{n}}$. This means $\ev{N \mid X_1} = \frac{n}{n-X_1 +1}$. Therefore, $\ev{N} = \ev{\dfrac{n}{n-X_1+1}} = n\ev{\dfrac{1}{(n+1)-X_1}}$. To compute the remaining expected value, we can just use LOTUS. Namely, we know $\ev{\dfrac{1}{n+1-X_1}} = \sum_{k=1}^n \dfrac{1}{n+1-k} \cdot \prob{X_1 = k} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \dfrac{1}{n+1-k} = \dfrac{1}{n}\left[\dfrac{1}{n} + \dots \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{1}\right] = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \dfrac{1}{k}$. Therefore, $\ev{T} = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^n \dfrac{1}{k}$ by plugging back in. With $n = 6$, the answer is $\dfrac{49}{20}$.

questions.title: Prime Divisor
questions.problem: Let $N = p_1^{e_1}\dots p_r^{e_r}$ be the prime factorization of $N$, where $e_i \geq 1$ for all $i$. Define $S$ as the set of all positive divisors of $N$. Find the probability that a randomly selected element of $S$ is divisible by $n = p_1^{f_1}\dots p_r^{f_r}$, where $0 \leq f_i \leq e_i$ for each $i$. Answer this when $N = 14^{69}$ and $n = 14^{50}$.
questions.solution: The key thing to note is that picking a uniformly random element of $S$ is equivalent to picking a uniformly random exponent for each of the $p_i$ independently. This is because the set $S = \{p_1^{m_1}\dots p_r^{m_r} : 0 \leq m_i \leq e_i\}$. In other words, if the primes are removed, it has all $r-$tuples $(m_1,\dots, m_r)$ with $0 \leq m_i \leq e_i$. Thus, the "joint support" of this random point is a $r-$dimensional rectangle on the lattice points, so the dimensions are independent in each direction. For $n$ to divide the chosen element, the power of $p_i$ must be at least $f_i$ for each $i$. In other words, if $s \in S$ is selected such that $s = p_1^{a_1}\dots p_r^{a_r}$, $n \mid a$ if and only if $f_i \leq a_i$ for all $i$. This is because you could write $s = n \cdot p_1^{a_1 - f_1}\dots p_r^{a_r - f_r}$, and the second term is an integer exactly when $a_i - f_i \geq 0$ (so that you don't have any reciprocals) i.e. $a_i \geq f_i$. Thus, if $A_i$ is the event that $a_i \geq f_i$, we want $\displaystyle \prob{\bigcap_{i=1}^r A_i} = \prod_{i=1}^r \prob{A_i}$. The above is by independence. $\prob{A_i}$ is fairly easily computed. This just means that $a_i$, which is uniform between $0$ and $e_i$ (inclusive of both), is at least $f_i$. There are $e_i - (f_i - 1)$ integers that are between $f_i$ and $e_i$, inclusive of both, and there are $e_i+1$ total integers from $0$ to $e_i$. Thus, as the exponent is selected uniformly at random, $\prob{A_i} = 1 - \frac{f_i - 1}{e_i + 1}$. Plugging this in, our final probability is $\prod_{i=1}^r \left(1 - \dfrac{f_i-1}{e_1 + 1}\right)$. With our specific numbers, $N = 14^{69} = 2^{69} \cdot 5^{69}$ and $n = 14^{50} = 2^{50} \cdot 7^{50}$, so $f_1 = f_2 = 50$ and $e_1 = e_2 = 69$, so the answer is $\left(1 - \dfrac{49}{70}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{100}$.

questions.title: Even Heads
questions.problem: Suppose that you flip $$$n$$$ coins that each have a probability 0 < < 1 $0 < p < 1$ of landing heads. Find the probability that an even amount of heads appear when = 6 $n = 6$ and = 1 / 3 $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: Let $$$$$p$$$$$ $$$$$$n$$$$$$ be the probability that when n coins are flipped, there are an even amount of heads. The probability for n heads is directly related to the probability for − $1$ n−1 heads, as you are just appending on another coin. Therefore, it's best to derive a recurrence relation for p n . We can compute p n by conditioning on the outcome of the nth coin. If the nth coin is heads (which occurs with probability p), then there must be an odd amount of heads that appear in the other − 1 n−1 flips for the total number of heads to be even. This occurs with probability 1 − − 1 1−p n−1 , as − 1 p n−1 is the probability of an even amount of heads in − 1 n−1 flips. Otherwise, with probability 1 − 1−p, the nth coin is tails, and there must be an even amount of heads in the other − 1 n−1 flips to have an even total. This occurs with probability − 1 p n−1 . Using the Law of Total Probability, we have the relationship = ( 1 − − 1 ) + ( 1 − ) − 1 = + ( 1 − 2 ) − 1 p n =p(1−p n−1 )+(1−p)p n−1 =p+(1−2p)p n−1 The initial condition is 1 = 1 − p 1 =1−p, as you have $$0$$ 0 heads with probability 1 − 1−p and 1 1 head with probability p. If there was no p in the recurrence above, it would be pretty easy to solve. Thus, to eliminate this p, as it is constant, we can consider − − 1 p n −p n−1 , as both of those will have the constant of p inside. Namely, we will obtain − − 1 = [ + ( 1 − 2 ) − 1 ] − [ + ( 1 − 2 ) − 2 ] = ( 1 − 2 ) ( − 1 − − 2 ) p n −p n−1 =[p+(1−2p)p n−1 ]−[p+(1−2p)p n−2 ]=(1−2p)(p n−1 −p n−2 ) This gives us a much easier recurrence relation to work with. We can now iterate this to say that − 1 − − 2 = ( 1 − 2 ) ( − 2 − − 3 ) p n−1 −p n−2 =(1−2p)(p n−2 −p n−3 ), and so on, until we reach 1 − 0 p 1 −p 0 . The number of iterations is − 1 n−1, as we go from − − 1 p n −p n−1 to 1 − 0 p 1 −p 0 and = ( − 1 ) + 1 n=(n−1)+1, so there must be − 1 n−1 iterations. Namely, this yields − − 1 = ( 1 − 2 ) − 1 ( 1 − 0 ) p n −p n−1 =(1−2p) n−1 (p 1 −p 0 ). We know 1 = 1 − p 1 =1−p from above. We can set 0 = 1 p 0 =1 for consistency, as if no coins are flipped, there are always 0 0 heads. Therefore, − − 1 = − ( 1 − 2 ) − 1 p n −p n−1 =−p(1−2p) n−1 , which can be rearranged to = − 1 − ( 1 − 2 ) − 1 p n =p n−1 −p(1−2p) n−1 . This gives us a recurrence that is now easier to deal with, as we have a constant at back that is dependent on n. questions.title: Over Half Heads
questions.problem: A fair coi$$n$$ is flipped 2 − 1 2n−1 times for some positive integer n. Find the probability that at least n heads appear when = 10 $n = 10$.
questions.solution: Si$$$$$n$$$$$ce heads and tails are equally li$$k$$ely, we can use this symmetry to simplify our calculation greatly. Consider any sequence that has ≤ ≤ 2 − $$1$$ n≤k≤2n−1 heads in it. We can pair this sequence with the sequence that has all of the heads and tails inverted. For example, with = 3 $n = 3$, the sequence $HHTHT$ gets matched to $TTHTH$. These two sequences are equally likely, as the coin is fair. Furthermore, note that the sequence that is paired with the one we selected has at most − 1 n−1 heads, as it would be ( 2 − 1 ) − (2n−1)−k heads, and since ≤ ≤ 2 − 1 n≤k≤2n−1, 0 ≤ ( 2 − 1 ) − ≤ − 1 0≤(2n−1)−k≤n−1, so it lies in the complement of the event that we want to compute the probability of. Since 2 − 1 2n−1 is odd, k and ( 2 − 1 ) − (2n−1)−k will never overlap with one another, as k must be an integer. We have created a one-to-one pairing between sequences with at least n heads and less than n heads. Since all the sequences are equally likely and we have a one-to-one matching between the sample points (i.e. sequences) that compose the events, the two events must have the same probability. The two events are also exhaustive, as every single sequence either has less than n or at least n heads in it. Thus, the sum of the probabilities of the events above must be 1 1. Since their probabilities are equal and sum to 1 1, both of them must have probability 1 / 2 $$1/2$$. In particular, this implies that the probability of at least n heads is 1 / 2 1/2.

Therefore, the number of groups is the number of record low speeds as we scan the cars from the first car (front) to the last.
