questions.title: Couple Pairs II
questions.problem: $n$ heterosexual married couples ($1$ male and $1$ female) are standing in a line. They all scatter around and form $n$ pairs uniformly at random. Find the variance of the number of couples that are paired up together when $n = 5$. Pairs can consist of members of the same gender.
questions.solution: We are looking to count the variance of number of some events that are not independent, so the best approach is to write this random variable as a sum of indicators and use the variance of a sum formula. Arbitrarily label the couples $1-n$, and let $P_i$ be the indicator that couple $i$ is paired up together. $T = P_1 + \dots + P_n$ gives the total number of couples that are paired up together. By the variance of a sum formula, $\var{T} = \var{P_1 + \dots P_n} = \sum_{i=1}^n \var{P_i} + \sum_{i \neq j} \cov{P_i}{P_j}$. Let's start with the first sum. Recall from "Couple Pairs I" that the random variables $P_1,\dots, P_n$ are exchangeable, so they have identical distributions. In particular, $P_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}\left(\dfrac{1}{2n-1}\right)$, as there is probability $\dfrac{1}{2n-1}$ of $P_i = 1$ i.e. couple $1$ is paired together; otherwise, $P_i = 0$. Therefore, $\var{P_i} = \dfrac{1}{2n-1} \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2n-1}\right) = \dfrac{2n-2}{(2n-1)^2}$. For the covariance terms, by the exchangeability of the $P_i$ random variables, $\cov{P_i}{P_j} = \cov{P_1}{P_2}$ for $i \neq j$. Therefore, we can just compute $\cov{P_1}{P_2}$. By using the common covariance formula, $\cov{P_1}{P_2} = \ev{P_1P_2} - \ev{P_1}\ev{P_2}$. From "Couple Pairs I", $\ev{P_1} = \ev{P_2} = \dfrac{1}{2n-1}$. The first term is the probability that both couples $1$ and $2$ are paired together. We know that the probability couple $1$ is paired together is $\dfrac{1}{2n-1}$. Once couple $1$ is paired together, we can play the same game with couple $2$. Namely, the husband in couple $2$ will have $2n-3$ potential partners remaining (couple $1$ is removed and there are $n-1$ couples left). Of these $2n-3$, exactly $1$ of them is his wife, so the conditional probability of couple $2$ also being paired together is $\dfrac{1}{2n-3}$. Thus, the probability that both couples $1$ and $2$ are paired together is $\ev{P_1P_2} = \dfrac{1}{2n-1} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2n-3}$. Plugging these in, $\cov{P_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{1}{(2n-1)(2n-3)} - \dfrac{1}{(2n-1)^2} = \dfrac{2}{(2n-1)^2(2n-3)}$. Plugging all of these into the sums from above, $\var{T} = n \cdot \dfrac{2n-2}{(2n-1)^2} + n(n-1) \cdot \dfrac{2}{(2n-1)^2(2n-3)} = \dfrac{2n(n-1)(2n-3) + 2n(n-1)}{(2n-1)^2(2n-3)} = \dfrac{4n(n-1)^2}{(2n-1)^2(2n-3)}$. With the specific values, the answer is $\dfrac{320}{567}$.

questions.title: Uniform Absolute Difference
questions.problem: Suppose that $X,Y \sim \unif{a}{b}$ IID for $a < b$. Compute $\ev{|X-Y|}$ for $a = 2$ and $b = 5$.
questions.solution: Note that $X = a + (b-a)U_1$ and $Y = a + (b-a)U_2$ for $U_1,U_2\sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID, as this transformation is what generates the $\unif{a}{b}$ distribution. We want to do this because working on the interval $(0,1)$ is easier. Plugging these in for $X$ and $Y$, we get $\ev{|X-Y|} = \ev{|a + (b-a)U_1 - (a + (b-a)U_2)|} = \ev{|(b-a)(U_1 - U_2)|} = |b-a|\ev{|U_1 - U_2|} = (b-a)\ev{|U_1 - U_2|}$. All that remains is to compute $\ev{|U_1 - U_2|}$, where $U_1,U_2 \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. The easiest way to do it is by the following thought experiment. Since $U_1,U_2 \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID, these can be placed on the interval $(0,1)$. $|U_1 - U_2|$ is the length of the interval between $U_1$ and $U_2$. Since these are uniform random variables, the two uniform random variables split up the unit interval into $3$ equally sized pieces on average. Thus, as $|U_1 - U_2|$ is one of these pieces, $\ev{|U_1 - U_2|} = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Other approaches to computing $\ev{|U_1 - U_2|}$ include direct LOTUS and also by the tail integral. For example, the event $\{|U_1 - U_2| \geq x\}$ is the union of two triangles whose side lengths are $1-x$. This can be seen by decomposing the event $\{|U_1 - U_2| \geq x\} = \{U_1 - U_2 \geq x\} \cup \{U_1 - U_2 \leq -x\}$ and plotting it in the plane. The area of each of these triangles would be $\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1-x)^2$, so the area of the region $\{|U_1 - U_2| \geq x\}$ is $(1-x)^2$. The total area of the support of $U_1$ and $U_2$ is $1$, so $\prob{|U_1 - U_2| \geq x} = (1-x)^2$. Using the tail integral formula for expected value, $\ev{|U_1 - U_2|} = \int_0^1 \prob{|U_1 - U_2| \geq x}dx = \int_0^1 (1-x)^2 dx  = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Regardless of how it is computed, we get that $\ev{|X-Y|} = \dfrac{b-a}{3}$. With the specific values, the answer is $1$.

questions.title: Many Primes Rolled
questions.problem: Abby and Brock each roll standard fair $6$-sided dice. Abby rolls her die $n$ times, while Brock rolls his die $n+1$ times. Find the probability that Brock rolls strictly more prime integers than Abby when $n = 100$.
questions.solution: $2,3,$ and $5$ are the prime integers that could be obtained on each roll. Therefore, $3$ of the $6$ equally likely outcomes on the dice are prime, meaning there is probability $1/2$ per roll of obtaining a prime integer. Since there is probability $1/2$ per roll, all sequences of prime/non-prime integers are equally likely, as we are only identifying each roll by whether it is prime or not. Using this fairness, we can exploit some symmetry within the first $n$ rolls, as both Abby and Brock roll $n$ times. In the first $n$ rolls, there is some positive probability, say $p$, of Abby and Brock having an equal number of primes rolled. Afterwards, given that they haven't rolled an equal number of prime integers, Abby and Brock are equally likely to be the person that has more primes rolled, as each person is rolling an identical die, so the number of primes that each person rolls are IID random variables, and hence exchangeable. This also makes intuitive sense, as given that they haven't rolled the same number of heads, since they are both rolling the same die, there is no reason to believe that one is more likely than the other to have more primes within $n$ rolls. Thus, the probability that Brock has strictly more primes in the first $n$ rolls than Abby is $\frac{1-p}{2}$, as $1-p$ is the probability Brock and Abby don't have an equal number of primes, and given they don't have equal numbers of primes, Brock has probability $1/2$ of having more primes. Similarly, the probability that Abby has strictly more primes than Brock in the first $n$ rolls is $\frac{1-p}{2}$. If Brock has strictly more primes than Abby in the first $n$ rolls, then no matter what happens on his last roll, he will have more primes than Abby in total, so his conditional probability of having more primes in this case is $1$. If Abby has strictly more primes than Brock after $n$ rolls, then no matter what happens on Brock's last roll, he can't have more primes than Abby, so his conditional probability of winning is $0$ in this case. Lastly, if they have equal amounts of primes between then in the first $n$ rolls, then with probability $1/2$, Brock rolls a prime integer on the last roll, giving him strictly more heads. Thus, using the Law of Total Probability, the total probability of Brock having strictly more primes than Abby is $\dfrac{1-p}{2} \cdot 1 + \dfrac{1-p}{2} \cdot 0 + p \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. This result is independent of $n$.

questions.title: Preside
questions.problem: A standard fair $n$-sided die is rolled until the value $n$ appears. Given that the first $n$ appears before the first $1$, find the expected number of times the die was rolled when $n = 8$.
questions.solution: The first task is to convert this into a probabilistic problem. Let $N_i$ be the random variable that represents the trial of the first occurrence of side $1 \leq i \leq n$. We want random variables set up like this, as we are looking to compute the expected number of trials until side $n$ was rolled given the information $N_n < N_1$ i.e. it took less trials to roll the first $n$ than $1$. Mathematically, this is $\ev{N_n \mid N_n < N_1}$. To compute this, the easiest way is by interpreting this conditional expectation as the expected value of the conditional distribution of $N_n \mid N_n < N_1$. Namely, this implies $\ev{N_n \mid N_n < N_1} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k\prob{N_n = k \mid N_n < N_1}$. We now compute the conditional probability. Namely, this is $\prob{N_n = k \mid N_n < N_1} = \dfrac{\prob{N_n = n \cap N_n < N_1}}{\prob{N_n < N_1}}$. We start with computing the numerator. Since the die is fair, we can compute the total number of sequences satisfying our event and divide by the total number of sequences. For $N_n = k$, the $n$th roll must be the first occurrence of the value $n$. Thus, the $k$th spot is fixed as $n$. In the first $k-1$ spots, any value besides $1$ and $n$ can appear, as trial $k$ is the first time $n$ appears, and the information given is that the first $n$ appears before the first $1$, so any of the other $n-2$ values can appear on each of the first $k-1$ rolls. Thus, this implies that there are $(n-2)^{k-1}$ sequences where the $k$th roll is $n$ and the first $k-1$ rolls are anything besides $1$ and $n$. The total number of outcomes is $n^k$, as there are $n$ options for each of the $k$ rolls, so the numerator is just $\prob{N_n = k \cap N_n < N_1} = \dfrac{(n-2)^{k-1}}{n^k} = \dfrac{1}{n} \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{2}{n}\right)^{k-1}$. To compute the denominator, note that $1$ and $n$ are equally likely to appear on each roll of the die. Therefore, conditioned on a roll being either $1$ or $n$, it's equally likely to be either $1$ or $n$, so the probability that the first $n$ comes before the first $1$ is just $\dfrac{1}{2}$, as each is equally likely to appear first. Plugging both of these in, $\prob{N_n = k \mid N_n < N_1} = \dfrac{2}{n} \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{2}{n}\right)^{k-1}$. In other words, $N_n \mid N_n < N_1 \sim \geom{2/n}$, as this is the form of the PMF above. Now that we know this, computing the conditional expectation is quite easy, as we know formulas for the geometric distribution. Namely, $\ev{N_n \mid N_n < N_1} = \dfrac{n}{2}$. With $n = 8$, the answer is $4$.

questions.title: Prize Finder II
questions.problem: You have $n \geq 1$ boxes in front of you. A prize of $\$p$ is hidden in $1 \leq k \leq n$ of the boxes uniformly at random. You open boxes one-at-a-time until you find the prize. You are also required to pay a fee of $\$x$ to open each box. What value of $x$ makes the expected profit from opening these boxes $0$ when $n = 9, k = 2$ and $p = 50$?
questions.solution: As there is more than one box with a prize now, the argument from "Prize Finder I" will not work. You are looking for the expected number of boxes that need to be opened until one with a prize inside is opened, as this is directly related to the expected cost. The $k$ boxes that have prizes inside can be treated as "dividers" of the sequence of opening. We want to do this because we are really sampling without replacement from the collection of boxes, which could really be seen as dealing without replacement from a deck of cards. In particular, we can take the approach of the "First Ace" problem in solving this. The $k$ boxes with prize money are dividers, which means that there are $n-k$ boxes left that do not have dividers. The $k$ boxes divide up the drawing process into $k+1$ regions of equal size in expectation by exchangeability, so there would be $\frac{n-k}{k+1}$ boxes per region, on average. Thus, in the region before the first box with a prize, there are $\frac{n-k}{k+1}$ boxes opened on average. After, we must add $1$ for the box with the prize money itself to find the expected number of boxes that must be opened until the prize money is obtained. This implies there are $\frac{n+1}{k+1}$ boxes opened on average until the first box with a prize is opened. This means the expected cost of obtaining the prize money is $\frac{n+1}{k+1}x$, as each box costs $\$x$ to open. The prize money is $\$p$ from opening the box. Therefore, for the expected profit to be $0$, the expected cost must be equal to the prize, which means $\frac{n+1}{k+1}x = p$. By rearrangement, $x = \frac{(k+1)p}{n+1}$. With the specified values, the answer is $15$.

questions.title: Prize Finder III
questions.problem: You have $n \geq 1$ boxes in front of you. There are $1 \leq k \leq n$ boxes with prizes in them of varying amounts. The $k$ prize amounts are $p_1,\dots, p_k$. You open boxes one-at-a-time until you find the prize. You are also required to pay a fee of $\\$ to open each box. What value of $x$ makes the expected profit from opening these boxes $0$ when $n = 9, k = 2$ and $p_i = 40i, i = 1,2$?
questions.solution: As there is more than one box with a prize now, the argument from "Prize Finder I" will not work. You are looking for the expected number of boxes that need to be opened until one with a prize inside is opened, as this is directly related to the expected cost. The $k$ boxes that have prizes inside can be treated as "dividers" of the sequence of opening. We want to do this because we are really sampling without replacement from the collection of boxes, which could really be seen as dealing without replacement from a deck of cards. In particular, we can take the approach of the "First Ace" problem in solving this. The $k$ boxes with prize money are dividers, which means that there are $n-k$ boxes left that do not have dividers. The $k$ boxes divide up the drawing process into $k+1$ regions of equal size in expectation by exchangeability, so there would be $\frac{n-k}{k+1}$ boxes per region, on average. Thus, in the region before the first box with a prize, there are $\frac{n-k}{k+1}$ boxes opened on average. After, we must add $1$ for the box with the prize money itself to find the expected number of boxes that must be opened until the prize money is obtained. This implies there are $\frac{n+1}{k+1}$ boxes opened on average until the first box with a prize is opened. This means the expected cost of obtaining the prize money is $\frac{n+1}{k+1}x$, as each box costs $\\$ to open. Given that you opened a box with prize money, each possible amount is equally likely to appear, so the expected prize in the box is $\displaystyle \dfrac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k p_i$. Therefore, for the expected profit to be $0$, the expected cost must be equal to the expected prize, which means $\dfrac{n+1}{k+1}x = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k p_i$. By rearrangement, $x = \displaystyle \dfrac{k+1}{(n+1)k}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i$. With the specified values, the answer is $18$.

questions.title: Intersected Set I
questions.problem: Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets that are independently and uniformly at random selected from $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$. Find the probability that $A$ and $B$ are not disjoint when $n = 4$.
questions.solution:
Every element of $[n]$ is equally likely to be in or not in each of $A$ and $B$, as the subsets are selected uniformly at random. Since $A$ and $B$ are selected from $[n]$ independently, for each $1 \leq i \leq n$, the events $\{i \in A\}$ and $\{i \in B\}$ are independent. Furthermore, since there are no restrictions on the elements that can or can't be in each of the subsets, for $i 
eq j$, the events $\{i \in A\}$ and $\{j \in A\}$ for $i 
eq j$ are also independent. The two statements above imply that for each $1 \leq i \leq n$, $i$ is equally likely to be in $A \cap B, A \cap B^c, A^c \cap B,$ or $A^c \cap B^c$, independently of all other $j 
eq i$. There are $4$ such equally likely options here. We want the probability that at least one $1 \leq i \leq n$ belongs to $A \cap B$, as this would imply that the intersection is non-empty. Since this is an "at least" statement, working the complement is typically nicer, as this event is just the event that no elements belong to $A \cap B$. In other words, each $1 \leq i \leq n$ belongs to either $A \cap B^c, A^c \cap B,$ or $A^c \cap B^c$. These are $3$ of the $4$ equally likely options for each element, so the probability that each individual element $i$ belongs to one of these three sets is $\dfrac{3}{4}$. Since there are $n$ elements in $[n]$, the probability that all $n$ elements are not in $A \cap B$ i.e. that $A \cap B$ is empty is $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}ight)^n$. Therefore, the probability that at least one element belongs to $A \cap B$ is $1 - \left(\dfrac{3}{4}ight)^n$. For $n = 4$, the answer is $\dfrac{175}{256}$.

questions.title: Intersected Set II
questions.problem: Let $A_1,\dots, A_r$ be subsets that are independently and uniformly at random selected from $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$. Find the probability that $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^r A_i$ is not empty when $r = 3$ and $n = 4$.
questions.solution: Every element of $[n]$ is equally likely to be in or not in each of $A_i$, as the subsets are selected uniformly at random. Since the $A_i$ subsets are selected from $[n]$ independently, for each $1 \leq m \leq n$, the events $\{m \in A_i\}$ and $\{m \in A_j\}$ for $i \neq j$ are independent. Furthermore, since there are no restrictions on the elements that can or can't be in each of the subsets, for $m_1 \neq m_2$ and $i$ fixed, the events $\{m_1 \in A_i\}$ and $\{m_2 \in A_i\}$ are also independent. The two statements above imply that for each $1 \leq i \leq n$, $i$ is equally likely to be in any sets in the form $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^r O_i$, where $O_i = A_i$ or $A_i^c$. In simple terms, since each element is equally likely to be in or not be in each set, each element is equally likely to belong to any intersection of all $r$ events/their complements. In the intersection above, we must count how many equally likely options there are for each element. Each of the $O_i$ has two options: $A_i$ or $A_i^c$, so as there are $r$ such sets being intersected, there are $2^r$ possible subsets that are equally likely. We want the probability that at least one $1 \leq i \leq n$ belongs to $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^r A_i$, as this would imply that the intersection is non-empty. Since this is an "at least" statement, working the complement is typically nicer, as this event is just the event that no elements belong to this intersection. In other words, each $1 \leq i \leq n$ belongs to one of the other $2^r - 1$ equally likely subsets. As there are $2^r$ total options, the probability that each individual element $i$ belongs to one of these other sets is $\frac{2^r - 1}{2^r} = 1 - \frac{1}{2^r}$. Since there are $n$ elements in $[n]$, the probability that all $n$ elements are not in $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^r A_i$ i.e. that this intersection is empty is $\left(1 - \frac{1}{2^r}\right)^n$. Therefore, the probability that at least one element belongs to $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^r A_i$ is $1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^r}\right)^n$. For the specified values, the answer is $1 - \left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^4 = \dfrac{1695}{4096}$.

questions.title: Midpoint
questions.problem: Suppose $X_1,X_2 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ IID. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the minimum and maximum order statistics, respectively. Find the probability that the range of $X_1$ and $X_2$ i.e. $O_2 - O_1$ is larger than their midpoint (defined as $\frac{O_1 + O_2}{2}$) when $\lambda = 3$
questions.solution: We want $\mathbb{P}\left[O_2 - O_1 > \dfrac{X_1 + X_2}{2}\right]$. The trick here is that, regardless of the actual values of $X_1$ and $X_2$, $X_1$ corresponds to one of $O_1$ or $O_2$, while $X_2$ corresponds to the other. Thus, $O_1 + O_2 = X_1 + X_2$ no matter what. Therefore, this is equal to $\mathbb{P}\left[O_2 - O_1 > \dfrac{O_1 + O_2}{2}\right]$. Rearranging the previous expression, we must compute $\mathbb{P}[O_2 > 3O_1]$. Since $O_1$ and $O_2$ are not independent, as $O_2 > O_1$ by definition, working with their marginal PDFs will not work. Instead the best approach is to work with their joint PDF, which can be obtained via the order statistics formulas, and integrate over the respective region for that. The joint PDF of the order statistics, by the order statistics formula, is given by $f_{O_1.O_2}(x,y) = \binom{2}{0,1,0,1,0}f(x)f(y)I_{(0,\infty)}(x)I_{(x,\infty)}(y)$. With $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, as $X_1,X_2 \sim \exponential{1}$ IID, we have $f(x,y) = 2\lambda^2e^{-\lambda(x+y)}I_{(0,\infty)}(x)I_{(x,\infty)}(y)$. Therefore, the probability is given by $\prob{O_2 > 3O_1} = \int_0^{\infty} \int_{3x}^{\infty} 2\lambda^2e^{-\lambda(x+y)} dydx = \int_0^{\infty} 2\lambda e^{-4\lambda x} dx = \dfrac{1}{2}$. This is independent of the value of $\lambda$, so our answer is $1/2$.

questions.title: Minecraft Speedrun II
questions.problem: $\textbf{BREAKING:}$ You're stuck in a Minecraft speedrun in 3D space from $(0,0,0)$ to $(x, y, z)$, but plot twist—you can only move forward, right, or up one block at a time. No diagonals, no Elytra, no Nether shortcuts. Just pure, unfiltered block-hopping. HOWEVER, you are now required to take one movement downwards ($-z$ direction). How many paths can you take? Solve this when $(x,y,z) = (2,4,6)$.
questions.solution: Each movement can be represented as $R,F,$ or $U$, representing a right, forward, or up movement. We know that to go from $(0,0,0)$ to $(x,y,z)$, there must be $x$ movements right, $y$ forward movements, and $z$ upwards movements if we only move right, forward, or upwards. However, we must also add in a downwards movement into the sequence. Thus, there is one $D$ representing a downwards movement and $z+1$ $U$s to represent upwards movements, so that the final position is $z$ in the vertical direction. Therefore, we are placing $x$ $R$s, $y$ $F$s, $1$ $D$, and $z+1$ $U$s onto $x+y+z + 2$ blanks. In other words, we can view a path as a string of length $x+y+z+2$ with the counts above of each letter. This implies that counting the number of paths is equal to counting the number of strings satisfying the above. By the multinomial coefficient, there are $\displaystyle \binom{x+y+z+1}{x,y,z+1,1} = \dfrac{(x+y+z+2)!}{x!y!(z+1)!1!}$ total such strings, and hence paths to $(x,y,z)$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{14!}{2!4!7!1!} = 360360$.

questions.title: Bust and Broke
questions.problem: You continually roll a fair $n$-sided die with the values $1$ to $n$ on the sides until you roll either $1$ or $n$ on the upface. If the upface is $1$, you get to cash out the sum of all of the upfaces up until that point (excluding the $1$). If the upface is $n$, you receive no payout. You do not have the option to stop before rolling either $1$ or $n$. Find your expected payout when $n = 8$.
questions.solution: This payout is a random sum of all of the rolls before the end. Thus, we need to set up such a sum. Let $X_i$ be the amount rolled on the $i$th turn, and let $N$ be the number of rolls needed to obtain either $1$ or $n$. $T = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} X_i$ gives the total amount obtained, as we don't include the value rolled on the $N$th turn (the turn that we stop). We actually receive this payout when $X_N = 1$ i.e. we stop on a $1$. We are looking to compute $\ev{T}$ in this question. As the amount we receive is dependent on whether the last roll is $1$ or $n$, we should condition on this. Therefore, we have $\ev{T} = \ev{T \mid X_N = 1}\prob{X_N = 1} + \ev{T \mid X_N = n}\prob{X_N = n}$. Since $X_N = 1$ or $n$ only (we only stop rolling on $1$ or $n$) and the die is fair, $\prob{X_N = 1} = \prob{X_N = n} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. If $X_N = n$, there is no payout, so $\ev{T \mid X_N = n} = 0$. Otherwise, if $X_N = 1$, we receive the payout, so $\ev{T \mid X_N = 1} = \ev{T} = \ev{\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} X_i} = \ev{N-1}\ev{X_1}$. The last term is by Wald's Identity. For $i < N$, $\ev{X_i}$ is just the expected value of a die that is not $1$ nor $n$. In other words, this is the expected value of a fair $n-2$ sided die with the values $2$ to $n-1$. This is discrete uniform over $\{2,\dots, n-1\}$, which has mean $\dfrac{(n-1)+2}{2} = \dfrac{n+1}{2}$. Since $N$ is the number of trials until either $1$ or $n$ appears, these appear with probability $2/n$ independently per trial. Thus, as $N$ counts the number of trials until this occurs, $N \sim \geom{2/n}$, so $\ev{N} = \dfrac{n}{2}$. This implies $\ev{T \mid X_N = 1} = \left(\dfrac{n}{2} - 1\right) \cdot \dfrac{n+1}{2}$. Therefore, plugging back into the formula for $\ev{T}$, we get $\ev{T} = \left(\dfrac{n}{2} - 1\right) \cdot \dfrac{n+1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} + 0 = \dfrac{n+1}{4}\left(\dfrac{n}{2} - 1\right)$. With $n = 8$, the answer is $\dfrac{27}{4}$.

questions.title: Sock Pairs
questions.problem: There are $n$ pairs of socks in a drawer. $0 \leq k \leq 2n$ socks are drawn out of the drawer. Find the expected number of pairs of socks that remain in the drawer when $n = 6$ and $k = 5$.
questions.solution: We are looking to compute the expected amount of dependent events that occur, so linearity of expectation is the best approach here. Namely, arbitrarily label the pairs $1-n$, and let $P_i$ be the indicator random variable that represents sock pair $i$ still being in the drawer after drawing out. We have that $T = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n P_i$ gives the total number of pairs that remain. Since the labels of the pairs were arbitrary, the random variables $P_1,\dots, P_n$ are exchangeable. This means that they are identically distributed, which implies, among other things, that the random variables all have the same mean, so by linearity of expectation, $\ev{T} = n\ev{P_1}$. $\ev{P_1}$ is the probability that pair $1$ remains in the drawer. For this to be true, the $k$ socks drawn must be from the other $2n-2$ socks that are not pair $1$. In other words, we pick $k$ socks from $2n-2$. As the drawing is uniformly at random, we can just count the number of ways to do this, and divide by the total number of ways to draw $k$ socks without restriction. There are $\binom{2n}{k}$ ways to pick out $k$ socks out of the drawer without restriction, as the order is irrelevant. The number of ways to pick $k$ socks that aren't pair $1$ is just $\binom{2n-2}{k}$, as we pick $k$ from the other $2n-2$ socks. Thus, the probability of having pair $1$ still in the drawer is $\ev{P_1} = \dfrac{\binom{2n-2}{k}}{\binom{2n}{k}}$. Plugging into the expected value statement, $\ev{T} = n \cdot \dfrac{\binom{2n-2}{k}}{\binom{2n}{k}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{21}{11}$.

questions.title: Which Quantity?
questions.problem: Suppose you roll a fair standard $6$-sided die $5$ times. Let $X_1,\dots, X_5$ be these rolls. Order the following quantities from smallest to largest: 1) $\ev{X_1^2}$, 2) $\ev{X_1X_2}$, 3) $\ev{X_{(3)}^2}$. Report your answer as the corresponding values concatenated smallest to largest.
questions.solution: The first simplification is to note that $\ev{X_1X_2} = \ev{X_1}\ev{X_2} = (\ev{X_1})^2$ by independence. This helps us because of the fact that $\var{X_1}$ relates $\ev{X_1^2}$ and $(\ev{X_1})^2$. Namely, we have that $\var{X_1} = \ev{X_1^2} - (\ev{X_1})^2 \geq 0$, so $(\ev{X_1})^2 \leq \ev{X_1^2}$. All that remains is $\ev{X_{(3)}^2}$ compared to $\ev{X_1^2}$. Since $X_{(3)}$ is the median of the $5$ dice, we can reasonably assume that $\ev{X_{(3)}}$ is very close to $\ev{X_1}$, as the middle value of the $5$ is the "average" of all $5$ dice, which should be close to the true average. Since we know that these are roughly equal, we should consider how to relate these to their second moments. By considering the variance once again, we have that $\var{X_{(3)}} = \ev{X_{(3)}^2} - (\ev{X_{(3)}})^2$ and $\var{X_1} = \ev{X_1^2} - (\ev{X_1})^2$. The terms that are subtracted from each second moment are roughly equal by the discussion above. Thus, we only need to consider which variance is greater. Since $X_1$ is uniform over $\{1,2,\dots, 6\}$, it has pretty high variance. However, $X_{(3)}$ is likely to be centered at roughly $3$ or $4$, and has very little tail probability in either direction outwards. Therefore, $\var{X_{(3)}} < \var{X_1}$, which implies that $\ev{X_{(3)}^2} < \ev{X_1^2}$. The question that remains is where it ranks compared to $\ev{X_1X_2}$. Note that $\ev{X_{(3)}^2} = \var{X_{(3)}} + (\ev{X_{(3)}})^2$. Since $\ev{X_{(3)}}$ is very closely equal to $\ev{X_{1}^2}$, we can conclude that $(\ev{X_{(3)}})^2$ is very close to $(\ev{X_1})^2 = \ev{X_1X_2}$. However, with the addition of the variance term, which is small, but non-negligible, we can conclude that $\ev{X_{(3)}^2} > \ev{X_1X_2}$. Therefore, the order is $2 < 3 < 1$, meaning the answer is $231$.

questions.title: Concert Ticket
questions.problem: $2n$ people, $n \geq 1$, are looking to go to a concert. The concert costs $\\$ to attend. $n$ of the people only have $\\$ bills, while the other $\\$ people only have $\\$ bills. The cashier at the concert has no change. If the people arrange in line uniformly at random, find the probability that all of the people can successfully purchase a ticket without changing order when $n = 9$.
questions.solution: A $\\$ bill splits into $2$ $\\$ bills. A person who gives a $\\$ bill will have to receive $\\$ back. Therefore, the $\\$ bill is the currency we want to track. To ensure we have change for the people with $\\$ bills, we need to ensure that the number of people that have paid with a $\\$ bill never exceeds the number of people that paid with a $\\$ bill. In other words, we can represent a person paying with a $\\$ bill as a $($ and $\\$ bill as a $)$. An arrangement of people that is valid is thus a proper parenthesization of length $2n$ i.e. the number of $)$ in the string never exceeds the number of $($. By the result of "Proper Parenthesization", there are $\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ such strings, which is also the number of arrangements of people in line. To count the number of ways to arrange the people in line, note that we are only identifying the people by whether or not they have a $\\$ bill or a $\\$ bill. Thus, we must pick the places of the $n$ people in line with the $\\$ bill. After this is done, the other $n$ places in line must be the people with the $\\$ bills. There are $\binom{2n}{n}$ ways to pick the $n$ spots from the $2n$ to be for the people with $\\$ bills, so this is the total number of ways to arrange the people in line. We can divide the above to get the probability, as the arrangement of the people in line is uniformly random. Thus, the probability of being able to have everyone obtain a ticket without switching order is $\frac{1}{n+1}$. The answer is $1/10$ for the specific values here.

questions.title: Logarithmic Uniforms I
questions.problem: Suppose that $X, Y \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Compute $\prob{\floor{\log_2(X)} = \floor{\log_2(Y)}}$.
questions.solution: This appears to be a weird transformation of the random variables $X$ and $Y$, so there's no clear cut way to efficiently evaluate this. We note that the support of $\floor{\log_2(X)}$ is the negative integers, as $\log_2(x) < 0$ for $0 < x < 1$, and the floor function makes it an integer. Therefore, the best approach here is to disjointify this event and sum up over all possible values that they could both share. This implies $\prob{\floor{\log_2(X)} = \floor{\log_2(Y)}} = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{-1} \prob{\floor{\log_2(X)} = k} \prob{\floor{\log_2(Y)} = k} = \sum_{k = -\infty}^{-1} \left(\prob{\floor{\log_2(X)} = k}\right)^2$. The interior comes from the fact that $X$ and $Y$ are IID, so the transformations of them are as well. The event $\{\floor{\log_2(X)} = k\}$ means that $k \leq \log_2(X) < k+1$, so $2^k \leq X < 2^{k+1}$. Note that $k \leq -1$, so this is a valid interval. Since $X$ is uniform, we can take ratios of interval lengths to compute probabilities. Namely, this probability is $2^{k+1} - 2^k = 2^k \cdot (2-1) = 2^k$, as this event is an interval of length $2^k$ inside an interval of length $1$ (since the total support is of length $1$). Therefore, the probability in question is given by $\sum_{k=-\infty}^{-1} (2^k)^2 = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{-1}4^k = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 4^{-k} = \dfrac{1/4}{1-1/4} = \dfrac{1}{3}$. In the above, the transformation $k \mapsto -k$ was performed to the indices to make the indices of the sum positive integers. After this was done, using the geometric series formula is easy.

questions.title: Logarithmic Uniforms II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X, Y \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. For a base $b > 1$, Compute $\prob{\floor{\log_b(X)} = \floor{\log_b(Y)}}$. Report the answer when $b = 4$.
questions.solution: This appears to be a weird transformation of the random variables $X$ and $Y$, so there's no clear cut way to efficiently evaluate this. We note that the support of $\floor{\log_b(X)}$ is the negative integers, as $\log_b(x) < 0$ for $0 < x < 1$, and the floor function makes it an integer. Therefore, the best approach here is to disjointify this event and sum up over all possible values that they could both share. This implies $\prob{\floor{\log_b(X)} = \floor{\log_b(Y)}} = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{-1} \prob{\floor{\log_b(X)} = k} \prob{\floor{\log_b(Y)} = k} = \sum_{k = -\infty}^{-1} \left(\prob{\floor{\log_b(X)} = k}\right)^2$. The interior comes from the fact that $X$ and $Y$ are IID, so the transformations of them are as well. The event $\{\floor{\log_b(X)} = k\}$ means that $k \leq \log_b(X) < k+1$, so $b^k \leq X < b^{k+1}$. This is from the definition of the floor function. Note that $k \leq -1$, so this is a valid interval. Since $X$ is uniform, we can take ratios of interval lengths to compute probabilities. Namely, this probability is $b^{k+1} - b^k = b^k \cdot (b-1)$, as this event is an interval of length $b^k(b-1)$ inside an interval of length $1$ (since the total support is of length $1$). Therefore, the probability in question is given by $\sum_{k=-\infty}^{-1} (b^k(b-1))^2 = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{-1}b^{2k}(b-1)^2 = (b-1)^2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (b^2)^{-k} = (b-1)^2 \cdot \dfrac{1/b^2}{1-1/b^2} = \dfrac{(b-1)^2}{b^2 - 1}$. In the above, the transformation $k \mapsto -k$ was performed to the indices to make the indices of the sum positive integers. After this was done, using the geometric series formula is easy. With $b = 4$, the answer is $3/5$.

questions.title: Sample Deviance
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are independent random variables such that $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \mu_i$ and $\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2$. Note that the variance is common, but the means are potentially different. Define $\overline{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{n}\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n \mu_i$. Compute $\mathbb{E}[(X_i - \overline{X})^2]$ when $n = 5, i = 3, \mu_i = i,$ and $\sigma^2 = 16$.
questions.solution: Directly expanding out the interior is going to be messy, as $\overline{X}$ doesn't have a nice expression. To approach this problem, we know how to compute $\ev{X_i - \overline{X}}$ quite easily, so if there were a nice way to compute $\var{X_i - \overline{X}}$, we could use the typical variance formula to compute $\ev{(X_i - \overline{X})^2}$. Writing out the expression explicitly, we have $\text{Var}(X_i - \overline{X}) = \mathbb{E}[(X_i - \overline{X})^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X_i - \overline{X}])^2$. By linearity of expectation, the second term is just $(\ev{X_i} - \ev{\overline{X}})^2 = (\mu_i - \overline{\mu})^2$. One can see that $\ev{\overline{X}} = \overline{\mu}$ from linearity of expectation on the definition of $\overline{X}$. To compute $\text{Var}(X_i - \overline{X})$, we know that by the variance of a sum formula, $\var{X_i - \overline{X}} = \text{Var}(X_i) + \text{Var}(\overline{X}) - 2\text{Cov}(X_i,\overline{X})$. The first two terms are $\sigma^2$ and $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$, respectively. We get $\var{\overline{X}} = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$ from noting that each of the $X_i$ random variables have common variance and are independent, so the variance of the sum (without the $1/n$ out front) is $n\sigma^2$. Since scalars impact the variance by a squaring factor, the variance of $\overline{X}$ is $\dfrac{1}{n^2} \cdot n\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$. The final term is best handled bilinearity of covariance, as $\overline{X}$ is the sum of independent random variables. This becomes $\text{Cov}(X_i,\overline{X}) = \dfrac{2}{n}\text{Cov}(X_i,X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_i + \dots + X_n) = \dfrac{2}{n}\left(\text{Cov}(X_i, X_1) + \dots + \text{Cov}(X_i,X_i) + \dots + \text{Cov}(X_i,X_n)\right)$. Note that for all $j \neq i$, $(X_i,X_j) = 0$, as the random variables are independent, meaning that they are also uncorrelated. The only remaining term is $\text{Cov}(X_i,X_i) = \text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2$. Thus, after plugging back in, we have that $\text{Var}(X_i - \overline{X}) = \dfrac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$. Plugging in once again and rearranging, $\mathbb{E}[(X_i - \overline{X})^2] = (\mu_i - \overline{\mu})^2 + \dfrac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$. With the specified values, $\mu_3 = 3$, $\overline{\mu} = \dfrac{1+2+3+4+5}{5} = 3,$ and the answer is $\frac{64}{5}$.

questions.title: Poweraid
questions.problem: Define the sets $A = \{1,3,5,7,9\}$ and $B = [4n] = \{1,2,\dots, 4n\}$ for some positive integer $n$. Let $X$ be a uniformly random element from $A$ and $Y$ be a uniformly random element from $B$. Find the probability that $X^Y \equiv 1 \hspace{3pt} (\text{mod} \hspace{3pt} 10)$ when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: For each $x \in  A$, there will be a different collection of integers in $B$ such that the condition is satisfied. For example, if $1$ is selected, then for any $y \in B$, $1^y = 1$, so this condition would be satisfied. However, if $5$ is selected, every power of $5$ also ends in $5$, so no integer from $B$ would satisfy this condition. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on the element from $A$ that is selected, and find which elements of $B$ would satisfy this condition for the selected element. Formalizing this, let $E$ be the event that $X^Y \equiv 1 \hspace{3pt} (\text{mod} \hspace{3pt} 10)$. We are going to condition on $X$, and find which $y \in B$ satisfy the condition. Namely, $\prob{E} = \prob{E \mid X = 1}\prob{X=1} + \dots + \prob{E \mid X = 9}\prob{X = 9}$. Since $X$ is selected uniformly at random from $A$, $\prob{X=1} = \dots = \prob{X = 9} = 1/5$, as there are $5$ integers in $A$. To compute the conditionals, we must determine which integers in $B$ satisfy the condition. Since the element of $B$ is selected uniformly at random, we can just take the ratio of the number of integers in $B$ that satisfy the condition to the total number of integers in $B$ (which is $4n$) to compute the probability. If $X = 1$, then by the discussion above, all integers in $B$ satisfy the condition, so $\prob{E \mid X = 1} = 1$. If $X = 5$, then none of the integers satisfy the condition, so $\prob{E \mid X = 5} = 0$. If $X = 9$, we have to do a little experimentation to see which powers of $9$ will result in a ones digit of $1$. The first few powers of $9$ are $9, 81, 729,$ and $6561$. This makes us conjecture that even powers of $9$ will result in a $1$. This can be verified: If $n$ is even, then $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Then we have that, in mod $10$, $9^n = 9^{2k} = (9^2)^k = 81^k = \equiv 1^k = 1$. Therefore, all even integers make the power of $9$ end in $1$. This is exactly $1/2$ of all of the integers in $[4n]$, so $\prob{E \mid X = 9} = 1/2$. If $X = 3$, we note that $3^2 = 9$, and even powers of $9$ end in a $1$. Thus, $9^{2k}$ ends in $1$ for integers $k$. Since $9 = 3^2$, this implies that $(3^2)^{2k} = 3^{4k}$ ends in $1$ for all integers $k$. Therefore, all multiples of $4$ in $[4n]$ will satisfy this condition for $3$. This is exactly $1/4$ of the total integers, so $\prob{E \mid X = 3} = 1/4$. If $X = 7$, we have something similar: $7^2 = 49$, which ends in $9$, so the same exact argument above holds! Therefore, $\prob{E \mid X = 7} = 1/4$. Plugging all of these in, we get that $\prob{E} = \dfrac{1}{5}\left[1 + \frac{1}{4} + 0 + \dfrac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\right] = \dfrac{2}{5}$. This result is independent of $n$.

questions.title: Last Exponential II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \sim \exponential{\lambda_1}$ and $X_2 \sim \exponential{\lambda_2}$ independently. Define $M = \max(X_1,X_2)$. Compute $\ev{M}$ when $\lambda_i = i$.
questions.solution:
To compute the expected value of a maximum, a typical approach may be to use the tail expected value $\ev{X} = \ctailsum{X}$. In the previous part, this approach was inefficient because $n$ was arbitrary, which made the integral intractable. Since $n = 2$ here, it may be able to work. Since $M_n$ is the maximum, we know how to compute probabilities of events of the form $\{M_n \leq x\}$ easily. Since the tail integral interior is $\prob{M_n > x}$, the easiest way to compute this is via the complement. We have that $\prob{M_n > x} = 1 - \prob{M_n \leq x} = 1 - \prob{\max(X_1,X_2) \leq x} = 1 - \prob{X_1 \leq x, X_2 \leq x} = 1 - \prob{X_1 \leq x}\prob{X_2 \leq x}$. Using the fact that $\prob{X \leq x} = 1  - e^{-\lambda x}$ for $X \sim \exponential{\lambda}$ and $x > 0$, $\prob{M_n > x} = 1 - (1-e^{-\lambda_1 x})(1 - e^{-\lambda_2 x})$. Plugging this into the integral, we have that $\ev{M_n} = \int_0^{\infty} 1 - (1-e^{-\lambda_1 x})(1 - e^{-\lambda_2 x}) dx = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-\lambda_1 x} + e^{-\lambda_2 x} - e^{-(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2) x}dx = \dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} 
 + \dfrac{1}{\lambda_2} - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{7}{6}$.

questions.title: Permutation Maxima
questions.problem: A permutation of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$, say $(i_1,\dots, i_n)$, is formed uniformly at random. We say that spot $k$ is a local maxima if $i_k$ is larger than the entry/entries adjacent to it. Find the expected number of local maxima in the permutation when $n = 20$.
questions.solution: All interior entries have $2$ entries that are adjacent, while the endpoints only have $1$ adjacent entry. Since we are looking to count the expected number of some event that occurs and the events are not independent, counting with indicators is the best tool. Let $M_i$ be the indicator of the event that the $i$th entry in the permutation, $1 \leq i \leq n$, is a local maxima. $T = M_1 + \dots + M_n$ gives the total number of local maxima. Note that $M_2,M_3,\dots, M_{n-1}$ are exchangeable, and therefore identically distributed, as each of the interior terms have two neighbors. However, $M_1$ and $M_n$ only have one neighbor, so these two are identically distributed, but not the same distribution as the other $n-2$ spots. Random variables with the same distribution have the same mean, so via linearity of expectation, $\ev{T} = (n-2)\ev{M_2} + 2\ev{M_1}$. $\ev{M_1}$ is just the probability that the entry in the first spot is larger than that of the second spot. Since all permutations are equally likely and all the values are distinct, each of the two spots are equally likely to be the larger one, so the probability is just $\ev{M_1} = 1/2$. $\ev{M_2}$ is the probability that $M_2$ is a local maxima i.e. that it is the largest among $M_1,M_2,$ and $M_3$. Once again, since each permutation is equally likely, the maximum among these three random variables is equally likely to be in any of the three spots, so $\ev{M_2} = 1/3$, as there is a $1$ in $3$ chance that $M_2$ is the maxima of the $3$ above random variables. Therefore, $\ev{T} = \frac{n-2}{3} + 1$. With the specified values, the answer is $7$.

questions.title: Hearty Variance
questions.problem: A hand of $n$ cards is dealt from a standard card deck. Find the variance of the number of hearts that are in the hand when $n = 26$.
questions.solution:
Let $T$ be the total number of cards in the hand that are hearts. For each card in the hand, it either is or is not a heart. Therefore, we can count $T$ by counting $1$ per heart in the hand and $0$ if the card is not a heart. In other words, arbitrarily label the cards in your hand $1-n$, and for $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $H_i$ be the indicator that card $i$ in your hand is a heart. Then $T = H_1 + \dots + H_n$ gives the total number of hearts that are in hand. The $H_i$ random variables are not independent, as if we know the first card is a heart, this information decreases the probability that each of the remaining cards are hearts. Therefore, the variance of a sum formula is most appropriate. Applying this formula, we get $\var{T} = \var{H_1 + \dots + H_n} = \sum_{i=1}^n \var{H_i}  + \sum_{i 
eq j}\cov{H_i}{H_j}$. Since the labels $1-n$ were assigned to the cards arbitrarily, the random variables $H_1,\dots, H_n$ are exchangeable, which implies they have the same distribution (and hence mean/covariance/covariances). Therefore, we can claim $\var{H_i} = \var{H_1}$ and $\cov{H_i}{H_j} = \cov{H_1}{H_2}$ for all $i 
eq j$. Plugging these in, we obtain $\var{T} = n\var{H_1} + n(n-1)\cov{H_1}{H_2}$. The term $n(n-1)$ arises from the fact that there are $n^2$ total pairs of random variables $H_i$ and $H_j$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq n$, and the first sum contains $n$ of those pairs where $i = j$, so there must be $n(n-1)$ pairs remaining where $i 
eq j$. All that remains is to compute each of these quantities. Since $H_1$ is an indicator of the event that the first card is a heart, and each of the $4$ suits is equally likely to appear for this draw, $H_1 \sim  ern{1/4}$, as $H_1 = 1$ with probability $1/4$ and $0$ otherwise. Thus, $\var{H_1} = 1/4 \cdot \left(1 - 1/4ight) = 3/16$. To compute $\cov{H_1}{H_2}$, we use the expansion of covariance to obtain $\cov{H_1}{H_2} = \ev{H_1H_2} - \ev{H_1}\ev{H_2}$. Since $H_1$ and $H_2$ are exchangeable, they have the same mean of $\ev{H_1} = 1/4$ from the known distribution of $H_1$. $\ev{H_1H_2}$ is equal to the probability that $H_1 = H_2 = 1$, which is exactly that both of the first two cards are hearts. The probability that the first card is hearts is $1/4$ from previous work. Given that the first card was a heart, the probability that the second card is also a heart is $12/51$, as there are $12$ hearts that remain in the other $51$ cards, so $\ev{H_1H_2} = 1/4 \cdot 4/17 = 1/17$. Plugging this in, we get $\cov{H_1}{H_2} = 1/17 - 1/16 = -1/272$. Therefore, $\var{T} = \dfrac{3}{16}n - \dfrac{1}{272}n(n-1) = \dfrac{n(52-n)}{272}$. This result makes a lot of intuitive sense, as when $n = 0$, there are always going to be no hearts, so the variance is $0$. Similarly, when $n=52$, you have drawn the entire deck, so you will have always $13$ hearts, meaning there is also $0$ variance. Furthermore, this function is symmetric about $n = 26$, which makes sense, as if you draw a hand of $k$ cards, you are implicitly also leaving a hand of $52 - k$ cards left in the deck that you did not select. Thus, you could create a hand of size $k$ by either picking $k$ cards and taking those or by picking $52 - k$ cards to discard. Both methodologies should yield the same variance, as they both yield a hand of size $k$, and they do. With the specified value, the answer is $\dfrac{169}{68}$.

questions.title: Shuffle Up I
questions.problem: The numbers in the string $1234$ are shuffled uniformly at random. Let $p_i$ be the probability that exactly $i$ of the characters are out of place. For example, $3241$ has $3$ characters out of place. Find $\sum_{i=0}^4 p_i^2$.
questions.solution: Since all $4! = 24$ permutations of the string are equally likely, we only must count the number of permutations where exactly $0 \leq i \leq 4$ of the values are out of order. $p_0$ is just the probability that none of the characters are out of order i.e. all are in the correct spots. This just means that the string is correct. There is only $1$ such correct string, which is the original string $1234$, so $p_0 = 1/24$. For $p_1$, note that it is impossible for exactly one element to be out of place, as if one element is out of place, it takes up the spot of a different element, so that other element also can't be in the correct spot. This implies $p_1 = 0$. $p_2$ is the probability that exactly $2$ characters are out of place. For this to occur, this means that two of the $4$ elements are in their correct place, and two of the elements were swapped in locations. For example, $3214$ is obtained by swapping $1$ and $3$. All outcomes with exactly $2$ characters out of place are generated by swapping two elements, so the number of outcomes satisfying this is just equal to the number of ways to select $2$ elements to swap, which is $\binom{4}{2} = 6$. Thus, $p_2 = 6/24 = 1/4$. $p_3$ is the probability that there are exactly $3$ characters out of place. For this to be true, there must be exactly one character fixed in place. Afterwards, none of the remaining $3$ characters can go into their original locations. There are $4$ ways to pick the character that is fixed. Afterwards, suppose that $abc$ are the three characters that are being permuted to different locations, with this as their original relative order. By writing out the $3! = 6$ permutations of these values, one can see that $2$ of these $6$ arrangements have no characters in their original spots, so there must be $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ ways to permute the characters such that $3$ of them differ in their location. Thus, $p_3 = 8/24 = 1/3$. Lastly, as $\displaystyle \sum_{i=0}^4 p_i = 1$ by the fact that the only possibilities are that there are $0,1,2,3,$ or $4$ characters out of place, $p_4 = 1\displaystyle - \sum_{i=0}^3 p_i = 1 - 1/24 - 6/24 - 8/24 = 9/24 = 3/8$. The answer is $\sum_{i=0}^4 p_i^2 = \dfrac{1^2 + 6^2 + 8^2 + 9^2}{24^2} = \dfrac{91}{288}$.

questions.title: Shuffle Up II
questions.problem: The numbers in the string $1234$ are shuffled uniformly at random. Given that the shuffled string is not $1234$, find the expected number of transpositions that need to be performed to make the permuted string the original string. For example, $3241 \rightarrow 1243 \rightarrow 1234$ can be transformed into the original string in two transpositions. Note that the transpositions do not need to be between adjacent entries in the string and that you take the most efficient sequence of transpositions to obtain $1234$.
questions.solution: To find the expected number of transpositions, it would be easier if we knew how many characters of the string were out of place. This is because the number of transpositions needed is dependent on how many characters are out of place. For example, if there are only $2$ characters out of place, then only one transposition is needed, but if there are more characters out of place, there are more transpositions that are needed. Let $O$ be the random variable representing the number of characters out of place given that the string is not $1234$. This restricts us to $23$ strings. However, each of those strings are equally likely, and the counts are the same as in "Shuffle Up I", so $\prob{O = 1} = 0, \prob{O = 2} = 6/23, \prob{O = 3} = 8/23,$ and $\prob{O = 4} = 9/23$. Similarly, let $T$ be the number of transpositions needed to obtain the original string. By performing the conditioning from above, $\ev{T} = \ev{\ev{T \mid O}} = \sum_{i=1}^4 \ev{T \mid O = i}\prob{O = i}$. We know from above that $\prob{O = 1} = 0$, so this term can be eliminated immediately. If $O = 2$, then exactly $1$ transposition is needed, as you just swap the two terms that are out of order. Therefore, $\ev{T \mid O = 2} = 1$ and $\prob{O = 2} = 6/23$. Similarly, if $O = 3$, then $3$ of the letters are out of place. It can quickly be seen that you need $2$ moves to shuffle them back into the original arrangement, so $\ev{T \mid O = 3} = 2$ and $\prob{O = 3} = 8/23$. The last case is when all $4$ characters are out of place. However, one can quickly see that there are two sub-cases to consider here. Some of the outcomes with all $4$ characters that are out of place consists of two swaps i.e. just switching around two pairs, while others need $3$ transpositions. An example of the first kind is $3412$, as you can swap $1$ and $3$, as well as $2$ and $4$, to get back to the original arrangement. An example of the second kind is $3421$, as the sequence is $3421 \rightarrow 1423 \rightarrow 1243 \rightarrow 1234$. The second type always takes $3$ transpositions, as we are always able to ensure one of the characters lands in the right position per turn. We know that there are $9$ total outcomes with all $4$ characters out of place, so we must determine how many of these $9$ belong to each case. To obtain an outcome of the first kind, we must pick two pairs of elements to swap around. There are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ ways to pick a single pair to swap around. Once we pick the first pair, we also automatically pick the second pair to swap. For example, if we selected $(1,3)$ to swap, then the other pair that we swap is $(2,4)$. However, this exact sequence of swaps also could have been created by selecting $(2,4)$ to swap, and this would inadvertently also swap $(1,3)$. Therefore, each set of two pairs of elements to swap is really repeated twice in the above, so we must divide by $2$ to remove the repetition. This yields $3$ ways to reach an outcome of the first kind. In particular, these are just $(1,2), (1,3),$ and $(1,4)$. These $3$ outcomes require $2$ transpositions to reach $1234$, while the other $9-3 = 6$ outcomes require $3$ transpositions. Given that $O = 4$, the probability we are in the first sub-case is $3/9 = 1/3$, as we have restricted ourselves to only the $9$ outcomes where $O = 4$. This also means the probability we are in the second sub-case is $2/3$. By Law of Total Expectation, we have that $\ev{T \mid O = 4} = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 2 + \frac{2}{3} \cdot 3 = \frac{8}{3}$, as we break up based on which sub-case the outcome is in. We also know that $\prob{O = 4} = \frac{9}{23}$. Plugging all of these in, we obtain $\ev{T} = 0 + \dfrac{6}{23} \cdot 1 + \dfrac{8}{23} \cdot 2 + \dfrac{8}{3} \cdot \dfrac{9}{23} = 2$.

questions.title: Differencing III
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\dots$ is a sequence of random variables with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. The sequence also has an auto-correlation function $\rho(i,j)$ i.e. $\rho(i,j) = \corr{X_i}{X_j}$. Define the new sequence of random variables $Y_i = X_{i+1} - X_i$ for $i \geq 1$. Compute the auto-correlation function for the sequence of $Y_i$ random variables in terms of the given information for the $X_i$ random variables. In other words, determine $\rho'(i,j) = \corr{Y_i}{Y_j}$. Evaluate this for $i = 10, \mu = 4, \sigma^2 = 9,$ and $\rho(i,j) = \dfrac{1}{1 + |i-j|}$. Note that $\corr{Y_i}{Y_j} = \dfrac{\cov{Y_i}{Y_j}}{\sqrt{\var{Y_i}\var{Y_j}}}$.
questions.solution: To compute $\rho'(i,j) = \corr{Y_i}{Y_j} = \dfrac{\cov{Y_i}{Y_j}}{\sqrt{\var{Y_i}\var{Y_j}}}$, we only need to compute the numerator, as the variance was determined in "Differencing II". Subbing in $Y_i$ and $Y_j$, $\cov{Y_i}{Y_j} = \cov{X_{i+1} - X_i}{X_{j+1} - X_j}$. When looking at a sum/difference of random variables, bilinearity of covariance is typically the best approach to computing covariance. Applying this here and taking out the constants, $\cov{X_{i+1} - X_i}{X_{j+1} - X_j} = \cov{X_{i+1}}{X_{j+1}} - \cov{X_{i+1}}{X_j} - \cov{X_i}{X_{j+1}} + \cov{X_i}{X_j}$. From "Differencing II", we know that $\cov{X_m}{X_n} = \rho(m,n)\sigma^2$, where $\rho(m,n)$ is the auto-correlation function of the $X_i$ sequence evaluated at $(m,n)$. Applying this here, we obtain $\cov{Y_i}{Y_j} = \sigma^2\left(\rho(i+1,j+1) - \rho(i+1,j) - \rho(i,j+1) +\rho(i,j)\right)$. Plugging this into the formula for correlation with the result from "Differencing II", we obtain $\rho'(i,j) = \dfrac{\sigma^2\left(\rho(i+1,j+1) - \rho(i+1,j) - \rho(i,j+1) +\rho(i,j)\right)}{\sqrt{2\sigma^2(1-\rho(i,i+1)) \cdot 2\sigma^2(1 - \rho(j,j+1))}} = \dfrac{\rho(i+1,j+1) - \rho(i+1,j) - \rho(i,j+1) +\rho(i,j)}{2\sqrt{(1-\rho(i,i+1))(1-\rho(j,j+1))}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $-\dfrac{1}{105}$.

questions.title: Group Formation II
questions.problem: There are $n$ people in a class that have to make groups for a project. To do this, they each are assigned a label $1$ to $n$. Each person writes their label on a slip of paper, and all the pieces of paper are thrown into a bowl. One by one, each guest picks a name from the bowl. Each guest will be a part of a group with the guest they pulled the name out of from the bowl. If a guest pulls out their own name, they are in a group all by themselves. If Guest A pulls out Guest B's name, Guest B pulls out Guest C's name, and Guest C pulls out Guest A's name, they are all a part of the same closed group and no one else will be able to join them. What is the average size of a group when $n = 100$? Round your answer to the nearest hundredth.
questions.solution: Drawing the numbers out of the bowl can be viewed as a random permutation of the labels. A group of people would be a cycle in this permutation, so this question is really asking for the expected size of a cycle in a uniformly random permutation of length $n$. From "Group Formation I", we know that there are an average of $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac{1}{i}$ cycles in the permutation. The expected length of the cycle is just the average number of elements in a cycle. Therefore, as there are $n$ elements, the average number of elements per cycle is just $\dfrac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n 1/i}$, the total number of elements divided by the expected number of cycles. This is because no cycle is any more/less likely to be larger/smaller than any other cycle. With $n = 100$, the answer is approximately $19.28$.

questions.title: Multiballs II
questions.problem: You have two urns in front of you, say $1$ and $2$. Urn $1$ has $m$ red and $n$ blue marbles inside, while Urn $2$ has $n$ red and $m$ blue marbles inside. Assume that $m,n \geq 2$. You select one urn uniformly at random and select $3$ marbles uniformly at random without replacement. In your selection, you observe $2$ red and $1$ blue marble. Find the probability that you drew from urn $1$ when $m = 7$ and $n = 4$.
questions.solution: We are given information here about what appears in the sequence of draws, so using the definition of conditional probability/Bayes' Theorem here is most relevant. Let $U_1$ and $U_2$ be the events that we select from urns $1$ and $2$, respectively. Similarly, let $S$ be the event that we obtain a selection of $2$ red and $1$ blue marble among $3$ marbles drawn without replacement. We are looking to compute $\prob{U_1 \mid S} = \dfrac{\prob{U_1 \cap S}}{\prob{S}}$. If we know which urn we selected, then it's quite easy to determine the probability of obtaining the selection above, as we know the counts of the marbles in the urn. Therefore, we should condition on the selected urn. Namely, $\prob{S \cap U_1} = \prob{S \mid U_1}\prob{U_1}$. $\prob{U_1} = 1/2$, as you select the urn uniformly at random to start. Then, given you selected urn $1$, you must select $2$ red and $1$ blue marble. Since the marbles are selected uniformly at random, we can compute the number of ways to obtain such a selection, and then divide by the number of ways to draw $3$ marbles unrestricted. As there are $m+n$ marbles in the urn and we select $3$, there are $\binom{m+n}{3}$ ways to do this without restriction. There are $n$ ways to pick the one blue marble, and there are $\binom{m}{2}$ ways to pick $2$ red marbles, as the order of selection is irrelevant by our choice of using the binomial coefficient. Thus, $\prob{S \mid U_1} = \dfrac{n\binom{m}{2}}{\binom{m+n}{3}}$. We compute $\prob{S}$ in a similar way. As per the above, we condition on the urn that is being drawn from to obtain $\prob{S} = \prob{S \mid U_1}\prob{U_1} + \prob{S \mid U_2}\prob{U_2}$. The first term is exactly the numerator. We also know that $\prob{U_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, as each urn is equally likely to be selected from at first. Then, given that we selected from urn $2$, we must find the probability of obtaining the desired selection. There are $\binom{m+n}{3}$ ways to pick the marbles without restriction once again. In this case, the roles of $m$ and $n$ are reversed, as the other bag has $n$ red and $m$ blue marbles. Therefore, $\prob{S \mid U_2} = \dfrac{m\binom{n}{2}}{\binom{m+n}{3}}$. Plugging all of this in, we obtain $\prob{U_1 \mid S} = \dfrac{\dfrac{n\binom{m}{2}}{\binom{m+n}{3}}}{\dfrac{n\binom{m}{2}}{\binom{m+n}{3}} + \dfrac{m\binom{n}{2}}{\binom{m+n}{3}}} = \dfrac{nm(m-1)/2}{nm(m-1)/2 + nm(n-1)/2} = \dfrac{m-1}{(m-1) + (n-1)}$. This answer makes intuitive sense. As we saw in "Multiballs I", a subset of the information here is symmetric between the two parts of our partition (in this case, the urns). Therefore, that subset of information really does not tell us any information at all, as that subset is equally likely to apply to either urn. Therefore, the only relevant information that we have is the extra red ball. We can now view this event, once we account for the symmetric information, as the probability of drawing $1$ red ball from urns with $m-1$ and $n-1$ of the counts of red and blue/blue and red balls, respectively. We say $m-1$ and $n-1$ because of the fact that one ball of each color is removed prior as per our information. Thus, as the ball is drawn uniformly at random, urn $1$ contains $m-1$ red balls, and urn $2$ contains $n-1$ red balls, the answer is just simply $\dfrac{m-1}{(m-1) + (n-1)}$. With the specific values, the answer is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.title: Multiballs III
questions.problem: You have two urns in front of you, say $1$ and $2$. Urn $1$ has $m$ red and $n$ blue marbles inside, while urn $2$ has $n$ red and $m$ blue marbles inside. Assume that $m,n \geq 1$ and $k \leq \min(m,n)$. You choose one urn uniformly at random and select $2k$ marbles uniformly at random without replacement. In your selection, you observe $k$ red and $k$ blue marbles. Find the probability that you drew from urn $1$ when $m = 7, n = 4,$ and $k=3$.

Let $U_1$ and $U_2$ be the events that we select from urns $1$ and $2$, respectively. If we know which urn we selected, then it's quite easy to determine the probability of obtaining the selection above, as we know the counts of the marbles in the urn. Therefore, we should condition on the selected urn. Namely, $\prob{S \cap U_1} = \prob{S \mid U_1}\prob{U_1}$. $\prob{U_1} = 1/2$, as you select the urn uniformly at random to start. Then, given you selected urn $1$, you must select $k$ red and $k$ blue marbles. Since the marbles are selected uniformly at random, we can compute the number of ways to obtain such a selection, and then divide by the number of ways to draw $2k$ marbles unrestricted. As there are $m+n$ marbles in the urn and we select $2k$, there are $\binom{m+n}{2k}$ ways to do this without restriction. The first term is exactly the numerator. We also know that $\prob{U_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, as each urn is equally likely to be selected from at first. In other words, drawing $k$ red and $k$ blue marbles gives no information at all regarding which urn was selected, as the information says that we draw $k$ marbles of each color, and the urns are also symmetric in their counts of each type of marble. This result is independent of $m$ and $n$, so the answer is $1/2$.

Since the marbles are selected uniformly at random, we can compute the number of ways to obtain such a selection, and then divide by the number of ways to draw $2k+1$ marbles unrestricted. In this case, the roles of $m$ and $n$ are reversed, as the other bag has $n$ red and $m$ blue marbles. Therefore, $\prob{S \mid U_2} = \dfrac{\binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{k+1}}{\binom{m+n}{2k+1}}$. We say $m-k$ and $n-k$ because of the fact that $k$ balls of each color are removed prior as per our information. Thus, as the ball is drawn uniformly at random, urn $1$ contains $m-k$ red balls, and urn $2$ contains $n-k$ red balls, the answer is just simply $\dfrac{m-k}{(m-k) + (n-k)}$. questions.title: Variant Convergent I
questions.problem: Select $X_1 \sim \unif{0}{1/2}$. For $n \geq 1$, select $X_n \mid X_{n-1} = x \sim \unif{x}{x+2^{-n}}$. Define $X_{\infty} = \displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} X_n$. Find $\ev{X_{\infty}}$. Note that $X_{n-1}$ determines the left endpoint of the interval from which $X_n$ is drawn, and the interval width shrinks as $n$ grows. The value of $X_n$ is always at least $X_{n-1}$.
questions.solution: The key insight here is to see that $X_n$ is just the value of $X_{n-1}$ with some uniform random variable added to it. In other words, $X_n = X_{n-1} + U_{n}$, where $U_2,\dots$ are independent random variables with $U_i \sim \unif{0}{2^{-n}}$. We can say this because of the fact that, given the value of $X_{n-1}$, the value of $X_n$ is just this uniform random variable added to the value of $X_{n-1}$. Therefore, we can say that $X_n = X_{n-1} + U_n = X_{n-2} + U_{n-1} + U_n = \dots = X_1 + U_2 + \dots + U_n$. Note that $X_1 \sim \unif{0}{1/2}$, so it still fits into the paradigm here. For convenience and consistency of notation, replace $X_1$ with $U_1$. We therefore have that $X_{\infty} = \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} U_n$, where $U_i \sim \unif{0}{2^{-i}}$ independently. By linearity of expectation, we can conclude that $\ev{X_{\infty}} = \ev{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} U_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\ev{U_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{2^{-i} + 0}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^i} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1/2}{1-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. We used the fact that $\var{X} = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}$ for $X \sim \unif{a}{b}$.

questions.title: Variant Convergent II
questions.problem: Select $X_1 \sim \unif{0}{1/2}$. For $n \geq 1$, select $X_n \mid X_{n-1} = x \sim \unif{x}{x+2^{-n}}$. Define $X_{\infty} = \displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} X_n$. Find $\var{X_{\infty}}$. Note that $X_{n-1}$ determines the left endpoint of the interval from which $X_n$ is drawn, and the interval width shrinks as $n$ grows. The value of $X_n$ is always at least $X_{n-1}$.

Since the random variables are independent, we can conclude that $\var{X_{\infty}} = \var{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} U_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\var{U_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(2^{-i} - 0)^2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{12}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{4^i} = \dfrac{1}{12} \cdot \dfrac{1/4}{1-1/4} = \dfrac{1}{36}$. We used the fact that $\var{X} = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}$ for $X \sim \unif{a}{b}$.

questions.title: Eventually Equal I
questions.problem: You flip a coin with probability $1/2 < p < 1$ of heads repetitively until the running total number of heads equals the running total number of tails. Find the probability that you ever stop flipping when $p = 3/4$.
questions.solution: Instead of viewing this as coin flips, it's easier to visualize what is occurring by framing it as a random walk of some particle. This is a natural choice, as random walks are often represented by random choice of direction, and we can map the two directions to the two outcomes of a coin. A heads will represent one movement to the right, while a tails will represent one movement to the left. An equal amount of heads and tails at some point would then visually represent the particle returning to the origin. Condition on the direction of the first movement, as the particle will need to move the opposite direction to return to the origin. Let $H_1$ and $T_1$ be the events that the particle moves right/left on the first turn (obtains head/tails) and $R$ be the event of a return to the origin. We have that $\prob{R} = \prob{R \mid H_1}\prob{H_1} + \prob{R \mid T_1}\prob{T_1}$. As per the question, we know $\prob{H_1} = p$ and $\prob{T_1} = 1-p$. Now, we need to compute the conditional probabilities. For both $\prob{R \mid H_1}$ and $\prob{R \mid T_1}$, we need to compute the probability that the particle returns to the origin when it has some probability, say $r$, of moving in the direction of the origin, and probability $1-r$ of moving away from the origin. Thus, we will compute $\alpha_r$, the probability of returning to the origin from $1$ step away when there is a probability $0 < r < 1$ of moving in the direction towards the origin and probability $1-r$ of moving away from the origin at each step. We would then have $\prob{R \mid H_1} = \alpha_{1-p}$, as the particle moves right at the first step, so it would need to move left to reach the origin, which occurs with probability $1-p$ per trial. By similar logic, $\prob{R \mid T_1} = \alpha_p$, as the particle needs to move right to reach the origin. To compute $\alpha_r$, we should condition on what happens in the first step. This is because of the fact that if the particle moves $1$ unit towards the origin at the first step, it already reaches the origin. Otherwise, it is now $2$ steps away from the origin, which isn't the same probability, so we should condition on which direction the particle moves from the $1$ step away position. If the particle moves towards the origin, which occurs with probability $r$ by definition, then the origin is reached. Otherwise, with probability $1-r$, the particle moves in the direction opposite of the origin, so it is now $2$ units away. For the particle to reach the origin from $2$ units away, the particle must eventually reach the state $1$ unit away from the origin, and then eventually reach the origin from there. The problem of reaching the state $1$ unit away from the origin from the one that is $2$ units away is exactly the same as the original problem, except everything is shifted by $1$ unit. The probability of this is just $\alpha_r$ as well. Then, once the particle hits the state $1$ unit away from the origin, there is probability $\alpha_r$ by definition that it hits the origin. By the Strong Markov Property (or intuitively reasoning that the hitting of the two states deal with independent sequences of coin flips), these are independent, so there is a probability $\alpha_r^2$ of hitting the origin given that the particle moves away at the first step. By the Law of Total Probability, we have obtained $\alpha_r = r + (1-r)\alpha_r^2$. Rearranging this, we obtain a quadratic equation in $\alpha_r$ given by $(1-r)\alpha_r^2 - \alpha_r + r = 0$. By the quadratic formula, the roots of this are given by $\alpha_r = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4r(1-r)}}{2(1-r)} = \dfrac{1 \pm 2r-1}{2(1-r)} = 1,\dfrac{r}{1-r}$. The question now becomes which root is the valid one. A theorem from stochastic processes says that the minimum root is the proper one. Note that $r < 1-r$ when $r < 1/2$, so for $r < 1/2$, $\alpha_r = \dfrac{r}{1-r}$, while for $r \geq 1/2$, the answer is $1$. As $1/2 < p < 1$ in this problem, $0 < 1-p < 1/2$. Therefore, we have that $\prob{R \mid H_1} = \alpha_{1-p} = \dfrac{1-p}{p}$, while $\prob{R \mid T_1} = \alpha_p = 1$. Plugging these into the Law of Total Probability expression from the beginning, we get $\prob{R} = \dfrac{1-p}{p} \cdot p + 1 \cdot (1-p) = 2(1-p)$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/2$.

The problem of reaching the state $1$ unit away from the origin from the one that is $2$ units away is exactly the same as the original problem, except everything is shifted by $1$ unit. The probability of this is just $\alpha_r$ as well. Then, once the particle hits the state $1$ unit away from the origin, there is probability $\alpha_r$ by definition that it hits the origin. By the Strong Markov Property (or intuitively reasoning that the hitting of the two states deal with independent sequences of coin flips), these are independent, so there is a probability $\alpha_r^2$ of hitting the origin given that the particle moves away at the first step. By the Law of Total Probability, we have obtained $\alpha_r = r + (1-r)\alpha_r^2$. Rearranging this, we obtain a quadratic equation in $\alpha_r$ given by $(1-r)\alpha_r^2 - \alpha_r + r = 0$. By the quadratic formula, the roots of this are given by $\alpha_r = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4r(1-r)}}{2(1-r)} = \dfrac{1 \pm 2r-1}{2(1-r)} = 1,\dfrac{r}{1-r}$. The question now becomes which root is the valid one. A theorem from stochastic processes says that the minimum root is the proper one. Note that $r < 1-r$ when $r < 1/2$, so for $r < 1/2$, $\alpha_r = \dfrac{r}{1-r}$, while for $r \geq 1/2$, the answer is $1$. As $0 < p < 1/2$ in this problem, $1/2 < 1-p < 1$. Therefore, we have that $\prob{R \mid H_1} = \alpha_{1-p} = 1$, while $\prob{R \mid T_1} = \alpha_p = \dfrac{p}{1-p}$. Plugging these into the Law of Total Probability expression from the beginning, we get $\prob{R} = 1 \cdot p + \dfrac{p}{1-p} \cdot (1-p) = 2p$. This result makes a lot of sense. When the probability of heads is $p$, the coin with probability $1-p$ of heads is essentially the same coin with the roles of heads and tails flipped, and this is what was observed with the past two results. One could have solved this problem by noting that if there is probability $0 < p < 1/2$ of heads per flip, there is probability $1/2 < 1-p < 1$ of tails per flip, and used the result of "Eventually Equal I" with the roles of heads and tails swapped to obtain the answer as $2(1-(1-p)) = 2p$. With the specified values, the answer is $2/3$.

questions.title: Generous Friend II
questions.problem: You and a rich friend play the following game: Each of you will select a positive integer according to any strategy of your respective choices. If you both select the same value $n$, you receive $\$n^2$ from your friend. Under an optimal strategy from both you and your friend, what is your expected payout to the nearest thousandth?
questions.solution: Consider this game on the finite set $[N] = \{1,2,\dots, N\}$. An initial strategy from each player could be to select a deterministic value $1 \leq i \leq N$. However, this is not optimal from each player, as you could just select $N$ every time and increase your expected value, while your friend could just select $1$ every time and decrease your expected value, so both players can do better. As this holds for all $N$, no type of "uniform" distribution on the positive integers will be optimal. The goal is to find some probability distribution on the positive integers such that you select $i \geq 1$ with probability $p_i$. To do this, we should use the indifference principle. This idea states that in an optimal strategy, you should be indifferent to what your friend chooses. In other words, no matter what your friend selects as their number, your payout remains constant. The expected payout contributed by term $k$ is just $k^2p_k$, as you receive a payout of $k^2$ with probability $p_k$. Thus, the optimal strategy will have that $1^2p_1 = 2^2p_2 = \dots = k^2p_k = \dots \iff p_k = \dfrac{1}{k^2}p_1$. However, we also must have that $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} p_k = 1 \iff p_1 \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{k^2} = 1 \iff p_1 = \dfrac{6}{\pi^2}$. We use the known sum $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{k^2} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{6}$. Therefore, we have that $p_k = \dfrac{1}{k^2}p_1 = \dfrac{6}{\pi^2 k^2}$ for any $k \geq 1$. This distribution is typically known as the $\text{Zeta}(2)$ distribution. In other words, the optimal strategy for both you and your friend is to select your values independently from a $\text{Zeta}(2)$ distribution. The expected payout would therefore be $\dfrac{6}{\pi^2}$, as this is the expected payout, regardless of the choice of your friend, for each $k \geq 1$, so averaging all of these together gives the same value.

questions.title: Exact N
questions.problem: Let $X_1,X_2,X_3 \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{1,2,\dots,N\}$. Let $p_N = \prob{X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = N}$. If it exists, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} Np_N$. If it doesn't exist, enter $-1$.
questions.solution: Computing the exact value of $p_N$ is possible but tedious. Instead, note that for $X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = N$, it must be the case that $X_1 + X_2 < N$, and then exactly one value of $X_3$ will ensure that $X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = N$. Therefore, the best approach is to approximate the probability that $X_1 + X_2 < N$, and then the remaining probability is easy to compute. Doing this, we have $\prob{X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = N} = \prob{X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = N \mid X_1 + X_2 < N}\prob{X_1 + X_2 < N}$. As $X_1$ and $X_2$ are discrete uniform on $[N] = \{1,2,\dots,N\}$, as $N \rightarrow \infty$, $\prob{X_1 + X_2 = N} \rightarrow 0$, as there are more and more values added to the support. Since the support of $X_1$ and $X_2$ individually are $[N]$, the support of $X_1 + X_2$ is $\{2,3,\dots, 2N\}$. Furthermore, $X_1$ and $X_2$ are each symmetric about their mean of $\dfrac{N+1}{2}$. Thus, the sum $X_1 + X_2$ must be symmetric about its mean of $2 \cdot \dfrac{N+1}{2} = N+1$. Thus, as $N \rightarrow \infty$, the portion of the support lying in the region $\{X_1 + X_2 < N\}$ converges to $\dfrac{1}{2}$. As this sum is symmetric about the mean, the probability mass lying on the left and right side of the center is equal, so this implies $\prob{X_1 + X_2 < N} \rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2}$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$. As for the first term, given that $X_1 + X_2 < N$, there is exactly one value of $X_3$ in $[N]$ such that $X_1 +X_2 + X_3 = N$. Namely, this value is $N - X_1 - X_2$. The probability that this particular value is obtained by $X_3$ is $1/N$, as each value is equally likely to be selected from $X_3$, so $\prob{X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = N \mid X_1 + X_2 < N} = \dfrac{1}{N}$. Therefore, in limit, $Np_N = N\prob{X_1 + X_2 + X_3 = N} \rightarrow N \cdot \dfrac{1}{N} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.title: Maxidice I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob have fair standard $n-$sided and $m-$sided dice, respectively, where $n \geq m$. Bob is allowed to roll his die twice and keep the maximum value, while Alice can only roll her die once. Find the probability that Alice rolls a strictly higher value than Bob on her die when $m = 15$ and $n = 20$.
questions.solution: Since $n \geq m$, we know that Alice has a higher potential ceiling of values that she can roll than Bob. Note that if Alice rolls a value that is strictly larger than $m$, she automatically has the higher value, as Bob can't roll higher than $m$. The probability she rolls a value that is at most $m$ is $m/n$, as this accounts for $m$ of the $n$ equally likely sides. This implies that the probability she rolls a strictly larger value than $m$ is $1 - m/n$. Otherwise, if she rolls a value at most $m$, there is positive probability that she can lose. She wins exactly when both of Bob's die rolls are strictly less than hers. In other words, the maximum of them is strictly less than hers. If we knew Alice's roll, this would be an easy item to compute, so the best approach is to condition on Alice's roll. Formalizing the above, let $A$ be the event that Alice rolls a strictly larger value than Bob, and $X$ be the value of Alice's roll. By conditioning on the value of $X$, we have that $\prob{A} = \prob{A \mid X > m}\prob{X > m} + \sum_{k=1}^m \prob{A \mid X = k}\prob{X = k}$. In the latter term, we split into individual terms of the form $\{X = k\}$ because of the fact that we want a fixed threshold in each term. However, as we know that the exact value of $X$ given it is $> m$ does not matter, we can just condition for $\{X > m\}$ in the first part. As per the above, Alice always wins if $X > m$, so $\prob{A \mid X > m} = 1$, and $\prob{X > m} = 1-m/n$. Otherwise, we know that $\prob{X = k} = 1/n$ for each $1 \leq k \leq n$, as the die is fair. For $\prob{A \mid X = k}$, we want to compute the probability that the maximum of the two rolls is strictly less than $k$. In other words, the values of Bob's rolls must be at most $k-1$. The probability of this per roll is $\frac{k-1}{m}$, as there are $k-1$ positive integers at most $k-1$ out of $m$ total values on the die. Thus, as he rolls twice, the probability that both are at most $k-1$ is $\prob{A \mid X = k} = \left(\frac{k-1}{m}\right)^2$.
