Plugging this into the sum, we obtain $\prob{A} = 1 - \frac{m}{n} + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^m \left(\dfrac{k-1}{m}\right)^2 = 1 - \dfrac{m}{n} + \dfrac{1}{nm^2}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}k^2 = 1 - \dfrac{m}{n} + \dfrac{m(m-1)(2m-1)}{6nm^2}$. To evaluate the sum, an index shift by $1$ was performed, and we used the summation formula $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^n k^2 = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ with $n = m-1$. With the specified values, the answer is $107/225$.

questions.title: Maxidice II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob have fair standard $n-$sided and $m-$sided dice, respectively, where $n \geq m$. Bob is allowed to roll his die $r$ times and keep the maximum value, while Alice can only roll her die once. Let $p_r$ be the probability that Alice rolls a strictly higher value than Bob on her die when Bob has $r$ opportunities to roll his die. If it exists, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{r \rightarrow \infty} p_r$ when $m = 15$ and $n = 20$.
questions.solution: This probability could be computed explicitly, but it's much better to think about this question on an intuitive level. As $r \rightarrow \infty$, it becomes more and more likely that Bob will roll at least one very high value for his die in the $r$ rolls. In fact, it becomes essentially guaranteed for very large $r$ that Bob will roll the value $m$ at some point in the $r$ rolls. As Alice needs to roll a strictly larger value than Bob, the only way to do this for large $r$ is for her to obtain a value larger than $m$ on her die, so that no matter what Bob rolls, he will never be able to break above the threshold of his die. The probability of Alice rolling a strictly larger value than $m$ is $1 - \dfrac{m}{n}$, as found in "Maxidice I", so $\displaystyle \lim_{r \rightarrow \infty}p_r = 1 - \dfrac{m}{n}$. By an extremely similar process to the one from "Maxidice I", one can explicitly show $p_r = 1 - \dfrac{m}{n} + \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^m \left(\dfrac{k-1}{m}\right)^r$. The only difference is that there are now $r$ dice that need to be at most $k-1$ in value instead of $2$, so the power changes. However, as $m$ and $n$ are fixed and $\dfrac{k-1}{m} < 1$ for all $1 \leq k \leq m$, as $r \rightarrow \infty$, the terms on the interior of the summation tend to $0$, as the common ratio $\dfrac{k-1}{m} < 1$. Thus, the terms of the sum all tend to $0$, meaning that the $1 - \dfrac{m}{n}$ term is all that remains. With the specified values, the answer is $1/4$.

questions.title: Bertrand's Paradox II
questions.problem: A random chord is formed by a uniformly random angle $\theta \sim \unif{0}{2\pi}$ with the positive $x-$axis, and then a uniformly random distance $R \sim \unif{0}{1}$ is selected. A chord is then drawn that is perpendicular to the diameter of the circle that makes an angle $\theta$ with the positive $x-$axis whose intersection point with the chord is a distance $R$ away from the origin. Find the probability that the length of this chord is at least $\sqrt{3}$.
questions.solution: In the same spirit as "Bertrand's Paradox I", we can note that the angle selected for the diameter is irrelevant, as the circle can just be rotated so that $\theta = 0$ and the length of the chord selected does not change. Thus, assume $\theta = 0$. From here, we need to find the length of chord when $R = r$. If $R = r$, then the chord is vertical and intersects the $x-$axis at $(r,0)$. As the diameter is $1$ and the horizontal leg is $r$, the length of the vertical leg is $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ by the Pythagorean Theorem. As this vertical chord extends both above and below the $x-$axis and the circle is symmetric, the chord must be of length $2\sqrt{1-r^2}$ when $R = r$. Thus, the random variable that represents the length of the chord is $L = 2\sqrt{1-R^2}$. Since we know the distribution of $R$, we want to compute $\prob{L \geq \sqrt{3}}$, and we can relate $L$ to $R$, the approach is to substitute in the definition of $L$ in terms of $R$ and derive an event in terms of $R$. Namely, this is $L \geq \sqrt{3} \iff 2\sqrt{1-R^2} \geq \sqrt{3} \iff 1 - R^2 \geq \dfrac{3}{4} \iff R^2 \leq \dfrac{1}{4} \iff R \leq \dfrac{1}{2}$. We can ignore the negative values of $R$, as $R \sim \unif{0}{1}$. Since $R$ is uniform, we can take ratios of lengths to compute probabilities. The total length of the support of $R$ is $1$, while the event in question has length $1/2$ in the support, so the probability is $1/2$.

questions.title: Bertrand's Paradox III
questions.problem: A random chord is formed by selecting a uniformly random point $X$ from the interior of the unit circle that represents the other endpoint of a line segment extending from the circle's center to that point. Then, the chord whose midpoint is $X$ and is perpendicular to the line segment with endpoints $(0,0)$ and $X$ is drawn. You may assume that there is only one such chord. Find the probability that this chord has length at least $\sqrt{3}$.
questions.solution: We can view this question in the same light as "Bertrand's Paradox II", as we created the line segment in that problem by selecting a uniform direction and then a uniformly random distance from the origin in the selected direction. In this problem, we are just choosing a uniformly random point on the interior. If $R$ represents the distance from the origin of the selected point, then we still want to compute $\prob{R \leq 1/2}$. However, now, the event $\{R \leq 1/2\}$ represents a circle in the plane with radius $1/2$ centered at the origin, as this is the set of all points of distance at most $1/2$ away from the origin. Since the point $X$ is selected uniformly at random from the interior of the circle, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The total area of the support is $\pi$, while the area of the event $\{R \leq 1/2\}$ is $\pi \cdot (1/2)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Therefore, the probability that the chord is length at least $\sqrt{3}$ is $1/4$. The three parts of this problem show that "random chord" needs to be defined carefully in the context of the problem, as different interpretations that all appear valid yield different answers!

questions.title: Even Socks
questions.problem: A drawer contains (a not necessarily equal amount of) red and black socks. When two socks are drawn uniformly at random without replacement, the probability that both are red is $1/2$. What is the minimum number of red socks in the drawer if the number of black socks is even?
questions.solution:
Suppose that there are $r$ red and $b$ black socks in the drawer. Our goal to find the pair $(r,b)$ such that $r$ is minimal and the probability of drawing $2$ reds from a drawer of $r$ red and $b$ black socks is $1/2$. Thus, the first important step would be to find the probability for any general $r$ and $b$, say $P(r,b)$. The probability that the first sock is red is $\dfrac{r}{r+b}$, as $r$ of the $r+b$ total socks are red. Then, there are $r-1$ red and $b$ black socks left, so the probability that the second sock is red given the first sock is red is $\dfrac{r-1}{r+b-1}$, as there are $r+b-1$ socks overall left. Thus, the probability that both socks are red is $P(r,b) = \dfrac{r}{r+b} \cdot \dfrac{r-1}{r+b-1}$. Now, we need to set this equal to $1/2$ to derive a relationship between $r$ and $b$. Namely, $P(r,b) = \dfrac{1}{2} \iff \dfrac{r(r-1)}{(r+b)(r+b-1)} = \dfrac{1}{2} \iff 2r(r-1) = (r+b)(r+b-1) \iff 2r^2 - 2r = r^2 + b^2 
+ 2rb - r - b$. From here, we must attempt to arrange all of the $r$ variables on one side. The idea is that we want to obtain a quadratic equation for $r$ in terms of $b$, so that we are able to solve for $r$ in terms of $b$, and then determine when this is an integer. We get $r^2 - (2b+1)r - (b^2 - b) = 0 \iff r_{1,2} = \dfrac{2b+1 \pm \sqrt{(2b+1)^2 +4(b^2 - b)}}{2} = \dfrac{2b+1 \pm \sqrt{8b^2 + 1}}{2}$. Note that $\sqrt{8b^2 + 1} > \sqrt{8b^2} = 2\sqrt{2}b > 2b$, so the root that subtracts $\sqrt{8b^2 + 1}$ will be negative, which isn't possible, as we can't have a negative amount of socks. Therefore, $r = \dfrac{2b+1 + \sqrt{8b^2 + 1}}{2}$ is the number of red socks we must have for a fixed number of black socks. Note that $b$ must be even here by the assumption of the question, so we can write $b = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Plugging this in, we have that $r = \dfrac{4k+1 + \sqrt{32k^2 + 1}}{2}$. Now, we must find the smallest positive integer $k$ such that this is an integer. For this to be an integer, it is necessary that $\sqrt{32k^2 + 1}$ is an integer, so let's find the smallest $k$ that makes this an integer. The interior must be a perfect square, so trying out a few small values of $k$, we get $33, 129,$ and $289$. However $289 = 17^2$, so $k = 3$ makes the square root an integer. Thus, when $k = 3$, $r = \dfrac{13 + 17}{2} = 15$, which is also an integer. As the number of black balls is $2k$, the minimal pair is $(r,b) = (15,6)$. One can verify that this does satisfy the equation: $\dfrac{15}{21} \cdot \dfrac{14}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Therefore, the answer is $15$.

questions.title: Coprime Fraction
questions.problem: Find the number of rational numbers $\dfrac{a}{b}$ such that $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime integers and $ab = 25!$.
questions.solution: For $a$ and $b$ to be relatively prime, their prime factorizations must not contain any primes in common. If they had a prime in common, then they would not be relatively prime. The possible primes in the prime factorization of $25!$ are just the primes that are less than $25$, which are: $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,$ and $23$. Since the product of $a$ and $b$ must be $25!$, we must assign the maximal power of each prime to exactly one of $a$ or $b$. This means, for example, that if the exponent of $2$ is $p_2$ in the prime factorization of $25!$, then $2^{p_2}$ must be in the prime factorization of exactly one of $a$ or $b$. Note that we need the exponent that is assigned to $a$ and $b$ to be maximal so that $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime. Otherwise, for example, if we assigned $2^{p_2 - 1}$ to $a$, we would have to assign a factor of $2$ to $b$ so that the product will be the same as what is in $25!$. However, $a$ and $b$ would no longer be relatively prime, as $2$ would divide both $a$ and $b$. Therefore, creating a fraction is really equivalent to just assigning each prime factor to one of $a$ or $b$. Since there are $2$ options for each of the $9$ prime factors, there are $2^9 = 512$ ways to assign the primes to either $a$ or $b$, so there are $512$ such fractions. Note that integers are rational numbers, so we don't need to worry about the case when $b = 1$. In general, if $\pi(n)$ represents the number of prime integers that are at most $n$, there would be $2^{\pi(n)}$ ways to create such a fraction.

questions.title: Parentheses Inventor
questions.problem: You invent a new language that has $k \geq 1$ forms of parentheses, say $(_1 )_1$ to $(_k )_k$. A proper $(k,n)-$parenthesization is a string of length $2n$ such that for all $1 \leq i \leq k$, the number of $)_i$ never exceeds the number of $(_i$ anywhere in the string. Find the number of proper $(k,n)-$parenthesizations when $k = 4$ and $n = 5$.
questions.solution: Since this quantity is related to parenthesizations, the first thought should be to relate it to Catalan numbers (we will refer to these as standard parenthesizations). Therefore, fix some standard parenthesization. There are $n$ pairs of parentheses in the string that satisfy the condition above. Now, all that is left is to note that a $(k,n)-$parenthesization can be obtained from a standard parenthesization by selecting one of the $k$ parentheses options for each of the $n$ pairs. For example, if $n = 3$ and $k = 3$, then the "standard parenthesization" $(())()$ could become, for example, $(_1(_2)_2)_1(_2)_2$ or $(_3(_3)_3)_3(_1)_1$. Essentially, for each of the pairs of parentheses, there are $k$ options for what subscript it has, so as there are $n$ pairs of parentheses total, each standard parenthesization gives rise to $k^n$ $(k,n)-$parenthesizations, as there are $k$ options for each of $n$ pairs. Now, we know from "Proper Parenthesization" that the number of "standard parenthesizations" is just $C_n = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$, so this implies that the number of $(k,n)-$parenthesizations is $C_n \cdot k^n$, as each gives rise to $k^n$ $(k,n)-$parenthesizations. With the specified values, the answer is $42 \cdot 4^5 = 43008$.

questions.title: Subby Choice II
questions.problem: A random subset $S$ of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$ is selected by first selecting $N \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{0,1,2,\dots,n\}$. Then, given that $N = k$, select a subset $S$ uniformly at random from $[n]_k$, the collection of all size $k$ subsets of $[n]$. Find the expected sum of the elements in $S$ when $n = 15$.
questions.solution: Note here that the selection among all subsets of $[n]$ is not uniform; instead, the distribution of the sizes of the subsets are uniform. If we knew the size of the subset, say $k$, then we know that as sampling without replacement is an exchangeable process, the expected value of each of the $k$ elements is just the expected value of the first element selected, which is $\dfrac{n+1}{2}$. Therefore, the idea here is to condition on the size of the subset, $N$. Namely, if $T$ represents the total sum of elements in $S$, then $\ev{T} = \ev{\ev{T \mid N}} = \sum_{k=0}^n \ev{T \mid N = k}\prob{N=k}$. As per the question $\prob{N = k} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$, as it is discrete uniform over a set of $n+1$ elements. Then, by the previous discussion above, $\ev{T \mid N = k} = k \cdot \dfrac{n+1}{2}$, as each of the $k$ elements selected without replacement are exchangeable, and therefore have the same mean. Plugging this in, we get $\ev{T} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sum_{k=0}^n k = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{4}$. Note that even though the distribution of $T$ in this problem and $T$ in "Subby Choice I" are different, they yield the same expected value. This is because of the symmetric way in which the subsets are picked, even if the subsets themselves don't share the same distribution. In particular, this symmetry arises from the fact that for each $A \subseteq [n]$, $A$ and $A^c$ have the same probability of being selected. This is from the fact that there are the same number of subsets of size $k$ as there are size $n-k$. We can also see that $[n] = A \cup A^c$, so the sum of the elements between the two subsets is just $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n i = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. As this accounts for two subsets, the mean sum of each subset is $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{4}$, and this holds for every subset $A \subseteq [n]$.

questions.title: Different Intersection II
questions.problem: Select two subsets of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$ in the following fashion: Let $N_1,N_2 \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ IID. Then, given $N_1 = n_1$ and $N_2 = n_2$, select $A$ and $B$ independently and uniformly at random selected from the collection of subsets of $[n]$ of sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$, respectively. Find $\ev{|A\cap B|}$ when $n = 12$.
questions.solution: If we know $n_1$ and $n_2$, then we can use the result of "Different Intersection I" to compute the expected number of elements in the intersection. Therefore, the approach is to condition on the values of both $N_1$ and $N_2$. By Law of Total Expectation, we have that $\ev{|A\cap B|} = \ev{\ev{|A \cap B| \mid N_1,N_2}} = \sum_{n_1=0}^n \sum_{n_2=0}^n \ev{|A \cap B| \mid N_1 = n_1, N_2 = n_2}\prob{N_1 = n_1,N_2 = n_2}$. Since $N_1$ and $N_2$ are selected independently, $\prob{N_1 = n_1, N_2 = n_2} = \prob{N_1 = n_1}\prob{N_2 = n_2} = \dfrac{1}{(n+1)^2}$, as $N_1$ and $N_2$ are selected uniformly at random from a discrete set of size $n+1$. Then, given $N_1 = n_1$ and $N_2 = n_2$, we now know the sizes of $A$ and $B$, so we can use the result of "Different Intersection I" to conclude that $\ev{|A\cap B| \mid N_1 = n_1, N_2 = n_2} = \dfrac{n_1n_2}{n}$. Plugging all of these in, we get that $\ev{|A\cap B|} = \sum_{n_1 = 0}^n\sum_{n_2 = 0}^n \dfrac{n_1n_2}{n} \cdot \dfrac{1}{(n+1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{n(n+1)^2}\sum_{n_1 = 0}^n n_1 \cdot \sum_{n_2=0}^n n_2 = \dfrac{1}{n(n+1)^2} \cdot \left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{n}{4}$. Note that we can write the remaining double sum as a product of two sums, as the terms inside are separable and the bounds are constant. Therefore, with $n = 12$, the answer is $3$.

questions.title: Different Intersection III
questions.problem: Fix $0 \leq n_1,\dots, n_k \leq n$. Let $A_1,\dots, A_k$ be subsets of $[n]$ that are independently selected, with $A_i$ being uniformly random from the collection of subsets of $[n]$ with size $n_i$. Find $\ev{\displaystyle \left|\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i\right|}$ when $n = 12, k = 4,$ and $a_i = 2i$.
questions.solution: There is no clear way to proceed in this problem by deriving the PMF of the intersection, so an alternative must be better. Note that the number of elements in $\displaystyle \left|\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i \right|$ is just the sum of indicators that represent whether or not each element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in the intersection. Therefore, the best approach is to use linearity of expectation on indicators. In particular, let $I_i$ be the indicator that element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i$. We set up the indicators this way so that we can count the expected number of elements in the intersection. Therefore, we have that $\displaystyle \left|\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i\right| = I_1 + \dots + I_n$ gives the total number of elements in the intersection. As the $k$ subsets are selected uniformly at random from the subsets of those respective sizes, each element has the same probability of being included in each of the $A_i$ sets. Therefore, the indicators are all exchangeable, and hence have the same mean. By linearity of expectation, we have $\ev{\left|\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i\right|} = n\ev{I_1}$. $\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that $1$ is in $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i$. Since the $A_i$ sets are selected independently, we have that $\prob{\displaystyle 1 \in \bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i} = \prob{1 \in A_1}\dots\prob{1 \in A_k}$. By the result of "Include The Element!", as $|A_i| = n_i$, $\prob{1 \in A_i} = \dfrac{n_i}{n}$. Plugging these in, we get $\ev{\left|\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i\right|} = n \cdot \dfrac{n_1}{n} \dots \dfrac{n_k}{n} = \dfrac{n_1\dots n_k}{n^{k-1}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $2/9$.

questions.title: Flipping Boxes
questions.problem: Infinitely many boxes labelled $1,2,\dots$ are lined up, with box $k$ having $r^k - 1$ black balls and $1$ white ball, where $r \geq 1$ is an integer. We flip a fair coin until the first heads appears, and if it takes $k$ flips to see the first head, then we draw $1$ ball from box $k$. Find the probability a white ball is selected when $r = 4$.
questions.solution:
The probability of obtaining a heads depends on which box is selected, and the box selected depends on how many flips there are until the first heads. Therefore, let $F_k$ be the event that it takes $k$ flips until the first heads appears and $W$ be the event of selecting a white ball. By applying the Law of Total Probability with partitioning on the $F_k$ events, $\mathbb{P}[W] = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}[W \mid F_k]\mathbb{P}[F_k]$. We first need to find $\mathbb{P}[F_k]$ for each $k \geq 1$. The event $F_k$ occurs when the first heads occurs on the $k$th flip. This is equivalent to saying the first $k-1$ flips were all tails, while the $k$th flip is heads. There are $2^k$ equally likely outcomes in $k$ flips (as the coin is fair), and only one of them has tails in the first $k-1$ flips and a head in the $k$th flip, so $\mathbb{P}[F_k] = 1/2^k$. Then, given $F_k$, we select from $r^k -1$ black balls and $1$ white ball. Thus, $\mathbb{P}[W \mid F_k] = 1/r^k$. Substituting in, $\mathbb{P}[W] = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^k \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{r}\right)^k = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 
\left(\dfrac{1}{2r}\right)^k$. This is a geometric series with common ratio and first term equal to $1/2r$, so $\mathbb{P}[W] = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2r}}{1 - \frac{1}{2r}} = \dfrac{1}{2r-1}$. With $r = 4$, the answer is $1/7$.

questions.title: Powerful Root I
questions.problem: Evaluate the integral $I(n) = \displaystyle \int_0^1 (1-x^n)^{1/n}~dx$ for integers $n \geq 1$. Report the answer to the nearest thousandth when $n = 4$.
questions.solution: In this integral, we see a term of $1-x^n$ raised to some power. This does seem somewhat reminiscent of the Beta integral. However, in the Beta integral, we only have powers of $x$ and $1-x$. This leads us to try to eliminate the $x^n$ by the $u-$substitution $u = x^n$. This means that $du = nx^{n-1}dx$ and $x = u^{1/n}$. The bounds the new integral are $0^n = 0$ and $1^n = 1$. Since we don't see a term of $x^{n-1}$ in our integral to immediately create the $du$, rearrange the $dx$ to get $dx = \dfrac{1}{n(u^{1/n})^{n-1}}du = \dfrac{u^{1/n-1}}{n}du$. Substituting the above into the integral, we obtain $I(n) = \int_0^1 (1-u)^{1/n} \cdot \dfrac{1}{n}u^{1/n - 1}~du = \dfrac{1}{n} \int_0^1 u^{\textcolor{red}{1/n} - 1}(1-u)^{\textcolor{blue}{(1 + 1/n)} - 1}~du$. We write the integral like this because of the fact that it now looks similar to the Beta integral with $\textcolor{red}{a = 1/n}$ and $\textcolor{blue}{b = 1 + 1/n}$, but without the normalization constant. Therefore, the integral evaluates to the normalization constant, so $I(n) = \dfrac{1}{n} \cdot \dfrac{\Gamma(1/n)\Gamma(1+1/n)}{\Gamma(1+2/n)} = \dfrac{\Gamma(1/n)\Gamma(1+1/n)}{n\Gamma(1+2/n)}$. When $n=4$, the answer is $\approx 0.927$.

questions.title: Normal Moments II
questions.problem: Suppose that $Z \sim N(0,1)$. Find $\ev{Z^n}$, where $n$ is a positive even integer. Report the answer when $n = 8$.
questions.solution: When computing $\ev{Z^k}$ for a general $k$, computing the $k$th derivative through the MGF or LOTUS explicitly is annoying. However, from the Taylor expansion of the MGF, one can read off the $k$th moment from the coefficient of $\theta^k$. Therefore, the best approach is to consider the Taylor series of the MGF. By taking $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$ in the MGF of the Normal distribution, the MGF of $Z$ is given by $M(\theta) = e^{\frac{1}{2}\theta^2}$. Luckily, we do know the Taylor series of $e^x$, so we can conclude that $M(\theta) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\theta^2\right)^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^k k !}\theta^{2k}$. Suppose $n$ is even i.e. $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$. The coefficient of $\theta^{2k}$ in the above is $\dfrac{1}{2^k k!}$. From the Taylor expansion of the MGF, we know it's also equal to $\dfrac{\ev{Z^{2k}}}{(2k)!}$. Therefore, we have the equality $\dfrac{\ev{Z^{2k}}}{(2k)!} = \dfrac{1}{2^k k!} \iff \ev{Z^{2k}} = \dfrac{(2k)!}{2^k k!}$. With the specified value, $n = 8 = 2 \cdot 4$, so $\ev{Z^8} = 105$.

questions.title: Normal Moments III
questions.problem: Suppose that $X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. Find $\ev{X^n}$, where $n$ is any positive integer. Report the answer for $\mu = 3, \sigma^2 = 4,$ and $n = 4$.
questions.solution: We know the moments of a standard Normal distribution from the previous parts of this problem. Recall that if $Z \sim N(0,1)$, then $X = \sigma Z + \mu \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. Therefore, we can write $\ev{X^n} = \ev{(\sigma Z + \mu)^n}$. To relate this quantity to the moments of $Z$, we must expand out the interior. This can be done with the binomial theorem. Namely, $\ev{X^n} = \ev{(\sigma Z+ \mu)^n} = \ev{\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(\sigma Z)^k \mu^{n-k}} = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}\sigma^k \mu^{n-k}\ev{Z^k}$. This is the furthest the expression can be simplified. With the specified values, the answer is $345$.

questions.title: Ordered Volume
questions.problem: Find the volume of the region $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, where we have that $S = \left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : 0 \leq x_1 < x_2 < \dots < x_n \leq 1\right\}$. Report the answer when $n = 4$.
questions.solution: Recall that if the PDF of some random variables $X_1,\dots, X_n$ in a bounded region $R \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is constant, then density is uniformly distributed throughout $R$, and that constant is $1/\text{Vol}(R)$. Using this idea, we want to somehow make the density throughout $S$ constant. A way to do this is to use $\unif{0}{1}$ random variables as the $X_1,\dots,X_n$ for our order statistics. The PDF of a $\unif{0}{1}$ distribution is constant, which illuminates the natural choice. The joint density of the $n$ order statistics for $X_1,\dots,X_n \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$ IID is given by the above formula with $f(x) = 1$, so that $f(x_1,\dots,x_n) = n!(1)^nI_{\{0 \leq x_1 < x_2 <\dots <x_n \leq 1\}}((x_1,\dots,x_n)) = n!I_{\{0 \leq x_1 < x_2 <\dots <x_n \leq 1\}}((x_1,\dots,x_n))$. The indicator has a lower bound of $0$ and an upper bound of $1$ because each of the $x_i$ are between $0$ and $1$, since Unif$(0,1)$ random variables are only supported on $(0,1)$. Thus, all of them must be at least $0$ and at most $1$. Note that the region in the indicator is now just $S$ from the question, and the term in front of the indicator is $n!$, which is constant. Thus, the joint density over $S$ is constant, and that means that the volume of $S$ is given by $n! = \dfrac{1}{\text{Vol}(S)} \iff \text{Vol}(S) = \dfrac{1}{n!}$. With $n = 4$, the answer is $1/24$.

questions.title: Minimum Twice!
questions.problem: Suppose that $X \sim \exponential{\lambda_1}$ and $Y \sim \exponential{\lambda_2}$ independently. For any $t > 0$, compute $\prob{Y \geq X \geq t}$ when $\lambda_i = i$ and $t = 3$. If the answer you receive is $p$, report $p \cdot 10^5$ to the nearest hundredth.
questions.solution: The event $\{Y \geq X \geq t\}$ is the same as saying both $Y \geq X$ and $\min(X,Y) \geq t$ hold. Thus, we can write $\{Y \geq X \geq t\} = \{Y \geq X\} \cap \{\min(X,Y) \geq t\}$. The key insight here is to note that the events $\{Y \geq X\}$ and $\{\min(X,Y) \geq t\}$ are independent. This is because knowing both of them are at least some value does not affect their relative ordering by the memorylessness property of Exponential distributions. Therefore, $\prob{Y \geq X \geq t} = \prob{Y \geq X}\prob{\min(X,Y) \geq t} = \prob{X = \min(X,Y)}\prob{X \geq t}\prob{Y \geq t}$. The last two probabilities are easy to compute through the CDF of the Exponential distribution. The first probability is $\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}$ by the result of "Less Than Exponential". Thus, we obtain $\prob{Y \geq X \geq t} = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}e^{-(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)t}$. If you didn't realize the above, the probability is not too difficult to explicitly compute. The more straightforward way is to integrate over the region corresponding to the event. The joint PDF of $X$ and $Y$ is $f(x,y) = \lambda_1 e^{-\lambda_1 x} I_{(0,\infty)}(x) \cdot \lambda_2 e^{-\lambda_2 y} I_{(0,\infty)}(y)$ by independence. This probability is equal to $\prob{Y \geq X \geq t} = \int_t^{\infty} \int_x^{\infty} f(x,y)~dy~dx = \int_t^{\infty} \lambda_1 e^{-(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)x}~dx = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}e^{-(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)t}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\frac{1}{3e^9}$.

questions.title: Even Multiple I
questions.problem: A fair coin is flipped repeatedly until the first heads appears. Given that the total number of flips performed is divisible by $r > 1$, where $r$ is an odd integer, compute the probability that the total number flips performed is even. Solve this when $r = 3$.
questions.solution: The distribution of the number of flips needed to observe the first heads is $N \sim \geom{1/2}$, as each flip is independent and has constant success probability. As $r$ is odd, multiples of odd integers alternate between even and odd. For example, $3,6,9,12,15,18,\dots$ alternate between even and odd for the $r = 3$ case. Since we want to compute a conditional probability, we should set up a conditional probability statement. Let $E$ be the event that $N$ is even and $R$ be the event that $N$ is divisible by $r$. We want to compute $\prob{E \mid R}$. By the conditional probability formula, this is $\prob{E \cap R}/\prob{R}$. If $R$ occurs, then $X = kr$ for some positive integer $k$, as $X$ must be a multiple of $r$. We have that $\prob{R} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{X = kr} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{kr} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{2^r}\right)^k = \dfrac{1/2^r}{1 - 1/2^r} = \dfrac{1}{2^r - 1}$. We evaluated the sum using the geometric series formula with common ratio $1/2^r$. If $E \cap R$ occurs, then $X$ must be a multiple of both $2$ and $r$. As $r$ is odd, $X$ must be a multiple of $2r$. Applying the same process as above, $\prob{E \cap R} = \dfrac{1/4^r}{1 - 1/4^r} = \dfrac{1}{4^r - 1}$. Plugging these in, $\prob{E \mid R} = \dfrac{2^r - 1}{4^r - 1} = \dfrac{1}{2^r + 1} = \dfrac{1/2^r}{1 + 1/2^r}$. The expression $\dfrac{1/2^r}{1 + 1/2^r}$ gives us another interpretation to look at. As $\prob{N = n} = 1/2^n$, we can note that $\prob{N = (k+1)r} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{(k+1)r} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^r \cdot \prob{N = kr}$. Thus, all of the even values (even multiples of $r$) are $1/2^r$ as likely to occur as the odd multiple coming right before them. If $p$ represents the probability that $N$ is odd, $p/2^r$ must be the probability that $N$ is even by the above scaling factor of $1/2^r$ for all even probabilities. $N$ must either be even or odd, so $p + p/2^r = 1 \iff p = \dfrac{1}{1 + 1/2^r}$. Therefore, the probability of an even is $p/2^r = \frac{1/2^r}{1 + 1/2^r}$. With the specified value, the answer is $1/9$.

questions.title: Even Multiple II
questions.problem: A coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip is flipped repeatedly until the first heads appears. Given that the total number of flips performed is divisible by $r > 1$, where $r$ is an odd integer, compute the probability that the total number flips performed is even. Solve this when $r = 3$ and $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: The distribution of the number of flips needed to observe the first heads is $N \sim \geom{p}$, as each flip is independent and has constant success probability. As $r$ is odd, multiples of odd integers alternate between even and odd. For example, $3,6,9,12,15,18,\dots$ alternate between even and odd for the $r = 3$ case. Since we want to compute a conditional probability, we should set up a conditional probability statement. Let $E$ be the event that $N$ is even and $R$ be the event that $N$ is divisible by $r$. We want to compute $\prob{E \mid R}$. By the conditional probability formula, this is $\prob{E \cap R}/\prob{R}$. If $R$ occurs, then $X = kr$ for some positive integer $k$, as $X$ must be a multiple of $r$. We have that $\prob{R} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{X = kr} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} p(1-p)^{kr-1} = \dfrac{p}{1-p}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left[(1-p)^r\right]^k = \dfrac{p}{1-p} \cdot \dfrac{(1-p)^r}{1-(1-p)^r}$. We evaluated the sum using the geometric series formula with common ratio $(1-p)^r$. If $E \cap R$ occurs, then $X$ must be a multiple of both $2$ and $r$. As $r$ is odd, $X$ must be a multiple of $2r$. Applying the same process as above, $\prob{E \cap R} = \dfrac{p}{1-p} \cdot \dfrac{(1-p)^{2r}}{1 - (1-p)^{2r}}$. Plugging these in, $\prob{E \mid R} = \dfrac{\frac{(1-p)^{2r}}{1 - (1-p)^{2r}}}{\frac{(1-p)^{r}}{1 - (1-p)^{r}}} = \dfrac{(1-p)^r}{1+(1-p)^r}$. The expression $\dfrac{(1-p)^r}{1+(1-p)^r}$ gives us another interpretation to look at. As $\prob{N = n} = p(1-p)^{n-1}$, we can note that $\prob{N = (k+1)r} = p(1-p)^{r(k+1) - 1} = (1-p)^r\prob{N = kr}$. Thus, all of the even values (even multiples of $r$) are $(1-p)^r$ as likely to occur as the odd multiple coming right before them. If $q$ represents the probability that $N$ is odd, $q(1-p)^r$ must be the probability that $N$ is even by the above scaling factor of $(1-p)^r$ for all even probabilities. $N$ must either be even or odd, so $q + q(1-p)^r = 1 \iff q = \dfrac{1}{1 + (1-p)^r}$. Therefore, the probability of an even is $q(1-p)^r = \dfrac{(1-p)^r}{1 + (1-p)^r}$. With the specified values, the answer is $8/35$.

questions.title: Limited Hitter II
questions.problem: A standard fair $n-$sided die is rolled infinitely. The cumulative sum of all observed rolls is recorded after each roll. For each integer $k \geq 1$, let $f(n,k)$ be the probability that the cumulative sum is ever exactly $k$. For a fixed $n$, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} f(n,k)$. Report the answer when $n = 6$.
questions.solution: The expected value of a fair $n-$sided die is $\frac{n+1}{2}$. Therefore, the die jumps, on average, $\frac{n+1}{2}$ values per roll, meaning that it hits approximately $1$ value per $\frac{n+1}{2}$ in the long-run. Thus, the proportion of values the cumulative sum hits is approximately $\frac{2}{n+1}$ in the long-run, meaning our limit is $\frac{2}{n+1}$. This intuition can actually be formalized with the theory of renewal processes and Blackwell's theorem. With $n = 6$, the answer is $2/7$.

questions.title: Limited Hitter III
questions.problem: $m \geq 1$ standard fair $n-$sided dice is rolled infinitely. The cumulative sum of all observed rolls at each turn is recorded. For example, when $m = 2$ and $n = 6$, if the two dice observed are $2$ and $5$, the value $7$ would be added to the running total. For each integer $m \geq 1$, let $f(n,k,m)$ be the probability that the cumulative sum is ever exactly $k$. For fixed $n$ and $m$, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} f(n,k,m)$. Report the answer when $n = 6$ and $m = 4$.
questions.solution: The expected value of a fair $n-$sided die is $\frac{n+1}{2}$. By linearity of expectation, the expected value of the sum of $m$ such dice is $m \cdot \frac{n+1}{2}$. Therefore, the die jumps, on average, $m \cdot \frac{n+1}{2}$ values per turn, meaning that it hits approximately $1$ value per $m \cdot \frac{n+1}{2}$ in the long-run. Thus, the proportion of values the cumulative sum hits is approximately $\frac{2}{m(n+1)}$ in the long-run, meaning our limit is $\frac{2}{m(n+1)}$. This intuition can actually be formalized with the theory of renewal processes and Blackwell's theorem. With $n = 6$ and $m = 4$, the answer is $1/14$.

questions.title: Limited Hitter IV
questions.problem: A $n-$sided die with the values $1-n$ is rolled infinitely. The side with value $i$ appears with probability $p_i > 0$. The cumulative sum of all observed rolls is recorded after each roll. For each integer $k \geq 1$, let $f(k)$ be the probability that the cumulative sum is ever exactly $k$. For a fixed $k$, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} f(k)$. Report the answer when $n = 8, p_i = 1/12$ for $i = 1,2,3,4$, and $p_i = 1/6$ for $i = 5,6,7,8$.
questions.solution: Just as in the previous examples, define $\mu = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n ip_i$. The die jumps, on average, $\mu$ values per turn, meaning that it hits approximately $1$ value per $\mu$ in the long-run. Thus, the proportion of values the cumulative sum hits is approximately $1\ \mu$ in the long-run, meaning our limit is $1/ \mu$. This intuition can actually be formalized with the theory of renewal processes and Blackwell's theorem. The three previous parts of this question can be regarded as special versions of this one. With the specific values in question, $\mu = 62/12 = 31/6$, so the answer is $6/31$.

questions.title: Limited Hitter V
questions.problem: A $n-$sided die is rolled infinitely. Suppose that the GCD of all the sides is $d \geq 1$. The side with value $i$ appears with probability $p_i > 0$. The cumulative sum of all observed rolls is recorded after each roll. For each integer $k \geq 1$, let $f(k)$ be the probability that the cumulative sum is ever exactly $k$. Compute $\displaystyle \lim_{r \rightarrow \infty} f(rd)$. Report the answer when $n = 8, p_i = 1/12$ for $i = 3,6,9,12$, and $p_i = 1/6$ for $i = 24,48,72,96$.
questions.solution: Just as in the previous examples, define $\mu = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n ip_i$. Note that $\displaystyle \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} f(k)$ does not exist, as the probability of cumulative sums that are not multiples of $d$ is $0$, whereas it's positive for multiples of $d$. We can now interpret this as: On average, the die jumps $\mu/d$ multiples of $d$ per roll, so it hits one multiple of $d$ on average per $\mu/d$ multiples. Therefore, the limiting proportion of multiples of $d$ that are hit is $d/\mu$, which is our limit. This intuition can actually be formalized with the theory of renewal processes and Blackwell's theorem. In this example, $d = 3$, as the GCD of all values on the die is $3$, and $\mu = 85/2$. Therefore, the answer is $6/85$.

questions.title: Distinct Values I
questions.problem: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n$ be IID non-negative integer-valued random variables with $p_i = \prob{X_1 = i}$. Find the expected number of distinct values among $X_1,\dots, X_n$ when $n = 40$ and $X_i \sim \poisson{1}$ IID. Round to the nearest tenth.
questions.solution: The concept of this problem seems similar to the coupon collector problem. In that problem, we set up indicators representing whether or not the coupon was collected. We can apply the same idea here to set up indicators as to whether or not each value appears among $X_1,\dots, X_n$. Using the above idea, let $I_i$ be the indicator that at least one of the $n$ random variables takes the value $i$. $T = I_0 + I_1 + \dots$ gives the total amount of distinct values that appear among the $n$ random variables. Since this is an infinite summation, we can't apply linearity of expectation directly. The expectation is still linear, and can be justified by the Monotone Convergence Theorem, although this detail is irrelevant. Assuming this, $\ev{T} = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \ev{I_i}$. $\ev{I_i}$ is the probability that at least one of $n$ random variables takes the value $i$. This probability is easier computed via the complement, which is the event that no random variables take the value $i$. The probability that any particular random variable takes the value $i$ is $p_i$, so the probability none of the $n$ random variables take the value $i$ is $(1-p_i)^n$ by independence. By complementation, the probability at least one random variable takes the value $i$ is $\ev{I_i} = 1-(1-p_i)^n$. Therefore, $\ev{T} = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}1 - (1-p_i)^n$. The coupon collector problem is this problem with $X_1,\dots, X_n \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{1,2,\dots, n\}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 4.5$.

questions.title: All In II
questions.problem: Kenny has $\$n$ in his pocket at a casino, where $n$ is an integer. His goal is to leave with $\$2n$. The dealer gives Kenny two choices for his game: Bet all $\$n$ at once or bet $\$1$ at a time until he goes broke or has $\$2n$. Regardless of the game, Kenny has probability $0 < p < 1$ of winning each round. If $p = 1/4$ and $n = 50$, which game should Kenny play to maximize his probability of leaving with twice as much money? Answer $1$ if he should bet all $\$n$ at once, $2$ if he should bet $\$1$ per round, or $3$ if he is indifferent.
questions.solution: Kenny falls into the Gambler's Ruin paradigm if he bets $\$1$ at a time. Since the game is no longer symmetric, we need to use the more complicated Gambler's Ruin formula for the probability of success. When there is probability $0 < p < 1$ of the Kenny winning each round, as per the Gambler's Ruin formula, his probability of leaving with $\$2n$ when betting $\$1$ at a time is given by $\dfrac{1 - \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n}{1 - \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^{2n}} = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n}$. Clearly, Kenny has probability $p$ of winning if he bets all at once. To see where these are equal, $p = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n} \iff p = \dfrac{p^n}{p^n + (1-p)^n} \iff p^{n+1} + p(1-p)^n = p^n \iff p^n(1-p) = p(1-p)^n$. In the last equation, we see that $p = 0,1$ create equality. We can divide by $p(1-p)$ on both sides to obtain $p^{n-1} = (1-p)^{n-1} \iff p = 1-p \iff p = 1/2$. Therefore, the two functions are equal at $0,1/2,$ and $1$. The intersection of $1/2$ was seen in "All In I". Note that there will be a better choice for all $0 < p < 1/2$ and $1/2 < p < 1$, as the only intersection in $(0,1)$ is at $p = 1/2$. To find which choice is better, we can break up based on $0 < p < 1/2$ and $1/2 < p < 1$. If $0 < p < 1/2$, then $\frac{1-p}{p} > 1$, as $p < 1-p$. Since $\frac{1-p}{p} > 1$, for any positive integer $n$, $\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n > \frac{1-p}{p}$. Using this fact, $\dfrac{1}{1+\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n} < \dfrac{1}{1 + \frac{1-p}{p}} = p$. This implies betting all at once is the better option. This result makes intuitive sense because of the Law of Large Numbers. When Kenny plays a large number of games, on average, he is going to lose money per round by LLN, so it's much more likely he will go broke, especially when $n$ is large. Even if Kenny is lucky for a while and wins a few games, the LLN will eventually make Kenny's disadvantage against the dealer show. In $1$ game, it is essentially pure luck as to whether he wins or not, so there aren't enough rounds for LLN to kick in and draw his winnings down to $0$. The answer to this question is $1$.

questions.title: All In III
questions.problem: Kenny has $\$n$ in his pocket at a casino, where $n$ is an integer. His goal is to leave with $\$2n$. The dealer gives Kenny two choices for his game: Bet all $\$n$ at once or bet $\$1$ at a time until he goes broke or has $\$2n$. Regardless of the game, Kenny has probability $0 < p < 1$ of winning each round. If $p = 3/4$ and $n = 50$, which game should Kenny play to maximize his probability of leaving with twice as much money? Answer $1$ if he should bet all $\$n$ at once, $2$ if he should bet $\$1$ per round, or $3$ if he is indifferent.
questions.solution: Kenny falls into the Gambler's Ruin paradigm if he bets $\$1$ at a time. Since the game is no longer symmetric, we need to use the more complicated Gambler's Ruin formula for the probability of success. When there is probability $0 < p < 1$ of the Kenny winning each round, as per the Gambler's Ruin formula, his probability of leaving with $\$2n$ when betting $\$1$ at a time is given by $\dfrac{1 - \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n}{1 - \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^{2n}} = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n}$. Clearly, Kenny has probability $p$ of winning if he bets all at once. To see where these are equal, $p = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n} \iff p = \dfrac{p^n}{p^n + (1-p)^n} \iff p^{n+1} + p(1-p)^n = p^n \iff p^n(1-p) = p(1-p)^n$. In the last equation, we see that $p = 0,1$ create equality. We can divide by $p(1-p)$ on both sides to obtain $p^{n-1} = (1-p)^{n-1} \iff p = 1-p \iff p = 1/2$. Therefore, the two functions are equal at $0,1/2,$ and $1$. The intersection of $1/2$ was seen in "All In I". Note that there will be a better choice for all $0 < p < 1/2$ and $1/2 < p < 1$, as the only intersection in $(0,1)$ is at $p = 1/2$. To find which choice is better, we can break up based on $0 < p < 1/2$ and $1/2 < p < 1$. If $1/2 < p < 1$, then $\frac{1-p}{p} < 1$, as $p > 1-p$. Since $\frac{1-p}{p} > 1$, for any positive integer $n$, $\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n < \frac{1-p}{p}$. Using this fact, $\dfrac{1}{1+\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)^n} > \dfrac{1}{1 + \frac{1-p}{p}} = p$. This implies betting $\$1$ per round is the better option. This result makes intuitive sense because of the Law of Large Numbers. When Kenny plays a large number of games, on average, he is going to make money per round by LLN, so it's much more likely he will eventually hit $\$2n$, especially when $n$ is large. Even if Kenny goes on a slightly unlucky streak for some time, the LLN gives him more opportunity to wield his edge in the game against the dealer. In $1$ game, it is essentially pure luck as to whether he wins or not, so there aren't enough rounds for Kenny's advantage to strongly take effect. The answer to this question is $2$.

questions.title: Line Hitter
questions.problem: A particle performs a simple symmetric random walk in the plane starting from the origin. Find the expected time until the particle hits the line $y = 1-x$. If the answer is infinite, report $-1$.
questions.solution: The particle can hit the line $y = 1-x$ immediately on the first turn by moving up or right. Alternatively, it can move one further away from the line by moving down or left. Since the walk is symmetric, with probability $1/2$ each, the particle moves one closer or one further from the line. This idea holds at every step, so we can frame this as a SSRW on the integers. Namely, the particle starts at position $0$ (distance $1$ away from the line), and it moves from position $i$ to $i+1$ (up/right in plane) and $i-1$ (down/left in plane) with probability $1/2$ each at each step. Therefore, this question is really asking us to find the expected time for the particle to hit position $1$ from $0$ in a SSRW. The discussion below concerns the computation of expected hitting time of $1$ from $0$ in the random walk on the integers when there is probability $0 < p < 1$ of moving right for $p \geq 1/2$. Let $T_i$ be the amount of steps needed to go from position $i$ to $i+1$. We want $\ev{T_0}$. Let $X_1$ be the step $(\pm 1)$ that the particle takes at the first step. Then by Law of Total Expectation, $\ev{T_0} = \ev{\ev{T_0 \mid X_1}} = \ev{T_0 \mid X_1 = 1}\prob{X_1=  1} + \ev{T_0 \mid X_1 = -1}\prob{X_1 = -1}$. We know the two probability terms are $p$ and $1-p$ by the question. If $X_1 = 1$, then $T_0 = 1$, as the particle reaches position $1$ in $1$ step, so $\ev{T_0 \mid X_1 = 1} = 1$. If $X_1 = -1$, then the particle moves to $-1$. Therefore, the particle needs to first move back from $-1$ to $0$ and from $0$ to $1$. We know that $T_{-1}$ would be the number of steps it takes to go from $-1$ to $0$. Afterwards, we have that $T_0$ would be the number of steps that are needed to go from $0$ to $1$ once it returns to $0$. We also need to add $1$ to this, as we used $1$ step on the first turn to go from $0$ to $-1$. Therefore, we have $\ev{T_0 \mid X_1 = -1} = \ev{1 + T_{-1} + T_0} = 1 + \ev{T_{-1}} + \ev{T_0}$. However, by the Markov Property, $\ev{T_{-1}} = \ev{T_0}$. Plugging this all into the Law of Total Expectation, $\ev{T_0} = 1 \cdot p + (1-p) \cdot (2\ev{T_0} + 1)$. By rearranging this equation for $\ev{T_0}$, we obtain that $\ev{T_0} = \dfrac{1}{2p-1}$. Since $p = \dfrac{1}{2}$ here, $\ev{T_0} = \infty$.

questions.title: Most Likely Odd
questions.problem: You repeatedly roll a fair standard $n-$sided die until the cumulative sum of all observed upfaces is odd. What is the most likely sum to stop on when $n = 20$?
questions.solution: The most likely value needs to be accessible from the most possible ways in the fewest number of rolls. We need the fewest number of rolls condition because the die only has a certain probability of showing each side, so every additional roll that needs to be performed significantly reduces the probability of that cumulative sum appearing. The fewest number of rolls is $1$, so this restricts our candidates to all the odd integers at most $n$. Let the largest odd integer at most $n$ be denoted $n^*$. Any sequence of rolls that stops at a cumulative sum of $k$, where $k < n^*$, has some amount of evens before it. For example, consider a standard $6-$sided die. To stop at $1$, $1$ must be rolled on the first turn. In this case, $n^* = 5$ can also be obtained on the first roll, so the probability of stopping on $5$ must be at least as large as stopping on $1$. To stop on $3$, you either roll $3$ on the first turn or roll $2$ then $1$. However, $4$ then $1$, which is equally probable to $2$ then $1$, results in a sum of $5$ as well. Therefore, all the paths that lead to a cumulative sum of $3$ have equivalents that lead to a cumulative sum of $5$, so stopping on $5$ must be at least as probability as stopping on $3$. Lastly, $5$ has additional sequences that lead to it, such as $2$ then $3$, which aren't encapsulated by the smaller values, so it must have strictly larger probability. This same idea generalizes: All paths that lead to stopping at a sum $k < n^*$ have equivalents that stop at $n^*$, with $n^*$ having additional sequences that aren't equivalent to paths for any smaller odd value. Therefore, $n^*$, the largest odd integer at most $n$, is the most likely value to stop at. With $n = 20$, the answer is $19$.

questions.title: Monkey Mash I
questions.problem: A monkey somehow has a keyboard. The keyboard has $m$ letters and a space bar. The monkey creates a string of length $n$ (inclusive of spaces) by mashing at letters uniformly at random on the keyboard. Find the expected number of words that the monkey creates when $m = 26$ and $n = 703$.
questions.solution: The number of words is equal to the number of starts of words. For example, "monkey t yping" has $3$ words that we can characterize by the first letter. For a word to start in position $i$, where $i > 1$, there must be a space followed by a letter. However, in position $1$, there is no space that comes before it, so a word starts at position $1$ when it has a letter there. Since the events of a word starting at position $i$ and $i+1$ are dependent (if a word starts at $i$, it can't start at $i+1$), counting with indicators is the best approach to computing the expected number of words. Let $I_i$ be the event that position $i$ is the start of a new word. $T = I_1 + \dots + I_n$ gives the total number of words that are in the string. By the discussion above, the condition for a word to start at positions $2$ to $n$ are all the same: space followed by letter. Thus, all of those random variables have the same mean. We have to separate out $I_1$ from the rest, as it has a different condition. By linearity of expectation, $\ev{T} = \ev{I_1} + (n-1)\ev{I_2}$. $\ev{I_2}$ is the probability that a space is followed by a letter. The probability of a space in each position is $\frac{1}{m+1}$, as it's $1$ of the $m+1$ total buttons the monkey can press. Otherwise, with probability $\frac{m}{m+1}$, the monkey presses a letter. By independence of the characters at each spot, $\ev{I_2} = \frac{m}{(m+1)^2}$. $\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that the first character in the string is a letter, which is $\frac{m}{m+1}$. Substituting in, $\ev{T} = \dfrac{m}{m+1} + (n-1) \cdot \dfrac{m}{(m+1)^2} = \dfrac{m(m+n)}{(m+1)^2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $26$.

questions.title: Sides Up
questions.problem: Suppose we have an $r-$sided dice numbered $1,2,\dots, r$ that we roll $n$ times. Side $i$ appears with probability $p_i$ independently between rolls. Let $A$ be the random variable that counts the number of sides that do not appear in any of the $n$ rolls. Find $\mathbb{E}[A]$ when $r = 4, n = 3, p_1 = p_2 = 1/5$, and $p_3 = p_4 = 3/10$.

questions.title: Uniform Trig
questions.problem: Suppose $U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$. Define the random variables $X = \cos(2\pi U)$ and $Y = \sin(2\pi U)$. Compute $\cov{X}{Y}$.
questions.solution:
Solution 1: $\cov{X}{Y} = \ev{XY} - \ev{X}\ev{Y} = \ev{\cos(2\pi U)\sin(2\pi U)} - \ev{\cos(2\pi U)}\ev{\sin(2\pi U)}$. Since $U \sim \unif{0}{1}$, $\mathbb{E}[\sin(2\pi U)] = \displaystyle \int_0^1 \sin(2\pi u) ~du = 0$. Also, $\mathbb{E}[\sin(2\pi U)\cos(2\pi U)] = \displaystyle \int_0^1 \sin(2\pi u)\cos(2\pi u)~du = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^0 v~dv = 0$ using the substitution $v = \sin(2\pi u)$. Therefore, $\cov{X}{Y} = 0$.

Solution 2: Note that $1-U \sim \unif{0}{1}$. This means $(\cos(2\pi U),\sin(2\pi U))$ has the same distribution as $(\cos(2\pi (1-U)), \sin(2\pi (1-U))) =(\cos(2\pi U),-\sin(2\pi U))$. So $(X,Y)$ has the same distribution as $(X,-Y)$, giving $\cov{X}{Y} = \cov{X}{-Y} = -\cov{X}{Y}$, which implies $\cov{X}{Y} = 0$.

questions.title: Coinsecutive VI
questions.problem: A potentially biased coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads is repeatedly flipped until the sequence $HT$ is observed. Find the expected number of flips performed when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: The idea here is to condition on what happens at the first flip and set up a Markov Chain. We need to think about our intermediate states that can occur before hitting $HT$. We could have no part of the sequence or one $H$ before hitting the sequence $HT$. Therefore, let $e_0$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe $HT$ given that no part of our sequence has been observed yet. Similarly, let $e_H$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe $HT$ given that the previous flip was $H$. By conditioning on the first flip, we have that $e_0 = (1-p) \cdot (e_0 + 1) + p \cdot (e_H + 1)$. This is because if we obtain a tails (which occurs with probability $1-p$), it is as if we are still in a "nothing" state, but the number of flips we have performed now is $1$ instead of $0$. Therefore, our process is in the same state, but now we add $1$ to the counter. If we flip a heads on the first flip (also occurring with probability $p$), then we are in the state where our previous flip was $H$. We have to add $1$ for the same fact that we have now flipped and it must be added to our running total. We now need to compute $e_H$ in terms of $e_0$. Conditioning on the next flip, we have that $e_H = (1-p) \cdot (1) + p \cdot (1 + e_H)$. If we obtain a tails on the next flip, then we have obtained the sequence $HT$. Therefore, it would have only taken one flip from $H$ to obtain our sequence of interest. If we obtain a heads on the next flip, then we remain in the state where the previous flip was a heads, but must add $1$ to our counter to account for the fact that we performed an additional flip. The above provides two equations with two unknowns, which we can solve for $e_0$. One can verify that $e_0 = 1/p + 1/(1-p)$ is the solution to this system. It makes sense that this solution is symmetric about $p = 1/2$ i.e. the expected time for $p$ and $1-p$ is the same, as we must observe both a single head and a single tail. With the specified value, the answer is $9/2$.

questions.title: Four Subhand
questions.problem: Suppose we are dealt $10$ cards from a standard deck. Find the probability that in this hand, there at least one $5$ card sub-hand matching a four-of-a-kind poker hand. Round to the nearest millionth.
questions.solution: We must count the total number of hands with a four-of-a-kind, and then divide by the total number of hands. There are $\binom{52}{10}$ total hands that can be created, as the order of selection is irrelevant. We have to use inclusion-exclusion on the numerator to account for the fact that we may have another four-of-a-kind in the other $5$ cards that we don't fix to be the four-of-a-kind itself. For example, consider the hand $2277778888$. This hand could be obtained by fixing the four $8$s or the four $7$s, so it is counted twice. The number of hands with at least one four-of-a-kind is given by $\displaystyle 13 \cdot \binom{48}{6}$. There are $13$ ranks we can select for the four-of-a-kind, and then we must choose $6$ more cards from the other $48$ remaining. Then, we subtract out the number of hands with $2$ four-of-a-kinds, which is given by $\binom{13}{2}\binom{44}{2}$. There are $\displaystyle \binom{13}{2}$ ways to pick the two ranks that are four-of-a-kinds, and then we must pick $2$ more cards from the last $44$. Thus, the answer is $\dfrac{\displaystyle 13\cdot \binom{48}{6} - \binom{13}{2}\binom{44}{2}}{\displaystyle \binom{52}{10}} \approx 0.010079$.

questions.title: Nearest Diagonal II
questions.problem: A point is selected uniformly at random from the unit square. Find the expected minimum distance of the point to either $y=x$ or $y=1-x$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Let $D$ be the distance to the nearest diagonal. We don't know the PDF of $D$ directly, which makes direct integration not possible. Instead, we can consider the tail integral formula $\ev{X} = \ctailsum{X}$. This is the best way because we don't know the PDF nor any direct symmetry in this scenario. In this scenario, we are looking at the perpendicular distance from the points to a diagonal. Thus, the maximum possible distance to the $y=x$ or $y=1-x$ lines occurs at the $4$ points $(0,1/2),(1,1/2),(1/2,1),$ and $(1/2, 0)$, which are all $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ distance away from the lines. To find the distance of a point $(x,y)$ from the line $ax + by + c = 0$, we can use the distance formula $d(ax+by+c=0, (x,y)) = \dfrac{|ax + by + c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$. For the $y = x$ line, from "Nearest Diagonal I", the distance of $(X,Y)$ to the line is given by $D_1 = |X-Y|/\sqrt{2}$. Similarly, we can write $y = 1-x$ as $x+y-1 = 0$, so the distance of a point $(X,Y)$ to this line is $D_2 = |X+Y-1|/\sqrt{2}$. The distance to the nearest diagonal is $D = \min(D_1,D_2)$. Using this, $\{D \geq d\} = \left\{\min(D_1,D_2) \geq d\right\} = \{|X-Y| \geq d\sqrt{2}, |X+Y-1| \geq d\sqrt{2}\}$. Drawing this region out in the plane, we get four disjoint right triangles whose base is of length $1-2d\sqrt{2}$ and height is $1/2 - d\sqrt{2}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are uniform, we can take a ratio of areas to compute probabilities. The area of the full support is $1$, while the area of the four triangles is given by $4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1-2d\sqrt{2}) \cdot (1/2 - d\sqrt{2}) = (1-2d\sqrt{2})^2$. Thus, $\prob{D \geq d} = (1-2d\sqrt{2})^2$. Plugging this into the continuous tail integral formula yields $\ev{D} = \int_0^{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}} (1-2x\sqrt{2})^2~dx = \dfrac{1}{6\sqrt{2}}$. This makes intuitive sense, as it's exactly half of the answer. One could see this by noting that the two boundaries are symmetric and eliminate the same amount of area each.

questions.title: Nearest Diagonal III
questions.problem: A point is selected uniformly at random from the unit square. Find the expected minimum distance of the point to one of $y=x, y=1-x, x=1/2,$ and $y=1/2$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Let $D$ be the distance to the nearest diagonal. We don't know the PDF of $D$ directly, which makes direct integration not possible. Instead, we can consider the tail integral formula $\ev{X} = \ctailsum{X}$. This is the best way because we don't know the PDF nor any direct symmetry in this scenario. In this scenario, we are looking at the perpendicular distance from the points to a diagonal. The maximum possible distance from a point to one of the lines is $\frac{1}{2(1+\sqrt{2})}$, which occurs at $8$ different points. $(\sqrt{2}/2,0)$ is such a point. Note that $(1/4,0)$, for example, is a distance $\sqrt{2}/8$ away from $y=x$. To find the distance of a point $(x,y)$ from the line $ax + by + c = 0$, we can use the distance formula $d(ax+by+c=0, (x,y)) = \dfrac{|ax + by + c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$. For the $y = x$ line, from "Nearest Diagonal I", the distance of $(X,Y)$ to the line is given by $D_1 = |X-Y|/\sqrt{2}$. Similarly, we can write $y = 1-x$ as $x+y-1 = 0$, so the distance of a point $(X,Y)$ to this line is $D_2 = |X+Y-1|/\sqrt{2}$. The last two lines are easy: The distance of a point $(x,y)$ to the line $x = 1/2$, is $|X-1/2|$, and similarly for $y = 1/2$. Call these $D_3$ and $D_4$. The distance to the nearest diagonal is $D = \min(D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4)$. Using this, $\{D \geq d\} = \left\{\min(D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4) \geq d\right\} = \{|X-Y| \geq d\sqrt{2}, |X+Y-1| \geq d\sqrt{2}, |X - 1/2| \geq d, |Y - 1/2| \geq d\}$. Drawing this region out in the plane, we get eight disjoint right triangles whose base and height are both of length $1/2 - d\left(1+\sqrt{2}\right)$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are uniform, we can take a ratio of areas to compute probabilities. The area of the full support is $1$, while the area of the eight triangles is given by $8 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}-d(1+\sqrt{2})\right)^2 = \left(1 - 2d(1+\sqrt{2})\right)^2$. Thus, $\prob{D \geq d} = \left(1 - 2d(1+\sqrt{2})\right)^2$. Plugging this into the continuous tail integral formula yields $\ev{D} = \int_0^{\frac{1}{2(1+\sqrt{2})}} \left(1 - 2x(1+\sqrt{2})\right)^2~dx = \dfrac{1}{6(1+\sqrt{2})}$.

questions.title: Flea Hop I
questions.problem: A flea starts at position $0$ and performs a random walk on the positive integers by jumping $1$ or $2$ positions to the right with respective probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, independent of other jumps. Let $p_n$ be the probability that the flea hops on position $n$. Find $p_4$ when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: The probability that the flea hits position $n$ is dependent on what the last jump was beforehand. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on the jump that comes right before hitting position $n$. This will allow us to derive a recurrence relation for $p_n$. To hit position $n$, the flea can come from two paths: Hitting position $n-2$ and jumping $2$ spots or hitting position $n-1$ and jumping $1$ spot. With probability $p_{n-1}$, the flea hits position $n-1$, and with probability $p$, it jumps $1$ spot to position $n$. With probability $p_{n-2}$, the flea hits position $n-2$, and with probability $1-p$, the flea jumps $2$ positions. Therefore, by Law of Total Probability, $p_n = pp_{n-1} + (1-p)p_{n-2} \iff p_n - pp_{n-1} - (1-p)p_{n-2} = 0$. This can be solved through the method of characteristic equations, as the recurrence is homogenous. The characteristic equation is given by $r^2 - pr - (1-p) = 0 \iff r_{1,2} = \dfrac{p \pm \sqrt{p^2 + 4(1-p)}}{2} \iff r_{1,2} = \dfrac{p \pm (p-2)}{2} = 1,p-1$. The general form of this characteristic equation is given by $p_n = c_1 + c_2(p-1)^n$. We have some initial conditions on the recurrence. Namely, $p_0 = 1$ makes sense because the flea always starts at position $0$. Additionally, $p_1 = p$ makes sense, as the only way to hit position $1$ is by jumping one step at the first movement. Plugging these in, $1 = c_1 + c_2$ and $p = c_1 + c_2(p-1)$. Substituting in $c_1 = 1 - c_2$ into the second equation yields $p = 1 + c_2(p-2) \iff c_2 = \frac{p-1}{p-2}$. Plugging this back into the first equation yields $c_1 = -\frac{1}{p-2}$. Our final expression for $p_n$ is $p_n = -\dfrac{1}{p-2} + \dfrac{(p-1)(p-1)^n}{p-2} = \dfrac{(p-1)^{n+1} - 1}{p-2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $165/243$.

questions.title: Flea Hop II
questions.problem: A flea starts at position $0$ and performs a random walk on the positive integers by jumping $1$ or $2$ positions to the right with respective probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, independent of other jumps. Let $p_n$ be the probability that the flea hops on position $n$. Find $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} p_n$ when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: Using the answer to "Flea Hop I", as $0 < p < 1$, $|p-1| < 1$, so $(p-1)^{n+1} \rightarrow 0$, so the limit is $\frac{1}{2-p}$. However, we can also reason this intuitively without solving the recurrence. On average, the flea moves $p \cdot 1 + (1-p) \cdot 2 = 2-p$ positions per turn. Therefore, in limit, the flea hops on $1$ out of every $2-p$ positions, so the limiting proportion of spots the flea lands on is $\frac{1}{2-p}$. With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $3/5$.

questions.title: Discrete Triangle I
questions.problem: A collection of $2n+1$ rods of lengths $1,2,\dots, 2n+1$ are in a bin. Three rods are selected uniformly at random from the bin. Find the probability that the three rods can form a triangle when $n = 5$.
questions.solution:
Let $a > b > c$ be the lengths of the three rods respectively. For a triangle to exist, the sum of $b$ and $c$ must be larger than $a$ i.e. $a < b+c$. Since these are discrete values, the number of ways that this can be done is dependent on whether $a$ is even or odd, as parity affects the number of options. Therefore, the idea is to count the number of ways to form a triangle for fixed $a$ being even or odd. Note that we can't apply conditional probability directly because we define $a$ as the maximum of the values, which is not uniform over the set. There are $n+1$ odd integers and $n$ even integers in the set $[2n+1] = \{1,2,\dots, 2n+1\}$. Let's consider a concrete example with $a = 10$. To count the number of ways to obtain a valid triangle, we condition on the value of $c$, the minimum side length. These are the possibilities for $b$ in each case: $$\begin{align*}
    c = 2&: 9\\
    c = 3&: 8,9\\
    c = 4&: 7,8,9\\
    c = 5&: 6,7,8,9\\
    c = 6&: 7,8,9\\
    c = 7&: 8,9\\
    c = 8&: 9
\end{align*}$$ To count the number of outcomes for general $a$, we follow this exact pattern. The middle has $a/2 - 1$ possibilities, and then each of the sides above and below the middle have $1  + 2 + \dots + (a-4)/2 = \dfrac{\frac{a-4}{2} \cdot \frac{a-2}{2}}{2} = \frac{(a-4)(a-2)}{8}$. Since there are two of these, the regions cumulatively have $\frac{(a-4)(a-2)}{4}$ above and below the middle. Adding the two components together (middle and off-middle), the number of triangles that can be formed for even $a$ is given by $\dfrac{(a-4)(a-2)}{4} + \dfrac{a-2}{2} = \dfrac{(a-2)^2}{4} = \left(\dfrac{a-2}{2}\right)^2$. Since $a$ is even, $a = 2r$ for some positive integer $r$, meaning there are $(r-1)^2$ total triangles by substituting. We can play the same game for odd $a$. Here is an example with $a = 11$. $$\begin{align*}
    c = 2&: 10\\
    c = 3&: 9,10\\
    c = 4&: 8,9,10\\
    c = 5&: 7,8,9,10\\
    c = 6&: 7,8,9,10\\
    c = 7&: 8,9,10\\
    c = 8&: 9,10\\
    c = 9&: 10
\end{align*}$$ For general odd $a$, there are two components that each contain $1 + 2 + \dots + (a-3)/2 = \dfrac{\frac{a-3}{2} \cdot \frac{a-1}{2}}{2} = \dfrac{(a-3)(a-1)}{8}$ combinations, so there are $\dfrac{(a-3)(a-1)}{4}$ combinations total for odd $a$. Odd $a$ can be written in the form $a = 2r+1$ for some non-negative integer $r$. Substituting this in, there are $r(r-2)$ triangles that can be formed when $a = 2r+1$. The total number of triangles that can be formed is found by summing the amount of triangles given $a$ is the largest side. We found the expressions for when $a = 2r$ and $a = 2r+1$ for positive integers $r$, so we can sum over all valid values of $r$ to obtain the total number of triangles. The smallest value of $r$ for which there is at least one triangle that can be formed is $r = 2$, and the maximum value of $a = 2n+1$, so $r = n$ is the largest possible value. Therefore, the total number of triangles is given by $\sum_{r=2}^n (r-1)^2 + r(r-1) = \sum_{r=2}^n 2r^2 - 3r + 1 = \dfrac{n(n-1)(4n+1)}{6}$. The total number of ways to draw $3$ rods from the bin of $2n+1$ rods is given by $\displaystyle \binom{2n+1}{3} = \dfrac{(2n+1)(2n)(2n-1)}{6}$. Plugging these in, the probability of the three sticks forming a triangle is given by $\dfrac{(n-1)(4n+1)}{2(2n+1)(2n-1)}$. With $n = 5$, the answer is $14/33$.

questions.title: Discrete Triangle II
questions.problem: A collection of $2n+1$ rods of lengths $1,2,\dots, 2n+1$ are in a bin. Three rods are selected uniformly at random from the bin. Let $p_n$ be the probability that three uniformly random rods drawn are able to form a triangle. If it exists, find $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} p_n$. If it doesn't exist, enter $-1$.
questions.solution: We could evaluate this using the result "Discrete Triangle I" or based on sole intuition. From the result of the previous part, we know that $p_n = \dfrac{(n-1)(4n+1)}{2(2n-1)(2n+1)}$. By the limit rules for rational functions, $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} p_n = 4/8 = 1/2$. This can also be reasoned intuitively as follows: For any fixed $a$ as the maximum, the two other rod lengths are uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,\dots, a-1\}$. These have mean $a/2$ and are symmetric, so the sum of the two lengths has mean $a$. Furthermore, as each of the two are symmetric about their means, the sum must be symmetric about it's mean, which is $a$. Therefore, as $a \rightarrow \infty$, the probability that the sum is exactly $a$ tends to $0$, and by symmetry of the sum, the sum is equally likely to be larger or smaller than $a$. Since the two probabilities must sum to $1$ in limit, the probability that the sum is larger than $a$ tends to $1/2$.

questions.title: Arc Up III
questions.problem: Two points are selected uniformly at random from the circumference of a semi-circle of radius $1$, including the diameter at the bottom. Let $A$ be the area of the triangle with vertices at the two selected points and the midpoint of the diameter. Let $D$ be the event that at most one point lies on the diameter. Compute $\ev{A \mid D}$ to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution: When given this information, the only part that changes is the probability of each case. The expected values do not change because the situations within each of the two cases has not changed. As per the last part, the probability of exactly one point on the diameter is $\frac{4\pi}{(2+\pi)^2}$, while the probability of both points on the circular portion is $\frac{\pi^2}{(2+\pi)^2}$. As these are the only two options now, given this information, the probability of having exactly one point on the diameter is given by $\frac{4\pi}{4\pi + \pi^2} = \frac{4}{4 + \pi}$. The updated probability of both points being on the circular portion is $\frac{\pi}{4 + \pi}$. Using these updated probabilities with the conditional expected values from the previous part, $\ev{A \mid D} = \dfrac{4}{4 + \pi} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\pi} + \dfrac{\pi}{4 + \pi} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\pi} = \dfrac{1 + \frac{2}{\pi}}{4 + \pi} = \dfrac{\pi + 2}{4\pi + \pi^2}$.

questions.title: Arc Up IV
questions.problem: Two points are selected uniformly at random from the circumference of a circle of radius $1$. Let $A$ be the area of the triangle with vertices at the two selected points and the center of the circle. Find $\ev{A}$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: In this scenario, the points selected are on the circumference of the full circle. This corresponds to the second case of "Arc Up II", but now on the entire circle. The angle $\theta$ between the two selected points follows the same distribution as in "Arc Up II" because the interior angle of the triangle can't be larger than $\pi$ radians. The base of the triangle is still $1$, and the height is still $\sin\theta$. Therefore, the answer is exactly the same as the specific case in "Arc Up II": $1/\pi$. This can also be intuitively reasoned from the fact that the two selected points will always lie in some semi-circle. As the selection of points is uniform, that semi-circle can arbitrarily be selected to be the upper half of the circle, which is exactly the scenario in "Arc Up II".

questions.title: Cubic Ant III
questions.problem: A spider and an ant start at the opposing corners of a cube. Every minute, the spider and ant choose one of the $3$ possible directions independently and uniformly at random to move in. Afterwards, they travel simultaneously. The spider catches the ant if they move along the same edge while travelling at the end of the minute. Find the expected number of minutes until the spider catches the ant.
questions.solution: The ant and the spider start a distance $3$ away from one another. Since they both move at each step, they can only ever be a distance of $3$ or $1$ away from one another. The expected amount of time until the spider catches the ant is dependent on how far away the spider is from the ant, so set up a $2-$state Markov chain. By the symmetry of the cube, the expected time for the spider and ant travel down the same edge is the same no matter which opposing edges they start it. WLOG, assume the ant and spider start at $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,1)$, respectively. Let $E_3$ and $E_1$ be the expected time for the ant and spider to intersect if they are current $3$ and $1$ units away from each other, respectively. The spider and ant are one unit away from each other if two of their coordinates are the same. By the symmetry of the cube and the movements being equally likely in any direction, the distribution of the distance of the ant and spider is the same, regardless of which movement the spider makes. WLOG, suppose the spider moves down to $(1,1,0)$ on the first turn. If the ant moves in the $+x$ or $+y$ directions to either $(1,0,0)$ or $(0,1,0)$, which occurs with probability $2/3$, they are distance $1$ away from each other. On average, an additional $E_1$ minutes will pass before they intersect. Otherwise, if the ant moves upwards to $(0,0,1)$, which occurs with probability $1/3$, the ant and spider are on opposite corners of the cube again, which means an additional $E_3$ minutes will pass on average before intersecting. Therefore, we have the equation $E_3 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{3}E_3 + \dfrac{2}{3}E_1$. The additional $1$ comes from the fact that $1$ minute passed in the spider and ant moving. Now, we must derive a recurrence for $E_1$. If the ant and spider are $1$ unit away from one another, they intersect exactly when they both choose to travel down the same segment. By the symmetry of the cube, the exact segment is irrelevant, so suppose the ant and spider are at $(0,0,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$, respectively. They choose to travel down the same segment with probability $1/9$, for which $0$ additional minutes would be needed. Otherwise, if the spider moves down and the ant moves in the $+x$ or $+y$ directions, the spider and ant still lie a distance $1$ away from each other, meaning an additional $E_1$ steps are needed. This occurs with probability $2/9$, as the spider moves downwards with probability $1/3$ and the ant moves in the $+x$ or $+y$ directions with probability $2/3$. If the spider doesn't move downwards, the $+x$ and $+y$ movements for the spider are symmetric, so we can consider one of them only. Suppose the spider moves in the $+x$ direction to $(1,0,1)$. If the ant moves up or in the $+x$ direction to $(0,0,1)$ or $(1,0,0)$, they are separated by $1$ unit, meaning an additional $E_1$ minutes are needed on average. Otherwise, if the ant moves to $(0,1,0)$, they are on opposite sides of the cube, meaning $E_3$ minutes more are needed on average. Therefore, $E_1 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{9}(0) +  \dfrac{2}{9}E_3 + \dfrac{2}{3}E_1 = 1 + \dfrac{2}{9}E_3 + \dfrac{2}{3}E_1$. We now have a system of two equations to solve for $E_1$ and $E_3$. We want $E_3$, as the ant and spider initially start $3$ units away from one another. One finds that $E_3 = 27/2$ after some basic algebraic work on the system.

questions.title: Teacher Salary
questions.problem: In an incentive to teach students well, the school board of some district mandates the new salary structure: Teachers will be paid $\frac{B}{1+X}$ as their salary, where $B > 0$ is a constant and $X$ is the number of students in their class that fail an exam. A given teacher has $n$ students that each have probability $0 < p < 1$ of failing, independently of other students. To the nearest dollar, find the expected salary of the teacher when $B = 10^6, p = 1/4,$ and $n = 24$.
questions.solution: The expected salary of the teacher is given by $\ev{\dfrac{B}{1+X}} = B\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}}$. Since $X$ counts the number of failures among independent trials (students) with constant success probability, $X \sim \binomial{n}{p}$. As we don't know a particularly quick way to compute an expected value of this form, LOTUS is the best approach. Substituting into the LOTUS formula, $\ev{\textcolor{red}{\dfrac{1}{1+X}}} = \sum_{k=0}^n  \textcolor{red}{\dfrac{1}{1+k}} \cdot \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \dfrac{n!}{(k+1)!(n-k)!}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. We combine the $\frac{1}{k+1}$ into the binomial coefficient because there is a $k!$ on the denominator, and $k! \cdot (k+1) = (k+1)!$. We see that $(k+1) + (n-k) = n+1$, so we should try to get $(n+1)!$ in the numerator to write this as $\binom{n+1}{k+1}$. This can be done by multiplying and dividing by $n+1$. Doing this, we get $\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^n \dfrac{(n+1)!}{(k+1)!(n-k)!}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n+1}{k+1}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. Since we have a $k+1$ in the binomial coefficient, it would be nice to shift that back to $k$, as we want to apply the binomial theorem again. By index shifting $j = k+1$, the new bounds are $j = 1$ to $j = n+1$, and we replace $k$ by $j-1$ everywhere in the summand. This yields $\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}} = \sum_{j=1}^{n+1} \binom{n+1}{j}p^{j-1}(1-p)^{(n+1)-j}$. This appears to be the form of the binomial theorem besides two things. The first is the $p^{j-1}$ term. We need $p^j$ there instead, so we take out $p^{-1}$ from it. The second is that the sum starts at $j = 1$. This is okay, as we can add and subtract the $j = 0$ term, $(1-p)^{n+1}$. Performing both of these actions, $\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}} = \dfrac{1}{p(n+1)}\left[\sum_{j=0}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}{j}p^j(1-p)^{(n+1)-j} - (1-p)^{n+1}\right] = \dfrac{1-(1-p)^{n+1}}{p(n+1)}$. The first sum evaluates to $1$ by the binomial theorem with $a = p, b = 1-p,$ and $n$ as $n+1$. By the above, the expected salary of the teacher is $B \cdot \dfrac{1-(1-p)^{n+1}}{p(n+1)}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\$159,880$.

questions.title: Lotto III
questions.problem: Let $N > 0$ be fixed. $2N$ people play the lottery each week. Each of the people are assigned a uniformly random integer in $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$, independently of other people. The lotto prize is $\$B$. One of the $N$ integers is selected uniformly at random to be the winning value. If there are multiple winners, the prize is split evenly among them. Given that you, one of the participants, has a winning ticket, find your expected payout when $B = 10^6$ and $N = 15$.
questions.solution: As per the previous part, $1+X$, where $X \sim \binomial{2N-1}{1/N}$, is the number of winners in the lotto. Therefore, the random variable that represents your payout is $\dfrac{B}{1+X}$. By linearity of expectation, your expected payout is $B\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}}$. It remains to compute the expected value. We will calculate it for general $\binomial{n}{p}$. As we don't know a particularly quick way to compute an expected value of this form, LOTUS is the best approach. Substituting into the LOTUS formula, $\ev{\textcolor{red}{\dfrac{1}{1+X}}} = \sum_{k=0}^n  \textcolor{red}{\dfrac{1}{1+k}} \cdot \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \dfrac{n!}{(k+1)!(n-k)!}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. We combine the $\frac{1}{k+1}$ into the binomial coefficient because there is a $k!$ on the denominator, and $k! \cdot (k+1) = (k+1)!$. We see that $(k+1) + (n-k) = n+1$, so we should try to get $(n+1)!$ in the numerator to write this as $\binom{n+1}{k+1}$. This can be done by multiplying and dividing by $n+1$. Doing this, we get $\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^n \dfrac{(n+1)!}{(k+1)!(n-k)!}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n+1}{k+1}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. Since we have a $k+1$ in the binomial coefficient, it would be nice to shift that back to $k$, as we want to apply the binomial theorem again. By index shifting $j = k+1$, the new bounds are $j = 1$ to $j = n+1$, and we replace $k$ by $j-1$ everywhere in the summand. This yields $\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}} = \sum_{j=1}^{n+1} \binom{n+1}{j}p^{j-1}(1-p)^{(n+1)-j}$. This appears to be the form of the binomial theorem besides two things. The first is the $p^{j-1}$ term. We need $p^j$ there instead, so we take out $p^{-1}$ from it. The second is that the sum starts at $j = 1$. This is okay, as we can add and subtract the $j = 0$ term, $(1-p)^{n+1}$. Performing both of these actions, $\ev{\dfrac{1}{1+X}} = \dfrac{1}{p(n+1)}\left[\sum_{j=0}^{n+1}\binom{n+1}{j}p^j(1-p)^{(n+1)-j} - (1-p)^{n+1}\right] = \dfrac{1-(1-p)^{n+1}}{p(n+1)}$. The first sum evaluates to $1$ by the binomial theorem with $a = p, b = 1-p,$ and $n$ as $n+1$. In this scenario, $n$ is $2N-1$ and $p = 1/N$.
