Therefore, your expected payout is $B \cdot \dfrac{1 - (1-1/N)^{2N}}{1/N \cdot 2N} = B \cdot \dfrac{1-(1-1/N)^{2N}}{2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\$436,894$.

questions.title: Die Duo II
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1/6$. Your friend's die has the values $111666$ on the sides. You get to select the sides of your own die under the following conditions: All values must be between $1$ and $6$, inclusive of both, and they must sum to $21$. An example would be $223455$. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to simultaneously maximize your winning probability and minimize your friend's winning probability? Enter the die's values in non-decreasing order from left to right.
questions.solution: Since there are no values strictly larger than $6$, the largest possible probability of winning is $1/2$, as you could have a die that has values all strictly larger than $1$, so you win guaranteed whenever your friend obtains a $1$. However, we also want to minimize the probability that your friend wins. For this to occur, we need to have as many values that are $6$ as possible and all sides are at least $2$. We can do better than one $6$, as a sum of $15$ still remains for the other $5$ sides of the dice. With two values of $6$, the remaining $4$ sides must sum to $9$. The only way to do this with all sides being strictly larger than $1$ is $2223$. Therefore, $222366$ is a good candidate. We can't use $3$ values as $6$, as the remaining three sides would be $111$, violating our other condition that all values must be strictly larger than $1$. Therefore, $222366$ is the optimal response.

questions.title: Die Duo III
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Your friend has a standard fair die. You get to select the sides of your own die under the following conditions: All values must be between $1$ and $6$, inclusive of both, and the die must have mean $7/2$. You may choose both the probabilities and the values on the die. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to maximize your winning probability? Enter the optimal winning probability.
questions.solution: Since your friend's die is unbiased in the sense that all values appear with equal probability, it has no particular weakness to exploit. If your values are biased with a lot of high values, you must also have lower numbers on your die so that the mean is $3.5$. Therefore, those lower values will fare poorly against your opponents die. All of this discussion leads to the following claim: Any die you select has the same probability of winning against your opponent. Suppose that $p_1,\dots, p_6$ are the probabilities that each value on your die appears. We know that $p_1 + \dots + p_6 = 1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^6 ip_i = 3.5$ by the conditions above. Let $W$ be the event of you rolling a strictly higher value than your opponent. Furthermore, let $X$ be the random variable representing one outcome of your die. The probability that you win is easy to compute if we know the value of your die, so the idea is to condition on your die's value. Namely, $\prob{W} = \sum_{i=1}^6 \prob{W \mid X = i}\prob{X = i}$. Since the die shows the value $i$ with probability $p_i$, $\prob{X = i} = p_i$. Given you roll $i$, your friend must roll at least $i+1$. There are $6 - (i+1) = 6-i$ values on their die that are larger than $i$. Therefore, $\prob{W \mid X = i} = \frac{6-i}{6}$. Plugging this in, $\prob{W} = \sum_{i=1}^6 \dfrac{6-i}{6}p_i = \sum_{i=1}^6 p_i - \dfrac{1}{6}\sum_{i=1}^6 ip_i = 1 - \dfrac{3.5}{6} = \dfrac{5}{12}$. All dice are equally good here, so the answer is $5/12$.

questions.title: Die Duo IV
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. You get to select the sides and probability of appearance for both dice. There is one restriction: Only values $1-6$ can be used. You and your friend both receive the die you created. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to simultaneously maximize your winning probability and minimize your friend's winning probability? Report the variance of the die you create.
questions.solution: Since the dice are independent and identical, given that the two dice aren't the same value, it is equally likely as to whether you or your friend won. Furthermore, since you can select the probabilities that each side appears, WLOG, the values $1-6$ all appear on the die. This is WLOG because you can set the probability of some side to $0$ if you don't want it to appear. Let $p$ be the probability that there is a tie between the dice. The probability that the dice show distinct values i.e. there is no tie is $1-p$. Given that there is no tie, you win with probability $1/2$ by the above discussion. Therefore, the probability you win is $\frac{1-p}{2}$. To maximize your winning probability, we need to minimize the probability of a tie, $p$. Suppose that side $i$ appears with probability $p_i$. You can obtain a tie by both rolling $1,2,\dots, 6$. By the independence of the dice, $p = \sum_{i=1}^6 p_i^2$. Our restrictions are $p_1 + \dots + p_6 = 1$ and $p_1,\dots, p_6 \geq 0$, as these are probabilities. The goal is to minimize $p$ under these restrictions. Intuitively, one can see that each of the $p_i$ values contributes the same to the total sum, as they are not weighted. Thus, in an optimal solution, there's no reason for $p_i$ to contribute more than any other, so it should be the case that $p_1 = \dots = p_6$. However, as we know their sum is $1$, the result is $p_1 = p_2 = \dots = p_6 = 1/6$. In other words, you should choose the standard fair die. The mean of this die is $7/2$. By LOTUS, the second moment is given by $\dfrac{1^2 + \dots + 6^2}{6} = \dfrac{91}{6}$. Using the variance formula, the variance of the value showing on this die is $\dfrac{91}{6} - \left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{35}{12}$. One can also verify the minimization by the method of Lagrange multipliers. Taking the gradient of the objective function $(p)$ and setting it equal to $\lambda$ multiplied by the constraint's gradient $(1)$, this yields the system $2x_i = \lambda$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$. Since $\lambda = 2x_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$, $2x_1 = \dots = 2x_n \iff x_1 = \dots = x_n$.

questions.title: Die Duo V
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6$ − 6−sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1$ / 6 $1/6$. You each get to select the sides of your own die under the following conditions: All values must be between 1 1 and 6 6, inclusive of both, and the die must have sides that sum to $21$ 21. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to maximize your winning probability? Enter the values of the die in non-decreasing order.
questions.solution: Both you and your friend can choose dice under the same restrictions. What's optimal for you is also optimal for them, so you and your friend will end up selecting the same dice. However, as both you and your friend receive the same dice, this problem is exactly that of "Die Duo IV": To maximize your probability of winning, you need to minimize the probability of a tie. Therefore, the answer is the standard die $123456$ 123456. This intuitively makes sense: By "Die Duo III", the standard fair die has constant winning probability, regardless of the die chosen by your opponent. In other words, the standard fair die has no "weaknesses", as it is uniformly distributed across all the values. If your friend were to select a die that has some repeated values, those could be exploited by changing your own die in response.

questions.title: Die Duo VI
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6$ − 6−sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1$ / 6 $1/6$. You each get to select the sides of both dice under the following conditions: All values must be between 1 1 and 6 6, inclusive of both, and the die must have sides that sum to $21$ 21. Note that the two dice no longer need to be the same. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What dice would you select for you and your friend maximize your winning probability? Report the optimal probability of you winning.
questions.solution: To maximize your probability of winning, you want to have a minimal number of values on your friend's die that beat you, but have many of your values be just $1$ 1 larger than theirs. The maximum value that can be put on your friend's die is $$$$$$6$$$$$$ 6, so suppose one 6 6 is placed on it. The other $$5$$ 5 values must have sum $15$ 15, so a natural choice is to make all of them $$$$3$$$$ 3. This is the smallest constant value that can be placed without having any more "large values". To beat your friend, you would want as many $$$4$$$ 4s as possible on your die, as that is the smallest value above 3 3. This can be easily obtained with the die $144444$ 144444. Adjusting any values upwards is non-optimal, as 5 5 nor 6 6 give you any marginal benefit (they still only beat 3 3), but you would also have to adjust another value down, meaning you lose an outcome of a 4 4. With these two dice, you win exactly when you roll 4 4 and your friend rolls 3 3. This occurs with probability 5 / 6 $5/6$ per die, so you win with probability 25 / 36 $$25/36$$. We now claim that 25 / 36 25/36 is optimal. The only way you would adjust your friend's die is if you put another 6 6 on it, as that could lower the values you need on your die. If a second 6 6 is added to your friend's die, 1 / 3 $1/3$ of the time, they would roll a 6 6, meaning you can't win. Therefore, your maximum winning probability would be 2 / 3 = 24 / 36 < 25 / 36 $2/3 = 24/36 < 25/36$ with such a die for your friend.

questions.title: Clubby King
questions.problem: You choose $4$ 4 cards without replacement from a standard deck. Find the probability you see at least $2$ 2 clubs, with one being king of clubs. Report your answer to the nearest millionth.
questions.solution: If you get a satisfactory hand, you must be the king of clubs in it. Therefore, it's natural to evaluate this probability by conditioning on the king of clubs being in your hand. Let $C$ be the event in question, and $K$ be the event that the king of clubs is in your hand. By the definition of conditional probability, [ ] = [ ∣ ] [ ] P[C]=P[C∣K]P[K] As $4$ 4 cards are drawn out of $52$ 52 and the king is equally likely to be in any spot, [ ] = 4 / 52 = 1 / 1$$$$3$$$$ P[K]=4/52=1/13. Given that the king of clubs is in your hand, you have at least two clubs exactly when at least one of the remaining three cards in the deck is a club. Since this is an "at least" probability, the easier quantity to compute would be the complement, which is that no clubs are in the remaining 3 3 cards. For no clubs to be in the remaining 3 3 cards, the 3 3 cards must be drawn from the other $39$ 39 that aren't clubs. There are ( 39 3 ) ( 3 39 ) ways to do this. We also know that there are $51$ 51 cards remaining in the deck after the king of clubs has been removed, so there are ( 51 3 ) ( 3 51 ) ways to pick 3 3 cards without restriction. By complementation, [ ∣ ] = 1 − [ ∣ ] = 1 − ( 39 3 ) ( 51 3 ) P[C∣K]=1−P[C c ∣K]=1− ( 3 51 ) ( 3 39 ) Plugging this in, [ ] = 1 13 [ 1 − ( 39 3 ) ( 51 3 ) ] ≈ 0.043166 P[C]= 13 1 [1− ( 3 51 ) ( 3 39 ) ]≈0.043166

questions.title: Estimated Sample
questions.problem: Fix an integer > 0 $K > 0$. Suppose ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } N∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,K} and ∣ = ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } X∣N=n∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n}. Find [ ∣ = ] E[N∣X=a] when = 100 $K = 100$ and = 5 $a = 5$. Round to the nearest integer.
questions.solution: By exp$$a$$nding out the definition of the conditional expected value, [ ∣ = ] = ∑ = [ = ∣ = ] E[$$$N$$$∣$X$=a]= j=a ∑ K kP[$N = k$∣X=a] The question provides the conditional distribution of ∣ X∣N, but we need the conditional distribution of ∣ N∣X here. We can relate these by Bayes' rule: [ = ∣ = ] = [ = , = ] [ = ] = [ = ∣ = ] [ = ] [ = ] P[N=k∣X=a]= P[X=a] P[N=k,X=a] = P[X=a] P[X=a∣N=k]P[N=k] On the numerator, for any 1 ≤ ≤ ≤ $1 \leq a \leq k \leq K$, given = N=k, ∣ = ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } X∣N=k∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,k}, so [ = ∣ = ] = 1 / P[X=a∣N=k]=1/k. questions.title: Bounded CDF II
questions.problem: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with CDF $F(x)$, PDF $f(x)$, and bounded support $[a,b]$. Let $Y$ be a random variable with CDF $G(y) = \frac{F(y)}{2-F(y)}$. Find the best possible lower bound for $\ev{Y}$ when $\ev{X} = 4$. If no such bound exists, enter $-100$.
questions.solution: We've abstractly defined the random variable $Y$ in terms the CDF of $X$. Therefore, the idea is to try to make the expression for $\ev{Y}$ look like something in terms of $\ev{X}$, and then bound some terms. We know that $\ev{Y} = \int_a^b yf_Y(y)~dy$. In this case, by the product rule $f_Y(y) = \dfrac{d}{dy}(F(y)) = \dfrac{2f(y)}{(2-F(y))^2}$. Plugging this in, $\ev{Y} = \int_a^b y \cdot \dfrac{2f(y)}{(2-F(y))^2}~dy = \int_a^b yf(y) \cdot \dfrac{2}{(2-F(y))^2}~dy$. Since $yf(y)$ is the proper integrand for the expectation, the goal is to bound $\frac{2}{(2-F(y))^2}$. Note that $0 \leq F(y) \leq 1$ for all real $y$, so the smallest possible value of the expression is when we subtract out the smallest possible value of $F(y)$, which is $0$. Therefore, $\frac{2}{(2-F(y))^2} \leq \frac{2}{(2-0)^2} = 1/2$. Substituting this in, $\ev{Y} = \int_a^b yf(y) \cdot \dfrac{2}{(2-F(y))^2}~dy \geq \dfrac{1}{2}\int_a^b yf(y)~dy = \dfrac{1}{2}\ev{X}$. Note that this bound can't be made any sharper, as the rise from $F(a) = 0$ to $F(b) = 1$ can be made arbitrarily slowly. With $\ev{X} = 4$, the answer is $2$.

questions.title: Bounded CDF III
questions.problem: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with CDF $F(x)$, PDF $f(x)$, and bounded support $[a,b]$. Let $Y$ be a random variable with CDF $G(y) = \frac{F(y)}{2-F(y)}$. Find the best possible upper bound for $\var{Y}$ when $\ev{X} = 4$ and $\var{X} = 9$. If no such bound exists, enter $-100$.
questions.solution: We've abstractly defined the random variable $Y$ in terms the CDF of $X$. Therefore, the idea is to write out the terms of $\var{Y}$ and bound them in terms of the quantities for $X$. We know that $\var{Y} = \ev{Y^2} - (\ev{Y})^2$. Since we want an upper bound on $\var{Y}$ we must bound $\ev{Y^2}$ from above and $\ev{Y}$ from below. This is because we want to subtract out as little as possible to get the upper bound. From "Bounded CDF II", we know that $\ev{Y} \geq \frac{1}{2}\ev{X}$, so our lower bound on the $(\ev{Y})^2$ term is $\frac{1}{4}(\ev{X})^2$. As for bounding $\ev{Y^2}$, we can apply the same methodology as the previous parts in writing out the integral and bounding it. Namely, $\ev{Y^2} = \int_a^b y^2f_Y(y)~dy = \int_a^b y^2f(y) \cdot \dfrac{2}{(2-F(y))^2}~dy \leq 2\int_a^b y^2f(y)~dy = 2\ev{X^2}$. The last integral was evaluated by noting the definition of $\ev{X^2}$. Using this, we can conclude $\var{Y} = \ev{Y^2} - (\ev{Y})^2 \leq 2\ev{X^2} - \dfrac{1}{4}(\ev{X})^2 = 2\left[\ev{X^2} - (\ev{X})^2\right] + \dfrac{7}{4}(\ev{X})^2 = 2\var{X} + \dfrac{7}{4}(\ev{X})^2$. With the specified values, the answer is $46$.

questions.title: Exceed Double Heads
questions.problem: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly, and the cumulative number of tails and heads are recorded. Find the probability that the cumulative number of heads obtained ever exceeds twice the amount of tails. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Just as gambler's ruin and random walks can easily be related, we can relate this question to the scenario of "Double Step Particle II" quite easily. In this scenario, we can view a head as a step leftwards, while a tail as $2$ steps right. The reason we view tails as two steps right is because the number of heads must strictly exceed twice the number of tails, so adding a tails to the running total adds $2$ to the threshold. Furthermore, the "particle" in this scenario starts one unit away from the origin. If a heads is flipped immediately, then the number of heads does exceed twice the number of tails, so the process ends in $1$ step. By the above discussion, this is a special case of "Double Step Particle II" with $k = 1$ and $p = 1/2$, so the answer is $\dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}$.

questions.title: Multistep Particle
questions.problem: Fix $0 < p < 1$ and a positive integer $r$. A particle performs an asymmetric random walk on the integers. The particle starts at position $k > 0$. Each turn, the particle moves from position $k$ to positions $k+r$ or $k-1$ with respective probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, independent of previous turns. Find the maximum value of $p$ such that no matter where the particle starts, it hits the origin at some point with probability $1$. Report this when $r = 24$. If there is no such threshold, enter $-1$.
questions.solution: By Law of Large Numbers, if the expected value of the movement the particle makes at each step is negative, it will eventually reach $0$ with probability $1$. Why is this true? Suppose $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are the IID movements made by the particle at each step. By the Law of Large Numbers, with probability $1$, $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\dfrac{X_1 + \dots + X_n}{n} \rightarrow \ev{X_1}$. In other words, for large $n$, $X_1 + \dots + X_n$ will be fairly close to $n\ev{X_1}$. However, if $\ev{X_1} < 0$, the expected movement will be negative over time, so the particle will eventually be, on average, $-k$ distance away from the starting position, no matter what $k$ is. It turns out this also holds for when $\ev{X_1} = 0$. This intuitively makes sense: With $\ev{X_1} = 0$, the particle may oscillate up and down for some time, and the swings may be large, so if they are "large enough", the particle will end up hitting position $0$. According to the discussion above, let $X_i$ be the $i$th movement the particle takes. Our condition is $\ev{X_i} \leq 0$, so $\ev{X_i} = pr + (1-p)(-1) \leq 0 \iff p \leq \dfrac{1}{r+1}$. With $r=  24$, the answer is $1/25$.

questions.title: Galen-Ashore I
questions.problem: The Galenshore distribution, denoted by $\text{Galenshore}(\alpha,\theta)$, where $\alpha, \theta > 0$, has PDF given by $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\theta^{2\alpha}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\theta^2x^2}I_{(0,\infty)}(x)$. Suppose that $X \sim \text{Galenshore}(\alpha,\theta)$. Compute $\ev{e^{-X^2}}$ when $\alpha = 3$ and $\theta = 2$.
questions.solution: This expected value doesn't have an immediately quick way to evaluate it, so the best approach is LOTUS. Applying LOTUS, we get $\ev{\textcolor{red}{e^{-X^2}}} = \int_{0}^{\infty} \textcolor{red}{e^{-x^2}} \cdot \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\theta^{2\alpha}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\theta^2x^2}~dx = \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\theta^{2\alpha}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-(\theta^2+1)x^2}~dx$. In this expected value, the general form of the integrand did not change! All that changed is $\theta$ in the exponent now becomes $\sqrt{\theta^2 + 1}$. We observe that the form of the integrand did not change at all, so we can evaluate this new integral with normalization. Namely, wherever $\theta$ currently exists, we need to multiply and divide so that it becomes $\sqrt{\theta^2 + 1}$. The goal of this is to get the integrand into the form of a $\text{Galenshore}(\alpha,\sqrt{\theta^2 + 1})$ PDF. The only other place where it exists is the $\theta^{2\alpha}$ out front, so we can take that out (we integrate with respect to $x$), multiply and divide by the new constant we want to have, and then say the integral is $1$. Performing this, $\ev{e^{-X^2}} = \theta^{2\alpha} \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-(\theta^2+1)x^2}~dx = \dfrac{\theta^{2\alpha}}{(\textcolor{orange}{\sqrt{\theta^2 + 1}})^{2\alpha}} \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}(\textcolor{orange}{\sqrt{\theta^2 + 1}})^{2\alpha}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-(\theta^2+1)x^2}~dx = \left(\dfrac{\theta^2}{\theta^2 + 1}\right)^{\alpha}$. With the specified values, the answer is $64/125$.

questions.title: Galen-Ashore II
questions.problem: The Galenshore distribution, denoted by $\text{Galenshore}(\alpha,\theta)$, where $\alpha, \theta > 0$, has PDF given by $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\theta^{2\alpha}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\theta^2x^2}I_{(0,\infty)}(x)$. Suppose that $Y \sim \text{Galenshore}(\alpha,\theta)$. Compute $\ev{Y^2}$ when $\alpha = 4$ and $\theta = 2$.
questions.solution: To compute $\ev{Y^2}$, we can take a similar approach to the previous question in terms of normalization. The reason for this is because we don't know any properties about the Galenshore distribution in general. By LOTUS, we get $\ev{\textcolor{red}{Y^2}} = \int_{0}^{\infty} \textcolor{red}{x^2} \cdot \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\theta^{2\alpha}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\theta^2x^2}~dx = \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\theta^{2\alpha}x^{2(\alpha+1) - 1}e^{-\theta^2x^2}~dx$. Once again, the form of the integrand did not change! The only change to the integrand was that $\alpha$ became $\alpha +1$, so the idea is to normalize the interior to the form of a $\text{Galenshore}(\alpha + 1,\theta)$ PDF. We see $\alpha$ in two places: $\Gamma(\alpha)$ and $\theta^{2\alpha}$. The first term can be remedied by noting $\Gamma(\alpha + 1) = \alpha\Gamma(\alpha)$, so we can replace $\Gamma(\alpha)$ with $\Gamma(\alpha + 1)/\alpha$. For the second term, we can multiply and divide by $\theta^2$ to give us $\theta^{2\alpha + 2} = \theta^{2(\alpha + 1)}$. Performing both of these, we get $\ev{Y^2} = \dfrac{\alpha}{\theta^2}\int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\textcolor{red}{\alpha + 1})}\theta^{2(\textcolor{red}{\alpha + 1})}x^{2(\textcolor{red}{\alpha+1}) - 1}e^{-\theta^2x^2}~dx = \dfrac{\alpha}{\theta^2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1$.

questions.title: Galen-Ashore III
questions.problem: Suppose that $X \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)$ with $\alpha > 1$ and $Y \mid X = x \sim \text{Galenshore}(1-x,\sqrt{x})$. For reference, the PDF of a $(\alpha,\theta)$ distribution is $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\theta^{2\alpha}x^{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\theta^2x^2}I_{(0,\infty)}(x)$. Compute $\mathbb{E}[Y^2]$ when $a  = 3$ and $b = 4$.
questions.solution: In this question, we know the distribution of $Y \mid X = x$. Thus, the best approach is to apply the Law of Total Expectation by conditioning on $X$. By LOTE, $\ev{Y} = \ev{\ev{Y \mid X}}$. As per the question, $Y \mid X = x \sim \text{Galenshore}(1-x,\sqrt{x})$. Therefore, $\ev{Y^2 \mid X = x}$ is just the answer from "Galen-Ashore II" with $\alpha = 1-x$ and $\beta = \sqrt{x}$. Substituting in, we get $\ev{Y} = \ev{\dfrac{1-X}{(\sqrt{X})^2}} = \ev{\dfrac{1-X}{X}} = \ev{\dfrac{1}{X}} - 1$. This question now turns to $X \sim \bet{a}{b}$. Once again, there's no clear way to compute this directly, so we apply LOTUS to obtain $\ev{\dfrac{1}{X}} = \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{x} \cdot \dfrac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}~dx = \int_0^1 \dfrac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}x^{(a-1)-1}(1-x)^{b-1}~dx$. By multiplying in the $1/x$, the form of the integral has not changed! The only part that changed is $\alpha$ became $\alpha - 1$. This illuminates why $\alpha > 1$ is needed! With this observation, we can now evaluate the integral by normalization to a $\bet{a-1}{b}$ distribution. We do this with the reduction property of the Gamma function. This yields $\ev{\dfrac{1}{X}} = \dfrac{(a-1)+b}{a-1}\int_0^1 \dfrac{\Gamma(\textcolor{red}{(a-1)} + b)}{\Gamma(\textcolor{red}{a-1})\Gamma(b)}x^{(\textcolor{red}{a-1}) - 1}(1-x)^{b-1}~dx = \dfrac{b}{a-1} + 1$. We can now conclude $\ev{Y^2} = \ev{\dfrac{1}{X}} - 1 = \dfrac{b}{a-1}$. With the specified values, the answer is $2$.

questions.title: Plug Walk I
questions.problem: The plug performs a random walk on the set $S = \{0,1,\dots, m\}$, where $m > 0$. The plug starts at position $0 \leq k < m$. Each step, the plug moves up or down $1$ step with equal probability. The plug has opps at $0$, so they move back upwards with probability $1$ whenever they hit $0$. Find the expected amount of steps that occurs until the plug first reaches position $m$ when $k = 4$ and $m = 20$.
questions.solution:
This is a random walk, but a martingale is not particularly helpful here due to the boundary condition. The boundary can't be accounted for in a martingale so a recurrence is best. Let $e_k$ be the expected number of steps needed to hit position $m$ given the plug is currently at position $k$. By definition, $e_m = 0$, as the plug is already at position $m$. Otherwise, if the plug is currently at position $k$, where $0 < k < m$, with probability $1/2$ each, they move to positions $k+1$ or $k-1$. An additional $e_{k+1}$ or $e_{k-1}$ steps are needed, dependent on where you move. One step is performed by doing this, so for $1 \leq k \leq m-1$, $e_k = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}e_{k-1} + \dfrac{1}{2}e_{k+1}$. If $k = 0$, you move back to position $1$ guaranteed, so $e_0 = 1 + e_1$. To solve this recurrence, we will substitute forward and try to see the pattern. Namely, $\begin{align*}
e_1 &= 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}e_0 + \dfrac{1}{2}e_2 \iff e_1 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}(1+e_1) + \dfrac{1}{2}e_2 \iff e_1 = 3 + e_2\\
e_2 &= 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}e_1 + \dfrac{1}{2}e_3 \iff e_2 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}(3+e_2) + \dfrac{1}{2}e_3 \iff e_2 = 5 + e_3\\
e_3 &= 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}e_2 + \dfrac{1}{2}e_4 \iff e_3 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}(5+e_3) + \dfrac{1}{2}e_4 \iff e_3 = 7 + e_4
\end{align*}$. We can see a pattern here: For $0 \leq k < n$, $e_k = e_{k+1} + (2k+1)$. Using this pattern, we can find $e_k$ for any $k$. $\begin{align*}
    e_k &= e_{k+1} + (2k+1)\\
    &= e_{k+2} + (2k+1) + (2(k+1) + 1)\\
    &= e_{k+3} + (2k+1) + (2(k+1) + 1) + (2(k+2) + 1)\\
    &\dots\\
    &= e_m + \sum_{i=k}^{m-1} 2i+1 = 2\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}i - \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} i\right) + (m-k)\\
    &= 2 \cdot \dfrac{m(m-1) - k(k-1)}{2} + (m-k)\\
    &= (m-k)(m+k)
\end{align*}$. With the specified values, the answer is $384$.

questions.title: Tied Up Gambler I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob repeatedly gamble against one another. They initially have $\$a$ and $\$b$, respectively, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. Alice wins each round with probability $p$, while Bob wins each round with probability $q$. Assume that $p \neq q$. However, with probability $1-p-q$, Alice and Bob tie. If there is a winner, the loser pays $\$1$ to the winner; otherwise, no exchange of money occurs. They repeatedly gamble until one person has all of the money. Find the probability that Alice goes bankrupt when $a = 15, b = 10, p = 0.3,$ and $q = 0.35$. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: This game is quite similar to the standard gambler's ruin scenario, but there is a possibility of a tie. An interaction between the players happens exactly when there is no tie, and the probability of Alice ruining only depends on the rounds where there is no tie. Thus, conditioning on a round not being a tie, by the idea of sample space reduction, the probability Alice wins it is $\frac{p}{p + q}$, while Bob wins with probability $\frac{q}{p+q}$. This reduces the problem to: What is the probability Alice ruins before obtaining $\$(a+b)$ when she starts with $\$a$ and has probability $\frac{p}{p+q}$ of winning each round? This is a question we have already answered for the standard gambler's ruin! Letting $p' = \frac{p}{p+q}$ and substituting in the respective quantities, the probability Alice ruins is $\dfrac{\left(\frac{1-p'}{p'}\right)^a - \left(\frac{1-p'}{p'}\right)^{a+b}}{1 - \left(\frac{1-p'}{p'}\right)^{a+b}} = \dfrac{\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^a - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{a+b}}{1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{a+b}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.803$.

questions.title: Tied Up Gambler II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob repeatedly gamble against one another. They initially have $\$a$ and $\$b$, respectively, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. Alice wins each round with probability $p$, while Bob wins each round with probability $q$. Assume $p \neq q$. However, with probability $1-p-q$, Alice and Bob tie. If there is a winner, the loser pays $\$1$ to the winner; otherwise, no exchange of money occurs. They repeatedly gamble until one person has all of the money. Find the expected number of rounds played until someone goes bankrupt. Answer when $a = 45, b = 30, p = 0.3,$ and $q = 0.35$. Round to the nearest integer.
questions.solution: This game is quite similar to the standard gambler's ruin scenario, but there is a possibility of a tie. An interaction between the players happens exactly when there is no tie. The total number of games that are played is dependent on the number of ties. In particular, with probability $p+q$, a given round has an outcome that results in one player giving money to the other player. The duration of the game only depends on these outcomes. Conditioning on a round not being a tie, by the idea of sample space reduction, the probability Alice wins it is $\frac{p}{p + q}$, while Bob wins with probability $\frac{q}{p+q}$. This reduces the problem of the expected number of games where there is an action to the following: What is the expected number of turns until someone ruins when the two gambler's start with $\$a$ and $\$b$, respectively, and have respective probabilities of $\frac{p}{p+q}$ and $\frac{q}{p+q}$ of winning each round? The answer to this was determined in "Expected Gambler's Duration I" to be $E = \dfrac{1}{2p'-1}\left[(a+b) \cdot \dfrac{1 - \left(\frac{1-p'}{p'}\right)^a}{1 - \left(\frac{1-p'}{p'}\right)^{a+b}} - a\right] = \dfrac{p+q}{p-q}\left[(a+b) \cdot \dfrac{1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{a}}{1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{a+b}} - a\right]$. However, only a proportion $1-p-q$ games on average are ones where is there is a result. To account for this, we must multiply the expected number of rounds by $\frac{1}{1-(1-p-q)} = \frac{1}{p+q}$. This factor comes from the fact that if $E$ rounds with an action are needed on average to have someone go bankrupt, and each round is an "action round" with probability $1-(1-p-q) = p+q$, then with $E/(p+q)$ rounds, we would have $E$ action actions on average. Therefore, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{p-q}\left[(a+b) \cdot \dfrac{1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{a}}{1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{a+b}} - a\right]$. With the specified values, the answer is approximately $885$.

questions.title: Envelope Trade I
questions.problem: There are two envelopes before you. You know that one of them contains $\$2x$, while the other contains $\$x$. However, you do not know what $x$ is. You take one envelope at random, observe the money inside, and have the option to switch to the other envelope. Should you switch the envelope? If any, which is the first incorrect line in the following argument? Answer with the number of the incorrect step. If the argument is correct, answer $-1$. (1) Let $M$ be the amount of money in the selected envelope. (2) The probability that $M$ is the smaller amount is $1/2$, while it is the larger amount with $1/2$. (3) The other envelope contains either $2M$ or $M/2$ inside. (4) If the envelope you selected is the smaller one, the other envelope contains $2M$. (5) If the envelope you selected is the larger one, the other envelope contains $M/2$. (6) The expected amount of money in the other envelope is $1/2 \cdot (M/2) + 1/2 \cdot 2M = 5M/4$. (7) Since the expected value by swapping $(5M/4)$ is larger than the expected value of not swapping $(M)$, the optimal action is to swap.
questions.solution: This argument can't be correct because it implies that you should switch indefinitely to increase your expected value: Your expected value multiplies by $5/4$ per swap according to this argument. Going line-by-line, This is just a definition, so there's no error here. This is also true, there's nothing wrong here. This is indeed true: The other envelope either contains twice as much or half as much as the one you selected. If you selected the one with $\$x$, the other has $\$2x$, so this is true. If you selected the one with $\$2x$, the other has $\$x$, so this is true. This is not true. This is the expected RATIO of the money in your envelope to that of the other. However, this does not yield the expected VALUE of the other envelope. Since the above step is wrong, this is also wrong. The first incorrect step is $6$, so the answer is $6$.

questions.title: Martingular Variance
questions.problem: Suppose that $\{Z_n\}_{n \geq 0}$ is a martingale, where $Z_0 = 0$. For $i \geq 1$, define $X_i = Z_i - Z_{i-1}$. Compute $\var{Z_n}$ when $n = 10$ and $\var{X_n} = n$.
questions.solution:
From definition, $\var{Z_n} = \ev{Z_n^2} - (\ev{Z_n})^2$. Since $Z_n$ is a martingale, for all positive integers $n$, $\ev{Z_n} = \ev{Z_0} = 0$. Therefore, we only need to compute $\ev{Z_n^2}$. In the question, we see a direct relationship between the $Z_n$ and $X_n$ random variables: $Z_0 = 0$ and $Z_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n$. Therefore, it's natural to consider $\var{X_k}$ for $k \geq 1$. Letting $\mathcal{F}_l$ be the accumulated information up to and including time $k$ of the $Z_n$ process, $\begin{align*}
    \var{X_k} = \var{Z_k - Z_{k-1}} &= \ev{(Z_k - Z_{k-1})^2} - (\ev{Z_k - Z_{k-1}})^2\\
    &= \ev{(Z_k - Z_{k-1})^2}\\
    &= \ev{\ev{(Z_k - Z_{k-1})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}}}\\
    &= \ev{\ev{Z_k^2 - 2Z_kZ_{k-1} + Z_{k-1}^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}}}\\
    &= \ev{\ev{Z_k^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}} - 2Z_{k-1}\ev{Z_{k-1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}} + \ev{Z_{k-1}^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}}}\\
    &= \ev{\ev{Z_k^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}}} - 2\ev{Z_{k-1}^2} + \ev{Z_{k-1}^2}\\
    &= \ev{Z_k^2} - \ev{Z_{k-1}^2} = \var{Z_k} - \var{Z_{k-1}}
\end{align*}$. We think to condition on $\mathcal{F}_{k-1}$ because the goal is to utilize the martingale property. With this in mind, we can clearly see that $\var{Z_n} =  \var{Z_n} - 0 = (\var{Z_n} - \var{Z_{n-1}}) + \dots (\var{Z_1} - \var{Z_0}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \var{X_i}$. With the specified values, the answer is $55$.

questions.title: Expected Second Roll
questions.problem: You have two fair standard dice that respectively have $m$ sides and $n$ sides. You select one uniformly at random and roll it. The value appearing is $1$. Find the expected value of your second roll if $m = 5$ and $n = 15$.
questions.solution: It helps to first frame this problem probabilistically. Let $1$ be the event that you observe $1$ on the selected die. Define $M$ and $N$ be the events that you selected the $m-$sided and $n-$sided dice, respectively. Lastly, let $R$ be the value of your second roll. In this problem, we are looking to compute $\ev{R \mid 1}$. To do this, it would be helpful if we knew what die was being rolled. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the die being rolled. By the Law of Total Expectation, $\ev{R \mid 1} = \ev{R \mid M \cap 1}\prob{M \mid 1} + \ev{R \mid N \cap 1}\prob{N \mid 1}$. We have conditional probabilities out back because we are given that a $1$ was rolled, so the probabilities must be updated accordingly. For the conditional expected values, the fact that the first roll was a $1$ is irrelevant, as the rolls are independent. Once the die is fixed, that provides all the needed information. The expected value of a fair $k-$sided die is $\frac{k+1}{2}$, so the two conditional expected values are $\frac{m+1}{2}$ and $\frac{n+1}{2}$, respectively. To compute the conditional probabilities, we can apply a standard Bayesian approach. By the definition of conditional probability and the Law of Total Probability $\prob{M \mid 1} = \dfrac{\prob{1 \cap M}}{\prob{1}} = \dfrac{\prob{1 \mid M}\prob{M}}{\prob{1 \mid M}\prob{M} + \prob{1 \mid N}\prob{N}}$. We reverse the direction of the conditionals because it's easy to compute the probability of obtaining $1$ if we know the selected die. As the initial selection is uniformly random, $\prob{M} = \prob{N} = 1/2$. Given that the die is fair and $k-$sided, the probability of rolling a $1$ is $1/k$, so $\prob{M \mid 1} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{m} \cdot \frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{m} \cdot \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{n}{m+n}$. This means $\prob{N \mid 1} = 1 - \prob{M \mid 1} = \dfrac{m}{m+n}$. Plugging all of the above quantities into the Law of Total Expectation formula, $\ev{R \mid 1} = \dfrac{m+1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{n}{m+n} + \dfrac{n+1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{m}{m+n} = \dfrac{2mn + m + n}{2(m+n)} = \dfrac{mn}{m+n} + \dfrac{1}{2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $17/4$.

questions.title: Rooted SDE
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Let $X_t$ be the process satisfying the SDE $dX_t = \kappa(\theta - X_t)dt - \sigma \sqrt{X_t}dW_t$ with $X_0 = x > 0$. It can be shown that if $\frac{2\kappa}{\theta} > \sigma^2$, $X_t > 0$ with probability 1, so $\sqrt{X_t}$ is defined almost surely. For $T > 0$, $\ev{X_T}$ can be written as a function $f(x,\kappa, \theta,\sigma,T)$. Report the value of $f(5,0.25,1,1,1)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: When approaching SDEs, it's often helpful to consider the dynamics of some function of $X_t$. In this case, we see that the first term looks one with a mean-reversion, so we can view $\kappa$ as a "discount rate" type quantity. Therefore, it's of interest to consider the dynamics of $e^{\kappa t}X_t$. By the product rule of stochastic calculus, $d(e^{\kappa t}X_t) = \kappa e^{\kappa t}X_tdt + e^{\kappa t}dX_t = \kappa e^{\kappa t} + e^{\kappa t}\left( \kappa(\theta - X_t)dt - \sigma \sqrt{X_t}dW_t\right)$. When distributing everything out, the first term cancels with the $-\kappa X_t dt$ term inside the parentheses, so the resulting SDE is given by $d(e^{\kappa t} X_t) = \kappa e^{\kappa t}dt - \sigma e^{\kappa t} \sqrt{X_t} dW_t$. To get an expression for $X_t$, we can first integrate $d(e^{\kappa t}X_t)$, and then multiply by $e^{-\kappa t}$ on both sides to remove the exponential term. Performing the integration, $e^{\kappa t} X_t - X_0 = \int_0^t \kappa e^{\kappa s}ds - \int_0^t \sigma e^{\kappa s} \sqrt{X_s} dW_s$. We must add $X_0$ to be the "constant of integration" (which is really a random variable). Multiplying by $e^{-\kappa t}$ on both sides, $X_t = X_0 e^{-\kappa t} + \int_0^t \kappa e^{\kappa(s-t)}ds - \int_0^t \sigma e^{\kappa(s-t)} \sqrt{X_s} dW_s$. As per the question, $X_0 = x$, where $x$ is a non-random constant, so we can substitute that in. The first integral is non-random, so this can also be treated as a constant. The second integral is Ito and the function inside is "sufficiently nice" (in the sense of Ito integration theory) to conclude that the mean of it is $0$. Thus, $\mathbb{E}[X_T] = xe^{-\kappa T} + \int_0^T \kappa e^{\kappa(s-T)}ds = xe^{-\kappa T} + \theta (1 - e^{-\kappa T}) = xe^{-\kappa T} + \theta (1 - e^{-\kappa T})$. With the specified values, the answer is approximately $4.115$. This result makes intuitive sense because $\theta$ can be viewed as the "mean reversion" term of the SDE, so $\ev{X_t}$ should approach $\theta$ as $t \rightarrow \infty$, which is does in this solution.

questions.title: MGF to Hit
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Define $T_a = \inf\{t > 0: |W_t| = a\}$. For $\lambda > 0$, compute $M(\lambda,a) = \ev{e^{-\lambda T_a}}$. Report $M(3,1)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Since the term on the interior is an exponential, it makes sense to consider the exponential martingale. Namely, we will want to consider the martingale $Z_t = e^{\theta W_t - \frac{\theta^2}{2}t}$. If you haven't shown this is a martingale, it is a good exercise to do so. The idea is to apply the Optional Stopping Theorem to $Z_t$, as the $t$ in the second term of the exponent will become $T_a$, getting us closer to the goal. Applying OST, $\ev{Z_{T_a}} = \ev{Z_0} \iff \ev{e^{\theta W_{T_a} - \frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a}} = 1$. For the LHS, $W_{T_a}$ is either $\pm a$ with probability $1/2$ each, as both are equidistant from $0$. Thus, we can apply LOTE to it and obtain $\ev{e^{\theta W_{T_a} - \frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\ev{e^{\theta W_{T_a} - \frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a} \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} W_{T_a} = a} + \ev{e^{\theta W_{T_a} - \frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a} \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} W_{T_a} = -a}\right] = \dfrac{e^{\theta a} + e^{-\theta a}}{2}\ev{e^{-\frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a}}$. By rearrangement, $\ev{e^{-\frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a}} = \dfrac{1}{\cosh{a\theta}} = \dfrac{2}{e^{a\theta} + e^{-a\theta}}$. To get $\ev{e^{-\lambda T_a}}$ from this, we must have $\theta^2/2 = \lambda$, meaning $\theta = \sqrt{2\lambda}$. Doing this, $\ev{e^{-\lambda T_a}} = \dfrac{2}{e^{a\sqrt{2\lambda}} + e^{-a\sqrt{2\lambda}}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.171$.

questions.title: Geometric Brownian Square
questions.problem: Suppose that $S_t$ is a Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) with drift $\mu$ and volatility $\sigma$ starting at $X_0 = x$. Compute $\ev{X_t^2}$ as a function $f(t,\mu,\sigma,x)$. Report $f(3,0.1,0.2,4)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: The GBM SDE is $dS_t = \mu S_t dt + \sigma S_t dW_t$ and has mean $\ev{S_t} = xe^{\mu t}$. The idea is to find a SDE that $dS_t^2$ satisfies, and use this to compute the expected value. To find the SDE of $S_t^2$, we apply Ito's lemma with $f(t,x) = x^2$, which yields $df(t,x) = dS_t^2 = 2S_tdS_t + \dfrac{1}{2}2d[S,S]_t$. To compute the quadratic variation $d[S,S]_t = dS_tdS_t$, we substitute in the SDE for $dS_t$ and obtain $d[S,S]_t = (\mu S_t dt + \sigma S_t dW_t)(\mu S_t dt + \sigma S_t dW_t) = \sigma^2 S_t^2 dt$. All terms that aren't $d[W,W]_t = dt$ vanish to $0$, as the time term has $0$ quadratic variation. Substituting in $dS_t$ and $d[S,S]_t$ into the SDE for $dS_t^2$, $dS_t^2 = 2S_t(\mu S_t dt + \sigma S_t dW_t) + \sigma^2 S_t^2 dt = (2\mu + \sigma^2)S_t^2dt  + 2\sigma S_tdW_t$. Note that $S_t^2$ satisfies the exact same SDE as $S_t$, but $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are now replaced with $2\mu + \sigma^2$ and $2\sigma$, respectively. Furthermore, we also have that $S_0^2 = x^2$, so $S_t^2$ is a GBM with initial location $x^2$, drift $2\mu + \sigma^2$, and volatility $2\sigma$. Using the formula for the expected value of a GBM presented at the beginning of the solution, we can conclude $\ev{S_t^2} = x^2e^{(2\mu + \sigma^2)t}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 23.505$.

questions.title: Brownian Martingale II
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Define $X_t = W_t^n - \int_0^t g(W_s)~ds$ for some continuous-time stochastic process $g(W_s)$ that is adapted to the Brownian Motion filtration. Find the process $g(W_s)$ that makes $X_t$ a martingale. Report the value of $\ev{g(W_t)}$ when $n = 6$ and $t = 1$.
questions.solution: $X_t$ is defined in terms of a function of $W_t$, so it's best to use Ito's lemma to determine when $X_t$ is a martingale. We will consider the dynamics of $W_t^n$, and then select $g(W_s)$ based on the result. Applying Ito's lemma with $f(w) = w^n$, $df(W_t) = dW_t^n = nW_t^{n-1}dW_t + \dfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)d[W,W]_t = nW_t^{n-1}dW_t + \dfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)W_t^{n-2}dt$. The integral has $0$ second-order variation, and the first order derivative is just $g(W_t)dt$. For $X_t$ to be a martingale, it must be the case that the coefficient in front of $dt$ is $0$ i.e. there is no drift. Therefore, $\dfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)W_t^{n-2} - g(W_t) = 0 \iff g(W_t) = \dfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)W_t^{n-2}$. With $n = 6$ and $t = 1$, $\ev{g(W_t)} = 15\ev{W_1^4} = 15 \cdot 3 = 45$. In the expected value, we use the facts that $W_1 \sim N(0,1)$ and $\ev{Z^{2n}} = \dfrac{(2n)!}{2^n n!}$ when $Z$ is standard normal.

questions.title: Brownian Bridge
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. The Brownian Bridge on $[0,1]$ is the process $X_t = W_t - tW_1$. You can think of this as a Brownian Motion that is conditioned on $W_0 = W_1 = 0$. For any $0 \leq s < t \leq 1$, compute $\ev{X_s \mid X_t = a}$ when $s = 1/4, t = 1/2,$ and $a = 4$.
questions.solution:
The idea here is to use the independent increments property of Brownian Motion. As $X_s$ is defined in terms of Brownian Motion, the idea is to split the Brownian Motion up into two segments: $(s,t)$ and $(t,1)$. We can write $X_s = W_s - sW_1 = \left(W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t\right) + \left(\dfrac{s}{t}W_t - sW_1\right) = \left(W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t\right) + \dfrac{s}{t}(W_t - tW_t) = \left(W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t\right) + \dfrac{s}{t}X_t$. The first term deals with a change in the Brownian Motion on $(s,t)$, while $X_t$ deals with a change in the Brownian Motion on $(t,1)$, so they should be independent by the independent increments property. This can be verified rigorously too by computing the covariance of the two terms. Showing they are uncorrelated is sufficient because of three facts: The two terms are Normally distributed by the properties of Normal distributions and Brownian Motion; Brownian Motion is a Gaussian process; Uncorrelated Normal random variables are independent. By the bilinearity of covariance, $\begin{align*}
    \cov{W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t}{X_t} &= \cov{W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t}{W_t - tW_1}\\
    &= \cov{W_s}{W_t} - t\cov{W_s}{W_1} - \dfrac{s}{t}\cov{W_t}{W_t} + s\cov{W_t}{W_1}\\
    &= s - st - s+ st = 0
\end{align*}$. In the above, we repeatedly use the fact that $\cov{W_s}{W_t} = \min(s,t)$ for Brownian Motion. We can now conclude $W_s - \frac{s}{t}W_t$ and $X_t$ are independent, so $\ev{W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} X_t} = \ev{W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t} = \ev{W_s} - \dfrac{s}{t}\ev{W_t} = 0$. Finally, we can conclude $\ev{X_s \mid X_t} = \ev{W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t + \dfrac{s}{t}X_t\hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} X_t} = \ev{W_s - \dfrac{s}{t}W_t \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} X_t} + \dfrac{s}{t}X_t = \dfrac{s}{t}X_t$. With the specified values, the answer is $2$.

questions.title: Reciprocal GBM
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Suppose that $X_t$ is a process such that $1/X_t$ is a GBM with drift $\mu$ and volatility $\sigma$ i.e. it satisfies the SDE $d\left(\dfrac{1}{X_t}\right) = \dfrac{1}{X_t} \cdot (\mu dt + \sigma dW_t)$. $X_t$ is a GBM with drift $\mu'$ and volatility $\sigma'$. Find $\mu'\sigma'$ when $\mu = -2$ and $\sigma = 1$.
questions.solution: We know the dynamics of $1/X_t$ in this question, and we are looking to obtain the dynamics of $X_t$. We can write $X_t = 1/(1/X_t)$, so the key is to apply Ito's lemma on $f(y) = 1/y$, where $Y_t = 1/X_t$. By basic calculus, $f'(y) = -1/y^2$ and $f''(y) = 2/y^3$. By Ito's formula, $df(Y_t) = dX_t = f'(Y_t)dY_t + \dfrac{1}{2}f''(Y_t)d[Y,Y]_t$. To compute $d[Y,Y]_t$, we can expand out the "square" of the SDE that $Y_t$ satisfies. This yields $d[Y,Y]_t = dY_tdY_t = Y_t^2(\mu dt + \sigma dW_t)^2 = \sigma^2 Y_t^2 dt$. All the other terms that have at least one $dt$ term in them vanish, as cross-variations and the quadratic variation of $t$ is $0$. Plugging this in, $dX_t = - \dfrac{1}{Y_t^2} \cdot Y_t(\mu dt + \sigma dW_t) + \dfrac{1}{Y_t^3} \cdot \sigma^2 Y_t^2 dt = \dfrac{1}{Y_t}\left((\sigma^2 - \mu)dt - \sigma dW_t\right) = X_t\left((\sigma^2 - \mu)dt - \sigma dW_t\right)$. This implies $X_t$ is also a GBM with drift $\sigma^2 - \mu$ and volatility $\sigma^2$. With the specified values, $\mu' = 3$ and $\sigma' = 1$, so the answer is $3$.

questions.title: Ito Variance V
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Compute $\displaystyle \var{\int_0^2 \sqrt{t}e^{\frac{W_t^2}{8}}~dW_t}$.
questions.solution: As we are looking to compute the variance of an integral, Ito's lemma should be your first thought. The alternate form of Ito's isometry can be applied here, as the integrand is adapted, square integrable, and is almost surely continuous. Namely, this tells us $\var{\int_0^2 \sqrt{t}e^{\frac{W_t^2}{8}}~dW_t} = \int_0^2 \ev{\left(\sqrt{t}e^{\frac{W_t^2}{8}}\right)^2}~dt = \int_0^2 t\ev{e^{\frac{1}{4}W_t^2}}~dt$. We must compute the expected value term in the integrand. To do this, we note that $W_t = \sqrt{t}Z$, where $Z \sim N(0,1)$, as $W_t \sim N(0,t)$ and variance scales quadratically. Therefore, $\ev{e^{\frac{1}{4}W_t^2}} = \ev{e^{\frac{t}{4}Z^2}} = M_{Z^2}\left(\dfrac{t}{4}\right)$. In the above $M_{Z^2}(\theta)$ is the MGF of $Z^2$. The expression is equivalent by noting the form of $M_X(\theta) = \ev{e^{\theta X}}$ with $X$ as $Z^2$ and $\theta$ as $t/4$. To evaluate this expected value, we note that $Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1$, where $\chi^2_n$ is the chi-square distribution with $n$ degrees of freedom. Even further, $\chi^2_n$ is the same as $\gam{n/2}{2}$, which has MGF $M_{Z^2}(\theta) = (1-2\theta)^{-n/2}$. Substituting in $\theta = t/4$ yields $M_{Z^2}(t/4) = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{2-t}}$. Plugging this back in, $\var{\int_0^2 \sqrt{t}e^{\frac{W_t^2}{8}}~dW_t} = \int_0^2 t \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{2-t}}~dt = \int_0^2 (2-u) \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{u}}~du = 2\sqrt{2}\int_0^2 u^{-1/2}~du  - \sqrt{2}\int_0^2 u^{1/2}~du = \dfrac{16}{3}$. The second integral is obtained by the $u-$substitution $u = 2-t$. This is a natural choice because integrating $1/\sqrt{u}$ is easy.

questions.title: Brownian Hitting III
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion and $T_a = \inf\{t > 0: |W_t| = a\}$. Compute $\text{Var}(T_a)$ when $a = 3$.
questions.solution: To compute the variance of $T_a$, we need to create a martingale out of $W_t$ that has a $t^2$ term in it. This will allow us to compute $E[T_a^2]$ when applying the OST. It is known that $X_t = W_t^4 - 6tW_t^2 + 3t^2$ is a martingale, and this contains a $t^2$ term. One can verify that this is a martingale by Ito's lemma on $f(t,w) = w^4 - 6tw^2 + 3t^2$. Under this assumption, we can apply OST quite naturally: $E[X_{T_a}] = E[X_0] \iff E[W_{T_a}^4 - 6W_{T_a}^2 T_a + 3T_a^2] = 0$. Since the Brownian Motion only assumes the values $\pm a$ at $T_a$, we can conclude $W_{T_a}^4 = a^4$ and $W_{T_a}^2 = a^2$ with probability $1$. Substituting these in, $$\begin{align*} E[X_{T_a}] &= a^4 - 6a^2 E[T_a] + 3E[T_a^2] = 0 \\ &\iff a^4 - 6a^2 \cdot a^2 + 3E[T_a^2] = 0 \\ &\iff E[T_a^2] = \dfrac{5}{3}a^4 \end{align*}$$ We evaluate $E[T_a]$ with the result of "Brownian Hitting II" for $a = b$. Now that we have the second moment, we can conclude $\text{Var}(T_a) = E[T_a^2] - (E[T_a])^2 = \dfrac{5}{3}a^4 - a^4 = \dfrac{2}{3}a^4$. With $a = 3$, the answer is $54$.

questions.title: Partitioned Brownian
questions.problem: Let $B_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Fix $t > 0$, and define $\Delta_{m,n} = B_{tm2^{-n}} - B_{t(m-1)2^{-n}}$, where $1 \leq m \leq 2^n$. For fixed $n$ and $t$, compute $E\left[\left(\sum_{m=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{m,n} - t\right)^2\right]$. Report the answer when $t = n = 4$.
questions.solution: Since this entire sum is squared, the best approach is to first expand out everything. By expanding out the interior, $$E\left[\left(\sum_{m=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{m,n} - t\right)^2\right] = E\left[\left(\sum_{m=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{m,n}\right)^2\right] - 2t E\left[\sum_{m=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{m,n}\right] + t^2$$ $\Delta_{m,n}$ concerns the change of the Brownian Motion on an interval of length $t/2^n$. By stationarity, $\Delta_{m,n} \sim N(0, t/2^n)$. Since the mean is $0$, $E[\Delta_{m,n}^2] = \text{Var}(\Delta_{m,n}) = t/2^n$. By linearity of expected value, the sum in the second term is $2^n \cdot t/2^n = t$. When we expand out the square, we obtain $$E\left[\left(\sum_{m=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{m,n}^2\right)^2\right] = E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2^n}\sum_{j=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{i,n}\Delta_{j,n}\right] = E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{i,n}^4\right] + \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq 2^n} E[\Delta_{i,n}]E[\Delta_{j,n}]$$ by breaking up the double sum into where $i = j$ and $i \neq j$. By independent increments, $\Delta_{i,n}$ and $\Delta_{j,n}$ are independent when $i \neq j$. For the first sum, if $Z \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$, then $E[Z^4] = 3\sigma^4$. The first sum evaluates to $2^n \cdot 3\left(\frac{t}{2^n}\right)^2$. There are $2^n \cdot 2^n - 2^n = 2^n(2^n - 1)$ terms in the second sum, as there are $(2^n)^2 = 4^n$ total terms, of which $2^n$ are accounted for in the $i = j$ sum. Each term in the second sum is $\left(\frac{t}{2^n}\right)^2$, so $$E\left[\left(\sum_{m=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{m,n}^2\right)^2\right] = \dfrac{3t^2}{2^n} + \dfrac{t^2(2^n-1)}{2^n} = t^2 \left(1 + \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right)$$ Plugging everything in: $$E\left[\left(\sum_{m=1}^{2^n} \Delta_{m,n} - t\right)^2\right] = t^2 \left(1 + \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right) - 2t^2 + t^2 = \dfrac{t^2}{2^{n-1}}$$ Substituting in the respective values yields an answer of $2$.

questions.title: Remaining Gum
questions.problem: Omar has $N$ pieces of 5gum in his left pocket and $N$ pieces of Orbit gum in his right pocket. He's dealing out gum to $M > 2N$ people in his probability class. Every time he deals out a piece of gum to someone, he picks which pocket to deal from uniformly at random. When Omar is asked to give someone gum and he looks in his pocket to find there are no pieces of gum remaining in it, he counts up the number of pieces of gum in his other pocket. Find the probability there are exactly $k$ pieces of gum in the other pocket, $0 \leq k \leq N$, when $N = 8$ and $k = 4$.
questions.solution: Let's think about the scenario at the experimental level. WLOG, we can assume that his right pocket is the one he notices to be empty. We can say this WLOG because both pockets are equally likely to be noticed as empty, so we can just fix one of them and multiply by $2$ to account for the other pocket. Let $X$ be the event that the right pocket gets emptied first, $Y$ be the event that the left pocket gets emptied first, and $G$ the number of pieces of gum in the other pocket. Then the law of total probability gives, $$\begin{align*} P[G = k] &= P[X] P[G = k | X] + P[Y] P[G = k | Y] \\ &= \frac{1}{2} P[G = k | X] + \frac{1}{2} P[G = k | Y] \\ &= P[R = k | X] \end{align*}$$ If Omar's right pocket is the one that's noticed to be empty, it must have been selected by Omar $N+1$ times: $N$ times to empty it out, and then $1$ more time to notice it's actually empty. For there to be exactly $k$ pieces of gum in his left pocket, it must have been selected $N-k$ times. This would ensure there are $N - (N-k) = k$ pieces of gum in the left pocket. For there to be exactly $k$ pieces of gum in Omar's left pocket upon him noticing his right pocket is empty, the following events must occur: Omar must select from his right pocket $N$ times in the first $2N-k$ draws, Omar must select from his left pocket $N-k$ times in the first $2N-k$ draws, and Omar must select from his right pocket on the $(2N-k+1)$st draw. Since each draw is independent, we can use a Binomial distribution. If we let $R$ represent the number of times he draws from his right pocket in the $2N-k$ trials, then $R \sim \text{Binom}(2N-k, 1/2)$. Accordingly, $$P[R = N] = \binom{2N-k}{N}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^N\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{N-k} = \binom{2N-k}{N}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2N-k}$$ The probability he draws from his right pocket again on the $(2N-k+1)$st trial is $1/2$, so the probability of Omar having exactly $k$ pieces of gum in his left pocket upon realizing his right pocket is empty is $$\binom{2N-k}{N}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2N-k+1}$$ We must multiply by $2$ to account for the other case. Therefore, the probability of Omar having exactly $k$ candies in his other pocket upon realizing one pocket is empty is $$\binom{2N-k}{N}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2N-k}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $495/4096$.

questions.title: Full Subset
questions.problem: Suppose $S$ is a set of $n$ elements. How many ways can two (not necessarily distinct) subsets of $S$, say $A$ and $B$, be selected such that $A \cup B = S$. Report the answer when $n = 8$. The order of $A$ and $B$ is irrelevant.
questions.solution: For $A \cup B = S$, every $x \in S$ must belong to at least one of $A$ or $B$. In other words, exactly one of the following is true: $x \in A \cap B^c$, $x \in A^c \cap B$, or $x \in A \cap B$. Thus, there are $3$ options for each of the elements of $S$, meaning there are $3^n$ possible ways to assign the elements of $x$. However, the order of the subsets is irrelevant, so we need to divide by $2$ to account for the ordering of $A$ and $B$. There is one caveat to this: If $A = B$, there are not two orderings of the subsets, so these must be excluded first before dividing by $2$, and then added back. Since $A \cup B = S$, the only possible way $A = B$ is if $A = B = S$, which is $1$ possibility. Thus, there are $\frac{3^n - 1}{2} + 1 = \frac{3^n + 1}{2}$ ways to select the subsets: We subtract the $1$ equality case from $3^n$, divide by $2$ to remove the ordering of $A$ and $B$, and then add back in the equality case. With $n = 8$, the answer is $3281$.

questions.title: Uniform Conditional Density
questions.problem: Suppose that $X \sim U(0,1)$ and that $Y|X=x \sim U(0,x)$. What is the density of $Y$ evaluated at $Y = 0.5$ rounded to 2 decimal places?
questions.solution: We can solve this problem using the relation, $f_{Y}(y) = \int f_{Y,X}(y,x)dx = \int f_{X}(x) f_{Y|X}(y|x) dx$. Since $X \sim U(0,1)$, we know that $f_{X}(x) = 1 \times \mathbf{1}\{0 \leq x \leq 1\}$. The key is to get the appropriate form of $f_{Y|X}(y|x)$. Since we are given that $Y|X=x \sim U(0,x)$ it is tempting to say that $f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{1}{x}$. However, it is important to keep in mind that this is only true when $0 \leq y \leq x$, as otherwise $f_{Y|X}(y|x)$ is equal to 0. Thus, the correct formula for $f_{Y|X}(y|x)$ is $f_{Y}(y) = \frac{1}{x}$ $\mathbf{1}\{0 \leq y \leq x\}$. Putting everything together we get that the density of $Y$ is, $$f_{Y}(y) = \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x} \mathbf{1}\{0 \leq y \leq x\} \mathbf{1}\{0 \leq x \leq 1\} dx = \int_{y}^{1} \frac{1}{x} dx = \text{ln}(1) - \text{ln}(y) = -\text{ln}(y)$$ Thus, the density of $Y$ evaluated at $0.5$ is $-\text{ln}(0.5) = 0.69$, when rounded to two decimal places.

questions.title: Normal Stepper
questions.problem: Suppose that a particle is at the origin in 2D space. That is, the particle is located at $(0,0)$. At every time step $t$, the particle will make a move in a random direction. This random direction is determined by randomly adding $(Z_{1t}, Z_{2t})$ to the particles current position, where each $Z_{it} \sim N(0,1)$ and are independent across all $i$ and $t$. What is the expected Euclidean distance to the origin of the particle after $n$ steps? Report the answer when $n = 100$, rounded to $2$ decimal places.
questions.solution: After $n$ steps, the particle's position is $(\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{1t}, \sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{2t})$. The Euclidean distance is $\sqrt{ (\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{1t})^{2} + (\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{2t})^{2} }$. Since the $Z_{it}$ are independent, $\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{1t} \sim N(0, n)$ and $\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{2t} \sim N(0, n)$. Call these $X$ and $Y$. The distance is $\sqrt{ X^{2} + Y^{2} }$. We can write this as $\sqrt{ (\sqrt{n} W_{1})^{2} + (\sqrt{n}W_{2})^{2} } = \sqrt{n} \sqrt{ W_{1}^{2} + W_{2}^{2}}$ where $W_{1}, W_{2} \sim N(0,1)$. Since $W_{i}^{2} \sim \chi^{2}_{1}$, we have $W_{1}^{2} + W_{2}^{2} \sim \chi^{2}_{2}$, and $W = \sqrt{ W_{1}^{2} + W_{2}^{2}} \sim \chi_{2}$. The mean of the chi distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom is $$E[W] = \sqrt{2} \frac{ \Gamma( \frac{k+1}{2}) }{ \Gamma(\frac{k}{2} )}$$ For $k = 2$, this gives $\sqrt{ \frac{\pi}{2} }$. Therefore, $$\begin{align*} E\left[\sqrt{ (\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{1t})^{2} + (\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_{2t})^{2} }\right] &= E\left[ \sqrt{n} \sqrt{ W_{1}^{2} + W_{2}^{2}} \right] \\ &= \sqrt{n} E[W] \\ &= \sqrt{n} \sqrt{ \frac{\pi}{2} } \end{align*}$$ With $n = 100$, the answer is $\approx 12.53$.

questions.title: Rowed Heads and Tails
questions.problem: You flip a fair coin until you get either $3$ heads in a row or $3$ tails in a row. What is the expected number flips you will perform?
questions.solution: We will approach this question by first conditioning on the outcome of the first flip and then follow the typical markov state approach to finding the expectation. Define the states $T_{i}$ and $H_{i}$, which stand for having a sequence of flips which ends with a consecutive sequence of $i$ tails and $i$ heads respectively. For example, $H_{2}$ means that our sequence of flips ends with $HH$. Denoting the number of flips we need before getting either 3 heads or 3 tails in a row by $N$, we have, $$E[N] = P[\text{roll H}]( 1 + E[ N | H_{1} ]) + P[\text{roll T}](1 + E[ N | T_{1} ])$$ Since the coin is fair, $P[\text{roll H}] = P[\text{roll T}] = \frac{1}{2}$. Writing out how all of our possible states relate to each other yields the system of equations, $$\begin{align*} E[ N | H_{1} ] &= \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | H_{2}]) + \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | T_{1}]) \\ E[ N | T_{1} ] &= \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | T_{2}]) + \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | H_{1}]) \\ E[ N | H_{2} ] &= \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | H_{3}]) + \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | T_{1}]) \\ E[ N | T_{2} ] &= \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | T_{3}]) + \frac{1}{2}(1 + E[N | H_{1}]) \\ E[ N | H_{3} ] &= 0 \\ E[ N | T_{3} ] &= 0 \end{align*}$$ Solving the system of equations yields, $$E[N] = 7$$

questions.title: Bears and Bulls
questions.problem: $7$ Bears and $7$ Bulls sit at a round table. What is the probability that at least $4$ bears sit together in a row?
questions.solution:
We need to count the number of seatings where at least $4$ bears sit together in a row. There are $7$ bears among $14$ total animals at a round table, giving $\binom{14}{7}$ total arrangements. For at least $4$ bears sitting together, we fix a block of $4$ consecutive seats among the $14$ seats. There are $8$ remaining seats from which we choose $3$ more bears: $\binom{8}{3}$. Since the table is circular with $14$ seats, there are $14$ positions for a block of $4$, giving $14 \binom{8}{3}$. We must also account for blocks of $5$: $14 \binom{7}{2}$, blocks of $6$, and blocks of $7$. By inclusion-exclusion: $$P[\text{at least 4 bears sit together in a row}] = \frac{14( \binom{8}{3} + \binom{7}{2} + \binom{6}{1} + \binom{7}{0})}{\binom{14}{7}} = \dfrac{49}{147}$$

Alternatively, let $S_{i}$ be the event that position $i$ starts a run of $4$ bears. Then $$P\left[ \bigcup_{i=1}^{14} S_{i} \right] = \sum_{i=1}^{14} P[S_{i}]$$ since the $S_{i}$ are structured so inclusion-exclusion simplifies. For each fixed starting position $i$, $P[S_{i}] = \frac{7}{14}\cdot\frac{7}{13}\cdot\frac{6}{12}\cdot\frac{5}{11}\cdot\frac{4}{10} = \frac{7}{286}$, where $\frac{7}{14}$ accounts for position $i$ being a bear and $\frac{7}{13}$ for the next. Thus $$\begin{align*} P\left[ \bigcup_{i=1}^{14} S_{i} \right] &= \sum_{i=1}^{14} \frac{7}{286} = \frac{49}{143} \end{align*}$$

questions.title: Head Start
questions.problem: You flip a fair coin $n$ times. Given that no consecutive heads appear in your sequence of flips, what is the probability that the first flip was a heads? Report the answer when $n = 15$.
questions.solution: This problem can be solved by recursion. First, let's generalize and suppose that we make $n$ flips. Since we are dealing with a fair coin, we will determine the probability by counting the total number of length $n$ sequences that start with a heads and don't have any consecutive heads, and divide that by the total number of sequences that don't have any consecutive heads. By Bayes rule, $$P[\text{first flip is H} \mid \text{No consecutive H in } n \text{ flips}] = \frac{P[\text{first flip is H}, \text{No consecutive H in } n \text{ flips}]}{P[\text{No consecutive H in } n \text{ flips}]}$$ Denote the number of sequences of $n$ coin flips with no consecutive heads as $f(n)$. In order for a length $n$ sequence to not have any consecutive heads, either the sequence ends in $TH$ or it ends in $T$. The number of length $n$ sequences ending in $HT$ is $f(n-2)$, since we can append $HT$ to any valid length $n-2$ sequence. Similarly, the number ending in $T$ is $f(n-1)$. Putting this together yields, $$f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2)$$ which is the Fibonacci sequence. Clearly, $f(1) = 2$ and $f(0) = 1$. This is exactly the Fibonacci sequence shifted by $2$ upwards, so $f(n) = F_{n+2}$. We now need to find the number of length $n$ sequences that start with a heads and don't have any consecutive heads. Denoting this as $g(n)$, any such sequence must start with $HT$. The number of valid sequences is the number of length $n-2$ sequences with no consecutive heads, since we can append $HT$ to the start. Thus, $g(n) = f(n-2) = F_n$. Putting everything together: $$P[\text{first flip is H} \mid \text{No consecutive H in } n \text{ flips}] = \frac{ f(n-2) }{f(n)} = \dfrac{F_n}{F_{n+2}}$$ When $n = 15$: $$P[\text{first flip is H} \mid \text{No consecutive H in } 15 \text{ flips}] = \frac{ f(13) }{f(15)} = \frac{610}{1597}$$

questions.title: 3, 2, 1, Go!
questions.problem: What is the expected number of rolls of a fair $6$-sided die before you either get a $3$ for the first time or two consecutive $1$s?
questions.solution: We can solve this problem by conditioning on the outcome of our rolls and then using the typical markov state approach. Let $R_{1}$ denote rolling a $1$, $R_{3}$ denote rolling a $3$, and $R^{*}$ denote rolling any other number. Using the law of total expectation, and denoting the number of rolls needed as $N$, $$\begin{align*} E[N] &= P[ R_{1} ]E[N | R_{1}]+ P[ R_{3} ]E[N | R_{3}] + P[ R^{*} ]E[N | R^{*}] \\ &= \frac{1}{6}( 1 + E[N | 1]) + \frac{1}{6}(1 + E[N | 3]) + \frac{4}{6}( 1 + E[N]) \end{align*}$$ where $E[N | k]$ denotes the expected number of additional rolls needed given that our last roll was equal to $k$. The fact that $E[N | R^{*}] = 1 + E[N]$ is because if our first roll is something other than a 3 or a 1, then we have used 1 roll but it's as if we just started, so we expect to use $E[N]$ more rolls. We can then condition on the result of the next roll: $$\begin{align*} E[ N | 1 ] &= P[ R_{1} ]E[N | 1, R_{1}]+ P[ R_{3} ]E[N | 1, R_{3}] + P[ R^{*} ]E[N | 1, R^{*}] \\ &= \frac{1}{6}(1 + E[N | 1,1]) + \frac{1}{6}(1 + E[N | 1,3]) + \frac{4}{6}(1 + E[N]) \\ & = \frac{1}{6}(1 + 0) + \frac{1}{6}(1 + 0) + \frac{4}{6}(1 + E[N]) \\ &= 1 + \frac{4}{6}E[N] \\ E[ N | 3 ] &= 0 \end{align*}$$ Above, $E[N | i,j]$ denotes the number of additional rolls needed given that our current sequence of rolls is $i,j$. Putting this altogether gives, $$\begin{align*} E[N] &= \frac{1}{6}( 1 + E[N | 1]) + \frac{1}{6}(1 + E[N | 3]) + \frac{4}{6}( 1 + E[N]) \\ &= \frac{1}{6}( 1 + 1 + \frac{4}{6}E[N] ) + \frac{1}{6}(1) + \frac{4}{6}(1 + E[N]) \end{align*}$$ and solving for $E[N]$ we get, $$E[N] = \frac{21}{4}$$

questions.title: Conditional Normal Region I
questions.problem: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. What is $P[X > 0| X + Y > 0]$?
questions.solution:
We can solve this geometrically. Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables, the condition $X + Y > 0$ is equivalent to $Y > -X$, which is the region above the line $y = -x$. The condition $X > 0$ is the right half-plane. $P[X > 0| X + Y > 0]$ asks what fraction of the probability mass in the region $X + Y > 0$ also satisfies $X > 0$. By the symmetry of the standard bivariate normal, $P[X > 0| X + Y > 0] = \frac{3}{4}$.

More rigorously: $$\begin{align*} P[X > 0| X + Y > 0] &= \frac{P[X > 0, X + Y > 0]}{P[X + Y > 0]} \\ &= \frac{P[X > 0, X + Y > 0]}{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= 2 P[X + Y > 0 | X > 0] \\ &= 2 P[Y > -X | X > 0] \end{align*}$$ since $X+Y \sim N(0,2)$ so $P[X + Y > 0] = \frac{1}{2}$. To evaluate $P[Y > -X | X > 0]$: $$\begin{align*} P[Y > -X | X > 0] &= \int_{0}^{\infty} \int_{-x}^{\infty} f(x,y)dydx \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \int_{-x}^{\infty} e^{ \frac{-(x^{2}+y^{2})}{2} } dydx \end{align*}$$ Converting to polar coordinates with $x = r\cos(\theta)$, $y = r\sin(\theta)$, $r = \sqrt{ x^{2} + y^{2} }$, the region corresponds to $\frac{-\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $0 \leq r \leq \infty$. The upper bound $\frac{\pi}{2}$ comes from the positive x-axis, and the line $y = -x$ gives $\frac{-\pi}{4}$. $$\begin{align*} \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{ -\frac{\pi}{4} }^{ \frac{\pi}{2} } \int_{-\infty}^{0} e^{ \frac{-r^{2}}{2}} r dr d\theta \end{align*}$$ Using the substitution $u = -\frac{r^{2}}{2}$, $du = -rdr$, when $r = 0$, $u = 0$; when $r = \infty$, $u = -\infty$: $$\begin{align*} \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{ -\frac{\pi}{4} }^{ \frac{\pi}{2} } \int_{0}^{-\infty} -e^{u} du d\theta &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{ -\frac{\pi}{4} }^{ \frac{\pi}{2} } \int_{-\infty}^{0} e^{u} du d\theta \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{ -\frac{\pi}{4} }^{ \frac{\pi}{2} } (1 - 0) d\theta \\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{3\pi}{4} \\ &= \frac{3}{8} \end{align*}$$ Therefore, $$\begin{align*} P[X > 0| X + Y > 0] &= 2 P[Y > -X | X > 0] = 2 \times \frac{3}{8} = \frac{3}{4} \end{align*}$$

questions.title: Neighborhood Cats Table
questions.problem: Suppose that $2n$ cats are eating at a circular bowl. Each cat at the bowl has a distinct label from $0,\dots,2n - 1$ which denotes the number of other cats at the bowl that the cat knows. Specifically, a cat with label $i$ knows $i$ of the other cats at the table. Assuming that cat A knowing cat B doesn't imply that cat B knows cat A, what is the expected proportion of cats that know at least one of the cats directly on either side of them when $n = 20$?
questions.solution: Let $X_{i}$ be a random variable defined as follows: $$X_{i} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if cat } i \text{ knows at least 1 neighbor} \\ 0 & \text{if cat } i \text{ doesn't know at least 1 neighbor} \end{cases}$$ The expected proportion of cats that know at least one neighbor can then be expressed as $$E\left[ \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} X_{i}}{2n}\right]$$ Note that the index $i$ starts at $0$ and ends at $2n-1$ since the labels start at $0$ and end at $2n-1$. By linearity of expectation: $$E\left[ \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} X_{i}}{2n}\right] = \frac{ \sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} E[X_{i}] }{2n} = \frac{ \sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} P[X_{i} = 1]}{2n}$$ Our task is now to determine $P[X_{i} = 1]$. Since this represents the probability that cat $i$ knows at least one neighbor, we consider the complement $1 - P[X_{i} = 0]$, where $P[X_{i} = 0]$ is the probability that cat $i$ doesn't know any of its direct neighbors. To find $P[X_{i} = 0]$, note that there are $\binom{2n-1}{i}$ ways to determine the $i$ other cats that cat $i$ knows since there are $2n-1$ other possible cats to know. The number of ways with the restriction that cat $i$ doesn't know its two immediate neighbors is $\binom{2n-3}{i}$. Thus, $$\begin{align*} P[X_{i} = 0] &= \frac{\binom{2n-3}{i}}{\binom{2n-1}{i}} = \frac{ (2n-1-i)(2n-2-i) }{(2n-1)(2n-2)} \end{align*}$$ We now have $$\frac{ \sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} P[X_{i} = 1]}{2n} = \frac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} 1 - \frac{ (2n-1-i)(2n-2-i) }{(2n-1)(2n-2)}$$ Simplifying the sum using the identities $\sum_{i=0}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ and $\sum_{i=0}^{n} i^{2} = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$: $$\begin{align*} \sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} 1 - \frac{ (2n-1-i)(2n-2-i) }{(2n-1)(2n-2)} &= \frac{4n}{3} \end{align*}$$ Finally, $$E\left[ \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{2n-1} X_{i}}{2n}\right] = \frac{1}{2n} \frac{4n}{3} = \frac{2}{3}$$

questions.title: Tricky Even Dice
questions.problem: You roll a fair 6-sided dice until you roll a 6. Given that you only rolled even numbers, what is the expected number of rolls you made?
questions.solution:
Given that only even numbers are rolled, each roll is equally likely to be a 2, 4, or 6, each with probability $\frac{1}{3}$. So the conditional probability of stopping (rolling a 6) on any given roll is $p = \frac{1}{3}$. Since $P[\text{roll a 6} | \text{only rolled evens}] = P[\text{roll a 2} | \text{only rolled evens}] = P[\text{roll a 4} | \text{only rolled evens}]$.

Let $N$ be the number of rolls and $V$ the event that only even numbers are rolled. Let $R_{i}$ for $i=1,...,6$ denote rolling $i$. Then $$\begin{align*} E[N | V] &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} P[R_{i} | V] E[N | R_{i}, V] \\ &= P[R_{2} | V] E[N | R_{2}, V] + P[R_{4} | V] E[N | R_{4}, V] + P[R_{6} | V] E[N | R_{6}, V] \end{align*}$$ since $P[R_{1} | V] = P[R_{3} | V] = P[R_{5} | V] = 0$. For each even $i$: $$P[ R_{i} | V] = \frac{ P[ V | R_{i} ]P[R_{i}] }{P[V]}$$ We compute $P[V]$: for a game lasting $k$ rolls, the first $k-1$ must be even non-6 and the last must be 6: $$P[V] = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} (\frac{1}{3})^{i-1}\frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{6} \frac{1}{\frac{2}{3}} = \frac{1}{4}$$ For $P[ V | R_{i} ]$: when $i=1,3,5$, $P[ V | R_{i} ] = 0$. When $i = 6$, $P[ V | R_{i}] = 1$. When $i = 2$ or $i = 4$: $$\begin{align*} P[V|R_{i}] &= \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} P[V | R_{i}, \{ \text{k rolls needed} \}] P[\{ \text{k rolls needed} \} | R_{i}] \\ &= \frac{1}{4} \end{align*}$$ Since $E[N | V, R_{6}] = 1$, and for $i=2$ or $i=4$, $E[N | V, R_{i}] = 1 + E[N|V]$: $$\begin{align*} E[N | V] &= \frac{1}{6}(1 + E[N|V]) + \frac{1}{6}(1 + E[N|V]) + \frac{2}{3}(1) \\ &= \frac{1}{3}(1 + E[N|V]) + \frac{2}{3} \end{align*}$$ Solving for $E[N | V]$: $E[N | V] = \frac{3}{2}$.

Alternatively, let $N$ be the number of rolls and $X$ the event of rolling only evens. Conditioned on $X$, each roll independently stops with probability $p = 2/3$ (rolling a 6 given even). Then $$E[N|X] = E[N] = \frac{1}{\frac{2}{3}} = \frac{3}{2}$$

questions.title: Subset Subset
questions.problem: You independently pick two random subsets, $A$ and $B$, from the set of all subsets of $[n] = \{ 1, 2, \dots, n \}$. What is the probability that $A$ is a subset of $B$ when $n = 5$?

questions.title: Meandering Cat
questions.problem: A cat is currently sitting at the origin of the 2-d plane. If there is an equally likely chance that the cat either moves directly, north, south, east, or west, what is the probability that the cat returns to the origin before hitting the boundary of the square defined by $(\pm 2, \pm 2)$?
questions.solution: This problem can be solved by using the typical Markov state approach. Define the states: $$\begin{align*} S_{0} &= \{ \text{The cat is at the origin} \} \\ S_{1} &= \{ \text{The cat is one step away from the origin} \} \\ S_{c} &= \{ \text{The cat is at one of the corners of the square } (\pm 1, \pm 1) \} \\ S_{2} &= \{ \text{The cat is on the border of the square } (\pm 2, \pm 2) \} \end{align*}$$ Define the event $O = \{ \text{The cat returns to the origin before hitting the square } (\pm 2, \pm 2) \text{, if it starts from the origin} \}$. Then, conditioning on the cat's first step: $$\begin{align*} P[O] &= P[O|S_{1}] \\ P[O | S_{1} ] &= \frac{1}{4}P[O | S_{0}] + \frac{1}{2} P[O|S_{c}] + \frac{1}{4} P[O|S_{2}] \\ P[O|S_{c}] &= \frac{1}{2} P[O | S_{1}] + \frac{1}{2} P[O | S_{2}] \\ P[O | S_{2}] &= 0 \\ P[O | S_{0}] &= 1 \end{align*}$$ This system follows from the fact that the cat is equally likely to move in any direction. For example, if the cat is at state $S_{1}$, it will return to the origin with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, move to one of the corners $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, and move to the edge $(\pm 2, \pm 2)$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$. Solving the system of equations yields $P[O] = \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.title: Even Doubles
questions.problem: Lewis is going to flip a coin until he either gets two consecutive heads or two consecutive tails for the first time. What is the probability that Lewis ends up flipping the coin an even number of times?
questions.solution: In order for Lewis to flip an even number of times, he must perform $2$ flips, $4$ flips, $\dots$, etc. If we let $F_{i}$ be the event that Lewis makes $i$ flips, then we are looking for $P[ F_{2} \cup F_{4} \cup ... ] = P[ \cup_{i = 1} F_{2i} ]$. Since each of these events are disjoint, this is simply equal to $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} P[F_{2i}]$. To find $P[F_{2i}]$, note that in order for Lewis' sequence to be of length $2i$, it must have ended in either TT or HH. Furthermore, the rest of the sequence had to have alternated between $H$ and $T$ for the $2i - 2$ preceding flips. Thus, for any possible sequence length there will be exactly two possible sequences that have that length. Since the length is $2i$, there are $2^{2i}$ total possible sequences. Therefore, $$\begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} P[F_{2i}] &= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{2}{2^{2i}} \\ &= 2 \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{i} \\ &= 2 \cdot \frac{ 1/4 }{1 - 1/4} \\ &= \frac{2}{3} \end{align*}$$

questions.title: Tail Coin Cut
questions.problem: Lewis is playing a game where he flips a fair coin until he gets his first tails. The game pays out $\text{min}(\$2^r, \$2^{n})$ where $n$ is the number of times Lewis flips the coin before stopping (including his last flip) and $k$ is a fixed positive integer. What is Lewis' expected payoff when $r = 7$?
questions.solution: Let the number of flips needed to get the first tails be $N$. Since $N$ counts the number of flips until the first occurrence of tails, $N \sim \text{Geom}(1/2)$. Lewis' expected payoff is given by, $$\begin{align*} E[\text{payoff}] &= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \text{min}\left(2^r, 2^{k}\right) P[n = k] \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \text{min}\left(2^r, 2^{k}\right) \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{r} 2^{k} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} + \sum_{k=r+1}^{\infty} 2^r \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{r} 1 + \sum_{k=r+1}^{\infty} 2^r \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} \\ &= r + \sum_{k=r+1}^{\infty} 2^{r} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} \\ &= r + \sum_{k=r+1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-r} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} \\ &= r + \sum_{k=r+1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k-r} \\ &= r + \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i} \\ &= r + \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} \\ &= r+1 \end{align*}$$ which follows from the properties of geometric series. Note that we split the series at $n = r$ since that is the point at which $2^{n} = 2^r$.

questions.title: Uniform Median Probability
questions.problem: What is the probability that the median of five $\text{Unif}(0,1)$ random variables is less than $\frac{2}{3}$?
questions.solution: In order for the median of five random variables to be less than $\frac{2}{3}$, it must be the case that either 3 of them are less than $\frac{2}{3}$, 4 of them are less than $\frac{2}{3}$, or all 5 of them are less than $\frac{2}{3}$. If we denote these events as $L_{3}, L_{3}$ and $L_{5}$, respectively, then since they are disjoint we have, $$\begin{align*} P[\text{median less than } \frac{2}{3}] &= P[L_{3}] + P[L_{4}] + P[L_{5}] \\ &= \binom{5}{3}(\frac{2}{3})^{3}(\frac{1}{3})^{2} + \binom{5}{4}(\frac{2}{3})^{4}(\frac{1}{3})^{1} + \binom{5}{5}(\frac{2}{3})^{5} \\ &= \frac{64}{81} \end{align*}$$ which follows from the fact that the number of random variables less than $\frac{2}{3}$ has a $\text{Binom}(5, \frac{2}{3})$ distribution, since $P[U < \frac{2}{3}] = \frac{2}{3}$ for any $U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$.

questions.title: Tom and Jerry
questions.problem: Tom (from Tom and Jerry) is randomly placed on a $5 \times 5$ grid. Tom will then start moving on the grid, and it randomly chooses to either move diagonally up to the left or diagonally up to the right with equal probability. There is cat food in the top left and top right corners. If Tom only makes moves that allow him to stay on the grid, what is the probability that Tom gets to eat cat food?
questions.solution: The brute force method would be to define each cell as a state, but since there are $5 \times 5 = 25$ cells, this gets unwieldy. Instead, we exploit symmetry. Number the cells as $(i,j)$ for $i = 1,\dots, 5$ and $j= 1,\dots, 5$.
