Ignoring states from which Tom cannot reach the corners, define: $$\begin{align*} S_{0} &= \{ \text{Tom is in } (1,1) \text{ or } (1,5) \} \\ S_{2,2} &= \{ \text{Tom is at position } (2,2) \text{ or } (2,4) \} \\ S_{3,1} &= \{ \text{Tom is at position } (3,1) \text{ or } (3,5) \} \\ S_{3,3} &= \{ \text{Tom is at position } (3,3) \} \\ S_{4,2} &= \{ \text{Tom is at position } (4,2) \text{ or } (4,4) \} \\ S_{5,1} &= \{ \text{Tom is at position } (5,1) \text{ or } (5,5) \} \\ S_{5,3} &= \{ \text{Tom is at position } (5,3) \} \end{align*}$$ Using the law of total probability and computing the transition probabilities from inspecting the grid: $$\begin{align*} P[C] &= P[S_{0}] P[C \mid S_{0}] + P[S_{2,2}] P[C \mid S_{2,2}] + P[S_{3,1}] P[C \mid S_{3,1}] + P[S_{3,3}] P[C \mid S_{3,3}] \\ &\quad + P[S_{4,2}] P[C \mid S_{4,2}] + P[S_{5,1}] P[C \mid S_{5,1}] + P[S_{5,3}] P[C \mid S_{5,3}] \\ &= \frac{8}{25} \end{align*}$$

questions.title: Uniform Choice
questions.problem: Lewis is playing a game where a random number is generated uniformly from the interval $(0,1)$. Lewis observes the number, and can then decide to either keep this number, or generate a second number, also uniformly from the interval $(0,1)$. Once Lewis makes his decision the game ends and he receives a payout that is equal to the last number that is generated. If Lewis plays optimally, what is his expected payout?
questions.solution: Since each number is generated uniformly from the interval $(0,1)$, the expected value of each generated number is $\frac{1}{2}$. Thus, if the first number is less than $\frac{1}{2}$, then Lewis will expect to earn more if he generates a second number. Similarly, if the first number is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$ then Lewis will expect to earn less if he generates a second number. Thus, Lewis' strategy will be to stay with the first number if it is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, and otherwise generate a new number. If we denote the first generated number as $U_{1}$, the second generated number as $U_{2}$, and his payoff as $V$, then the law of total expectation gives us, $$\begin{align*} E[V] &= P[U_{1} < \frac{1}{2}] E[V | U_{1} < \frac{1}{2}] + P[U_{1} > \frac{1}{2}] E[V | U_{1} > \frac{1}{2}] \\ &= \frac{1}{2} E[U_{2}] + \frac{1}{2} E[V | U_{1} > \frac{1}{2}] \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{4} \\ &= \frac{5}{8} \end{align*}$$ The second equality follows from the fact that if $U_{1} < \frac{1}{2}$ then Lewis will generate the second number and so his payoff is $E[U_{2}]$. The third equality follows from the fact that if $U_{1} > \frac{1}{2}$, then $U_{1}$ has a $\text{Unif}(\frac{1}{2}, 1)$ distribution, which has expected value $\frac{3}{4}$.

questions.title: Coin Flip Order
questions.problem: Lewis, Scout, and Rupert each have their own fair coin. They all starting flipping and count the number of flips they need before getting their first heads. If the number of flips needed for Lewis is denoted as $L$, the number of flips needed for Scout is denoted as $S$, and the number of flips needed for Rupert is denoted as $R$, what is $\prob{ L \leq S \leq R}$?
questions.solution:
Let $A$ be the event that all three flip the same number of times, $B$ be the event that exactly two of them flip the same number of times, and $C$ be the event that all three flip different numbers of times.

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{L \leq S \leq R} = \prob{A} \prob{L \leq S \leq R | A} + \prob{B} \prob{L \leq S \leq R | B} + \prob{C} \prob{L \leq S \leq R | C}
\end{align*}$

If $L =S =R$, then $L \leq S \leq R$ is automatically satisfied, so $\prob{L \leq S \leq R | A} = 1$.

If $L < S < R$ (all distinct), by symmetry the probability of any particular ordering is $\frac{1}{3!} = \frac{1}{6}$, since there are $3!$ equally likely orderings. Thus $\prob{L \leq S \leq R | C} = \frac{1}{6}$.

For event $E$ (that the tied pair is adjacent in the desired ordering):

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{L \leq S \leq R | B} &= \prob{E | B} \prob{L \leq S \leq R | B, E} + \prob{E^{c} | B} \prob{L \leq S \leq R | B, E^{c}} \\
    &= \frac{1}{3}\frac{1}{2} + \frac{2}{3}\frac{1}{4} \\
    &= \frac{1}{3}
\end{align*}$

Here $\prob{L \leq S \leq R | B, E} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\prob{L \leq S \leq R | B, E^{c}}$ involves the non-adjacent tie. In the $E^{c}$ case, the probability is $\frac{1}{2}$ that the lone value is on the correct side, and given that, $\frac{1}{2}$ that the ordering $L \leq S \leq R$ holds, so $\prob{L \leq S \leq R | B, E^{c}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$.

Now we compute $\prob{A}, \prob{B}$, and $\prob{C}$. For each flip $k$, the probability of getting heads on exactly that flip is $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k}$. Let $L_{i}$, $S_{i}$, and $R_{i}$ denote the events that Lewis, Scout, and Rupert respectively get their first heads on flip $i$.

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{A} &= \prob{ \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}  L_{i} \cap S_{i} \cap R_{i} }  \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \prob{ L_{i} \cap S_{i} \cap R_{i} } \\   
    &= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \prob{ L_{i} } \prob{S_{i}} \prob{ R_{i} } \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i} \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{i} \\
    &= \frac{ \frac{1}{8} }{ 1 - \frac{1}{8}} \\
    &= \frac{1}{7}
\end{align*}$

The events $\{L_{i} \cap S_{i} \cap R_{i}\}$ are disjoint for different $i$.

For $\prob{B}$:

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{B} &= 3\prob{ \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}  L_{i} \cap S_{i} \cap R^{c}_{i} } \\
    &= 3\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \prob{ L_{i} } \prob{S_{i}} \prob{ R^{c}_{i} } \\
    &= 3\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \prob{ L_{i} } \prob{S_{i}} \left(1 - \prob{ R_{i} } \right)\\
    &= 3\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i}\left(1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i}\right) \\
    &= 3\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{i} - \frac{3}{7} \\ 
    &= 3\frac{ \frac{1}{4} }{ 1 - \frac{1}{4}} - \frac{3}{7} \\ 
    &= 1 - \frac{3}{7} \\
    &= \frac{4}{7}
\end{align*}$

From $\prob{A}$ and $\prob{B}$, we get $\prob{C} = 1 - \prob{A} - \prob{B} = 1 - \frac{1}{7} - \frac{4}{7} = \frac{2}{7}$.

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{L \leq S \leq R} &= 1 \cdot\frac{1}{7} + \frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{2}{7} + \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{4}{7} = \frac{8}{21}
\end{align*}$

Alternatively, we can directly compute $\prob{L \leq S \leq R}$ by summing over all valid orderings:

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{L \leq S \leq R} &= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sum_{j=i}^{\infty} \sum_{k=j}^{\infty} \prob{L = i \cap S = j \cap R = k} \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sum_{j=i}^{\infty} \sum_{k=j}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{i}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{j}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k} \\
    &= \frac{8}{21}
\end{align*}$

questions.title: Small Back
questions.problem: You draw four cards from a standard $52-$card deck without replacement. Suppose that each card has a point value associated with the card number, where Jack, Queen, and King are equal to $11, 12,$ and $13$, respectively and Aces are equal to $1$. After observing the $4$ cards, you return the smallest of the $4$ back into the deck. What is the expected value of the card you return to the deck? Round to the nearest hundredth.
questions.solution:
Denote the values of the four cards as $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3},$ and $X_{4}$. We are interested in finding $\ev{\text{min}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},X_{4})} = \ev{ X_{(1)} }$. The exact distribution of $X_{(1)}$ is not immediately known, so directly using LOTUS is not viable. One might think to use a First Ace approach, but the issue is that there are multiple replicates of each rank in the deck. We do know that the tail expected value works nicely with maximum and minimum order statistics, so this is a viable approach. This yields

$\begin{align*}
    \ev{ X_{(1)} } &= \sum_{k=1}^{13} \prob{ X_{(1)} \geq k} \\
    &= \sum_{k=1}^{13} \frac{ \binom{52 - 4(k-1)}{4} }{ \binom{52}{4} } \\
    &= \frac{9073}{2975}
\end{align*}$

The second equality follows from the fact that for any value $1 \leq k \leq 13$, if the minimum of the four cards is greater than or equal to $k$ then all of the cards must be greater than or equal to $k$. For example, if $k = 2$, then none of the $4$ cards can be aces. Thus, there are $52 - 4 = 48$ possible cards to choose from, and the number of ways we can choose $4$ of these $48$ cards is given by $\binom{48}{4}$. Since each card is equally likely to be chosen, and since there are $52$ cards in the deck, the probability that we pick no aces will be given by $\frac{ \binom{48}{4} }{ \binom{52}{4} }$. Following this logic for general $k$ yields that there are $k-1$ ranks below $k$, so there are $52-4(k-1)$ cards to pick from.
questions.hint: Use the tail sum formula for expected value of the minimum order statistic.

questions.title: Repaired Couples
questions.problem: Four couples, each consisting of two people are sitting in a room. The eight people are randomly paired up together. What is the probability that at least one of the couples is paired up?
questions.solution:
Let $C_{i}$ be the event that the $ith$ couple ends up in the same pair. By the principle of inclusion-exclusion, this is equal to,

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{\bigcup_{i=1}^{4} C_{i}} &= \sum_{i=1}^{4} \prob{C_{i}} - \sum_{ i \neq j} \prob{ C_{i} \cap C_{j} } + \sum_{ i \neq j \neq k} \prob{ C_{i} \cap C_{j} \cap C_{k}} -  \sum_{ i \neq j \neq k \neq t} \prob{ C_{i} \cap C_{j} \cap C_{k} \cap C_{t}} \\
    &= 4 \prob{C_{1}} - \binom{4}{2} \prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2}} + \binom{4}{3} \prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2} \cap C_{3} } - \binom{4}{4} \prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2} \cap C_{3} \cap C_{4} } 
\end{align*}$

which follows from the fact that the couples are all exchangeable (meaning that, for example, $\prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2}} = \prob{ C_{3} \cap C_{4}}$ and so on).

To find $\prob{C_{1}}$, fix one member of the couple. Since there are 7 other people and one of those people is the other couple member, there is a $\frac{1}{7}$ chance that they end up together. Alternatively, note that there are $\frac{8!}{2^{4}4!} = 105$ total ways to pair people up, and if we fix one of the pairs so that both members of the first couple are together then there are $\frac{6!}{2^{3}3!} = 15$ ways to pair up the remaining people. Since all pairings are equally likely, this also yields $\prob{C_{1}} = \frac{15}{105} = \frac{1}{7}$.

To find $\prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2}}$, we can use Bayes rule so that $\prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2}} = \prob{C_{2} | C_{1} } \prob{C_{1}}$. For $\prob{C_{2} | C_{1} }$, note that if the two members of $C_{1}$ are paired together, it's as if we have the exact same problem except now with $8 - 2 = 6$ people and 3 couples. Thus,

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2}} &= \prob{C_{2} | C_{1} } \prob{C_{1}} \\
    &= \prob{C_{2} | \text{6 people and 3 couples}} \frac{1}{7} \\
    &= \frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{7} \\
    &= \frac{1}{35}
\end{align*}$

The third equality follows from the same logic as was used to calculate $\prob{C_{1}}$.

To find $\prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2} \cap C_{3}}$, another application of Bayes rule yields,

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2} \cap C_{3}} &= \prob{C_{1}}\prob{C_{2} | C_{1}}\prob{C_{3} | C_{2}, C_{1}} \\
    &= \frac{1}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{3} \\
    &= \frac{1}{105}
\end{align*}$

Finally, since there are only $4$ couples, $\prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2} \cap C_{3} \cap C_{4} } = \frac{1}{105}$, since only $1$ out of the $105$ ways of pairing up the people has all of the original couples end up paired together. Alternatively, if three of the couples end up paired together, then the fourth couple must also necessarily end up together, so $\prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2} \cap C_{3} \cap C_{4} } = \prob{ C_{1} \cap C_{2} \cap C_{3} } = \frac{1}{105}$.

Putting everything together gives

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{\bigcup_{i=1}^{4} C_{i}} &= \frac{4}{7} - \frac{6}{35} + \frac{4}{105} - \frac{1}{105} \\
    &= \frac{3}{7}
\end{align*}$

questions.title: Five Aces
questions.problem: You are playing a game with $10$ regular card decks of $52$ cards each. All $10$ decks are combined together and shuffled, and then cards continue to be pulled from the top of the deck and revealed to you. The game stops once $5$ Aces have been pulled from the deck. Your job is to guess the total number of cards that need to be turned over until the $5$th Ace is pulled. Supposing that your strategy is to choose the number of cards that maximizes your probability of winning, what number of cards should you choose?
questions.solution:
Denote the event that you win as $W$. To solve this problem, we will let $n$ represent the number of cards that we choose and our goal will be to write $\prob{W}$ as a function of $n$, and then maximize it with respect to $n$.

For any $n$ that we choose, in order to win we need to have exactly $4$ aces in the first $n-1$ cards, one ace as the $n$th card, and the remaining $520 - n$ cards have no restrictions, except that only $35$ aces can be present (since $5$ were already placed in the previous $n$ cards).

Since every ordering of cards occurs with equal probability, we can use typical counting techniques to find the probability. For the first $n-1$ cards, we have $40$ aces to choose from, so there are $\binom{40}{4}$ possible combinations of aces that can appear in the first $n-1$ cards, and $\binom{520 - 40}{(n - 1) - 4} = \binom{480}{n-5}$ ways to pick the remaining $n-5$ non ace cards. Thus, there are $\binom{40}{4}\binom{480}{n-5}$ ways for the first $n-1$ cards to be picked.

For the $n$th card, we know that it must be an ace, and after 4 aces have been chosen to be in the first $n-1$ cards, there are $36$ possible choices for the ace that appears at the $n$th position. Note that once this occurs, we have now also determined which cards will end up in the $520 - n$ cards that appear after the ace at the $nth$ position, and thus we don't need to account for it.

Furthermore, there are $(n-1)!$ ways we can order the first $n-1$ cards, and $(520 - n)!$ ways we can order the last $520 - n$ cards. Finally, since there are 520 cards, there are $520!$ possible arrangements. Putting this altogether, the probability of winning is,

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{W} = \frac{ \binom{40}{4}\binom{480}{n-5}36(n-1)!(520-n)!}{ 520! }
\end{align*}$

At first glance this expression appears impossible to optimize. However, note that since we are trying to find the $n$ that maximizes $\prob{W}$, we are searching for the $n$ that satisfies $\prob{W | \text{choose $n + 1$}} \leq \prob{W | \text{choose $n$}}$. Intuitively, if $n$ maximizes our probability of winning then increasing $n$ should reduce it. This is the same as saying

$\begin{align*}
    \frac{ \prob{W | \text{choose $n + 1$}} } { \prob{W | \text{choose $n$}} } \leq 1 \\
\end{align*}$

If we write out the above and cancel out terms using the definition of factorials, we will eventually end up with,

$\begin{align*}
    \frac{ n (485 - n) }{ (n-4)(520 -n) } &\leq 1 \\
\end{align*}$

which is equivalent to,

$\begin{align*}
     n(485-n) - (n-4)(520-n) &\leq 0 \\
     \rightarrow 485n - n^{2} + n^{2} - 524n + 2080 &\leq 0 \\
     \rightarrow -39n + 2080 &\leq 0 \\
     \rightarrow n &\geq \frac{160}{3}
\end{align*}$

Since $\frac{160}{3} \approx 53.33$, we will choose $n = 54$.

Note that there are many different ways to determine the numerator that all lead to the same answer. For example, we could instead imagine that we place an ace at the $nth$ position first, which can occur in 40 ways. Then, amongst the $n-1$ first cards we set the location of the 4 aces which can be done in $\binom{n-1}{4}$ ways. Amongst the remaining $520-n$ cards, we then set the location of the remaining 35 aces which can be done in $\binom{520-n}{35}$ ways. There are then $40!$ ways to order the 40 aces, and $480!$ ways to order the non-aces, so that the probability is,

$\begin{align*}
    \prob{W} = \frac{ \binom{n-1}{4}\binom{520-n}{35}40!480!}{ 520! }
\end{align*}$

which can be shown to be equivalent to the expression above.

questions.title: Increasing Chain of Uniforms
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_{1}, X_{2}, ...$ are independent $\unif{0}{1}$ random variables that are generated one by one, sequentially. Define $N$ as the first index such that $X_{n} \neq \text{max}\{ X_{1}, X_{2}, ..., X_{n} \}$ and suppose that we stop generating random variables once we generate $X_{n}$. Find $\ev{N}$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
To compute the expected value, there are a few options when the exact distribution isn't easily known: Renewal equation or tail sum. In this question, the event of the tail sum is easy to describe, so we take this method. Specifically, we have,

$\begin{align*}
    \ev{N} &= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \prob{N > k} = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{N> k}
\end{align*}$

since we will definitely have to generate more than one $X_{j}$. Our task now is to find $\prob{N > k}$. Note that our stopping condition is that the random variable we generate is not larger than all of the previous random variables generated. Thus, in order for $N$ to be greater than some number $k$, we must have generated the first $i$ random variables in such a way that $X_{k} > X_{k-1} > ... > X_{1}$, since otherwise our process would've stopped on or before index $k$.

Since each of the random variables are independent and identically distributed, the probability of any ordering of $k$ of them is $\frac{1}{k!}$, since there are $k!$ possible orderings, all of which are equally likely. We thus have,

$\begin{align*}
    \ev{N} &= 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{N> k} = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!} \\
    &=  \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!} \\
    &= e \\
    & \approx 2.718
\end{align*}$

questions.title: Multiplicative Minimum I
questions.problem: Let $U_1,U_2,\dots \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Define $M_n = n\min\{U_1,\dots, U_n\}$. If it exists, compute the limiting distribution of $M_n$, say $M$, as $n \rightarrow \infty$ and report $\prob{M \geq 2}$ to the nearest thousandth. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$.
questions.solution:
Since $M_n$ is defined as a function of the minimum of order statistics, to find the limiting distribution, it's best to evaluate expressions of the form $\prob{M_n \geq z}$ for positive real $z$. This is because events in the form $\{\text{min}\{X_1,\dots, X_n\} \geq z\}$ are easier to work with by separating out the expression and utilizing independence. We know $z > 0$ because the minimum of positive real numbers also must be a positive real number.

Writing the expression, we get

$\prob{M_n \geq z} = \prob{n\min\{U_1,\dots, U_n\} \geq z} = \prob{U_1 \geq z/n,\dots, U_n \geq z/n} = \left(\prob{U_1 \geq z/n}\right)^n = \left(1 - \dfrac{z}{n}\right)^n$

The third equality is by expanding out the definition of the minimum. The fourth equality is by noting that $U_1,\dots, U_n$ are IID. The last equality follows by taking ratios of interval lengths, as $U_1$ is Uniform.

As $n \rightarrow \infty$ in the above, this approaches $e^{-z}$ by the limit definition of $e$. This shows $\prob{M \geq z} = e^{-z}$ for all $z > 0$. In particular, this means $M \sim \exponential{1}$, as one can obtain the CDF by complementation.

With the specified value of $z = 2$, the answer is $e^{-2}$.

questions.title: Brownian Exit I
questions.problem: Let $B_t$ be a $n-$dimensional Brownian Motion. Fix $r > 0$, and define $\tau = \inf\{t > 0: |B_{t}| = r\}$ i.e. the first time the Brownian Motion hits a ball of radius $r$ about the origin. Find $\ev{\tau}$. Report the answer with $n = 4$ and $r = 12$.
questions.solution:
In the univariate case, we compute the expected value via the martingale $B_t^2 - t$. Since we can write $B_t = (W_{1,t},\dots, W_{n,t})$, where $W_{i,t}$ are all independent Brownian Motions, $W_{i,t}^2 - t$ is a martingale for each $1 \leq  i \leq n$.

The natural analog of squaring for vectors is the square magnitude, so a natural candidate would involve $|B_t|^2 = W_{1,t}^2 + \dots  + W_{n,t}^2$. As the sum of martingales is a martingale and we know $W_{i,t}^2 - t$ are all martingales, $M_t = |B_t|^2 - nt$ is a martingale.

Applying the Optional Stopping Theorem to $M_t$, we get

$\ev{M_{\tau}} = \ev{M_0} \iff \ev{|B_{\tau}|^2 - n\tau} = \ev{|B_0|^2 - 0} \iff \ev{\tau} = \dfrac{r^2}{n}$

When $n = 1$, this gives the answer we would expect. Intuitively, the expected time is just $1/n$ times as large as the one-dimensional case because the $n-$dimensional Brownian Motion accumulates variance at a rate of $n$ per unit time ($1$ in each of the $n$ directions).

With the specified values, the answer is $36$.

questions.title: Brownian Exit II
questions.problem: Let $B_t$ be a $n-$dimensional Brownian Motion. Fix $r > 0$ and $x \in \R^n$, where $r > |x|$. Define $\tau = \inf\{t > 0: |B_{t} - x| = r\}$ i.e. the first time the Brownian Motion hits a ball of radius $r$ with center $x$. Find $\ev{\tau}$. Report the answer with $n = 4, x = (2,4,6,8),$ and $r = 12$.
questions.solution:
This question is very similar to "Brownian Exit I" with just a different centering of the ball. Thus, we should consider a similar martingale to $|B_t|^2 - nt$. Since we now want to center at $x = (x_1,\dots, x_n)$, a natural idea is to include $|B_t - x|^2$ in the martingale. The question becomes: What goes out back?

Looking at $|B_t - x|^2$ component-wise,

$|B_t - x|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (W_{i,t} - x_i)^2 \implies \ev{|B_t - x|^2} = \sum_{i=1}^n \ev{(W_{i,t} - x_i)^2} = \sum_{i=1}^n t + x_i^2 = nt + \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = nt + |x|^2$

Since $|x|^2$ is a constant, it doesn't affect the formation of our martingale, so $M_t = |B_t - x|^2 - nt$ is a martingale.

Applying the Optional Stopping Theorem to $M_t$,

$\ev{M_{\tau}} = \ev{M_0} \iff \ev{|B_{\tau} - x|^2 - n\tau} = \ev{|B_0 - x|^2 - 0} \iff \ev{\tau} = \dfrac{r^2 - |x|^2}{n}$

When $n = 1$, this gives the answer we would expect. Intuitively, the expected time is just $1/n$ times as large as the one-dimensional case because the $n-$dimensional Brownian Motion accumulates variance at a rate of $n$ per unit time ($1$ in each of the $n$ directions).

With the specified values, the answer is $6$.

questions.title: Many Consecutive Heads I
questions.problem: A fair coin is flipped $n$ times. Find the probability that there is no run of $k$ consecutive heads, $1 \leq k \leq n$, among the $n$ flips when $n = 10$ and $k = 3$.
questions.solution:
Since all of the sequences of flips are equally likely, the best approach is to count the number of sequences that satisfy this condition. As $k$ is fixed, we only need to count the number of sequences of length $n$ satisfying this condition. Since the sequences of length $n$ inherently appear related to those of shorter lengths (a length $n$ sequence is just a length $n-1$ sequence with an extra flip), a recursive approach appears best. This is also reasonable because we solved the $k = 2$ case like this in a different problem.

The recurrence here will depend on both $n$ and $k$, so let $N_{n,k}$ be the number of sequences of length $n$ with no runs of $k$ heads. To get a recurrence, we condition on the possible endings of the sequence. Since we want less than $k$ heads, the possible endings are $T, TH, THH, \dots$, until it's tails with $k-1$ heads following. One can intuitively understand this as breaking up the problem by conditioning on the position of the last tails in the sequence.

Furthermore, all of these cases are disjoint. For the sequence with $i$ heads after the tail, any valid sequence of length $n-(i+1)$ can be attached before the ending sequence, so there are $N_{n-(i+1),k}$ valid sequences of length $n$ that have the ending sequence of a tails and $i$ heads. Therefore, we have derived the recurrence

$N_{n,k} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}N_{n-(i+1),k} = \sum_{i=1}^k N_{n-i,k}$

Since this is a $k$th order recurrence relation (we go back $k$ terms from the present), we need $k$ initial conditions $N_{0,k},\dots, N_{k-1,k}$. However, this is quite easy: $N_{i,k}$ counts the number of sequences of length $i$ with no runs of $k$ consecutive heads, so if $i < k$, all of the $2^i$ possible sequences do not have $k$ consecutive heads, so we can conclude $N_{i,k} = 2^i$ for $0 \leq i \leq k-1$.

There's no simple closed-form for the sequence $N_{n,k}$, but the sequence does typically go by the name $k-$step Fibonacci numbers $F_n^{(k)}$. In particular, since $N_{0,k} = 1$ and $N_{1,k} = 2$, which is two steps ahead in the standard Fibonacci number sequence (Normally, the first two terms are $0$ and $1$), we can conclude that $N_{n,k} = F_{n+2}^{(k)}$. Note that the first $k$ terms of $F_n^k$ are $0,1,1,2,\dots, 2^{k-1}$.

Therefore, the probability in question is given by $\dfrac{F_{n+2}^{(k)}}{2^n}$.

With $n = 10$ and $k = 3$, the answer is $63/128$.

questions.title: Maximum Different Dice
questions.problem: Avi rolls $n$ standard fair dice with $1,2,\dots, n$ sides. Find the expected maximum value Avi obtains when $n = 4$.
questions.solution:
Let $M$ denote the maximum of the $n$ dice. The key observation is that events of the form $\{M \leq k\}$ are easy to compute, and we can use the discrete tail sum formula $\ev{X} = \dtailsum{X}$.

Using the tail sum approach:

$\ev{M} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{M \geq k} = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 - \prob{M \leq k-1} = n - \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \prob{M \leq k}$

Note that $\prob{M \leq 0} = 0$ since the minimum die value is $0$ (actually $1$, but we use this for the sum). For $1 \leq k \leq n-1$, the event $\{M \leq k\}$ means all $n$ dice show at most $k$. Since each die has $n$ faces with values $1$ through $n$, the probability each die shows at most $k$ is $k/n$. By independence:

$\begin{align*}
    \ev{M} &= n - \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \prob{M \leq k} \\
    &= n - \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \prob{M \leq k} \\
    &= n - \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (\frac{k}{n})^{n} \\
\end{align*}$

With $n = 4$:

$\begin{align*}
    \ev{M} = 4 - \sum_{k=1}^{3} (\frac{k}{4})^{4} = \frac{463}{128}\\
\end{align*}$

Alternatively, using LOTUS directly:

$\begin{align*}
    \ev{M} &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} k \prob{M = k} \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} k\big( \prob{ M \leq k} - \prob{M < k} \big) \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} k\left( \left( \frac{k}{n} \right)^{n} - \left( \frac{k-1}{n} \right)^{n} \right) \\
\end{align*}$

Here $\{ M < k \}$ is the same as $\{ M \leq k \}$ shifted down by one since dice take integer values.

With $n = 4$:

$\begin{align*}
    \ev{M} &= \sum_{i=1}^{4} k\left( \left( \frac{k}{4} \right)^{4} - \left( \frac{k-1}{4} \right)^{4} \right) \\
    &= \frac{463}{128}
\end{align*}$
questions.hint: Use the tail sum formula for the expected value of a maximum: express via events of the form $\{M \leq k\}$.

questions.title: Bus Park
questions.problem: A parking lot consists of $n$ parking spaces. $(n-1)/2 \leq m \leq n-1$ cars randomly park and each takes up a singular parking space. However, the Magic School Bus arrives. It is large and needs $2$ consecutive spaces to park in. Find the probability that it is able to park to the nearest thousandth when $n = 20$ and $m = 15$.
questions.solution:
In this problem, we should consider our sample space as the total number of ways that the cars can park, and then figure out how many of those arrangements are conducive to letting the bus park. The total number of ways the $m$ cars can park is $\binom{n}{m}$, as the order of parking is irrelevant.

Counting the number of valid arrangements is equivalent to counting the number of arrangements that have at least two consecutive empty spots. Instead of counting these, it's easier to count the complement, which is the number of arrangements with at most one empty spot between any consecutive cars.

Since $m$ cars are parking, there will be $n-m$ total empty spots. Any arrangement of the $m$ cars will create $m+1$ regions: Before the first car, between the first and second cars, and so on. We must arrange the $n-m$ empty spots into the $m+1$ regions such that there is at most one open spot per region. This is equivalent to saying: Choose $n-m$ regions to receive one open spot between them. There are $\binom{m+1}{n-m}$ ways to do this, as we choose $n-m$ of the $m+1$ regions to receive an open spot.

Since the above counts the number of arrangements that have at most one open spot between any consecutive cars, this is the number of arrangements where the bus can't park. Therefore, the probability that the bus can park is

$1  - \dfrac{\binom{m+1}{n-m}}{\binom{n}{m}} = 1 - \dfrac{\binom{m+1}{n-m}}{\binom{n}{n-m}}$

With the specified values, the answer is approximately $0.718$.
questions.hint: Count the complement: arrangements where no two consecutive spots are empty.

questions.title: Line Angle
questions.problem: Suppose that $B_1$ and $B_2$ are IID Cauchy random variables. This means that they have PDF $f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}$ for all real $x$. The lines $y = B_1x$ and $y = B_2x$ are formed. Find the expected value of the angle (in radians) that lies between the lines. Round to the nearest hundredth.
questions.solution:
To find the angle between the lines, we can consider the angle that each line makes with the origin and subtract them. Each line really forms a triangle with base $1$ and height $B_i$, so the angle formed with the origin is $\arctan(B_i), i = 1,2$. Since we aren't sure which is larger, the absolute value of their difference will give the angle between the lines, so we want to compute $\ev{|\arctan(B_1) - \arctan(B_2)|}$.

Since there is no clear easy way to compute this expected value, it may be helpful to compute the distribution of $\arctan(B_1)$, as the random variables are IID. To do this, we use the CDF method. Letting $F(x)$ be the CDF of $B_1$ and $Y = \arctan(B_1)$,

$F_Y(y) = \prob{Y \leq y} = \prob{\arctan(B_1) \leq y} = \prob{B_1 \leq \tan(y)} = F(\tan(y))I_{(-\infty,\infty)}(\tan(y))$

$\tan(y)$ takes all real values on the interval $-\pi/2 < y < \pi/2$, so the support of $Y$ is $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$. Taking the derivative of the CDF yields

$f_Y(y) = \dfrac{d}{dy}F(\tan(y)) = f(\tan(y)) \cdot \sec^2(y)I_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2)}(y) = \dfrac{1}{\pi(1 + \tan^2(y))} \cdot \sec^2(y)I_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2)}(y) = \dfrac{1}{\pi}I_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2)}(y)$

In the last step, we used the trig identity $1 + \tan^2(y) = \sec^2(y)$. The above work implies that $\arctan(B_1) \sim \unif{-\pi/2}{\pi/2}$, so letting $U_i = \arctan(B_i) \sim \unif{-\pi/2}{\pi/2}$ for $i = 1,2$, we are really looking to compute $\ev{|U_1 - U_2|}$.

This is solved in "Uniform Absolute Difference" with $a = -\pi/2$ and $b = \pi/2$ to be $\pi/3$, which is the answer.

questions.title: Timely Hit
questions.problem: Let $S_n$ be a simple symmetric random walk. Define $T_n = \inf\{t: S_t = n\}$ for positive integers $n$ i.e. the first hitting time of $n$. For any positive integer $t$, compute $\prob{T_n \leq t}$. Evaluate the probability when $n = 5$ and $t = 13$.
questions.solution:
For the event $\{T_n \leq t\}$ to occur, it must be the case that the walk hit position $n$ within the first $t$ time units. We can find the distribution of $S_n$ quite easily with some shifting around. If $\{T_n \leq t\}$ occurs, it indicates to us that we should stop the walk at time $T_n$ and see what happens afterwards.

By definition $S_{T_n} = n$, so the moment we reach position $n$, we can look forward to three options: $S_t > n, S_t < n,$ and $S_t = n$. As the walk is symmetric, the events $\{S_t > n\}$ and $\{S_t < n\}$ are equally likely: Once we've stopped the walk at time $T_n$, being positive or negative among the final $t - T_n$ steps is equally likely. The last case is that $S_t = n$, which is separate from the other cases.

By this stopping time argument, we can conclude that

$\prob{T_n \leq t} = \prob{S_t > n} + \prob{S_t < n} + \prob{S_t = n} = 2\prob{S_t > n} + \prob{S_t = n}$

The last probabilities can't be expressed in a simple form for general $n$ and $t$, but with specific values, they can be computed quite easily.

With our specific values, $\prob{S_{13} = 5}$ is just the event that there are $9$ steps right and $4$ steps left, which occurs with probability

$\prob{S_{13} = 5} = \binom{13}{9}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2^{13}}=  \dfrac{715}{8192}$

For the first term, we can just sum up the probabilities that there are more than $9$ steps right to yield

$\prob{S_{13} > 5} = \dfrac{\binom{13}{13} + \dots + \binom{13}{10}}{2^{13}} = \dfrac{378}{8192}$

Therefore, the probability in question is

$\prob{T_5 \leq 13} = 2 \cdot \dfrac{378}{8192} + \dfrac{715}{8192} = \dfrac{1471}{8192}$

questions.title: King and Ace
questions.problem: Scott turns over cards one-by-one from a standard deck of cards without replacement. Find the expected number of cards Scott needs to turn over to observe both a king and an ace.
questions.solution:
Solution 1:

There are $8$ cards that are kings or aces, and $52 - 8 = 44$ cards that are neither. By a negative hypergeometric argument, the expected number of cards to see the first king or ace is $44/(8 + 1) = 44/9$, so the expected position of the first king or ace is $44/9 + 1 = 53/9$.

Given that the first special card appeared, we know $1$ of the $3$ remaining positions for the other type. There are $52 - 53/9 = 415/9$ remaining cards, of which $4$ are of the other type. Among the remaining $415/9 - 4 = 379/9$ non-target cards and $4 + 1 = 5$ slots, the expected wait is $379/45$, so the expected position of the second type is $379/45 + 1 = 424/45$ cards later.

The total expected number of cards is $\dfrac{53}{9} + \dfrac{424}{45} = \dfrac{689}{45}$.

Solution 2:

Using the identity $\max(x,y) = x + y - \min(x,y)$, let $X$ be the number of cards to see the first king and $Y$ be the number of cards to see the first ace. We want $\max(x,y)$, so

$\ev{\max(X,Y)} = \ev{X} + \ev{Y} - \ev{\min(X,Y)}$

For $\ev{X}$ (and $\ev{Y}$ by symmetry): there are $4$ kings and $52 - 4 = 48$ non-kings. The expected position of the first king is $48/5 + 1 = 53/5$. So $\ev{X} = \ev{Y} = 53/5$.

For $\ev{\min(X,Y)}$: the first card that is either a king or an ace has expected position $53/9$ (as computed above).

Therefore, $\ev{\max(X,Y)} = 2 \cdot \dfrac{53}{5} - \dfrac{53}{9} = \dfrac{689}{45}$.

questions.title: Walk Modulus
questions.problem: A bug performs a simple symmetric random walk on the integers. Let $S_n$ be the position of the bug at time $n$, with $S_0 = 0$. Compute $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \ev{\left|\dfrac{S_n}{\sqrt{n}}\right|}$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
$S_n$ is the sum of the individual movements at each step. Furthermore, $\sqrt{n}$ can be interpreted as some type of standard deviation of the position at time $n$, so the sum of IID random variables standardized typically yields a Central Limit Theorem argument.

Let $X_i$ be the movement the bug takes at time $i$. We know that $X_i = \pm 1$ with equal probability $1/2$. Thus, $\ev{X_i} = 0$ and $\var{X_i} = 1$ are simple to compute. We can write $S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n$, where each $X_i$ is IID. By linearity of expectation and linearity of variance on independent random variables, $\ev{S_n} = 0$ and $\var{S_n} = n$.

Thus, the standardized version of the walk is $Z_n = \dfrac{S_n - \ev{S_n}}{\sqrt{\var{S_n}}} = \dfrac{S_n}{\sqrt{n}}$.

As $n \rightarrow \infty$, by the Central Limit Theorem, $Z_n \rightarrow N(0,1)$. Plugging this in, our goal is to compute $\ev{|Z|}$, where $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

Since $|Z|$ isn't exactly a nice function, LOTUS is the best option here. Namely, this is

$\ev{|Z|} = \int_{\mathbb{R}} |x| \cdot \npdf{x}dx$

Note that $f(x) = \npdf{x}$ and $|x|$ are both even functions. Recall that an even function $g$ is one such that $g(-x) = g(x)$ for all real $x$. Thus, their product is also even, so the integrand is even about $0$. This implies that the area above $0$ and below $0$ are equal, so we can just compute one of them and double the integral's value.

This becomes $\displaystyle 2\int_0^{\infty} x \cdot \npdf{x}dx$. We can remove the absolute values because of the fact that $x > 0$ from the bounds, so $|x| = x$.

From here, the best approach is a $u-$substitution with $u = \dfrac{x^2}{2}$, so that $du = xdx$. The reason for this choice is because we see a polynomial of degree $1$ out front $(x)$ and polynomial of degree two in the exponent $(x^2)$, so the derivative of a second degree polynomial yields a first degree polynomial. The bounds remain the same by just plugging in $x = 0$ and $\infty$ into the $u-$substitution. The new integral is

$\ev{|Z|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-u}du = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\pi}}$

Therefore, our answer here is $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\pi}} \approx 0.798$.

questions.title: Same Friends I
questions.problem: A party consists of $n$ people. Each pair of people is friends with probability $0 \leq p \leq 1$, independently between pairs. Being friends is symmetric: $A$ and $B$ are friends if and only if $B$ and $A$ are friends. A person can't be friends with themselves. Find the expected number of pairs of people who have the same set of friends. Report the answer with $p = 2/3$ and $n = 10$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
In this question, we're asked to compute the expected amount of some dependent events that occur, so counting with indicators and applying linearity of expectation is the best approach. The events are dependent because if $A$ and $B$ are friends, they can't have the same set of friends, as nobody can be friends with themselves.

As there are $n$ people at the party, there are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs of people at the party, so let $I_i$ be the indicator that the $i$th pair of people have the same set of friends. $T = I_1 + \dots + I_{\binom{n}{2}}$ gives the total number of pairs of people that have the same set of friends.

Since the pairs are all exchangeable (the labels on the pairs of people are arbitrary), all the indicators have the same mean, so $\ev{T} = \binom{n}{2}\ev{I_1}$.

$\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that the first pair of people have the same set of friends. For this to occur, the two people must not be friends with each other and must have the same decision (friends or not friends) with each of the other $n-2$ people at the party.

The probability that the people aren't friends is $1-p$. To calculate the probability that the two people have the same decision on each of the other $n-2$ people at the party, we break up into two cases: friends and not friends. The probability that both are friends with a given person is $p^2$, as it's probability $p$ for each, while the probability that they both aren't friends with a given person is $(1-p)^2$. Adding these two disjoint cases together yields a total probability of $p^2 + (1-p)^2$ for the two people having the same decision on a given other person.

As they must agree on the decision for each of the other $n-2$ people to have the same set of friends, we can conclude that

$\ev{I_1} = (1-p)\left(p^2 + (1-p)^2\right)^{n-2}$

Plugging this into the original linearity of expectation statement, our answer is

$\ev{T} = \binom{n}{2}(1-p)\left(p^2 + (1-p)^2\right)^{n-2}$

This answer satisfies some properties we would intuitively expect: If $p = 1$, the answer is $0$, as everyone would be friends with everyone else, meaning that no two people have the exact same set of friends. Furthermore, when $p = 0$, the answer is $\binom{n}{2}$, as nobody has any friends, meaning that everyone has the same friend group.

With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.136$.

questions.title: Same Friends II
questions.problem: A party consists of $n$ people. Each pair of people is friends with probability $0 \leq p \leq 1$, independently between pairs. Being friends is symmetric: $A$ and $B$ are friends if and only if $B$ and $A$ are friends. A person can't be friends with themselves. Find the expected number of pairs of people who have at least one mutual friend. Report the answer with $p = 1/3$ and $n = 10$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
In this question, we're asked to compute the expected amount of some dependent events that occur, so counting with indicators and applying linearity of expectation is the best approach.

As there are $n$ people at the party, there are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs of people at the party, so let $I_i$ be the indicator that the $i$th pair of people have at least one friend in common. $T = I_1 + \dots + I_{\binom{n}{2}}$ gives the total number of pairs of people that have at least one friend in common.

Since the pairs are all exchangeable (the labels on the pairs of people are arbitrary), all the indicators have the same mean, so $\ev{T} = \binom{n}{2}\ev{I_1}$.

$\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that the first pair of people have at least one friend in common. Since this is an "at least" probability, it's best to consider the complement, which is that they have no friends in common. For this to occur, on each of the other $n-2$ people that aren't themselves, they can't both be friends with that person.

The probability that both are friends with a given person is $p^2$, so the probability that they aren't both friends with the given person is $1-p^2$. To have no friends in common, the above must occur on all $n-2$ people that aren't themselves, so the probability of this is $(1-p^2)^{n-2}$ by independence.

By complementation, the probability there is at least one common friend between a pair of people is

$\ev{I_1} = 1 - (1 - p^2)^{n-2}$

Substituting this into the original linearity of expectation statement, our answer is

$\ev{T} = \binom{n}{2}\left(1 - (1-p^2)^{n-2}\right)$

This answer satisfies some properties we would intuitively expect: If $p = 1$, the answer is $\binom{n}{2}$, as everyone would be friends with everyone else, meaning that everyone has at least one friend in common. Furthermore, when $p = 0$, the answer is $0$, as nobody has any friends, so there are no common friends.

With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 27.462$.

questions.title: Rooted Limit
questions.problem: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be a sequence of IID non-negative random variables with $\ev{X_1} = 1$ and $\var{X_1} = \sigma^2 > 0$. Define $S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n$. Find the limiting distribution of $\sqrt{S_n} - \sqrt{n}$, say $Z$, and report the value of $\prob{Z > 1}$ to the nearest thousandth when $\sigma^2 = 4$.
questions.solution:
The expression in question seems to be the sum of random variables with some type of mean subtracted out, so Central Limit Theorem (CLT) should be our first thought.

Since $\ev{X_i} = 1$ and $\var{X_i} = \sigma^2$ for all positive integers $i$, $\ev{S_n} = n$ and $\var{S_n} = n\sigma^2$. CLT would then imply that the limiting distribution of $Z_n = \frac{S_n - n}{\sigma \sqrt{n}}$ is $Z \sim N(0,1)$.

We need to get from $S_n - n$ to $\sqrt{S_n} - \sqrt{n}$, and the key is to factor $S_n - n = (\sqrt{S_n} - \sqrt{n})(\sqrt{S_n} + \sqrt{n})$.

Substituting this in,

$Z_n = \dfrac{(\sqrt{S_n} - \sqrt{n})(\sqrt{S_n} + \sqrt{n})}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1}{\sigma}\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{S_n}{n}} + 1\right)\cdot (\sqrt{S_n} - \sqrt{n})$

As $n \rightarrow \infty$, by the Law of Large Numbers, $S_n/n \rightarrow \ev{X_1} = 1$, and as $\sqrt{x}$ is continuous, $\sqrt{S_n/n} \rightarrow \sqrt{1} = 1$. Thus, the term out front tends to $2/\sigma$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$.

Therefore, we can conclude $Z_n = \frac{2}{\sigma}\left(\sqrt{S_n} - \sqrt{n}\right)$ has $Z \sim N(0,1)$ as its limiting distribution. By multiplying the constant to the other side, the limiting distribution of $\sqrt{S_n} - \sqrt{n}$ is $N(0,\sigma^2/4)$ distributed.

Using the specified values, the answer is $\Phi(-1) \approx 0.159$.

questions.title: Square Summation
questions.problem: Let $S(n)$ be the number of ways to write $n = a^2 + b^2$, where $(a,b)$ is a pair of integers. For example, $S(1) = 4$, as $1$ can be written in four ways: $1 = 0^2 + 1^2 = 1^2 + 0^2 = (-1)^2 + 0^2 = 0^2 + (-1)^2$. Evaluate $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n S(n)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
We can view the limit in hand as informally saying: What is the average number of ways in which a randomly selected positive integer can be written as the sum of two squares?

We can view the above problem geometrically: $S(n)$ is counting the number of lattice points (pairs with integer coordinates) $(a,b)$ on the boundary of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = n$.

Now, let's consider the sum for a fixed upper bound $N$. In other words, we want to consider $S(1) + \dots + S(N)$. $S(N)$ counts the number of lattice points on the boundary of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = N$. Similarly, $S(N-1)$ counts the number of lattice points on the boundary of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = N-1$, which is contained inside the circle $x^2 + y^2 = N$. A similar argument can be made for $S(i)$, where $1 \leq i \leq N$.

In particular, we can view $S(1) + \dots + S(N)$ as the number of lattice points $(x,y)$ inside the circle $x^2 + y^2 \leq N$, as every lattice point $(x,y)$ inside this larger circle will be counted on the boundary of exactly one "sub-circle". The only exception to this is $(0,0)$, but this single point doesn't matter in limit.

Our question now becomes: How many lattice points are there inside the circle $x^2 + y^2 \leq N$? This is a circle of radius $\sqrt{N}$, so the area of the circle is, in limit, equal to the number of lattice points inside. The area of such a circle would be $\pi N$, so there are roughly $\pi N$ lattice points inside the circle for large $N$.

Thus, for large $N$, $S(1) + \dots + S(N) \approx \pi N$, meaning

$\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n S(i) = \dfrac{1}{n} \cdot \pi n = \pi$
questions.hint: Think geometrically: lattice points inside a circle.

questions.title: Cube Summation
questions.problem: Let $S(n)$ be the number of ways to write $n = a^2 + b^2 + c^2$, where $(a,b,c)$ is a pair of integers. Evaluate $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{1}{n^{3/2}}\sum_{i=1}^n S(n)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
We can view the limit in hand as informally saying: Asymptotically, how fast does the number of ways in which a randomly selected positive integer can be written as the sum of three squares grow?

We can view the above problem geometrically: $S(n)$ is counting the number of lattice points (pairs with integer coordinates) $(a,b,c)$ on the boundary of the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = n$.

Now, let's consider the sum for a fixed upper bound $N$. In other words, we want to consider $S(1) + \dots + S(N)$. $S(N)$ counts the number of lattice points on the boundary of the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = N$. Similarly, $S(N-1)$ counts the number of lattice points on the boundary of the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = N-1$, which is contained inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = N$. A similar argument can be made for $S(i)$, where $1 \leq i \leq N$.

In particular, we can view $S(1) + \dots + S(N)$ as the number of lattice points $(x,y,z)$ inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \leq N$, as every lattice point $(x,y,z)$ inside this larger sphere will be counted on the boundary of exactly one "sub-sphere". The only exception to this is $(0,0,0)$, as $0^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 = 0$, but this single point doesn't matter in limit.

Our question now becomes: How many lattice points are there inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \leq N$? This is a sphere of radius $\sqrt{N},$ so the volume of the sphere is, in limit, equal to the number of lattice points inside. The volume of such a sphere would be $\frac{4}{3}\pi N^{3/2}$, so there are roughly $\frac{4}{3}\pi N^{3/2}$ lattice points inside the sphere for large $N$.

Thus, for large $N$, $S(1) + \dots + S(N) \approx \frac{4}{3}\pi N^{3/2}$, meaning

$\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{1}{n^{3/2}}\sum_{i=1}^n S(i) = \dfrac{1}{n^{3/2}} \cdot \dfrac{4}{3}\pi n^{3/2} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \approx 4.189$
questions.hint: Think geometrically in 3D: lattice points inside a sphere.
