questions.title: Question The Coin
questions.problem: Your friend flips a fair coin $n$ times and records the sequence. Your goal is to guess the sequence that your friend flipped. You are allowed to ask a single yes/no question about their sequence (ex: Is the there a tails somewhere in the sequence?). Afterwards, you must guess the sequence. What is the maximum probability of being correct that can be achieved when $n = 10$?
questions.solution:
The best approach is to first try out a few simple questions. A very simple question is: Is the first flip heads? With this, there are now only $n-1$ flips that remain, so there are $2^{n-1}$ possible equally likely sequences that remain, yielding a probability of $1/2^{n-1}$ of being correct with this question. This question, along with any other question asked, can be generalized by the following, where $\Omega$ is the set of all $2^n$ possible sequences of coin flips: Is the coin sequence $\omega \in A \subseteq \Omega$? A question is really reducing the sample space to some subset $A$ of the total sample space. In the question above, $A$ is the set of all coin sequences starting with heads. Surprisingly, as long as $A 
eq \Omega$ and $A 
eq \emptyset$, every question yields a probability of $2^{-(n-1)}$ of being correct! The proof of this is via the Law of Total Probability. Let $C$ be the event that you guess the sequence correctly, and $Q_A$ be the event that your friend says yes to the question "Is $\omega \in A$?" The idea is to condition on what your friend responds. Namely, we have that $\prob{C} = \prob{C \mid Q_A}\prob{Q_A} + \prob{C \mid Q_A^c}\prob{Q_A^c}$. Since the coin is fair, all sequences are equally likely, $\prob{Q_A} = |A|/2^n$, as $|A|$ of the sequences lie in $A$ out of $2^n$ total. Given $Q_A$, all sequences are equally likely, as no information is received on which specific sequence you have within $A$ by asking if the sequence is in $A$. Thus, $\prob{C \mid Q_A} = 1/|A|$. The above implies, by complementation, $\prob{Q_A^c} = 1 - |A|/2^n$. Given that $\omega 
otin A$, we again are uniformly at random from the remaining $2^n - |A|$ sequences, as we don't receive any information as to which specific sequence among the remaining ones your friend flipped when they say no. Thus, $\prob{C \mid Q_A^c} = \dfrac{1}{2^n - |A|}$. Plugging these in, $\prob{C} = \dfrac{|A|}{2^n} \cdot \dfrac{1}{|A|} + \left(1 - \dfrac{|A|}{2^n}ight) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2^n - |A|} = \dfrac{2}{2^n} = 2^{-(n-1)}$. Therefore, as long as your question eliminates at least one outcome, but not all of them, the question provides you a probability of $2^{-(n-1)}$ of guessing correctly. In particular, with $n = 10$, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{512}$.

questions.title: Paperless Play II
questions.problem: You play rock, paper, scissors with a friend, but they can't use paper. If you win, you receive $\$a$ from your friend. If you lose, you pay $\$b$ to your friend. No payments happen if there is a tie. Under optimal strategy from both yourself and your friend, find your expected payout on one round of the game when $a = 1$ and $b = 2$.
questions.solution: As your friend can only play rock and scissors, you should never play scissors yourself, as it is not possible for you to win against your friend with scissors. Therefore, we only have to work with rock and paper for yourself. In such a problem where an optimal strategy must be determined for multiple players, finding a Nash equilibrium is typically the best approach. Both players must run a mixed strategy, as if either ran a pure strategy, the other one could pick a pure strategy on the option that beats the one the other player selected, which is not optimal. Let $p$ be the probability that you play rock. Similarly, let $q$ be the probability that your friend plays rock. $1-p$ and $1-q$ are the respective probabilities of you playing paper and your friend playing scissors. The idea is to find an equation $E(p,q)$ that represents your expected payout of a round dependent on $p$ and $q$. Afterwards, we want to take partial derivatives in $p$ and $q$, set them equal to $0$, and determine the values of $p$ and $q$ that are optimal for each player. If you and your friend both play rock, nothing occurs, so the expected profit is $0$. If you play rock and your friend plays scissors, which occurs with probability $p(1-q)$, you win $\$a$. If you play paper and your friend plays rock, which occurs with probability $q(1-p)$, you also win $\$a$. Lastly, if you play paper and your friend plays scissors, which occurs with probability $(1-p)(1-q)$, your friend wins $\$b$. Thus, your expected profit, as a function of $p$ and $q$, is given by $E(p,q) = a[p(1-q) + q(1-p)] - b(1-p)(1-q)$. To solve for the optimal $p$ and $q$, we take partial derivatives of this function in $p$ and $q$ and set them equal to $0$. Namely, we have that $\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial p} = a+b-(2a+b)q = 0 \iff q = \dfrac{a+b}{2a+b} \hspace{50pt} \dfrac{\partial E}{\partial q} = a+b-(2a+b)p = 0 \iff p = \dfrac{a+b}{2a+b}$. These are the optimal values of $p$ and $q$ for each player. Note that $E(p,q) = E(q,p)$ for all $p$ and $q$, so it makes sense that these optimal values are also symmetric. Plugging this in and simplifying intensely, the expected payout for you is $E\left(\dfrac{a+b}{2a+b},\dfrac{a+b}{2a+b}\right) = \dfrac{a^2}{2a+b}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/4$.

questions.title: Pick The Unknown
questions.problem: You have $3$ cards in front of you labelled $n,n+1,$ and $n+2$. However, you do not know what $n$ is prior to playing. All of the cards are initially face down. You flip one card and observe the value. You are then given the opportunity to hold (in which you receive a payout equal to the value of the drawn card), or you can hit. If you hit, you flip one of the other $2$ remaining cards, and you face the same decision. Note that you can't go back to the value of a previous card after you decide to hit. Design the optimal strategy. Find the expected payout of this strategy when $n = 20$.
questions.solution: The key to this question is closely analyzing what information/choice do you have after each draw. After the first card is drawn, you have no information as to what $n$ is, so the card you drew is equally likely to be any of the minimum, middle, or maximum. This would imply that the expected payout with this strategy is $n+1$, the value of the middle card. If you stop after all $3$ cards are drawn, you also get no choice as to what card you get (just pick the last one), so your expected value with this strategy is also $n+1$, as each of the three cards would be equally likely to be the last card drawn. However, with the second draw, you do have an information advantage that is afforded to you by the cards drawn. For example, if you drew $n$ and then $n+2$ in the first two draws, you would know that the last card has to be $n+1$, meaning you would stay at $n+2$. Therefore, there is information that is given by the first $2$ cards based on how far apart they are. Thus, the optimal approach to this question is to condition based on the values of the first two cards that appear. For simplicity, let $a$ be the value of the first card, and $b$ be the value of the second card. The most naturally thing to consider is the difference $b-a$ between the two cards, as this tells us how far apart the two cards that we drew were. The inferences that we can make are dependent on this. The two easiest cases are $b-a = 2$ and $b-a = -2$, of which the $b-a = 2$ example was shown above. If $b-a = 2$, then $b$ must be the maximum card value among the three, so the payout in this case is $n+2$. If $b-a = -2$, then $a$ must be the smallest card value among the three, so you should draw the last card, which would be $n+1$ in value. This case yields a payout of $n+1$. If $b-a = 1$, then you either selected $n+1$ and then $n+2$, or you selected $n$ and then $n+1$. Since $n$ is unknown to you, you have no idea if the two cards you selected are the two highest or the two lowest. Therefore, from your current position, you can either gain $1$ more or lose $2$ with equal probability (the higher number you picked is either the highest card, in which the remaining is the lowest, or it is the middle card, in which the remaining is the highest card). Thus, hitting again is negative expected value, as you lose more than you gain on average, so you should stay at the second card selected. The payouts in these cases are $n+2$ and $n+1$, respectively. Otherwise, if $b-a = -1$, then it's just the same argument as above in reverse, as you either selected $n+2$ and then $n+1$ or $n+1$ and then $n$. In this case, you either lose $1$ (go from $n+1$ to $n$) or gain $2$ (go from $n$ to $n+2$) with equal probability, so it is positive expected value to go for the last card. The payouts are $n$ and $n+2$, respectively. All $3! = 6$ permutations of the card values are equally likely, so the expected payout of the game is just the average of all of the payouts, which is $\dfrac{3 \cdot (n+2) + 2 \cdot (n+1) + n}{6} = n + \dfrac{4}{3} > n+1$. With $n = 20$, the answer is $\dfrac{64}{3}$.

questions.title: Dominating Two
questions.problem: You and the friend play the following game: You and your friend each select an integer in $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$, where $n \geq 3$. The winner is the person who picks the strictly larger number OR who picks exactly $2$ below the larger number. For example, if your friend selected $75$ and you selected $73$, you would be the winner. If the two numbers are equal, nothing occurs. The winner receives $\$1$ from the loser. Assuming both you and your friend play optimally, the optimal strategy is a mixed strategy where you choose your value according to some appropriately selected random variable $X$. Find $\ev{X}$ when $n = 100$.
questions.solution: The first important observation is that the game is symmetric between the two players, as they both receive the same payout from each other and are making the same choice, so their optimal strategies will be the same. Now, we must go about determining the strategy. Since the larger number is generally better (except for perhaps having a number $2$ below it dominate you by the rules of the game), a natural thing to think about is when larger numbers dominate smaller numbers. Suppose that $k$ were to be selected. Note that $k+3$ is strictly better than $k$, as $k+3$ beats everything $k$ beats, as well as $k+2$. Note that both $k$ and $k+3$ lose to $k+1$ and win against $k+2$, while $k+3$ also beats $k$, so $k+3$ strictly dominates $k$. Thus, if you were to select $k$, you should instead select $k+3$. This implies that the strategy of you and your friend should be to select one of $n-2,n-1,$ or $n$, as these are the three largest integers in the set to select from, and you can't add $3$ to any of these and get a valid option in the set. The question now becomes: Which of these should you play? The first item to note is that each of the three options wins against $1$ option and loses against another option. Namely, $n-2$ wins against $n$ and loses to $n-1$, $n-1$ wins against $n-2$ and loses to $n$, while $n$ wins against $n-1$ and loses to $n-2$. This appears very reminiscent to rock-paper-scissors! The optimal strategy should be the same for both players, so if there were a pure strategy Nash equilibrium, then this would always result in a tie, as they select the same value. However, this is not optimal, as by the above, one of the players can improve their strategy by selecting a different value that would beat the "shared" value from before. Thus, the players must both run a mixed strategy. Let $p_{n-2},p_{n-1},$ and $p_n$ be the three probabilities that correspond to playing each of the options. Note that the probabilities for you and your friend are the same by the fact that you share the same strategy. We must have that $p_{n-2} + p_{n-1} + p_n = 1$ by definition. One may intuitively first think that a uniform distribution among these three choices is best i.e. each of them is selected with probability $1/3$. This would indeed be correct! Note that if you select a non-uniform distribution between the choices, your opponent can re-weigh their selection of probabilities to exploit your choice. In other words, if you put more probability mass on one of the choices, your opponent can exploit that by adding more probability mass on the option that beats the one where you put more mass. For example, suppose that you assign a distribution of $p_{n-2} = 0.5, p_{n-1} = 0.3$ and $p_n = 0.2$. If your friend were to run a pure strategy of choosing $n-1$, the expected payout for you would be $0.5 \cdot (-1) + 0.3 \cdot 0 + 0.2 \cdot 1 = -0.3 < 0$. Thus, the best choice is to remain indifferent so that your friend can't exploit your preference. In other words, this means both you and your friend should select uniformly at random from $\{n-2,n-1,n\}$ on each trial. This has mean $n-1$, as it is uniformly random, so the answer is $n-1$ in general. With the specific values, the answer is $99$.

questions.title: Pay The Smalls
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play the following game: Bob generates a uniformly random number in $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Alice can select any number in $[n]$. Whoever has the larger number pays out the amount of the smaller number to the person with the smaller number. For example, with $n = 50$, if Alice says $30$ and Bob says $40$, then Bob pays Alice $30$. If there is a tie, no transaction occurs. Assuming Alice plays optimally, what is her expected payout when $n = 20$?
questions.solution: In this question, we are looking to optimize Alice's expected payout. Therefore, to choose the best option, the best approach is to create an expected payout function when Alice selects $x$, say $E(x)$, and then maximize in $x$. One can treat $x$ as continuous, take a derivative, and then account for the discreteness later. Suppose that Alice selects $x$. Furthermore, let $B \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{1,2,\dots, n\}$ be the number that Bob selects. Since the payout is determined by whether or not Bob is larger or smaller than $x$, we should determine the expected payout based on whether $B < x$ or $B > x$. We can ignore the $B = x$ case, as there is no payout if this occurs. If $B > x$, then Alice has the smaller number, and $x$ is her payout. Since $B$ is discrete uniform, we can just count outcomes to compute probabilities. If $B > x$ then this means that $B$ takes a value in the set $\{x+1,\dots, n\}$. There are $n-x$ integers in this set, and the total support of $B$ is size $n$, so $\prob{B > x} = \dfrac{n-x}{n}$, and the expected payout for Alice in this case is $x$. Otherwise, if $B < x$, then Alice has the larger number. This means that Alice pays Bob some money. Given that $B < x$, $B$ is uniform among the remaining values, which is a property of uniform distributions. Therefore, given that $B < x$, $B$ is uniform on the set $\{1,2,\dots, x-1\}$. The average amount that Alice has to pay is just the mean of $B$, as it is the value that Bob selects if his is smaller. The mean of the above distribution is just $\dfrac{(x-1) + 1}{2} = \dfrac{x}{2}$, so Alice must pay $x/2$ on average if $B < x$. The set above has $x-1$ integers in it, so $\prob{B < x} = \dfrac{x-1}{n}$. Combining the above, we obtain $E(x) = x \cdot \dfrac{n-x}{n} - \dfrac{x}{2} \cdot \dfrac{x-1}{n} = \dfrac{(2n+1)x - 3x^2}{2n}$. To find the value of $x$ that maximizes $E(x)$, we can treat $x$ as continuous and take the derivative. Thus, we have that $E'(x) = \dfrac{2n+1 - 6x}{2n} = 0 \iff 2n+1 = 6x \iff x = \dfrac{2n+1}{6}$. Since $x$ must be an integer, the actual value can't be the one above for general $n$. However, we are able to say which of the floor or ceiling it is. Since $E(x)$ is a downwards facing parabola in $x$, we can conclude that whichever integer is closest to $\dfrac{2n+1}{6}$ will have the largest expected value, as it will be closest to the maximum and the parabola is symmetric about the axis of symmetry. Therefore, $x^* = \text{round}\left(\dfrac{2n+1}{6}\right)$ is the optimal value of $x$. In the case $n = 20$, $x^* = 7$, and $E(7) = \dfrac{41 \cdot 7 - 3 \cdot 7^2}{2 \cdot 20} = \dfrac{7}{2}$.

questions.title: Stone Pick III
questions.problem: Alice and Bob pick alternate turns in the following game: Initially, there are $n \geq 1$ stones in the middle. Either player can choose to take $1$ to $r$ stones from the pile. Assume that $r+1 \nmid n$. The player who draws the last stone wins. Alice gets to determine if she goes first or second. Assuming Alice selects her position in the game optimally and both Alice and Bob play optimally, in how many turns (total actions by the players) does Alice win the game, inclusive of the draw that makes Bob lose, when $n = 107$ and $r = 7$?
questions.solution: We want Alice's optimal strategy to be independent of what Bob does. Using the same idea as "Stone Pick II", Alice should want to leave Bob with a multiple of $r+1$ stones left for him to pick from at each turn. Therefore, on Alice's first turn, she should select the (unique) number of stones $k$ such that Bob has a multiple of $r+1 \mid n-k$ i.e. Bob has a multiple of $r+1$ stones for him to select from. Afterwards, the exact same strategy described earlier will apply, as Alice will always leave Bob with some multiple of $r+1$ stones at each turn. Therefore, Alice should choose to go first, and she will win in $1 + 2 \cdot \floor{\frac{n}{r+1}}$ turns, as $r+1 \mid n-k$, which is the number of cycles the game goes through. Each cycle contains $2$ actions by the players, and then $1$ additional action is needed for Alice to select $k$ stones on the first turn, where $k$ is defined above. With the specific values, the answer is $27$.

questions.title: Roll Again IV
questions.problem: Kelly plays a game where she has $n$ standard fair $6$-sided die and rolls all of them. Once she observes the values, she can choose to hold or reroll. If Kelly holds, she receives the sum of the upfaces as her payout (in dollars) under the caveat that if $2$ or more of the dice show the same value $i$, each of them are switched to $7-i$. If Kelly chooses to roll again, she may hold any subset of the dice fixed and reroll the rest. Kelly must pay $\$1$ per die per reroll. There are no restrictions on how many times Kelly can reroll the dice. Under optimal play from Kelly, what is her expected payout when $n = 4$?
questions.solution: A key complication in this problem is the switching condition. However, if we look at it carefully, it doesn't actually change any expected values! This is because obtaining $k \geq 2$ values of $i$ has the exact same probability as obtaining $k$ values of $7-i$, and these two outcomes would switch to one another. For an example with concrete numbers, $(1,1)$ is equally likely to appear as $(6,6)$ on two dice. The pair $(6,6)$ would payout $1+1 = 2$, while $(1,1)$ would pay out $6+6 = 12$, so the average payout of these pairs is $7$, which is the exact same as two dice that weren't switched in value. Therefore, we can completely ignore this condition. The optimal stopping strategy is exactly the same as in "Roll Again III", as her expected payout is only dependent on the value showing on a given die and not on the other dice. The stopping condition is also the same for all of the dice because they are identical and independent. By the result of the previous part, the optimal strategy is to hold whenever the die shows at least $3$ or $4$, as they have the same expected value, and the expected payout is $\$4$ per die. By linearity of expectation, the expected value of the sum is $4n$. With $n = 4$, the answer is $16$.

questions.title: Roll or Hold
questions.problem: You are presented with the following game: You repeatedly roll a fair $n$-sided die with the values $0,1,\dots, n-1$ on the sides. After each roll, assuming it's non-zero, you have the option to end the game and receive a payout equal to the face showing on your die or to roll again. If you ever roll a $0$, the game ends and you receive no payout. Find the optimal strategy for this game. Report your expected payout under this strategy when $n = 8$.
questions.solution: The optimal strategy, just like many other die games, is to cash out the first time your roll is at least some threshold value $1 \leq t \leq n$. At each turn, you should have the same strategy because future rolls are independent of prior rolls. The problem is determining the threshold $t$. To do this, we will make a function $E(t)$ that gives the expected payout of the game when the threshold is $t$, and then we can optimize it in $t$. To find $E(t)$, let's break down what happens in the game. You repeatedly roll until we obtain a value that is at least $t$. Given that you roll a value at least $t$, the value is uniform on $\{t,t+1,\dots,n-1\}$, so the average payout value is $\frac{n+t-1}{2}$. However, there is a possibility that you roll a $0$ before a value that's at least $t$. To find the probability of rolling a $0$ before any value at least $t$, we can consider all orders of appearance of the values $0,t,t+1,\dots,n-1$. You don't receive a payout exactly when a $0$ is first to appear in the order, so the probability you don't receive a payout is $\frac{1}{n-t+1}$, as there are $n-t+1$ values in the sequence, and $0$ is equally likely to appear in any spot. Thus, you receive a payout with probability $\frac{n-t}{n-t+1}$. We can now conclude $E(t) = \dfrac{n-t}{n-t+1} \cdot \dfrac{n+t-1}{2} = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n-t+1}\right) \cdot \dfrac{n+t-1}{2}$. The goal is to optimize this in $t$. We can treat $t$ as continuous and then discretize it later. Taking the derivative in $t$, we obtain $\dfrac{dE}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{(n-t+1)(1) - (n+t-1)(-1)}{2(n-t+2)^2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{2n}{(n-t+1)^2}\right) = 0 \iff t = n+1 \pm \sqrt{2n}$. Since the threshold can't be larger than $n$, $\hat{t} = n+1 - \sqrt{2n}$ is the optimal threshold. Since this isn't necessarily an integer, we need to discretize it by taking the ceiling and floor and seeing which yields a larger expected value. Therefore, the optimal value is whichever of $\floor{\hat{t}}$ or $\ceil{\hat{t}}$ yields a higher value of $E(t)$. With $n = 8$, the answer is $5$, yielding an expected value of $4.5$.

questions.title: Add Again?
questions.problem: Aahna plays the following game: She generates a uniformly random number $U_1 \sim \unif{0}{1}$. She has two options: Hit or Hold. If she decides to hold, she leaves with her current balance. Otherwise, if she hits, she generated another uniformly random number $U_2 \sim \unif{0}{1}$, and she adds it to her balance. If her balance ever exceeds $1$, she loses and receives no payout. Otherwise, while her balance is less than $1$, she faces the same option to hit or hold. Assuming Aahna plays optimally, she will stop the first time her balance exceeds $t$ for some $0 < t < 1$. Find $t$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: The key to this problem, as with many optimal strategy problems, is the principle of indifference. If Aahna plays optimally, the threshold $t$ should satisfy the principle of indifference: Aahna will be indifferent to holding vs. hitting again if her balance is $t$. Therefore, the idea is to calculate Aahna's expected payouts under each action given her balance is $t$, and then solve for $t$. If Aahna has balance $t$ and holds, her payout is $t$. Otherwise, if she decides to hit, she will add a $U \sim \unif{0}{1}$ random variable to $t$. For her balance to be at most $1$, it must be the case that $U < 1-t$, so that $t + U < t + (1-t) = 1$. Since $U$ is Uniform, we can take ratios of lengths to compute probabilities and conclude that $\prob{U < 1-t} = 1-t$. Given that $U < 1-t$, we need to find the expected value of Aahna's balance. By the properties of conditioning on Uniform distributions, $U \mid U < 1-t \sim \unif{0}{1-t}$, which has mean $\frac{1-t}{2}$. Therefore, Aahna's expected payout upon hitting would be $t + \frac{1-t}{2} = \frac{1+t}{2}$. This is her expected payout because the principle of indifference would imply that Aahna should hold whenever her balance is larger than $t$. Aahna's expected payout given she hits is $(1-t) \cdot \dfrac{1+t}{2} = \dfrac{1-t^2}{2}$. This is from the Law of Total Expectation with conditioning on $U < 1-t$ vs. $U \geq 1-t$. In the second case, her payout is $0$, so we can ignore it. We must solve the equation $t = \dfrac{1-t^2}{2} \iff t^2 + 2t - 1 = 0 \iff t = \pm \sqrt{2} - 1$. Since the threshold must be strictly in $(0,1)$, we can conclude that $t^* = \sqrt{2} - 1$ is optimal.

questions.title: Bring Coin?
questions.problem: You and your friend want to go watch the new Kung Fu Panda movie, but your parents are not very thrilled about it. They allow you to do so if you succeed in the following game: Both you and your friend are given a coin with probability $0 < r < 1$ of landing heads and are put in separate rooms. Each of you makes a decision as to whether you bring out the coin or not. If neither person brings out the coin, you can't go to the movie. If exactly one person brings out their coin, they must flip it and obtain a head to attend the movie. If both people bring out their coin, they must both flip and obtain heads to attend the movie. Assuming both you and your friend play rationally, find the optimal strategy. Report the probability that you and your friend can attend the movie when $r = 1/3$.
questions.solution: The first key piece to solving is noting that you and your friend must share the same strategy, as the game is symmetric between the players. Because of this, it's clear to see that it's not optimal to never bring out the coin, as neither person would bring a coin, leading to no chance of attending the movie. However, always bringing out the coin may not be optimal either, as the probability that both people land heads is significantly lower than if just one person needs to land a head. Therefore, both you and your friend should run a mixed strategy. This means that each person independently decides to bring out the coin with probability $0 < p < 1$. The problem is finding the optimal choice of $p$. The second key is noting that $p$ should satisfy the principle of indifference: For the optimal value of $p$, the probability that you can attend the movies should be the same, regardless of whether or not you bring the coin. Thus, we must calculate the probability that you attend the movie in each case. If you don't bring the coin, your friend must bring the coin, which occurs with probability $p$, and land heads, which occurs with probability $r$. Therefore, the probability you attend the movies in this case is $pr$. If you do bring out the coin, there are two cases with positive probability: If your friend also brings out their coin (probability $p$), both of you must land heads, which occurs with probability $r^2$ by independence. If your friend doesn't bring their coin (probability $1-p$), you must land a head, which occurs with probability $r$. Aggregating the two cases above yields a total probability of attending the movies of $pr^2 + (1-p)r$. Equating the two options, we must solve for $p$ in $pr = pr^2 + (1-p)r$. By expanding, we get that $pr = pr^2 + (1-p)r \iff pr = pr^2 + r - pr \iff pr(2-r) = r \iff p = \dfrac{1}{2-r}$. Division by $r$ is fine since it's assumed that $r > 0$. Therefore, both you and your friend should independently bring out their coins with probability $\frac{1}{2-r}$, yielding a probability of attending the movies of $pr = \frac{r}{2-r}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/5$.

questions.title: Bucket Allocation I
questions.problem: You and $100$ other players are each given $3$ tickets to distribute into three buckets with prizes $\$20, \$80,$ and $\$200$. One winning ticket is drawn from each bucket, and the winner gets the associated prize. A single person can win multiple buckets. You are the last person to put in your tickets and are told that the number of tickets in each bucket are currently allocated proportionally to the size of the prize of the bucket. Assuming you want to maximize expected profit, how should you allocate your tickets? Report the expected profit to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution: The key is to mimic the strategy of the other people as closely as possible: Since the number of tickets in each bucket is already such that there is constant expected payout per bucket, the best approach is to get as close to the same distribution as you can. Prior to you putting in any tickets, there will be $300$ total tickets from the other $100$ people; by the question, there will be $20, 80,$ and $200$ tickets in the three respective buckets. Since the total amount of money in the buckets is $\$300$, you should put $200/300 = 2/3$ of your tickets in the $\$200$ bin, which means $2$ of the three tickets go in the $\$200$ bin. One may wonder why putting all $3$ tickets in the $\$200$ bin is sub-optimal; intuitively, when putting all $3$ tickets in that bin, you limit yourself to that one bucket, while each additional ticket added yields a smaller incremental increase in probability of being the winner. Thus, the other ticket should go in either the $\$80$ or $\$20$ bucket. By a simple expected value calculation, if you put your ticket in the $\$80$ bucket, there is a probability $1/81$ of you winning (your ticket and the $80$ tickets already in the bucket) $\$80$, so your expected value is $80/81$. Similarly, if you put your ticket in the $\$20$ bucket, there is a probability $1/21$ of you winning $\$20$, so your expected value is $20/21$. As $20/21 < 80/81$, you should put the last ticket in the $\$80$ bucket. This allocation yields a net expected value of $\dfrac{2}{202} \cdot 200 + \dfrac{1}{81} \cdot 80 \approx 2.9679$. For good measure, here are the expected values of some other common strategies: All $3$ in the $\$200$ bucket: $2.9557$. One in each bucket: $2.9351$.

questions.title: Bucket Allocation III
questions.problem: You and $100$ other players are each given $3$ tickets to distribute into three buckets with prizes $\$20, \$80,$ and $\$200$. One winning ticket is drawn from each bucket, and the winner gets the associated prize. A single person can win multiple buckets. Assuming each person plays optimally to maximize their expected payout, what is your strategy? If $e_i$ is the expected number of tickets you place in the bucket with $\$i$ in it, report $e_{20}^2 + e_{80}^2 + e_{200}^2$.
questions.solution: The idea of the indifference between the buckets from "Bucket Allocation I" is what should be applied here. If one were to employ a strategy that is more reliant to generate expected value from a certain bucket, say the $\$200$ one, another player could bias their distribution away from the $\$200$ bucket to have a higher probability of winning one of the other buckets. Every person must have the same optimal strategy because each person has the same set of information about the game. Therefore, everyone should be betting proportionally to the amount in each bucket. Since $2/3$ of the money is in the $\$200$ bucket, every person should put $2$ tickets in there. The last ticket is what differs from the previous problem. Since every person runs the same strategy, it's sub-optimal to always select the $\$80$ bin: If everyone else chooses the $\$80$ bin, you can unilaterally improve your strategy by putting your ticket in the $\$20$ bin, guaranteeing you $\$20$. Therefore, a mixed strategy is most appropriate. Since $4/5$ of the remaining $\$100$ is in the $\$80$ bucket, to bet proportionally to the prize of the bucket, you should place your last ticket in the $\$80$ bucket with probability $4/5$, while you place it in the $\$20$ bucket with probability $1/5$. We can conclude that $e_{20} = 1/5, e_{80} = 4/5,$ and $e_{200} = 2$, so the answer is $117/25$.

questions.title: Good Moves
questions.problem: A particle walks $(0, 0)$ to $(n, n)$ in a path of length $2n$ under the condition that it moves right or up one unit at each step. Two consecutive moves in the form $(a, b) -> (a + 1, b) -> (a + 1, b + 1)$ are called a good pair of moves. How many paths can the particle take that have exactly $0 \leq m \leq n$ good pairs of moves? Report the answer when $n = 12$ and $m = 4$.
questions.solution: As we want to have exactly $m$ good movements in our sequence, it's in our best interest to first fix the $m$ sequences of good moves, denoted by $RU$ (right and up), and add in the other movements between them. Any valid sequence can be formed by first placing the $m$ good movements in our sequence, and then add in the $n-m$ right and $n-m$ upwards movements between them. The remaining $R$ and $U$ movements are identical (among movements of the same type) besides their ordering. However, we need to be careful that there are no sequences of $RU$ in any between regions, as that would make there be more than $m$ good moves in the sequence. The condition to make this happen is that all the in between movements must have all the $U$'s before the first $R$. Otherwise, if there is at least one $U$ remaining to be placed after the first $R$ is, there is a switch $RU$ somewhere in the "between" sequence. This implies a crucial fact for the problem: Given any amount of $R$ and $U$ for a "between" sequence, the only possible sequence of movements is in the form $U\dots UR\dots R$. Each of these sequences between is uniquely determined by the counts of $R$ and $U$ in them, so we need to compute the number of distinct ways to assign counts of $R$ and $U$ to each of the $m+1$ regions formed by the $m$ good moves. This sounds like a stars and bars problem on both $R$ and $U$ individually. Let $x_1,\dots, x_{m+1}$ be the number of $R$ in each region. There are $n-m$ $R$ left to be assigned, so we must have $x_1 + \dots + x_{m+1} = n-m$, where each $x_i \geq 0$. The number of solutions to this, by stars and bars, is $\binom{n-m + (m+1) - 1}{(m+1)-1} = \binom{n}{m}$. The exact same stars and bars process works for the assignment of $U$ as well. By the product rule, there are $\binom{n}{m}^2$ ways to assign the counts of $R$ and $U$ to the "between" regions, which also must be the number of paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ that have exactly $m$ good moves. With the specified values, the answer is $\binom{12}{3}^2 = 48400$.

questions.title: Fun Run
questions.problem: $r$ elements of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ are selected with replacement and arranged in order of selection. A fun run is a decreasing or an increasing subsequence of maximal length. For example, with $n = 6$ and $r = 10$, $54261453$ has $5$ fun runs: $542, 26, 61, 145, 53$. Given that no number is selected more than once in succession, find the expected number of fun runs when $n = 12$ and $r = 11$.
questions.solution: In the example, we can clearly see that the starts of fun runs are either larger or smaller than the values on either side of them. This is because they must end an increasing/decreasing chain, so they break a pattern. Counting the number of fun runs is equivalent to counting the number of positions that start a fun run, so linearity of expectation seems to be a good approach. Thus, let $I_i$ be the indicator that position $i$ is the start of a fun run, $1 \leq i \leq n$. $T = I_1 + \dots + I_n$ gives the total amount of fun runs. By linearity of expectation, $\ev{T} = \ev{I_1} + \ev{I_2} + \dots + \ev{I_n}$. The first position always is the start of a fun run, as it's the first value, so $\ev{I_1} = 1$. Similarly, the last position is never the start of a fun run, as no values come after it, so $\ev{I_n} = 0$. For the other $n-2$ indicators in the middle, the condition is all the same: Position $i$ must have a strictly larger or smaller value than the two positions on either side of it. $\ev{I_i}$ is the probability that position $i$ is strictly larger or smaller than both of positions $i-1$ and $i+1$. Since values can't be the same in succession, we will want to break this into two cases: Positions $i-1$ and $i+1$ are distinct vs. the same. If positions $i-1$ and $i+1$ both have distinct values, position $i$ must also have a value that's not the value of position $i-1$ nor $i+1$ by the given information. Given that the three values are distinct, the probability that position $i$ is either the maximum or minimum is $2/3$, as it's equally likely to be any of the three orders. If positions $i-1$ and $i+1$ agree, then position $i$ must be different than both of positions $i-1$ and $i+1$ in this sub-case by our given information. Since position $i$ is distinct from the (repeated) value of positions $i-1$ and $i+1$, it is either the maximum or minimum by definition, so it starts a new run with probability $1$. Now, we need to consider the probabilities of each case above. When $3 \leq i \leq n-1$, $i-1 \geq 2$, so there are always $r-1$ possible values for each of position $2$ to $n$ (any of the other $r-1$ values that aren't in the prior position). We split on this because there are $n$ options for the first position, which is included in comparison when $i = 2$. Thus, for $3 \leq i \leq n-1$, there are $r-1$ equally likely possibilities for position $i-1$, and one possibility will be selected for position $i+1$. By the above, the probability positions $i-1$ and $i+1$ are equal is $\frac{1}{r-1}$, so they are different with probability $\frac{r-2}{r-1}$. For $i = 2$, there are $r$ positions for the first spot and $r-1$ positions for the third spot, so a counting approach is better here. There are $r(r-1)^2$ ways to pick the values for the first three spots without any restrictions. Under the restriction that the first and third spots are the same, there are $r$ ways to pick the value in those two spots, and $r-1$ ways to pick the value in the second spot (any value but the one selected above). Therefore, the probability of having positions $1$ and $3$ the same is $\frac{r(r-1)}{r(r-1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{r-1}$. This is the same as what was obtained for $3 \leq i \leq n-1$, so we can conclude that for all $2 \leq i \leq n-1$, $\ev{I_i} = \dfrac{1}{r-1} \cdot 1 + \dfrac{r-2}{r-1} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{2r-1}{3(r-1)}$. In the above, we applied Law of Total Probability by conditioning on whether or not positions $i-1$ and $i+1$ were equal. Substituting in, we can conclude $\ev{T} = 1 + (n-2) \cdot \dfrac{2r-1}{3(r-1)} = \dfrac{(n-2)(2r-1)}{3(r-1)} + 1$. With the specified values, the answer is $8$.

questions.title: House Salesman I
questions.problem: Priyanshu is looking to purchase a very nice house in Bangalore. The price (in Lakh Rupees) is $P \sim \unif{a}{b}$. He can bid any amount he wants for the house, and if he bids at least the true value of $P$, he gets the house. If he doesn't win the bid, nothing happens. Since Priyanshu is a great salesman, he can sell the house for a multiple of $1+p$ times the true house price, where $0 < p < 1$. How much should Priyanshu bid on the house when $a = 100, b = 1000,$ and $p = 0.5$.
questions.solution: Priyanshu's expected profit is based on how much he bids for the house. If we knew his bid for the house, we could calculate the expected profit directly. Therefore, the natural idea is to calculate his expected profit as a function of his bid $x$, say $E(x)$, and then optimize in $x$. Our first key observation to simplifying the problem is that Priyanshu should always bid $a \leq x \leq b$. If he bids less than $a$, he will never win the bid, meaning his expected profit is $0$. If he bids more than $b$, he would always win the bid by just betting $b$, as the maximum possible value of the house is $b$. Thus, we can calculate $E(x)$ for $a \leq x \leq b$. Priyanshu wins the house when its true value is at most $x$. The probability of this is $\frac{x-a}{b-a}$, as the price $P$ is Uniform, so we can take ratios of lengths to compute probabilities. Given he wins with a bid of $x$, the price of the house is $\unif{a}{x}$ distributed by the properties of Uniform distributions. The mean price of the house is $\frac{x+a}{2}$ in this case, and Priyanshu would sell the house for $1+p$ times that amount. He paid $x$ for the house, so Priyanshu's expected profit given he wins is the expected amount he sells the house for minus the amount he paid. If he doesn't win the bid, nothing happens, so his profit is $0$. By the Law of Total Expectation, $E(x) = \dfrac{x-a}{b-a} \cdot \left[(1+p) \cdot \dfrac{x+a}{2} - x\right] + \left(1 - \dfrac{x-a}{b-a}\right) \cdot 0 = \dfrac{p-1}{2(b-a)}(x-a)\left(x - a \cdot \dfrac{1+p}{1-p}\right)$. $E(x)$ is quadratic in $x$, so the maximum occurs at the midpoint of the roots. Thus, the optimal choice of $x$ is $x^* = \dfrac{a + a \cdot \frac{1+p}{1-p}}{2} = \dfrac{a}{1-p}$. Recall that this is the optimal choice of the bid. We take the minimum of this with $b$, as there's no reason to ever bid more than $b$, so the optimal bid is $\min\{\frac{a}{1-p},b\}$. With the specified values, the answer is $200$.

questions.title: Weighted Rolls
questions.problem: You and your friend both play a game: you both pick a number (doesn't necessarily need to be an integer), and then roll two weighted $6$-sided dice with the values $1-6$ on the sides. The person who gets closest to the sum wins. The dice are non-uniform: there is a $40\%$ chance of rolling a sum of $12$, and a $6\%$ chance of rolling each of the other $10$ sums $2-11$. Assuming both you and your friend play optimally, if you go first, what is your strategy? Report your probability of winning as a percentage.
questions.solution: To find the optimal strategy, it's best to first find the smallest value $x$ at which there is at least $50\%$ probability of the sum being at least $x$. It's natural to do this because this would be the point where you and your friend may want to center your bet around. We can easily see that the dice show at least $11$ with probability $46\%$, while the sum is at least $10$ with probability $52\%$. Thus, let's consider different cases on your guess $x$ and how your friend would respond. Suppose you guess $x > 10$. Since there is a $46\%$ chance of the dice showing $11$ or $12$, there is a $54\%$ chance of the dice showing $10$ or below, so your friend should give a response of $x - \varepsilon$ for some very small $\varepsilon$ to ensure they are closer for anything $10$ or below. Suppose you guess $x = 10$. If your friend guesses anything larger than $10$, there is a $46\%$ chance of them winning (either $11$ or $12$ appears), meaning there is a $54\%$ chance you win. Alternatively, if they guess anything less than $10$, they have a $48\%$ chance of winning (sum $2$ to $9$ appears), meaning you have a $52\%$ chance of winning. Suppose you guess $x < 10$. If your friend guesses anything higher than you, say $x + \varepsilon$, they are closer than you for at least $10-12$, which gives them at least a $52\%$ chance of winning. By the above, the only case when you have a larger than $50\%$ chance of winning is when you guess $x = 10$. Your friend has at most a $48\%$ chance of winning in this case by guessing $10 - \varepsilon$ for some very small $\varepsilon$, as they capture the numbers $2-9$. Under the optimal strategy, you guess $10$, and you get a $52\%$ chance of winning.

questions.title: Product Rolls I
questions.problem: Suppose you roll two standard fair $4$-sided dice. You can pay $\$2$ to reroll either of the dice, and this decision can be made as many times as you'd like. Your payout is the product of the upfaces of your final roll. Assuming optimal play, what is your expected value?
questions.solution: Suppose the two dice show the values $x_1$ and $x_2$, where $x_1 < x_2$. If you make the decision to roll again, you should clearly roll the die showing $x_1$, as the expected product of the dice would be larger if you have a larger multiplier. By iterating this methodology, the optimal strategy must be to continually reroll the dice until both are sufficiently large. More explicitly, the strategy is to reroll both dice until they both show at least $t$ for some $t = 1,2,3,4$. The goal is to find the expected value of our payout with each threshold. The key here is to use independence of the values on the dice: If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are the values on each die, $\ev{X_1X_2} = \ev{X_1}\ev{X_2}$. If $t = 1$, we stop on the first roll always, as the minimum possible value is always at least $1$, so the expected value of each die is $\frac{1+2+3+4}{4} = 2.5$, meaning the expected payout is $(2.5)^2 = 6.25$. If $t = 2$, upon stopping, the value on each die is $2,3,$ or $4$ with equal probability, so each die shows $3$ on average, meaning the expected product is $3^2 = 9$. To calculate the expected cost, we note that there is probability $3/4$ per roll of the dice showing at least $2$. We can calculate the expected cost to get at least $2$ on one die, and then double it to account for the other die. On average, it would take $1/(3/4) = 4/3$ rolls to get at least $2$ on the die, meaning we have to perform $1/3$ rerolls on average. The cost of the reroll is $\$2$, so the expected cost of obtaining at least $2$ on each die is $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1/3 = 4/3$. The first two represents the fact that there are $2$ dice. The expected profit would be the expected payout minus the expected cost, so this is $9 - 4/3 = 23/3 \approx 7.67$. If $t = 3$, upon stopping, the value on each die is $3$ or $4$ with equal probability, so each die shows $3.5$ on average, meaning the expected product is $(3.5)^2 = 12.25$. To calculate the expected cost, there is probability $1/2$ per roll of obtaining at least $3$ on a given die, so the expected number of total rolls needed to obtain at least $3$ is $2$, meaning $1$ reroll is needed on average. Thus, the expected cost to get both dice to at least $3$ is $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 4$. The expected profit is $12.25 - 4 = 8.25$. Lastly, if $t = 4$, the payout is always $4^2 = 16$ upon stopping. However, there is probability $1/4$ per roll of obtaining a $4$, so $4$ rolls of each die are needed on average to get a $4$, meaning $3$ rerolls would be needed. Thus, the expected cost of rerolling is $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 12$, so the expected profit is $16-  12 = 4$. By the above, we can see that $t = 3$ yields the optimal expected payout of $8.25$.

questions.title: Even Multiheads
questions.problem: Suppose that you have $n_1$ coins with probability $0 < p_1 < 1$ of heads per flip and $n_2$ coins with probability $0 < p_2 < 1$ of heads per flip. You flip all $n_1 + n_2$ coins. Find the probability that there are an even amount of heads to the nearest ten-thousandth when $n_1 = 4, n_2 = 6, p_1 = 1/4,$ and $p_2 = 1/8$.
questions.solution: To get an even amount of heads in total, it may help to break down the problem based on the sub-collections of coins that have the same success probability. To get an even amount of heads total, both sub-collections of coins must have an even amount or odd amount of heads. Therefore, the idea is to break up into two cases: Both sub-collections have an even amount of heads and both have an odd amount of heads. In the remaining part of this question, we will apply the result of "Even Heads", which states that the probability of an even amount of heads in $n$ flips of coins with probability $p$ of heads per flip is $p_E(p,n) = \frac{1 + (1-2p)^n}{2}$. The probability of an even amount of heads in each sub-collection is $p_E(p_1,n_1)p_E(p_2,n_2)$. Similarly, the probability of an odd amount of heads in each sub-collection is $(1-p_E(p_1,n_1))(1-p_E(p_2,n_2))$. This is by complementation, as the total number of heads in each sub-collection is either even or odd. Adding up these two disjoint cases together yields a total probability of $p_E(p_1,n_1)p_E(p_2,n_2) + (1-p_E(p_1,n_1))(1-p_E(p_2,n_2)) = \dfrac{1 + (1-2p_1)^{n_1}(1-2p_2)^{n_2}}{2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.5056$.

questions.title: Chess Mean Return I
questions.problem: A king starts at the bottom left corner of a standard $8 \times 8$ chessboard. A king can move to any adjacent square (vertical, horizontal, or diagonal) at any step, as long as it stays on the chess board. Find the expected time for the king to return to the bottom left corner if the king moves uniformly at random among all of its possible moves at each step.
questions.solution: This Markov Chain is time-reversible: Any path that can be taken to get from the bottom left to any position can also be taken backwards to get back to the bottom left. Using this, we can use the classic theorem that relates the stationary distribution to expected return time. All that needs to be done is find the stationary distribution. We can view this random walk as one of a graph, where the degree of each square is equal to the number of squares that it can be reached by. By noting this, the stationary probability on each square is equal to its degree as a proportion of the total degree of the graph. Intuitively, this makes sense; The proportion of time that the Markov Chain spends in a given state is directly proportional to how many "entry points" there are to that state. By a simple counting argument, there are $36$ squares with $8$ entry points (the inner $6 \times 6$ square), $24$ squares with $5$ entry points (the outer boundary of the $8 \times 8$ square, minus the corners), and $4$ squares with $3$ entry points (the $4$ corners), yielding a total degree of $36 \cdot 8 + 24 \cdot 5 + 4 \cdot 3 = 420$. Thus, the limiting proportion on the bottom left corner is $3/420 = 1/140$, so the expected return time is $140$, the reciprocal of the limiting proportion.

questions.title: Chess Mean Return II
questions.problem: A knight starts at the bottom left corner of a standard $8 \times 8$ chessboard. A knight can move $(\pm 2, \pm 1)$ or $(\pm 1, \pm 2)$ in any direction, as long as it stays on the chess board. Find the expected time for the knight to return to the bottom left corner if the knight moves uniformly at random among all of it's possible moves at each step.
questions.solution:
This Markov Chain is time-reversible: Any path that can be taken to get from the bottom left to any position can also be taken backwards to get back to the bottom left. Using this, we can use the classic theorem that relates the stationary distribution to expected return time. All that needs to be done is find the stationary distribution. We can view this random walk as one of a graph, where the degree of each square is equal to the number of squares that it can be reached by. By noting this, the stationary probability on each square is equal to it's degree as a proportion of the total degree of the graph. Intuitively, this makes sense; The proportion of time that the Markov Chain spends in a given state is directly proportional to how many "entry points" there are to that state. By a simple counting argument, we can find the number of entry points to each square on the board to be $\begin{align*}
    \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
        \hline
        & & & & 4 & 4 & 3 & 2 \\
        \hline
        & & & & 6 & 6 & 4 & 3 \\
        \hline
        & & & & 8 & 8 & 6 & 4 \\
        \hline
        & & & & 8 & 8 & 6 & 4\\
        \hline
        & & & & & & &\\
        \hline
        & & & & & & &\\
        \hline
        & & & & & & &\\
        \hline
        & & & & & & &\\
        \hline
    \end{array}
\end{align*}$ Since the board and moves are symmetric, we can just multiply the degree of this corner by $4$ to get the total degree of the board to be $336$. The bottom left corner has degree $2$, so the limiting proportion of time the knight spends in the bottom left corner is $1/168$, meaning the expected return time is $168$.

questions.title: Last Ball Drawn
questions.problem: A box contains $b \geq 1$ black and $w \geq 1$ white balls. Besides this box, there is a large pile of black balls (you may assume it's infinitely large). Each turn, $2$ balls are drawn uniformly at random from the box. If they are of the same color, a black ball from the pile is put into the box; otherwise, the white ball is put back into the box. This procedure is iterated until the box empties out and one ball is put back in. Find the probability that this last ball is white when $b = 20$ and $w = 10$.
questions.solution: In these types of problems, the most common approach is to iterate backwards from the end and notice patterns from the process along the way. A first observation is that the number of total balls after each draw decreases by $1$: Two balls are drawn out, and one is placed in. The most important item to note is that parity of the number of white balls never changes: If two balls of different colors are drawn out, the white ball is replaced, so there are the same number of white balls. If two balls of the same color are drawn out, it's either $2$ black (in which the number of white balls is unchanged) or $2$ white (in which the number of white balls decreases by $2$, which keeps the parity the same). Since the parity never changes, the last ball placed in is white exactly when the last two balls are of different colors, so there must be $1$ white and $1$ black ball in the box. This is possible exactly when there are an odd number of white balls to start, as the parity of the number of white balls never changes. Since the total number of balls at each step decreases by $1$, the process does end with two balls being drawn. With all of the above in mind, we can conclude that the last ball is white if and only if there were initially an odd amount of white balls, in which this occurs with probability $1$. Otherwise, if the amount of white balls is even to start, the last two balls drawn must be white, meaning a black is replaced, so there is probability $0$ of the last ball being white in this case. Since $w = 10$ here, which is even, the answer is $0$.

questions.title: Fair Cards
questions.problem: You are invited to play the following game by your friend: A standard deck of $52$ cards ($26$ red and $26$ black) is shuffled, and cards are dealt out in pairs from the top. If the cards are both red, you receive them. If the cards are both black, your friend receives them. If the cards differ in color, they are discarded. Once the deck is completely empty, both players count up their cards. If your friend has more cards than you, you don't need to pay them anything, but you receive $\$c$ for each additional card you have over your opponent. When $c = 5$, how much would you pay to play this game?
questions.solution: All of the cards in deck coming in pairs that are of different colors are discarded. Since there is $1$ red and $1$ black card in each discarded pair, once all of these pairs are discarded, there are an equal amount of red and black cards remaining in the deck, and all of these are paired up with another card of the same color. Since there are the same number of red and black cards remaining in the deck, each paired up with a card of it's respective color, both players will always have the same number of cards at the end! Thus, you never receive any payout from the game, as with probability $1$, you and your friend always have the same number of cards. Regardless of $c$, the fair value of the game is $\$0$. To see this in action, consider a small deck with $10$ cards, $5$ of each color. Here's an example shuffling: $RRBRRBRBBB$. This can be split into $5$ pairs: $RR|BR|RB|RB|BB$. The middle three regions are discarded because they have opposing colors, and each player gets $2$ cards in the end.

questions.title: Obtuse Triangle
questions.problem: Suppose that $X,Y \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$ IID. Find the probability that sides of lengths $X,Y,$ and $1$ form an obtuse triangle. Report your answer to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: For any triangle to be formed at all, the sum of any two sides must be larger than the third side. In this case, we must have $X < 1 + Y, Y < 1+ X,$ and $1 < X+Y$. The first two are satisfied automatically, as $X$ and $Y$ are supported only on $[0,1]$. Thus, our first condition is $X+Y > 1$. The above guarantees that a triangle can be formed, but when is it obtuse? We can relate the side lengths of a triangle to it's angles via the Law of Cosines. Since $0 \leq X,Y \leq 1$, the angle opposite of the side of length $1$ is largest, so it must be the obtuse angle. Denote this angle as $\theta$. For our triangle to be obtuse, $\theta > \pi/2$, so $\cos\theta < 0$. Using the Law of Cosines, we can conclude that the triangle is obtuse exactly when $1^2 = X^2 + Y^2 - 2XY\cos\theta \geq X^2 + Y^2$ We get $\geq$ because $\cos\theta < 0$, so the last term in the expression is positive. Therefore, our two conditions to have an obtuse triangle are $X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1$ and $X+Y>1$. As $X$ and $Y$ are Uniform, it's best to consider ratios of areas. Plotted in the plane, we can see that the region is the quarter circle in the first quadrant, minus the triangle with vertices $(0,1), (1,0),$ and $(0,0)$. The area of the quarter circle is $\pi/4$, while the triangle has area $1/2$. Thus, their difference, which is the region of interest, has area $\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi - 2}{4}$. As the total support has area $1$, the probability of an obtuse triangle is $\dfrac{\pi - 2}{4} \approx 0.285$

questions.title: Stripe Stick II
questions.problem: Two marks are independently selected at uniformly random points along a stick of length $1$. The stick is then divided into $n$ regions by selecting $n-1$ cutting points uniformly at random. Find the probability that the two marks lie in the same region when $n = 5$.
questions.solution: The two marks lie in the same region exactly when there is no cut between them. We can view the problem as $n+1$ IID Uniform random variables, where two of them are the marks, and the other $n-1$ are the cuts. We can treat them as one in the same because the cutting points and mark points are IID. Arbitrarily fix the locations of these points. Since all arrangements of locations of the marks are equally likely, we can convert this into a counting problem on how many arrangements satisfy the condition of no cutting point being between the marks. The total number of ways to pick the location of the $2$ marks among the $n+1$ points is $\binom{n+1}{2}$. Of these, there are $n$ ways to have the marks consecutive: First and second, second and third, and so on, until the $n$th and $(n+1)$st points. As all are equally likely, the probability of the two marks being in the same region is $\dfrac{n}{\binom{n+1}{2}} = \dfrac{2}{n+1}$ With $n = 5$, the answer is $1/3$.
questions.hint: Consider the marks and cuts as one combined set of uniform random variables.

questions.title: Under Oath II
questions.problem: Alice, Bob, and Chad are witnesses to a crime. When asked questions, Alice, Bob, and Chad respectively tell the truth with probability $p_A, p_B,$ and $p_C$ (and lie with respective probabilities $1-p_A,1-p_B,$ and $1-p_C$). The detective asks Alice a question, she gives an answer, and Bob makes a determination on the validity/invalidity of Alice's statement. Chad tells us that Bob confirms Alice is telling the truth. Find the probability that Alice told the truth when $p_A = p_B = p_C = 1/3$.
questions.solution: This is a conditional probability problem, as we are given information about the response from Chad. Let $E$ be the event that Chad says Bob confirms Alice's statement is true, and $T$ be the event that Alice is actually telling the truth. We are looking to compute $\prob{T \mid E} = \frac{\prob{T \cap E}}{\prob{E}}$. To compute the probabilities, to consider the combinations of outcomes leading to each case, as the scenario is quite complicated. For the numerator, Alice must tell the truth. If Alice tells the truth, the there are two cases: Bob was truthful or was lying. If Bob was truthful, then Chad was truthful too, as Alice and Bob agree. Otherwise, if Bob was was lying, Chad is lying too, as Alice and Bob do not agree. The probability of these two events, respectively, are $p_Ap_Bp_C$ and $p_A(1-p_B)(1-p_C)$, so their sum is the numerator, as these are disjoint cases. As for the denominator, the term from the numerator is included, and we also need to account for the case where Alice is lying. If Bob is also lying, then Chad is truthful, since Alice and Bob are both in agreement. If Bob is telling the truth when Alice is lying, Chad is lying, as Alice and Bob don't agree. The probability of these two cases are $(1-p_A)(1-p_B)p_C$ and $(1-p_A)p_B(1-p_C)$, respectively. The sum of all four terms (the two here and the two from the numerator) represents the denominator. Combining all of this, we can conclude $\prob{T \mid E} = \dfrac{p_A(p_Bp_C + (1-p_B)(1-p_C))}{p_A(p_Bp_C + (1-p_B)(1-p_C)) + (1-p_A)(p_B(1-p_C) + p_C(1-p_B))}$
questions.hint: Consider all combinations of truth-telling and lying for Alice, Bob, and Chad that result in Chad's statement.

questions.title: Ladder Fall
questions.problem: $n$ people labelled $1-n$ are climbing a ladder, with person $1$ at the bottom and person $n$ at the top. Each person falls off the ladder themselves with probability $p$. If person $i$ falls off the ladder, they knock off everyone below them as well. Find the expected amount of people that fall off the ladder when $n = 10$ and $p = 0.2$ to the nearest hundredth.
questions.solution: We are looking to compute the expected amount of dependent events: If person $i$ falls down, all people $j < i$ also fall. Thus, linearity of expected value is the best approach. Let $I_i$ be the indicator of the event that the $i$th person falls off the ladder. $T = I_1 + \dots + I_n$ gives the total amount of people that fall off the ladder, as it counts $1$ per person who falls off. By linearity of expectation, $\ev{T} = \sum_{i=1}^n \ev{I_i}$ $\ev{I_i}$ is the probability that person $i$ falls off the ladder. For this to occur, it must be the case that person $i$ falls off themselves, or someone above them fell onto them. As a result, the complement, which is that they don't fall off, might be easier to compute. For person $i$ to not fall off, they must not fall off themselves, and nobody above them can fall off. Therefore, no people in the set $\{i,i+1,\dots, n\}$ can fall off for person $i$ to not fall off. By independence, the probability of this is $(1-p)^{n-i+1}$, as there are $n-i+1$ integers in the set, and each doesn't fall off with probability $1-p$. By complementation, the probability that person $i$ doesn't fall off the ladder is $\ev{I_i} = 1 - (1-p)^{n-i+1}$ Substituting into the summation from before, $\ev{T} = \sum_{i=1}^n 1-  (1-p)^{n-i+1} = n - \sum_{i=1}^n (1-p)^i = n - \dfrac{(1-p) - (1-p)^{n+1}}{1-(1-p)} = n - \dfrac{1-p}{p}(1 - (1-p)^n)$ With the specified values, the answer is $6.43$.

questions.title: Dice Divisibility
questions.problem: You roll $n$ standard fair $r$-sided dice and add up all of the values. What is the probability that the sum is divisible by $r$? Report the answer when $n = 100$ and $r = 10$.
questions.solution: This appears complicated at first, as one would normally consider enumerating the possibilities. However, we can take a more clever approach, as the divisibility by $r$ aligns with the values $1-r$ on the dice, which hints there may be some clean trick that can be done. Note that whenever a die is rolled, exactly one of the $r$ values on the die will make the cumulative sum divisible by $r$. For example, with $r = 10$, if the current sum is $9$, only a $1$ will make the sum divisible by $10$. This is easily generalized, no matter what the current sum is: The sum of the first $n-1$ dice is irrelevant, as exactly $1$ of the $r$ values on the last die will make the sum of all $n$ dice divisible by $r$. Therefore, the probability is exactly $1/r$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/10$.

questions.title: Double Up
questions.problem: Which of the following games yields a higher probability of success? Game $1:$ Roll at least $1$ six in $6$ rolls of a standard fair die. Game $2:$ Roll at least $1$ pair of sixes in $36$ rolls of a pair of dice.
questions.solution: For starters, it may help to compute the probabilities explicitly. The probability of at least one $6$ in $6$ rolls is best computed by complementation, as it's an "at least one" probability statement. The complement is that there are no sixes rolled, which occurs with probability $(5/6)^6$, so the probability of at least one $6$ is $1 - (5/6)^6$. As for the second game, we perform the same action: The probability of not getting a pair of sixes in a given roll is $35/36$, so the probability of at least one pair of sixes in $36$ rolls is $1 - (35/36)^{36}$. These two expressions have a similar form, as $1 - \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)^6 = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^6$ A similar idea holds for the other expression with $36$ instead of $6$. These appear to be in the form of the definition of $e$, and we know that the limit $(1 + x/n)^n$ approaches $e^x$ from below (think about it for the base case $x = 1$ if you want some intuition). Therefore, as $6 < 36$, $\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^6 < \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{36}\right)^{36} \iff 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{6}\right)^6 > 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{36}\right)^{36}$ This means that game $1$ is more favorable to play.

questions.title: Swappy Coin
questions.problem: A fair coin is flipped $n$ times. We say that a swap occurs at position $i$ if positions $i-1$ and $i$ differ in parity. For example, the sequence $HHHTHHT$ has $3$ swaps. Find the probability of exactly $k$ swaps in $n$ flips when $n = 10$ and $k = 4$.
questions.solution: Using the condition for swaps outlined in the question, we are looking to count the number of positions $i$ in which the outcomes in positions $i-1$ and $i$ differ. Therefore, from a sequence of length $n$, we can create a sequence of length $n-1$ such that the $i$th element of the sequence takes the value $1$ if positions $i$ and $i+1$ differ (we need to define this way because the first position indicates whether the first and second outcomes differ), and $0$ if not. For example, the sequence $HHHTHHT$ becomes $001101$. A natural question is: Are positions $i \neq j$ independent in the new string? If $|j-i| > 1$, positions $i$ and $j$ concern disjoint collections of flips, so they must be independent. However, if $j = i+1$ (or vice versa), there could be intersection. Thus, we need to verify $\prob{I_i = 1, I_{i+1} = 1} = \prob{I_i = 1}\prob{I_{i+1} = 1}$ for these to be independent. The LHS event is the event of receiving $HTH$ or $THT$ in three consecutive spots, as positions $i$ and $i+1$ must differ, as well as positions $i+1$ and $i+2$, and this is satisfied by these $2$ sequences. The probability of this is $2/8 = 1/4$. The probability that any specific indicator is $1$ is just $1/2$, as the second flip needs to differ from the first flip. As $1/4 = 1/2 \cdot 1/2$, the indicators over varying positions are indeed independent, and have probability $1/2$ per position. Therefore, the distribution of the number of swaps $S$ in $n$ flips is just the distribution of the number of occurrences of $1$ in the string of length $n-1$, where each character is $0$ or $1$ with equal probability. As this counts the number of occurrences in a fixed number of trials, $S \sim \text{Binom}(n-1,1/2)$, so $\prob{S = k} = \binom{n-1}{k}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}$ With the specified values, the answer is $63/256$.

questions.title: Decimal to Fraction II
questions.problem: Suppose that $x = 0.c_1\dots c_m\overline{a_1\dots a_n}$ in base $10$ decimal form, where each $0 \leq a_i,c_i \leq 9$. Write $x = a/b$ where $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime integers. Find $a+b$ when $m = 2, n = 4, c_1c_2 = 42,$ and $a_1a_2a_3a_4 = 1747$.
questions.solution: In this question, we are going to employ a similar idea to "Decimal to Fraction I" in trying to create the same remainder by some multiplication. Note now that there is a fixed term of $c_1\dots c_m$ at the start of the decimal expansion of $x$ now. Therefore, to ensure we get to the repeating part, we should first consider $10^m x$. Namely, $10^m x = (10^{m-1}c_1 + \dots 10c_{m-1} + c_m).\overline{a_1\dots a_n}$ Now, to get another integer whose decimal part is $\overline{a_1\dots a_n}$, we can multiply by $10^{m+n}$, as that will run through the first cycle of $a_1\dots a_n$, and then the decimal repeats. Doing this, we get $10^{m+n}x = (10^{m+n-1} c_1 + \dots 10^{n+1}c_{m-1} + 10^nc_m + 10^{n-1}a_1 + \dots 10a_{n-1} + a_n).\overline{a_1\dots a_n}$ Now, to get an integer, we subtract $10^m x$ from $10^nx$, as they now have the same expansion past the decimal point, which yields $10^{m+n}x - 10^mx = (10^{m+n-1} c_1 + \dots 10^{n+1}c_{m-1} + 10^nc_m + 10^{n-1}a_1 + \dots 10a_{n-1} + a_n) - (10^{m-1}c_1 + \dots 10c_{m-1} + c_m)$ Rearranging and combining, we obtain $x = \dfrac{c_1(10^{m+n-1} - 10^{m-1}) + \dots + c_m(10^n - 1) + a_1 \cdot 10^{n-1} + \dots a_{n-1} \cdot 10 + a_n}{10^{m+n} - 10^m}$ With the specified values, we have that $x = \dfrac{421747 - 42}{10^6 - 10^2} = \dfrac{84341}{19980}$. Therefore, the answer is $84341 + 199980 = 284321$.

questions.title: Murderous Circle
questions.problem: Suppose that there are $N$ people standing in a circle labeled $1$ through $N$ in order, where person $1$ has person $2$ on their left and person $N$ on their right. Define $X = 2^r$, where $r$ is the maximum power such that $2^r \leq N$. Person $1$ takes a sword and kills the person to their left. Afterwards, they pass the sword to the next living person on their left, and the process continues circularly until one person remains. The survivor's number can be expressed in the form $aN+bX+c$. Find $abc$.
questions.solution: The general set-up of this problem suggests that there is something special about powers of $2$. In particular, it somewhat makes sense that the answer here would be related to a power of $2$, as at each rotation of the circle, you are essentially "halving" the number of people that remain in the circle, so as you are repeatedly rotating around a circle and halving, the answer should involve some modular arithmetic and powers of $2$. First, let's consider the case where $N = 2^k$ for some positive integer $k$ and explicitly work out some cases for small values of $k$. If $k = 1$, then clearly person $1$ wins, as they immediately kill person $2$. If $k = 2$, person $1$ kills person $2$, person $3$ kills person $4$, and then person $1$ kills person $3$. This means person $1$ also wins here. More generally, one might assume that person $1$ will always win in the case where $N$ is a power of $2$. This hunch would be correct. The reason that person $1$ will always win is because of the fact that powers of $2$ can always halve without a remainder, so the "relative position" of person $1$ never really changes. Now, suppose that $N$ is not a power of $2$. This means that $N$ is $N-X$ away from the largest power of $2$ at most $N$ by the definition of $X$. If $N-X$ people are killed in the circle, then the first person that begins with the knife immediately afterwards will be the last person standing. This is because there would now be a power of $2$ number of people left in the circle, which means that the first person to start would be the last person standing. For example, with $N = 3$, we have that person $1$ kills person $2$ and person $3$ kills person $1$. This is because of the fact that the moment person $1$ kills person $2$, there would be $2$ people left in the circle (which is a power of $2$), and hence person $3$ is the first one to act with the knife at this time, so they are the last one standing. Therefore, the question now becomes what indexed person is the one with the knife at this point? Since $N-X$ people need to be killed off, each of the first $N-X$ even-numbered people will be killed off. This means that people $2,4,\dots, 2(N-X)$ are killed off. Afterwards, there will be $X$ people left in the circle, which means that person $2(N-X) + 1$ will be the first person to act afterwards. Therefore, the last person standing in the circle will be numbered $2N - 2X+1$. In particular, by the form of the question at hand, the product $abc = (2)(-2)(1) = -4$.

questions.title: Fibonacci Ratio II
questions.problem: Let $F_n$ be the $n$th Fibonacci number, where $F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1,$ and $F_{n} = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$ for $n \geq 2$. If it exists, find $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{F_{n+2}}{F_n}$.
questions.solution: To compute this limit, we are going to want to use the recurrence relation on the numerator. This is easier because of the direct relationship between $F_{n+2}$ and the preceding two terms. Call the limit in the question $L$. Then we have that $L = \displaystyle \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} = \dfrac{F_{n+1} + F_{n}}{F_n} = 1 + \displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{F_{n+1}}{F_{n}}$ Note that the limit on the RHS above is just that of "Fibonacci Ratio I" and was found to be $\dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$. Therefore, we have that $L = \dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.

questions.title: Tripled? I
questions.problem: A child is playing baseball and tracking his batting average. This child is the next Babe Ruth, so at some point, his batting average is below $75\%$. However, later that day, his batting average is above $75\%$. Is it guaranteed that his batting average was ever exactly $75\%$? Answer $1$ if the answer is yes and $0$ if the answer is no.
questions.solution: Imagine the balls being put into two stacks: "hit" and "not hit". For his batting average to be below $75\%$ at one point, the "hit" stack must be less than $3$ times as tall as the "not hit" stack. However, later that day, the "hit" stack must exceed $3$ times the height of the not hit stack. Thus, no matter how tall the "not hit" stack is, at some point, there must have been exactly $3$ times as many balls in the "hit" stack as the "not hit" stack for there to be a change from below $75\%$ to above $75\%$, as all of these are integers. Therefore, the answer is $1$.

questions.title: Tripled? II
questions.problem: A child is playing baseball and tracking his batting average. This child is the next Babe Ruth, so at some point, his batting average is below $60\%$. However, later that day, his batting average is above $60\%$. Is it guaranteed that his batting average was ever exactly $60\%$? Answer $1$ if the answer is yes and $0$ if the answer is no.
questions.solution: Imagine the balls being put into two stacks: "hit" and "not hit". For his batting average to be below $60\%$ at one point, the "hit" stack must be less than $3/2$ as large as tall as the "not hit" stack. However, later that day, the "hit" stack must exceed $3/2$ times the height of the not hit stack. The approach of the previous question doesn't work because a $3/2$ multiple of the stack may be a non-integer. This hints at the fact that we can cook up an example where the $3/2$ multiple of the smaller stack is a non-integer. For example, suppose the child makes $1$ of his first two shots, so each stack is of size $1$. If the child makes the next shot, his proportion of shots made is $2/3$, which is larger than $3/5$. Thus, it's not guaranteed, and the answer is $0$.

questions.title: Different Marbles II
questions.problem: You have $n$ bags. If bags can be placed inside one another, what is the minimum number of marbles needed to ensure there are a different number of marbles in each bag? Report the answer when $n = 15$.
questions.solution: Assume that the bags are initially empty. Imagine a "Russian nesting doll" type arrangement, where there is a bag that contains all of the other $n-1$ bags, the next bag contains the other $n-2$, and so on, until $0$. Note that every bag contains a distinct number of bags. If we place $1$ marble in all of the bags that aren't the one that contains no bags, every bag contains a distinct number of bags, meaning also a distinct number of marbles. Therefore, $n-1$ marbles are needed in this scenario, so the answer is $14$.

questions.title: Convergent Tower
questions.problem: Suppose that $y = x^{x^{x^{x\dots}}}$. What is the largest value of $x$ such that this converges to a finite value? If there is no largest value, report $-1$. Otherwise, round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Suppose that $x > 0$. Since $f(y) = x^y$ is a continuous function, if the infinite tower $x^{x^{x^{x\dots}}}$ converges to some limit $y$, then $y = x^y$ by grouping the terms together. Since we want to solve for the largest $x$ such that this holds, we isolate $x$ and see $x = y^{1/y}$. To maximize $x$, we must maximize the RHS in $y$. To make things easier, as the logarithm is strictly increasing, maximizing $y^{1/y}$ is equivalent to maximizing $\ln(y)/y$. By applying the quotient rule and setting the derivative equal to $0$, $\dfrac{d}{dy}\left(\dfrac{\ln(y)}{y}\right) = \dfrac{1 - \ln(y)}{y^2} = 0 \iff \ln(y) = 1 \iff y = e$ If $y = e$, then $x = e^{1/e}$. Since $(e^{1/e},e)$ actually satisfies $y = x^y$, the limit exists, and the answer is $e^{1/e}$.

questions.title: Hours and Minutes I
questions.problem: In how many positions do the minute and hour hands overlap on the face of an analog clock?
questions.solution: Starting at the $12:00$ position, in $t$ hours, the minutes hand completes $t$ revolutions around the clock, while the hour hand has completed $t/12$ revolutions (there are $12$ hours on the clock). The first time the minute and hour hands overlap, the minute hand has completed one lap more than the hour hand. Thus, $t = t/12 + 1$, or $t = 12/11$ hours. In general, on the $n$th time the hands meet, the minutes hand has completed $n$ more laps than the hours hand, so the time $t$ at which the hands meet for the $n$th time, solves $t = t/12 + n$. The number of positions of intersection is exactly the number of intersections in $12$ hours. With $t = 12$ (there are $12$ hours on a clock), we must have $12 = 12/12 + n \iff n = 11$. Thus, there are $11$ intersections.

questions.title: Boy or Girl?
questions.problem: In an infinitely large community of individuals, every couple wants to have a baby girl. In fact, they keep having children until they have a baby girl. As time increases, what is the fraction of girls in this community?
questions.solution: Naturally, the percentage of boys and girls will remain at a $50/50$ split in an infinitely large population because the probability that a girl is born is unaffected by the couples' preferences. Note that this doesn't hold if the population is of a finite size, as the argument here relies on the Law of Large Numbers to make the proportion of children in the population. Thus, the percentage of girls in the population is $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.title: Special Multiple
questions.problem: Find the lowest multiple of $35$ that only has the digits $1$ and $0$.
questions.solution: We have two conditions: The number must have a units digit of zero, and it must be divisible by $7$. To check if a number is divisible by $7$, we can multiply the units digit by $2$, and subtract it from the rest of the number. Since the units digit is already $0$, this means we are simply looking for a number composed of ones and $0$s that is divisible by $7$, and we add a $0$ on to the end of it. The first number that satisfies this is $1001$, so the answer to this problem is $10010$.

questions.title: Largest Sum
questions.problem: Find the largest number that cannot be expressed as a sum of $5$ and $21$.
questions.solution: We want the largest number not expressible as a non-negative combination of $5$ and $21$.
