It measures the influence of a point on a single regression coefficient.

It measures the influence of a point on all of the regression coefficients.

It measures the contribution of each fitted coefficient to the fitted value of a given point.

None of the above.
questions.solution: Let $\hat{Y}_{i(-i)}$ be the predicted value corresponding to $(X_{i1},\dots, X_{ip})$ when the regression is run on all data points besides $(X_{i1},\dots, X_{ip}, Y_i)$, the $i$th data point. Furthermore, let $H_{ii}$ be the influence of the $i$th data point, and $e_i$ be the $i$th residual. The DFFits of the $i$th data point is $F_i = \dfrac{\hat{Y}_i - \hat{Y}_{i(-i)}}{\sqrt{MSE_{(-i)}H_{ii}}}$. Intuitively, we can see that DFFits is a measure of the influence of a point on its fitted value, as it measures the difference between the fitted value of the $i$th point with and without including that point. Thus, the first choice is correct.

questions.title: DFBetas Use
questions.problem:
Which of the following best encapsulates the use of DFBetas?

Let $\hat{\beta}_k$ be the $k$th regression coefficient in our original regression, while $\hat{\beta}_{k(-i)}$ is the $k$th regression coefficient when the $i$th data point is removed. Recall that DFBetas is defined by $B_{ki} = \dfrac{\hat{\beta}_k - \hat{\beta}_{k(-i)}}{\sqrt{MSE \cdot C_{kk}}}$.

It measures the influence of a point on its fitted value.

It measures how much a point affects the fitted values of the whole line.

It measures the influence of a point on another point's fitted value.

It measures the influence of one regression coefficient estimate on another regression coefficient.

It measures the influence of a point on a single regression coefficient.

It measures the influence of a point on all of the regression coefficients.

It measures the contribution of each fitted coefficient to the fitted value of a given point.
questions.solution: Let $\hat{\beta}_k$ be the $k$th regression coefficient in our original regression, while $\hat{\beta}_{k(-i)}$ is the $k$th regression coefficient when the $i$th data point is removed. Recall that DFBetas is defined by $B_{ki} = \dfrac{\hat{\beta}_k - \hat{\beta}_{k(-i)}}{\sqrt{MSE \cdot C_{kk}}}$. In the above, $C_{kk} = [(X^TX)^{-1}]_{kk}$ is the $k$th diagonal entry of $(X^TX)^{-1}$. Since DFBetas takes the difference between regression coefficients when the $i$th data point is and isn't included in the model, DFBetas measures the impact of the $i$th data point on the regression coefficients. Thus, the $5$th choice is correct.

questions.title: Adjusting R-Squared
questions.problem:
Which of the following pieces of information are $\textbf{necessary}$ to compute the $R_{adj}^2$ of a regression model?

$(1) \: \: R^2$

$(2) \: \: p$

$(3) \: \: MSR$

(4) The residuals $e_1,\dots, e_n$

$(5) \: \: n$

(6) The coefficients $\hat{\beta}_0,\dots, \hat{\beta}_p$

(7) None of the above.
questions.solution: We can write $R^2_{adj} = 1 - (1-R^2) \cdot \dfrac{n-1}{n-(p+1)}$, where $p$ is the number of predictors. If you've never seen this derivation, here is the work: $1 - (1 - R^2) \cdot \dfrac{n-1}{n-(p+1)} = 1 - \left(1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{SSE}{SST}\right)\right) \cdot \dfrac{n-1}{n-(p+1)} =1 - \dfrac{SSE/(n-p-1)}{SST/(n-1)} = R^2_{adj}$. In this formula, we need $R^2, p,$ and $n$ only; the rest of the information is irrelevant! Therefore, Options (1), (2), and (5) are all that's required.

questions.title: HFT Data
questions.problem:
Which of the following is most likely be an issue encountered when modeling high-frequency trading data? High-frequency data is time-series data that is observed on very short time-scales.

High autocorrelation between observations

A too small amount of data

The data is high dimensional

None of the above
questions.solution: Since high-frequency data is a times-series whose values are observed with very small amounts of time between each observation, one would expect that there would be a lot of autocorrelation between observations. The intuitive reasoning for this is that there is less "time" in between observations for other properties of the time-series (for example, a mean drift) to affect the values. This is especially true for real-life data. Thus, the correct answer is Option (1). Option (2) is incorrect because high-frequency data, by its nature produce a lot of data. Option (3) is incorrect. Dimensionality refers to the number of features that a dataset has. Specifically, in the context of a time-series, if we had a random time series vector $X_{t}$ that is of dimension $1 \times p$, the dimensionality of the time series would refer to the size of $p$ relative to the number of observations in the time series. Since the time series is high frequency, it is highly likely that $p$ is less than the number of observations in the time series.

questions.title: Common Point I
questions.problem:
Suppose we perform the OLS regression $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon$ and obtain the fitted line $\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i$. Which of the following points, if any, always lies on the fitted line.

$(0,0)$

$(0,\overline{Y})$

$(\overline{X},0)$

$(\overline{X},\overline{Y})$

All of the above.

None of the above.

questions.title: Error Covariance
questions.problem:
Let $\hat{y} = Hy$, where $H = X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$, and $\hat{e} = y - \hat{y}$ is the residual vector of OLS regression with $p$ predictors and an intercept. Under the standard OLS assumptions, compute $\cov{\hat{e}}{\hat{y}}$.

$H$

$(X^TX)^{-1}$

$\sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1}$

$0 \in \R^{n \times n}$

None of the above
questions.solution:
This question is actually the same as Predictors and Residuals I, except that we have presented the problem in a different way. To compute this covariance, we should plug in the expressions for both of them in terms of $y$, as they both relate to $y$. We have that $\begin{align*}
\cov{\hat{e}}{\hat{y}} &= \cov{(I-H)y}{Hy}\\
&= (I-H)\cov{y}{y}H^T \\
&= \sigma^2(I - H)H^T\\
&= \sigma^2(H^T - HH^T)\\
&= \sigma^2(H - H^2)\\
&= \sigma^2(H - H) = 0
\end{align*}$ We used symmetry and idempotence to simplify the result, as long as the typical regression assumption that $\cov{y,y} = \var{y} = \sigma^{2}$. From the geometric perspective of regression, this answer should intuitively make sense because $\hat{e}$ and $\hat{y}$ are orthogonal.

questions.title: Why Multicollinearity? II
questions.problem:
When performing OLS, why is multicollinearity an issue intuitively?

Multicollinear predictors add no new information.

Multicollinear predictors make the model less interpretable.

Multicollinear predictors make our estimates of the parameters less accurate.

None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (1) is correct. On an intuitive level, including linear combinations of predictors doesn't add any new information to the model, as the individual information already exists within the model. For example, if we were to run the regression $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{1}X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \beta_3(X_{1i} + X_{2i}) + \varepsilon_i$, we could expand out the third predictor, define $\beta_1' = \beta_1 + \beta_3$ and $\beta_2' = \beta_2 + \beta_3$, and rewrite the model as $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1'X_{1i} + \beta_2'X_{2i} + \varepsilon_i$. By doing this, we have eliminated the predictor $X_1 + X_2$ and encapsulated the same information. Option (2) is correct. If the predictors are highly correlated, it can be difficult to disentangle the effects of different coefficients. One way this can be seen mathematically is by recalling that, under the typical regression assumptions, $\var{\hat{\beta}} = \sigma^{2}(X^{T}X)^{-1}$. If there is a high degree of multicollinearity in $X$, then $(X^{T}X)^{-1}$ can be very large causing high variance in the fitted predictors. This means that fitting the model on new data might cause the coefficients to change dramatically, rendering it impossible to interpret the values of their fitted coefficients. Option (3) is correct, by the discussion above for Option (2) about the variance of fitted coefficients.

questions.title: Leave One Out Regression
questions.problem: Suppose that we want to perform leave one out cross validation (LOOCV) on an OLS regression model. Which of the following statements are true? LOOCV will be very computationally intensive, since we need to re-run the full regression for each left-out datapoint. LOOCV requires us to use Lasso to select the variables we use. LOOCV will be computationally easy, since there is a quick formula in the case of OLS. LOOCV will be very computationally intensive, since we need to re-run the full regression for each predictor variable. LOOCV will be computationally easy, since the result we get will be the same as if we ran LASSO. None of the above.

questions.title: Cook Distances Use
questions.problem: Which of the following best encapsulates the use of Cook Distances? It measures the influence of a point on it’s fitted value. It measures the influence of a single point on the fitted values for every datapoint It measures the influence of a single on another single point's fitted value. It measures the influence of one regression coefficient estimate on another regression coefficient. It measures the influence of a point on a single regression coefficient. It measures the influence of a point on all of the regression coefficients.

questions.title: Dual Regression
questions.problem: Suppose we perform OLS regression $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon$ and obtain the residuals $e_1,\dots, e_n$. Afterwards, suppose we perform a second regression $e = \beta_0' + \beta_1'X_i + \varepsilon'$. If anything, what can be said about this second regression? $R^2 = 1$ The residuals will all be $0$. The best-fit line will be $\hat{e}_i = 0$, where $\hat{e}_i$ is the fitted value of the $i$th residual. The best-fit line will be $\hat{e}_i = \overline{Y}$, where $\overline{Y}$ is the average of the data used in the first regression. Nothing can be said in generality about this second regression. None of the above.
questions.solution:
First, keep in mind that, as is well known, the residuals of the first regression will have mean $0$, since it is OLS fitted with an intercept. Let's now inspect the fitted value of $\beta_{1}'$. We know that, $\begin{align*}
    \hat{\beta_{1}'} &= \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_{i} - \bar{X})(e_{i} - \bar{e}) }{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2} } \\
    &= \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_{i} - \bar{X}) e_{i} }{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2} } \\
    &= \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}e_{i} - \bar{X} \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i} }{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2} } \\
    &= \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}e_{i} }{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2} } \\
    &= \frac{ 0 }{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2} } \\
    &= 0
\end{align*}$ where the second and fourth equalities follow from the aforementioned fact that the sum of the residuals is 0. The penultimate equality follows from the fact that in OLS, the residuals and predictors are orthogonal, so their dot product is 0. We can now inspect the fitted value of $\beta'_{0}$, which is, $\begin{align*}
    \hat{\beta_{0}'} &= \bar{e} - \bar{X}\hat{\beta'_{1}} \\
    &= 0 - \bar{X} 0 \\
    &= 0
\end{align*}$ Thus, all fitted coefficients are 0, and the fitted value for each $e_{i}$ will be $\hat{e}_{i} = 0$. Option (3) is therefore the correct answer.

questions.title: Known Weights II
questions.problem: Suppose we want to perform a WLS $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$, and we know that the data $Y_i$ is the sum of $n_i$ IID observations of the same process. Which of the below would be the most typical value to use for the weight, $w_i$, of the $i$th data point? $w_i = n_i$ $w_i = n_i^2$ $w_i = 1/n_i$ $w_i = 1/n_i^2$ Nothing can be said in generality about the weight. None of the above.

questions.title: Lasso Limit
questions.problem: As $\lambda$ becomes very large in Lasso regression, what happens to the fitted coefficients? Many of the parameters will become $0$ to create a more sparse model. The parameters decrease to a certain non-zero value. The estimator converges to the OLS estimator. The parameters will converge to $0$, but never be exactly $0$. Nothing can be said in generality.

questions.title: Confidence Intervals II
questions.problem: What is the interpretation of a credible interval for a parameter $\theta$ at confidence level $100(1-\alpha)\%$? It's a non-random interval such that the true value of the parameter $\theta$ lies in the interval with probability $1-\alpha$. It's a random interval such that the true value of the parameter $\theta$ lies in the interval with probability $1-\alpha$. It's a random interval such that if one were to generate a large number of samples $X$ and create an interval each time, the proportion of intervals that contain the true value of $\theta$ tends to $1-\alpha$. It's a non-random interval such that if one were to generate a large number of samples $X$ and create an interval each time, the proportion of intervals that contain the true value of $\theta$ tends to $1-\alpha$. None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (2) is correct. A credible interval is the Bayesian analogue to the frequentist confidence interval. Since credible intervals come from a Bayesian perspective, they assume that $\textbf{both}$ the data and the parameter for which we are creating the credible interval are random. We get this interpretation because the output is a posterior distribution on the parameter $\theta$ given our data, so we can find intervals of that posterior distribution such that the true value lies in the interval with probability $1-\alpha$.

questions.title: QQ Plots
questions.problem: In regression diagnostics, QQ plots are typically used to determine which of the following? 1. If the response variable should be transformed. 2. If a predictor variable is missing. 3. If the residuals follow a Normal distribution. 4. If the response variable is normally distributed.
questions.solution: A QQ plot shows the quantiles of one set of data versus the quantiles of another set, the purpose of which is to determine if the two datasets come from the same distribution. In the context of regression, QQ-plots are typically used to plot the standardized residual values versus the quantiles of a standard Normal distribution, which is used to check if the residuals follow a Normal distribution. Option (1) is incorrect. Just because the QQ-plot provides evidence, for or against, the Normality of the residuals, it doesn't mean that the response should be transformed. Option (2) is incorrect. The residuals being non-Normal does not necessarily imply a predictor is missing. Indeed, all of the "necessary" predictors could be in the model, but the residuals still need not be necessarily Normal. Option (3) is correct, per the discussion above. Option (4) is incorrect. QQ-plots are often applied to the residuals, not the response.

questions.title: Binary Swap
questions.problem: Suppose you have an OLS regression model that regresses $y$ with $p$ predictors and an intercept, where the first predictor is a binary variable of some characteristic (takes the value $0$ if not present and $1$ if it's present). Let $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ be the intercept and coefficient on the binary variable, respectively. Suppose we switch the binary indicator such that it takes the value $0$ if it's present and $1$ if it's not present. Which coefficient values, if any, change in the new regression? $\beta_i \mapsto 1 - \beta_i$ for all $0 \leq i \leq p$. $\beta_0$ is unchanged, but $\beta_i \mapsto 1 - \beta_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq p$. $\beta_i \mapsto - \beta_i$ for all $0 \leq i \leq p$. $\beta_0 \mapsto -\beta_0$ and $\beta_1 \mapsto -\beta_1$, while the rest are unchanged. $\beta_0 \mapsto 1-\beta_0$ and $\beta_1 \mapsto -\beta_1$, while the rest are unchanged. $\beta_0 \mapsto -\beta_0$ and $\beta_1 \mapsto 1-\beta_1$, while the rest are unchanged. $\beta_0 \mapsto 1-\beta_0$ and $\beta_1 \mapsto 1-\beta_1$, while the rest are unchanged. None of the above.
questions.solution: To frame the above mathematically, suppose we have a regression model $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \dots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \varepsilon_i$, where $X_{i1} = 0$ or $1$ only. From this, we obtain the fitted model $\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_{i1} + \dots + \hat{\beta}_p X_{ip}$. Now, we invert the binary variable $X_{i1}$ such that all $0$ become $1$, and vice versa. Mathematically, we can represent this as $X_{i1} \mapsto 1 - X_{i1}$. With this substituted predictor, we want to determine the fitted coefficients of the regression. To relate these regressions, it's easiest to just substitute in $X_{i1}$ with $1 - X_{i1}$ and see the form of the new regression. This yields $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1(1 - X_{i1}) + \dots + \beta_pX_{ip} \iff Y_i = (\beta_0 + \beta_1) + (-\beta_1)X_{i1} + \dots + \beta_pX_{ip}$ In this form, it's clear to see that if we define $\beta_0' = \beta_0 + \beta_1, \beta_1' = -\beta_1,$ and $\beta_i' = \beta_i$ for $2 \leq i \leq p$, the above is written in the form $Y_i = \beta_0' + \beta_1'X_{i1} + \dots + \beta_{p}'X_{ip}$ Therefore, we can conclude that $\hat{\beta}_0' = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1$, while $\hat{\beta}_1' = -\hat{\beta}_1$. This is none of the above answers, so the last answer is correct.

questions.title: Binary Residuals I
questions.problem: Suppose you have an OLS regression model that regresses $y$ with $p$ predictors and an intercept, where the first predictor is a binary variable of some characteristic (takes the value $0$ if not present and $1$ if it's present). What is the sum of residuals for only those datapoints whose binary indicator is equal to 1? $0$ $p$ $n$ $p+1$ There is no general formula.
questions.solution:
For any predictor with data $X_{i1},\dots, X_{in}$, we know that the residuals $e$ and the predictor data $X_i$ are orthogonal, so their dot product $\sum_j X_{ij}e_j = 0$. This is due to the fact that the residual vector, $e$, is orthogonal to the column space of $X$. Thus, any vector in the column space of $X$ will be orthogonal to $e$. Since $X_1$ is our binary indicator, we know $\sum_j X_{1j}e_j = 0$. As we want to consider all data points when $X_{1j} = 1$, it makes sense to break the above into two sums: $j$ such that $X_{1j} = 1$, and $j$ such that $X_{1j} = 0$. Doing this, we get, $\begin{align*}
    0 &= \sum_{j} X_{1j}e_j \\
    &= \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 1}X_{1j}e_j + \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 0}X_{1j}e_j \\
    &= \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 1}1 \cdot e_j + \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 0}0 \cdot e_j = 0 \\
    &= \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 1}1 \cdot e_j \\
    &= \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 1} e_j
\end{align*}$ Thus, $\sum_{j:X_{1j} = 1} e_j = 0$.

questions.title: Binary Residuals II
questions.problem: Suppose you have an OLS regression model that regresses $y$ with $p$ predictors and an intercept, where the first predictor is a binary variable of some characteristic (takes the value $0$ if not present and $1$ if it's present). If there's a nice expression, what is the sum of all residuals when the binary indicator is $0$? NOTE: Complete Binary Residuals I before attempting this problem. $0$ $p$ $n$ $p+1$ There is no general formula.
questions.solution:
In Binary Residuals I, we showed that the sum of all residuals where the level of the binary indicator is $1$ equals $0$. Since the regression is fitted with an intercept, the sum of all residuals is $0$. This is true because if we have an intercept, then our $X$ matrix contains a column of 1's, as we know that $\sum_j X_{ij}e_j = 0$ for any column $X_{i}$ in $X$, and so $\sum_j 1 e_j = \sum_j e_j = 0$. As every data point has the binary indicator equal to $0$ or $1$, for the sum of all residuals to be $0$ and sum of all residuals with binary level $1$ to be $0$, it must also be the case that the sum of all residuals with binary level $0$ must be $0$. Mathematically, we can write this as, $\begin{align*}
    0 &= \sum_j e_j \\
    & = \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 1} e_j + \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 0}e_j \\
    &= 0 + \sum_{j:X_{1j} = 0}e_j \\
\end{align*}$ which follows from the answer to Binary Residuals I. Thus, $\sum_{j:X_{1j} = 0}e_j = 0$.

questions.title: Non-Normal Inference I
questions.problem: Suppose you run OLS $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i$ with a large amount $n$ of data points, under the standard regression assumptions, except that $\varepsilon_i$ are assumed to be non-Normal. Is the typical $T-$test statistic for the hypothesis test $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ against $H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0$ under the Normal error model still approximately valid? No because exact normality is always needed to use the test statistic. No because hypothesis tests in general can't be performed outside of the Normal error model. Yes because the Central Limit Theorem implies the test statistic is approximately Normal. Yes because the test statistic holds very closely for all error distribution forms and sample sizes, and Normality is never assumed. Yes, as long as the errors come from a distribution with finite mean and variance, due to the Central Limit Theorem. None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (1) is incorrect. While it is true that exact Normality is needed for the test statistics to exactly have a $T-$distribution, this exact Normality almost never holds in practice, and $T-$tests will still be used. Option (2) is incorrect. Hypothesis tests can, in theory, be used under any error model. It just may be difficult to come up with a reasonable test statistic and its associated distribution. Option (3) is incorrect. While it is true $\textbf{in general}$ that the central limit theorem will imply the test statistic has an approximately Normal distribution, this will not be the case for $\textbf{any}$ error model. For example, if the errors are Cauchy distributed then the central limit theorem will not hold. Option (4) is incorrect. To derive the exact distribution of the $T-$test statistic, Normality is assumed. Option (5) is correct. As long as the errors come from a distribution with finite mean and variance, the Central Limit Theorem will guarantee that in large sample sizes, the test statistic will be approximately $T$-distributed.

questions.title: FT Tests III
questions.problem: In OLS with $p > 1$ predictors, consider testing $H_0: \beta_1 \leq 0$ against $H_1: \beta_1 > 0$. Suppose that we calculate the $t-$statistic and the $F-$statistic for this test, and denote their values as $T_{s}$ and $F_{s}$ respectively. How do $T_{s}$ and $F_{s}$ relate to each other? $F_s = T_s^2$ $F_s = T_s$ $T_s = F_s^2$ $F_s = |T_s|$ In general, there is no relationship between $F_s$ and $T_s$. The $F$ statistic doesn't exist for this hypothesis test. The $T$ statistic doesn't exist for this hypothesis test.
questions.solution: The hypothesis test in this question is a composite hypothesis test, since the null hypothesis is that $\beta_{1} \leq 0$, rather than testing strict equality. Recall that the $F$ test is used to test if one model is a subset of another model. This means that it can only test null hypotheses in which the null is that a set of coefficients are exactly 0 or not. Thus, the $F$ statistic does not exist for this sort of hypothesis test and Option (6) is the correct answer.

questions.title: FT Tests IV
questions.problem: In OLS with $p > 1$ predictors, consider testing $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 0$ against $H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0$ or $\beta_2 \neq 0$. Suppose that we calculate the $t-$statistic and the $F-$statistic for this test, and denote their values as $T_{s}$ and $F_{s}$ respectively. How do $T_{s}$ and $F_{s}$ relate to each other? Consider what sort of null hypothesis the $T$ test is used for. $F = T^2$ $F = T$ $T = F^2$ $F = |T|$ In general, there is no relationship between $F$ and $T$. The $F$ statistic doesn't exist for this hypothesis test. The $T$ statistic doesn't exist for this hypothesis test.
questions.solution: The null hypothesis in this question is simultaneously testing whether or not multiple coefficients are equal to $0$. While the $F$ test is appropriate in this case, the $T$ test can only be used when a single coefficient is being tested. Thus, Option (7) is the correct answer.

questions.title: R-Squared Test
questions.problem: Suppose that you perform a regression using the model $Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}X + \epsilon$, and when checking the model diagnostics you see that the $R^{2}$ is equal to $0.99$. What does this imply about the result of the following test: $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ vs. $H_1: \beta_{1} \neq 0$? One should reject $H_0$ with this information. One should fail to reject $H_0$ with this information. It doesn't imply anything about the statistical significance of $\beta_1$. Both $\beta_{0}$ and $\beta_{1}$ are statistically significant. None of the above.

questions.title: Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov Limitations
questions.problem: Which of the following are limitations of the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test when used to compare two empirical distribution functions? It cannot be used if the data distributions are not normal. It is not applicable for very small sample sizes due to low power. It may be overly sensitive to outliers in the data. The test isn't applicable unless the data is standardized. None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (1) is incorrect. The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is distribution agnostic. That is, it can compare any (assumed continuous!) empirical distributions from two different datasets and conduct a hypothesis test on the equality of the distributions the datasets came from. Option (2) is correct. With too few data points, the distributions are poorly determined, so the test may have large differences in the empirical CDFs solely due to a lack of data. For example, imagine what data sampled from a normal distribution might look like if you only had 3 datapoints. Would you be able to tell the data came from a Normal distribution? Option (3) is correct. Just like many other tests on normality, the KS test is sensitive to outliers between the compared CDFs. Option (4) is incorrect. The test can be applied for data that is not standardized, but the test will detect differences in both mean and variance.

questions.title: Two-Sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov
questions.problem: Which of the following statements is true about the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test? It requires the assumption that the distributions being compared are continuous. It can be applied to testing both continuous and discrete distributions. It is sensitive to differences in both location and scale of the distributions. It requires the sample sizes of the two datasets being compared to be equal. None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (1) is correct. The KS test is designed for continuous distributions and compares the empirical distribution functions of the two samples. It assumes that the distributions are continuous to calculate the maximum difference between their CDFs. Applying the KS test to discrete distributions can lead to misleading results, as the nature of jumps in CDFs of discrete distributions affects the test statistic and its corresponding p-value. Option (2) is incorrect. While technically the KS test can be calculated for discrete data, it is not appropriate to do so because the test does not account for the discrete nature of distribution functions, which can create multiple issues in accuracy and interpretation. The test's assumptions and methodology are better suited for continuous data. Option (3) correct. The KS test is sensitive to all types of differences between distributions, including differences in location, scale, and shape. The test statistic, which is the maximum difference between the two empirical CDFs, captures any form of discrepancy between the distributions. Option (4) incorrect. The KS test does not require that the sample sizes of the two groups be equal. The test is valid for different sample sizes, although extreme disparities in sample sizes can affect the power of the test. The test statistic and the critical values can be adjusted according to the sample sizes, allowing for flexibility in comparing samples of unequal sizes.

questions.title: Invalid Ryan-Joiner
questions.problem: Under which of the following conditions would the Ryan-Joiner test likely be inappropriate? When the sample size is very large (e.g., over $5000$). When the data is ordinal. When the data contains multiple outliers. None of the above.
questions.solution: Option (1) is correct. Most normality tests, including the Ryan-Joiner test, are sensitive to large sample sizes. With a very large sample size, even very small deviations from normality can result in the test rejecting the null hypothesis (that the data are normally distributed). Thus, the Ryan-Joiner test might frequently indicate non-normality in large samples due to minor deviations that are statistically significant but not practically significant. Option (2) is correct. The Ryan-Joiner test assumes that data are continuous and measured on an interval or ratio scale, as it has to measure a correlation. When bucketing data together in an ordinal setting, much valuable information about the exact data points is lost. Option (3) is correct. The presence of outliers can significantly affect the outcome of the Ryan-Joiner test. This test, like many other normality tests, can be sensitive to outliers as they can skew the distribution and lead to incorrect conclusions about the normality of the dataset.

questions.title: Weighted Least Squares I
questions.problem: For $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $Y_i \mid \beta, \sigma^2 \sim N(\beta X_i,\sigma^2/w_i)$ independently, where $X_1,\dots, X_n, w_1,\dots, w_n$ are known constants. Note that $\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ are not known. Let $\hat{\beta}$ be the value of $\beta$ that minimizes $SSE(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta X_i)^2$. Which of the below is the correct expression for $\hat{\beta}$? $\dfrac{\sum w_{i} X_iY_i}{\sum X_i^2}$ $\dfrac{\sum w_{i} X_iY_i}{\sum w_{i}^{2} X_i^2}$ $\dfrac{\sum X_iY_i}{\sum X_i^2}$ $\dfrac{\sum X_iY_i}{\sum w_{i}^{2}X_i^2}$ $\dfrac{\sum w_iX_iY_i}{\sum w_iX_i^2}$

questions.title: Categorical Downside
questions.problem: Which of the following are some downsides of using categorical predictors? Categorical predictors may not make sense to standardize. Categorical predictors can't be used in an OLS model. Categorical predictors can contain a range of real values, and thus be less informative that the raw values themselves. Categorical predictors are necessarily ordered, and that must be dealt with in the model. Categorizing naturally continuous predictors makes you unable to recover the exact values of predictors in each category. None of the above.
questions.solution: The first answer choice is correct because the mean of the groups is not necessarily representative of the overall mean of the data. For example, suppose you collect $100$ data points and bucket them with $-1$ or $1$ according to the sign. If one were to get $50$ negative and $50$ positive data points, the mean of the bucketed data is $0$, as there are equal amounts of data with values $-1$ and $1$. However, this is misleading as it tells us nothing about the mean of the data that's underlying: All of the negative values could be like $-1$, while the positive values could be very large. The second choice is incorrect. One possible method to do this is one-hot encoding. The third choice is correct because each category contains a range of real values, so you may not know where in a given range your predictor is. This can decrease the accuracy of your model. The fourth choice is correct, and is often prevalent in survey data. People may have different interpretations of "high" or "low" levels of some metric (ex: amount of alcohol consumed, amount of hours of sleep, etc.), so this can lead to poor prediction. The fifth choice is correct by a similar reasoning to one: For example, if one is told a hurricane is Category $1$, one can't discern whether the wind speed was $75$ mph or $90$ mph from this information alone. This can abstract away useful information for the model.

questions.title: Perturbed Ridge
questions.problem: Suppose that you perform OLS and Ridge regression using the same data matrix, $X$. Denote the fitted coefficients as $\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ and $\hat{\beta}_{Ridge}$, respectively. Suppose that you then add some random noise to $X$ and perform each regression again, getting fitted coefficients $\hat{\beta}^{*}_{OLS}$ and $\hat{\beta}^{*}_{Ridge}$. In general, which do you expect to be larger, $||\hat{\beta}_{OLS} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{OLS}||$ or $||\hat{\beta}_{Ridge} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{Ridge}||$? $||\hat{\beta}_{OLS} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{OLS}|| \geq ||\hat{\beta}_{Ridge} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{Ridge}||$ since Ridge regression limits the size of the fitted regression coefficients. $||\hat{\beta}_{OLS} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{OLS}|| \geq ||\hat{\beta}_{Ridge} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{Ridge}||$ since Ridge stabilizes the regression estimates by adding a term to the diagonal of $X^{T}X$. $||\hat{\beta}_{OLS} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{OLS}|| \leq ||\hat{\beta}_{Ridge} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{Ridge}||$ since Ridge regression limits the size of the fitted regression coefficients. $||\hat{\beta}_{OLS} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{OLS}|| \leq ||\hat{\beta}_{Ridge} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{Ridge}||$ since Ridge stabilizes the regression estimates by adding a term to the diagonal of $X^{T}X$. $||\hat{\beta}_{OLS} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{OLS}|| = ||\hat{\beta}_{Ridge} - \hat{\beta}^{*}_{Ridge}||$ since the $X$ matrix is being changed by the same random amount for each of the regressions.

questions.title: Bayesian Lasso Prior
questions.problem: In the Bayesian formulation of Lasso regression, what prior distribution is assumed for $\beta$? Normal Exponential Cauchy Laplace Since the Lasso estimator has no closed form, it can't be obtained via assuming any prior on $\beta$. None of the above.

questions.title: Normal Coefficient Prior
questions.problem: Suppose that you perform Bayesian linear regression according to the standard assumptions, but additionally assume that $\beta \sim N(0, \alpha I)$ for some $\alpha > 0$. What effect is increasing $\alpha$ most likely to have on the fitted coefficients? Increasing $\alpha$ will cause the coefficients to become closer to the coefficients fitted by standard OLS. Increasing $\alpha$ will cause the coefficients to become larger in the positive direction Increasing $\alpha$ will cause the coefficients to become larger in the negative direction Increasing $\alpha$ will cause the coefficients to be closer to 0. Increasing $\alpha$ will not affect the fitted coefficients.

questions.title: Bayesian Regularization Advantage
questions.problem: What potential advantage is provided by using the Bayesian formulations of Lasso and Ridge regression? The Bayesian formulations can handle multicollinearity more effectively by providing point estimates. The Bayesian formulations provide interval estimates that quantify uncertainty about the coefficients. The Bayesian formulations automatically determine the optimal regularization parameter. The Bayesian formulations provide more accurate parameter estimates.
questions.solution: Option (1) is incorrect. The Bayesian formulation of Lasso and Ridge will behave equivalently to the optimization formulation, since both formulations will lead to the same estimate for $\beta$. Option (2) is correct. Since the Bayesian formulation involves the estimation of a posterior distribution, that is, the distribution of $\beta$ given $X$, it is possible to create interval estimates for $\beta$ using this distribution. Option (3) is incorrect. Just as in the optimization formulation, the optimal value for the regularization parameter must be found according to some criteria. Option (4) is incorrect. As mentioned, the estimate of $\beta$ from Bayesian formulation of Lasso and Ridge is equivalent to the optimization formulation.

questions.title: Predictors and Residuals I
questions.problem: Suppose that an OLS regression $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ is performed to obtain $\hat{y} = X\hat{\beta}$. Compute $\cov{\hat{y}}{e}$, where $e$ is the vector of residuals, and $\hat{y}$ is the vector of fitted values, under the standard regression modeling assumptions. $\sigma^2I_n$ $0 \in \R^{n \times n}$ $0 \in \R^n$ $\sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$ None of the above
questions.solution:
Solution 1: $\begin{align*}
    \hat{y} = X\hat{\beta}_{OLS} =  X(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty 
\end{align*}$ $\begin{align*}
    e = y - \hat{y} = y - X\hat{\beta}_{OLS} = y - X(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty
\end{align*}$ $\begin{align*}
    \cov{\hat{y}}{e} &= \cov{(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty}{(I - X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T)y}\\
    &= (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\cov{y}{y}(I - X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T)^{T}\\
    &= \sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1}X^T(I - X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T)\\
    &= \sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1}X^T - \sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1}X^TX(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\\
    &= 0    
\end{align*}$ where $\cov{y}{y} = \var{y} = \sigma^{2} I$. Solution 2: $\hat{y}$ is a linear function of $y$ and $X$. Since $e = y - \hat{y}$, and $\hat{y}$ is the projection of $y$ onto the column space of $X$, we know that $\langle \hat{y}, e \rangle = 0$. Since $\ev{XY}$ denotes expectation, and $\hat{y}$ and $e$ are orthogonal, $\ev{\hat{y}e}= 0$. Therefore $\cov{\hat{y}}{e}$: $\begin{align*}
    \cov{\hat{y}}{e} &= \ev{\hat{y}e} - \ev{\hat{y}}\ev{e} \\
    &= \ev{\hat{y}e} - \ev{\hat{y}}0 \\
    &= \ev{\hat{y}e} \\
    &= 0
\end{align*}$ since $\ev{e} = \ev{y - \hat{y}} = X\beta - X\beta = 0$.

questions.title: Orthogonal Covariates
questions.problem: Suppose we perform ridge regression $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ on $p$ predictors with no intercept with regularization parameter $\lambda$, where the matrix $X$ is orthogonal, with each column having square norm equal to $n$. How are the ridge coefficients related to the OLS coefficients, if at all? $\hat{\beta}_R = \frac{1}{\lambda}\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ $\hat{\beta}_R = \frac{1}{n+\lambda}\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ $\hat{\beta}_R = \frac{n}{n+\lambda}\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ $\hat{\beta}_R = \frac{\lambda}{n+\lambda}\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ $\hat{\beta}_R = \frac{p}{p+\lambda}\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ $\hat{\beta}_R = \frac{\lambda}{p+\lambda}\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ There is no general relationship between the two fitted coefficients.
questions.solution:
If the matrix $X$ is orthogonal, $X^TX = nI_{p}$, as there are $p$ columns that are orthogonal, and each column has norm equal to $n$. Therefore, the ridge estimate is given by $\begin{align*}
    \hat{\beta}_R &= (X^TX + \lambda I_p)^{-1}X^Ty\\
    &= ((n+\lambda)I_p)^{-1}X^Ty\\
    &= \dfrac{1}{n+\lambda}X^Ty\\
    &= \dfrac{n}{n+\lambda} \cdot (nI_p)^{-1}X^Ty\\
    &= \dfrac{n}{n+\lambda} \cdot (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\\
    &= \dfrac{n}{n+\lambda} \cdot \hat{\beta}_{OLS}
\end{align*}$ The idea to perform the manipulation with $\frac{n}{n+\lambda}$ in the fourth equality is because of the known form of $\hat{\beta}_{OLS} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty$. Thus, Option (3) is correct.

questions.title: Estimating Beta
questions.problem: In the standard linear regression model, $Y = X\beta + \epsilon$, there are many possible unbiased estimators for $\beta$, so why is $\hat{\beta}_{OLS}$ commonly used? Select all that apply. It has a geometric interpretation via a projection onto the subspace spanned by the data. It is the MLE for $\beta$ under IID Normal errors. It has the lowest variance of any unbiased estimator for $\beta$. It has the lowest variance of any linear unbiased estimator for $\beta$. It has the lowest variance of any estimator for $\beta$.

questions.title: Uniform MLE II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1\mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim \text{Unif}[-\theta,\theta]$ IID. If it exists, find the MLE of $\theta$ with the dataset $\{1,2,3,-4,2\}$. If it doesn't, report $-1$. NOTE: It may be helpful to solve Uniform MLE I before attempting this question.

questions.title: Uniform MLE III
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1\mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim \text{Unif}(0,\theta)$ IID. If it exists, find the MLE of $\theta$, $\hat{\theta}_{MLE}$ with the data $\{1,2,3,4,0.5\}$. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$.
questions.solution: This question is the exact same as "Uniform MLE I", but the interval is now open. The computations are exactly the same, but we have an open interval $(0,\theta)$ instead of closed interval $[0,\theta]$. To maximize the likelihood, we must choose the smallest $\theta$ satisfying $\theta > \max(x_1,\dots, x_n)$. We don't have $\geq$ now because it must be the case that $\theta > x_i$ for each $1 \leq i \leq n$, rather than $\theta \geq x_i$. The issue is that there is no smallest $\theta$ satisfying the condition: We can't select $\theta = \max(x_1,\dots, x_n)$ itself because that isn't strictly greater than the maximum, but for any choice of $\theta' > \max(x_1,\dots, x_n)$, we can select $\theta'' = \frac{\theta' + \max(x_1,\dots,x_n)}{2} < \theta'$ and larger than $\max(x_1,\dots, x_n)$. Since there is no "smallest $\theta$" satisfying our condition, the MLE does not exist.

questions.title: Uniform MLE IV
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim \text{Unif}[\theta, \theta +1]$ IID. If it exists, find the MLE of $\theta$ with the data $\{1,1.5,1.2,2\}$. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$.

questions.title: Uniform MLE V
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim \text{Unif}[a,b]$ IID, where $\theta = (a,b)$ is unknown. If it exists, find the MLE of $\theta, \hat{\theta}_{MLE} = (\hat{a}_{MLE}, \hat{b}_{MLE})$ with the data $\{1,2,3,4,-5\}$ and report $\hat{a}_{MLE}\hat{b}_{MLE}$. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$. NOTE: It may be helpful to complete Uniform MLE II before attempting this question.

questions.title: Normal MLE II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ IID, where $\mu$ is known but $\sigma^{2}$ is unknown. If it exists, find the MLE of $\sigma^2$ with the data $\{1,-2,4,-1\}$ and $\mu = 1$. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$.

questions.title: Normal MLE III
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ IID, where $\theta = (\mu,\sigma)$ is unknown. Find the MLE of $\theta, \hat{\theta}_{MLE} = (\hat{\mu}_{MLE}, \hat{\sigma}_{MLE})$ with the data $\{1,-2,4,-1\}$ and report $\hat{\mu}_{MLE}\hat{\sigma}_{MLE}$ to the nearest thousandth. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$.

questions.title: Normal Fisher Information I
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \mu, \dots, X_n \mid \mu \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ IID, where $\sigma^2 > 0$ is known. Find the Fisher Information of $\mu$, $I(\mu)$. What is the value of the Fisher Information when $\mu = 7, \sigma^{2} = 5$, and $n = 10$?

questions.title: Normal Fisher Information II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \sigma^2, \dots, X_n \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ IID, where $\mu$ is known. Find the Fisher Information of $\sigma^2$, $I(\sigma^2)$. What is the value of the Fisher Information when $n= 10, \mu = 2$, and $\sigma^{2} = 2$?

questions.title: Normal Fisher Information III
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \sigma, \dots, X_n \mid \sigma \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ IID, where $\mu$ is known. Find the Fisher Information of $\sigma$, $I(\sigma)$. What is the value of the Fisher Information when $n= 10, \mu = 2$, and $\sigma^{2} = 2$?

questions.title: Normal Fisher Information IV
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \theta, \dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ IID, where $\theta = (\mu,\sigma^2)$ is unknown. Find the Fisher Information of $\theta$, $I(\mu,\sigma^2)$, and report the determinant when $n = 16$ and $\sigma^2 = 4$. If it doesn't exist, report $-1$.

questions.title: Variable Ratio
questions.problem: Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be independent random variables with $\frac{\ev{X_1}}{\sqrt{\var{X_1}}} = 3, \frac{\ev{X_2}}{\sqrt{\var{X_2}}} = 1,$ and $\var{X_1} = \var{X_2}$. For $0 \leq w \leq 1$, define $Z_w = wX_1 + (1-w)X_2$. Find the value of $w$ such that $\frac{\ev{Z_w}}{\sqrt{\var{Z_w}}}$ is maximized.
questions.solution: The best approach to this problem is to explicitly compute $\ev{Z_w}$ and $\var{Z_w}$ as a function of $w$, and then we can try to maximize the function as stated in the question. We can do this because $Z_w$ is known in terms of $X_1$ and $X_2$, who have known means and variances. By linearity of expectation, $\ev{Z_w} = \ev{wX_1 + (1-w)X_2} = w\ev{X_1} + (1-w)\ev{X_2} = 3w\sigma_1 + (1-w)\sigma_1 = (1 + 2W)\sigma_1$ In the above, $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\var{X_1}} = \sqrt{\var{X_2}}$ is the standard deviation. We can write the expectation in this way because of the relations given in the question. As for the variance, we can similarly say $\var{Z_w} = \var{wX_1 + (1-w)X_2} = (w^2 + (1-w)^2)\sigma_1^2 = (1-2w(1-w))\sigma_1^2$ Plugging these expressions into the function in the question, say $S(w)$, $S(w) = \dfrac{\ev{Z_w}}{\sqrt{\var{Z_w}}} = \dfrac{(1+2w)\sigma_1}{\sqrt{(1-2w(1-w))\sigma_1^2}} = \dfrac{1+2w}{\sqrt{1-2w(1-w)}}$ To optimize this function in $w$, we should take the derivative and set it equal to $0$. This yields $S'(w) = \dfrac{3-4w}{\left(1 - 2w(1-w)\right)^{3/2}} = 0 \iff 3-4w = 0 \iff w = 3/4$ We can see that this is a maximum because the derivative is positive for $w < 3/4$ and negative for $w > 3/4$. Therefore, $3/4$ is the answer.

questions.title: Flippy RPS
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play rock, paper, scissors (RPS) with the following twist: Before each turn, Bob must flip a fair coin. If it lands heads, he must play rock on that given turn. The winner pays the loser $\$1$, and no transfer of money occurs in a tie. Alice does not know the outcome of Bob's coin flip. Under optimal play from both players, what's the expected value of the game for Alice?
questions.solution: In these RPS questions, we often need to work with the indifference principle to find the optimal strategy. Let's first get intuition for the problem and what the optimal strategy should look like for each player. Given Alice's advantage, she should have a strategy that yields positive expected value. Since Bob plays rock at least $50\%$ of the time (whenever the coin is heads and any additional probability in his strategy), if Alice is to play scissors, she loses at least $50\%$ of the time. Given that she loses at least $50\%$ of the time, it's optimal for Alice to never play scissors. In other words, she should only play rock and paper. Since Alice is to never play scissors, it's not optimal for Bob to play rock more than what is guaranteed by the coin, as Bob will never win with rock, making it a negative expected value choice. By the above, we've concluded two things: Alice should only play paper and rock. In his strategy that excludes the coin flip, Bob should only play paper and scissors. Let $p_A, p_B, r_A,$ and $s_B$ be the probabilities at which Alice and Bob play paper $(p)$, rock $(r)$, and scissors $(s)$. From the above discussion, $s_A = 0$ and $r_B = 1/2$, as Alice never plays scissors and Bob never plays rock in addition to the coin flip. Thus, we have that $p_A + r_A = 1$ and $p_B + s_B = 1/2$. The indifference principle here states that, in an optimal strategy, Alice and Bob should be indifferent to playing either option, regardless of the other player's action. Mathematically, the expected profit/loss for each player should be constant, regardless of what the other player selects. Solving for Bob's probabilities first, we compute the expected payout for Alice given her choice. If she chooses rock, she wins $\$1$ when Bob plays scissors, and loses $\$1$ when he plays paper. Nothing happens when he plays rock, so $\ev{A \mid \text{Rock}} = 1 \cdot s_B - 1 \cdot p_B = s_B - p_B$ Similarly, if Alice plays paper, she wins $\$1$ when Bob plays rock (probability $1/2$) and loses $\$1$ when he plays scissors (probability $s_B$). Therefore, $\ev{A \mid \text{Paper}} = 1 \cdot 1/2 - 1 \cdot s_B = 1/2 - s_B$ The indifference principle states that the two expected values above are equal, as Alice should be indifferent to playing rock and paper, so the expected values should be equal. This yields $s_B - p_B = 1/2 - s_B \iff p_B = 2s_B - 1/2$ Since $p_B + s_B = 1/2$, we can substitute the above in and conclude $s_B = 1/3$ and $p_B = 1/6$. This result means that, in the long-run, Bob plays rock, paper, and scissors with limiting proportions $1/2$ (solely by the coin flip), $1/6$ (given the coin isn't heads, probability $1/3$), and $1/3$ (given the coin isn't heads, probability $2/3$). We now repeat the same analysis from Bob's perspective. Bob should be indifferent to playing paper or scissors, since he can't control when he plays rock. If Bob plays scissors, he wins $\$1$ when Alice plays paper (probability $p_A$) and loses $\$1$ when Alice plays rock (probability $r_A$). Therefore, $\ev{B \mid \text{Scissors}} = 1 \cdot p_A  - 1 \cdot r_A = p_A - r_A$ Similarly, if Bob plays paper, he wins $\$1$ when Alice plays rock (probability $r_A$), and loses $\$1$ when Alice plays scissors (probability $0$). Therefore, $\ev{B \mid \text{Paper}} = 1 \cdot r_A - 1 \cdot 0 = r_A$ The indifference principle states that Bob should be indifferent to playing scissors or paper, so we set the two equations above equal under the additional constraint $p_A + r_A = 1$ to yield $r_A = p_A - r_A \iff p_A = 2r_A \iff r_A = 1/3, p_A = 2/3$ Now that we've found the optimal probabilities, what is Alice's expected payout? Plugging in $s_B = 1/3$ and $p_B = 1/6$ into the equations for Alice's expected payout, by the principle of indifference, Alice's expected payout, regardless of what Bob does, is $1/6$. Therefore, Alice's expected gain is $1/6$ from this game. Note that we did not actually need to solve for Alice's strategy here, as the expected value was computed by directly plugging in probabilities to the first pair of equations.

questions.title: Expected Exponentials
questions.problem: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ IID. For any $t > 0$, let $N_t = \min\{n: X_1 + \dots + X_n > t\}$. Find $\ev{N_t}$ when $\lambda = 2$ and $t = 4$.
questions.solution: The number of random variables that need to be added to exceed $t$ is exactly $1$ more than the expected number of random variables that can be summed to be at most $t$. For example, if, on average, $3$ random variables sum to at most $1$, it takes $4$ random variables (on average) to exceed $1$. We state this because we can relate this problem to the Poisson process: The Poisson process has interarrival times that are Exponentially distributed. The number of renewals of the Poisson process by time $t$ (i.e. the number of random variables added such that $X_1 + \dots + X_n \leq t$) is $\text{Poisson}(\lambda t)$ distributed by the definition of a Poisson process. The mean of this distribution is $\lambda t$, so the mean number of renewals by time $t$ (hence, in this case, mean number of random variables who sum to at most $t$) is $\lambda t$. It takes exactly one additional for the sum to exceed $t$, so $\lambda t + 1$ is the expected number of Exponential random variables needed to exceed $t$. With the specified values, the answer is $9$.

questions.title: Close Squares
questions.problem: Two distinct squares are selected from an $n \times n$ grid of squares, where $n \geq 2$. Find the probability that the two squares share a side when $n = 8$.

questions.title: Increasing Subsequences
questions.problem: Consider the set $[2n] = \{1,2,\dots, 2n\}$ for some positive integer $n$. How many permutations of $[2n]$ $(a_1,\dots, a_{2n})$ are such that the two subsequences of all even-valued elements and all odd-valued elements are monotonic (either strictly increasing or decreasing)? Report the answer when $n = 5$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we need to create a permutation of the elements in $[2n]$ such that the two subsequences of odd-valued elements and even-valued elements are monotonic. To create the monotonic sequences, two things must happen: The locations of the even-valued elements and odd-valued elements must be selected. The elements must be arranged. WLOG, we can start with the even-valued elements, as there are an equal amount of odd-valued and even-valued elements in $[2n]$. $n$ of these elements are even, so we must select the $n$ spots for them to go in. Since we are only selecting a subset of the indices to assign the even-valued elements to go to, the order of selection of places is irrelevant, so there are $\binom{2n}{n}$ ways to pick the $n$ spots from the $2n$ that the even elements lie. Once those are selected, there are two arrangements of the values onto the blanks: Either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing. Once the locations of the even elements are selected, the odd elements go in the other $n$ spots of the permutation that are currently open. Therefore, there is no flexibility in how to choose the spots. There are two ways to arrange the odd elements in these remaining spots: Strictly increasing or decreasing. By the multiplication principle, the total number of permutations that yield two monotonic subsequences of even and odd integers is $2 \cdot 2 \cdot \binom{2n}{n} = 4\binom{2n}{n}$. With $n = 5$, the answer is $1008$.

questions.title: Either-Or Sequence
questions.problem: A fair coin is repeatedly flipped until the sequence $HHT$ or $HTH$ appears. Find the expected number of flips performed.
questions.solution:
Let $E_0$ denote the expected number of flips from the start. On any flip, we get $H$ or $T$ each with probability 1/2. If the first flip is $H$, we move to state $E_H$. If $T$, we reset to $E_0$. Thus $E_0 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}E_H + \dfrac{1}{2}E_0$. From state H, with probability $1$/2 we get $H$ (state $HH$), and with probability 1/2 we get $T$ (state $HT$). From $HH$, if we flip $T$ we complete $HHT$ and are done. If we flip $H$, we stay at $HH$. The expected flips to leave this state is $\geom{1/2}$ with mean $2$. So $E_{HH} = 2$. From $HT$, with probability $1/2$ we flip $H$ completing $HTH$ (done in $1$ flip), and with probability 1/2 we flip $T$ returning to $E_0$. So $E_{HT} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}E_0$. We have $E_H = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}E_{HH} + \dfrac{1}{2}E_{HT}$. Solving the system gives $E_0 = 6$.

Alternatively, let $E$ denote the expected number of flips. After $2$ flips (expected, to get the first $H$), with probability $1/2$ we get another $H$ giving $HH$, and with probability $1/2$ we get $T$ giving $HT$. From $HH$: with probability $1/2$ we get $T$ completing $HHT$ in $1$ flip; with probability $1/2$ we get $H$ staying at $HH$ (expected $2$ more flips for a $T$). From $HT$: with probability $1/2$ we get $T$ giving $HTT$, which has probability $1/4$ of occurring. Then in $1$ flip of $T$ we restart. But with probability $1/4$ from $HT$ we get $H$ completing $HTH$ in $1$ flip. Combining: $E = 2 + 1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 2 + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (1 + E) + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 1 \iff E = 6$.
questions.hint: Consider the states: no progress, after H, after HH, after HT. The sequences HHT and HTH both start with H.

questions.title: Doubly Even Heads II
questions.problem: A coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip is repeatedly flipped until the sequence $HH$ appears for the first time. Find the probability that the coin is flipped an even amount of times. Report the answer when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: The approach of the second solution to the previous part no longer works, as the outcomes aren't all equally likely. This is why we separated out the specific case of $p = 1/2$ for the first part of this problem. We must use the Markov chain approach described in the previous part for this question. Let $h$ be the probability that we obtain $HH$ for the first time in an even amount of flips. By the discussion of the previous part, the key strategy is to condition on the outcome of the first flip, based on whether it is $H$ or $T$. If the first flip is $H$, we will see that additional conditioning is needed. If the first flip is $T$ (probability $1-p$), this does not contribute to us getting $HH$ at all, so it's as if the process starts all over again with the counter set at $1$. Obtaining $HH$ in an even amount of flips from here would amount to the same situation of obtaining $HH$ in an odd number of flips from before: We need an odd number of additional flips past the $T$ to get $HH$ in an even total. The distribution of the number of additional flips is unchanged because of the memorylessness property of the Geometric distribution. Therefore, the conditional probability of landing $HH$ in an even number of flips in this case is $1-h$, since this is the probability that $HH$ is obtained in an odd number of flips from the start (must be either even or odd, and even with probability $h$). If $H$ is obtained on the first flip, there are two cases: $HH$ and $HT$. If it's $HH$ (probability $p^2$), we're immediately done, and no further turns are needed. If it's $HT$ (probability $p(1-p)$), we've used two flips, and the $T$ cancels any overlap, so it's as if we started the process again with the counter beginning at $2$. We need an even number of additional flips to get an even total, and this occurs with probability $h$ by the above discussion. By the Law of Total Probability, $h = (1-p)\cdot(1-h) + p^2 \cdot 1 + p(1-p) \cdot h \iff h =  \dfrac{p^2 - p + 1}{p^2 - 2p + 2} = \dfrac{p^2 + (1-p)}{p^2 + 2(1-p)}$. This solution satisfies some properties we would expect: As $p \rightarrow 1$, the answer tends to $1$, as it's nearly guaranteed that the first two flips will be $HH$. Similarly, as $p \rightarrow 0$, the answer tends to $1/2$, which is intuitive because the advantage of $HH$ appearing on the first trial, which inflates the probability of it showing on an even number of flips, vanishes. This advantage goes away because it takes a very long time to see heads, so the outcomes with few flips are quite improbable. Lastly, with $p = 1/2$, we get the answer of $3/5$ from the previous part. With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $7/13$.
questions.hint: Use a Markov chain approach. Condition on whether the first flip is H or T, then further condition within the H case.

questions.title: Randomly Correlated
questions.problem: Fix an integer $n \geq 2$. Let $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n$ be identically distributed random variables with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. The random variables are pairwise correlated with some common random coefficient $\rho \sim \unif{-\frac{1}{n-1}}{1}$. Compute $\ev{\var{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}}$. Report the answer when $n = 10, \mu = 4,$ and $\sigma^2 = 9$.
questions.solution:
In this question, $\var{X_1 + \dots + X_n}$ is indeed random, as their pairwise correlations are random, which influence the variance of the sum. If the pairwise correlation $\rho$ was known, it wouldn't be hard to compute the variance of this sum, since we can use our standard formula for the variance of a sum. Thus, the appropriate step is to apply Law of Total Expectation by conditioning on $\rho$. By Law of Total Expectation, $\ev{\var{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}} = \ev{\ev{\var{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i} \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} \rho}}$. Given $\rho$, we can compute the variance via the variance of a sum formula: $$\begin{align*}
    \ev{\var{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i} \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} \rho} &= \ev{\sum_{i=1}^n \var{X_i} + \sum_{i < j} \cov{X_i}{X_j} \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} \rho}\\
    &= \ev{\sum_{i=1}^n \sigma^2 + \sum_{i < j} \rho \sigma^2 \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} \rho}\\
    &= \ev{n\sigma^2 + n(n-1)\rho \sigma^2 \hspace{3pt} \Big| \hspace{3pt} \rho}\\
    &= n\sigma^2(1 + (n-1)\rho)
\end{align*}$$ The expectation reduces from the third line to the fourth because everything is non-random and we've conditioned on $\rho$. Therefore, we can conclude $\ev{\var{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}} = \ev{n\sigma^2(1 + (n-1)\rho)} = n\sigma^2\left(1 + (n-1)\ev{\rho}\right) = n\sigma^2\left(1 + (n-1) \cdot \frac{1 - \frac{1}{n-1}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{n^2\sigma^2}{2}$. This result is exactly the variance of the sum if the pairwise correlation is $\frac{n-2}{2(n-1)}$, the average value of $\rho$. It isn't a coincidence! The variance depends linearly on $\rho$, so we could have just found the result by computing the expected value of $\rho$ and plugging it in directly. With the specified values, the answer is $450$.
questions.hint: Use Law of Total Expectation conditioning on rho. The variance of a sum formula involves pairwise covariances. The expected value of rho under the given uniform distribution simplifies things.

questions.title: Tiny Card
questions.problem: $n$ cards labelled $1$ to $n$ are distributed into two piles, say $A$ and $B$, with each card put into the piles uniformly at random and independently of other cards. Find the expected value of the minimum card in pile $A$. If there are no cards in a given pile, we say the minimum is $0$. Report the answer when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we are looking at the expected value of the minimum of some quantity. We don't know the exact distribution of the minimum, so directly computing via LOTUS is infeasible. The other main technique we know for computing expectations is the tail summation $\ev{X} = \dtailsum{X}$. The event $\{X \geq k\}$ is easy to interpret: The minimum card in the pile $A$ is at least $k$, which exactly means that cards $1$ to $k-1$ are in the other pile, and there is at least one card in pile $A$. This is an event that's easy to compute the probability of, so we should apply the tail summation method. As stated above, to evaluate $\prob{X \geq k}$, we only need to find the probability that cards $1$ to $k-1$ are in pile $B$, and at least one of cards $k$ to $n$ are in pile $A$. The second condition is to ensure that the pile is not empty. There is probability $1/2$ per trial of a given card going into pile $B$. By independence, the probability that all of the cards $1$ to $k-1$ go into pile $B$ is $1/2^{k-1}$. As for the second condition, we need at least one of cards $k$ to $n$ to be in pile $A$, as the pile can't be empty. Since we are looking to evaluate an "at least one" probability, it's typically easier to compute the complementary probability, which is that none of the cards $k$ to $n$ are in pile $A$. There are $n-(k-1)$ cards ranging in value from $k$ to $n$, so the probability that all of them are in pile $B$ is $1/2^{n-(k-1)}$. Thus, the probability at least one card is in pile $A$ is $1 - 1/2^{n-(k-1)}$. Multiplying this probability with the one above, we find that $\prob{X \geq k} = \dfrac{1}{2^{k-1}}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^{n-(k-1)}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2^{k-1}} - \dfrac{1}{2^n}$. We can also compute the probability in a different way. If pile $A$ is empty, then it most definitely does not contain the cards of ranks $1$ to $k-1$. Defining the two events $E$ that pile $A$ is empty and $A_k$ that cards $1$ to $k-1$ are not in pile $A$, we essentially said that $E \subseteq A_k$. The event that the minimum in pile $A$ is at least $k$ is $\{X \geq k\} = A_k \cap E^c$ by the discussion from two paragraphs ago. Since we are looking to evaluate the probability of one and NOT another, we use the standard subset decomposition $\prob{X \geq k} = \prob{A_k \cap E^c} = \prob{A_k} - \prob{A_k \cap E}$. The first probability is exactly what we found above, $1/2^{k-1}$. Since $E \subseteq A_k$, the second term is just $\prob{E} = 1/2^n$, as each of the $n$ cards go into pile $B$ with probability $1/2$. Substituting in yields the same result. Regardless of your methodology, plugging into the summation yields $\ev{X} = \sum_{k=1}^n \left(\dfrac{1}{2^{k-1}} - \dfrac{1}{2^n}\right) = \dfrac{1 - \frac{1}{2^n}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} - \dfrac{n}{2^n}= 2 - \dfrac{n+2}{2^n}$. We stop the upper bound at $n$ because the minimum of the $n$ cards can't be larger than $n$. As a sanity check, with $n = 1$, we get $1/2$, which makes sense: The card is in pile $A$ with probability $1/2$, in which the minimum is $1$, and otherwise it's $0$. Additionally, as $n \rightarrow \infty$, the expected value converges to $2$, which also makes sense: When taking the limit, we are essentially looking at the first trial at which the card goes into pile $A$, which would be $\geom{1/2}$ distributed, and this has mean $2$. With $n = 10$, the answer is $2 - \frac{12}{1024} = \frac{509}{256}$.
questions.hint: Use the tail summation formula for expectations. The event that the minimum is at least k means cards 1 through k-1 are all in pile B.

questions.title: MGF Moments II
questions.problem: Suppose $X$ is a random variable with MGF given by $M_X(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{1 - \theta^2/2}$ for $|\theta| < \sqrt{2}$. If possible, find $\ev{\cos(X)}$. If it's not possible, report the answer of $-1$.
questions.solution: To evaluate $\ev{\cos(X)}$, we need some way to relate $\cos(X)$ to the moments of $X$. From the first part, we know all the moments, so can we relate them? The answer is yes! Just as we formed the Taylor series of the MGF, we can look at the Taylor series expansion of $\cos(x)$, as that would express it as a polynomial. Namely, $\cos(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-1)^{k}x^{2k}}{(2k)!}$. Plugging in $x$ as $X$ and taking expectations on both sides, we get $\ev{\cos(X)} = \ev{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-1)^kX^{2k}}{(2k)!}} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-1)^k}{(2k)!}\ev{X^{2k}} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{(-1)^k}{(2k)!} \cdot \dfrac{(2k)!}{2^k}$. Bringing in the expected value technically requires justification, since it's an infinite sum. However, for the purposes of interviews, we can assume that linearity of expectation holds fine for the infinite case. If you're interested in learning more, search up Fubini's Theorem. In the last step, we plugged in our expression for $\ev{X^{2k}}$ from the first part. We see that the $(2k)!$ terms cancel, and the remaining sum is quite simple: $\ev{\cos(X)} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^k = \dfrac{1}{1-(-1/2)} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
questions.hint: Use the Taylor series of cos(x) and relate it to the moments of X.

questions.title: Uniformly Correlated
questions.problem: Suppose that $X,Y \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Define $U = \min(X,Y)$ and $V = \max(X,Y)$. Evaluate $\cov{U}{V}$.
questions.solution: There does not appear to be a short and slick trick to computing the covariance, so the definition would be the most appropriate approach. Intuitively, we expect this covariance to be positive, as an increase in the value of the minimum, for example, limits the maximum to only be larger values, so we'd expect an increase (on average) in the maximum as well. Writing out the calculation, we get $\cov{U}{V} = \ev{UV} - \ev{U}\ev{V}$. Calculating $\ev{U}$ and $\ev{V}$ is quite easy. One can note any of the following three facts: If $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are IID $\unif{0}{1}$, then the $i$th order statistic $X_{(i)} \sim \bet{i}{n-i+1}$. If $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are IID $\unif{0}{1}$, the values break up the interval $(0,1)$ into $n+1$ exchangeable regions. Since $U$ and $V$ are non-negative, we can write $\ev{U} = \int_0^1 \prob{U \geq u}~du$, and likewise with $V$. Regardless of your method, it's quick to see that $\ev{U} = 1/3$ and $\ev{V} = 2/3$. As for $\ev{UV}$, one could note either of the following facts: Regardless of the values of $X$ and $Y$, $UV = XY$, as one of $X$ and $Y$ is the minimum, while the other is the maximum. Multiplying the minimum and maximum just permutes $X$ and $Y$. The joint PDF of the $i$th and $j$th order statistic of IID random variables with PDF $f(x)$ and CDF $F(x)$ is given by $\binom{n}{i-1,1,j-i-1,1,n-j}(F(x))^{i-1}f(x)(F(y) - F(x))^{j-i-1}f(y)(1-F(y))^{n-j}$. In this case, $f(x) = 1$ and $F(x) = x$. We will do the computations for both approaches. If you recognize the first fact, $\ev{UV} = \ev{XY} = \ev{X}\ev{Y} = 1/4$. We can split it because $X$ and $Y$ are independent. This observation is quite powerful and makes life easy. As for most people, you may take the second approach. The joint PDF of $U$ and $V$ is given by $f_{U,V}(u,v) = \binom{2}{0,1,0,1,0}1 \cdot 1 = 2$. As for the support, we require that $0 < U < V < 1$ by definition, since the maximum must always be at least as large as the minimum, so $f_{u,v}(u,v) = 2I_{(0,1)}(u)I_{(u,1)}(v)$. We seek to compute $\ev{UV}$. This is easiest by LOTUS, as we know the joint PDF now. This yields $\ev{UV} = \int_0^1 \int_{u}^1 2uv~dv~du = \int_0^1 u(1-u^2)~du = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}$. Regardless of your methodology, we find that $\cov{U}{V} = 1/4 - 1/3 \cdot 2/3 = 1/36$.
questions.hint: Use the definition of covariance. Compute E[U], E[V], and E[UV] separately. Note that UV = XY regardless of which is the min or max.

questions.title: Ordered Sum
questions.problem: Let $X_1,\dots, X_n$ be IID random variables with finite expectation $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Denote the $n$ order statistics corresponding to the $X_i$ random variables as $O_1,\dots, O_n$. If possible, when $n = 5, \mu = 4,$ and $\sigma^2 = 9$, evaluate $\ev{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n O_i}$. If it's not possible, report $-1$.
questions.solution: At first glance, this problem seems to be intractable. How can we make a claim in such generality when we have no idea about any distributional form of the $X_i$ random variables? A first thought would be to look at the PDFs of the order statistics, but we would need the joint distribution of all $n$ order statistics, which could take a very difficult form. Just like common advice on dating apps, we should look at what's on the inside the expectation: the sum of the order statistics. $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n O_i$ sums up all $n$ order statistics. Since we consider all $n$ order statistics, each of the $X_i$ random variables corresponds to exactly one of the $O_j$ random variables, regardless of the values. For example, with $n = 3$, if $X_1 = 5, X_2 = 7,$ and $X_3 = 2$, then $O_1 = X_3, O_2 = X_1,$ and $O_3 = X_2$. In other words, no matter what the values of $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are, ordering them is just a permutation of the values. Since the $O_j$ random variables are just permuted versions of the $X_i$ random variables, it's very natural to see that $\sum_{i=1}^n O_i = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. This is exactly the key break we needed, as the LHS is quite easy to evaluate the expectation of! Namely, $\ev{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n O_i} = \ev{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n X_i} = \sum_{i=1}^n \ev{X_i} = n\mu$. With the specified values, the answer is $20$.
questions.hint: The sum of the order statistics equals the sum of the original random variables. Ordering is just a permutation.

questions.title: Sum 15
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play the following game: Each player selects a distinct integer from $[9] = \{1,2,\dots, 9\}$ at each turn. The first player that obtains $3$ numbers that sum to $15$ wins. Alice gets to choose whether she selects first or second. Assuming both players are optimal, what should Alice choose? First to act / Second to act / Alice is indifferent.
questions.solution:
The goal of both players is to select $3$ integers that sum to $15$. Here are the possible ways to get $15$ from $3$ distinct integers, which can be found by brute force: $$\begin{align*}
    15 &= 1 + 6 + 8\\
    &= 1 + 5 + 9\\
    &= 2 + 4 + 9\\
    &= 2 + 5 + 8\\
    &= 2 + 6  + 7\\
    &= 3 + 4 + 8\\
    &= 3 + 5 + 7\\
    &= 4 + 5 + 6
\end{align*}$$ In the above, we enumerated by the lowest integer in the winning path. It's helpful to visualize this as a tic-tac-toe grid, where each row, column, and diagonal sum to $15$. This works because there are exactly $8$ winning sequences, and there are exactly $8$ ways to win in a tic-tac-toe grid. Since $5$ occurs in $4$ "winning sequences", and the middle spot of a tic-tac-toe grid has $4$ winning sequences, $5$ must go in the middle. The corners each have $3$ winning sequences they contribute to, so these must be $2,4,6,$ and $8$. The middle squares on the exterior each contribute to $2$ winning sequences, which are $1,3,7,$ and $9$ here. By placing into the grid and arranging such that the sums are actually formed, we get the following result: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
    \hline
    8 & 1 & 6 \\ \hline
    3 & 5 & 7 \\ \hline
    4 & 9 & 2 \\ \hline
\end{array}$$ Under optimal play in tic-tac-toe, the best result is a draw. Therefore, neither player will ever win! Accordingly, the answer is "Alice is indifferent".
questions.hint: Map this game to tic-tac-toe using a magic square. Each row, column, and diagonal of the 3x3 magic square sums to 15.

questions.title: Friends of Friends
questions.problem: How many friends do your friends have? Formally, let's define a social network as a graph of undirected edges $G = (V, E)$, where $V$ is the set of vertices and $E$ is the set of edges. The vertices $V$ represent individuals in the social network, and the edges $E$ represent friendships: Vertex $v_1$ is connected to vertex $v_2$ by an edge if and only if they are friends. Friendship is assumed to be symmetric, and a person can't be friends with themselves. Let $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ denote the mean and variance of the number of friends in the network. The average number of friends that a typical friend has can be modeled by choosing a random person (who has at least one friend), and then calculating how many friends their friends have on average. This amounts to choosing, uniformly at random, an edge of the graph (representing a pair of friends), an endpoint of that edge (a friend of the other vertex), and then calculating the degree of the selected endpoint. Determine the expected number of friends that the friends of a person chosen in this manner have. Report the answer when $\mu = 5$ and $\sigma^2 = 10$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we will need to use some basic graph theory. Our goal is to relate everything to $|V|, |E|,$ and $d(v)$, where $d(v)$ is the degree (number of edges) of a vertex. $d(v)$ can also just be interpreted as the number of friends person $v$ has. The mean $\mu$ would just be equal to the sum of all degrees of the vertices (number of friends per person) divided by the number of people. More formally, $\mu = \dfrac{1}{|V|}\sum_{v \in V}d(v) = \dfrac{2|E|}{|V|}$. In the above, we use the fact that the sum of degrees of a graph is exactly twice the number of edges. Intuitively, each edge touches two vertices, so it increases the total degree of the graph by $2$. First, let's evaluate the probability that a certain person is selected using our method above. Note that in all parts of this question, our probability space is really the vertices $V$, so we are creating a random variable on $V$. This would represent the "friend of a friend". Let $X$ be the random person selected. For person $v \in V$ to be selected, two things need to happen: One of the edges touching $v$ must be selected, and once the edge is selected, person $v$ must be the selected endpoint. There are $d(v)$ edges touching $v$ out of $|E|$ total, so the first probability is $d(v)/|E|$. Given that an edge involving person $v$ was selected, person $v$ is one of the two possible people that can be selected, so person $v$ is selected with probability $1/2$. Therefore, for all $v \in V$, the probability that person $v$ is selected is $\prob{X = v} = \dfrac{d(v)}{|E|} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{d(v)}{2|E|}$. In this problem, we are looking to compute $\ev{d(X)}$, the expected number of friends of the random person we have selected. By LOTUS, we have that $\ev{d(X)} = \sum_{v \in V} \textcolor{red}{d(v)}\prob{X = v} = \sum_{v \in V} d(v) \cdot \dfrac{d(v)}{2|E|} = \dfrac{1}{2|E|}\sum_{v\in V} (d(v))^2$. Note that $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ are fixed quantities, with $\sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{|V|}\sum_{v \in V} (d(v))^2 - \mu^2$. This is the analogue of $\ev{X^2} - (\ev{X})^2$ for this probability space. Therefore, we can see that $\sum_{v \in V} (d(v))^2 = |V| \cdot (\sigma^2 + \mu^2)$. Plugging this into the previous expression, $\ev{d(X)} = \dfrac{1}{2|E|} \cdot |V|(\sigma^2 + \mu^2) = \dfrac{|V|}{2|E|} \cdot (\sigma^2 + \mu^2) = \dfrac{1}{\frac{2|E|}{|V|}} \cdot (\sigma^2 + \mu^2) = \dfrac{\sigma^2 + \mu^2}{\mu} = \mu + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{\mu} > \mu$. This result implies that your friends, on average, have more friends than you! How do we explain this? Mathematically, the degree (number of friends) of your friends is not just a simple average of the degrees of people in the network. It's weighted by the degree itself. Formally, if you select a friend at random, you're more likely to pick someone with a higher degree because they appear in more edges. With the specified values, the answer is $7$.
questions.hint: Use the handshaking lemma: the sum of degrees equals 2|E|. The mean is mu = 2|E|/|V|. Express the variance in terms of the sum of squared degrees. Use LOTUS to compute the expected degree of the selected friend.

questions.title: Multiplicatively Decreasing II
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$. You play the following game starting on turn $i = 1$: Initialize turn to $i = 1$. Generate $X_i \sim \unif{0}{\alpha^{i-1}}$, where $0 < \alpha < 1$, independently of other random variables. As long as $i < n$, you can choose to either receive a payout of $X_i$ (the game ends), or you can choose to reject $X_i$. If $i = n$, you must cash out $X_n$. If you reject $X_i$, $i$ gets incremented to $i+1$, and the process goes back up to the second step. More simply stated, this is the same game as the first part, but you have at most $n$ values that can be generated. Assuming you play optimally, what is your expected payout from this game? Report the answer when $n = 3$ and $\alpha = 1/2$. Give the exact fraction.
questions.solution:
This game appears to have a recursive flavor to it, as when we consider a $\unif{0}{\alpha^k}$ random variable, this is exactly $\alpha$ times a $\unif{0}{\alpha^{k-1}}$ random variable. Since we can only play this game up to $n$ rounds, we must track both the current upper bound on the Uniform we are generating, as well as the number of remaining values we are allowed to generate. Our goal is to relate the expected payout of the next turn given the value on the current turn. For ease of notation, denote $E_{z,k}$ to be the expected payout of the game when the first random variable being generated is $\unif{0}{z}$ and there are $1 \leq k \leq n$ values that can be generated, inclusive of the value where the maximum is $z$. We are looking to compute $E_{1,n}$, as the first value generated in this sequence is $\unif{0}{1}$, and there are $n$ turns remaining. There is one key fact here: By the multiplicative property of Uniform random variables stated above, for a fixed $1 \leq k \leq n$, $E_{z,k} = zE_{1,k}$ for all $0 < z < 1$, as it's the same problem with all Uniform random variables scaled by $z$. The expected payout of this game is dependent on what the first value is, since this influences our decision. Therefore, to evaluate $E_{1,n}$, we should condition on the first generated value. If the value generated is $x$, then our optimal strategy says that we should take $\max(x,E_{\alpha,n-1})$, since our two options are to cash out (receive $x$), or continue on (the first value generated is now $\unif{0}{\alpha}$ with $n-1$ more values that can be generated, so $E_{\alpha,n-1}$ is the expected payout). We have to integrate this with respect to the density of $X_1$. Since $X_1 \sim \unif{0}{1}$, $f_{X_1}(x) = 1$ on $(0,1)$. Performing the integration, $$\begin{align*}
    E_{1,k} &= \int_0^1 \max(x,E_{\alpha,k-1})~dx\\
    &= \int_0^{E_{\alpha,k-1}} \max(x,E_{\alpha,k-1})~dx + \int_{E_{\alpha,k-1}}^1 \max(x,E_{\alpha,k-1})~dx\\
    &= \int_0^{E_{\alpha,k-1}} E_{\alpha,k-1}~dx + \int_{E_{\alpha,k-1}}^1 x~dx\\
