This implies that $\mathbb{E}[T] = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^N \dfrac{N}{N-i+1} = \dfrac{N}{N} + \dfrac{N}{N-1} + \dots + \dfrac{N}{2} + \dfrac{N}{1} = \displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^N\dfrac{1}{i}$. With $N = 100$, the expected value is about $518.74$, so the answer is $519$.

questions.title: Undirected Graph Search II
questions.problem: You are given a complete undirected graph with $N \geq 2$ nodes. You first select a uniformly random node to go to, and then each step after, you select to move to any of the nodes ($\textbf{excluding}$ the one you are presently on) in the graph uniformly at random. Find the expected number of turns that are performed until you visit all of the nodes with $N = 101$ and round to the nearest integer.
questions.solution: Without loss of generality, say the nodes are labelled $1-N$. We first take $1$ step to reach a starting node. Once we reach the first node, we also know that the second movement results in a distinct node that has not been visited, as you can't move to the node you are currently on. Afterwards, we can then view a "random step" here as the same as rolling a fair $(N-1)$-sided die that has all of the nodes except the one you currently reside on. One might ask why this is the case. In this random walk on the graph, you can't return to the node you are currently standing on. Therefore, you only have $N-1$ equally likely nodes to move to. Once the problem is reframed in this way, the problem now becomes: On average, how many rolls are needed to see all of the sides of a fair $N$-sided die? Once we have this, we can replace $N$ with $N-1$ and add $1$ to the solution to account for the initial movement onto some node. The idea here is to use linearity of expectation by decomposing into the number of rolls between each consecutive new value. We can see this since the number of rolls needed between observing new values is a geometric random variable, as it measures the number of trials needed to observe the occurrence of some event. Here is a concrete example with $N = 6$. Let $X_i$ be the number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value given that we have already observed $i-1$ distinct values on the die. Then $T = X_1 + \dots + X_6$ gives the total number of rolls needed to observe all $6$ sides. For example, if our sequence of rolls is $1131344213456$, then $X_1 = 1, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 3, X_4 = 2, X_5 = 4,$ and $X_6 = 1$. We can now perform similar, but instead of stopping at $6$, we stop at $N$. In particular, define $X_i$ the exact same way as above: The number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value given that we have already observed $i-1$ distinct values on the die. We have that $R = X_1 + \dots + X_N$ gives the total number of rolls needed to observe all $N$ sides. By linearity of expectation, we have that $\ev{R} = \sum_{i=1}^N\ev{X_i}$. We now need to find $\ev{X_i}$ for each $i$. Let's interpret each random variable separately. $X_i$ is the number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value on the die, given that $i-1$ distinct values have already been observed. This means that $i-1$ of the $N$ sides on each turn do not give us a new value. This means that $N - (i-1) = N-i+1$ of the sides do yield a new value. Therefore, the probability on each roll that a new value is observed is $\dfrac{N-i+1}{N}$. Since this is a waiting time until some event, we should employ a geometric random variable. In particular, $X_i \sim \text{Geom}\left(\dfrac{N-i+1}{N}\right)$, so $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{N}{N-i+1}$. This implies that $\mathbb{E}[T] = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^N \dfrac{N}{N-i+1} = \dfrac{N}{N} + \dfrac{N}{N-1} + \dots + \dfrac{N}{2} + \dfrac{N}{1} = \displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^N\dfrac{1}{i}$. Abiding by the first paragraph, we must replace $N$ with $N-1$ and add $1$ to obtain the solution to our desired problem. Therefore, with $N$ nodes on the graph, the answer is $1 + (N-1)\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\dfrac{1}{k}$. With $N = 101$, the expected value is about $519.74$, so the answer is $520$.

questions.title: Comparable Flips II
questions.problem: You and your friend are sharing a coin. You continually flip the coin and note the sequence of heads and tails that appears. By denoting $H$ as heads and $T$ as tails, you win if $HTH$ appears before $HHT$; otherwise, your friend wins. What is the probability that you win?
questions.solution: Since both sequences start with $H$, we can really consider the sequences starting from the first head being obtained. This is because, eventually, an $H$ is going to appear on the coin. There are $4$ possible outcomes to occur in the next two flips after the heads. Let's consider each separately. If $HTH$ appears, then you win. If $HHT$ appears, then your friend wins. If $HHH$ appears, your friend wins. This is because a tails must eventually appear, so once it does, the sequence $HHT$ would occur. Lastly, if $HTT$ appears, then the game is essentially reset, as neither of the sequences have overlap with the ending of this sequence. Therefore, as $HTT$ resets the game, to have a winner be determined, it must be the case that one of the three other outcomes has to happen. As only one of the three equally likely outcomes that ends the game is in your favor, the answer is $1/3$.

questions.title: Conditional Geometric I
questions.problem: Let $X,Y \sim \geom{p}$ IID for $0 < p < 1$. Find $\ev{\min(X,Y)}$ when $p = 1/2$.
questions.solution: When looking at minimums, we know how to deal with events in the form $\{\min(X,Y) \geq k\}$. We also know the tail sum formula $\ev{X} = \dtailsum{X}$ for non-negative integer-valued discrete random variables $X$, which is exactly in the form of the above. Therefore, we should apply the tail sum formula to $\min(X,Y)$. The only item we will need is $\prob{X \geq k}$ for a geometric random variable. Assuming $k$ is an integer, we can interpret this using our known methods to interpret geometric random variables. In particular, we can view this as saying that the first heads on a coin with probability $p$ of heads takes at least $k$ flips or more to obtain, meaning the first $k-1$ flips were all tails. This occurs with probability $(1-p)^{k-1}$, as there is probability $1-p$ for each of the $k-1$ flips that they are tails. Therefore, using this, $\ev{\min(X,Y)} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{\min(X,Y) \geq k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{X \geq k, Y \geq k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{X \geq k}\prob{Y \geq k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (1-p)^{k-1} \cdot (1-p)^{k-1}$. The trick to compute the final sum $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (1-p)^{2(k-1)}$ is to write it as $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} [(1-p)^2]^{k-1}$. This is now a geometric series with common ratio $(1-p)^2$, so it sums to $\dfrac{1}{1-(1-p)^2} = \dfrac{1}{p(2-p)}$, as the first term in the geometric series is $1$. Therefore, with $p = 1/2$, $\ev{\min(X,Y)} = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

questions.title: Quicker Heads I
questions.problem: Jack and Jill are both repeatedly flipping coins that have probability $0 < p < 1$ of showing heads on each flip. Find the probability that Jack obtains his first heads in strictly fewer flips than Jill when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: Let $X$ and $Y$ respectively represent the number of flips that are needed to observe the first heads for both Jack and Jill. This question is asking you to compute $\prob{X < Y}$. The distributions of $X$ and $Y$ are $\geom{p}$ IID, as they measure the number of flips needed to obtain a heads on a coin with probability of success $p$ per trial. The easiest way is to compute $\prob{X = Y}$. This is because $\prob{X \neq Y} = \prob{X < Y} + \prob{X > Y} =  1-\prob{X = Y}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, and hence exchangeable, $\prob{X > Y} = \prob{X < Y}$. Using this fact, we can determine that $\prob{X < Y} = \dfrac{1-\prob{X = Y}}{2}$. To compute $\prob{X = Y}$, all we need to do is sum up $\prob{X = k, Y = k} = \prob{X = k}\prob{Y = k}$ over all possible values of $k$, as we are disjointifying based on the different values of $k$ that both $X$ and $Y$ can take. The equality above is by the independence of $X$ and $Y$. This means $\prob{X = Y} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \prob{X=k}\prob{Y=k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} p(1-p)^{k-1} \cdot p(1-p)^{k-1} = p^2 \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} [(1-p)^2]^{k-1} = \dfrac{p^2}{1-(1-p)^2} = \dfrac{p}{2-p}$. The summation is evaluated using the geometric series formula with common ratio $(1-p)^2$. We now get $\prob{X < Y} = \dfrac{1-\dfrac{p}{2-p}}{2} = \dfrac{1-p}{2-p}$. Note that this answer does make intuitive sense. As $p \rightarrow 1$, the probability tends to $0$, which aligns with the fact that if $p$ is very large, they will most likely both obtain heads on the first flip, so it would not be strictly quicker. Similarly, if $p \rightarrow 0$, we see that the probability tends to $1/2$, which makes sense, as it's extremely unlikely that either person will obtain a heads anytime soon, so the probability that they get the heads at the exact same time is very close to $0$. With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $2/5$.

questions.title: Cubic Ant I
questions.problem: An ant walks along the edges of a cube and moves to one of the three adjacent vertices with equal probability at each step. Find the expected number of steps needed for the ant to reach the vertex opposite of where it started.
questions.solution: The best approach here is to set up a Markov chain based on how far away the ant is from its starting place (either $0$, $1$, or $2$ away). This is because the ant is really moving between states right now that only depend on how far away it is from its destination (and hence, the starting place). Let $E_i$ be the expected number of steps that the ant needs to make to reach the opposite corner given that it is currently at a vertex $i$ units away from the starting location. We want to find $E_0$. We have that $E_0 = 1 + E_1$ directly, as the ant will always move to a location that is $1$ unit away from the starting point on the first step. WLOG, suppose the ant moved upwards at the first step to be in state $1$. This is WLOG because the cube is symmetric, so it doesn't matter which actual vertex the ant moved to. From this position, the ant can move back to the starting point (probability $1/3$) or move left/right to be $2$ steps away from the starting point (probability $2/3$). Therefore, we have that $E_1 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{3}E_0 + \dfrac{2}{3}E_2$. This comes from the Law of Total Expectation. Suppose now that the ant is in a state that is $2$ units away from the starting point. With probability $1/3$, the ant moves to the opposite corner. Otherwise, with probability $2/3$, the ant moves back to a state that is $1$ unit away from the starting point. This means that $E_2 = 1 + \dfrac{2}{3}E_1$. We now need to solve the system of equations above for $E_0$. By using your favorite linear algebraic tools or a calculation, the result is that $E_0 = 10, E_1 = 9,$ and $E_2 = 7$. $E_0$ is what we are interested in, so $E_0 = 10$.

questions.title: Prior Event II
questions.problem: Suppose you simulate some experiment repeatedly. Let $A$ and $B$ be any events that can occur on each trial of the experiment such that $\prob{A} = p_1$, $\prob{B} = p_2$, and $\prob{A \cap B} = p_3 < \min(p_1,p_2)$. The simulation ends when exactly one of $A$ or $B$ occurs on some trial. Find the probability that $A$ occurred when $p_1 = 2/3, p_2 = 1/2,$ and $p_3 = 1/3$.
questions.solution: Exactly one event occurring means the event $(A\cap B^c) \cup (A^c \cap B)$ occurred. Recall that $A \cap B^c$ means that $A$ occurred and $B$ did not occur, and vice versa with $A^c \cap B$. To end the simulation, we know one of those two events occurs and are disjoint. The probability we are looking to compute here is $\prob{A\cap B^c \mid (A\cap B^c) \cup (A^c \cap B)}$, as we know exactly one of $A$ or $B$ occurred to end the experiment, so we want to find the probability that $A$ was the one that occurred and ended the experiment. Note that $(A \cap B^c) \cup (A^c \cap B) \subseteq A \cup B$, so $\prob{(A \cap B^c)\cup (A^c \cap B)} \leq \prob{A \cup B} \leq 1$. Furthermore, we know that $A \cap B^c$ and $A^c \cap B$ are disjoint events, as it's impossible for both $A$ and $A^c$ to occur (and likewise with $B$). Therefore, we can apply the result of "Prior Event I" to the events $A\cap B^c$ and $A^c \cap B$. To do this, we can write $\prob{A \cap B^c} = \prob{A} - \prob{A \cap B} = p_1 - p_3$ and $\prob{A^c \cap B} = \prob{B} - \prob{A \cap B} = p_2 - p_3$. This decomposition arises from writing $A = (A\cap B) \cup (A \cap B^c)$ i.e. by disjointifying $A$ based on $B$. Plugging this in, we get $\prob{A \cap B^c \mid (A \cap B^c) \cup (A^c \cap B)} = \dfrac{p_1 - p_3}{p_1 + p_2 - 2p_3}$. With our specified values, we get the answer $\dfrac{1/3}{1/3 + 1/6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.title: Ones and Twos I
questions.problem: You roll a standard $6$-sided fair die until the number $1$ appears on the upface. Find the expected number of times that the value $2$ was rolled before stopping.
questions.solution: If we know how many rolls are performed, this expected value is much easier to compute. Therefore, it would be best to use Law of Total Expectation with conditioning on the number of rolls that occur total. The number of rolls that are needed to observe the first $1$ on the die is $N \sim \geom{1/6}$, as there is a $1/6$ probability per roll that the value $1$ appears. Let $T$ be the number of times that the value $2$ appears. We want to compute $\ev{T}$. By using the idea above, $\ev{T} = \ev{\ev{T \mid N}}$. It now remains to compute $\ev{T \mid N}$. Given that there are $N$ rolls, this means that the $N$th roll was a $1$, while the first $N-1$ rolls are any value but $1$. Conditional on the roll not being a $1$, there is a probability $1/5$ that the roll was a $2$, as there are $5$ remaining equally likely values on the die. Therefore, $T \mid N \sim \binomial{N-1}{1/5}$, as each roll is independent of the previous rolls. By taking the expected value, $\ev{T \mid N} = \frac{N-1}{5}$, so $\ev{T} = \ev{\dfrac{N-1}{5}} = \dfrac{1}{5} \cdot \ev{N} - \dfrac{1}{5}$. Since $N \sim \geom{1/6}$, $\ev{N} = 6$, so $\ev{T} = 1$ as a result. An intuitive way to reason this is that, on average, there are $6$ total rolls, of which the last is a $1$. Therefore, there is a conditional probability $1/5$ for each of the first $5$ rolls to be the value $2$, meaning that the expected number of times $2$ appears is $5 \cdot 1/5 = 1$.

questions.title: Valid Table II
questions.problem: A craftsman carves a perfect circular disk for the top of a table. $N \geq 3$ legs are attached uniformly at random to the circumference of the circular disk. Find the probability that the table stands. You may assume the legs are infinitely thin and have mass $0$. Additionally, you may assume the material is of uniform density. Solve this when $N = 6$. Note: It would be helpful to solve Same Arc before attempting this question.
questions.solution: The table will fall whenever the center of mass (this coincides with the center of the table because it has uniformly density) lies outside the plane of the polygon formed by the legs. This is really asking the following question: What's the probability that the origin is contained in a randomly chosen polygon with vertices uniformly at random from the circumference? For the origin to be contained inside the $N$-gon, one can see pictorially that this occurs if and only if the $N$ points selected for the polygon do not lie in the same semi-circle. If they do, there exists a diameter of the circle, which goes through the origin, for which all of the points are contained on a single side of the diameter. Therefore, since all of the points are contained on the same side of the diameter, the polygon that is formed can't contain the origin. From "Same Arc", we know the probability that all of the points lie in the same arc of $x$ radians is $N \cdot \left(\dfrac{x}{2\pi}\right)^{N-1}$, where $N$ is the number of points. In this case, $x = \pi$, as we are looking at a diameter. With this, we get the answer is $\dfrac{N}{2^{N-1}}$. Therefore, there is a $\dfrac{N}{2^{N-1}}$ probability that the table falls, meaning that there is a $1 - \dfrac{N}{2^{N-1}}$ probability that the points are not contained in the same semi-circle, which means the table stands. With $N = 6$, the answer is $\dfrac{13}{16}$.

questions.title: Overflow I
questions.problem: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be IID with mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$, and $\ev{\dfrac{1}{S_k}} = a_k$. Define $S_k = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^k X_i$. Compute $\ev{\dfrac{S_m}{S_n}}$ when $m \leq n$. For this question, compute it with $\mu = 3, \sigma^2 = 18, a_k = \frac{2}{3k}, m = 25,$ and $n = 50$.
questions.solution: To compute this, we can write out the terms explicitly first and use linearity of expectation. This becomes $\ev{\dfrac{S_m}{S_n}} = \ev{\dfrac{X_1 + \dots + X_m}{X_1 + \dots + X_m + \dots + X_n}} = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n \ev{\dfrac{X_i}{X_1 + \dots + X_n}}$. Now, we need to compute $\ev{\dfrac{X_i}{X_1 + \dots + X_n}}$ for each $1 \leq i \leq m$. The trick here is to note that since $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are IID, they are exchangeable. Therefore, every permutation of the values has the same distribution. In particular, this means that $\dfrac{X_1}{X_1 + \dots + X_n},\dots, \dfrac{X_n}{X_1 + \dots + X_n}$ all have the same distribution, and hence mean. Furthermore, note that $1 = \dfrac{X_1}{X_1 + \dots  + X_n} + \dots + \dfrac{X_n}{X_1 + \dots + X_n}$. By exchangeability, $n\ev{\dfrac{X_1}{X_1 + \dots + X_n}} = 1$, meaning $\ev{\dfrac{X_1}{X_1 + \dots + X_n}} = 1/n$. This makes intuitive sense, as $X_1$ contributes one of $n$ IID values to the denominator, so it, on average, is a proportion $\dfrac{1}{n}$ of the total sum. Applying the exchangeability to the sum, we have that $\ev{\dfrac{S_m}{S_n}} = m \ev{\dfrac{X_1}{X_1  + \dots + X_n}} = \dfrac{m}{n}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/2$.

questions.title: Products of Uniforms I
questions.problem: Let $X,Y,Z \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Compute $\prob{Y \leq XZ}$.
questions.solution:
Solution 1: Condition on $Y$. $\prob{Y \leq XZ} = \displaystyle \int_0^1 \prob{Y \leq XZ \mid Y = y}f_Y(y)dy$. Since $Y \sim \unif{0}{1}$, $f_Y(y) = 1$. Therefore: $\begin{align*}
\prob{Y \leq XZ} &= \displaystyle \int_0^1 \prob{Y \leq XZ \mid Y = y}f_Y(y)dy \\
&= \int_0^1 \prob{y \leq XZ } dy\\
&= \ev{XZ} \\
&= \ev{X} \ev{Z} \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{4}
\end{align*}$ where $X, Z$ are independent of $Y$.

Solution 2: Condition on $Z$. We can write $\prob{Y \leq XZ} = \displaystyle \int_0^1 \prob{Y \leq XZ \mid Z = z}f_Z(z)dz$. Since $Z \sim \unif{0}{1}$, $f_Z(z) = 1$. Given $Z = z$, $\prob{Y \leq XZ \mid Z = z} = \prob{Y \leq zX}$. For $0 < z < 1$, this is the area under the line $y = zx$ in the unit square (the $xy$-plane scaled to $z$ height and $1$ width). So $\prob{Y \leq XZ \mid Z = z} = \prob{Y \leq zX} = \dfrac{z}{2}$, as $(X,Y)$ is uniform on the unit square and the area below $y = zx$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ is $\dfrac{z}{2}$. Therefore $\prob{Y \leq XZ} = \displaystyle \int_0^1 \dfrac{z}{2}dz = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Solution 3: Direct integration. $\begin{align*}
\prob{Y \leq XZ} &=  \int_0^1  \int_0^1  \int_0^{xz} f_{XYZ}(x,y,z) dy dx dz \\
&=  \int_0^1  \int_0^1  \int_0^{xz} f_{X}(x)f_{Y}(y)f_{Z}(z) dy dx dz \\
&=  \int_0^1  \int_0^1  \int_0^{xz} dy dx dz \\
&=  \int_0^1  \int_0^1 xz dx dz \\
&= \ev{XZ} \\
&= \ev{X} \ev{Z} \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{2} \\
&= \frac{1}{4}
\end{align*}$ where $X,Y$ and $Z$ are independent.

questions.title: Last Color Standing
questions.problem: Beth has $r$ red marbles, $b$ blue marbles, and $g$ green marbles in an urn. She draws out the marbles one at a time without replacement. Find the probability there is at least one green and one blue marble left in the urn right after the last red marble is selected. Find this probability when $r = 10, b = 20, g = 30$.
questions.solution: Imagine there were only two colors in the urn. The probability that one is the last color to be drawn is easy to compute. To ensure that there is at least one of both green and blue left in the urn when the last red is drawn, condition on which of green or blue is the absolute last marble drawn from the urn, and then consider the orderings of the remaining two colors. Imagine the draws of the marbles being counted in order from $1$ to $r+b+g$. Let $T_r, T_b,$ and $T_g$ be the positions of the final red, blue, and green marbles, respectively. We want to compute $\prob{T_r < T_b, T_r < T_g}$, as we want the final red to occur before the final green and final blue. There are two cases: $T_r < T_g < T_b$ or $T_r < T_b < T_g$. Let's disjointify on these two cases. Namely, we want to compute $\prob{T_r < T_b < T_g} + \prob{T_r < T_g < T_b}$. To compute each of these, we should condition on the information that we stated at the beginning: Condition on what is absolute last. Namely, we want to now compute $\prob{T_r < T_b < T_g \mid T_g \hspace{3pt}\text{last}}\prob{T_g\hspace{3pt} \text{last}} + \prob{T_r < T_g < T_b \mid T_b \hspace{3pt} \text{last}}\prob{T_b \hspace{3pt} \text{last}}$. We can compute $\prob{T_b \hspace{3pt} \text{last}}$ and $\prob{T_g \hspace{3pt} \text{last}}$ quite easily. Since sampling without replacement is an exchangeable process, the probability that the last ball drawn is green/blue is the same as the probability the first ball drawn is green/blue. These probabilities are $\frac{g}{r+b+g}$ and $\frac{b}{r+b+g}$, respectively. Now, we need to compute the conditionals. We will start with $\prob{T_r < T_b < T_g \mid T_g \hspace{3pt}\text{last}}$. Given green is last, we only now care about the orderings of the red and blue marbles relative to one another. There are $r$ red and $b$ blue marbles, so as we are only looking at the relative orderings of red and blue marbles, we want to find the probability that the last marble among red and blue is blue (so that the red marbles run out first). This occurs with probability $\frac{b}{r+b}$ by the same argument that the last marble drawn has the same distribution as the first marble. We now repeat the same argument to compute $\prob{T_r < T_g < T_b \mid T_b \hspace{3pt} \text{last}}$. Restricting to reds and greens, the probability that the last marble among the $r+g$ is green is $\dfrac{g}{r+g}$. Combining all of these, our final answer is $\dfrac{g}{r+g} \cdot \dfrac{b}{r+b+g} + \dfrac{g}{r+b+g} \cdot \dfrac{b}{r+b}$. With our specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{7}{12}$.

questions.title: Varied Numbers
questions.problem: An urn consists of $2k$, $k \geq 1$, balls of each of $m \geq 2$ colors, of which red and blue are two of them. We select balls one-by-one without replacement from the $2mk$ total balls. Given that in the first $mk$ draws there were exactly $r$ more red balls than blue, find the probability the next ball drawn is blue when $k = 12, m = 8,$ and $r = 6$.
questions.solution: The goal here is to use the information we have in two different ways. Let $R$ and $B$ represent the event that the $(mk+1)$st ball drawn is red and blue, respectively. Since sampling without replacement is an exchangeable process, the probability of drawing a red/blue on any turn is the same. Thus, the probability that the $(mk+1)$st ball drawn is blue is the same as the first ball. For the first ball, red and blue are $2$ of the $m$ equally likely possibilities of colors, so $\prob{R} + \prob{E} = \dfrac{2}{m}$. Additionally, we know that $r$ more red balls than blue balls in the first $mk$ drawn. Therefore, there are $r$ more blue than red ones in the remaining $mk$ balls. Other than the extra balls, there are equally many red and blue balls, so regardless of their exact number, the probabilities cancel. Thus, the differential probability is $\dfrac{r}{mk}$, as there are an additional $r$ blue balls left in the remaining $mk$. This means $\prob{B} - \prob{R} = \dfrac{r}{mk}$. We now have a system of equations with $2$ equations and $2$ unknowns. Adding these together yields $2\prob{B} = \dfrac{2}{m} + \dfrac{r}{mk} \iff \prob{B} = \dfrac{2k + r}{2mk}$. With our specific values, the answer is $\prob{B} = \dfrac{5}{32}$.

questions.title: Figure Collector
questions.problem: Your favorite brand of cereal packs toys in their boxes. Each box is equally likely to have one of $N$ distinct toys inside, independent between boxes. Find the expected number of boxes that you need to open to observe all of the toys when $N = 40$. Round to the nearest integer.
questions.solution: Label the toys $1-N$. Opening a box is now equivalent to rolling a fair $N$-sided die. The question now becomes: Find the expected number of rolls needed to observe all of the sides of a fair $N$-sided die. The idea here is to use linearity of expectation by decomposing into the number of rolls between each consecutive new value. We can see this since the number of rolls needed between observing new values is a geometric random variable, as it measures the number of trials needed to observe the occurrence of some event. Here is a concrete example with $N = 6$. Let $X_i$ be the number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value given that we have already observed $i-1$ distinct values on the die. Then $T = X_1 + \dots + X_6$ gives the total number of rolls needed to observe all $6$ sides. For example, if our sequence of rolls is $1131344213456$, then $X_1 = 1, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 3, X_4 = 2, X_5 = 4,$ and $X_6 = 1$. We can now perform similar, but instead of stopping at $6$, we stop at $N$. In particular, define $X_i$ the exact same way as above: The number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value given that we have already observed $i-1$ distinct values on the die. We have that $R = X_1 + \dots + X_N$ gives the total number of rolls needed to observe all $N$ sides. By linearity of expectation, we have that $\ev{R} = \sum_{i=1}^N\ev{X_i}$. We now need to find $\ev{X_i}$ for each $i$. Let's interpret each random variable separately. $X_i$ is the number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value on the die, given that $i-1$ distinct values have already been observed. This means that $i-1$ of the $N$ sides on each turn do not give us a new value. This means that $N - (i-1) = N-i+1$ of the sides do yield a new value. Therefore, the probability on each roll that a new value is observed is $\dfrac{N-i+1}{N}$. Since this is a waiting time until some event, we should employ a geometric random variable. In particular, $X_i \sim \text{Geom}\left(\dfrac{N-i+1}{N}\right)$, so $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{N}{N-i+1}$. This implies that $\mathbb{E}[T] = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^N \dfrac{N}{N-i+1} = \dfrac{N}{N} + \dfrac{N}{N-1} + \dots + \dfrac{N}{2} + \dfrac{N}{1} = \displaystyle N\sum_{i=1}^N\dfrac{1}{i}$. With $N = 40$, the expected value is about $171.14$, so the answer is $171$.

questions.title: Runs!
questions.problem: A coin that comes up heads with probability $0 < p < 1$ per flip is flipped $n$ times. The outcomes are recorded in order of appearance. On average, how many runs/connected components will there be when $n = 100$ and $p = 1/3$? A run is defined as the longest contiguous sequence of flips of the same parity (heads or tails). For example, $HHTTTHTHH$ has $5$ runs.
questions.solution: The best approach is to derive a recurrence relation for $C_n$, the expected number of connected components/runs. This approach is most appropriate since the number of runs in $n$ coin flips is directly related to the number of runs in the first $n-1$ coin flips and the parity of the last coin. More explicitly, suppose $C_n$ is the expected number of runs in a sequence of $n$ flips. An additional run occurs with the addition of the last coin exactly when the $(n-1)$st and $n$th coins differ in parity. Otherwise, there are the same number of runs in $n-1$ flips. This approach is most viable because the probability we get a "match" between the $(n-1)$st and $n$th squares depends on which color the $(n-1)$st square is. A way to derive the recursive equation easier is to find the probability that two consecutive coins differ in parity. This quantity is the expected number of connected components that are added when we add a coin to the line, as we would have $1$ additional connected component with this probability and $0$ otherwise. To do this, we just need to find the probability of $HT$ or $TH$, which we can really find just one of them and double it. The probability of $TH$ is just $p(1-p)$, so the probability any two consecutive coins differ is $2p(1-p)$. Therefore, for any coin after the first, there is a $2p(1-p)$ probability that we add another connected component by including that coin; otherwise, we do not add any new connected component. Since we do this for every single coin past the first, when there are $n$ coins in a line, we would get $1$ connected component from the first coin and $2p(1-p)$ connected components on average from each of the other $n-1$ coins in the line. Therefore, the expected number of runs is $1 + (n-1)2p(1-p)$. With the specific numbers in the question, the answer is $45$.

questions.title: Double 5
questions.problem: Albert rolls a standard fair $$$$$6$$$$$ − 6−sided die with the values 1 − 6 1−6 on the sides. He continually rolls the die and keeps track of the outcomes in the order they appear. Albert rolls until he sees either $2$ 2 $5$ 5s (not necessarily consecutive) OR both a $$$$4$$$$ 4 and a 6 6. Find the probability that Albert stops rolling due to seeing a 4 4 and a 6 6.
questions.solution: The key observation here is that we only care about the order of the $$$$$$$$$$$$4$$$$$$$$$$$$ , $$$$$$$$5$$$$$$$$ , $4,5,$ and $$$$$$$$$$$$$$$6$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$ 6. All other rolls that aren't these don't effect the probability of interest. Conditional on the die showing 4 − 6 4−6, each value appears with probability $1$ / 3 $$1/3$$. Now, we should consider the orders in which we stop on 4 4 and 6 6. The first case is that the first two values are 4 4 and 6 6 in some order. This occurs with probability 2 3 ⋅ 1 2 = 1 3 3 2 ⋅ 2 1 = 3 1 . The reason for this is that the first value is a 4 4 or 6 6 with probability 2 / 3 $$$2/3$$$. Once that choice is eliminated, the next value appearing is 5 5 or 6 6 with equal probability, so the probability it is a 6 6 is 1 / 2 $$$1/2$$$. The next case is that there is 1 1 5 5 in the middle of a sequence of the above form. In other words, $456$ 456 or $654$ 654. The probability that the first value is a 4 4 or 6 6 is 2 / 3 2/3. Afterwards, the probability that the next value is a 5 5 is 1 / 2 1/2, as we are now restricted to the other of 4 4 or 6 6 not rolled on the first turn and 5 5, both of which are equally likely. Lastly, the probability that the third roll is the other of 4 4 or 6 6 is 1 / 2 1/2 by the same argument as above. Thus, the probability of this case is 2 3 ⋅ 1 2 ⋅ 1 2 = 1 6 3 2 ⋅ 2 1 ⋅ 2 1 = 6 1 . The final case is that there is a 5 5 to start, and then both a 4 4 and 6 6 occur afterwards. The probability that the first value is a 5 5 is 1 / 3 1/3. Afterwards, the probability that the next value is either a 4 4 or 6 6 is 2 / 3 2/3, as we want either a 4 4 or 6 6 instead of a 5 5. Now, we eliminate the value rolled on the second turn from our sample space, and we restrict ourselves to 5 5 and the other of 4 4 or 6 6 not rolled on the previous turn. The probability that this next value rolled is the other of 4 4 or 6 6 is 1 2 2 1 . Therefore, the probability of this case is 1 2 ⋅ 2 3 ⋅ 1 3 = 1 9 2 1 ⋅ 3 2 ⋅ 3 1 = 9 1 . Adding up these three cases together, the probability of stopping on a 4 4 and 6 6 is 11 18 18 11 . The idea here is to condition on the die being 4 − 6 4−6 and continually restrict your sample space.

Each string has a certain number of $0$ , $1$ , … , 9 0,1,…,9 inside. questions.title: Sequential Ace
questions.problem: Scott turns over cards one-by-one from a standard deck of cards without replacement. Find the expected number of cards Scott needs to turn over to observe the third ace.
questions.solution: The $i$dea here is to use linearity of expectation by decomposing into the regions between aces, before the first ace, and after the last ace. By the symmetry of the problem, the expected sizes of the regions will be equal, and we can simply solve for the expectation. In particular, the $4$ 4 aces in the deck will split it up into $$5$$ 5 regions: cards before the first ace, between the first and second, and so on. Label these regions $1$ − 5 1−5, and let X i be the number of cards in region i. We are looking for [ 1 ] + 1 E[X 1 ]+1. We must add in 1 1 for the fact that 1 X 1 is the number of cards that comes before the first ace, and we want the number of cards that must be observed, including the ace itself. Note that there are 52 − 4 = $48$ 52−4=48 cards in the deck that are not aces. By the exchangeability of the different regions, as sampling without replacement is an exchangeable process and the labels of the regions are irrelevant, we have that [ 1 ] = ⋯ = [ 5 ] E[X 1 ]=⋯=E[X 5 ]. Therefore, as there are 48 48 cards to be assigned to the 5 5 regions, we would expect 48 / 5 $48/5$ cards per region on average. The number of cards that need to be drawn to observe the third ace is the sum of all the cards in each of the three regions before the third ace and the $$3$$ 3 aces themselves. There are 3 3 aces that are drawn to see the third ace, and the number of cards in the three regions is 48 5 ⋅ 3 = 144 5 = 28.8 5 48 ⋅3= 5 144 =28.8 on average. Thus, the total number of cards that are drawn until and including the third ace is 28.8 + 3 = 31.8 $28.8 + 3 = 31.8$.

questions.title: Urn Distributor
questions.problem: Adam has $$7$$ 7 white and $8$ 8 black balls in his bag. How many distinct ways can Adam distribute them into $5$ 5 distinct urns such that each urn has exactly $$$3$$$ 3 balls?
questions.solution: The balls, other than the$$i$$r color, are identical. Note that once the white balls are distributed in some satisfactory way such that there are at most $$$$$$$$$3$$$$$$$$$ 3 balls in any urn, there exists exactly one way to put the black balls in so that every urn has exactly 3 3 balls. Namely, if ( $1$ , 2 , 3 , $$$4$$$ , $$$5$$$ ) (a 1 ,a 2 ,a 3 ,a 4 ,a 5 ) is a tuple that represents the number of white balls in all the urns, then ( 3 − 1 , … , 3 − 5 ) (3−a 1 ,…,3−a 5 ) represents the number of black balls that should go in the urns to ensure there are exactly 3 3 balls per urn. Thus, we really want to count the number of ways to distribute the white balls in a satisfactory way. In other words, we must count the number of non-negative integer solutions to 1 + ⋯ + 5 = $7$ a 1 +⋯+a 5 =7, with 0 ≤ ≤ 3 0≤a i ≤3 for all i. The numbers 3 3 and 7 7 are special here. Note that it is only possible for at most one urn to have more than 3 3 white balls, as if there were two urns with more than 3 3 white balls i.e. at least 4 4, there would need to be at least $8$ 8 white balls total. Thus, we can avoid the typical route of inclusion-exclusion and just count via the complement. In other words, we should count how many of solutions here have at least one > 3 a i >3. The total number of solutions, with no restrictions, is just ( 7 + 5 − 1 5 − 1 ) = 330 ( 5−1 7+5−1 )=330 by stars-and-bars. Of those, to get a solution with one ≥ 4 a i ≥4, we must pick one of a i variables to be larger than 3 3. There are 5 5 ways to pick this. Without loss of generality, say we chose 1 a 1 . Afterwards, once this is done, we can ignore the upper bound restrictions on 2 a 2 to 5 a 5 , since we know that only one urn can have strictly more than 3 3 balls in it. The number of solutions that are invalid is just 5 5 multiplied by the number of solutions to the equation 1 + ⋯ + 5 = 7 a 1 +⋯+a 5 =7 with 1 ≥ 4 a 1 ≥4 and 2 , … , 5 ≥ 0 a 2 ,…,a 5 ≥0. To do this, the key is to fix 4 4 balls into urn 1 1 at the start, and now there are 3 3 balls left to distribute to the 5 5 urns in an unrestricted manner, as the condition of having at least 4 4 in urn one is satisfied. The number of solutions to the above equation is equal to the number of solutions to 1 + ⋯ + 5 = 3 a 1 +⋯+a 5 =3 with ≥ 0 a i ≥0 for all i. By stars-and-bars, the number of solutions to this is ( 3 + 5 − 1 5 − 1 ) = 35 ( 5−1 3+5−1 )=35. Therefore, there must be 35 ⋅ 5 = 175 $35 \cdot 5 = 175$ solutions we must exclude. By complementation, the total number of distributions that are valid is 330 − 175 = 155 330−175=155, which is the answer.

Two dice are considered indistinguishable if the number of faces that show value i for 1 ≤ ≤ 6 $1 \leq i \leq 6$ is the same for all i between the two dice, regardless of orientation. Assume that each of the 6 6 sides appear with equal probability.
questions.solution: We must ensure that all values $$$$2$$$$ ≤ ≤ $$$1$$2$ $2 \leq k \leq 12$ have positive probability of appearing. The easiest values to determine on the die to consider first are the extreme values, as they are the ones that have the fewest possible ways to obtain them. Namely, 2 2 and 12 12 must have positive probability of appearing, which is only possible through 2 = 1 + 1 $2 = 1 + 1$ and 12 = $$$6$$$ + 6 $12 = 6  + 6$, meaning 1 1 and 6 6 must be on the die. Similarly, let's look at the next most extreme values of $$$$$$$$3$$$$$$$$ 3 and $11$ 11. As 3 = 1 + 2 $3 = 1 + 2$ and 11 = 6 + $$5$$ $11 = 6 + 5$, these are only possible to obtain with positive probability when 2 2 and 5 5 are also on the die. Now, let's see which sums are possible to obtain with the values 1 , 2 , 5 , $1,2,5,$ and 6 6 thus far, and we can figure out what to add from there. The possible sums with two dice with these $$$$$$$$4$$$$$$$$ 4 values thus far are 2 ( 1 + 1 ) , 3 ( 2 + 1 ) , 4 ( 2 + 2 ) , 6 ( 5 + 1 ) , 7 ( 5 + 2 ) , 8 ( 6 + 2 ) , 10 ( 5 + 5 ) , 11 ( 5 + 6 ) , 12 ( 6 + 6 ) $2 (1+1),3 (2+1),4 (2+2),6 (5+1),7 (5+2),8 (6+2),10 (5+5),11 (5+6), 12 (6+6)$ Only 5 5 an $9$ 9 are not possible to obtain yet. We could obtain 9 = 6 + 3 = 5 + 4 $9 = 6+3 = 5+4$, so either 3 3 or 4 4 must be on the die as well. Once either 3 3 or 4 4 is on the die, there are no restrictions what the last value is, as all of the possible sums are now represented. Therefore, we need to count the number of combinations where at least one of 3 3 or 4 4 is among the last two values. There are 2 2 options for which of 3 3 or 4 4 goes on the die, and once that is settled, there are 6 6 options for the last value on the die, as any value can be placed on it. This yields 2 ⋅ 6 = 12 $2 \cdot 6 = 12$ ways to pick the final 2 2 values of the dice. However, note that the option of putting 3 3 and 4 4 is counted twice in the above. It is counted in the case where we fix 3 3 on the die and 4 4 is the choice for the unrestricted spot, as well as when we fix 4 4 and 3 3 is in the unrestricted spot. Therefore, this outcome is double-counted, meaning that we must subtract 1 1 to remove the double-counting of this outcome. This implies there are 12 − 1 = 11 12−1=11 distinct dice that satisfy this condition.

questions.title: Product Of 5
questions.problem: $5$ standard fair $6$-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the product of their upfaces is $144$.
questions.solution:
As we are taking a product of values here, a natural idea to consider is the prime factorization. This allows us to determine what factors should be present among the dice. We can write $144 = 2^4 \cdot 3^2$, so we need $4$ factors of $2$ and two factors of $3$. In particular, the dice can never show $5$, as $5$ does not divide $144$. Any dice that show $1$ do not change the product, so the idea is to condition on the number of $1$s that appear, as this influences what must appear in the remaining dice.

If no ones appear, then there are two general forms that lead to a product of $144$: $22236$ and $42233$. We obtain these by considering the powers of $2$ and $3$ that need to appear. As the dice are fair, we can just count all the permutations. As we know the total number of dice and we are assigning labels with a fixed amount per group, the multinomial coefficient is best. The two cases respectively have $\binom{5}{3,1,1} = 20$ and $\binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30$ permutations, so there are $50$ outcomes corresponding to this case.

If $1$ one appears, there are three forms that suffice: $14433$, $16622$, and $16243$. We obtained these by conditioning on the number of $6$s that appear. These forms respectively have $\binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30$, $\binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30$, and $5! = 120$ ways of appearing, so there are $180$ outcomes for this case.

If $2$ ones appear, there is only one form that suffices: $11466$. There are $\binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30$ permutations of these values onto the dice.

By the above, there are $50 + 180 + 30 = 260$ permutations total that lead to a product of $144$. With no restrictions, there are $6^5 = 7776$ total outcomes of $5$ dice, so the probability of a product of $144$ is $260/7776 = 65/1944$.

questions.title: Updated First Round
questions.problem: A gambler starts with $\$k$ in a casino, where $k$ is a positive integer. The gambler bets $\$1$ per round in a fair game until they either have $\$m$, where $m \geq k$, or $\$0$. Given that the gambler ends with $\$m$, find the probability that they won the first round when $k = 10$ and $m = 20$. If necessary, round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
We need to update the probability that the gambler wins the first round with the information that they quit upon winning $\$m$. This is a classic conditional probability scenario, so we should apply the definition here. Let $W$ be the event that the gambler wins the first bet and $M$ be the event that the gambler cashes out with $\$m$. We are looking to compute $P[W \mid M]$.

As per the definition, $P[W \mid M] = \dfrac{P[W \cap M]}{P[M]}$.

We know how to compute the bottom probability from the known formulas for gambler's ruin to be $P[M] = k/m$. As for the numerator, we reverse the direction of the conditional to obtain $P[W \cap M] = P[M \mid W]P[W]$. With no information, the gambler wins each round with probability $1/2$, so $P[W] = 1/2$. Given that the gambler won the first round, they have $\$(k+1)$, so the probability they leave with $\$m$ is $P[M \mid W] = \frac{k+1}{m}$.

Substituting these in yields $P[W \mid M] = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{k+1}{m}}{\frac{k}{m}} = \dfrac{k+1}{2k}$.

Interestingly, this is independent of $m$. With the specified values, the answer is $11/20$.

questions.title: Variance of BM Sum
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. For $0 \leq s < t$, compute $\text{Var}(W_s + W_t)$. Report the answer when $s = 1$ and $t = 3$.
questions.solution:
Since this is a sum of random variables that are not independent (the Brownian Motion process has autocorrelation), we should apply the variance of a sum formula. Namely, $\text{Var}(W_s + W_t) = \text{Var}(W_s) + \text{Var}(W_t) + 2\text{Cov}(W_s, W_t)$.

As $W_a \sim N(0,a)$ for any $a > 0$, the first two terms are $s$ and $t$, respectively. For $\text{Cov}(W_s, W_t)$, the covariance, by "Autocorrelation of BM", is $\min(s,t) = s$.

Therefore, $\text{Var}(W_s + W_t) = t + 3s$.

With the specified values, the answer is $6$.

Another approach to this is by the independent increments property. The idea here is to split up the interior into two independent components of the Brownian Motion. As $s < t$, we can write $W_t = W_s + (W_t - W_s)$, as $W_s$ and $W_t - W_s$ are independent. Substituting this in, $\text{Var}(W_s + W_t) = \text{Var}(W_s + W_s + (W_t - W_s)) = \text{Var}(2W_s + (W_t - W_s))$.

Since $W_s$ and $W_t - W_s$ are independent, we can apply variance linearly, as well as the stationary property, to conclude $\text{Var}(W_s + W_t) = \text{Var}(2W_s) + \text{Var}(W_t - W_s) = 2^2\text{Var}(W_s) + \text{Var}(W_{t-s}) = 4s + (t-s) = t + 3s$, so that with the provided values the answer is $3 + 3 = 6$.

questions.title: Arithmetic Progression I
questions.problem: Three distinct integers from $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$ are selected uniformly at random, where $n$ is an even positive integer. Find the probability that the three numbers form an arithmetic progression when $n = 100$. For example, if the three selected numbers are $26$, $38$, and $14$, this would be an arithmetic progression $14 \rightarrow 26 \rightarrow 38$ with common difference $12$.
questions.solution:
Since $n$ is even, we can write $n = 2k$ for some positive integer $k$. The three values selected must be in form $a, a+d, a + 2d$, where $a$ is the minimum value of the three that are selected, while $d$ is the common difference between the elements.

The idea is to break up based on the common difference, as there are many possible common differences. The minimum possible common difference is $d = 1$, which means the three values are consecutive. The starting point $a$ could be any value from $a = 1$ to $a = 2k-2$, as the maximum would be $2k-2, 2k-1, 2k$. Thus, there are $2k-2$ possible arithmetic progressions with $d = 1$.

If $d = 2$, the values must be the form $a, a+2, a+4$. The smallest possible value would be $a = 1$, while the maximum possible value is $a = 2k-4$, as this is the arithmetic progression $2k-4,2k-2,2k$. Thus, there are $2k-4$ possible progressions here.

With this pattern in mind, we can now generalize to difference $d$. The smallest possible value is $a = 1$, while the largest is $a = 2(k-d)$, as this corresponds to the progression $2k-2d, 2k-d, 2k$. Thus, with common difference $d$, there are $2(k-d)$ possible selections of the values.

Since every sequence of three values can have only one possible common difference, the outcomes are disjoint for varying $d$. This allows us to add up all of the different counts per common difference to obtain the total number of arithmetic progressions. The total number of selections yielding an arithmetic progression is $2(k-1) + 2(k-2) + \dots + 2 = 2\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}i = k(k-1)$.

With no restrictions, there are $\binom{n}{3} = \binom{2k}{3}$ ways to select three values from $[n]$. As all selections are equally likely, the probability of an arithmetic progression is $\dfrac{k(k-1)}{\binom{2k}{3}} = \dfrac{k(k-1)}{\frac{(2k)(2k-1)(2k-2)}{3\cdot 2 \cdot 1}} = \dfrac{3}{2(2k-1)} = \dfrac{3}{2(n-1)}$.

With $n = 100$, the answer is $1/66$.

questions.title: Arithmetic Progression II
questions.problem: Three distinct integers from $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$ are selected uniformly at random, where $n$ is an odd positive integer. Find the probability that the three numbers form an arithmetic progression when $n = 15$. For example, if the three selected numbers are $26$, $38$, and $14$, this would be an arithmetic progression $14 \rightarrow 26 \rightarrow 38$ with common difference $12$.
questions.solution:
Since $n$ is odd, we can write $n = 2k+1$ for some positive integer $k$. The three values selected must be in form $a, a+d, a+2d$, where $a$ is the minimum value of the three that are selected, while $d$ is the common difference between the elements.

The idea is to break up based on the common difference, as there are many possible common differences. The minimum possible common difference is $d = 1$, which means the three values are consecutive. The starting point $a$ could be any value from $a = 1$ to $a = 2k-1$, as the maximum would be $2k-1, 2k, 2k+1$. Thus, there are $2k-1$ possible arithmetic progressions with $d = 1$.

If $d = 2$, the values must be the form $a, a+2, a+4$. The smallest possible value would be $a = 1$, while the maximum possible value is $a = 2k-3$, as this is the arithmetic progression $2k-3,2k-1,2k+1$. Thus, there are $2k-3$ possible progressions here.

With this pattern in mind, we can now generalize to difference $d$. The smallest possible value is $a = 1$, while the largest is $a = 2(k-d)+1$, as this corresponds to the progression $2k-2d+1, 2k-d+1, 2k+1$. Thus, with common difference $d$, there are $2(k-d)+1$ possible selections of the values.

Since every sequence of three values can have only one possible common difference, the outcomes are disjoint for varying $d$. This allows us to add up all of the different counts per common difference to obtain the total number of arithmetic progressions. The total number of selections yielding an arithmetic progression is $2(k-1)+1 + 2(k-2)+1 + \dots + 1 = k + 2\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}i = k^2$.

With no restrictions, there are $\binom{n}{3} = \binom{2k+1}{3}$ ways to select three values from $[n]$. As all selections are equally likely, the probability of an arithmetic progression is $\dfrac{k^2}{\binom{2k+1}{3}} = \dfrac{k^2}{\frac{(2k+1)(2k)(2k-1)}{3\cdot 2 \cdot 1}} = \dfrac{3k}{(2k+1)(2k-1)} = \dfrac{3 \cdot \frac{n-1}{2}}{n(n-2)} = \dfrac{3(n-1)}{2n(n-2)}$.

With $n = 15$, the answer is $7/65$.

questions.title: Uniform Probability I
questions.problem: Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent $U(0,1)$ random variables. Calculate $P(X^5 + Y > 1)$.
questions.solution:
Solution 1:

We condition on $X$ and use the law of total probability:

$$\begin{aligned} P(X^5 + Y > 1) &= \int_{0}^{1} P(X^5 + Y > 1 \mid X = x) f_X(x)\, dx \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} P(Y > 1 - x^5 \mid X = x)\, dx \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} P(Y > 1 - x^5)\, dx \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} 1 - (1 - x^5)\, dx \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} x^5\, dx \\ &= \frac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Solution 2:

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent $U(0,1)$ random variables, the joint density is $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y) = 1$ on the unit square. We compute directly:

$$\begin{aligned} P(X^5 + Y > 1) &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{1-x^5}^{1} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\, dy\, dx \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{1-x^5}^{1} 1\, dy\, dx \\ &= \frac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

questions.title: It's Black and White
questions.problem: Suppose that you have two standard fair $8$-sided dice, one of which is colored black and one of which is colored white. Find the fair value of the following game: Each dice is rolled at the same time. If the two dice show the same value, the game ends. If the white dice shows a value at least $2$ greater than the black dice, you earn $\$1$ and get to roll again. In any other case you earn nothing, but are allowed to roll again.
questions.solution:
We will approach this question by conditioning the outcome on the first roll, and will follow the typical Markov state approach to finding the expectation. Define the following states: $S_0$ = Both dice show the same value, $S_1$ = The white die shows a value at least $2$ greater than the black die, and $S_2$ = The dice show different values, and the white die is not at least $2$ greater than the black die.

Denoting our payout from the game as $V$, we then have $$E[V] = P[S_0]E[V \mid S_0] + P[S_1]E[V \mid S_1] + P[S_2]E[V \mid S_2]$$

To get $P[S_0]$, we can simply note that no matter what the value of the first die is, the other die equals it with probability $1/8$, as one of the $8$ equally likely values is the one on the first die. Thus, $P[S_0] = 1/8$.

To get $P[S_1]$, if the black dice is equal to some value $k$, then the white dice can be any value between $k+2$ and $8$, inclusive. If $k \leq 6$, then there will be $8 - (k+2) + 1 = 7 - k$ numbers between $8$ and $k$ that satisfy the condition. Since this amount is dependent on $k$, we sum over all values of $k$ to get $$P[S_1] = \frac{1}{64}\sum_{k=1}^{6}(7-k) = \frac{21}{64}$$

Note that we don't need to consider $k = 7$ or $k = 8$, since there are no satisfactory values in these cases.

Finally, we can simply get $P[S_2]$ by complementation: $1 - P[S_0] - P[S_1]$, which yields $P[S_2] = \frac{35}{64}$.

As for the expected values, the key is to realize that after making a roll, the game either ends (in case we go to $S_0$), or it repeats itself. Keeping in mind our definitions of the states, we have:

$$\begin{aligned} E[V \mid S_0] &= 0 \\ E[V \mid S_1] &= 1 + E[V] \\ E[V \mid S_2] &= E[V] \end{aligned}$$

The addition of $1$ in $S_1$ is because we receive $\$1$, and the game repeats.

Putting everything together yields: $$E[V] = \frac{1}{8}(0) + \frac{21}{64}(1 + E[V]) + \frac{35}{64}(E[V]) \rightarrow E[V] = \frac{21}{8}$$

questions.title: Convex Quadrilateral
questions.problem: Suppose that $10$ points are randomly placed on the edge of a circle, and you draw all possible chords between the points. If you uniformly and randomly select $4$ chords, what is the probability that these $4$ chords form a convex quadrilateral? A convex quadrilateral is any four-sided polygon where every interior angle is less than $180$ degrees.
questions.solution:
Since any group of $4$ chords are equally likely to be picked, we can determine the probability by calculating the number of ways that $4$ chords can be chosen such that a convex quadrilateral can be formed, and divide that by the total number of ways that we can pick $4$ chords from all of the chords that were drawn.

First, since there are $10$ points and we are drawing a chord between each pair of points, we have $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ total chords. This thus gives us $\binom{45}{4} = 148995$ total ways in which we can pick $4$ chords from all of the chords that were drawn.

Now, note that any choice of $4$ chords forming a convex quadrilateral will correspond to choosing $4$ distinct points on the circle. For any $4$ points on the circle, there will be exactly one selection of chords such that the resulting shape is a convex quadrilateral. Thus, the number of ways to pick $4$ chords such that a convex quadrilateral can be formed is simply given by the number of ways we can choose $4$ of our $10$ points, which is $\binom{10}{4} = 210$.

The final answer is $$\frac{210}{148995} = \frac{2}{1419}$$

questions.title: Bestie Card
questions.problem: Rupert is playing a game where he first picks some integer $k \in \{1, 2, ..., 52\}$. Given $k$, he then draws the first $k$ cards from a regular shuffled deck of $52$ cards. If the last card that Rupert draws is an ace, and if there exists exactly one ace remaining in the deck then Rupert wins. What $k$ should Rupert pick to maximize his probability of winning?
questions.solution:
Solution 1:

Let $k$ be the number of cards drawn and $W$ be the event that Rupert wins. We compute $P[W]$. Among the first $k$ cards, we need position $k$ to be an ace, positions $1$ through $k-1$ to contain exactly $2$ other aces, and the remaining $52 - k$ cards to contain exactly $1$ ace.

The number of favorable arrangements of the $k$-th card being an ace with exactly $2$ aces in positions $1$ to $k-1$ is $\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{k-3}(k-1)!$. Here $\binom{4}{2}$ chooses which $2$ of the $4$ aces go in the first $k-1$ positions, $\binom{48}{k-3}$ picks $k-3$ non-ace cards from the $48$ non-aces, and $(k-1)!$ orders the first $k-1$ cards. The ace at position $k$ can be any of the remaining $2$ aces, and the remaining $52 - k$ cards can be arranged in $(52 - k)!$ ways. The total arrangements are $52!$.

$$\begin{aligned} P[W] &= \frac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{k-3}(k-1)! \cdot 2 \cdot (52-k)!}{52!} \\ &= \frac{12(k-1)(k-2)(52-k)}{52 \cdot 51 \cdot 50 \cdot 49} \\ &= \frac{-12k^3 + 660k^2 - 1896k + 1248}{52 \cdot 51 \cdot 50 \cdot 49} \end{aligned}$$

Setting the derivative to $0$ to find the optimal $k$:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dk}(-12k^3 + 660k^2 - 1896k + 1248) &= -36k^2 + 1320k - 1896 = 0 \\ k &= \frac{55}{3} \pm \frac{\sqrt{2551}}{3} \\ k &\approx 1.5 \text{ or } 35.17 \end{aligned}$$

Since $k = 1.5$ is not an integer and $k$ must be at least $2$ (we need at least $2$ aces in the drawn cards), we check $k = 35$ and $k = 36$ near the second root. We find $P[W] \approx 0.03523$ for $k = 35$ and $P[W] \approx 0.03516$ for $k = 36$, so the optimal $k$ is $k = 35$.

Solution 2:

Alternatively, $P[W]$ can be expressed as: among the first $k-1$ positions choose $2$ for aces ($\binom{k-1}{2}$), the $k$-th card is $1$ of the remaining $2$ aces, and one of the last $52 - k$ positions holds the final ace ($52 - k$ choices). Then multiply by $4!$ (arrangements of the $4$ aces) and $48!$ (arrangements of non-aces):

$$P[W] = \frac{\binom{k-1}{2}(52-k) \cdot 4! \cdot 48!}{52!}$$

This yields the same optimal $k = 35$.

questions.title: Uniform Angle Overlap
questions.problem: Suppose that we have a unit circle sitting on the $(x,y)$ plane centered at $(0,0)$. We randomly generate an angle $\theta \sim \text{Unif}(0, 2\pi)$, and move along the perimeter of the circle $\theta$ radians counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$, coloring the perimeter orange as we go. We then generate two more angles, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, independently from $\text{Unif}(0, 2\pi)$. An arc along the perimeter of the circle of length $\beta$ radians starting from the point that is $\alpha$ radians counterclockwise from $(1,0)$ is then colored green. What is the probability that the orange and green regions are disjoint?
questions.solution:
Solution 1:

For the regions to be disjoint, we need $\alpha > \theta$ (so the green arc starts after the orange arc ends) and $\alpha + \beta \leq 2\pi$ (so the green arc doesn't wrap around). Since $\beta \leq 2\pi$ and the green arc must not overlap, we also need $\alpha \leq \beta$ in terms of the constraint.

We compute $P[\theta < \alpha,\, \alpha \leq \beta \leq 2\pi]$:

$$\begin{aligned} P[\theta < \alpha,\, \alpha \leq \beta \leq 2\pi] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{\theta}^{2\pi} \int_{\alpha}^{2\pi} f_{\theta}(\theta)f_{\alpha}(\alpha)f_{\beta}(\beta)\, d\beta\, d\alpha\, d\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{\theta}^{2\pi} \int_{\alpha}^{2\pi} \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{1}{2\pi}\, d\beta\, d\alpha\, d\theta \\ &= \frac{1}{8\pi^3} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{\theta}^{2\pi} \int_{\alpha}^{2\pi} d\beta\, d\alpha\, d\theta \\ &= \frac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Solution 2:

Conditioning on $\alpha$:

$$\begin{aligned} P[\theta < \alpha,\, \alpha \leq \beta \leq 2\pi] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} P[\theta < a] \cdot P[a \leq \beta \leq 2\pi] \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi}\, da \\ &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \frac{a}{2\pi} \left(1 - \frac{a}{2\pi}\right) \frac{1}{2\pi}\, da \\ &= \frac{1}{8\pi^3} \int_{0}^{2\pi} a(2\pi - a)\, da \\ &= \frac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

questions.title: Parity Streaks
questions.problem: Fix positive integers $h$ and $t$. What is the expected number of flips of a fair coin needed in order to either have $h$ more heads flipped than tails or $t$ more tails flipped than heads? Report the answer when $t = 10$ and $h = 8$.
questions.solution:
In this scenario, on each flip, the number of heads or the number of tails increases by $1$ with equal probability. We can view the stopping conditions as boundaries: Either $h$ more heads than tails or $t$ more tails than heads. This type of "change in either direction by $1$" and "boundary" scenario should be reminiscent of a simple symmetric random walk.

The question is: How can we frame this problem as such? We must think about some quantity that either rises by $1$ or drops by $1$ at each turn. This observation makes it natural: We should look at the difference of heads and tails, say $H - T$, on each turn. If there is a heads, this quantity increases by $1$, and if there is a tails, it decreases by $1$. In other words, we can model the difference between the number of heads and tails we have flipped as a simple symmetric random walk on the integers.

The process now ends when this walk hits $h$ or $-t$, as those are the cases where we have $h$ more heads than tails and $t$ more tails than heads.

The above is now a well-known problem: For a symmetric random walk, the expected hitting time of an element in the set $\{-x, y\}$ for $x, y > 0$ is $xy$. In this case, $x = t$ and $y = h$, so the answer is $ht$.

With our specified values, the answer is $80$.

questions.title: Cutting Wood
questions.problem: Lewis is cutting a piece of wood of length $L$ into three pieces. In order to cut the wood, he independently and uniformly at random chooses two cutpoints, one on each side of the midpoint of the piece of wood. What is the probability that the distance between Lewis' two cutpoints is less than $\frac{L}{3}$? Record the answer when $L = 2$.
questions.solution:
First, note that the value of $L$ is irrelevant here. The reason for this is that the two points are distributed uniformly, and the quantities we care about all depend on $L$. Thus, we can simply fix $L = 1$ and proceed.

Let the two cutpoints that Lewis chooses be denoted as $X_1$ and $X_2$, where $X_1$ is the cutpoint to the left of the midpoint and $X_2$ is the cutpoint to the right of the midpoint. Since they are chosen uniformly at random we have $X_1 \sim \text{Unif}(0, \frac{1}{2})$ and $X_2 \sim \text{Unif}(\frac{1}{2}, 1)$.

We are thus interested in finding $P[X_2 - X_1 \leq \frac{1}{3}]$. Since we have two sources of randomness here, let's condition on one of them and use the law of total probability:

$$\begin{aligned} P[X_2 - X_1 \leq \tfrac{1}{3}] &= \int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} P[X_2 - X_1 \leq \tfrac{1}{3} \mid X_1 = x]\, f_{X_1}(x)\, dx \\ &= \int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} P[X_2 \leq \tfrac{1}{3} + x]\, 2\, dx \end{aligned}$$

which follows from the fact that $X_1 \sim \text{Unif}(0, \frac{1}{2})$, and that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent.

Since $X_2 \sim \text{Unif}(\frac{1}{2}, 1)$, we can see that $P[X_2 \leq \frac{1}{3} + x] = 2(\frac{1}{3} + x - \frac{1}{2}) = 2(x - \frac{1}{6})$.

However, we must be careful with the bounds of integration. Since $X_2$ is always at least $\frac{1}{2}$, then $P[X_2 \leq \frac{1}{3} + x] = 0$ for any $x$ such that $\frac{1}{3} + x < \frac{1}{2}$, i.e., for $x < \frac{1}{6}$. Thus, the lower bound on our integral is $\frac{1}{6}$, since the interior expression is $0$ on $[0, \frac{1}{6})$.

We thus have: $$P[X_2 - X_1 \leq \tfrac{1}{3}] = \int_{\frac{1}{6}}^{\frac{1}{2}} 2\left(x - \tfrac{1}{6}\right) \cdot 2\, dx = \frac{2}{9}$$

questions.title: Rewin I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play in a tennis match indefinitely. One of them starts serving at random, and the winner of the previous point is who serves in the next point. Alice wins each point she serves with probability $p_1$, while she wins every point Bob serves with probability $p_2$. Find the proportion of points that are won by Alice. Report the answer when $p_1 = 2/3$ and $p_2 = 1/3$.
questions.solution:
To find the proportion of points, we need to find the expected amount of points that are played between consecutive points that Alice wins. At an intuitive level, if there are, on average, $\mu$ points that occur between consecutive points Alice wins, her proportion of wins is $1/\mu$, as she wins $1$ out of every $\mu$ points on average.

We can view this as a Markov chain with two states: Alice serving and Bob serving. Let $T_A$ and $T_B$ be the expected time until Alice wins a point given Alice and Bob, respectively, are serving.

To find $E[T_A]$, we condition on who wins the point Alice just served. If Alice wins, which occurs with probability $p_1$, it takes just $1$ point for Alice to win again. If Bob wins, which occurs with probability $1 - p_1$, it takes $1 + E[T_B]$ points on average for Alice to win. We add $1$ because there was a point that just occurred.

Alice wins each point Bob serves with probability $p_2$, so $T_B \sim \text{Geom}(p_2)$, as this counts the distribution of the waiting time until Alice wins. This has mean $E[T_B] = 1/p_2$, so we obtain the equation:

$$E[T_A] = p_1 \cdot 1 + (1-p_1)\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{p_2}\right) = 1 + \dfrac{1-p_1}{p_2}$$

$E[T_A]$ represents the number of points played between consecutive wins of Alice, so the proportion of points Alice wins is:

$$\dfrac{1}{E[T_A]} = \dfrac{p_2}{1 - (p_2 - p_1)}$$

With the values in question, the answer is $1/2$.

questions.title: Linear Brownian I
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion, and define $T = \inf\{t > 0: W_t = a + bt\}$. In other words, $T$ is the hitting time of the Brownian Motion to the line $y = a + bx$. Assume that $a$ and $b$ are of opposite signs, with $b \neq 0$. Compute $E[T]$ when $a = 5$ and $b = -1$.
questions.solution:
By the definition of $T$, we know that $W_T = a + bT$, so $E[W_T]$ would indeed yield $E[T]$. As Brownian Motion is a martingale, it's natural to apply OST to $W_t$. Namely,

$$E[W_T] = E[W_0] \iff E[a + bT] = 0 \iff E[T] = -\dfrac{a}{b}$$

This result makes intuitive sense: On average, the Brownian Motion is $0$ at all times, so the expected time for the line to hit the Brownian Motion should be equal to the point at which the line hits $0$, which is $-a/b$.

With the specified values, the answer is $5$.

questions.title: Geometric Brownian Hit
questions.problem: Let $X_t$ be a Geometric Brownian Motion starting at $S_0$ with drift $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ such that $2\mu > \sigma^2$. Define $T_x = \inf\{t > 0: X_t = x\}$, i.e. the hitting time of $x$. Assuming that $x > S_0$, find $E[T_x]$. Report the answer when $S_0 = 1$, $x = e$, $\sigma = 2$, and $\mu = 3$.
questions.solution:
By the definition of a GBM, $X_t = S_0\exp\left((\mu - \sigma^2/2)t + \sigma W_t\right)$, where $W_t$ is a standard Brownian Motion. Therefore, we can write:

$$T = \inf\left\{t > 0: S_0\exp\left((\mu - \sigma^2/2)t + \sigma W_t\right) = x\right\} = \inf\left\{t > 0: W_t = \dfrac{\ln(x/S_0)}{\sigma} - \dfrac{\mu - \sigma^2/2}{\sigma}\, t\right\}$$

This is exactly the form of "Linear Brownian" with $a = \frac{\ln(x/S_0)}{\sigma}$ and $b = -\frac{\mu - \sigma^2/2}{\sigma}$. Since $x > S_0$, the first term is positive. Similarly, as $2\mu > \sigma^2$, the coefficient of $t$ is negative, so the result applies here.

By the definition of $T$, we know that $W_T = a + bT$, so $E[W_T]$ would indeed yield $E[T]$. As Brownian Motion is a martingale, it's natural to apply OST to $W_t$. Namely,

$$E[W_T] = E[W_0] \iff E[a + bT] = 0 \iff E[T] = -\dfrac{a}{b}$$

Plugging these in:

$$E[T_x] = \dfrac{\ln(x/S_0)}{\mu - \sigma^2/2}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $1$.

questions.title: Stone Pick I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob pick alternate turns in the following game: Initially, there are $n \geq 1$ stones in the middle. Either player can choose to take $1$ to $r$ stones from the pile. Assume that $n \equiv 1 \pmod{r+1}$. The player who draws the last stone loses. Alice gets to determine if she goes first or second. Assuming Alice selects her position in the game optimally and both Alice and Bob play optimally, in how many turns (total actions by the players) does Alice win the game, inclusive of the draw that makes Bob lose, when $n = 101$ and $r = 4$?
questions.solution:
We want Alice's optimal strategy to be independent of what Bob does. The condition that $n \equiv 1 \pmod{r+1}$ gives a hint as to the actions of the players.

The first person to draw picks any arbitrary amount of stones. The trick here is to have the second player pick an amount of stones such that the sum of the two quantities the players drew is $r+1$. For example, if $r = 4$ and the first player draws $3$ stones, the second player draws $2$ stones.

Creating multiples of $r+1$ is the key because $n$ has a remainder of $1$ when divided by $r+1$, and the person to draw the last stone loses. Therefore, the idea is to remove multiples of $r+1$ at each pair of turns by the players so that there is $1$ stone left, and then the first player to act must draw that stone, meaning they lose.

Therefore, Alice should choose to go second, and she will win in $1 + 2 \cdot \dfrac{n-1}{r+1}$ turns, as $r+1 \mid n-1$, which is the number of cycles the game goes through. Each cycle contains $2$ actions by the players, and then $1$ additional action is needed for Bob to select the last stone.

With the specific values, the answer is $41$.

questions.title: Stone Pick II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob pick alternate turns in the following game: Initially, there are $n \geq 1$ stones in the middle. Either player can choose to take $1$ to $r$ stones from the pile. Assume that $n \equiv 1 \pmod{r+1}$. The player who draws the last stone wins. Alice gets to determine if she goes first or second. Assuming Alice selects her position in the game optimally and both Alice and Bob play optimally, in how many turns (total actions by the players) does Alice win the game, inclusive of the draw that makes Bob lose, when $n = 101$ and $r = 4$?
questions.solution:
We want Alice's optimal strategy to be independent of what Bob does. The condition that $n \equiv 1 \pmod{r+1}$ gives a hint as to the actions of the players.

The goal is to now draw the last stone. Therefore, the first person to draw should pick a single stone on the first turn. Afterwards, player $1$ can apply the same strategy as the one described in "Stone Pick I" to win. We flipped the game around, so it makes sense that Alice will now want to be the first player to go instead of the last.

This results in a winning strategy because player $2$ will have $(r+1)k$ stones in the pile at each turn he acts on if player $1$ applies the strategy of the previous part. Therefore, when there are $r+1$ stones left, player $2$ can't win from that position. No matter how many stones player $2$ picks from that position, player $1$ can draw the remaining stones, as there will be at most $r$ of them, and win.

Therefore, Alice should choose to go first, and she will win in $1 + 2 \cdot \dfrac{n-1}{r+1}$ turns, as $r+1 \mid n-1$, which is the number of cycles the game goes through. Each cycle contains $2$ actions by the players, and then $1$ additional action is needed for Alice to select $1$ stone on the first turn.

With the specific values, the answer is $41$.

questions.title: Between Uniforms
questions.problem: Alice, Bob, and Chet play a game where each one selects a real number between $0$ and $1$. The winner is the person who selects a value between the other two values. Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be the numbers that Alice, Bob, and Chet select, respectively. It is known that $A \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$ and $B \sim \text{Unif}(1/2, b)$, where $1/2 < b < 1$. Chet gets to select whatever number he wants. What value should Chet select to maximize his probability of winning when $b = 3/4$?
questions.solution:
Solution 1:

Let $t$ be the value Chet selects. We want to maximize $f(t) = P[A < t < B] + P[B < t < A]$.

We compute each term: $P[A < t, B > t] = P[A < t]P[B > t] = t \cdot \dfrac{b-t}{b-1/2}$ and $P[B < t, A > t] = P[B < t]P[A > t] = (1-t) \cdot \dfrac{t-1/2}{b-1/2}$.

Combining, $f(t) = \dfrac{t(b-t) + (1-t)(t-1/2)}{b-1/2}$.

Taking the derivative and setting it to zero: $f'(t) = \dfrac{2b+3-8t}{2b-1} = 0 \iff t^* = \dfrac{2b+3}{8}$.

With $b = 3/4$, the answer is $9/16$.

Solution 2:

Note that $E[A] = 1/2$ and $E[B] = (1/2+b)/2$. The optimal value for Chet is the midpoint of the two means, which gives $\frac{2b+3}{8}$.

questions.title: Card Composition
questions.problem: You have infinitely many cards with labels $1, 2, \dots, n$ to create a deck of cards. You may put in as many or as few cards as you'd like of each type. After you're done, you show the deck to your friend, they guess a number, and you draw out a card from your deck. If the card you draw matches your friend's guess, you pay them the amount on the card. Assuming both you and your friend play optimally, what is your friend's expected payout when $n = 100$? Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
The key to solving here is the principle of indifference. In the context of this problem, your friend's expected gain from the game should be the same, irrespective of what value they guess. Intuitively, if this expected value was non-constant, they would be able to guess a number with higher expected gain, exploiting your deck.

Suppose that $p_i$ is the proportion of the deck that is composed of cards with value $i$. The principle of indifference says that $1p_1 = 2p_2 = \dots = np_n \iff p_i = \dfrac{1}{i}p_1$.

Since $\sum_{i=1}^n p_i = 1$, we can conclude that $\sum_{i=1}^n p_i = p_1 \sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac{1}{i} = 1 \iff p_1 = \dfrac{1}{1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/n}$.

By the above, we can conclude that $p_i = \dfrac{1}{i}p_1 = \dfrac{1/i}{1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/n}$.

Since the expected payout is constant regardless of the value your friend selects, we can conclude that the expected payout is $ip_i = \dfrac{1}{1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/n}$.

With $n = 100$, the answer is approximately $0.193$.

questions.title: Big Envelope
questions.problem: You have two envelopes in front of you with $\$X$ and $\$2X$, where $X \sim \text{Unif}(0, a)$ for some $a > 0$ that is known. You select one of them uniformly at random and look at the value inside. After looking inside, you have the option to keep the envelope you have or switch. Under optimal strategy, what is the probability we obtain the envelope with $\$2X$ when $a = 100$?
questions.solution:
To maximize the expected value, we want to determine a strategy based on what value is observed in the first envelope. Clearly, if the observed value is larger than $a$, you shouldn't switch, as the other envelope can only contain less money. However, if the observed money is at most $\$a$, we must be careful in determining which envelope we are looking at.

The envelope with $\$X$ in it contains at most $a$ always, while the one with $\$2X$ only contains at most $\$a$ $50\%$ of the time. Therefore, given we see at most $a$ in the envelope, it's more likely to be the one with $\$X$ rather than $\$2X$, so we switch. In particular, if the value is less than $\$a$, it's twice as likely to be the one with $\$X$ as opposed to $\$2X$.

Using the above strategy, we can find the probability of selecting the envelope with $\$2X$. There are two cases where we obtain the envelope with $\$2X$.

If the first envelope selected has more than $\$a$ inside, we don't swap. For the first envelope to have more than $\$a$, two things must be true: $X > a/2$ (probability $1/2$ by uniformity) and the envelope with $\$2X$ is selected (probability $1/2$ by random selection). By the above, the probability the first envelope has more than $\$a$, meaning you don't switch, is $1/4$.

Therefore, the probability the first envelope selected has at most $\$a$ is $3/4$. To switch to the one with $\$2X$ inside, you must select the one with $\$X$ inside on the first draw. Given the envelope has at most $\$a$, it's twice as likely to be the one with $\$X$ inside, so the probability of switching to the one with $\$2X$ must be $2/3$, as the probabilities sum to $1$.

By the Law of Total Probability, the probability of obtaining the envelope with $\$2X$ is $\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

questions.title: Partial Sums I
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are all IID random variables with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Define $S_j = X_1 + \dots + X_j$, with $S_0 = 0$. If possible, compute $E[S_k \mid S_n]$, where $0 \leq k \leq n$. Report the answer when $X_1, \dots, X_n \sim \text{Exp}(1)$ IID, $k = 4, n = 10$, and $S_{10} = 15$.
questions.solution: It helps to solve this problem by substituting in the definitions of $S_k$ and $S_n$. Plugging them in, we want to compute $E[X_1 + \dots + X_k \mid X_1 + \dots + X_k + \dots + X_n] = E[X_1 \mid X_1 + \dots + X_n] + \dots + E[X_n \mid X_1 + \dots + X_n]$. Since $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are IID, $X_1 \mid S_n, \dots, X_n \mid S_n$ are identically distributed, as the information in $S_n$ is symmetric between the random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$. By taking expectations, we can conclude $E[X_1 \mid S_n] = \dots = E[X_n \mid S_n]$. We want to relate the individual expectations to something we know the conditional expectation of. By the definition of conditional expectation, $E[S_n \mid S_n] = S_n$, as it's known, and we also have that $E[S_n \mid S_n] = E[X_1 \mid S_n] + \dots + E[X_n \mid S_n] = S_n$. All of the terms on the LHS are equal, so we can write this as $nE[X_1 \mid S_n] = S_n \iff E[X_1 \mid S_n] = \dfrac{S_n}{n}$. This should make intuitive sense: Since there are $n$ IID random variables contributing to the value of $S_n$, each one should contribute proportion of the sum $S_n$ on average, meaning the conditional expected value is $1/n \cdot S_n$. Now, we can compute $E[S_k \mid S_n]$ easily as follows: $E[S_k \mid S_n] = E[X_1 \mid S_n] + \dots + E[X_k \mid S_n] = kE[X_1 \mid S_n] = \dfrac{k}{n}S_n$. With the specified values, the answer is $6$.

questions.title: Partial Sums II
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1, \dots, X_k$ are all IID random variables with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Define $S_j = X_1 + \dots + X_j$, with $S_0 = 0$. If possible, compute $E[S_k \mid S_n]$, where $0 \leq n \leq k$. Report the answer when $X_1, \dots, X_k \sim \text{Exp}(1)$ IID, $k = 10, n = 4$, and $S_4 = 5$.
questions.solution: Since $n \leq k$ here, we want to relate the value of $S_k$ to $S_n$. To do this, we can expand out the definitions of $S_k$ and $S_n$ to note $S_k = X_1 + \dots + X_k = [X_1 + \dots + X_n] + X_{n+1} + \dots + X_k = S_n + X_{n+1} + \dots + X_k$. We want to do this because the information of $S_n$ is given, so we can write $E[S_k \mid S_n] = E[S_n + X_{n+1} + \dots + X_k \mid S_n] = E[S_n \mid S_n] + E[X_{n+1} \mid S_n] + \dots + E[X_k \mid S_n]$. The first conditional expectation is $S_n$, as $S_n$ is given. $X_i$, where $n+1 \leq i \leq k$, is independent of $S_n$, as $S_n$ only includes information about the first $n$ random variables, and the random variables are IID. Using this fact, the conditional expectation can be dropped to the unconditional expectation: $E[X_i \mid S_n] = E[X_i] = \mu$ for all $n+1 \leq i \leq k$. Substituting all of these in, we can conclude $E[S_k \mid S_n] = S_n + \mu + \dots + \mu = S_n + (k-n)\mu$. With the specified values, the answer is $11$.

questions.title: Minimum Match
questions.problem: Two dice with the values $1 - n$ on the sides are rolled, with side $i$ having probability $p_i$ of appearing. You are to choose $p_1, \dots, p_n$ in any way you'd like, but they must be common between the two dice. What is the minimum probability that the two dice show the same value? Report the answer for $n = 10$.
questions.solution: Intuitively, the fair die is the "most random" in the sense of having no bias towards any side. If there was a side that had probability more than $1/n$ of appearing, the dice would be more "biased" to showing the same value, and hence has less variance in the outcomes, leading to a higher probability of a single side showing. This intuition is helpful in claiming that $1/n$ may be the minimum. We can prove this rigorously with the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality. This inequality is often helpful in bounding problems. We require $p_1 + \dots + p_n = 1$ by the definition of a probability distribution. The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality states $\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i\right)^2 \leq \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2$. As $p_1 + \dots + p_n = 1$, we can also write $(p_1 + \dots + p_n)^2 = 1$, so $$\begin{align*} 1 &= (p_1 + \dots + p_n)^n\\ &= (1 \cdot p_1 + \dots + 1 \cdot p_n)^2\\ &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^n 1 \cdot p_i\right)^2\\ &\leq \sum_{i=1}^n 1^2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2\\ &= n\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2 \end{align*}$$ By the last line, we can conclude $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2 \geq 1/n$. The LHS of this expression is exactly the probability that the two dice show the same values, as they are independent and can show the values $1, 2, \dots, n$ in common. With $n = 10$, the answer is $1/10$.

questions.title: Sum First II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob alternate rolling pairs of standard fair $6$-sided dice, with Alice going first. The game ends when Alice rolls a sum of $6$ or when Bob rolls a sum of $7$, whichever comes first. A turn is when either Alice or Bob rolls. Find the variance of the number of turns in the game. Report the answer to the nearest hundredth.
questions.solution:
