All that remains is to count the pairs with $|(j-i) \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n| = 1$: pairs of the form $(k,k+1)$ or $(k+1,k)$ for $1 \leq k \leq n-1$, plus $(1,n)$ and $(n,1)$. There are $2(n-1) + 2 = 2n$ such pairs.

Plugging in:
$$\var{T} = np(1-p)(1-p(1-p)) + 2np^2(1-p)^2 = np(1-p) + np^2(1-p)^2 = np(1-p)(1 + p(1-p))$$

With the specified values, the answer is $44/9$.

questions.title: Placed Turnover
questions.problem: Rishi has $n$ fair coins lined up in positions $1$ to $n$. He flips all $n$ of them, and then performs the following iterative process: He counts how many heads there are among the $n$ coins. If there are exactly $k$ heads among the $n$ coins, the coin in position $k$ is turned over. This process iterates until all of the coins show tails. For example, with $n = 3$, if Rishi gets $TTH$, the sequence of turnovers is: $TTH \rightarrow HTH \rightarrow HHH \rightarrow HHT \rightarrow HTT \rightarrow TTT$, ending the process in $5$ turnovers. Find the expected number of turnovers Rishi needs to perform. Report the answer when $n = 40$.
questions.solution:
Since this problem is very complicated, let us enumerate all outcomes for small $n$ and look for a pattern.

When $n = 1$: outcomes $H$ and $T$ take $1$ and $0$ turnovers, so the expected value is $1/2$.

When $n = 2$: $TT$ takes $0$, $HH$ takes $2$, $HT$ takes $1$, and $TH$ takes $3$ turnovers. Expected value: $(0+1+2+3)/4 = 3/2$.

When $n = 3$: enumerating all eight outcomes gives expected value $\frac{0+1+2+3+3+4+5+6}{8} = 3$.

The pattern between these is:
$$\begin{align*}
    \dfrac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{1 \cdot 2}{4}\\
    \dfrac{3}{2} &= \dfrac{2 \cdot 3}{4}\\
    3 &= \dfrac{3 \cdot 4}{4}
\end{align*}$$

So our guess is that the expected number of turnovers is $\frac{n(n+1)}{4}$.

To verify this, we perform induction on $n$. The base case $n = 1$ is verified. Suppose that for all $1 \leq k \leq n-1$, the expected number of turnovers with $k$ coins is $\frac{k(k+1)}{2}$. We must show that the expected number with $n$ coins is $\frac{n(n+1)}{4}$.

We condition on the parity of the last coin. Let $T_r$ be the expected number of turnovers when there are $r$ coins.

Case 1: The last coin is tails. It never gets turned over (impossible for there to be $n$ heads), so it is as if that coin did not exist. $T_{n-1}$ turnovers are needed on average.

Case 2: The last coin is heads. The only way the process can terminate is for all coins to show heads, after which we progressively flip each coin from right to left taking $n$ moves. By a symmetry argument (flipping the direction and target gives an equivalent game), the expected number of turnovers until all the first $n-1$ coins are all heads is also $T_{n-1}$. So $T_{n-1} + n$ turnovers are needed on average in case 2.

By the Law of Total Expectation:
$$T_n = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot T_{n-1} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (T_{n-1} + n) = T_{n-1} + \dfrac{n}{2}$$

This is a linear recurrence with $T_1 = 1/2$, so:
$$\begin{align*}
T_n &= T_{n-1} + \dfrac{n}{2}\\
&= T_{n-2} + \dfrac{n-1}{2} + \dfrac{n}{2}\\
&\hspace{40pt} \vdots\\
&= T_1 + \dfrac{2}{2} + \dots + \dfrac{n}{2}\\
&= \dfrac{1 + 2+ \dots + n}{2}\\
&= \dfrac{n(n+1)}{4}
\end{align*}$$

With $n = 40$, the answer is $410$.

questions.title: Andrew Tate's Elevator II
questions.problem: Andrew Tate was captured by the matrix and now works a day job in a building that is $n$ floors tall. His desk is on the $m$th floor of the building. There are $r$ elevators in the building that continuously move from floors $1$ to $n$ and back, and only stop when a button has been pressed to stop at a certain floor. Assume all of the following: The time it takes for each elevator to stop at a floor is negligible. The time it takes for people to board is negligible. The elevators move at the same constant speed. Andrew Tate wants to leave at a uniformly random time throughout the day. Andrew Tate will board the first elevator that reaches his floor once he decides to leave. What is the probability that the elevator Andrew Tate boards to leave work is going down? Report the answer when $m = 10, n = 50,$ and $r = 4$ to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution:
This problem is a generalization for more than one elevator. Each elevator is at a uniformly random point along its path at the time Andrew wants to go home.

Some intuitive properties our formula should satisfy: If $m = n$, the answer should be $0$. If $m = 1$, the answer should be $1$. If $m = (n+1)/2$, the answer should be $1/2$, as there is a length $(n-1)/2$ above and below this floor.

The key insight is that there are two regions: one where the elevator is equally likely to come from above or below, and one where it is not. If $m$ is below the midpoint, the equally likely region has total path length $4(m-1)$, so the probability of any given elevator being in the equally likely region is $\frac{2(m-1)}{n-1}$.

Let $E$ be the event that there is at least one elevator in the equally likely region, and $D$ be the event that the first elevator reaching floor $m$ is going down. By the Law of Total Probability:
$$\prob{D} = \prob{D \mid E}\prob{E} + \prob{D \mid E^c}\prob{E^c}$$

Since there are $r$ elevators operating independently:
$$\prob{E} = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{2(m-1)}{n-1}\right)^r$$

Given at least one elevator in the region, $\prob{D \mid E} = 1/2$. If no elevator is in the region (and $m$ is below the midpoint), all elevators are above, so $\prob{D \mid E^c} = 1$.

Plugging in when $m$ is below the midpoint:
$$\prob{D} = \left(1 - \dfrac{2(m-1)}{n-1}\right)^r + \dfrac{1 - \left(1 - \frac{2(m-1)}{n-1}\right)^r}{2} = \dfrac{1 + \left(1 - \frac{2(m-1)}{n-1}\right)^r}{2}$$

When $m$ is above the midpoint:
$$\prob{D} = \dfrac{1 - \left(1 - \frac{2(n-m)}{n-1}\right)^r}{2}$$

Since $m = 10$ is below the midpoint of $n = 50$, we use the former formula, which results in the answer $\approx 0.5801$.

questions.title: Andrew Tate's Elevator III
questions.problem: Andrew Tate was captured by the matrix and now works a day job in a building that is $n$ floors tall. His desk is on the $m$th floor of the building. There are $r$ elevators in the building that continuously move from floors $1$ to $n$ and back, and only stop when a button has been pressed to stop at a certain floor. Assume all of the following: The time it takes for each elevator to stop at a floor is negligible. The time it takes for people to board is negligible. The elevators move at the same constant speed. Andrew Tate wants to leave at a uniformly random time throughout the day. Andrew Tate will board the first elevator that reaches his floor once he decides to leave. What is the probability that the elevator Andrew Tate boards to leave work is going down? Report the answer when $m = 40, n = 50,$ and $r = 4$ to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution:
The analysis is the same as Andrew Tate's Elevator II. Since $m = 40$ is above the midpoint of $n = 50$, we use the formula:
$$\prob{D} = \dfrac{1 - \left(1 - \frac{2(n-m)}{n-1}\right)^r}{2}$$

which results in the answer $\approx 0.4387$.

questions.title: Game Prediction
questions.problem: A single-elimination tournament of $2^n$ teams consists of $n$ rounds. You, as a good sports better, want to bet on the outcome of all $2^n - 1$ matches in the tournament. In other words, for each game, you want to choose a winner for that game. Your payout is computed as follows: $\$1$ for each game you predict correctly in round $1$. $\$2$ for each game you predict correctly in round $2$. More generally, you receive $\$2^{k-1}$ for each game you predict correctly in round $k$, with $k = n$ (the finals) being the last round. All of the bets must be placed in advance of the tournament, and the initial bracket is visible to you. In game $i$, the two teams participating, say $A_i$ and $B_i$, have respective probabilities of $p_i$ and $1-p_i$ of winning the game. Since you know nothing about sports, you flip a fair coin to decide which team to bet on in each game. You do this by starting with all games in round $1$, then move to round $2$, and so on. Assuming that each game has an independent outcome, what is your expected payout when $n = 10$ and $p_i = 1/3$ for all $i$?
questions.solution:
Since we are looking to compute the expected total payout throughout all the rounds, linearity of expectation is the best approach. We label the games $1$ to $2^n -1$, where games $1$ to $2^{n-1}$ are in round $1$, games $2^{n-1} + 1$ to $2^{n-1} + 2^{n-2}$ are in round $2$, and so on.

Let $I_1,\dots, I_{2^n - 1}$ be the indicators that games $1$ to $2^{n} - 1$ are guessed correctly. Our payout would be:
$$T = (I_1 + \dots I_{2^{n-1}}) + 2(I_{2^{n-1} + 1} + \dots + I_{2^{n-1} + 2^{n-2}}) + \dots + 2^{n-1}I_{2^n - 1}$$

What is the probability we guess correctly in game $i$, given we know who participates? Suppose we assign heads to guessing team $A_i$ and tails to guessing team $B_i$. Our guess is correct in two cases: Heads and $A_i$ actually wins (probability $p_i/2$), or Tails and $B_i$ actually wins (probability $(1-p_i)/2$). Adding these yields probability $1/2$ of guessing correctly, regardless of who wins.

Intuitively: No matter who won, the coin gives you the side that corresponds to the winner with probability $1/2$.

This allows us to conclude that all indicators corresponding to a given round have the same mean:
$$\ev{T} = 2^{n-1}\ev{I_1} + 2 \cdot 2^{n-2} \ev{I_{2^{n-1} +1}} + \dots + 2^{n-1}\ev{I_{2^n -1}} = 2^{n-1}\left(\ev{I_1} + \ev{I_{2^{n-1} + 1}} + \dots + \ev{I_{2^n - 1}}\right)$$

The expected value of the indicator in the $k$th round is the probability of guessing that game correctly. To guess the winner of the $k$th round game correctly, two things must happen: the winner of the $k$th round must be guessed correctly (call this person $P$), AND in each of the first $k-1$ rounds that person $P$ played, you must have guessed them to be the winner. Since the probability of guessing correctly per game is $1/2$, independent of other games, the probability of guessing the $k$th game correctly is $1/2^k$.

Plugging in:
$$\ev{T} = 2^{n-1}\left(1/2 + 1/4 + \dots + 1/2^n\right) = 2^{n-2} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \dfrac{1}{2^i} = 2^{n-2} \cdot \dfrac{1-1/2^n}{1-1/2} = \dfrac{2^n - 1}{2}$$

With $n = 10$, the answer is $1023/2$.

questions.title: Repeatedly Smaller Uniforms II
questions.problem: Fix a real number $0 < t < 1$. You generate the sequence of random variables $X_1,X_2,\dots$ sequentially such that $X_i \mid X_{i-1} \sim \unif{0}{X_{i-1}}$, where $X_0 = 1$. Define $N_t = \inf\{n : X_n \leq t\}$ i.e. the first index $n$ such that $X_n \leq t$. Find $\var{N_{1/4}}$ to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution:
We know $X_1 \geq X_2 \geq \dots$ by construction. Since all of the random variables are Uniform, we use the property: If $U \sim \unif{0}{a}$, then $U/a \sim \unif{0}{1}$.

Since $\var{X} = \ev{X^2} - (\ev{X})^2$, we consider Law of Total Expectation on $\ev{N_t^2}$:
$$\ev{N_t^2} = \ev{\ev{N_t^2 \mid X_1}} = \int_0^1 \ev{N_t^2 \mid X_1 = x}~dx$$

Breaking up based on whether $x \leq t$:
$$\ev{N_t^2} = \int_0^t \ev{N_t^2 \mid X_1 = x}~dx + \int_t^1 \ev{N_t^2 \mid X_1 = x}~dx$$

If $x \leq t$, then $N_t = 1$. If $x > t$, since $X_2 \mid X_1 = x \sim \unif{0}{x}$ and $\frac{X_2}{x} \mid X_1 = x \sim \unif{0}{1}$, rescaling by $1/x$ stretches $t$ to $t/x$. Thus for $x > t$:
$$\ev{N_t^2 \mid X_1 = x} = \ev{(1 + N_{t/x})^2}$$

(Adding $1$ for the turn already spent.)

Plugging in and using $\ev{N_v} = 1 - \ln(v)$ from the first part:
$$\ev{N_t^2} = \int_0^t 1~dx + \int_t^1 \ev{(1 + N_{t/x})^2}~dx = t + \int_t^1 \left(1 + 2\ev{N_{t/x}} + \ev{N_{t/x}^2}\right)~dx = 1-2\ln(t) + \int_t^1 \ev{N_{t/x}^2}~dx$$

Let $f(v) = \ev{N_v^2}$, so $f(t) = 1 - 2\ln(t) + \int_t^1 f(t/x)~dx$, with initial condition $f(1) = 1$.

Using the substitution $u = t/x$, $du = -t/x^2~dx$, giving $dx/t = -1/u^2~du$:
$$f(t) = 1 - 2\ln(t) + t\int_t^1 \dfrac{f(u)}{u^2}~du$$

Differentiating both sides (product rule on RHS):
$$f'(t) = -\dfrac{2}{t} + \int_t^1 \dfrac{f(u)}{u^2}~du + t \cdot \left(0  - \dfrac{f(t)}{t^2}\right) = -\dfrac{2}{t} + \int_t^1 \dfrac{f(u)}{u^2}~du - \dfrac{f(t)}{t}$$

From the original recurrence: $\int_t^1 \dfrac{f(u)}{u^2}~du = \dfrac{f(t) + 2\ln(t) - 1}{t}$. Plugging in:
$$f'(t) = \frac{f(t) + 2\ln(t) - 1}{t} - \dfrac{f(t)}{t} - \dfrac{2}{t} = \dfrac{2\ln(t)}{t} - \dfrac{3}{t}$$

Solving: $f(t) = (\ln(t))^2 - 3\ln(t) + C$. With $f(1) = 1$: $1 = 0 + C \iff C = 1$, so:
$$f(t) = \ev{N_t^2} = (\ln(t))^2 - 3\ln(t) + 1$$

The variance is:
$$\var{N_t} = \ev{N_t^2} - \left(\ev{N_t}\right)^2 = (\ln(t))^2 - 3\ln(t)+ 1 - (1 - \ln(t))^2 = -\ln(t)$$

With $t = 1/4$, the answer is $\approx 1.3863$.

questions.title: Quicker Hands
questions.problem: A standard deck of cards is uniformly at random split into two sub-decks of $13$ and $39$ cards. Afterwards, cards are dealt from the top of each deck one-by-one until the first Ace appears, in which case, the deck showing the Ace is declared the winner. If an Ace shows up at the same time from each deck, neither deck is declared a winner. To the nearest ten-thousandth, find the probability that the deck of $13$ cards is the winner.
questions.solution:
Let $A_0,A_1,\dots, A_4$ denote the events that $0$ through $4$ Aces are in the $13$-card deck. Let $W$ denote the event that the $13$-card deck wins.

By the Law of Total Probability:
$$\prob{W} = \sum_{i=0}^4 \prob{W \mid A_i}\prob{A_i}$$

The probability of $i$ Aces in the $13$-card deck is:
$$\prob{A_i} = \dfrac{\binom{4}{i} \binom{48}{13-i}}{\binom{52}{13}}$$

(Choose $i$ of the $4$ Aces and $13-i$ of the $48$ non-Aces, divided by total ways to choose $13$ from $52$.)

Clearly $\prob{W \mid A_0} = 0$ and $\prob{W \mid A_4} = 1$.

For $\prob{W \mid A_1}$: The $13$-card deck has $1$ Ace and the $39$-card deck has $3$. Let $P$ be the position of the Ace in the $13$-card deck (uniform on $\{1,\dots,13\}$). For the $13$-card deck to win, its Ace must appear before any Ace in the $39$-card deck. Given $P = k$, the $39$-card deck must have all $3$ Aces in positions $k+1,\dots, 39$:
$$\prob{W \mid A_1} = \dfrac{1}{13}\sum_{k=1}^{13}\dfrac{\binom{39-k}{3}}{\binom{39}{3}} \approx 0.5665$$

For $\prob{W \mid A_3}$: The $39$-card deck has $1$ Ace. Let $P$ be its position (uniform on $\{1,\dots,39\}$). If $k > 11$, the $13$-card deck always wins ($\prob{W \mid A_3, P = k} = 1$). For $1 \leq k \leq 11$, the $13$-card deck wins unless all $3$ of its Aces are in positions $k,k+1,\dots, 13$:
$$\prob{W \mid A_3} = \dfrac{1}{39}\sum_{k=1}^{39}\prob{W \mid A_3, P = k} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{39}\sum_{k=1}^{11}\dfrac{\binom{14-k}{3}}{\binom{13}{3}} \approx 0.9103$$

For $\prob{W \mid A_2}$: Let $P$ be the position of the first Ace in the $13$-card deck. Computing $\prob{P = k \mid A_2}$ (the probability that the first of $2$ Aces among $13$ cards is at position $k$, for $1 \leq k \leq 12$):
$$\prob{P = k \mid A_2} = \dfrac{2 \cdot 11! \cdot (13-k)!}{(12-k)!13!}$$

Given $P=k$, the $39$-card deck (with $2$ Aces) must have both Aces after position $k$:
$$\prob{W \mid A_2} = \sum_{k=1}^{12} \dfrac{\binom{39-k}{2}}{\binom{39}{2}} \cdot \dfrac{2 \cdot 11! \cdot (13-k)!}{(12-k)!13!} \approx 0.7780$$

Combining everything gives $9472/20825 \approx 0.4548$.

questions.title: Which Rank?
questions.problem: Fix positive integers $k,m,$ and $n$, with $1 \leq k \leq m$. You perform the following process: Generate $X_1,\dots, X_m \sim f(x)$ IID, where $f(x)$ is some known PDF (you may assume the CDF is $F(x)$ for simplicity). Order $X_1,\dots, X_m$ to get the order statistics $X_{(1)},\dots, X_{(m)}$. We will now refer to $X_{(i)}$ as the rank $i$ random variable. Generate $X_{m+1},\dots, X_{m+n} \sim f(x)$ IID. Order $X_1,\dots, X_{m+n}$ to get the order statistics $Y_{(1)}, \dots, Y_{(m+n)}$. In words, you generate $m$ IID random variables, order them, generate $n$ more IID random variables, and order again. For the random variable that is rank $k$ in the first ordering, what is its expected rank after the second ordering? Report the answer when $f(x) = e^{-x}I_{(0,\infty)}(x), k = 10, m = 15,$ and $n = 24$.
questions.solution:
Let $R_k$ denote the rank of $X_{(k)}$ (rank $k$ in the first ordering) after the second ordering. We want $\ev{R_k}$.

Conditioning on $X_{(k)}$:
$$\ev{R_k} = \ev{\ev{R_k \mid X_{(k)}}} = \int_{\R} \ev{R_k \mid X_{(k)} = x} \cdot f_{X_{(k)}}(x)~dx$$

where the order statistic PDF is:
$$f_{X_{(k)}}(x) = \binom{m}{k-1,1,m-k}(F(x))^{k-1} f(x)(1 - F(x))^{m-k}$$

Given $X_{(k)} = x$, the rank of $X_{(k)}$ in the combined ordering equals $k$ (its original rank among the first $m$) plus the number of the $n$ new variables that fall below $x$. Each new variable falls below $x$ with probability $F(x)$, independently. Thus the number below $x$ is $\binomial{n}{F(x)}$ with mean $nF(x)$.

So $\ev{R_k \mid X_{(k)} = x} = k + nF(x)$, and:
$$\ev{R_k} = \int_{\R} (k + nF(x)) \cdot \binom{m}{k-1,1,m-k}(F(x))^{k-1} f(x)(1 - F(x))^{m-k}~dx$$

Since $f(x)$ and $F(x)$ appear in terms of $F(x)$ raised to powers and $f(x)$, we use the substitution $u = F(x)$, $du = f(x)~dx$, with bounds $F(-\infty) = 0$ to $F(\infty) = 1$:
$$\begin{align*}
    \ev{R_k} &= \int_0^1 (k + nu) \cdot \dfrac{m!}{(k-1)!(m-k)!} u^{k-1}(1-u)^{m-k}~du\\
    &= \int_0^1 (k+nu)\cdot\dfrac{\Gamma(k + (m-k+1))}{\Gamma(k) \Gamma(m-k+1)} u^{k - 1} (1-u)^{(m-k+1) - 1}~du
\end{align*}$$

Using $n! = \Gamma(n+1) = \Gamma(k + (n-k+1))$, the integrand involving $u^{k-1}(1-u)^{m-k}$ is exactly the PDF of a $\bet{k}{m-k+1}$ distribution. Letting $B \sim \bet{k}{m-k+1}$:
$$\ev{R_k} = \ev{k + nB}$$
$$\ev{R_k} = k + n\ev{B} = k + n \cdot \dfrac{k}{m+1} = k\left(1 + \dfrac{n}{m+1}\right)$$

With the given values: $k=10$, $m=15$, $n=24$, the answer is $25$.

Intuition: Among the first $m$ order statistics $X_{(1)},\dots, X_{(m)}$, they create $m+1$ gaps in the real line. When we add $n$ new variables drawn from the same distribution, they distribute uniformly among these $m+1$ gaps (on average $n/(m+1)$ per gap). The expected number below $X_{(k)}$ is $k \cdot \dfrac{n}{m+1}$ (since there are $k$ gaps below $X_{(k)}$), giving expected rank $k + k \cdot \dfrac{n}{m+1} = k\left(1 + \dfrac{n}{m+1}\right)$.

questions.title: Overwatch Tournament
questions.problem: An Overwatch tournament of $2^n$ players is occurring! Each player is given a distinct rank $1$ to $2^n$, where $1$ is the best and $2^n$ is the worst. In this problem, "lower ranking" refers to the actual numerical rank. Players are matched up in the following fashion: The $i$th lowest ranked player in the round is paired up with the $(i+1)$st lowest ranked player (ex: lowest and second lowest are paired, third and fourth lowest, etc.) The player with the lower rank in each pair has probability $1/2 < p < 1$ of winning and moving to the next round. This process iterates until there is only $1$ person remaining, who is declared the winner. Find the expected rank of the tournament's winner. Report the answer when $n = 8$ and $p = 2/3$.
questions.solution:
We look for symmetry that allows us to track expected ranks through rounds. If the game in a given round consists of $(a,b)$ where $a < b$, the expected rank of the winner is $ap + b(1-p) = a + (1-p)(b-a)$.

In round $1$, the expected ranks of the winners in the games $(2i-1, 2i)$ where $1 \leq i \leq 2^{n-1}$ is $2i-1 + (1-p) \cdot 1 = 2i - p$.

In the second round, the games have expected ranks $(4i-2-p, 4i-p)$, so winners have expected rank $4i-2-p + (1-p) \cdot 2 = 4i-3p$ for $1 \leq i \leq 2^{n-2}$.

In the third round, games have expected ranks $(8i-4-3p, 8i-3p)$, so winners have expected rank $8i-4-3p + (1-p) \cdot 4 = 8i-7p$ for $1 \leq i \leq 2^{n-3}$.

We conjecture that of the games in the $k$th round, the expected ranks are:
$$(2^ki - 2^{k-1} - (2^{k-1} - 1)p, 2^ki -(2^{k-1} - 1)p) = (2^{k-1}(2i-1)  - (2^{k-1} - 1)p, 2^{k-1} \cdot 2i - (2^{k-1} - 1)p)$$

We prove by induction. The base case $n = 1$ is verified. Assuming it holds for round $k$, the expected rank of the winner of that round's games (with expected ranks $(2^ki - 2^{k-1} - (2^{k-1} - 1)p, 2^ki -(2^{k-1} - 1)p)$) is:
$$2^ki - 2^{k-1} - (2^{k-1} - 1)p + (1-p) \cdot 2^{k-1} = 2^ki - (2^k - 1)p$$

This holds for all $1 \leq i \leq 2^{i-k}$, and the games in the next round have the form predicted for round $k+1$, completing the induction.

The winners of the games in the $k$th round have expected ranks $2^ki - (2^k - 1)p$. The winner of the tournament is the winner of the $n$th round. As the finals has only $1$ game, $i = 1$. Therefore, the answer is:
$$2^n - (2^n - 1)p$$

With the specified values ($n=8$, $p=2/3$): $256 - 255 \cdot 2/3 = 256 - 170 = 86$.

questions.title: Plug Walk II
questions.problem: The plug performs a random walk on the set $S = \{0,1,\dots, m\}$, where $m > 0$. The plug starts at position $0 \leq k < m$. Each step, the plug moves up $1$ step with probability $p$ or down $1$ step with probability $1-p$. The plug has opps at $0$, so they move back upwards with probability $1$ whenever they hit $0$. Find the expected amount of steps that occurs until the plug first reaches position $m$ when $k = 4,m = 20,$ and $p = 0.45$. Round to the nearest integer.
questions.solution:
This is a random walk with a reflecting boundary at $0$. Let $e_k$ be the expected number of steps needed to hit position $m$ given the plug is currently at position $k$.

By definition, $e_m = 0$. For $1 \leq k \leq m-1$:
$$e_k = 1 + (1-p)e_{k-1} + pe_{k+1}$$

If $k = 0$, you move back to position $1$ guaranteed, so $e_0 = 1 + e_1$.

By substitution, we find a pattern: $e_k = c_{k+1} + e_{k+1}$, where $c_{k+1}$ is some constant dependent on $p$.

Plugging the pattern back into the recurrence:
$$e_k = 1 + (1-p)(c_k + e_k) + pe_{k+1} \iff e_k = \dfrac{1 + (1-p)c_k}{p} + e_{k+1}$$

Thus the recurrence for $c_k$ is:
$$c_{k+1} = \left(\dfrac{1}{p} - 1\right)c_k + \dfrac{1}{p}$$

This is a non-homogeneous linear recurrence. By back substitution with $c_1 = 1$ (from $e_0 = 1 + e_1$):
$$\begin{align*}
    c_k &= \left(\dfrac{1}{p} - 1\right)^{k-1}c_1 + \dfrac{1}{p}\sum_{j=0}^{k-2}\left(\dfrac{1}{p}-1\right)^j\\
    &= \left(\dfrac{1}{p} - 1\right)^{k-1} + \dfrac{1}{p} \cdot \dfrac{1 - \left(\frac{1}{p} - 1\right)^{k-1}}{1 - (1/p - 1)}\\
    &= \dfrac{1-2p\left(\frac{1}{p} - 1\right)^k}{2p-1}
\end{align*}$$

Now $e_k = \sum_{j=k+1}^{m}c_j = \sum_{j=1}^{m}c_j - \sum_{j=1}^{k}c_j$. Using geometric series:
$$f(k) = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j = \dfrac{k(2p-1)-2p(p-1)\left(\left(\frac{1}{p}-1\right)^k - 1\right)}{(2p-1)^2}$$

Therefore $e_k = f(m) - f(k)$.

With the specific values in the question, the answer is $\approx 2490$.

questions.title: First Color Empty II
questions.problem: Fix three positive integers $r,b,$ and $g$. A box contains $r$ red, $b$ blue, and $g$ green marbles. You repeatedly draw out marbles one-at-a-time without replacement until you've drawn out all of the marbles of any color (i.e. the box only contains $2$ colors of marbles left). Find the expected number of marbles that are drawn out when $r=3,b=6,$ and $g=9$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
Define $R,B$ and $G$ to be the number of marbles drawn out until the last red, blue, and green marbles (respectively) are selected from the box. The random variable representing the number of draws we perform is $\min(R,B,G)$.

We use the maximum-minimum principle. For any real numbers $x_1,\dots, x_n$:
$$\max\{x_1,\dots, x_n\} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i - \sum_{i < j} \min\{x_i,x_j\} + \sum_{i < j < k}\min\{x_i,x_j,x_k\} + \dots + (-1)^{n+1}\min\{x_1,\dots, x_n\}$$

Applying with $n = 3$ and $x_1,x_2,x_3$ as $R,B,$ and $G$:
$$\ev{\max(R,B,G)} = \ev{R} + \ev{B} + \ev{G} - \ev{\min(R,B)} - \ev{\min(R,G)} - \ev{\min(B,G)} + \ev{\min(R,B,G)}$$

Replacing each pairwise minimum using $\ev{\min(R,B)} = \ev{R} + \ev{B} - \ev{\max(R,B)}$ and rearranging for all $3$ pairs:
$$\ev{\min(R,B,G)} = \ev{R} + \ev{B} + \ev{G} - \ev{\max(R,B)} - \ev{\max(R,G)} - \ev{\max(B,G)} + \ev{\max(R,B,G)}$$

We use a "First Ace" approach: with $d$ dividers and $n$ objects, the expected position of the last divider is $d + n \cdot \frac{d}{d+1} = d\left(1 + \frac{n}{d+1}\right)$.

Applying this framework:
- $\ev{R}$ has $d = r$ and $n = b+g$
- $\ev{B}$ has $d = b$ and $n = r+g$
- $\ev{G}$ has $d = g$ and $n = r+b$
- $\ev{\max(R,B)}$ has $d = r+b$ and $n = g$
- $\ev{\max(R,G)}$ has $d = r+g$ and $n = b$
- $\ev{\max(B,G)}$ has $d = b+g$ and $n = r$
- $\ev{\max(R,B,G)} = r+b+g$ (time until all colors are drawn)

Plugging in:
$$\begin{align*}
    \ev{\min(R,B,G)} &= r\left(1 + \frac{b+g}{r + 1}\right) + b\left(1 + \frac{r+g}{b + 1}\right) + g\left(1 + \frac{b+r}{g + 1}\right)\\
    &- (r+b)\left(1 + \frac{g}{r+b+1}\right) - (r+g)\left(1 + \frac{b}{r+g+1}\right) - (g+b)\left(1 + \frac{r}{g+b+1}\right)\\
    &+ r+b+g
\end{align*}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 13.185$.

questions.title: Yo Mama II
questions.problem: Yo mama performs a simple symmetric random walk starting at the origin. There is an absorbing boundary at position $-2n$ for some positive integer $n$. If yo mama ever reaches this boundary, it stays there for the rest of time. After $4n$ steps, what is the variance of the position of the particle? Report the answer when $n = 5$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
In this question, there is a specific difference from the standard random walk problem: There is a "lower bound" at the absorbing boundary. In a standard SSRW with no boundary, the answer to this question is $0$, as yo mama moves with equal probability up or down at each step.

To illustrate, take the example of $n = 5$. A path that ends at $-8$ would have $14$ down movements and $6$ up movements. In a standard SSRW, a path taking the first $14$ steps down and $6$ up at the end is valid, but with the absorbing boundary, this path would end at $-10$.

Using the reflection principle: if we reflect a path ending at $-2n-2k$ at the first time it hits $-2n$, we get a path ending at $-2n+2k$, equally probable to the unreflected path. Recall $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$. If $S_{4n}$ is the position at time $4n$, we showed $E[S_{4n}] = 0$, so $\text{Var}(S_{4n}) = E[S_{4n}^2]$.

The variance of an unrestricted walk of length $4n$ is $4n$ (each step has variance $1$, with $\pm 1$ equally likely). We subtract the differential in mean square from the absorbing threshold. The number of paths ending at $-2n-2k$ is $\binom{4n}{3n+k}$ out of $2^{4n}$ total paths.

The term we subtract is $\sum_{k=1}^n 8k^2 \cdot \dfrac{\binom{4n}{3n+k}}{2^{4k}}$. Thus, our final answer is $$\text{Var}(S_{4n}) = 4n - \sum_{k=1}^n 8k^2 \cdot \dfrac{\binom{4n}{3n+k}}{2^{4k}}$$

With $k = 5$, the answer is $\approx 19.913$.

questions.title: Swappy Perm
questions.problem: Fix two positive integers $k$ and $n$. Consider the list $(1,2,\dots, n)$ for some positive integer $n$. You generate a random permutation by choosing $k$ pairs of positions uniformly at random one-at-a-time and swapping the elements in those positions. For example, one such sequence with $n = 4$ and $k = 3$, $(1,2,3,4) \rightarrow (1,2,4,3) \rightarrow (4,2,1,3) \rightarrow (3,2,1,4)$. With $n = 16$ and $k = 5$, find the expected amount of integers that are in the same position after this swapping process as they were in to start. Report the answer to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
Using linearity of expectation with indicator variables $I_i$ for whether $i$ is fixed: $T = I_1 + \dots + I_n$, so $E[T] = nE[I_1]$ by symmetry.

Define $P(r)$ as the probability of $1$ being fixed after $r$ transpositions. By conditioning on whether $1$ is currently fixed: $$P(r) = \dfrac{n-2}{n}P(r-1) + \dfrac{2}{n(n-1)} \cdot (1 - P(r-1)) = \dfrac{2}{n(n-1)} + \dfrac{n-3}{n-1}P(r-1)$$

With initial condition $P(0) = 1$, solving yields: $$P(r) = \dfrac{1}{n}\left(1 + (n-3) \cdot \left(1-\frac{2}{n-1}\right)^{r-1}\right)$$

Thus $E[T] = nE[I_1] = 1 + (n-3) \cdot \left(1-\frac{2}{n-1}\right)^{k-1}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 8.334$.

questions.title: LinkedIn Networking III
questions.problem: You message $N$ quant researchers on LinkedIn in an attempt to get a referral. You created a personalized message for each, but forgot which one corresponds to each person. Therefore, you send each of them a random message, with each message being used exactly once. Let $T$ be the number of quant researchers that receive the message you intended for them. For any positive integer $n$, find $E[T^n]$. Report the answer when $n = 6$ and $N = 20$.
questions.solution:
We define $T = M_1 + \dots + M_N$ where $M_i$ indicates whether the $i$th researcher gets the correct message. Since $M_i^n = M_i$ for indicators, and $E[M_1\dots M_k] = \frac{1}{N(N-1)\dots(N-(k-1))}$, expanding $E[T^n]$ gives $$E[T^n] = \sum_{k=1}^n C(n,k) \cdot N_k \cdot \frac{1}{N_k} = \sum_{k=1}^n C(n,k)$$

where $C(n,k) = \left\{\begin{array}{c} n \\ k\end{array}\right\}$ are the Stirling numbers of the second kind. Thus $E[T^n] = B(n)$, the $n$th Bell number. With $n = 6$, the answer is $203$.

questions.title: LinkedIn Networking IV
questions.problem: You message $N$ quant researchers on LinkedIn in an attempt to get a referral. You created a personalized message for each, but forgot which one corresponds to each person. Therefore, you send each of them a random message, with each message being used exactly once. Let $T$ be the number of quant researchers that receive the message you intended for them. Find the MGF of $T$, and evaluate it at $\theta = 1/2$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
The MGF is $M(\theta) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{E[T^n]}{n!}\theta^n$ where $E[T^n] = B(n)$. Using the Bell number recurrence $B(n+1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}B(k)$, we derive the ODE $M'(\theta) = M(\theta)e^{\theta}$.

Solving with initial condition $M(0) = 1$ gives $M(\theta) = e^{e^{\theta} - 1}$. Evaluated at $\theta = 1/2$, the answer is $1.913$.

questions.title: Conditional RNG
questions.problem: You generate $r$ independent uniformly random integers with replacement from the set $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Given that the maximum value generated is $1 \leq k \leq n$, find the expected sum of all $r$ values. Report the answer to the nearest hundredth when $r = 6, n = 20,$ and $k = 15$.
questions.solution:
Let $M$ be the maximum and $X$ a single draw. Using $P[M = k] = \dfrac{k^r - (k-1)^r}{n^r}$ and conditional probability, we find $P[X = k \mid M = k] = \dfrac{k^{r-1}}{k^r - (k-1)^r}$.

Values $1$ to $k-1$ are equally likely given not $k$, so: $$E[X \mid M = k] = \dfrac{k^{r-1}}{k^r - (k-1)^r} \cdot k + \left(1 - \dfrac{k^{r-1}}{k^r - (k-1)^r}\right) \cdot \dfrac{k}{2} = \dfrac{k}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2(1-(1-1/k)^r)}$$

The expected sum is $r \cdot \left(\dfrac{k}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2(1-(1-1/k)^r)}\right)$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 53.85$.

questions.title: Integral Factorial
questions.problem: Consider the summation $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{n!}{n^n}$. Find a function $f(x)$ such that $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{n!}{n^n} = \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{f(x)}{(1 - f(x))^2}~dx$$ Evaluate $f(1)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
To convert this summation into an integral, we need to somehow express one of the terms as an integral: $n!$ or $1/n^n$. We know $n!$ has an integral representation from the Gamma function: $n! = \Gamma(n+1) = \int_0^{\infty} t^{n}e^{-t}~dt$.

However, this alone will not allow us to get rid of the factor of $1/n^n$ out front. Thus, a natural approach is to substitute $t = ns$, so $dt = n~ds$. This is because there is a $t^n$ out front, so we should get a factor of $n^n$ from the integral. Doing this, we have $n! = \int_0^{\infty} (ns)^n e^{-ns} \cdot n~ds = n^{n+1} \int_0^{\infty} s^n e^{-ns}~ds$.

Plugging in this expression, we get $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{n!}{n^n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n\int_0^{\infty} s^n e^{-ns}~ds = \int_0^{\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n(se^{-s})^n~ds = \int_0^{\infty} se^{-s} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n \cdot (se^{-s})^{n-1}~ds$$

The inner sum is in the form of $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} nx^{n-1}$ with $x = se^{-s}$. A natural thought is to evaluate this via normalization to the expected value of a Geometric random variable, which has PMF $p(1-p)^{n-1}$. Namely, $(se^{-s})^{n-1} = (1-p)^{n-1} \iff p = 1 - se^{-s}$.

We need to multiply by $1-se^{-s}$, and then we have the summation we desire. The expected value of a $\text{Geom}(p)$ random variable is $1/p$, so we conclude that $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{n!}{n^n} = \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{se^{-s}}{(1 - se^{-s})^2}~ds$$

This exactly matches the form in question, so $f(x) = xe^{-x}$. Our answer is $f(1) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368$.

questions.title: Acute Triangles
questions.problem: Three points are selected uniformly at random from the circumference of the unit circle. Find the probability that the triangle formed by the three points is acute.
questions.solution:
In this problem, we need to find the probability that all angles in a triangle formed via the selection of three uniformly random points are acute. All of the angles must be less than $90$ degrees. Recall that the sum of the degrees of the angles in a triangle is $180$. As an obtuse angle must be $> 90$ degrees, there can only be at most $1$ obtuse angle in the triangle.

Thus, a natural idea is to find the complementary probability: We want the probability that some particular angle is obtuse, and then multiply it by $3$ to account for the three possible angles that could be obtuse.

Let $A, B,$ and $C$ be the three points that are selected from the circumference of the circle. Let's find the probability angle $C$ is obtuse. WLOG, since the distribution of points is uniformly random on the circumference, we will say that point $A$ is fixed at $(1,0)$, as we could rotate the circle.

Now, to find the probability that $C$ is obtuse, we can get some quick results: If $B$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of the $x$-axis (i.e. one has positive $y$-coordinate and the other has negative), angle $C$ is acute. If $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of the $x$-axis, the point that is closer to $A$ forms an obtuse angle.

Therefore, for $C$ to be obtuse, two conditions must be satisfied: $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of the $x$-axis (probability $1/2$, as the selection is uniform), and $C$ must be closer to $A$ than $B$ is (probability $1/2$, both orderings are equally likely). These two events are clearly independent.

Therefore, we can conclude that angle $C$ is obtuse with probability $1/2 \cdot 1/2 = 1/4$. By our work earlier, angles $A$ and $B$ are obtuse with probability $1/4$ each as well, with all events disjoint. Therefore, the probability that some angle of the triangle is obtuse is $3/4$, meaning that the triangle is acute with probability $1 - 3/4 = 1/4$.

questions.title: Tiny Product
questions.problem: Fix a real value $0 < t < 1$. Let $X_1,X_2,\dots \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$ IID. Define $N_t = \inf\{n: X_1X_2\dots X_n < t\}$ i.e. the smallest integer $n$ such that the product $X_1 \dots X_n \leq t$. Find $E[N_{1/2}]$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
In this problem, we need to compute the expected number of IID $\text{Unif}(0,1)$ random variables that must multiplied together to have a cumulative product less than $t$. Products of random variables can be challenging to handle directly, but by taking logarithms, we can convert the problem into one involving sums.

One useful fact about $\text{Unif}(0,1)$ random variables is that if $X \sim \text{Unif}(0,1), -\ln(X) \sim \text{Exp}(1)$. Thus, define $Y_i = -\ln(X_i) \sim \text{Exp}(1)$ IID. We find that $$X_1X_2\dots X_n < t \iff \sum_{i=1}^n -\ln(X_i) > -\ln(t) \iff S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i > -\ln(t)$$

Therefore, $N_t$ is equivalently $\inf\{n: Y_1 + \dots + Y_n > -\ln(t)\}$. The sum of $n$ independent exponential random variables with rate $1$ is $S_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n,1)$. However, for our purpose, it's more convenient to consider a Poisson process.

A Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ is a counting process $\{ N(s), s \geq 0 \}$ where the interarrival times between events are $Y_i \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$. Since $Y_i \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$, we can interpret $\{ S_n \}_{n \geq 0}$ as the arrival times of a Poisson process with rate $\lambda = 1$, as it's the sum of the first $n$ interarrival times. The Poisson process counts the number of events that have occurred up to time $s$ i.e. $N(s) = \max\{ n \geq 0 : S_n \leq s \}.$

The expected number of random variables needed to have their sum exceed $s$ is exactly $1$ more than the expected number of random variables that can be summed to at most $s$. Recall that $N_t = \inf\{n: Y_1 + \dots + Y_n > -\ln(t)\}$. This implies that $E[N_t] = 1 + E[N(-\ln(t))] = 1 - \ln(t)$.

As a sanity check, we see that $E[N_1] = 1$ and $E[N_t]$ tends to $\infty$ as $t \rightarrow 0$. With $t = 1/2$, the answer is $\approx 1.693$.

questions.title: Conditionally Walking
questions.problem: Fix positive integers $a$ and $b$. Alvin (the Chipmunk) performs a simple symmetric random walk (SSRW) on the integers starting at position $0$ until he hits either position $a$ or position $-b$. Given that he lands on position $a$, what is the expected number of steps he took? Report the answer when $a = 6$ and $b = 8$.
questions.solution:
This is a variant of the standard problem for a SSRW where we actually condition on which boundary is hit. In a standard SSRW, the expected time to hit EITHER $a$ or $-b$ is $ab$. Therefore, we should use this fact to try to solve the time conditional on hitting $a$.

Let $T$ be the number of steps that Alvin took before hitting one of the boundaries, and let $S_n$ be his position after $n$ steps. We are looking to compute $E[T \mid S_T = a]$. By the Law of Total Expectation via conditioning on $S_T$, we find $$E[T] = ab = E[T \mid S_T = a]P[S_T = a] + E[T \mid S_T = -b]P[S_T = -b] = \dfrac{b}{a+b}E[T \mid S_T = a] + \dfrac{a}{a+b}E[T \mid S_T = -b]$$

While the above is good information, it's not enough to uniquely solve for the two variables. Therefore, we will need a second equation. One finds that the expected time to hit either $a$ or $-b$ by using the martingale $Z_n = S_n^2 - n$. Thus, we should consider making a martingale to get another equation using $S_n^3$ instead of $S_n^2$.

One can verify that $W_n = S_n^3 - 3nS_n$ is a martingale. Using the Optional Stopping Theorem: $$0 = E[S_T^3 - 3TS_T] = \dfrac{b}{a+b} \cdot (a^3 - 3aE[T \mid S_T = a]) + \dfrac{a}{a+b} \cdot (-b^3 + 3bE[T \mid S_T = -b])$$

Rearranging gives: $E[T \mid S_T = a] - E[T \mid S_T = -b] = \dfrac{(a+b)(a-b)}{3}$.

By multiplying the first equation by $a+b$, multiplying the second equation by $a$, and adding, we get $$(a+b)E[T \mid X_T = a] = ab(a+b) + \dfrac{a(a+b)(a-b)}{3} = \dfrac{a(a+b)(a+2b)}{3} \iff E[T \mid X_T = a] = \dfrac{a(a+2b)}{3}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $44$.

questions.title: Third Party Dice
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play the following game: Both players simultaneously roll a standard fair $6$-sided die. Each player gets to observe their own roll, but not the value of the other player's roll. Both players hand their die to Chad, who puts in an amount of dollars in an opaque box equal to the sum of the two rolls. Alice and Bob alternate turns bidding for the box, with Alice starting. Bids can only be placed as integer values. Each turn, Alice or Bob can decide to pass or increment the bid. The first person to pass lets the other player buy the box at the value of their last bid. Find the optimal strategy for each player. Under Alice's optimal strategy, what is the maximum amount she should bid if her roll is a $4$?
questions.solution:
A key observation is that from the viewpoint of a player with a private roll $r$ the value of the box is $v = r+s$. In the above, $s$ is the opponent's (unknown) roll. In view of the uniform distribution on $\{1,2,\dots, 6\}$ the ex-ante expectation of the box is $r + 7/2$.

In equilibrium we conjecture that each player adopts a cutoff strategy: for a player whose die shows $r$ there is a cutoff $\beta(r)$ so that they continue bidding (i.e. raises the bid by $\$1$) as long as the current bid $b$ satisfies $b < \beta(r)$, and drops out when $b\ge \beta(r)$. A reasonable assumption is that the equilibrium cutoff $\beta(r)$ is strictly increasing in $r$.

If player $i$ has roll $r$ and his opponent has roll $s$ with $r>s$, the bidding war will continue until the current bid reaches $\beta(s)$. At that point, the opponent with roll $s$ will drop out, as $\beta(s) < \beta(r)$. This means that the player with roll $r$ wins the box at price $\beta(s)-1$. Their net profit will be $(r+s)-(\beta(s)-1)$.

For the opponent of roll $s$ to be exactly indifferent at their cutoff, we require that if they were to win (had they been the higher type), their profit would be zero. Setting $r=s$ we obtain the indifference condition: $(s+s)-(\beta(s)-1)=0 \leftrightarrow 2s-\beta(s)+1=0 \leftrightarrow \beta(s) = 2s+1$.

Since the roles of the players are symmetric, we conclude that a symmetric equilibrium is given by $\beta(s)$ above. Simply stated, this means no player will ever bid more than twice their initial roll, as they bid with roll $s$ only when $b < 2s+1$ i.e. $b \leq 2s$. For the question specifically, this means that Alice should never bid more than $\$8$, so $8$ is the answer.

questions.title: Biased Poker Tournament III
questions.problem: There are $101$ players (you plus $100$ poker pros) in a round-robin poker tournament. This means that each person plays every other person once. All of the poker pros start have $100$ chips to start with for each of the $100$ matches they play, but you receive $20{,}000$ chips before the tournament, and are allowed to distribute them in any way you'd like among the $100$ matches. For example, you could put $1000$ chips on each of $20$ matches. In each match, the chance to win is proportional to your chips; that is, if you have $a$ chip and your opponent has $b$ chips, your probability of winning the match is $\dfrac{a}{a+b}$. The chips of the losing player do not get added to the stack of the winning player. A win awards $1$ point, while a loss does not award anything. After all the matches are complete, the prizes are awarded as follows: $1$st place: $\$1{,}000{,}000$; $2$nd place: $\$500{,}000$; $3$rd place: $\$400{,}000$; $4$th place: $\$300{,}000$; $5$th place: $\$200{,}000$; $6$th to $10$th place: $\$100{,}000$. No prize for anyone else. Any ties in points when converting to rank will be resolved by a uniformly random permutation of the ranks (ex: if three people are tied for $1$st, ranks $1, 2,$ and $3$ will be assigned uniformly at random). One of the other players offers to buy $5000$ chips off you at the start. If you agree to sell, they will receive $5000$ chips from you, and will be allowed to allocate those $5000$ chips to any of their $100$ games in any way they please. Assuming optimal play from the pro player, how much would you sell those chips to him for? Choose the closest answer below.
questions.solution:
To compute the fair value of those $5000$ chips, we need to estimate the change in expected payout from the tournament if you have $20000$ chips vs. if you and someone else each have $15000$ chips.

If you are the only one with bonus chips, it's very probable that you win the entire tournament, and if you don't, it's nearly guaranteed that you landed in the top $5$. Thus, we can conservatively estimate the expected winnings from the tournament when you have $20000$ chips as $\$900{,}000$.

If you only have $15000$ chips, firstly, it's much less probable you win the entire tournament, as you'd have $150$ chips to allocate per match instead of $200$. This means your probability of winning each match is $3/5$ instead of $2/3$. However it's still very likely you end up in the top $5$, but the probability mass is shifted more towards $2$nd to $5$th instead of $1$st.

Your new mean would be $3/5 \cdot 100 = 60$, while your variance is $100 \cdot 3/5 \cdot 2/5 = 24$. The individual gambler's have mean points $49.5 + (1 - 0.6) = 49.9$ and variance $\approx 25$ as well. Thus, the event that a particular other gambler beats you is now approximately $1.5$ standard deviations, rather than $2.5$.

Because there is also another player with the same amount of chips as you, it's likely that you and them will be ranked $1$ and $2$ in the tournament. As a crude estimate, we can say that there is approximately $20\%$ chance of you winning, $30\%$ of ranking second, and $50\%$ chance that you're in ranks $3$ to $10$ uniformly at random. Under this probability distribution, we find an expected payout of $$1000000 \cdot 0.2 + 500000 \cdot 0.3 + \dfrac{400000 + 300000 + 200000 + 5 \cdot 100000}{16} = \$437{,}500$$

The difference in expected value here is $\$462{,}500$, which is closest to $\$500{,}000$, so this is the answer. By Monte Carlo simulation, one can verify that the true values are approximately $\$870{,}000$ and $\$410{,}000$, making the fair value of the $5000$ chips approximately $\$460{,}000$.

questions.title: Brownian Sine
questions.problem: Fix some positive real number $a$. Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion, and let $T_a = \inf\{t > 0: |W_t| = a\}$. Compute $E[\sin(T_1)]$ to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution:
When we see computations involving the expected value of a sine or cosine of a function, the first thought should be to either $1)$ use LOTUS if the distribution is known or $2)$ convert to a complex exponential and consider the real/imaginary parts separately. Namely, we can write $\sin(T_a) = \text{Im}\left(e^{iT_a}\right)$. By the above, we can instead consider the expression $E[\sin(T_a)] = \text{Im}\left(E[e^{iT_a}]\right)$.

We consider the exponential martingale $Z_t = e^{\theta W_t - \frac{\theta^2}{2}t}$. Applying the Optional Stopping Theorem, $E[Z_{T_a}] = E[Z_0] \iff E[e^{\theta W_{T_a} - \frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a}] = 1$. Since $W_{T_a}$ is either $\pm a$ with probability $1/2$ each (both are equidistant from $0$), we apply LOTE and obtain $$E[e^{-\frac{\theta^2}{2}T_a}] = \dfrac{1}{\cosh{a\theta}} = \dfrac{2}{e^{a\theta} + e^{-a\theta}}$$

To get $E[e^{-\lambda T_a}]$ from this, we must have $\theta^2/2 = \lambda$, meaning $\theta = \sqrt{2\lambda}$. Doing this, $E[e^{-\lambda T_a}] = \dfrac{2}{e^{a\sqrt{2\lambda}} + e^{-a\sqrt{2\lambda}}}$.

We need this result with $\lambda = -i$, as that would yield the form $e^{iT_a}$ on the interior. We find $E[e^{iT_a}] = \dfrac{2}{e^{a\sqrt{-2i}} + e^{-a\sqrt{-2i}}}$.

We compute $\sqrt{-2i}$: since $-i = 0 - 1i = \cos(3\pi/2) + i\sin(3\pi/2) = e^{\frac{3\pi}{2} i}$, we get $\sqrt{-2i} = \sqrt{2} e^{\frac{3\pi}{4} i} = \sqrt{2}(\cos(3\pi/4) + i\sin(3\pi/4)) = -1 + i$.

Plugging this in, $E[e^{iT_a}] = \dfrac{2}{e^{a(-1+i)} + e^{-a(-1+i)}} = \dfrac{1}{\cosh(a(1-i))}$.

Expanding $\cosh(a(1-i)) = \cosh(a)\cos(a) - i\sinh(a)\sin(a)$. Conjugating the denominator and simplifying using $\cosh^2(x) = 1 + \sinh^2(x)$ and $\sin^2(a) + \cos^2(a) = 1$, we find $$E[e^{iT_a}] = \dfrac{\cosh(a)\cos(a)}{\cos^2(a) + \sinh^2(a)} + i \dfrac{\sinh(a)\sin(a)}{\cos^2(a) + \sinh^2(a)}$$

Now that we have separated the expression into the real and imaginary components, we can conclude $$E[\sin(T_a)] = \text{Im}\left(E[e^{iT_a}]\right) = \dfrac{\sinh(a)\sin(a)}{\cos^2(a) + \sinh^2(a)}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.5911$.

questions.title: More Dice, More Problems
questions.problem: Suppose Alice comes across an infinite collection of dice that are $n$-sided with values $1,2,\dots, n$ on the sides. The dice are all biased the same way i.e. side $i$ shows up with probability $p_i$. For some positive integer threshold $s$, Alice and Bob play the following game, with Alice starting: Alice rolls $1$ die from the collection. Call her roll $T_1$. If $T_1 > s$, Alice wins the game. Otherwise, Bob rolls $T_1$ dice from this collection. Call the sum of his $T_1$ rolls $T_2$. If $T_2 > s$, Bob wins the game. Otherwise, Alice rolls $T_2$ dice from the collection. Call the sum of her $T_2$ rolls $T_3$. If $T_3 > s$, Alice wins the game, otherwise, repeat in the same fashion as the above until someone rolls a sum of dice at least $s$. Find Alice's probability of winning the game in the case where $s = 2, n = 6$, and the dice are fair.
questions.solution:
To compute the probability of Alice winning, we need to keep track of the state of the game at all times. Let $a_r$ be the probability that Alice wins the game given that she is currently rolling $1 \leq r \leq s$ dice. Note that $1-a_r$ is the probability that Bob wins the game given that it's his turn and he is currently rolling $r$ dice.

We now want to find a recurrence relation for $a_r$. There are two cases to consider: If the sum of Alice's $r$ dice is at least $s$, she wins on that turn with probability $P\left[\sum_{i=1}^r D_i > s\right]$. Otherwise, if the sum of her rolls is some value $r \leq t \leq s$, Bob rolls $t$ dice on his turn. Alice will win with probability $1 - a_t$ in that case.

Putting it all together, we find that $$a_r = P\left[\sum_{i=1}^r D_i > s\right] + \sum_{t=r}^s P\left[\sum_{i=1}^r D_i = t\right] \cdot (1-a_t)$$

The probability that Alice wins the game is $a_1$, as she initially rolls $1$ die. This is a system of $s$ equations with $s$ unknowns $(a_1,\dots, a_s)$.

Employing this approach in our problem, we have that $s = 2$ and that there are $6$-sided fair dice. By using standard facts, we reach the equations $$a_1 = 2/3 + 1/6 \cdot (1-a_1) + 1/6 \cdot (1-a_2)$$ $$a_2 = 35/36 + 1/36 \cdot (1-a_2)$$

The second equation yields $a_2 = 36/37$. Plugging into the first: $a_1 = 2/3 + 1/6 \cdot (1-a_1) + 1/6 \cdot (1 - 36/37) \iff 7/6a_1 = 2/3 + 1/6 + 1/37 \iff a_1 = 186/259$.

The answer with the specific values is $186/259$.

questions.title: Forward Fill
questions.problem: Let $y_1,\dots, y_n$ be a sequence of $n$ real numbers. Choose a positive integer $1 \leq k \leq n-1$ and select $k$ distinct indices $1 < i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_k \leq n$. We construct a new sequence $x_1,\dots, x_n$ as follows: $x_j = y_1$ for $1 \leq j < i_1$; $x_j = y_{i_m}$ for $i_m \leq j < i_{m+1}$ and $1 \leq m < k$; $x_j = y_{i_k}$ for $i_k \leq j \leq n$. In other words, you take the subset of indices that you selected and "forward fill" them until the next selected index to create a new sequence of length $n$. For example, if our original sequence is $(100,135,96,88,64,167,133)$ and we select indices $i_1 = 3$ and $i_2 = 5$, our resulting sequence is $(100, 100, 96, 96, 64, 64, 64)$. If the $k$ indices are selected uniformly at random, forming the random sequence $X_1,\dots, X_n$, for any $1 \leq j \leq n$, compute $E[X_j]$. Report the answer with the starting sequence $(100,135,96,88,64,167,133), k = 2,$ and $j = 3$.
questions.solution:
To compute $E[X_j]$, we must first consider the values that $X_j$ can take. As we are forward filling one of the previous values, the only possible values for $x_j$ are $y_1,\dots, y_j$. Therefore, a simple approach would be to use the direct definition: $E[X_j] = \sum_{i=1}^j y_i P[X_j = y_i]$.

The event $\{X_j = y_i\}$ means that the value $y_i$ is forward filled to position $j$. For this to be the case: Index $i$ must be selected, and no other index in the set $\{i+1,i+2,\dots, j\}$ can be selected.

For general $2 \leq i \leq j$: The probability of $i$ being selected is $k/(n-1)$. The probability the remaining $k-1$ indices avoid $\{i+1,\dots,j\}$ is $\dfrac{\binom{n-2 - (j-i)}{k-1}}{\binom{n-2}{k-1}}$.

For $i = 1$: All $k$ indices must be in the set $\{j+1,\dots, n\}$, giving probability $\dfrac{\binom{n-j}{k}}{\binom{n-1}{k}}$.

Simplifying using $\dfrac{k}{n-1} = \dfrac{\binom{n-2}{k-1}}{\binom{n-1}{k}}$, we get $$E[X_j] = y_1 \cdot\dfrac{\binom{n-j}{k}}{\binom{n-1}{k}} + \sum_{i=2}^j y_i \cdot \dfrac{\binom{n-2 - (j-i)}{k-1}}{\binom{n-1}{k}}$$

Plugging the values in yields: $$E[X_3] = 100 \cdot \dfrac{\binom{4}{2}}{\binom{6}{2}} + 135 \cdot \dfrac{\binom{4}{1}}{\binom{6}{2}} + 96 \cdot \dfrac{\binom{5}{1}}{\binom{6}{2}} = 100 \cdot 2/5 + 135 \cdot 4/15 + 96 \cdot 5/15 = 40 + 36 + 32 = 108$$

questions.title: Covered Circle
questions.problem: There is a unit circle in the plane that is colored white initially. Every minute, we take a red paintbrush and paint some uniformly randomly selected semi-circle of the entire circle red. Find the expected number of minutes until the entire circle is painted red.
questions.solution:
In this problem, we set up a function $f(x)$ that represents the expected number of minutes to paint the circle entirely red given that an arc of radian length $x$ has not been covered yet. Each semi-circle covers $\pi$ radians. The first painting will always reduce us down to $\pi$ radians unpainted. Therefore, we restrict to $0 \leq x \leq \pi$, and the answer we seek is $f(2\pi) = 1 + f(\pi)$, as it takes $1$ minute to do the first painting.

After careful analysis of the three possible cases (completely covers remaining white, stays in red, or partially covers), we derive the integral equation: $$f(x) = 1 + \dfrac{\pi - x}{2\pi} \cdot f(x) + \dfrac{1}{\pi} \cdot \int_0^x f(y)~dy$$

This is an integral equation for $f(x)$, so we convert it into a differential equation by taking the derivative in $x$ on both sides: $$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}f(x) + \dfrac{\pi - x}{2\pi}f'(x)$$

Rearranging: $\left(1 - \dfrac{\pi-x}{2\pi}\right)f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}f(x) \iff \dfrac{\pi+x}{2\pi}f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}f(x)$.

This is a separable differential equation: $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)} = \dfrac{1}{\pi+x} \iff \ln{|f(x)|} = \ln{|\pi+x|} + C_1 \iff f(x) = C \cdot (\pi+x)$.

To get our initial condition, we plug $x = 0$ into the original equation, yielding $f(0) = 2$. This gives $2 = C\pi \iff C = 2/\pi$, so $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{\pi}x + 2$.

The answer is $1 + f(\pi) = 1 + 4 = 5$.
questions.hint: 1 Hint 2 Hint 3 Hint 4 Hint 5 Hint 6 Hint 7

questions.title: Minecraft Steve
questions.problem: Lucky day! Steve struck luck while mining. He has $m$ diamonds and $n$ gold ingots in his inventory. Since he is so lucky, he is going to perform the following procedure $r$ times: He removes one item from his inventory uniformly at random. He replaces the discarded item with one diamond and one gold ingot. Find the expected number of diamonds in Steve's inventory at the end of $r$ draws. Report the answer when $m = 20, n = 25,$ and $r = 44$.
questions.solution:
At the start, Steve has $m+n$ items. After $r$ turns, he will have $m+n+r$ total items. The difference between the number of diamonds and gold ingots changes by $\pm 1$ at each turn.

For some $0 \leq k \leq r$, let $D_k$ and $G_k$ represent the number of diamonds and gold ingots respectively. Define $R_k = D_k - G_k$. We also define $T_k = D_k + G_k$, so $D_k = \dfrac{T_k + R_k}{2}$ and $G_k = \dfrac{T_k - R_k}{2}$.

We compute: $$E[R_{k+1} - R_k \mid R_k] = 1 \cdot \dfrac{G_k}{T_k} + (-1) \cdot \dfrac{D_k}{T_k} = -\dfrac{R_k}{T_k} = -\dfrac{R_k}{m+n+k}$$

Since $R_k$ is known at time $k$: $E[R_{k+1} \mid R_k] = R_k\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{m+n+k}\right)$.

By the Law of Total Expectation: $E[R_{k+1}] = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{m+n+k}\right)E[R_k]$.

Iterating backwards with $R_0 = D_0 - G_0 = m-n$ and telescoping: $$E[R_k] = (m-n) \cdot \dfrac{m+n-1}{m+n+k-1}$$

We can now compute $E[D_k]$: $$E[D_k] = E\left[\dfrac{T_k + R_k}{2}\right] = \dfrac{m+n+k}{2} + \dfrac{(m-n)(m+n-1)}{2(m+n+k-1)}$$

With the specified values: $$E[D_{44}] = \dfrac{89}{2} + \dfrac{(20-25)(44)}{2 \cdot 88} = \dfrac{89}{2} - \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{173}{4}$$

questions.title: Consecutive Lineup
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$. There are $2n$ students in a class labeled $1,2,\dots, 2n$. When it is time for their school portraits, the teacher must line up half of the students to be in the first batch. The teacher has a peculiar rule: If students $k$ and $k+1$ are in the first batch, then student $k$ must take their picture before student $k+1$ in line. Find the number of acceptable lineups that can be made when $n = 5$.
questions.solution:
This problem has a unique twist because of the extra condition: if both students $k$ and $k+1$ are chosen, then student $k$ must appear before student $k+1$ in the lineup. We represent the situation with binary strings of length $2n$, where a $1$ indicates a selected student and a $0$ an unselected one. There are exactly $n$ ones and $n$ zeros.

The key observation is that any block (maximal sequence) of consecutive ones must appear in increasing order in the final lineup. With $n$ zeros in the string, they divide it into $n+1$ regions (or gaps). Let $o_1, o_2, \dots, o_{n+1}$ be the number of ones in each region. These must satisfy $o_1 + o_2 + \cdots + o_{n+1} = n$.

For fixed numbers $o_1, \dots, o_{n+1}$, the number of arrangements where the order inside each gap is respected is $\binom{n}{o_1, o_2, \dots, o_{n+1}}$.

Summing over all solutions essentially says: How many ways can each of the $n$ ones be placed into the $n+1$ regions? Each $1$ is a distinct object (person) that we want to place into one of the $n+1$ gaps. For each $1$, there are exactly $n+1$ choices of location, and these choices are made independently. Hence, the total number of assignments is $(n+1)^n$.

With $n = 5$, the answer is $6^5 = 7776$.

questions.title: Spotted Chord
questions.problem: Point $A$ is selected uniformly at random from the interior of a circle of radius $1$ with center $O$. Draw a chord $BC$ through point $A$ at an uniformly random angle $\theta$ to the radius which passes through the point A i.e. line segment $OA$. Find the mean length of the chord $BC$. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
We begin by noting that if you fix a point $A$ inside the circle at a distance $r$ from the center $O$, any chord through $A$ is uniquely determined by the angle $\theta$ between chord $BC$ and line segment $OA$.

Any chord can be described by its perpendicular distance $d$ from the center. For a circle of radius $R=1$, the half-length of the chord is $\text{(half-length)} = \sqrt{R^2 - d^2} = \sqrt{1-d^2}$, so the chord length is $L = 2\sqrt{1-d^2}$.

With point $A$ at distance $r$ from center $O$, by trigonometry: $d = OP = r\sin\theta$. Thus $L = 2\sqrt{1-r^2\sin^2\theta}$.

For distributions: $\theta \sim \text{Unif}(0, \pi/2)$ (perpendicular angle to $OA$), and the PDF of $r$ is $f_r(t) = 2t$ on $(0,1)$ (from the CDF $P[r \leq t] = t^2$). These are independent.

Therefore: $$E[L] = E[2\sqrt{1 - r^2\sin^2\theta}] = \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^1 2\sqrt{1 - s^2\sin^2t} \cdot 2s~ds \cdot \dfrac{1}{\pi/2}~dt = \dfrac{8}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi/2} \int_0^1s \sqrt{1 - s^2\sin^2t}~ds~dt$$

Using the substitution $u = s^2$ and evaluating the inner integral, then applying the identity $1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta$ and careful integration, we arrive at $$E[L] = \dfrac{8}{3\pi}\left[\sin t + \csc t - \cot t\right]\Big|_0^{\pi/2} = \dfrac{16}{3\pi}$$

Therefore, the answer is $16/3\pi \approx 1.698$.

questions.title: Power Square Divisibility
questions.problem: Find the number of positive integers $n$ at most $10{,}000$ such that $2^n - n^2$ is divisible by $7$.
questions.solution:
For $2^n - n^2$ to be divisible by $7$, it must be the case that $2^n$ and $n^2$ leave the same remainder when divided by $7$.

For $2^n$: The remainders cycle as $2, 4, 1$ with period $3$. Specifically: $2^{3n} \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$, $2^{3n+1} \equiv 2 \pmod{7}$, $2^{3n+2} \equiv 4 \pmod{7}$.

For $n^2$: The remainders cycle with period $7$. Specifically: $(7n)^2 \equiv 0$, $(7n+1)^2 \equiv 1$, $(7n+2)^2 \equiv 4$, $(7n+3)^2 \equiv 2$, $(7n+4)^2 \equiv 2$, $(7n+5)^2 \equiv 4$, $(7n+6)^2 \equiv 1$ (all mod $7$).

Since the cycle will repeat every $21$ positive integers, we look at integers satisfying the conditions from $1$ to $21$. Equating remainders, we find that in each set of $21$ consecutive integers, there are $6$ that satisfy the condition: All integers equivalent to $2, 4, 5, 6, 10,$ or $15$ modulo $21$.

We note that $10000 = 21 \cdot 476 + 4$. In each of the $476$ full groups, there are $6$ integers satisfying the condition. In the last group of $9997$ to $10000$ (remainders $1$ to $4$ mod $21$), remainders $2$ and $4$ satisfy the condition.

Thus, there are $6 \cdot 476 + 2 = 2858$ integers at most $10000$ satisfying the condition.

questions.title: Median Spread
questions.problem: Suppose that $X$ is a random variable with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Define the median of $X$, say $m$, to be the smallest real value $x$ such that $P[X < x] \leq 1/2 \leq P[X \leq x]$. For a given $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$, the possible values of $m$ form an interval $[a,b]$. Report $ab$ when $\mu = 6$ and $\sigma^2 = 16$.
questions.solution:
From the definition of the median, all we know is that it partitions our distribution into two pieces. Since we think that the median can represent some type of centering, it's instructive to look at the quantity $|\mu - m|$.

We follow logical steps: $|\mu - m| = |E[X] - m| = |E[X - m]| \leq E[|X - m|]$. The last step uses the fact that $y \leq |y|$ for all real $y$.

Now, consider the function $h(c) = E[|X-c|]$. Taking derivatives shows that $h'(c) = P[X \leq c] - P[X > c]$. The function $h(c)$ is minimized when $h'(c) = 0$, which occurs at the median $m$ where $P[X \leq m] = 1/2$.

Since the median $m$ minimizes $E[|X-c|]$ over all real $c$, taking $x = \mu$ gives $E[|X-m|] \leq E[|X-\mu|]$.

To bound $E[|X-\mu|]$: Since $|X-\mu|=\sqrt{(X-\mu)^2}$ and $f(x) = -\sqrt{x}$ is convex, applying Jensen's inequality to $(X-\mu)^2$ yields $E[|X-\mu|] \leq \sqrt{E[(X-\mu)^2]} = \sigma$.

Chaining it all together: $|\mu-m| \leq \sigma$, so $\mu - \sigma \leq m \leq \mu+\sigma$.

The bound is sharp (there exists a random variable $X$ achieving equality, e.g. $X$ taking values $\pm 1$ with probability $1/2$ each where $\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$, and the median is $-1$).

With the specified values, the answer is $(6-4)(6+4) = 20$.

questions.title: Socky Drawer
questions.problem: Miguel takes socks out of his drawer that contains $n \geq 4$ pairs of socks, where each pair has a distinct color. He draws out $2$ socks per day without replacement. Find the probability that the third day Miguel takes out socks is the first day he obtains a matching pair when $n = 6$. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
For day $3$ to be the first day that Miguel draws matching socks, he must draw $2$ distinct colored socks in each of the first two days. The probability on day $3$ is dependent on how many remaining pairs are left in the drawer by that point. The number of pairs left is directly determined by what Miguel does on day $2$, as there are a couple of cases:

WLOG, say on day $1$ that Miguel picks $2$ socks of colors $1$ and $2$.

- Miguel could pick the other socks of colors $1$ and $2$, leaving $n - 2$ complete colors (both socks of the color are in).
- Miguel could pick one of colors $1$ or $2$, and a sock of another color, say $3$, leaving $n - 3$ complete colors and $2$ colors with one sock.
- Miguel could pick two socks of colors $3$ and $4$ on the second day, leaving $n - 4$ complete pairs and $4$ pairs with $1$ sock each.

Due to this dependence on what happens in day $2$, the best thing to do is to condition on the number of pairs that overlap between days $1$ and $2$ in Miguel's selection.

The two color selections in day $1$ are irrelevant: No pairs have been selected yet, and all the colors are arbitrary, so as long as he removes $2$ distinct color socks, we are good. Regardless of which color Miguel draws for the first of the pair, $2n - 2$ of the remaining $2n - 1$ socks are not the same as the first. Therefore, the probability that he selects distinct colors on the first day is $\frac{2n-2}{2n-1}$.

There will now be $n - 2$ complete pairs of socks in the drawer, as well as $2$ singleton socks.

Let $M$ be the event that day $3$ is the first day that Miguel draws matching socks, and $O_i, i = 0,1,2$, be the events that Miguel draws $i$ sock colors in common between days $1$ and $2$. By the Law of Total Probability,
$$P[M] = P[M \mid O_0]P[O_0] + P[M \mid O_1]P[O_1] + P[M \mid O_2]P[O_2]$$

In these types of problems, computing the probability that there is complete overlap and complete disjointness is typically easiest. Note that there are $\binom{2n-2}{2}$ ways to draw $2$ socks on day $2$, as there are $2n-2$ socks that remain in the drawer. Exactly $1$ of those pairs are the same colors as day $1$, as only $1$ of each of those colors remain in the drawer. The above implies that
$$P[O_2] = \frac{1}{\binom{2n-2}{2}}$$

As for $P[O_0]$, we can't have either sock overlap in color with the ones from the first day. We will consider this part with ordering for now, and then remove ordering later. There are $2n-4$ socks that are not of the colors of the socks from day $1$. Once that sock is selected, there are $2n-6$ socks remaining that can be selected that are none of the prior colors. Then, we must divide by $2$ to remove the ordering. This implies
$$P[O_0] = \frac{\frac{(2n-4)(2n-6)}{2}}{\binom{2n-2}{2}}$$

We can't just do $\binom{2n-4}{2}$ because that would allow us to select any two socks from the remaining $2n-4$, of which some of those are pairs of the same color.

As for the event of one overlap, there are $2$ ways to pick the color of the sock that overlaps with one of the colors from the first day, and then $2n-4$ ways to pick the other sock. This already disregards the order of selection, so
$$P[O_1] = \frac{2(2n-4)}{\binom{2n-2}{2}}$$

Note that $P[O_0] + P[O_1] + P[O_2] \neq 1$ because there is positive probability of selecting matching socks on the second day.

Now, we compute the conditional probabilities for each case. If the sock colors drawn in days $1$ and $2$ are both the same, there are still $n - 2$ pairs of socks left. Thus, there are $n - 2$ pairs of socks for day $3$ that can be drawn out of $\binom{2n-4}{2}$ possible pairs. Therefore,
$$P[M \mid O_2] = \frac{n-2}{\binom{2n-4}{2}}$$

By the same logic, if there is $1$ sock color overlap between the first two days, one additional sock color was removed, so there are $n - 3$ pairs that remain. As there are still $2n-4$ total socks left,
$$P[M \mid O_1] = \frac{n-3}{\binom{2n-4}{2}}$$

Lastly, if all $4$ socks drawn in the first two days are different colors, then there are $n - 4$ pairs that remain, so
$$P[M \mid O_0] = \frac{n-4}{\binom{2n-4}{2}}$$

Plugging all of these into Law of Total Probability,
$$P[M] = \frac{(n-4) \cdot \frac{(2n-4)(2n-6)}{2} + (n-3) \cdot 2(2n-4) + (n-2) \cdot 1}{\binom{2n-2}{2}\binom{2n-4}{2}}$$

With the specific value of $n$, the answer is $\approx 0.072$.

questions.title: Uniformly Decreasing Chain
questions.problem: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$ IID. Define $N$ as the first index such that $X_N$ is not the minimum of the first $N$ random variables i.e. $N = \min\{n : X_n \neq \min(X_1, \dots, X_n)\}$. Compute $E[X_{N-1}]$, the expected value of the smallest random variable among the $N$. Report your answer to the nearest thousandth. Note: You may find it helpful to solve Uniformly Increasing Chain first.
questions.solution:
The expected value is determined by the current smallest value. For example, if the current smallest value is close to $1$, then there will be a lot of room to decrease. However, if the current minimum observed is already quite small, then there is not much room to decrease. Therefore, let $m(x)$ represent the expected minimum given that the current minimum of the chain is $x$.

Since the expectation here is dependent on the next draw, the approach is to condition on the next value observed. Let this next value be $X \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$. Using the Law of Total Expectation, we obtain
$$m(x) = \int_0^1 m(x \mid X = t) f_X(t) \, dt$$

The notation $m(x \mid X = t)$ represents the conditional expectation of the minimum of the chain given that the next draw was $t$ and the current minimum is $x$. Since $X$ is uniform on $(0,1)$, $f_X(t) = 1$.

To evaluate the interior, we need to break this up based on the value of $t$. If $t \geq x$, then we are no longer in a decreasing chain, which implies that $m(x \mid X = t) = x$. Otherwise, if $t < x$, so the new minimum is $t$. This would imply that $m(x \mid X = t) = m(t)$, as this represents the expected minimum when the (new) current minimum is $t$.

Plugging in, we obtain
$$m(x) = \int_0^1 m(x \mid X = t) \, dt = \int_0^x m(t) \, dt + \int_x^1 x \, dt = \int_0^x m(t) \, dt + x(1-x)$$

To determine the function $m(x)$, the approach is to convert this integral equation into a differential equation by taking the derivative on both sides. This yields
$$m'(x) = m(x) + (1-2x) \iff m'(x) - m(x) = 1-2x$$

The initial condition for this differential equation is $m(0) = 0$, as if the current observed minimum is $0$, it is not possible to go any lower.

This is a linear first-order differential equation, so the method of integrating factors is most appropriate here. The integrating factor here is $\mu(t) = e^{\int (-1) \, dx} = e^{-x}$, as the function in front of $m(x)$ is $g(x) = -1$. Multiplying this through and rewriting with the product rule, we obtain
$$m'(x)e^{-x} - m(x)e^{-x} = (1-2x)e^{-x} \iff \frac{d}{dx}(m(x)e^{-x}) = (1-2x)e^{-x}$$

Now, integrating on both sides, we obtain
$$m(x)e^{-x} = \int (1-2x)e^{-x} \, dx = (2x+1)e^{-x} + C \iff m(x) = (2x+1) + Ce^x$$

Plugging in the initial condition of $m(0) = 0$, we can solve for $C$. Namely, this is $0 = 1 + C \iff C = -1$. Therefore, our particular solution is
$$m(x) = 1 + 2x - e^x$$

$m(1)$ is the solution to this question, as when we start, there is no minimum value yet, so to ensure that the first value we select is always the minimum, we must take $1$ as the minimum before any values have been selected, as this is the maximum possible value that any of the $\text{Unif}(0,1)$ random variables can assume. Therefore, the answer is $m(1) = 3 - e$.

If you have completed "Uniformly Increasing Chain", you have seen the answer to that was $M(1) = e - 2$. Note that $3 - e + e - 2 = 1$, and this is not a coincidence! Note that if $X \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$, $1-X \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$ as well. Therefore, the random variables here, which look to measure the minimum of the chain $X_1, X_2, \dots$, could be replaced with $1-X_1, 1-X_2, \dots$, which are still $\text{Unif}(0,1)$. The minimum of the chain $X_1, X_2, \dots$ would be the maximum of the chain $1-X_1, 1-X_2, \dots$, as we would be subtracting the least amount possible. Since $X_i + (1-X_i) = 1$ for all $i$, we can conclude that this will also hold for the index $N$ from this question, which implies that the expected value of the maximum of the chain from "Uniformly Increasing Chain" and the minimum of the chain from this question should sum to $1$, which indeed holds true.

questions.title: Vote Count I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob are running for presidency of a school club. It is known that Alice has $a$ votes and Bob has $b$ votes, where $a > b$. The votes are counted one-by-one, and a running tally is recorded. Find the probability that Alice is always strictly ahead in the vote count when $a = 40$ and $b = 20$.
questions.solution:
Utilize the reflection principle in this question. For Alice to be strictly ahead of Bob throughout the counting of the votes, they are never able to tie. If the first vote is for Bob, Alice and Bob must tie at some point, as Alice has more votes than Bob, so they must equalize at some point.

For any sequence of drawing where the first vote is for Alice and it reaches a tie, reflect the votes up until the first point of equalization. This means that all votes for Alice are flipped to be for Bob, and vice versa. An important note is that the reflected sequence is still one with $a$ votes for Alice and $b$ votes for Bob, respectively, as they have an equal amount of votes up until the point of equalization. This reflected sequence becomes one where the first vote is for Bob, as the first vote in the original sequence was for Alice.

This reflected sequence could be any sequence that starts with a vote for Bob. What this proves is that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the sequences where a tie is reached with the first vote being for Alice and sequences where the first vote is for Bob.

The probability that Alice always leads the vote is just $1 - P[\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point}]$. Any sequence that ties starts with a vote for either Alice or Bob. However, by the above, the number of sequences where the first vote is Alice and there is a tie is equal to the number of sequences where there is a tie and the first vote is for Bob. Thus,
$$P[\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point}] = 2P[\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob}]$$

However, all sequences where Bob is the first vote tie at some point, so
$$P[\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob}] = P[\text{First vote is for Bob}]$$

Since $b$ of the $a+b$ total votes are for Bob, the probability that the first vote is for Bob is $\frac{b}{a+b}$. Plugging this in, we obtain that the probability Alice always leads is
$$1 - 2 \cdot \frac{b}{a+b} = \frac{a-b}{a+b}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $\frac{1}{3}$.

questions.title: Vote Count II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob are running for presidency of a school club. It is known that Alice has $a$ votes and Bob has $b$ votes, where $a > b$. The votes are counted one-by-one, and a running tally is recorded. Find the probability that Alice is never behind in the vote count when $a = 40$ and $b = 20$. Note: Solve Vote Count I before attempting this question.
questions.solution:
The situation of this question is very similar to that of the first part, so we should try to use the result of the first part. The difference between a sequence where Alice always has strictly more votes than Bob versus can tie would be $1$ vote. In other words, any sequence where Alice is never behind Bob can be converted into a sequence where Alice is always strictly ahead of Bob by appending a vote for Alice at the beginning of the sequence.

Similarly, we can also convert a sequence where Alice is always ahead of Bob with $a+1$ votes for Alice and $b$ for Bob into a sequence where Alice is never behind Bob with $a$ and $b$ votes for each person, respectively, by eliminating the first vote for Alice.

This implies that the number of sequences where Alice is never behind Bob with $a$ and $b$ votes for each, respectively, is equal to the number of sequences where Alice is always ahead of Bob when they respectively have $a+1$ and $b$ votes.

Note that this does not imply that the probabilities are equal, as the number of sequences of votes that can be drawn when there are $a+1$ and $b$ votes for the candidates is not equal to when there are $a$ and $b$ votes.

By "Vote Count I", the probability of the latter event is already known to be $\frac{a+1-b}{a+b+1}$. Thus, as all sequences are equally likely to occur, the number of sequences that satisfy the latter event is just equal to the probability multiplied by the number of sequences. The total number of votes drawn is $a+b+1$. Since it only matters which candidate the vote is for, we can pick the locations of the $b$ votes for Bob in $\binom{a+b+1}{b}$ ways, and the other $a+1$ spots belong to Alice. Thus, the number of sequences that satisfy our event of interest is
$$\frac{a-b+1}{a+b+1}\binom{a+b+1}{b} = \frac{a-b+1}{a+b+1} \cdot \frac{(a+b+1)!}{b!(a+1)!} = \frac{a-b+1}{a+1} \cdot \frac{(a+b)!}{a!b!} = \frac{a-b+1}{a+1}\binom{a+b}{a}$$

The above is also equal to the number of sequences where Alice is never behind in the count when there are $a$ and $b$ votes. There are $\binom{a+b}{a}$ ways to draw out the votes with no restrictions when there are $a$ and $b$ votes for the candidates. Since each sequence is equally likely, the probability of Alice never being behind Bob is the ratio of the above, which is just
$$\frac{a-b+1}{a+1}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $\frac{21}{41}$.

questions.title: Zeta Zonk VI
questions.problem: We say that $X$ follows a $\text{Zeta}(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $P[X=k] = \frac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$. Here, $\zeta(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X, Y \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Define $G$ to be the greatest common divisor (GCD) of $X$ and $Y$. For any positive integer $m$, compute $P[G = m]$. Evaluate when $s = 2$ and $m = 3$. Round your answer to the nearest thousandth. Note: Solve Zeta Zonk I - V before attempting this question.
questions.solution:
For $X$ and $Y$ to have GCD $m$, $m$ must divide both $X$ and $Y$ and $X/m$ must be relatively prime to $Y/m$.

If we knew that $m \mid X$ and $m \mid Y$, we can apply the result of "Zeta Zonk V" to know that the conditional distributions of $X$ and $Y$ given they are multiples of $m$ are still $\text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Therefore,
$$P[G = m] = P[\gcd(X/m, Y/m) = 1 \mid \{m \mid X\} \cap \{m \mid Y\}] \cdot P[m \mid X] \cdot P[m \mid Y]$$

The last two terms are both $m^{-s}$ by our previous work. By the discussion above, the conditional distributions of $X/m$ and $Y/m$ given $m \mid X$ and $m \mid Y$ are $\text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Therefore, the first term is just asking the probability that two IID $\text{Zeta}(s)$ distributions are relatively prime. By the result of "Zeta Zonk IV", the answer is $\frac{1}{\zeta(2s)}$.

Plugging these in,
$$P[G = m] = \frac{1}{m^{2s} \zeta(2s)}$$

and further plugging in for $s = 2$ and $m = 3$ yields
$$P[G = m] = \frac{1}{3^4 \zeta(4)} \approx 0.011$$

questions.title: Zeta Zonk VII
questions.problem: We say that $X$ follows a $\text{Zeta}(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $P[X=k] = \frac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$. Here, $\zeta(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Let $N$ be the event that $X$ is $n$-free (i.e. every integer that is the $n$th power of some other integer that isn't $1$ does not divide $X$). Find $P[N]$ when $s = 3/2$ and $n = 4$. Return your answer to the nearest thousandth. Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - VI before attempting this question.
questions.solution:
We want the probability that $X$ is $n$-free. This means that no $n$th power divides $X$. However, the $n$th power of a positive integer has the same factors as the integer it is the $n$th power of. Since every positive integer has a unique prime factorization, we can just write this as the event that $X$ is not divisible by $p_k^n$ for any prime $p_k$.

The probability that $p_k^n \mid X$ is just $1/(p_k^n)^s = 1/p_k^{ns}$ by the same exact methodology of the previous parts. We showed previously the $D_k$ events are independent, so this also carries over to the $n$th powers.

By independence, the probability $X$ is $n$-free is
$$\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p_i^{ns}}\right) = \frac{1}{\zeta(ns)}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $945/\pi^6$.

questions.title: Zeta Zonk VIII
questions.problem: We say that $X$ follows a $\text{Zeta}(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $P[X=k] = \frac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$. Here, $\zeta(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X_1, \dots, X_n \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$ IID.
