Compute the probability that $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are coprime (i.e. the only positive integer dividing all of them is $1$) when $n = 3$ and $s = 2$. Report your answer rounded to the nearest thousandth. Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - VII before attempting this question.
questions.solution:
For $X_1, \dots, X_n$ to be relatively prime, they must share no common prime divisor. From the previous parts, we know that
$$P[p_k \mid X_1] = \dots = P[p_k \mid X_n] = \frac{1}{p_k^s}$$

Since $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are independent, the events $\{p_k \mid X_1\}, \dots, \{p_k \mid X_n\}$ are independent. Therefore, the probability that $p_k$ divides $X_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ is $1/p_k^{ns}$.

For each prime $p_k$, we want the probability that $p_k$ does not divide all of the $X_i$, so this is $1 - 1/p_k^{ns}$ by complementation. The events above are independent for varying $k$ from "Zeta Zonk II".

Therefore, the probability that $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are coprime i.e. no prime divides all of them is
$$\prod_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p_k^{ns}}\right) = \frac{1}{\zeta(ns)}$$

This last product was evaluated by the result of "Zeta Zonk II". With the specified values, the answer is $945/\pi^6$.

questions.title: Zeta Zonk IX
questions.problem: We say that $X$ follows a $\text{Zeta}(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $P[X=k] = \frac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$. Here, $\zeta(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X, Y \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Define $G$ to be the greatest common divisor (GCD) of $X_1, \dots, X_n$. For any positive integer $m$, compute $P[G = m]$. Evaluate when $s = 2$, $n = 3$, and $m = 3$. Round your answer to the nearest thousandth. Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - VIII before attempting this question.
questions.solution:
For $X_1, \dots, X_n$ to have GCD $m$, $m$ must divide all of $X_1, \dots, X_n$ and $X_1/m, \dots, X_n/m$ must be coprime.

If we knew that $m \mid X_1, \dots, m \mid X_n$, we can apply the result of "Zeta Zonk V" to know that the conditional distributions of $X_1, \dots, X_n$ given they are multiples of $m$ are still $\text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Therefore,
$$P[G = m] = P[\gcd(X_1/m, \dots, X_n/m) = 1 \mid \{m \mid X_1\} \cap \dots \cap \{m \mid X_n\}] \cdot P[m \mid X_1] \dots P[m \mid X_n]$$

The $n$ terms out back are all $m^{-s}$ by our previous work. By the discussion above, the conditional distributions of $X_1/m, \dots, X_n/m$ given $m \mid X_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ are $\text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Therefore, the first term is just asking the probability that $n$ IID $\text{Zeta}(s)$ distributions are coprime. By the result of "Zeta Zonk VIII", the answer is $\frac{1}{\zeta(ns)}$.

Plugging these in,
$$P[G = m] = \frac{1}{m^{ns} \zeta(ns)}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $\frac{35}{27\pi^6}$.

questions.title: Variable Gambler
questions.problem: You got to Vegas successfully. They call you the variable gambler. You play a slot machine such that you win with probability $1/2$ your first turn. After the first turn, you win with probability $1/2$ if you lost the previous turn and with probability $0 < p < 1/2$ if you won the previous turn. Let $p_n$ be the probability that you win on the $n$th turn. Evaluate $p_4$ when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution:
The probability that you win on your current turn is dependent on whether you won or lost in the previous turn. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on whether you won or lost on the previous turn.

If you won on the previous turn, which occurs with probability $p_{n-1}$, then you win with probability $p$ on this turn. Otherwise, if you lost on the previous turn, which occurs with probability $1-p_{n-1}$, you win on this turn with probability $1/2$. Applying the Law of Total Probability, we get
$$p_n = p \cdot p_{n-1} + (1-p_{n-1}) \cdot 1/2 \iff p_n = (p - 1/2)p_{n-1} + 1/2$$

To solve this recurrence, the best method is by differencing, as it has a constant of $1/2$ out back. Since we will get to a term with $p_1$ in it, it helps to define $p_1 = 1/2$, which is consistent with the information in the question.

We will derive a recurrence for $r_n = p_n - p_{n-1}$. Namely,
$$p_n - p_{n-1} = [(p - 1/2)p_{n-1} + 1/2] - [(p - 1/2)p_{n-2} + 1/2] = (p-1/2)(p_{n-1} - p_{n-2})$$

This is now a fairly easy recurrence to solve:
$$p_n - p_{n-1} = (p-1/2)(p_{n-1} - p_{n-2}) = (p-1/2)^2(p_{n-2} - p_{n-3}) = \dots = (p-1/2)^{n-2}(p_2 - p_1)$$

Recall that $p_1 = 1/2$. We can use the recurrence to obtain $p_2 = 1/2 \cdot p + 1/2 \cdot 1/2 = (2p+1)/4$, so $p_2 - p_1 = (2p-1)/4$.

We now have a simple recurrence to solve, since the term out back is summable:
$$\begin{align*}
p_n &= p_{n-1} + \frac{2p-1}{4} \cdot \left(p - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{n-2}\\
&= p_{n-2} + \frac{2p-1}{4} \cdot \left[\left(p - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{n-3} + \left(p - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{n-2}\right]\\
&= \dots \\
&= p_1 + \frac{2p-1}{4} \sum_{k=0}^{n-2} \left(p - \frac{1}{2}\right)^k\\
&= \frac{1}{2} + \frac{2p-1}{4} \cdot \frac{1-(p-1/2)^{n-1}}{1-(p-1/2)}\\
&= \frac{1-(p-1/2)^n}{3-2p}
\end{align*}$$

The geometric series formula was used with common ratio $p - 1/2$. With the specified values, the answer is $\frac{185}{432}$.

questions.title: Transposition Trier I
questions.problem: You start with the tuple $\hat{0} = (0, 0, \dots, 0) \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Every turn, you select one of the $n$ elements uniformly at random. If the element you select is $i$, you replace it with $1-i$ in the tuple. Find the expected number of turns until you obtain $\hat{0}$ again when $n = 10$.
questions.solution:
Since the next state is dependent only on the current state, a Markov chain is best here. We will create a Markov Chain on the $2^n$ possible tuples themselves, as this will allow us to more clearly see the relationship between the states. There are $2^n$ tuples because each element can either be $0$ or $1$ at each time.

The transition matrix $P$ on $\{0,1\}^n = \{(a_1, \dots, a_n) : a_i = 0, 1\}$ is given by
$$P[(a_1, \dots, a_n), (b_1, \dots, b_n)] = \begin{cases} 1/n & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^n |a_i - b_i| = 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

This transition matrix encapsulates the fact that only one element can differ by $1$ at each step (either a single $0$ turns to $1$, or vice versa). There are exactly $n$ such states that can be reached from any other state in $1$ step, as there are $n$ choices of which element to flip.

Note that both the rows and columns of $P$ sum to $1$: If $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ is your target state, there are exactly $n$ other states such that if an element is flipped, you obtain $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$. These $n$ states are the same ones that can be reached from $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$. As the rows and columns both sum to $1$, $P$ is doubly stochastic.

Doubly stochastic matrices have a special property: Their stationary distributions $\pi$ are discrete uniform over the state space. This is useful because we are able to compute expected return times from the stationary distribution. Namely, if $\pi = [\pi_i]_{i=1}^r$ is the stationary distribution of a Markov Chain with $r$ states and $\tau_i$ is the random variable representing the first return to state $i$, $E[\tau_i] = 1/\pi_i$.

In this case, $r = 2^n$, as there are $2^n$ possible states of this Markov Chain, so $\pi_{(a_1, \dots, a_n)} = 2^{-n}$ for all tuples $(a_1, \dots, a_n) \in \{0,1\}^n$.

Using the above machinery, we can conclude that
$$E[\tau_{(0,0,\dots,0)}] = \frac{1}{\pi_{(0,0,\dots,0)}} = 2^n$$

With $n = 10$, the answer is $1024$.

questions.title: Transposition Trier II
questions.problem: You start with the tuple $\hat{0} = (0, 0, \dots, 0) \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Every turn, you select one of the $n$ elements uniformly at random. If the element you select is $i$, you replace it with $1-i$ in the tuple. Find the expected number of turns until you reach the state $(0, 0, \dots, 1)$, where there are $n-1$ zeroes in the above. Report the answer when $n = 10$. Note: It is helpful to solve Transposition Trier I before attempting this question.
questions.solution:
In "Transposition Trier I", we can break up the return of the chain to $\hat{0}$ into two steps: Flipping a $0$ to a $1$, and then flipping that $1$ back to $0$. Since the elements are selected uniformly at random and are all the same "distance" (in terms of amount of $1$s that need to be flipped) from $0$, the expected time to return to $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$ from any state with exactly one $1$ in it must be the same. This amount is known to be $2^n$ by the previous part of this question.

On the first turn, no matter what element is flipped, there will be exactly one $1$ in the resulting tuple. As $2^n$ total turns are needed on average to return to $\hat{0}$ and the first turn always moves to a state with exactly one $1$ in it, on average, $2^n - 1$ turns are needed to get from $(0, 0, \dots, 1)$ to $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$.

We now claim that $2^d - 1$ is also the expected number of steps needed to reach $(0, 0, \dots, 1)$ from $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$. Imagine relabeling all the states such that $(0, 0, \dots, 1)$ is now $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$. One possible way to do this is by the relabelling $(a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}, a_n) \mapsto (a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}, 1-a_n)$. You could imagine this as relabelling the vertices of the $n$-dimensional unit cube by reflecting it about the $n$th axis.

Under this relabelling, $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$ is now $(0, 0, \dots, 1)$, so the problems of reaching $(0, 0, \dots, 1)$ from $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$ under the new cube and reaching $(0, 0, \dots, 0)$ from $(0, 0, \dots, 1)$ on the new cube are the exact same, so they must have the same expected time.

With $n = 10$, the answer is $1023$.

questions.title: Vasicek Model
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Let $R_t$ satisfy the SDE $dR_t = (a - bR_t) \, dt + \sigma \, dW_t$. Assume that $a, b, \sigma > 0$, as well as $R_0 = r > 0$. $E[R_T]$ can be written as a function $f(a, b, r, \sigma, T)$. Report the value of $f(0.2, 0.1, 1, 0.15, 1)$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution:
When looking to solve SDEs, it is typically useful to consider the dynamics of some function of the process. In this case, we can see that $a$ and $b$ play into the long-term dynamics of the process. Notably, $b$ is the "compound rate" attached to $R_t$, so it would be useful to consider the dynamics of $e^{bt} R_t$.

By applying the product rule to $f(t, r) = r e^{bt}$, we get
$$d(e^{bt} R_t) = be^{bt} R_t \, dt + e^{bt} \, dR_t = be^{bt} + e^{bt}[(a - bR_t) \, dt + \sigma \, dW_t] = ae^{bt} \, dt + \sigma e^{bt} \, dW_t$$

$R_t$ has now vanished from the RHS! To solve for $R_t$, we can integrate both sides and multiply by $e^{-bt}$ to isolate $R_t$. Namely,
$$e^{bT} R_T - R_0 = \int_0^T ae^{bt} \, dt + \int_0^T \sigma e^{bt} \, dW_t$$

There are now a couple simplifications that can be made. First, $R_0 = r$ by the question statement. Secondly, in expectation, as the integrand of the Ito integral is deterministic and square-integrable, the second integral is a mean $0$ martingale, meaning it vanishes in expectation. The first integral is fully deterministic, so it can be treated as a constant.

Taking expected values, we get
$$e^{bT} E[R_T] = r + \int_0^T ae^{bt} \, dt = r + \frac{a}{b}(e^{bT} - 1) \iff E[R_T] = re^{-bT} + \frac{a}{b}(1 - e^{-bT})$$

With the parameters in question, the answer is $\approx 1.095$.

questions.title: Variable Starting Brownian
questions.problem: Let $W_t$ be a Brownian Motion and $\tau_{a,b} = \inf\{t > 0 : W_t \in \{a, -b\}\}$. The starting point of the Brownian Motion is $\text{Unif}(-b, a)$ distributed. Find $E[\tau_{a,b}]$ when $a = 4$ and $b = 2$.
questions.solution:
In the event that the starting point is non-random, say $x_0$, we know that $E[\tau_{a,b} \mid W_0 = x_0] = (a - x_0)(x_0 + b)$, the product of the distances of the starting point to each barrier.

Thus, if we know the starting place of the Brownian Motion, it's not difficult to compute the expected value. The proper method is to condition on the starting point $X_0$ of the Brownian Motion. By the above and the law of total expectation,
$$E[\tau_{a,b}] = E[E[\tau_{a,b} \mid W_0]] = E[(a - W_0)(W_0 + b)]$$

As per the question, $W_0 \sim \text{Unif}(-b, a)$. The best approach is to expand out the definition of $W_0$ to simplify the terms, and then apply linearity of expected value.
$$E[(a - W_0)(W_0 + b)] = ab + (a-b)E[W_0] - E[W_0^2]$$

It's easy enough to compute $E[W_0] = \frac{a + (-b)}{2} = \frac{a-b}{2}$. We can compute $E[W_0^2]$ by LOTUS to be
$$E[W_0^2] = \int_{-b}^a x^2 \cdot \frac{1}{a - (-b)} \, dx = \frac{1}{a+b} \int_{-b}^a x^2 \, dx = \frac{a^3 + b^3}{3(a+b)} = \frac{a^2 - ab + b^2}{3}$$

Substituting these in,
$$E[\tau_{a,b}] = ab + \frac{(a-b)^2}{2} - \frac{a^2 + b^2 - ab}{3} = \frac{(a+b)^2}{6}$$

With the specified values, the answer is $6$.

questions.title: Tourney Switch
questions.problem: Fix $0 < p < 1$. Alice and Bob play in a best of $2n-1$ tennis tournament. The winner of each round receives $1$ point, and the first to $n$ points wins. The player with fewer points has probability $p$ of winning the next match, while the player with more points has probability $1-p$ of winning the next match. If Alice and Bob have an equal amount of points, Alice has probability $p$ of winning. Find the probability that Alice wins the tournament when $n = 10$ and $p = 2/3$.
questions.solution:
The situation with up to $2n-1$ games gets very complicated for large $n$, so let's first consider the situation for when $n = 1$ and $2$, as these are solvable by hand.

With $n = 1$, the probability is just $p$, as this just asks for the probability Alice wins the first game which is $p$, as they start out tied.

When $n = 2$, there are three possible sequences leading to Alice winning: $WW$, $WLW$, and $LWW$, where $L$ is a loss and $W$ is a win for Alice. The probability of $WW$ is just $p(1-p)$, as she wins her first game with probability $p$, and then she wins her second game with probability $1-p$, as she's leading after the first game. By a similar methodology, the probability of $WLW$ and $LWW$ are $p^3$ and $p^2(1-p)$.

Adding these up, the probability Alice wins the best of $3$ is
$$p(1-p) + p^2(1-p) + p^3 = p[(1-p) + p - p^2 + p^2] = p$$

This doesn't seem like a coincidence any more! A natural guess is that the probability Alice wins is $p$, regardless of $n$.

We can prove this via strong induction. The base case of $n = 1$ is already shown above. Our strong induction hypothesis is that Alice has probability $p$ of winning a best of $2k-1$ tournament for all $1 \leq k \leq n$. Our goal is to prove that she has probability $p$ of winning in a best of $2n+1$ tournament.

We have to think carefully about how to actually utilize our induction hypothesis. Conditioning on the first step isn't sufficient here because the tournament is unbalanced afterwards i.e. one player only needs $n$ wins, while the other needs $n+1$ wins.

A more natural thing to condition on is if Alice and Bob tie at any point in the process. Let $A_{2n+1}$ be the event that Alice wins the best of $2n+1$ tournament and $T$ be the event that Alice and Bob are tied at some point after the start. By the Law of Total Probability,
$$P[A_{2n+1}] = P[A_{2n+1} \mid T] \cdot P[T] + P[A_{2n+1} \mid T^c] \cdot P[T^c]$$

For simplicity, let $P[T] = t$, which makes $P[T^c] = 1-t$. If there is no tie at any point in the tournament, the winner of the first game is the winner of the tournament, so Alice must win the first game in this case. This occurs with probability $P[A_{2n+1} \mid T^c] = p$.

If there is a tie at some point in the tournament, which occurs with probability $t$, starting from the tie point, the remainder of the tournament is just a smaller version of the original one. By our strong induction hypothesis, the probability Alice wins a best of $2k-1$ tournament for $1 \leq k \leq n$ is $p$, so $P[A_{2n+1} \mid T] = p$ by the strong induction hypothesis.

Plugging this in,
$$P[A_{2n+1}] = pt + p(1-t) = p$$

The result is now proven, allowing us to conclude the probability Alice wins the tournament is $p$, regardless of $n$. With the specified values, the answer is $2/3$.

questions.title: Uniform Product Density
questions.problem: Suppose that $X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4$ are i.i.d $\text{Unif}(0,1)$ random variables. Find the value of the PDF of $Y = X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4$ at $y = \frac{1}{2}$ and return the answer rounded to $2$ decimal points.
questions.solution:
Since we want to find the pdf of $Y$, we will proceed by first finding the cdf of $Y$. The cdf of $Y$ is $P[Y \leq z] = P[X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4 \leq z]$, but this looks difficult to deal with. Our next step will be to try to turn the product into something more manageable.

Since logarithms turn multiplication into addition, we will take the natural log of both sides. For reasons that will become clear shortly, we will also multiply each side by $-1$. Performing these operations gives,
$$P[Y \leq z] = P[X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4 \leq z] = P[-\log(X_1) + -\log(X_2) + -\log(X_3) + -\log(X_4) \geq -\log(z)]$$

Let's now inspect $-\log(X_1)$. What is the distribution of this random variable? We can find it by considering its cdf, so that for $w \in [0, \infty)$,
$$\begin{align*}
P[-\log(X_1) \leq w] &= P[\log(X_1) \geq -w] \\
&= P[X_1 \geq e^{-w}] \\
&= 1 - P[X_1 \leq e^{-w}] \\
&= 1 - e^{-w}
\end{align*}$$

where the last equality follows from the fact that $X_1$ is uniform. Differentiating with respect to $w$ in order to get the pdf yields $f_{-\log(X_1)}(w) = e^{-w}$, which can be recognized as the pdf of an exponential random variable with $\lambda = 1$.

Thus we can write the cdf of $Y$ as,
$$\begin{align*}
P[Y \leq z] &= P[-\log(X_1) + -\log(X_2) + -\log(X_3) + -\log(X_4) \geq -\log(z)] \\
&= P[G \geq -\log(z)] \\
&= P[e^{-G} \leq z]
\end{align*}$$

Where $G$ is a $\text{Gamma}(4, 1)$ random variable, since $\sum_{i=1}^4 -\log X_i$ is a sum of 4 independent $\text{Exp}(1)$ random variables.

Since the pdf of a random variable is simply the derivative of the cdf, the above also gives us
$$f_Y(z) = \frac{\partial}{\partial z} P[Y \leq z] = \frac{\partial}{\partial z} P[e^{-G} \leq z] = f_{e^{-G}}(z)$$

Thus, if we find the pdf of $e^{-G}$, we will have also found the pdf of $Y$. Since $h(G) = e^{-G}$ is a strictly decreasing and differentiable function of $G$, we can find the pdf of $e^{-G}$ using the typical method of transformations. If we let $Z = h(G) = e^{-G}$, then for $z$ such that $-\log(z) \in (0, \infty)$ we have,
$$\begin{align*}
f_{e^{-G}}(z) = f_Z(z) &= f_G(h^{-1}(G)) \left| \frac{\partial}{\partial z} h^{-1}(G) \right| \\
&= \frac{1}{\Gamma(4)} (-\log(z))^3 e^{\log(z)} \frac{1}{z} \\
&= \frac{1}{\Gamma(4)} (-\log(z))^3
\end{align*}$$

Note that the condition $-\log(z) \in (0, \infty)$ follows from the fact that the Gamma distribution is defined only on $(0, \infty)$. Since the method of transformations requires us to evaluate $f_G(h^{-1}(G)) = f_G(-\log(z))$, we must have that $-\log(z) \in (0, \infty)$.

Plugging in $z = 0.5$ yields the answer $0.06$.

questions.title: Over N
questions.problem: Lewis has a fair $n$-sided die with sides numbered from $1$ to $n$. If Lewis rolls the die until the cumulative sum of all his rolls is greater than or equal to $n$, what is the expected number of rolls Lewis will make if $n = 6$?
questions.solution:
The straightforward approach to this problem is to condition on Lewis' first roll and then use the law of total expectation. Instead, let $E_k(n)$ denote the expected number of rolls needed to get a cumulative sum of at least $n$, assuming that the current sum is $k$. Our goal is to find $E_0(n)$, since Lewis is starting off with a total sum of 0 before he starts rolling.

Let $R_i$ be the event that Lewis' next roll takes value $i$. Conditioning on the outcome of Lewis' next roll and using the law of total expectation yields,
$$\begin{align*}
E_k(n) &= P[R_1](1 + E_{k+1}(n)) + \dots + P[R_n](1 + E_{k+n}(n)) \\
&= 1 + \frac{1}{n}E_{k+1}(n) + \dots + \frac{1}{n}E_{k+n}(n) \\
&= 1 + \frac{1}{n}E_{k+1}(n) + \dots + \frac{1}{n}E_{n-1}(n)
\end{align*}$$

which follows from the fact that the die is fair, and that if Lewis' sum is at least $n$, he doesn't need to roll anymore so that $E_k(n) = 0$ for $k \geq n$.

First, note that $E_{n-1}(n) = 1$, since if Lewis is only $1$ away from $n$, then no matter what he rolls next, his cumulative sum will be at least $n$.

Let's now analyze $E_{n-2}(n)$. We have
$$E_{n-2}(n) = 1 + \frac{1}{n}E_{n-1} = 1 + \frac{1}{n}$$

Looking at $E_{n-3}(n)$ yields
$$E_{n-3}(n) = 1 + \frac{1}{n}E_{n-2} + \frac{1}{n}E_{n-1} = 1 + \frac{1}{n}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right) + \frac{1}{n}(1) = 1 + \frac{2}{n} + \frac{1}{n^2}$$

Looking at one more term gives
$$\begin{align*}
E_{n-4}(n) &= 1 + \frac{3}{n} + \frac{3}{n^2} + \frac{1}{n^3} \\
&= \frac{\binom{3}{0}}{n^0} + \frac{\binom{3}{1}}{n^1} + \frac{\binom{3}{2}}{n^2} + \frac{\binom{3}{3}}{n^3} \\
&= \sum_{i=0}^{3} \frac{\binom{3}{i}}{n^i}
\end{align*}$$

By induction, one can show that
$$E_{n-k}(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \frac{\binom{k-1}{i}}{n^i}$$

Solving this sum using the binomial theorem:
$$E_{n-k}(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \binom{k-1}{i} \left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^i (1)^{k-1-i} = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^{k-1}$$

Since Lewis begins with a sum of $0$, we are interested in $E_0(n)$, which is equal to
$$E_0(n) = E_{n-n}(n) = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^{n-1}$$

When $n = 6$, this yields $\left(1 + \frac{1}{6}\right)^5 = \frac{16807}{7776}$.

questions.title: FT Tests I
questions.problem:
In OLS with $1$ predictor, consider testing $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ against $H_1: \beta_1 \neq 0$. Suppose that we calculate the $t$-statistic and the $F$-statistic for this test, and denote their values as $T_s$ and $F_s$ respectively. How do $T_s$ and $F_s$ relate to each other?

- $F_s = T_s$
- $F_s = T_s^2$
- $F_s = \sqrt{T_s}$
- $F_s = |T_s|$
- In general, there is no relationship between $F_s$ and $T_s$.
- The $F$-statistic doesn't exist for this hypothesis test.
- The $T$-statistic doesn't exist for this hypothesis test.
questions.solution:
Before beginning any calculations, we should first check if this sort of hypothesis can even be tested via an $F$ and $T$ test. Since we're testing the value of a single coefficient, it is clear that a $T$ test is appropriate. What about an $F$ test? Recall that an $F$ test is used to test the fit of one "large" model to a "smaller" model which is a subset of the large one. In this case, the "large" model would be $Y = \beta_0 + X\beta_1$ and the "small" model would be $Y = \beta_0$, where the "small" model is a subset of the large model (specifically with $\beta_1 = 0$). Thus, an $F$ test can be used.

The $t$-statistic for testing $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ is given by
$$T_s = \frac{\hat{\beta_1}}{SE(\hat{\beta}_1)}$$

where $SE(\hat{\beta}_1)$ is the standard error of $\hat{\beta_1}$ and is equal to
$$SE(\hat{\beta}_1) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2}{(n-2)\sum_{i=1}^n (\bar{X} - X_i)^2}}$$

The $F$-statistic for testing $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ is given by
$$F_s = \frac{RSS_1 - RSS_2}{RSS_2} \cdot \frac{n - p_2}{p_2 - p_1}$$

where $RSS_1$ is the residual sum of squares of the model without $\beta_1$, $RSS_2$ is the residual sum of squares of the model with $\beta_1$, $n$ is the total number of datapoints, $p_1$ is the number of predictors in the model without $\beta_1$ (including the intercept), and $p_2$ is the number of predictors in the model with $\beta_1$ (including the intercept). Plugging these values in for our scenario yields
$$F_s = \frac{RSS_1 - RSS_2}{RSS_2} \cdot \frac{n-2}{2-1} = (n-2)\frac{RSS_1 - RSS_2}{RSS_2}$$

Our task now is to input the correct terms for $RSS_1$ and $RSS_2$, and then simplify. First, recall that in the linear regression model with an intercept and one extra predictor, we have $\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{X}$.

Through algebraic manipulation of the numerator (expanding, using the definition of $\hat{\beta}_1$, and simplifying), one can show that
$$RSS_1 - RSS_2 = \hat{\beta_1}^2 \sum_{i=1}^n (\bar{X} - X_i)^2$$

Thus, we can write $F_s$ as
$$\begin{align*}
F_s &= (n-2) \frac{\hat{\beta_1}^2 \sum_{i=1}^n (\bar{X} - X_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2} \\
&= \frac{\hat{\beta_1}^2}{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2}{(n-2)\sum_{i=1}^n (\bar{X} - X_i)^2}} \\
&= T_s^2
\end{align*}$$

Thus, we can see that $F_s = T_s^2$ is the correct answer.

questions.title: Bounding Zero
questions.problem: Let $X$ be any non-negative random variable with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ such that $P[X = 0] < 1$. Find the tightest possible upper bound on $P[X = 0]$. Report the answer when $\mu = 5$ and $\sigma^2 = 25$.
questions.solution:
If we're looking to find a bound on some probability, we should automatically think to use one of our inequalities. Neither Chebyshev's nor Markov's inequality will work here, as we'd need to use $c = 0$. Thus, we need to think of a different approach.

Recall that the event $\{X = 0\}$ does not contribute to $E[X]$ at all, since the value $0$ would be weighted by either its probability or density, which is still $0$ after taking the product. Since the random variable is non-negative, there is no probability density/mass for any negative values, so we can conclude $E[X] = E[X I_{X > 0}]$.

Note that $E[I_A] = P[A]$ for any event $A$, so if we can somehow separate out the product $X I_{X > 0}$ into its individual components, we would get $P[X > 0]$ somewhere. We can't separate out the expectation into its product directly, as $X$ and $I_{X > 0}$ are generally not independent. However, the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality allows us to do exactly this. Namely, for any random variables $X$ and $Y$,
$$|E[XY]| \leq \sqrt{E[X^2] E[Y^2]}$$

Applying this with $X$ and $I_{X > 0}$, we get
$$E[X] = |E[X I_{X > 0}]| \leq \sqrt{E[X^2] E[I_{X > 0}^2]}$$

Since $I_{X > 0}$ only takes the values $0$ and $1$, squaring it doesn't change the values it takes, so $I_{X > 0}^2 = I_{X > 0}$. Squaring both sides of the inequality and rearranging, we get
$$(E[X])^2 \leq E[X^2] E[I_{X > 0}] \iff E[I_{X > 0}] = P[X > 0] \geq \frac{(E[X])^2}{E[X^2]}$$

Since $X$ is non-negative, we can get $P[X = 0] = 1 - P[X > 0]$, so
$$1 - P[X > 0] = P[X = 0] \leq 1 - \frac{(E[X])^2}{E[X^2]} = \frac{E[X^2] - (E[X])^2}{E[X^2]} = \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{E[X^2]} = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + \mu^2}$$

The denominator is by the relation $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$. The ratio on the RHS is clearly always at most $1$.

With the specified values, the answer is $1/2$.

We can also see that this inequality is sharp: There exists a random variable $X$ such that $\leq$ becomes $=$. One such example is $X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1/2)$.
questions.hint: Consider using an inequality that allows you to bound the probability. The event $\{X = 0\}$ does not contribute to $E[X]$, so try working with $E[X] = E[X I_{X > 0}]$ and apply Cauchy-Schwarz.

questions.title: Cubic Ant V
questions.problem: An ant walks along the edges of a cube that has vertices at $\{0,1\}^3 = \{(x,y,z) : x,y,z \in \{0,1\}\}$, starting at $(0,0,0)$. There is a spider located at $(1,1,0)$ that eats ants whenever they visit $(1,1,0)$. The ant moves to one of the three adjacent vertices with equal probability at each step. Find the probability that the ant makes it to $(1,1,1)$.
questions.solution:
In more simple terms, we are asking the probability that the ant hits $(1,1,1)$ before $(1,1,0)$. Since the ant is performing a random walk, a Markov chain approach is most appropriate.

One natural concern is that there are $8$ states as of now, which correspond to the $8$ vertices. Thus, we would want to find some symmetry in the path of the ant to reduce the complexity of the Markov chain. Drawing out the cube and placing the spider on it, we see $4$ groups of vertices:

- Group $1$: $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,1)$
- Group $2$: $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$
- Group $3$: $(0,0,0)$
- Group $4$: $(0,0,1)$

Groups $1$ and $2$ are obtained by essentially reflecting the cube about the diagonal plane passing through $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,0)$, since their paths to both $(1,1,1)$ and $(1,1,0)$ are just reflected. $(0,0,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are solitary, as they are directly on the path of reflection. Thus, we've reduced our problem to $4$ states.

Let $p_1, p_2, p_3,$ and $p_4$ be the probabilities of reaching $(1,1,1)$ before $(1,1,0)$ from each of the $4$ groups, respectively. We now need to apply Law of Total Probability repeatedly. $p_3$ is our answer to the question, since the ant starts at $(0,0,0)$.

If the ant is currently in group $1$, one of the three directions brings it to $(1,1,1)$, in which it wins automatically. The other two directions bring the ant to groups $2$ and $4$, with respective probabilities $p_2$ and $p_4$ of success. By the Law of Total Probability,
$$p_1 = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3}p_2 + \frac{1}{3}p_4$$

If the ant is currently in group $2$, one of the three directions brings it to the spider, in which it dies. In the other two directions, the ant reaches groups $1$ and $3$, so
$$p_2 = \frac{1}{3}p_1 + \frac{1}{3}p_3$$

If the ant is currently in group $3$, two of the three directions bring the ant to group $2$, while the other brings the ant to group $4$:
$$p_3 = \frac{2}{3}p_2 + \frac{1}{3}p_4$$

Lastly, if the ant is currently in group $4$, two of the three movements bring it to group $1$, while the last movement brings it to group $3$:
$$p_4 = \frac{2}{3}p_1 + \frac{1}{3}p_3$$

By solving this system of four equations, we find that $p_3 = 3/7$.
questions.hint: Use symmetry to reduce the 8 vertices of the cube into 4 groups, then set up a system of equations using Law of Total Probability.

questions.title: Circularly Together
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$. $3n$ people sit around a circular table with $3n$ seats uniformly at random. Among these $3n$ people, there are $3$ groups consisting of $n$ people each. Find the probability that at least one of the three groups sits down with all $n$ people of that group adjacent to one another. Arrangements that are rotations of one another are not considered distinct. Report the answer with $n = 5$ to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution:
Let's first frame this problem probabilistically. Let $G_i$ be the event that all $n$ people of group $i$, $i = 1, 2, 3$, are seated together at the table. We are looking for $P[G_1 \cup G_2 \cup G_3]$, since we want the probability that at least one of the three groups sit together.

The events $G_1, G_2,$ and $G_3$ are clearly not disjoint (more than one group can sit continuously at the table). Furthermore, they are not independent: The knowledge that all members of group $1$ sit together increases the probability that the other groups sit together. Because of this, inclusion-exclusion is likely the best approach.

As the group labels are arbitrary (all $3$ groups have the same number of people), we can say that
$$P[G_1 \cup G_2 \cup G_3] = \binom{3}{1}P[G_1] - \binom{3}{2}P[G_1 \cap G_2] + P[G_1 \cap G_2 \cap G_3]$$

Let's start with $P[G_1]$. All $n$ people in group $1$ need to be sat together, so the typical strategy is to treat the $n$ people as a block. In this paradigm, we need to create a circular permutation of the block and the other $2n$ people at the table. This is a circular permutation of $2n+1$ objects, so there are $(2n)!$ arrangements here. However, we also need to account for the number of ways to arrange the people within the block, which is $n!$, since every permutation of those $n$ people will yield a distinct arrangement. Therefore, there are $(2n)! \cdot n!$ total permutations for this case.

The number of circular permutations of $3n$ people is $(3n-1)!$, so
$$P[G_1] = \frac{(2n)! \cdot n!}{(3n-1)!}$$

For $P[G_1 \cap G_2]$, treat the two groups as $2$ blocks. We now are forming a circular permutation of $n+2$ objects, meaning there are $(n+1)!$ distinct permutations here. We need to account for the internal arrangements of each block: $(n!)^2$. So the total is $(n!)^2(n+1)!$. Therefore,
$$P[G_1 \cap G_2] = \frac{(n+1)!(n!)^2}{(3n-1)!}$$

For the last probability, there are only $3$ blocks to be arranged circularly, so there are $2!$ circular arrangements of the three blocks. Each block has $n!$ internal arrangements, so the total is $2 \cdot (n!)^3$. Therefore,
$$P[G_1 \cap G_2 \cap G_3] = \frac{2 \cdot (n!)^3}{(3n-1)!}$$

Plugging it all in, the probability of our event is
$$P[G_1 \cup G_2 \cup G_3] = \frac{3 \cdot (2n)! \cdot n! - 3 \cdot (n+1)!(n!)^2 + 2 \cdot (n!)^3}{(3n-1)!}$$

As a sanity check, the answer is $1$ when $n = 1$, which makes sense: Each person is their own group, so by definition, all the members of each group sit together. With $n = 5$, the answer is $\approx 0.0147$.
questions.hint: Use inclusion-exclusion on the events that each group sits together. Treat each group as a block and count circular permutations.

questions.title: Choose Your Order
questions.problem: You a$$n$$d your friend are playing Mario Kart. Each turn, either you or your friend gets to select the map. If you select the map, you have probability 1 p 1 of winning the turn. If your friend selects the map, you have probability 2 p 2 of winning the turn. Consider the following two possible conventions for map selection: Method $$$A$$$: Method A: Alternating every turn Method $$$B$$$: Method B: The player selecting continues to select until they lose You get to select the map of the first turn. Each time someone wins, they receive a point. The first person to reach n points wins the tournament. Assuming you know both 1 p 1 and 2 p 2 , under an optimal strategy, which convention would you choose when = 10 $n = 10$ to maximize your probability of winning? Method A Method B You are indifferent to the two methodologies If 1 ≤ 2 p 1 ≤p 2 , choose method A, otherwise choose method B If 1 ≤ 2 p 1 ≤p 2 , choose method B, otherwise choose method A There's no way to determine the optimal strategy without more information None of the above SUBMIT
questions.solution: I$$$$$$$$$$$$$n$$$$$$$$$$$$$ this problem, we must be creative about how to generate an approach. The hardest part about the two methods is that it's unclear how long each lasts, since it's dependent on the sequence of wins and losses that occurred. Furthermore, based on this sequence of wins and losses, it influences the probability of winning in the next turn. Thus, it's not reasonable to compute this explicitly. Instead, we want to draw some common thread connecting the games. In the worst case, the tournament ends in 2 − 1 2n−1 turns, as someone must have n points by this time. Therefore, to put the two methodologies on equal footing, we will run the tournament for 2 − 1 2n−1 turns, regardless if someone has won before this point. Let's call this the "extended tournament". In the extended tournament, even if someone has won before 2 − 1 2n−1 turns has passed, in method A, the players will continue to alternate turns. In method B, after someone has lost, we will let the loser will serve all remaining rounds. Why do we construct method B in the extended tournament as above? Our goal is to relate these two tournaments somehow. Since you choose first, in method A, you will have chosen in exactly n of the 2 − 1 2n−1 turns. Thus, to put the two tournaments on equal footing, we need to ensure that regardless of when someone wins and who winsw in method B, you will have chosen in exactly n of the 2 − 1 2n−1 games. To do this, we note that in our construction, the number of times you choose is always equal to n, regardless if you win or lose and when. How is the above the case? Suppose you lose in ≤ ≤ 2 − 1 n≤$k$≤2n−1 turns. Under method B, you get to pick while you're winning, so if you lose in k turns, you must have won − k−n times, since your friend got n points. Thus, the turns at which you get to select are The first turn ( 1 ) $(1)$ The − k−n turns that follow after the − k−n wins The remaining ( 2 − 1 ) − (2n−1)−k turns after you lose Therefore, the total number of times you select is 1 + ( − ) + ( 2 − 1 − ) = 1+(k−n)+(2n−1−k)=n. Similarly, if you are the winner, you select in the first turn and the − 1 n−1 games that follow your first − 1 n−1 wins. You don't get to select on the turn after your nth win because selection power immediately gets turned over to the loser once a winner is declared. Why do this entire "extended tournament" construction? Other than just putting the tournaments on equal footing, the extended tournaments and the original ones are equivalent: You win the extended version of the tournament if and only if you win the original version (play until a winner is declared). This is very clear: Since there are 2 − 1 2n−1 total turns in the extended tournament, the person who reaches n points first can't be overtaken by the other person, as there would be at most − 1 n−1 other turns for them to win. Thus, we can make a determination on the optimal choice in the extended tournament, and the same result will carry over to the original question. In each extended tournament, with both methodologies, you are now choosing n times, while your friend is choosing − 1 n−1 times. As the probability of winning is constant per each person that selects, the order in which the turns appear is irrelevant: You have the same probability of winning the tournament under either methodology. This is because you have the same stopping condition (need to obtain n points from the tournament), and both extended tournaments consist of n selections for you and − 1 n−1 selections for your opponent. Since the counts of how many times each player selects is the same per tournament, the ordering of these selections is irrelevant. Therefore, the answer is "You are indifferent to the two methodologies" (quite counter-intuitive!) If you don't believe in the above statement, consider an extreme case where 1 = 1 p 1 =1 and 2 = 0 p 2 =0 i.e. you win on every turn you select, and lose on every turn you don't. No matter how you order your n selections in the extended tournament, you always win, as you get to select n times, meaning you have n guaranteed wins.
